Norma Jean (Feltman) AllenSeptember 7, 1935 – October 5, 2026Shared by: Mortimore Funeral Home and Cremation ServicesNorma Jean Allen, 91, was called to eternal peace on October 5, 2026, while in her home as independent as ever!
Norma was born on September 7, 1935, in St. Louis, Michigan, to Clarence and Clara (Meyer) Feltman. On July 4, 1953, at seventeen, she married FD Allen. Over sixty-five years, they built a life of children and adventure, moving to Wyoming in 1981 to buy a hotel and farm. Norma continued the adventure after her husband passed away in 2018.
Norma loved her family! She found great joy in conversation, sharing stories and catching up on life events all while beating you at a game of rummy. Norma always had goodies, and if she knew what you liked, you can bet it would show up in her kitchen!
She was in the height of her glory as a grandma, great-grandma, and great-great-grandma! She was proud of her grandchildren and loved to share what they were up to. Pure happiness and contentment graced Norma’s face at every holiday and family gathering as she watched her loved ones spend time together (and enjoy her noodles).
Norma was preceded in death by her parents, siblings, and husband. She is survived by her five children, Ray (Alice), Debbie (Dennis Coleman), Wanda (Chuck Niersel), Tony (Jamie), Bill (Jan), nine grandchildren and spouses, twelve great-grandchildren, and three great-great-grandchildren.
In honor of Norma’s wishes, we will not hold a service. Instead, please enjoy a treat and cherish your loved ones as a way to offer respect and condolences.








Waltrina Watson AscheMay 3, 1941 – September 19, 2026Cheyenne, Wyoming.Shared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral HomeWaltrina “Trina” Watson Halamka Asche completed her earthly journey on September 19, 2026. She was born on May 3, 1941, in El Paso, Texas, to John R. Watson and Julia A. (“Judy”) Pritchett Watson. She passed away in Cheyenne, Wyoming, at the Davis Hospice Center.
Trina was the oldest of three girls and was preceded in death by her parents, an infant brother John R. Watson III, and her youngest sister Barbara Links. She is survived by her children Franklyn Elliot Halamka (Lisa) and Triana Ann Halamka Burrill (Dave), four grandchildren, seven great-grandchildren, her sister Nana Wilson (John), five nieces and nephews, and countless others who loved her and called her “Grandma Trina.”
Waltrina always considered herself a Texan and cherished the rich heritage of her ancestry. Both her parents’ families settled in Texas prior to the Civil War. In later years, she took special joy in discovering more about her family’s history.
Trina graduated from Grossmont High School in El Cajon, California. She began nursing school and worked for a time as a “candy striper” and nurse’s aide at the Motion Picture Hospital. Trina married Frank Karél Halamka on December 31, 1961. This union brought forth her two children, Franklyn and Triana. Later she was married to Fred Asche from 1976 to 1982. While her children were growing up, Trina worked in various fields, finally settling into the home care industry in the Minneapolis/St Paul area. After retirement, she became a well-known Pampered Chef consultant in the Torrington, Wyoming area.
Throughout her life, one of her greatest gifts was her servant’s heart. She was always ready to help anyone in need, no matter the time or cost. Her greatest desire was to serve others and lighten their burdens.
Waltrina loved her church family and studying Scripture, participating in several Bible studies. She enjoyed sewing, doing jigsaw and crossword puzzles, visiting with friends, and most of all, keeping up with her family’s lives, no matter where they were. Listening to Southern Gospel Music was another passion; she said it reminded her of the time in her life when she came to know Jesus.
Services for Waltrina will be held at Cheyenne Evangelical Free Church, 7006 N. College Drive, Cheyenne, WY 82009 on October 21, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. A light lunch will follow.
Memorials can be made to Cheyenne Evangelical Free Church, The Gideons International, or Davis Hospice Center.








Talbert DeVaughan BowenOctober 30, 1978 – October 10, 2026Shared by: Vase Funeral HomeTalbert “Dee” DeVaughan Bowen III was born on October 30th. 1978 in Colorado Springs, Colorado. He passed away on October 10th, 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah at 47 years old. He spent the majority of his life in Wyoming, calling Green River his home.
Dee enjoyed his career working in the oilfield as a CDL driver. Cool or neat rocks often followed him home from the road to add to his collection and share with his grandkids. They would also often be found weighing down his wife’s purse.
In 2019 his “really great beard” scored him his beautiful wife. They met at Peterbilt in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Dee and Rachel were married in 2021 where he devastatingly missed his opportunity to say “Foreeeeverrrr,” at the wedding. He liked her that day.
He loved spending his time with his family, fishing, golfing with his wife, as well as riding and being free on his motorcycle. He especially enjoyed grilling, smoking, and making soups, often earning its position as a highlight of every weekend. “I cook how I like it – with love!” Dee loved his family very much and loved to express it anytime he could. You would often overhear Dee telling his grandchildren that they were ugly and to remember to use their brains. When times were tough you could find Dee at his place of peace, a river in the mountains. He always did his best thinking on the river.
Survivors include his wife, Rachel Bowen of Green River, Wyoming; father, Talbert Bowen II of Sterling, Colorado; four sons, Talbert Bowen IV companion Samantha Brough of Rock Springs, Wyoming; Christopher Bowles of Rock Springs, Wyoming; Jeffrey Bowles and wife Ashlinn of Green River, Wyoming; Kevin and Hallee Bowles of West Jordan, Utah; three daughters, Brianna Bowen of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Josephine Bowen of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Robyn Bowles and companion Hayden Larson of Rock Springs, Wyoming; two brothers, Alan Bowen and Alyssa of Lone Star, Colorado; Donnie Morgan and wife Tiffany of Casper, Wyoming; one half- sister Adra Cochran of Casper, Wyoming; ten grandchildren, Liam Bowen; Brooklyn McAllister; Harper Bowen; Daphne Williams; Brody Bowles; Brixlie Bowles; Berkley Bowles; Bristol Bowles; Skye Bowles; Rynnley Larson; several aunts, uncles, cousins, nieces and nephews.
He was preceded in death by his paternal grandfather, Talbert Bowen I; grandmother-in-law, Dorothy Wimmer “grandma Rifle”.
A celebration of life will be held at a later date. His final wish was for everyone to skip the heavy hearts and remember the good times. In lieu of tears, pour a shot of Irish Whisky to celebrate his memory.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Dee’s memory to Support Now:  https://www.supportnow.org/the-bowen-family-7658f776-9703-4427-b433-2880939ab76c
Condolences may be left Vase Funeral Homes.










Genevieve BriandSept. 4, 1968 – Oct. 3, 2026Laramie, WyomingShared by: Haskell Funeral HomeGenevieve Briand was born in Nantes, France, and passed away suddenly but peacefully at home in Byron on October 3, 2026.
Genevieve Briand was born September 4, 1968 to Denis and Marie-Jo Briand in Nantes, France and passed away suddenly but peacefully at home in Byron on October 3, 2026. She grew up in Le Cep, France at her family’s farm and eventually made it to Ecole Superieure d’Agriculture in Angers France which is a sister school of the University of Wyoming. In 1990 she did a summer internship in Wyoming with the Ag department at the University of Wyoming. She liked it enough to return in 1992 to work on a Ph.D. in economics at the University of Wyoming. In the fall of 1995, she met her future husband Dan Bodtke and they were married May 24, 1997 in Capenter, Wyoming. After which she started her journey to become a US citizen and finish her degree.  Dan took a job in Pullman, Washington so Gen had to delay her studies. She finished her Ph.D. in Agricultural Economics at Washington State University in 2002 and became a US Citizen in April 2005. In December 2005 she welcomed her daughter Gwynff into her life. In 2015 she returned to Wyoming and settled in Byron to be closer to Dan’s parents. While she taught economics in person and online for various places including Eastern Washington, Washington State, University of Idaho, John Hopkins, Montana State and NWC, her main passion in life was family. She spent many hours doing craft projects to share memories with family members. She was vibrant and full of life and will be dearly missed.
Genevieve is survived by her father Denis Briand (France); brother Martin Briand, wife Cecilia and children (France); sister Florence Briand, partner Romuald and children (France); husband Dan Bodtke; daughter Gwynff Bodtke; parents in law Dale and Cynthia Bodtke; brother in law David Bodtke, wife Dawn and children; aunt and uncle Marie-Madeleine and Jean-Claude Choquet and children (France); and many extended family members and friends.
Viewing will be 1 to 3 PM on Sunday October 11th and 7:45 to 8:45 AM on Monday October 12th at Haskell Funeral Home in Lovell. Memorial service will be held at 9 AM on October 12th at Haskell Funeral Home in Lovell. A short graveside service will immediately follow at the Byron Cemetery. A memorial service will be held in France at a later date.








Dorthea ButlerOctober 26, 1935 – September 27, 2026Rock SpringsShared by: Vase Funeral Home
Dorothea Butler, our beloved mother, grandmother and great-grandmother of Rock Springs, Wyoming passed away September 27, 2026 in Visalia, California at age 90 after a courageous battle with cancer.
Born on October 26, 1935 in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Dorothea was the daughter of Joe and Dorothy Pivik. After graduating from Rock Springs High, she pursued a bookkeeping career at City Hall, Saint Cyril and Methodius Catholic School, and Ben’s Foodliner until retirement. She also volunteered for The American Heart Association.
In her early years, Dorothea enjoyed playing bridge with friends and camping with family. She was best known for her passions of gardening and cooking. She loved spending time outdoors taking care of her flowers and plants. When not in the yard, she was in the kitchen making dinners for family and friends. She was very proud of her grandchildren, great-grandchild and loved spending time with them. We will always remember her for her sharp wit and humor.
Dorothea is survived by three daughters Dorothy (Jerry) Smith, Mary (Kelvin) O’Malley-Holub and Kelly O’Malley; four grandchildren Jarrad Smith, Danielle (Greg) Overmohle, Anna (Mark) Brassey, Kyle Holub; one great-grandchild Elizabeth Jo Overmohle.
She was preceded in death by her parents Joe and Dorothy Pivik; sister Marilyn Scott and brother Art Pivik; stepsister Angela Rahonce; stepbrothers Joe Pivik Jr., Carl Pivik, Rudy Pivik and Edward Pivik; spouses Patrick O’Malley, Albert Nelson, Michael Butler and companion Dan Blevins.
In accordance with Dorothea’s wishes, a traditional cremation has taken place a Celebration of Life will be conducted in the spring of 2027.
Condolences may be left at Vase Funeral Homes.








Emil Dale CalvertSept 7, 1969 — Oct 6, 2026Cheyenne, WyomingShared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral Home
Emil Dale “Skip” Calvert was born September 7, 1969, in Casper, Wyoming, to Floyd and Sharon K. Gums Calvert. He passed away on October 6, 2026, in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Skip left us far too soon. He gained his eternal rest with our Lord and savior Jesus Chrst.
Emil was known to some as Skip Calvert. Skip loved rodeo and rode bareback and bulls in high school.
In 1995, he moved to Cheyenne, Wyoming. He worked in heating and air conditioning in Cheyenne from 1997 to 2026. He spent more than 20 years with Climate Control.

He is survived by his parents, Floyd and Sharon Calvert of Casper, Wyoming; his sister, Tessa, and her husband, Eric Garnhart, of Casper; his daughter, Doriann Kay Calvert; and his son, Matthew Allen Calvert of Cheyenne, Wyoming.
He was preceded in death by an infant son, Johnathan Blaine Calvert, his grandparents; Emil and Margaret Gums, Earl and Jerrie Calvert; and one uncle, John Calvert.
As for his new granddaughter Lillian Izabella, a message from Skip’s son Matthew: “As we bring a new life into this world, she will always remember Grandpa, and he will always be a part of us and our hearts.” We will meet you in Heaven when our Lord calls us home.








Mary Lou CampbellJul 2, 1950 — Oct 5, 2026Alpine, WyomingShared by: Schwab Mortuary & CrematoryMary Lou Campbell, 76, peacefully departed this life on October 5, 2026, at her home in Alpine, Wyoming, surrounded by her loving husband and family.
Mary was born on July 2, 1950, in Jackson, Wyoming, to Phil and Pauline Baux. The third daughter of Phil and Pauline, Mary enjoyed an eventful and joyful childhood growing up in Jackson Hole. She attended Jackson Elementary School and graduated from Jackson-Wilson High School in 1968.
Shortly after graduation, Mary moved to Denver, Colorado, where she lived for a brief time. When her mother, Pauline, became ill, however, Mary returned home to Jackson to help care for her mother, father, and younger sister. It was an early example of something that would come to define Mary throughout her life: when her family needed her, she was there.
After returning to Jackson, Mary met Robert Lee Campbell, who had recently returned home after serving his country in the Vietnam War. The two fell in love and were married in 1973, beginning a marriage and partnership that would span 53 years.
Mary became a mother in 1975 with the birth of her first child. She and Robert built their life together in Jackson Hole, where their family eventually grew to include three children. Their home was one filled with love, forgiveness, laughter, and happiness, and Mary was always at its heart.
Anyone who knew Mary knew how much she loved the holidays, but Halloween and Thanksgiving held an especially dear place in her heart. She loved the colorful change of the seasons—the brilliant autumn leaves, the decorations, the gathering of family, and the feeling that came with that special time of year. An avid holiday decorator, Mary transformed her home with the seasons, creating a place where her family could gather and where memories were made year after year.
Mary also expressed her love through cooking. Over the years, she passed along cherished recipes and a love of preparing food to her children and grandchildren. Those recipes became more than instructions written on a card or remembered from time spent together in the kitchen; they became part of Mary’s legacy. Each time one of her children or grandchildren prepares one of her dishes, a little piece of Mary returns to the kitchen and to the family table.
In that way, the traditions Mary created will continue. Holidays will come, autumn leaves will change, kitchens will once again fill with familiar aromas, and her recipes will be prepared and shared by the generations who follow her. Around those tables, Mary will continue to bring her family together. Though she is no longer physically among us, in those familiar tastes, traditions, stories, and moments together, we are reunited with her in spirit.
In 1994, Mary took on another treasured role when she became a grandmother for the first time. In the years that followed, her family continued to grow with grandchildren and, eventually, great-grandchildren. Through holiday after holiday and ordinary day after ordinary day, Mary cared for her family through their successes, their celebrations, their challenges, and their sorrows. She offered the kind of love that forgave easily, welcomed people home, and remained steadfast through whatever life brought.
Mary remained the heart of her family until the very end.
She is survived by her husband of 53 years, Robert Lee Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming; her sister, Cindy (Ronnie) of Victor, Idaho; her children, Kiley (Christina) Campbell and Beau Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming; her grandchildren, Chandler (Syd) of Fort Collins, Colorado, Cassandra (Chris) of Jackson, Wyoming, Josie Campbell of Etna, Wyoming, Shaylee and Rylie Dobben of Hyrum, Utah, Ethan and Ava Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming, and Adri and Rory of North Carolina; as well as several great-grandchildren who will dearly miss her presence in their lives.
Mary was preceded in death by her parents, Phil and Pauline Baux; her sisters, Jean Davison and Carolyn Brooks; and her youngest son, Lucas Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming.
Mary’s life cannot be measured simply by the years between her birth and her passing. It can be measured in the family she nurtured, the home she created, the holidays she made magical, the people she cared for when they needed her, and the generations who will carry her memory forward.
For more than five decades, Mary and Robert built a life together. For more than half a century, she was a wife, a mother, a sister, and eventually a grandmother and great-grandmother. Through all those years and all those roles, one thing remained constant: Mary loved her family, and her family knew they were loved.
That love remains.
Graveside services for Mary Lou Campbell will be held Friday, October 9, 2026, at 1:00 p.m.








Jeffrey J. CastagnaJune 24, 1961 – Oct. 10, 2026Green River, WyomingShared by: Vase Funeral HomeJeffery James Castagna, 65, passed away peacefully at his home in Green River, Wyoming, on October 10, 2026, after a courageous walk with glioblastoma, carried out with immense strength and grace.
Born in Bemidji, Minnesota, on June 24, 1961, Jeff developed a lifelong appreciation for the outdoors, craftsmanship, and community. As an avid outdoorsman, he found true peace in nature through hunting, archery, and fishing with flies he carefully tied himself. Through his camera lens, he pursued his love of photography—documenting wildlife and landscapes, as well as capturing every highlight at his grandchildren’s sporting events. Whether out in nature enjoying God’s creation or spending time with family and close friends, Jeff was right where he wanted to be.
Jeff was also a talented carpenter and draftsman. With a keen eye for design and functionality, he took pride in crafting cherished treasures and spaces that brought utility, warmth, and a true sense of home to those around him.
Above all, Jeff was a dedicated educator. His greatest joy in life came from teaching—he derived deep fulfillment from guiding his students, helping them unlock their potential, and inspiring them to discover their own unique strengths and passions. He spent 35 years pouring into the lives of his students at Sweetwater County School District #1. He loved knowing that he was teaching them lifelong skills that they could use regardless of career choice. He stayed in touch with many of his students and took great pride when they shared the impact he had made in their lives.
Jeff possessed a deep, genuine kindness that left a lasting mark on everyone fortunate enough to know him. Embodying a true sense of “Minnesota nice”, his warmth wasn’t loud or performative. It was rooted in a quiet humility and a sincere, thoughtful consideration for others. Whether he was offering a helping hand, sharing a peaceful moment by the water, or simply listening, Jeff made people feel seen, valued, and welcome.
Jeff met the love of his life, Kelly, in 2015. Following a four-year courtship, the couple tied the knot in Tennessee in August 2019—a perfect backdrop that allowed Jeff to cross the Great Smoky Mountains off his bucket list.
He is survived by his wife Kelly Castagna; his chosen daughter, Robyn Meeks; his stepsons, Bobby Brown Jr. (Jerika) and Michael Brown (Ashley); and his cherished grandchildren, Travin, Quintin, Cazden, Raleigh, Lathan, Slayten, and Lexleigh, Sister-in-law, Barb Castagna; his niece and nephew, Laura Castagna and David Castagna; as well as his chosen family, Mark, Kristi, and Joy Hansen, who held a special place in his heart.
Jeff was preceded in death by his parents, James and Bonnie Castagna, and his brother, Steven Castagna.
In Jeff’s memory, let us carry his spirit forward by weaving his quiet kindness into our daily live by slowing down, listening deeply, and treating everyone around us with thoughtful consideration.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Jeffrey’s memory to the Tunnel to Tower Foundation, P.O. Box 70719, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 17176, or KLOVE Radio Station, 2000 Reams Fleming Boulevard, Franklin, Tennessee 37064. 
Cremation will take place; a Private Family Remembrance will take place at a later date.
Condolences can be expressed at Vase Funeral Homes.

Ruth FalkOctober 8, 1946 – October 3, 2026Sheridan, WyomingShared by: Champion Kane Funeral HomeRuth Falk, 79, of Sheridan, Wyoming, passed away on October 3, 2026 at her home.
Born in Denver, Colorado, to Frederick and Elizabeth Falk, Ruth grew up and lived in Phoenix, Arizona, before moving to Sheridan in 2018.
Ruth worked as a nurse for more than 30 years before retiring. She was a hard worker who showed up for others. Where there was a need, she filled it.
An avid reader, Ruth also enjoyed crocheting during her night shifts at the hospital. Her family still has the blankets to prove it, lasting reminders of the time and care she put into her work.
Love was not always easy for Ruth to give or receive, but she kept trying, often expressing her care by helping others. She loved her grandchildren.
Ruth is survived by her children, Malcolm Hernandez III and Suzanne Kulvinskas, and Suzanne’s husband, Erik Kulvinskas; her grandchildren, Stasys Kulvinskas, Chrysyn Kulvinskas, Lilia Erladson, Shaheen Esmaeili, Yasmin Esmaeili; and her siblings, Mary Gawron, Helen Tyler, Thom Falk, and Margaret Gifford. Darron Cole FerrisJan 19, 2004 — Oct 8, 2026Fort Washakie, WyomingShared by: Hudson’s Funeral Home & On-Site CrematoryDarron Cole Ferris was born on January 19, 2004, in Lander, Wyoming, to Neomi Hebah and Herman Ferris Jr. of Fort Washakie. He passed away in Fort Washakie on October 8, 2026.
Darron Cole attended Fort Washakie Head Start, Fort Washakie Elementary, and Fort Washakie Junior High. He completed his high school years at Wyoming Indian High School while also taking college courses at Casper College. After returning home, he began his work career at TWE Irrigation.
Darron enjoyed fishing, being outdoors, and spending time with his family and friends. He was involved in his traditional ways, attending the Shoshone Sundances and sweats. He was always happy and loved to joke and tease. Laughter was a great part of Darron’s life.
One of Darron’s greatest accomplishments was his daughter, A’vani, whom he loved with all his heart. Darron’s life was just starting to thrive and grow. He left us all too soon, leaving a mark on our hearts that will always be a blessing and a love we will never forget.

Robert “Bob” GallagherDec 23, 1936 — Sep 25, 2026Cody, WyomingShared by: Thompson Funeral Home and Cremation ServicesRobert (Bob) Gallagher passed away September 25, 2026 at Spirit Mountain Hospice House in Cody, Wyoming, with his daughters by his side. He was 89 years old. His only concern at the time of his passing was that he would be remembered as a Cody Bronc. We assured him that he would continue to be remembered as a Panther, a Montana Grizzly, and an OU Sooner, despite passing away at a Cody location. The Spirit Mountain Hospice House proved to be a beautiful place to spend his last few days here on this earth.
Bob was born in Missoula, Montana on December 23, 1936. He was the third of eight children born to Virginia and James Gallagher. Bob was preceded in death by his parents, his wife, Marlene, and his siblings, Jim, Irene, Don, Gerry, and Pat. He is survived by two younger sisters, Judy and Rose. He is also survived by his three daughters, Leslie (Jim) Christensen, Tracy (Nick) Metzler, and Gina. Bob has nine grandchildren; Cole (Tori), Kennedi, Lani, Brooke (Jake), Fena, Christa, Jackson (Caroline), McCall and Sofi and two great grandchildren, James and Carter. Grandpa was so very proud of each of his grandchildren; all of them so individually-perfect in his eyes.
From a very young age, Bob was resourceful and determined. At the ripe old age of five, he had his own paper route, upselling his older buddies at churches, theatres, and hotels. Apparently, the little businessman took up smoking at age five, but gave it up by age six. This paper route allowed Bob to attend the National Boy Scout Jamboree at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania in 1950 with 47,000 other boy scouts. It was a trip of a lifetime for him!
Being one of eight children, and living in a one bedroom home in Missoula, Bob decided sleeping outside in his sleeping bag was a better option than sleeping indoors. Although the Montana winters were cold, he and his dog, Rex, enjoyed not only sleeping outside under the stars, but also got in lots of fishing on the Blackfoot River. As a high school student, Bob was the manager of the local bowling alley, and later, the Fox Theatre. The money he earned from these jobs allowed his family to move into a larger home, complete with indoor plumbing!
At the age of 18, Bob’s luckiest day came when he rolled into the Frontier Drive-in, meeting a cute girl on rollerskates who was working there. They began to date, fell in love, and Bob and Marlene Flynn were married on August 17, 1957. Bob and Marlene were married at the Lutheran Church in Missoula. They gave birth to their first daughter, Leslie, while living in Missoula. Bob was then working for Safeway Grocery Stores and was transferred to Powell to become its new manager in 1965. Daughters Tracy and Gina were born in Powell in 1965 and 1967.
Within a few years of residing in Powell, Bob and Marlene purchased Big Charley’s Drive-In Restaurant. Bob quickly learned how to manage cooking for several carloads of people at once, while taking to-go phone orders, which was not an easy task. Leslie, Tracy, & Gina helped out by filling cokes and putting hamburger buns in the warmer, while the little green volkswagen bug delivered hamburgers, fries, and cokes around the community.
After a fun run with Big Charley’s, Bob and Marlene decided to open their own dine-in restaurant. After months of trying out new recipes and remodeling an old gas and service station in downtown Powell, they opened Hansel & Gretel’s in 1973. Hansel & Gretel’s became a popular restaurant for the community and the entire Big Horn Basin. Sports teams often came for pizza and fries after games and it was a great place for many to meet up with friends. It was a family endeavor, with the entire family engaged to make it all work. Bob and Marlene spent 36 years owning and operating Hansel and Gretel’s before retiring in 2009.
Bob was also known in Powell for sponsoring and playing on the H & G’s Basketball Team in the Powell Men’s League, running annually in the Powell Airport Hill Run and the Beartooth Mountain Run, hunting, fishing, spending time at his cabin in Sunlight Basin, serving in Kiwanis, and attending and participating on the church council at Hope Lutheran Church.
Bob lived his last four years at the Heartland Assisted Living Community. He loved the other residents, the staff, and the food at the Heartland. He frequently commented, “If you have to be someplace, this is a great place to be!” We are forever grateful to those at the Heartland for welcoming him there and making it home for his last few years.
A funeral service will be held Monday, October 12, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. at Hope Lutheran Church.

Duane faced challenges throughout his life that might have defeated many people, but he met them with incredible courage and quiet perseverance. When he fell or was knocked down, he got up again—and again—without complaint or self-pity. He wanted to do things that might have seemed out of reach, and he did not give up. His own struggles gave him great empathy for others facing difficulties. He loved children and was kind and patient with animals.
Duane attended school in Buffalo, graduating from Buffalo High School with the class of 1977. He was a member of the school’s FFA chapter and showed a steer from the family ranch at the Johnson County Fair. He also competed with other projects, one of which went on to the State Fair.
In his teenage years, Duane, a leftie, loved practicing his baseball pitching. He rode his gasoline-powered minibike with joy and abandon and enjoyed working in the ranch shop, welding and helping repair equipment. He was always game for gathering and splitting firewood and enjoyed target shooting with both pistol and rifle.
After high school, Duane attended vocational school in Cheyenne. He held various jobs around Buffalo and worked on the family ranch. He had a talent for small-engine repair and operated his own lawnmower repair business.
Duane loved hunting and fishing in the Bighorn Mountains and visiting Yellowstone National Park with his family. He enjoyed family gatherings and the feasts and festivities that came with those good times. Comedy movies and television delighted him, and he had a quick sense of humor and a joyous laugh.
The greatest strength in Duane’s life came through his genuine faith in Jesus. He enjoyed volunteering at Bighorn Baptist Church. His greatest joy and blessing on Earth was his beloved wife, Barb, who brought him true happiness and endless love and meant all the world to him. God truly brought them together. Duane and Barb were married on January 4, 2004, in Buffalo, Wyoming.
On November 8, 2013, Duane was admitted to Amie Holt Care Center where he lived for the remainder of his life.
Duane was preceded in death by his parents; his maternal grandparents, John and Amy Kumor; his paternal grandparents, Philip Henry and Irma Wohlbrandt; many aunts and uncles; and several cousins on both sides of the family.
He is survived by his wife, Barb; his brothers, John (Chris) and Phil (Tani); his sister, Lorena; and four nieces and their spouses and children.
Visitation will be held on Thursday, October 8, 2026, from 1 to 9 p.m. at Harness Funeral Home. A service will take place on Friday, October 9, 2026, at 10 a.m. followed by a graveside service at Willow Grove Cemetery, where Duane will be laid to rest in the family plot. A meal will follow at Calvary Chapel. Mike Leibee of Calvary Chapel will lead the service.
Memorial contributions may be made to Calvary Chapel in remembrance of Duane, a kind and courageous man whose faith, laughter, and love will remain with the family he leaves behind for a while.
Goodbye for now, Duane.

Farren James Zabriskie06 Oct 1947 – 05 Oct 2026Buffalo, WyomingShared by: Harness Funeral HomeFuneral services for Farren James Zabriskie, a 78-year-old Buffalo resident who passed away on Monday, October 5, 2026, will be held Saturday, October 31, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. at the Harness Funeral Home Chapel in Buffalo. Farren Jame Zabriskie, known to everyone simply as F’kin Farren, passed away on October 5, 2026, in Buffalo, Wyoming, one day shy of his 79th birthday, after health-related complications. He was born on October 6, 1947, in Berkeley, California, and spent a life that was equal parts hard work, good humor, and the kind of stubborn decency that makes a person unforgettable. He was a Christian, a proud veteran, a devoted family man, and a man who seemed to understand that if life was going to be complicated, it might as well be handled with a grin and a strong cup of coffee.
Farren grew up with a work ethic that could outlast a Wyoming winter and a practical streak that made him useful in just about any situation. He graduated from Hillcrest High School in Midvale, Utah, and later earned an Associate of Adolescent Psychology from Central Wyoming College. That combination of education and common sense suited him well, because Farren had a way of understanding people that did not require a degree, although he had one anyway. He spent his life learning, observing, and figuring out how to get things done, which was handy considering he never seemed to meet a job he could not improve with grit, patience, and a little bit of sarcasm.
His work history read like the greatest hits of American labor. Farren worked as a carpenter, in concrete, in coal mines, in construction, at the Wyoming State Training School in Lander, Wyoming, and in various odd jobs that probably could have filled an entire second obituary by themselves. He was also a Union Ironworker with Local 229 and Local 27, and he took that role seriously. He knew what it meant to show up, to sweat, to build, and to keep going when the day got long. If there was a heavy object that needed moving or a problem that needed solving, Farren was the kind of man you wanted nearby, preferably before the situation got worse.
He served his country honorably in the United States Marine Corps during the Vietnam era from 1966 to 1969, including AutoMech-CamPen-6weeks, and he carried those years with the quiet pride of someone who had done his duty and then some. His military honors included the National Defense Service Medal, the Vietnam Campaign Medal with device, the Vietnam Service Medal with 6, the Republic of Vietnam Cross of Gallantry with Palm, the Good Conduct Medal, 1st Award, and the Presidential Unit Citation. Those medals told part of the story, but anyone who knew Farren would say his real decoration was the way he lived afterward, with loyalty, resilience, and an ability to keep his sense of humor even when life was clearly trying to be difficult.
Farren was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Angie Rosalez Zabriskie, and he carried her memory with him always. He is survived by his brothers, Lee (Linda) Zabriskie, Paul (Wendy) Zabriskie, and Carl Zabriskie; his sons, Chance (Teri Ann) Zabriskie, Dylan Zabriskie, and Waylon (Alli) Zabriskie; his sons by marriage, Paul Luthi and Tyson Mcdougall; his daughters by marriage, Lindsay Avila and Shannon Nesheim; 12 grandchildren; and 14 great-grandchildren. His family was a source of pride and joy to him, and he loved them in the straightforward, no-nonsense way that meant he showed up, helped out, and made sure everyone knew where they stood. He was loving, selfless, and generous, which is a fine way to be remembered and, frankly, a rare enough combination to deserve its own medal.
Farren also knew how to enjoy life, which he did without apology. He loved his local watering hole, the Century Club, where the atmosphere undoubtedly benefited from his presence and where he probably left more memorable stories than anyone could reasonably count. He took pride in helping others who needed help unconditionally, which was one of those traits that made people trust him immediately. He loved the wind blowing through his hair on his motorcycle, and he had a special appreciation for his Harley Davidsons and old hot rod vehicles, because subtlety was never the point and neither was Farren. He enjoyed listening to music of all kinds and singing along, whether the song needed help or not. He also took great joy in the outdoors, whether he was fishing, camping with family and friends, or watching the sun rise and set as if he had someplace important to be, which he usually did not. He loved to sightsee and travel, and one suspects he did so with the confidence of a man who believed every road had a story and most of them were worth hearing twice.
In the spirit of Farren’s humor and larger-than-life personality, one fitting line comes from the beloved comedian George Carlin, who said, “Don’t sweat the petty things and don’t pet the sweaty things.” Farren would have appreciated that kind of wisdom, because he understood that life was serious enough on its own and did not need any extra nonsense added for free. He had a comedian’s timing without trying to be one, and a straight man’s delivery that made his dry wit even funnier. He could make people laugh simply by telling the truth in a way that was too honest to ignore and too funny to forget.
Farren’s life was built on service, work, loyalty, and love. He leaves behind a legacy that is as solid as the things he built and as warm as the stories he told. He will be remembered for his big heart, his steady hands, his generous spirit, and his ability to find the good in people, even when they had not fully earned it yet. He was the sort of man who made a place better just by being in it, and now that he has gone, the world feels a little quieter, a little rougher around the edges, and a lot less interesting.

She was born on August 9, 1947, to Phyllis and Marion Towns.  She was raised on her family’s farm in Hillsdale and graduated from Hillsdale High School in 1965. 
After graduation, she married William K. Zwieg on February 20, 1966.  Their story began in Cheyenne, Wyoming.  Judy and Bill had two kids: William Glen Zwieg, born in 1967, and Brenda (Zwieg) Benson, born 1969.  They later moved to Hanna, Wyoming, where her husband worked in the mines until 1984.  They then moved to Laramie.
She worked a number of different positions during her time in Laramie, including Godfather’s Pizza, Advanced Auto Parts, Laramie Ford, and finally the University of Wyoming as an Office Associate Senior, where she retired.
 She enjoyed sewing, crafting, making floral arrangements, and cake decorating.  Later on, she was an active volunteer for the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation.  She enjoyed attending Wyoming Cowgirls basketball games and spending time with her family.

Norma Jean (Feltman) AllenSeptember 7, 1935 – October 5, 2026Shared by: Mortimore Funeral Home and Cremation ServicesNorma Jean Allen, 91, was called to eternal peace on October 5, 2026, while in her home as independent as ever!
Norma was born on September 7, 1935, in St. Louis, Michigan, to Clarence and Clara (Meyer) Feltman. On July 4, 1953, at seventeen, she married FD Allen. Over sixty-five years, they built a life of children and adventure, moving to Wyoming in 1981 to buy a hotel and farm. Norma continued the adventure after her husband passed away in 2018.
Norma loved her family! She found great joy in conversation, sharing stories and catching up on life events all while beating you at a game of rummy. Norma always had goodies, and if she knew what you liked, you can bet it would show up in her kitchen!
She was in the height of her glory as a grandma, great-grandma, and great-great-grandma! She was proud of her grandchildren and loved to share what they were up to. Pure happiness and contentment graced Norma’s face at every holiday and family gathering as she watched her loved ones spend time together (and enjoy her noodles).
Norma was preceded in death by her parents, siblings, and husband. She is survived by her five children, Ray (Alice), Debbie (Dennis Coleman), Wanda (Chuck Niersel), Tony (Jamie), Bill (Jan), nine grandchildren and spouses, twelve great-grandchildren, and three great-great-grandchildren.
In honor of Norma’s wishes, we will not hold a service. Instead, please enjoy a treat and cherish your loved ones as a way to offer respect and condolences.








Waltrina Watson AscheMay 3, 1941 – September 19, 2026Cheyenne, Wyoming.Shared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral HomeWaltrina “Trina” Watson Halamka Asche completed her earthly journey on September 19, 2026. She was born on May 3, 1941, in El Paso, Texas, to John R. Watson and Julia A. (“Judy”) Pritchett Watson. She passed away in Cheyenne, Wyoming, at the Davis Hospice Center.
Trina was the oldest of three girls and was preceded in death by her parents, an infant brother John R. Watson III, and her youngest sister Barbara Links. She is survived by her children Franklyn Elliot Halamka (Lisa) and Triana Ann Halamka Burrill (Dave), four grandchildren, seven great-grandchildren, her sister Nana Wilson (John), five nieces and nephews, and countless others who loved her and called her “Grandma Trina.”
Waltrina always considered herself a Texan and cherished the rich heritage of her ancestry. Both her parents’ families settled in Texas prior to the Civil War. In later years, she took special joy in discovering more about her family’s history.
Trina graduated from Grossmont High School in El Cajon, California. She began nursing school and worked for a time as a “candy striper” and nurse’s aide at the Motion Picture Hospital. Trina married Frank Karél Halamka on December 31, 1961. This union brought forth her two children, Franklyn and Triana. Later she was married to Fred Asche from 1976 to 1982. While her children were growing up, Trina worked in various fields, finally settling into the home care industry in the Minneapolis/St Paul area. After retirement, she became a well-known Pampered Chef consultant in the Torrington, Wyoming area.
Throughout her life, one of her greatest gifts was her servant’s heart. She was always ready to help anyone in need, no matter the time or cost. Her greatest desire was to serve others and lighten their burdens.
Waltrina loved her church family and studying Scripture, participating in several Bible studies. She enjoyed sewing, doing jigsaw and crossword puzzles, visiting with friends, and most of all, keeping up with her family’s lives, no matter where they were. Listening to Southern Gospel Music was another passion; she said it reminded her of the time in her life when she came to know Jesus.
Services for Waltrina will be held at Cheyenne Evangelical Free Church, 7006 N. College Drive, Cheyenne, WY 82009 on October 21, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. A light lunch will follow.
Memorials can be made to Cheyenne Evangelical Free Church, The Gideons International, or Davis Hospice Center.








Talbert DeVaughan BowenOctober 30, 1978 – October 10, 2026Shared by: Vase Funeral HomeTalbert “Dee” DeVaughan Bowen III was born on October 30th. 1978 in Colorado Springs, Colorado. He passed away on October 10th, 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah at 47 years old. He spent the majority of his life in Wyoming, calling Green River his home.
Dee enjoyed his career working in the oilfield as a CDL driver. Cool or neat rocks often followed him home from the road to add to his collection and share with his grandkids. They would also often be found weighing down his wife’s purse.
In 2019 his “really great beard” scored him his beautiful wife. They met at Peterbilt in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Dee and Rachel were married in 2021 where he devastatingly missed his opportunity to say “Foreeeeverrrr,” at the wedding. He liked her that day.
He loved spending his time with his family, fishing, golfing with his wife, as well as riding and being free on his motorcycle. He especially enjoyed grilling, smoking, and making soups, often earning its position as a highlight of every weekend. “I cook how I like it – with love!” Dee loved his family very much and loved to express it anytime he could. You would often overhear Dee telling his grandchildren that they were ugly and to remember to use their brains. When times were tough you could find Dee at his place of peace, a river in the mountains. He always did his best thinking on the river.
Survivors include his wife, Rachel Bowen of Green River, Wyoming; father, Talbert Bowen II of Sterling, Colorado; four sons, Talbert Bowen IV companion Samantha Brough of Rock Springs, Wyoming; Christopher Bowles of Rock Springs, Wyoming; Jeffrey Bowles and wife Ashlinn of Green River, Wyoming; Kevin and Hallee Bowles of West Jordan, Utah; three daughters, Brianna Bowen of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Josephine Bowen of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Robyn Bowles and companion Hayden Larson of Rock Springs, Wyoming; two brothers, Alan Bowen and Alyssa of Lone Star, Colorado; Donnie Morgan and wife Tiffany of Casper, Wyoming; one half- sister Adra Cochran of Casper, Wyoming; ten grandchildren, Liam Bowen; Brooklyn McAllister; Harper Bowen; Daphne Williams; Brody Bowles; Brixlie Bowles; Berkley Bowles; Bristol Bowles; Skye Bowles; Rynnley Larson; several aunts, uncles, cousins, nieces and nephews.
He was preceded in death by his paternal grandfather, Talbert Bowen I; grandmother-in-law, Dorothy Wimmer “grandma Rifle”.
A celebration of life will be held at a later date. His final wish was for everyone to skip the heavy hearts and remember the good times. In lieu of tears, pour a shot of Irish Whisky to celebrate his memory.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Dee’s memory to Support Now:  https://www.supportnow.org/the-bowen-family-7658f776-9703-4427-b433-2880939ab76c

Genevieve BriandSept. 4, 1968 – Oct. 3, 2026Laramie, WyomingShared by: Haskell Funeral HomeGenevieve Briand was born in Nantes, France, and passed away suddenly but peacefully at home in Byron on October 3, 2026.
Genevieve Briand was born September 4, 1968 to Denis and Marie-Jo Briand in Nantes, France and passed away suddenly but peacefully at home in Byron on October 3, 2026. She grew up in Le Cep, France at her family’s farm and eventually made it to Ecole Superieure d’Agriculture in Angers France which is a sister school of the University of Wyoming. In 1990 she did a summer internship in Wyoming with the Ag department at the University of Wyoming. She liked it enough to return in 1992 to work on a Ph.D. in economics at the University of Wyoming. In the fall of 1995, she met her future husband Dan Bodtke and they were married May 24, 1997 in Capenter, Wyoming. After which she started her journey to become a US citizen and finish her degree.  Dan took a job in Pullman, Washington so Gen had to delay her studies. She finished her Ph.D. in Agricultural Economics at Washington State University in 2002 and became a US Citizen in April 2005. In December 2005 she welcomed her daughter Gwynff into her life. In 2015 she returned to Wyoming and settled in Byron to be closer to Dan’s parents. While she taught economics in person and online for various places including Eastern Washington, Washington State, University of Idaho, John Hopkins, Montana State and NWC, her main passion in life was family. She spent many hours doing craft projects to share memories with family members. She was vibrant and full of life and will be dearly missed.
Genevieve is survived by her father Denis Briand (France); brother Martin Briand, wife Cecilia and children (France); sister Florence Briand, partner Romuald and children (France); husband Dan Bodtke; daughter Gwynff Bodtke; parents in law Dale and Cynthia Bodtke; brother in law David Bodtke, wife Dawn and children; aunt and uncle Marie-Madeleine and Jean-Claude Choquet and children (France); and many extended family members and friends.
Viewing will be 1 to 3 PM on Sunday October 11th and 7:45 to 8:45 AM on Monday October 12th at Haskell Funeral Home in Lovell. Memorial service will be held at 9 AM on October 12th at Haskell Funeral Home in Lovell. A short graveside service will immediately follow at the Byron Cemetery. A memorial service will be held in France at a later date.








Dorthea ButlerOctober 26, 1935 – September 27, 2026Rock SpringsShared by: Vase Funeral Home
Dorothea Butler, our beloved mother, grandmother and great-grandmother of Rock Springs, Wyoming passed away September 27, 2026 in Visalia, California at age 90 after a courageous battle with cancer.
Born on October 26, 1935 in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Dorothea was the daughter of Joe and Dorothy Pivik. After graduating from Rock Springs High, she pursued a bookkeeping career at City Hall, Saint Cyril and Methodius Catholic School, and Ben’s Foodliner until retirement. She also volunteered for The American Heart Association.
In her early years, Dorothea enjoyed playing bridge with friends and camping with family. She was best known for her passions of gardening and cooking. She loved spending time outdoors taking care of her flowers and plants. When not in the yard, she was in the kitchen making dinners for family and friends. She was very proud of her grandchildren, great-grandchild and loved spending time with them. We will always remember her for her sharp wit and humor.
Dorothea is survived by three daughters Dorothy (Jerry) Smith, Mary (Kelvin) O’Malley-Holub and Kelly O’Malley; four grandchildren Jarrad Smith, Danielle (Greg) Overmohle, Anna (Mark) Brassey, Kyle Holub; one great-grandchild Elizabeth Jo Overmohle.
She was preceded in death by her parents Joe and Dorothy Pivik; sister Marilyn Scott and brother Art Pivik; stepsister Angela Rahonce; stepbrothers Joe Pivik Jr., Carl Pivik, Rudy Pivik and Edward Pivik; spouses Patrick O’Malley, Albert Nelson, Michael Butler and companion Dan Blevins.
In accordance with Dorothea’s wishes, a traditional cremation has taken place a Celebration of Life will be conducted in the spring of 2027.

Emil Dale CalvertSept 7, 1969 — Oct 6, 2026Cheyenne, WyomingShared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral Home
Emil Dale “Skip” Calvert was born September 7, 1969, in Casper, Wyoming, to Floyd and Sharon K. Gums Calvert. He passed away on October 6, 2026, in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Skip left us far too soon. He gained his eternal rest with our Lord and savior Jesus Chrst.
Emil was known to some as Skip Calvert. Skip loved rodeo and rode bareback and bulls in high school.
In 1995, he moved to Cheyenne, Wyoming. He worked in heating and air conditioning in Cheyenne from 1997 to 2026. He spent more than 20 years with Climate Control.
On September 6, 1997, he married Heather Smith in Cheyenne. They had two children, Dorian K. Calvert and Matthew Allen Calvert. Heather and Skip divorced later.
He is survived by his parents, Floyd and Sharon Calvert of Casper, Wyoming; his sister, Tessa, and her husband, Eric Garnhart, of Casper; his daughter, Doriann Kay Calvert; and his son, Matthew Allen Calvert of Cheyenne, Wyoming.
He was preceded in death by an infant son, Johnathan Blaine Calvert, his grandparents; Emil and Margaret Gums, Earl and Jerrie Calvert; and one uncle, John Calvert.
As for his new granddaughter Lillian Izabella, a message from Skip’s son Matthew: “As we bring a new life into this world, she will always remember Grandpa, and he will always be a part of us and our hearts.” We will meet you in Heaven when our Lord calls us home.








Mary Lou CampbellJul 2, 1950 — Oct 5, 2026Alpine, WyomingShared by: Schwab Mortuary & CrematoryMary Lou Campbell, 76, peacefully departed this life on October 5, 2026, at her home in Alpine, Wyoming, surrounded by her loving husband and family.
Mary was born on July 2, 1950, in Jackson, Wyoming, to Phil and Pauline Baux. The third daughter of Phil and Pauline, Mary enjoyed an eventful and joyful childhood growing up in Jackson Hole. She attended Jackson Elementary School and graduated from Jackson-Wilson High School in 1968.
Shortly after graduation, Mary moved to Denver, Colorado, where she lived for a brief time. When her mother, Pauline, became ill, however, Mary returned home to Jackson to help care for her mother, father, and younger sister. It was an early example of something that would come to define Mary throughout her life: when her family needed her, she was there.
After returning to Jackson, Mary met Robert Lee Campbell, who had recently returned home after serving his country in the Vietnam War. The two fell in love and were married in 1973, beginning a marriage and partnership that would span 53 years.
Mary became a mother in 1975 with the birth of her first child. She and Robert built their life together in Jackson Hole, where their family eventually grew to include three children. Their home was one filled with love, forgiveness, laughter, and happiness, and Mary was always at its heart.
Anyone who knew Mary knew how much she loved the holidays, but Halloween and Thanksgiving held an especially dear place in her heart. She loved the colorful change of the seasons—the brilliant autumn leaves, the decorations, the gathering of family, and the feeling that came with that special time of year. An avid holiday decorator, Mary transformed her home with the seasons, creating a place where her family could gather and where memories were made year after year.
Mary also expressed her love through cooking. Over the years, she passed along cherished recipes and a love of preparing food to her children and grandchildren. Those recipes became more than instructions written on a card or remembered from time spent together in the kitchen; they became part of Mary’s legacy. Each time one of her children or grandchildren prepares one of her dishes, a little piece of Mary returns to the kitchen and to the family table.
In that way, the traditions Mary created will continue. Holidays will come, autumn leaves will change, kitchens will once again fill with familiar aromas, and her recipes will be prepared and shared by the generations who follow her. Around those tables, Mary will continue to bring her family together. Though she is no longer physically among us, in those familiar tastes, traditions, stories, and moments together, we are reunited with her in spirit.
In 1994, Mary took on another treasured role when she became a grandmother for the first time. In the years that followed, her family continued to grow with grandchildren and, eventually, great-grandchildren. Through holiday after holiday and ordinary day after ordinary day, Mary cared for her family through their successes, their celebrations, their challenges, and their sorrows. She offered the kind of love that forgave easily, welcomed people home, and remained steadfast through whatever life brought.
Mary remained the heart of her family until the very end.
She is survived by her husband of 53 years, Robert Lee Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming; her sister, Cindy (Ronnie) of Victor, Idaho; her children, Kiley (Christina) Campbell and Beau Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming; her grandchildren, Chandler (Syd) of Fort Collins, Colorado, Cassandra (Chris) of Jackson, Wyoming, Josie Campbell of Etna, Wyoming, Shaylee and Rylie Dobben of Hyrum, Utah, Ethan and Ava Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming, and Adri and Rory of North Carolina; as well as several great-grandchildren who will dearly miss her presence in their lives.
Mary was preceded in death by her parents, Phil and Pauline Baux; her sisters, Jean Davison and Carolyn Brooks; and her youngest son, Lucas Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming.
Mary’s life cannot be measured simply by the years between her birth and her passing. It can be measured in the family she nurtured, the home she created, the holidays she made magical, the people she cared for when they needed her, and the generations who will carry her memory forward.
For more than five decades, Mary and Robert built a life together. For more than half a century, she was a wife, a mother, a sister, and eventually a grandmother and great-grandmother. Through all those years and all those roles, one thing remained constant: Mary loved her family, and her family knew they were loved.
That love remains.
Graveside services for Mary Lou Campbell will be held Friday, October 9, 2026, at 1:00 p.m.








Jeffrey J. CastagnaJune 24, 1961 – Oct. 10, 2026Green River, WyomingShared by: Vase Funeral HomeJeffery James Castagna, 65, passed away peacefully at his home in Green River, Wyoming, on October 10, 2026, after a courageous walk with glioblastoma, carried out with immense strength and grace.
Born in Bemidji, Minnesota, on June 24, 1961, Jeff developed a lifelong appreciation for the outdoors, craftsmanship, and community. As an avid outdoorsman, he found true peace in nature through hunting, archery, and fishing with flies he carefully tied himself. Through his camera lens, he pursued his love of photography—documenting wildlife and landscapes, as well as capturing every highlight at his grandchildren’s sporting events. Whether out in nature enjoying God’s creation or spending time with family and close friends, Jeff was right where he wanted to be.
Jeff was also a talented carpenter and draftsman. With a keen eye for design and functionality, he took pride in crafting cherished treasures and spaces that brought utility, warmth, and a true sense of home to those around him.
Above all, Jeff was a dedicated educator. His greatest joy in life came from teaching—he derived deep fulfillment from guiding his students, helping them unlock their potential, and inspiring them to discover their own unique strengths and passions. He spent 35 years pouring into the lives of his students at Sweetwater County School District #1. He loved knowing that he was teaching them lifelong skills that they could use regardless of career choice. He stayed in touch with many of his students and took great pride when they shared the impact he had made in their lives.
Jeff possessed a deep, genuine kindness that left a lasting mark on everyone fortunate enough to know him. Embodying a true sense of “Minnesota nice”, his warmth wasn’t loud or performative. It was rooted in a quiet humility and a sincere, thoughtful consideration for others. Whether he was offering a helping hand, sharing a peaceful moment by the water, or simply listening, Jeff made people feel seen, valued, and welcome.
Jeff met the love of his life, Kelly, in 2015. Following a four-year courtship, the couple tied the knot in Tennessee in August 2019—a perfect backdrop that allowed Jeff to cross the Great Smoky Mountains off his bucket list.
He is survived by his wife Kelly Castagna; his chosen daughter, Robyn Meeks; his stepsons, Bobby Brown Jr. (Jerika) and Michael Brown (Ashley); and his cherished grandchildren, Travin, Quintin, Cazden, Raleigh, Lathan, Slayten, and Lexleigh, Sister-in-law, Barb Castagna; his niece and nephew, Laura Castagna and David Castagna; as well as his chosen family, Mark, Kristi, and Joy Hansen, who held a special place in his heart.
Jeff was preceded in death by his parents, James and Bonnie Castagna, and his brother, Steven Castagna.
In Jeff’s memory, let us carry his spirit forward by weaving his quiet kindness into our daily live by slowing down, listening deeply, and treating everyone around us with thoughtful consideration.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Jeffrey’s memory to the Tunnel to Tower Foundation, P.O. Box 70719, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 17176, or KLOVE Radio Station, 2000 Reams Fleming Boulevard, Franklin, Tennessee 37064. 
Cremation will take place; a Private Family Remembrance will take place at a later date.
Condolences can be expressed at Vase Funeral Homes.

Nelson Patrick White Eagle Sr.Feb 26, 1939 — Oct 9, 2026Ethete, WyomingShared by: Hudson’s Funeral Home & On-Site CrematoryNelson Patrick White Eagle Sr., Hiitooxu’oot passed away peacefully in his home in Ethete, Wyoming in the early hours of October 9, 2026.
Born February 26, 1939 to Josephine White and Herbert White Eagle on the Wind River Reservation.
Nelson’s childhood and upbringing was spent with his grandparents, Steven and Susie, as they instilled traditional Arapaho teachings and values into his life which immensely reflected through his journey and reverence as a humble Arapaho man here on earth.
Nelson was taken to St. Stephen’s Catholic Indian Boarding School where he learned how to survive and perservere as he endured the federal government’s policy to “Kill the Indian and Save the Man” and through his sheer wit, strength, power of prayer, and resilience hung on tightly to his Arapaho teachings and Arapaho Language. Nelson was one of very few fluent speakers left from the Northern Arapaho Tribe.
Nelson was a natural athlete and played basketball at St. Stephen’s, along with his brother Crawford, was a member of the St. Stephen’s Indian Basketball Championship team.
In 1950 Nelson was drafted into the United States Army and spent his tour in Germany and was also proud serving alongside Elvis. He was designated as an expert marksman and also enjoyed playing football. It was on his tour where he learned his love for eating seafood and other delacacies not acustomed to his pallet of traditional foods such as elk, deer, and antelope. There wasn’t a food Nelson wasn’t willing to try, but if he had his favorite to choose from, it would have been crab legs.
In his prime Nelson was a Champion Fancy Dancer. He was well known in Canada and the Plains for his quick, fast, and agile ability to spin and move to the beat of the drum. It was on the pow-wow trail where he met the love of his life Bonnie Jean Goings at Oglala Lakota Nation Powwow. They were married in 1961 and began their lives together in Ethete, Wyoming, where they started their family with the eldest and only daughter Roxanne, and four sons Nelson Jr.(Pat), Steven, Judson, and Henry. Nelson took two of his children Roxanne and Steve on a European Tour for a cultural exchange and exhibition, where they danced in different places.
During the Indian Relocation Act Nelson and Bonnie moved to Oakland California where Nelson learned how to make computer chips. He also became a talented silversmith and learned the art of silversmithing from his grandpa John Pedro. Over the years he created beautiful pieces he gifted, sold, and traded through out Indian Country.
Nelson was a member of the Native Ameircan Church (NAC)N and spent a majority of his early years practing the NAC traditional way of life.
Nelson was an avid hunter and knew the Wind River Mouintains and Owl Creek’s like the back of his hand. He enjoyed exploring the mountains and taking his frIends and family to his favotire places. If you asked him where he found an elk, bear, ram, or fosil, he was known for saying, “it was at No Tell’em Creek”.
Nelson proudly served on the Northern Arapaho Business Council (NABC) having served 4 consecutive terms. His successes through NABC history included developing social and economic development strategies, identifying and utilizing The Northern Arapaho Tribe’s natural and human resources to complete successful projects. Examples are the community facilities and infrastructure improvements.
Nelson helped strategize and champion the Northern Arapaho Tribe right to conduct Class II and Class III Gaming on the Wind River Indian Reservation. Enabling the development of the Wind River Casino Enterpise and later expanding the tribes gaming footprint through building Little Wind Casino. The Northern Arapaho Tribe was one of the first tribes to win an Indian Gaming lawsuit and not have to compact with the state due to Governor Jim Geringer’s failing to negotiate in good faith.
Nelson and his fellow councilman were involved in enabling oil and gas settlements, tribal vehiclle registration, and numerous other economic development projects. Nelson promoted education that led to building its resource capacity and building relationships to help bring higher education learning to the reservation and the Northern Arapaho people. He prioritized cultural and Arapaho language revitalization. Nelson was a mentor to all of his people. He utilized his life experiences in guiding those who sought his wisdom, always giving back to the Arapaho people, as he was taught.
Nelson’s service to his people extended into having served on the Northern Arapaho Tribal Industries Board of Directors.
Nelson humbly dedicated his entire lifetime preserving the Northern Arapaho way of life. He unconditionally loved the Arapaho people with his entirety just as he loved his family. He shall always be revered as our beloved Keeper and Ceremonial Leader of this era who not only showed us what being Arapaho means but lived it every day.
He was a Chief in every true sense of the word. But what made his leadership so powerful wasn’t loudness or pride—it was his deep humility. He didn’t lead by standing above people; he led by standing beside them. He carried the weight of responsibility with strength, grace, and quiet wisdom. When he spoke, people listened, not because he demanded attention, but because his words carried the truth, dignity, and care of a man who genuinely loved his people and his family.
As a husband and a father, he set the standard. He showed what it meant to be steady when times are tough, to protect and care for those you love, and to walk through life with honor. Even through these responsibilities, his humor shone through. You could always ensure laughter lifted the air. The values he lived by every day—integrity, respect, and unconditional love—are the very foundation of the family he built. His guidance, his wisdom, and his legacy will live on in every life he touched, in every memory we hold, and in every generation that follows in his footsteps.
Nelson is surivived by his wife Bonnie; Daughters Roxanne Hines (Dave), Rebecca Armajo, and Lisa Redman. Son’s; Nelson *Pat* White Jr. (Hattie), Steven White Sr. (Alanita), Judson White, Henry White. Grandchildren; Amanda White (Trevor Trosper), Alan White (Lauren), Peggen Hines Frank (Willie), Samatha and Stacie Oldman, Steven White Jr. (Latonya), Winterhawk Goodman, Alison White Eagle, Frank White, Charles White, Nelson White III, Loveeda White (Christian Lopez), Marybel and Alejandra Maldanado, Jared White, Martin Brown III, Keva White, Michael Willow, Hobson White, Olivia and Rachel DuShane. Great Grandchildren; Ampo Mills, Dorianna White, Anessa White Eagle, Hehani Pte Skan White, Arianni White Eagle, Elliana White Eagle, Kaylanna White Eagle, MahpiyaOite White Eagle, Kayliah White Eagle, Auracellia White, Azailia White.
Brother: Marcus Willow. Sisters: Laverne White, Alvera Willow, Mavis Willow, Gloria C’Bearing, Charlotte “Chippa” Goggles, Salina Quiver.
Nieces: Dr. Dodie White Eagle, Lynn Hernadez, Hanna Clifford, Fay Hernandes, Maxine White, Rita Ann Brown, Rickina Armour, Audra White Eagle, Sherri White, Bernadette White, Lisa White, Tricia Willow, Carrie Benson, Chloe and Chloeleah Goings, Julie Goings, Jocelyn White, Philma Willow
Nephews: Tynan BearComesOut, Crawford White Jr, Vince White, Nelson Thomas White, Theodore Blindwoman, Marcus White, Colley Willow, Austin Willow, Houston Willow, Derrick Willow, Sr., Curtis Benson, Martin Goings, and Byron Willow.
Please give forgiveness if we have left anyone out, Nelson had a very large family whom he cherrished and adored and is surived by many brothers, sisters, nieces, nephews and grandchildren and great grandchildren.

Duane Roger Wohlbrandt02 Jun 1958 – 02 Oct 2026Buffalo, WyomingShared by: Harness Funeral HomeFuneral services for Duane Roger Wohlbrandt, 68-year-old Buffalo resident who passed away at Amie Holt Care Center on Friday, October 02, 2026, will be held Friday, October 9, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. at the Harness Funeral Home Chapel in Buffalo, with Mike Leibee officiating. Duane Roger Wohlbrandt
Goodbye for Now
Duane Roger Wohlbrandt, a lifelong resident of Buffalo, Wyoming, passed away on October 2, 2026, at the age of 68. He was born on June 2, 1958, in Mammoth Hot Springs, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, to Leroy “Wally” and Shirley Kumor Wohlbrandt.
Duane faced challenges throughout his life that might have defeated many people, but he met them with incredible courage and quiet perseverance. When he fell or was knocked down, he got up again—and again—without complaint or self-pity. He wanted to do things that might have seemed out of reach, and he did not give up. His own struggles gave him great empathy for others facing difficulties. He loved children and was kind and patient with animals.
Duane attended school in Buffalo, graduating from Buffalo High School with the class of 1977. He was a member of the school’s FFA chapter and showed a steer from the family ranch at the Johnson County Fair. He also competed with other projects, one of which went on to the State Fair.
In his teenage years, Duane, a leftie, loved practicing his baseball pitching. He rode his gasoline-powered minibike with joy and abandon and enjoyed working in the ranch shop, welding and helping repair equipment. He was always game for gathering and splitting firewood and enjoyed target shooting with both pistol and rifle.
After high school, Duane attended vocational school in Cheyenne. He held various jobs around Buffalo and worked on the family ranch. He had a talent for small-engine repair and operated his own lawnmower repair business.
Duane loved hunting and fishing in the Bighorn Mountains and visiting Yellowstone National Park with his family. He enjoyed family gatherings and the feasts and festivities that came with those good times. Comedy movies and television delighted him, and he had a quick sense of humor and a joyous laugh.
The greatest strength in Duane’s life came through his genuine faith in Jesus. He enjoyed volunteering at Bighorn Baptist Church. His greatest joy and blessing on Earth was his beloved wife, Barb, who brought him true happiness and endless love and meant all the world to him. God truly brought them together. Duane and Barb were married on January 4, 2004, in Buffalo, Wyoming.
On November 8, 2013, Duane was admitted to Amie Holt Care Center where he lived for the remainder of his life.
Duane was preceded in death by his parents; his maternal grandparents, John and Amy Kumor; his paternal grandparents, Philip Henry and Irma Wohlbrandt; many aunts and uncles; and several cousins on both sides of the family.
He is survived by his wife, Barb; his brothers, John (Chris) and Phil (Tani); his sister, Lorena; and four nieces and their spouses and children.
Visitation will be held on Thursday, October 8, 2026, from 1 to 9 p.m. at Harness Funeral Home. A service will take place on Friday, October 9, 2026, at 10 a.m. followed by a graveside service at Willow Grove Cemetery, where Duane will be laid to rest in the family plot. A meal will follow at Calvary Chapel. Mike Leibee of Calvary Chapel will lead the service.
Memorial contributions may be made to Calvary Chapel in remembrance of Duane, a kind and courageous man whose faith, laughter, and love will remain with the family he leaves behind for a while.
Goodbye for now, Duane.

Farren James Zabriskie06 Oct 1947 – 05 Oct 2026Buffalo, WyomingShared by: Harness Funeral HomeFuneral services for Farren James Zabriskie, a 78-year-old Buffalo resident who passed away on Monday, October 5, 2026, will be held Saturday, October 31, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. at the Harness Funeral Home Chapel in Buffalo. Memorial donations in Farren’s memory may be made to the Tunnel to Towers Foundation at www.T2T.org. Online condolences may be shared at www.harnessfuneralhome.com.
Farren Jame Zabriskie, known to everyone simply as F’kin Farren, passed away on October 5, 2026, in Buffalo, Wyoming, one day shy of his 79th birthday, after health-related complications. He was born on October 6, 1947, in Berkeley, California, and spent a life that was equal parts hard work, good humor, and the kind of stubborn decency that makes a person unforgettable. He was a Christian, a proud veteran, a devoted family man, and a man who seemed to understand that if life was going to be complicated, it might as well be handled with a grin and a strong cup of coffee.
Farren grew up with a work ethic that could outlast a Wyoming winter and a practical streak that made him useful in just about any situation. He graduated from Hillcrest High School in Midvale, Utah, and later earned an Associate of Adolescent Psychology from Central Wyoming College. That combination of education and common sense suited him well, because Farren had a way of understanding people that did not require a degree, although he had one anyway. He spent his life learning, observing, and figuring out how to get things done, which was handy considering he never seemed to meet a job he could not improve with grit, patience, and a little bit of sarcasm.
His work history read like the greatest hits of American labor. Farren worked as a carpenter, in concrete, in coal mines, in construction, at the Wyoming State Training School in Lander, Wyoming, and in various odd jobs that probably could have filled an entire second obituary by themselves. He was also a Union Ironworker with Local 229 and Local 27, and he took that role seriously. He knew what it meant to show up, to sweat, to build, and to keep going when the day got long. If there was a heavy object that needed moving or a problem that needed solving, Farren was the kind of man you wanted nearby, preferably before the situation got worse.
He served his country honorably in the United States Marine Corps during the Vietnam era from 1966 to 1969, including AutoMech-CamPen-6weeks, and he carried those years with the quiet pride of someone who had done his duty and then some. His military honors included the National Defense Service Medal, the Vietnam Campaign Medal with device, the Vietnam Service Medal with 6, the Republic of Vietnam Cross of Gallantry with Palm, the Good Conduct Medal, 1st Award, and the Presidential Unit Citation. Those medals told part of the story, but anyone who knew Farren would say his real decoration was the way he lived afterward, with loyalty, resilience, and an ability to keep his sense of humor even when life was clearly trying to be difficult.
Farren was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Angie Rosalez Zabriskie, and he carried her memory with him always. He is survived by his brothers, Lee (Linda) Zabriskie, Paul (Wendy) Zabriskie, and Carl Zabriskie; his sons, Chance (Teri Ann) Zabriskie, Dylan Zabriskie, and Waylon (Alli) Zabriskie; his sons by marriage, Paul Luthi and Tyson Mcdougall; his daughters by marriage, Lindsay Avila and Shannon Nesheim; 12 grandchildren; and 14 great-grandchildren. His family was a source of pride and joy to him, and he loved them in the straightforward, no-nonsense way that meant he showed up, helped out, and made sure everyone knew where they stood. He was loving, selfless, and generous, which is a fine way to be remembered and, frankly, a rare enough combination to deserve its own medal.
Farren also knew how to enjoy life, which he did without apology. He loved his local watering hole, the Century Club, where the atmosphere undoubtedly benefited from his presence and where he probably left more memorable stories than anyone could reasonably count. He took pride in helping others who needed help unconditionally, which was one of those traits that made people trust him immediately. He loved the wind blowing through his hair on his motorcycle, and he had a special appreciation for his Harley Davidsons and old hot rod vehicles, because subtlety was never the point and neither was Farren. He enjoyed listening to music of all kinds and singing along, whether the song needed help or not. He also took great joy in the outdoors, whether he was fishing, camping with family and friends, or watching the sun rise and set as if he had someplace important to be, which he usually did not. He loved to sightsee and travel, and one suspects he did so with the confidence of a man who believed every road had a story and most of them were worth hearing twice.
In the spirit of Farren’s humor and larger-than-life personality, one fitting line comes from the beloved comedian George Carlin, who said, “Don’t sweat the petty things and don’t pet the sweaty things.” Farren would have appreciated that kind of wisdom, because he understood that life was serious enough on its own and did not need any extra nonsense added for free. He had a comedian’s timing without trying to be one, and a straight man’s delivery that made his dry wit even funnier. He could make people laugh simply by telling the truth in a way that was too honest to ignore and too funny to forget.
Farren’s life was built on service, work, loyalty, and love. He leaves behind a legacy that is as solid as the things he built and as warm as the stories he told. He will be remembered for his big heart, his steady hands, his generous spirit, and his ability to find the good in people, even when they had not fully earned it yet. He was the sort of man who made a place better just by being in it, and now that he has gone, the world feels a little quieter, a little rougher around the edges, and a lot less interesting.
