name: Delaware
title: Breast Cancer Awareness Month enters second half with events across Delaware
text:
Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition activities range from music and soccer to survivor support, wellness programs and Halloween fundraisers through Oct. 31
WILMINGTON, Del. — Breast Cancer Awareness Month may be halfway over, but the Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition has a busy schedule of events, support programs and community fundraisers planned across the state through the end of October.
After major early-month events including Dewey Goes Pink and the coalition’s Monster Mile Walk for a Cause at Dover Motor Speedway, the focus now shifts to a series of smaller community events and programs that illustrate the broader work of the organization.
DBCC’s mission extends beyond October fundraising. The organization works year-round to increase access to breast cancer screening, provide education and patient navigation and offer programs for people diagnosed with breast cancer and their families.
That means the final weeks of October include everything from music and high school soccer to cooking, mental-health discussions, survivor groups and an overnight nature retreat.
Community events keep Delaware pink
Community partners have scheduled a series of fundraisers benefiting DBCC across all three counties.
On Thursday, Oct. 15, Twisted Irons Craft Brewing Co. is scheduled to hold its Drive Out Cancer event in New Castle County.
A day later, Sussex County joins the effort with the first Pink Out Party at Big Chill Surf Cantina on Friday, Oct. 16. Additional Sussex County businesses are supporting the coalition throughout October, including Russo by the Sea Italian Market and the East Sussex Moose Lodge.
On Saturday, Oct. 17, Pink Gumbo 6 will bring music, breast cancer awareness and survivor stories to The Delaware Contemporary on Wilmington’s Riverfront.
The event, presented by 3G Management and Entertainment, runs from 6 to 9:30 p.m. and features local performers, vendors and speakers. A portion of the proceeds will benefit DBCC.
The event combines the traditional pink associated with breast cancer awareness with what organizers describe as a “gumbo” of musical styles, cultures and people united around awareness and early detection.
Schools and sports join the campaign
Students are also helping turn October pink.
The Concord High School boys soccer program will hold its fifth annual game supporting DBCC on Tuesday, Oct. 20, beginning at 3:30 p.m. at Concord High School, 2501 Ebright Road in Wilmington.
The team has been raising money throughout the season and plans to present its donations during the event.
That same week, golf and social events will continue the fundraising effort in Sussex and New Castle counties.
Cripple Creek Golf & Country Club in Dagsboro is hosting its Go Pink or Go Home activities Oct. 20 and 21, including a Pink Champagne on Ice gathering. DBCC lists the events among its October community partnerships.
DBCC also has a Play Fore Pink golf event scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 22, at Newark Country Club. The event includes golf, lunch, dinner and a silent auction. Individual golf registration was listed as sold out on DBCC’s registration page, although foursomes and dinner-only participation remained available when the page was reviewed.
Newark will remain part of the awareness campaign on Sunday, Oct. 25, when the 10th annual DeerPark Goes Pink 5K is scheduled to raise money for the coalition. DBCC lists the longtime event among its New Castle County community fundraisers.
Support continues beyond fundraising
Some of the coalition’s most significant October activities will happen away from races and fundraising events.
DBCC’s calendar includes regular Breast Cancer Conversation support sessions, Young Survivors in Action programming and My Sister’s Keeper gatherings, along with wellness and nutrition programs.
A Breast Cancer Conversation is scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 15, followed by a virtual Young Survivors in Action healing meditation Saturday, Oct. 17.
On Tuesday, Oct. 20, DBCC will host its Forever Fighters program, a Yes2Health In the Kitchen session and a My Sister’s Keeper gathering in Georgetown.
A Yes2Health Active Cooking cookbook club for breast cancer survivors follows Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Additional Breast Cancer Conversation and My Sister’s Keeper programs are scheduled Oct. 27, with the New Castle My Sister’s Keeper group meeting from 6 to 7 p.m.
Mental health part of survivorship
The coalition also is using Breast Cancer Awareness Month to focus on the emotional effects of cancer.
Its “In the Loop” cancer survivorship and mental health series continues Wednesday, Oct. 28, with a session titled “Stress, Mind, and Body — What do I have in front of me?”
The programming reflects a broader approach to survivorship that extends beyond medical treatment to emotional health, nutrition, social connection and long-term wellness.
Nature retreat closes out the month
Breast cancer survivors will have another opportunity to connect during DBCC’s Nurture with Nature overnight retreat Oct. 30 and 31 at Ashland Nature Center in Hockessin.
The Nurture with Nature program uses outdoor activities as a way for survivors to connect with one another while experiencing hiking, nature and other outdoor activities.
The overnight program includes time at Ashland Nature Center, a morning hike and a session on mindful birding and forest bathing.
The program is one of several DBCC initiatives designed specifically around life after a breast cancer diagnosis.
Halloween ends month with a cause
Breast Cancer Awareness Month concludes with a Halloween-themed fundraiser in Smyrna.
The Halloween Hustle 5K Run/Walk is scheduled for 8 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, at Smyrna High School.
Participants are encouraged to wear costumes, and runners, walkers, families and first-time participants are invited. Proceeds from the event benefit DBCC.
The event provides a fitting conclusion to a month in which Delaware communities have supported the organization through races, restaurants, golf tournaments, athletic events, concerts and social gatherings.
Awareness can lead to action
For DBCC, October also provides an opportunity to remind Delawareans that breast cancer awareness should ultimately lead to screening and early detection.
The coalition helps residents schedule mammograms and navigate financial, transportation, insurance and language barriers. Its Women’s Health Screening Program can connect uninsured or underinsured Delawareans with free or reduced-cost screening programs and offers transportation and interpretation assistance when needed.
DBCC also provides breast health education and support resources in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole.
While October brings additional attention to breast cancer, the coalition’s programs and support services continue throughout the year.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY teachers PAC donated to conservative group to try to influence GOP primaries
text:
The JCTA PAC gave $200,000 to a Republican PAC to try to influence primaries. (file art)The Jefferson County Teachers Association’s PAC donated $200,000 to a pro-Republican PAC in the May primary. Now, the same conservative PAC is running attack ads against candidates endorsed by the teachers union. 
Federal Election Commission records show JCTA’s PAC, Better Schools Kentucky, donated the funds to the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition on April 1, ahead of Kentucky’s primary elections. Other donations to the coalition at the time included $250,000 from GOPAC Election Fund and $140,000 from the Kentucky Chamber Advocacy Committee, two PACs that generally support conservative causes
Months later, the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition is behind ads against Democratic candidates endorsed by Better Schools Kentucky for the state legislature. Kentucky Registry of Election Finance records show the coalition spent about $27,250 on ads against Suhas Kulkanri in the 48th House District and about $101,400 on ads against Tim Hall in the 31st House District. 
Commonwealth Conservative Coalition has also spent money against other Democrats this general election cycle, such as about $39,500 in ads against incumbent Rep. Adam Moore in the 45th House District, about $22,800 against Johnny Ray Turner in the 95th House District and $40,000 against Sarah Cole McIntosh in the 36th House District. 
Better Schools Kentucky also gave the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition $200,000 ahead of the 2024 primary, according to the FEC. 
Responding to questions from the Kentucky Lantern, Devyn Melvin, JCTA’s communications director, said in an email Better Schools Kentucky “is a non-partisan, teacher-led organization that is public-education focused and teacher focused.”
The General Assembly has had a Republican supermajority for several years. Melvin said the JCTA PAC was trying to support the candidates in Republican primaries that would be the most pro-public education.
“BSK has not made any contributions in the general election. BSK has made contributions to SuperPACS in the primaries in order to elect pro-public education candidates,” the statement said. “We support candidates who have a record of standing up for public education.”
According to KREF records, Commonwealth Conservative Coalition spent about $370,000 on ads supporting and opposing candidates in Republican primaries across the state this year. Some of those included backing incumbents like Rep. Kimberly Poore Moser in the 64th House District, Rep. Deanna Frazier Gordon in the 81st and Rep. Kim Banta in the 63rd. Banta ultimately lost her primary. In the general election so far, the coalition has spent more than $230,000.
BSK added that it hasn’t made “contributions to SuperPACs in the general election” and is focusing on school board candidates. 
“Teachers look forward to working with anyone who will support public education and stand by the people who educate our kids- teachers,” the statement said. 
Don Parkinson, who is listed as the treasurer for the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition on the FEC’s site, did not return emails and phone calls seeking comment. 
Jason Perkey, a senior adviser for Hall, questioned why JCTA’s PAC gave money to a group that ultimately spent it on races outside of Jefferson County. Regardless if JCTA’s money was spent during the primary or the general election by the second PAC, it was still donated to the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition, he added. Some of the candidates supported, like Moser and Gordon, voted in favor of a 2024 constitutional amendment that would have allowed the General Assembly to fund nonpublic schools, which JCTA opposed. The amendment failed to pass that fall. 
“I think the overarching argument about investing in races that will impact their membership and students across Kentucky is the right intention, but they could have found an organization that was trying to elect people who want the best for our public schools, teachers and students,” Perkey said. 
Perkey added that Hall is “very grateful and honored to have the support from the JCTA” and teachers in Jefferson County. Hall is running against incumbent Republican Rep. Susan Tyler Witten. 
Kulkarni said in a statement to the Lantern that it was “no surprise that corporations and special interests are pouring money” into support for the incumbent he is facing, Republican Rep. Ken Fleming. 
“We believe this is exactly what’s wrong with Frankfort: a system of pay-to-play politics where corporations get the tax breaks, Ken gets the campaign contributions, and working families and small businesses pay the price,” Kulkarni continued. “We believe voters are seeing through these schemes. The enthusiasm pouring into our campaign has been tremendous, and we feel very good about the support we’re receiving.”
State law prevents any candidate from coordinating with PACs. Kentucky’s general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Suspicious letter to Mississippi Secretary of State Watson intercepted
text:

The U.S. Postal Service and Homeland Security intercepted a letter sent to Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office, as federal authorities warn of letters with suspicious substances being sent to congressional and election offices across the country.
Watson spokeswoman Liz Jonson said in a statement on Thursday, “Based on the events in other states, we were notified to expect a suspicious letter, but it was intercepted by USPS and HSI before it got to our office.”
Jonson said the letter has been turned over to the FBI.
The Associated Press obtained a message from the U.S. Senate sergeant at arms warning that law enforcement officials were seeking to intercept letters, and reported that federal authorities were urging congressional and election offices nationwide to treat the letters as “potentially hazardous.”
The AP reported that mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to evacuation this week of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma, and the Ohio secretary of state said a package intended for his office was intercepted.
The news comes just weeks before midterm Election Day, and is similar to a threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings with a white powder. Some of those mailings contained traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Correction 10/15/2026: This story has been updated with the correct spelling of Liz Jonson’s name.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minneapolis council fails to override mayoral veto of ban on driverless robotaxis
text:
A Waymo vehicle exits a charging lot on January 15, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)The Minneapolis City Council failed to override a mayoral veto of an ordinance that would have required Waymo and other robotaxi companies to put human “safety monitors” behind the wheel and pay them minimum rates.
The proposal aimed to protect the jobs of the state’s roughly 10,000 rideshare drivers, who have become well organized since successfully campaigning for statewide minimum pay rates and job protections.
Council Member Robin Wonsley, the lead author of the ordinance, vowed to continue the fight immediately after the vote Thursday, giving formal notice that she would introduce another proposal to regulate autonomous vehicles for commercial purposes.
“To our residents, I want you to know we see you, and that there’s members of this body that’s continuously fighting for you,” Wonsley said. “We cannot simply allow Big Tech to come into our communities and steal thousands of jobs from immigrant workers.”
In vetoing the ordinance, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said in a statement, “Requiring a driver in a driverless car doesn’t make sense.”
“Minneapolis is open for business, open to innovative technology, and open to a variety of transportation options,” he said.
The council voted 7-5 to override his veto, falling short of the nine votes necessary.
Waymo began testing its technology in Minnesota last year, and the company says it currently provides more than 500,000 fully autonomous rides every week in 15 major U.S. cities, none of which require human monitors. It’s unclear when commercial service may begin in Minnesota.
The appearance of Waymo also prompted the St. Paul City Council to take action. The council voted Wednesday to direct city staff to study autonomous vehicles and suggest regulations that protect workers and the general public.
The fight over autonomous vehicles is expected to return to the state Capitol in January after lawmakers failed to agree on legislation regulating the nascent industry in the closely divided Legislature.
While robotaxi companies promise safer and more comfortable rides than Uber and Lyft, the white Jaguar Waymos covered in cameras are rolling emblems of artificial intelligence’s power to automate jobs — a power that is stoking fear throughout the labor force, from attorneys to truck drivers.
Robotaxi opponents warn that allowing drivers to be displaced by Waymos allows Silicon Valley to vacuum up income that would be reinvested in the state.
Wonsley pointed to a recent study by the union-backed think tank North Star Policy Action that estimates rideshare drivers in Minnesota earn about $209 million a year and contribute $561 million in total economic activity across the state through spending on housing, health care, car repairs and other necessities.
That income represent a minuscule portion — just 0.04% — of Minnesota’s $476 billion in total personal income.
“This is income that helps keep our city afloat,” Wonsley said. “Without that, that puts our city in very, very precarious conditions.”
The fight by workers against automation is a familiar one, though rarely successful.
The Luddites, English textile workers whose name became shorthand for rejecting technological progress, were unable to stop the mechanized loom.
Railroad firemen held onto their jobs through union contracts for decades after diesel engines left them no coal to shovel — though they were eventually forced to retire or retrain.
Elevator operators and typesetters have all but disappeared. Taxi dispatchers are largely obsolete, too, after Uber and Lyft automated those jobs.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Legal battle over Kosta Diamantis’ state pension began without him
text:
The legal battle over whether Connecticut can permanently revoke pension benefits for Konstantinos Diamantis, a former state official who was convicted of soliciting bribes from school construction contractors, kicked off on Thursday in a small courtroom in Hartford.
But as the legal arguments began, the defense table was conspicuously empty. 
Diamantis was not present, which is not a surprise given that he fled to Greece before he could be sentenced last month on federal bribery, extortion and conspiracy charges. And there was no attorney in the courtroom to make an appearance on Diamantis’ behalf.
Despite Diamantis’ absence, lawyers from Attorney General William Tong’s office proceeded with their case, which seeks to permanently cease payments of more than $70,000 per year that Diamantis has been collecting since leaving state employment in 2021.
The attorney general’s office asked a state Superior Court judge on Thursday to issue an injunction, which would allow the state to hold Diamantis’ monthly pension payments in escrow until the court rules whether to permanently reduce or revoke those benefits.
But state Superior Court Judge James Graham questioned why it was necessary to place Diamantis’ future pension payments in escrow, given that the Connecticut Comptroller’s office halted the direct deposits on those payments in September.
Graham said the comptroller’s earlier decision to stop wiring money to Diamantis “begged the question” as to why the state was seeking a temporary injunction now. 
Assistant Attorney General Eric Babbs told the judge that they were seeking clarity from the court on the issue, and he said Diamantis’ decision to flee the country made this case a unique situation.
Diamantis, who was sentenced to seven years in prison and is now considered a federal fugitive, has filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging Connecticut Comptroller Sean Scanlon’s decision to stop the direct deposits on his monthly pension benefits.
In that case, Diamantis alleged that Scanlon and Tong violated his due process rights by cutting off his pension payments before a judge had the opportunity to review such a request in state court. 
On Thursday, Diamantis responded to questions from the Connecticut Mirror by attacking Tong and Scanlon and by, once again, questioning the jury verdict in his federal criminal case.
“Why should my pension be held in escrow. They are owed to me until and unless the court rules I should be denied my future pensions,” Diamantis said via text message, adding that he expected to appeal any ruling that did not go in his favor. 
Diamantis also denounced the attorney general’s office for moving forward with its lawsuit in state court without properly notifying him of the proceedings.
“I did not know about the action in court taking place. Zero knowledge of Mr. Tong’s action,” Diamantis said. “All I know is he and/or the comptroller illegally stopped my pension that I earned before any action was filed in court.” 
Judge Graham also raised questions in court on Thursday about whether the attorney general’s office did enough to try to serve Diamantis in the case. 
Babbs, the assistant attorney general, told the judge that they delivered a court summons to Diamantis’ former residence in Farmington. He also explained that they were unable to serve Diamantis at his current address in Greece because they did not know where he was currently living. 
Babbs said the attorney general’s office also contacted Norm Pattis, who has represented Diamantis in federal court, to try to deliver the summons. 
Pattis told the CT Mirror, however, that he was not representing Diamantis as part of the Attorney General’s lawsuit in state court. 
Judge Graham recognized the difficulty the state attorneys were facing in trying to make contact with someone who is currently an “international fugitive.” 
But he instructed the attorney general’s office to work on the issue and to draft a motion arguing why they believe their attempts to contact Diamantis are adequate in this case.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Court disbars former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The Mississippi Supreme Court permanently disbarred former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba on Thursday, two months after he offered to surrender his law license. 
Lumumba, who did not immediately respond to a request for comment, is awaiting sentencing on a federal felony charge after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery in a case stemming from an FBI operation that ensnared multiple officials in Mississippi’s capital city.
Sentencing was initially scheduled for last month. U.S. District Judge Daniel P. Jordan III postponed the hearing to early November, but Lumumba’s attorneys are awaiting a ruling on a motion to further postpone the sentencing.
Lumumba was to be sentenced along with his co-defendants – former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens and former Jackson City Councilmember Aaron Banks. They each face up to five years in prison and fines of up to $250,000. 
Others involved in the scheme have also yet to be sentenced, including former Jackson City Councilmember Angelique Lee. 
In 2024, a sweeping federal indictment alleged that in exchange for $50,000 in campaign donations, Lumumba directed a city employee to shorten a bid deadline to benefit a pair of out-of-town developers that were working with Owens. 
Unknown to the local politicians, the developers were undercover FBI agents.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Griswold, Allen question each other’s qualifications in Colorado attorney general debate
text:
4th Judicial District Attorney Michael Allen, left, a Republican, and Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat, met for their only scheduled debate ahead of the November race to be Colorado's next attorney general. (Photos courtesy of candidates)Secretary of State Jena Griswold and El Paso County District Attorney Michael Allen attacked each other’s records and leadership of their current offices in the only scheduled debate in the Colorado attorney general’s race Wednesday.
The candidates vying to be Colorado’s top law enforcement official debated their approaches to challenging the Trump administration, protecting Colorado water rights, data centers and more at an event hosted by the Colorado Sun at the University of Denver,
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser is term-limited and won the Democratic nomination for governor in November.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Griswold, a Democrat, criticized Allen, a Republican, for his stance on federal immigration enforcement, highlighting comments he made praising the “trigger discipline” of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Renee Good. Allen wants to change Colorado laws that prohibit state law enforcement from cooperating with ICE. 
“When we have masked men in unmarked cars grabbing people that may or may not be citizens, not following due process, we are in danger as a democracy,” Griswold said.
She said she would continue to run an online portal Weiser’s office implemented that allows Coloradans to report misconduct by federal law enforcement officers, and said the “fundamental role of the next attorney general is to stand up between immigrant communities and ICE.” Allen, the district attorney for Colorado’s 4th Judicial District in El Paso and Teller counties, said he would evaluate whether the portal is necessary.
Allen said immigration policy should never be based on discrimination and that he would defend anybody who is victimized by law enforcement, whether by a federal or state agency.
As a Republican whose opinions conflict with several state laws, including those around abortion and gun regulations, Allen said he would still enforce and apply the law regardless as attorney general. He mentioned, for example, his role in prosecuting the shooter who killed five people and injured several others at Club Q in Colorado Springs in 2022.
“I prosecuted that case and filed hate crime charges, and said from the courthouse steps, that every person, regardless of where they come from, whatever, everyone has inherent human dignity,” Allen said. “And I used the power of the prosecution to hold the shooter in that case fully accountable to the law.”
Allen repeatedly flagged concerns about Griswold’s legal experience, particularly her limited experience as a trial attorney. Griswold argued that the office of attorney general is not a trial attorney, but an executive who manages an office of 700 people. The solicitor general argues cases on behalf of the state, such as those before the U.S. Supreme Court.
Griswold defended her leadership during election-related legal challenges, including the removal of former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters after she led a breach of her own election equipment to search for evidence of fraud in the 2020 election.
“During my time as Secretary of State, I set the legal direction of my department through some serious election and democracy issues,” Griswold said.
Allen acknowledged former President Joe Biden won the 2020 election, contradicting persistent false claims from some Republicans who say that Trump won the election.
Scrutiny of Griswold’s record
Griswold faced intense criticism after she disclosed in 2024 that a document posted to her office’s website included a hidden but accessible worksheet containing passwords to election equipment in counties throughout the state. County clerks said that while election security in the state remained strong following the breach, many were upset that Griswold did not inform them about the breach until after the Colorado Republican Party learned about and announced it.
More recently, a mistake within Griswold’s office resulted in the personal information for more than 130,000 confidential voters being publicly accessible for over a week. Allen is one of the voters whose information was temporarily made public.
Griswold said while she takes responsibility for the mistaken exposure of election equipment passwords, she is proud of the work her office has done to improve Colorado’s election processes and security.
Two years after Griswold was elected, her office hired a consultant to evaluate leadership within the secretary of state’s office amid high turnover in the office. She rejected claims of high turnover within her office and said she ran an executive office “in a very difficult atmosphere” amid thousands of threats against her and her staff.
Allen did not say he would continue Weiser’s streak of pursuing lawsuits against the Trump administration and said he does not have evidence to determine if he should. He has previously criticized Weiser for the lawsuits that Allen views as politically motivated. Griswold said confidently that she would continue lawsuits challenging unlawful actions from the Trump administration.
Wednesday’s debate was the only time Griswold and Allen are scheduled to meet face-to-face before the November election. During the primary election season, Griswold faced criticism for skipping roughly a dozen debates and forums with her three Democratic primary opponents. 
The attorney general heads the Colorado Department of Law and oversees enforcement of consumer protection and antitrust laws, defends state laws in legal challenges, and advocates for law enforcement and community safety.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Facing lawsuits, Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI offers to buy homes homes near Southaven data centers
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
With residents suing over noise and pollution, Elon Musk’s company is trying to buy up homes around his expansive data center operations in Southaven. 
A few owners have rejected the offers while others are contemplating it or have decided to take the buyout. But some renters believe they’re being left behind.
This is the latest development in over a year of tensions between Southaven residents and SpaceXAI, formerly xAI, as the $2-trillion company continues to expand its data center presence in the greater Memphis area. Some residents are opposed to the project that has resulted in noise and pollution complaints, multiple lawsuits and frustration on the part of locals and city officials.
Residents living near SpaceXAI’s power plant in Southaven have reported receiving offers to buy their homes from MZX Tech LLC, a subsidiary of SpaceXAI. 
In a letter that some residents received, Burch Realty Group, a local realtor that claimed to be working on behalf of MZX Tech, offered to buy their house in exchange for “among other things, a release of all claims” related to the class action lawsuit brought by a group of Southaven residents against SpaceXAI.
The litigation is over noise created by the company’s temporary gas turbines, and plaintiffs seek a court order to reduce the “near-constant noise, vibrations, and other nuisance-level harms.” They seek financial compensation for the disruption they say has been ongoing for over a year. 
Class action eligibility boundary proposed by lawyers representing residents bringing a class action lawsuit against SpaceXAI. The area is defined as “Stateline Road West to the North; U.S. Highway 51 to the East; Nail Road to the South; and a vertical boundary line to the West that is 1 mile West of Hom Lake Road.” The judge has not yet ruled on whether to accept these boundaries. (Credit: Google Earth and Airbus, modified by Julie Lee/Mississippi Today)
Anyone living in the affected area, including renters, are eligible for the class action, said Robert Wiygul, one of the attorneys representing residents.
Cushman & Wakefield, not mentioned in the letter, is another realty group that has made at least one buyout offer to local homeowners.
A representative from Cushman & Wakefield referred Mississippi Today to SpaceXAI and a representative from Burch Realty Group could not be reached for comment.
Mississippi Today spoke to several homeowners, who were reluctant to speak on the record or share details of the offers they received.
The NAACP is bringing a separate case against SpaceXAI over the same turbines, which it claims violates the federal Clean Air Act. State and local officials have said the company has not broken any state or local laws, and the federal government has said the company’s operations are vital for national security. 
In the letter to Southaven residents, MZX Tech “denies all of the allegations against it” and says it “requires property for business purposes.” The company did not disclose what business purposes it intends to use the houses for. 
However, in an Oct. 1 blog post, Southaven Mayor Darren Musselwhite said in addition to improving public perception, the buyout serves the purpose of acquiring homes for SpaceXAI employees. The project is expected to create hundreds of new jobs in the area and attract new residents.
The surge in construction is already bringing jobs and increased traffic. Residents report that surrounding parking lots are filled to capacity with employees’ cars and that privately chartered buses are routinely travelling to and from the site.
SpaceXAI is currently hiring for at least 160 jobs based in the Memphis area, according to its job board. 
SpaceXAI did not respond to a request for comment. But in August, the company wrote on social media, “We don’t just build in Memphis – we live, work and invest here. We are committed to being good neighbors and responsible partners.”
A letter from MZX Tech LLC, a subsidiary of SpaceXAI, that residents living near SpaceXAI’s power plant reported receiving. The letter offers to buy their homes “in exchange for, among other things, a release of all claims” related to a class action lawsuit against the company.
If you’ve been impacted by the SpaceXAI buyouts, Mississippi Today is interested in hearing your story. You can email Julie Lee at jlee@mississippitoday.org.
Mayor says purchase offers are good corporate citizenship
In response to media coverage of the buyout, Southaven Mayor Musselwhite addressed the news directly his recent blog post and at a Board of Aldermen meeting on Oct. 6.
“This buyout is not to say, ‘Well, scrap that. We can’t stop the noise.’ No, that’s still number one.” Musselwhite said at the meeting. He said that SpaceXAI has accelerated its plans to convert the louder, temporary turbines to permanent ones that are “much more quiet.” The buyout is instead a “parallel approach” to “eliminate negative impact or perception of negative impact” and “has been part of a comprehensive plan for many months,” he wrote in his blog post. 
“I told them that this should be part of your goodwill to the community, part of your being a good corporate citizen,” he said at the meeting. “Whether it is or it isn’t, if they view it as a negative, give them an option to sell.”
Musselwhite claimed media had needlessly alarmed people and stirred up controversy by sharing what he called misinformation that the company was forcing people out of their homes.
“Nobody is being forced to be bought out,” Musselwhite said, calling coverage “slanted” and “false.”
“It’s totally voluntary,” he said. 
As for renters, Musselwhite said that on any given day renters are at risk of being asked to move. “That’s nothing new. It has nothing to do with any development in Southaven.”
What about renters?
Danielle Dillard, 37, a renter who lives less than a mile from the power plant, disagreed. “If this wasn’t happening, my landlord wouldn’t have said a word. And even if he did, he definitely wouldn’t have given me 60 days’ notice,” she said. “And it wouldn’t be happening to multiple people because multiple homeowners don’t just decide to sell houses at the same time.”
Danielle Dillard, 37, shown with her children, rents a house in Southaven less than a mile from SpaceXAI’s power plant. Dillard was told she had 60 days to move out after her landlord took a buyout. (Credit: Courtesy of Danielle Dillard.)
In late September, Dillard learned that her landlord took the buyout offer. He told her she had 60 days to move out, she said. She had just signed to extend her lease a month before. 
Dillard had seen news of the buyout—“I sent it to my friend, and I was like, this is crazy”—but didn’t think it would apply to her. 
Dillard’s landlord offered to move her into a different home, she said, but it was 25 minutes away and wasn’t comparable to her current home. Dillard has four kids, three of whom are school-aged and live with her.
Neither her landlord nor SpaceXAI has offered to cover her moving expenses, Dillard added. She said she emailed SpaceXAI asking if there was anything they were offering renters, but never heard back.
Dillard still has not found another place to live. 
One-third to two-thirds of the Southaven and Horn Lake neighborhoods in the class action area are occupied by renters, according to 2020-2024 census estimates. In Mississippi at large, about a quarter of households are occupied by renters versus about a third nationwide.





Under Mississippi law, neither landlords nor tenants are allowed to end an active, fixed-term lease early, unless the contract has an early termination clause or parties voluntarily agree to end the lease early, according to lawyers Mississippi Today spoke with.
Tenants “can’t just automatically be kicked out at the landlord’s whim, or because the landlord found some other more lucrative offer,” said Sam Buchanan Jr., executive director of the Mississippi Center for Legal Services Corporation. Tenants have the right to see their lease through, unless the landlord has a reason to evict them based on a “material breach” of the contract. 
Dillard’s lease did not contain a termination clause, but her landlord sent her an “agreement to vacate property” that she said she didn’t know she had any option but to sign. 
“It was never optional,” she said. 
Buchanan Jr. recommends that before renters sign an agreement they may not fully understand, that they first seek out an expert for an independent opinion.
Robert Wiygul, the attorney representing plaintiffs in the lawsuit against SpaceXAI, urged people considering an offer to weigh their options carefully. 
“For every individual, they have to look at whether a buyout is going to actually make them whole for what they’ve lost,” he said. 
Jen Jenkins of The New York Times contributed research.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Cotton, Arkansas Republicans announce $1M get-out-the-vote effort for midterm election
text:
U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton shakes hands with supporters at Republican Party headquarters in downtown Little Rock on Tuesday, March 3, 2026 after being declared the winner of his party’s primary. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and Arkansas Republicans announced a $1 million effort to get out the vote ahead of the November election as Democrats are making an effort to unseat top GOP leaders.
The two-term Republican lawmaker announced his campaign is funding the effort in partnership with the state GOP. Cotton announced his campaign and the Cotton Majority PAC have raised more than $2 million.
“The Cotton campaign is thrilled with this record fundraising quarter, which will finance a massive get-out-the-vote campaign to help Arkansas Republicans up and down the ballot,” James Arnold, Cotton campaign spokesman, said in a news release. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
President Donald Trump’s low approval numbers have raised Democrats’ hopes for an upset in the heavily Republican state. Democrats have not won a statewide or U.S. House race in Arkansas since 2010.
State Republican Party Chairman Joseph Wood called the announcement the “most extensive turnout operation in the Arkansas Republican Party’s history.”
A poll from Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College in August showed a tight race between Cotton and Democratic challenger Hallie Shoffner. National political forecasters, however, have rated the Senate race as solidly Republican.
Cotton and conservative groups have heavily outspent Shoffner in the race, which also includes Libertarian Jeff Wadlin. America One, a conservative super PAC, has spent more than $4.4 million this year on the race, according to Federal Election Commission filings. 
Cotton’s absence takes center stage at debate between Arkansas’ US Senate candidates

Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, was first elected in 2014 and won reelection in 2020 against Libertarian challenger Ricky Dale Harrington Jr., who won a third of the vote. 
Democrats have also been focusing heavily on central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, where Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill is being challenged by Democratic nominee Chris Jones.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee recently added the race to its “Red to Blue” program targeting Republican-held districts the party believes it can flip. The Cook Political Report recently moved the race in Democrats’ favor, classifying it from “solid” to “likely” Republican.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Proposition 133 could punish trafficking victims and harm reproductive health access
text:
Volunteers organize, check and count ballots at the Denver Clerk and Recorder's office during the Colorado primary election on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)With ballots now arriving in mailboxes, Coloradans will decide on the deceptive Proposition 133, a measure titled “Penalties for Human Trafficking of a Minor.” Despite its title, the measure could punish victims for crimes they were forced or coerced to commit, make survivors less likely to seek help, and create new concerns about access to legally protected healthcare.
Organizations like the Colorado Coalition Against Sexual Assault that work directly with survivors of sexual violence and human trafficking are raising the alarm about the dangers of Proposition 133. No Colorado organization that works on sexual violence or human trafficking was consulted on this measure, and almost all of them oppose it, including the Laboratory to Combat Human Trafficking, Colorado Organization for Victim Assistance, Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network, Rocky Mountain Victim Law Center and the Rose Andom Center.
Colorado already treats child sex trafficking as a serious felony, punishable by eight to 48 years in prison per offense, followed by mandatory parole. Proposition 133 would replace those penalties with life imprisonment without parole, undermining judicial discretion, and expand the conduct covered by the law, potentially harming legally protected health care in our state.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Proposition 133’s deception promises to protect children and deter heinous crimes. A deeper examination reveals a dangerous reality: The measure seeks to add new, vague language to Colorado’s human trafficking statute, criminalizing anyone who “knowingly trades anything of monetary value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor.” The measure fails to define this language further, creating an ambiguity that is not an accident — it is a political strategy.
Proposition 133 was placed on the ballot by Protect Kids Colorado, an anti-abortion rights network also advancing Propositions 134 and 135 to target transgender students and gender-affirming care. The campaign’s own materials promote all three measures as part of a shared agenda. It’s also supported by the Heritage Foundation, the authors of Project 2025.
Leaders of this network have publicly characterized state protections for interstate healthcare travel as facilitating the “trafficking” of children. Because Colorado has become a critical access point for reproductive and gender-affirming healthcare in the region, this poorly defined trafficking language creates a direct risk.
Anti-abortion activists could attempt to weaponize this provision against anyone helping a minor obtain legal abortion care — including medical providers, parents, or support organizations providing transportation, lodging, or funding. A law does not need to result in a successful court conviction to cause profound harm. The mere threat of prosecution creates an ambiguity that causes families and providers to hesitate, severely reducing healthcare access through sheer intimidation.
While the measure creates a backdoor tool for political activists, its explicit mandates inflict immediate trauma on human trafficking survivors. Proposition 133 falsely claims to protect children, but in reality, it gives traffickers another tool to exploit them.
Traffickers don’t simply target, groom, and exploit victims sexually. They also often force them to recruit other victims, post advertisements, or participate in criminal activity. This is known as forced criminality.
Legally, it is nearly impossible for a victim without resources and legal support to defend themselves by proving they didn’t do something. Proving victimization in a court of law requires extensive documentation that traumatized victims rarely possess since traffickers control every aspect of their lives, including access to technology. Instead of holding institutions and abusers accountable, this extreme measure treats victims the same as their exploiters.
For example, under Proposition 133, an 18-year-old who has been exploited since childhood and coerced into facilitating encounters would face the exact same harsh punishment as their perpetrator. A 14-year-old victim forced by their abuser to recruit another minor could face a mandatory sentence designed for their trafficker before they even turn 18.
Proposition 133 offers the illusion of protection while exposing survivors to new risks, eliminating judicial discretion, and raising serious concerns about the misuse of criminal law against legally protected healthcare.
A ballot measure should be judged by what it actually does, not what its sponsors promise. Proposition 133 fails that test.

Box 147, Lyndonville, VT 05851; or Indivisible St. Johnsbury.

David Robert Martin, born David Robert Zisowitz on October 5, 1944, died of congestive heart failure in Lyndonville, Vermont on September 12th, 2026. Raised in Queens, New York, David was a born tinkerer. As a child he was given the freedom to explore all of the tools in his father Sam’s workshop, wiring a doorbell through his family’s house from the kitchen to the workshop so his mother Mae could tell Sam when to come down for dinner. For most of his childhood he thought he was going to be a scientist, but life took him in unexpected directions. 
In his early 20’s David found himself at loose ends. On New Year’s Eve 1966 his girlfriend suggested they go to Englewood, NJ to a lively party at the Patch house. There, David met Penny Patch and Chris Williams, and by the end of the night he was invited to come to Northeastern Vermont to build an A-frame with them and friends on East Haven Mountain. Penny and David got to know each other first as friends, a friendship that remained at the core of their 56 year love affair. 
In 1974, David, Penny and Seth left Toad Hall for Russo’s shed, then Janet’s barn in Lost Nation, and a brief stint in Upstate New York where their daughter Lizzie was born. Then they four moved back to Lost Nation where, in one season, David built a 3-story house for them. 
Lost Nation was a vital community of backwoods hippies, decidedly free of back-to-the-land romanticism.  There, amidst the challenge of daily survival, he developed lifelong friends, an artistic community, and a deep connection with the northern forest.  
Everything David came across might be made into pieces of art, be they broken down tractor parts, old sewing machines, copper telephone wire, or discarded wood. Beloved summer vacations on the remote coast of Maine saw him carting back rocks, shells, driftwood, and lobster trap bits. He saw spirits in these objects, using them to construct his many creatures. 
For over 20 years, David was also a teacher in St. Johnsbury that every kid longed for: empathetic, full of humor, and with a love of exploration. His joy was infectious to little children. While co-teaching with Kitty (Beattie) Toll at the Middle School he was ushered into publishing his first children’s stories by longtime friends Joe Spieler and Amy Ehrlich. This gave him the opportunity to take early retirement and focus on writing. Between the 1990s and 2026 he published approximately 35 books for young readers, many written due to his work with Reading Recovery. He often performed for local kids, telling his stories, juggling, and singing with his guitar. His work with CLIF (Children’s Literacy Foundation) brought him to schools all over the northeast. David served on the Cobleigh Library board for ten years, playing an important role in getting the first bookmobile going. 
David loved life so very much. He found joy in all of the people and places surrounding him and was brought to tears more often from smiles than from sadness. He cherished his relationship with each of his grandchildren. He played sports, games, and make-believe with them. He wrote them stories and sang them songs. He carried them as babies, danced with them, and took them outside whenever they visited. He built them any number of objects. 
His love of sports was present lifelong, beginning with games of stoopball and stickball in Jamaica, Queens, and a strong memory of listening to Bill Mazeroski’s famous home run to beat the Yankees in 1960 while sitting in a barber chair.  His own sandlot career was highlighted by his time playing softball for the Burke Hollow Athletic Club.  He took up different sports over the years including cycling, cross country skiing, tennis, and running, causing him to need multiple joint replacements.
David and his soulmate Penny Patch, lived a rich and joyful life together, full of music, dancing, listening and laughing. They supported each other through each change in their lives, constantly adding to their circle of friends. His life was full. A vocal member of the local Indivisible group, he was always fighting injustice. David, with his many old friends and new, worked to protect our Democracy. He was a founding member of The Whistle Pig Riot Brass Band, singing and playing music in support of those who need protection.
He always showed up for a friend or neighbor or family member in need of a move, or a bed, or a song. You could always tell a David Martin job – solid, thoughtful, and fastened tightly, often with a whimsical flourish.
David’s family wishes to thank all of his medical care teams: Dartmouth Hitchcock Advanced Heart Failure, Corner Medical, Caledonia Home Health and Hospice.
David is survived by his wife Penny Patch; children Seth Williams and Lizzie Martin; brother Ben Martin; grandchildren Luna and Jude Williams, Winslow and Graham Porter. There is so much more family he loved as friends and friends he loved as family. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  David Martin.
