name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Ballard sues to force Indiana Election Commission to act on complaints
text:
Independent/Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard responds to a question during the Indiana Secretary of State Debate hosted by the Indiana Debate Commission, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at WFYI Public Television Studios in Indianapolis. Ballard participated in the debate with Republican Max Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh and Libertarian Lauri Shillings. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard filed suit Thursday to force the Indiana Election Commission to rule on four pending campaign finance complaints against his opponents before the Nov. 3 election.
Two complaints are against Republican Max Engling and two are against Democrat Beau Bayh.
“The Commission has consistently met in September, but not this year,” Ballard said in an accompanying letter to commission chairwoman Beth Boyce. “Early voting began October 6. The complaint asks only that the Commission convene and decide, as the statute assigns it to do, whether there is substantial reason to believe a violation occurred — before the election, while it still matters to voters.”
Ballard said if Boyce calls a meeting before Oct. 26, “the court’s involvement becomes unnecessary.”
One of Ballard’s proposals in the race has been to make the Indiana Election Commission nonpartisan. It currently has two Democratic members and two Republicans, with no tiebreaker.
“I am a candidate in this race, bound by the same laws these complaints invoke. I am not asking the Commission to rule for or against anyone. I am asking it to meet.”
The lawsuit says the commission has sent the campaigns letters requesting responses but has no meetings scheduled. The complaints were filed on July 24, Sept. 15 and Sept. 17.
“Plaintiff does not contend that the Commission must find a violation, or must investigate every complaint regardless of merit,” the lawsuit said. “He contends that a complaint properly filed with the Commission presents a question the statute assigns to the Commission to decide — whether there is substantial reason to believe a violation occurred — and that the Commission may not simply decline to decide it while the election to which the complaint relates is conducted.”
The four complaints allege the following:

That Engling accepted an illegal $60,000 donation from Hoosier Leadership for America, Inc., exceeding the $5,000 cap. Engling later returned the entire donation.
That Engling’s campaign finance filings didn’t identify who paid for a hospitality suite the night before the GOP state convention.
That Bayh attended several hosted events where he was a featured speaker but reported no in-kind donations from the host groups.
That Bayh attended several events sponsored by county Democratic parties but reported no in-kind donations from those groups.

This story will be updated.

name: Nevada Current
title: Ford seeks to upset Lombardo, become Nevada’s first Black governor
text:
Aaron Ford, Joe Lombardo. (Photos: Dana Gentry, April Corbin Girnus/Nevada Current)Among the stack of lawsuits Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford has filed in his two terms is one of particular significance to the state and its bread-and-butter gambling industry – the effort to keep prediction markets out of states with regulated sports betting.
But on Wednesday, Ford briefly eschewed his adversarial posture and in a fundraising pitch, touted prediction platform Kalshi’s take on his chances against Gov. Joe Lombardo, whom he hopes to defeat in November. 
Screengrab of Kalshi line on the Nevada governor’s race.
The market has the race in a virtual tie, with momentum for Ford on the upswing. It’s likely not a place Ford or Lombardo thought the challenger would ever be. 
Lombardo, a two-term Clark County sheriff turned governor, declined to be interviewed for this story.
Ford is Nevada’s first Black attorney general and would be its first Black governor, a longshot in a state long known as the Mississippi of the West. 
He grew up poor in Dallas, Texas, and was arrested four times on misdemeanor charges as a young man – once for public intoxication, once for stealing a tire (he paid $100 restitution and the charge was dismissed) and twice for failing to appear in court. He was never convicted.  He was also investigated but not charged for being in his ex-girlfriend’s home without permission.
Ford’s encounters with the law have been a prominent focus of lawman Lombardo’s campaign.
Lombardo has recently criticized Ford for placing the clemency bid of a Nevada inmate who was convicted of voluntary manslaughter in the shooting death of a pregnant woman and her baby, on the state Pardons Board agenda, portraying the move as Ford coddling a criminal. 
“Aaron Ford cares more about criminals than victims,” Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson says in a new campaign ad for Lombardo, adding the two have “worked together to put violent criminals behind bars.”   
It’s a tough pill to swallow for Ford, given Lombardo’s embrace of President Donald Trump, a 34-time felon who pardoned insurrectionists. 
“It’s a Willie Horton redo,” Ford said, referring to the notorious campaign ad George H.W. Bush used to paint Michael Dukakis as soft on crime. “I’m criticized for putting an item on the agenda.” 
Ford says it’s “the height of hypocrisy for Gov. Lombardo to campaign with a person who is convicted of 34 felonies and who has been adjudicated a rapist and is in the Epstein files 5,300 times, and also beg for his endorsement.”
The AG added he’s not taking advice from Lombardo on issuing pardons, “especially when the  guy he’s endorsed pardoned January 6 assailants who assaulted law enforcement officers. It’s the height of hypocrisy. It’s also politics. He’s losing this race, and he’s desperate.”
“We stood up for crime victims and cracked down on domestic abusers,” Wolfson says in Lombardo’s campaign ad. 
In August the Current reported that in 2020, Wolfson and Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, who was undersheriff to Lombardo at the time, ignored a recommendation as board members of Hope for Prisoners to terminate the founder, Jon Ponder, a three-time convicted bank robber and domestic abuser. An investigation substantiated allegations that Ponder engaged in sexual misconduct with program participants and employees. 
Jon Ponder and Gov. Joe Lombardo after Lombardo was given the “Champion of HOPE” Award at at luncheon July 7, 2025. (Photo posted on social media by Hope for Prisoners)
Lombardo, the sheriff at the time, has refused for years to address the allegations or say if Metro conducted an investigation of HFP, which is one of Metro’s community partners.
Ponder was arrested and charged in August with sexual assault and other crimes. He has since been indicted on two dozen counts, including four counts of sexual assault, dating back to 2015 and extending through this year.  
Ford said it’s “crucial for more information to come to light, not just about what Ponder was doing, but about who knew about it and failed to stop it. There are allegations that Wolfson and Lombardo may have known about it, but that’s for an investigation to uncover.”
He called Ponder’s alleged crimes “appalling, and I’m praying for the victims to receive the full measure of justice.”
He declined to comment further, given the pending case. 
A Democrat has not defeated an incumbent Republican governor in Nevada since 1982, when then- Attorney General Richard Bryan mounted an anti-high energy cost crusade against Nevada Power, precursor to NV Energy, and defeated Gov. Robert List. 
Ford is hoping for the same result. He’s challenging a ruling from the Lombardo-appointed Public Service Commission that is slated to change the way electricity bills are calculated beginning in January, and he’s lashing out at out Lombardo’s support for data centers, their potential for increasing energy costs, and their insatiable thirst for water in a state that is enduring drought. 
Last month, Lombardo, who has declared a data center gold rush, doubled down on his commitment to the industry, but issued an executive order curtailing some tax incentives.
The order came days after Axios reported that a Trump pollster warned GOP candidates that “unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position” and they should avoid using the phrase “build more data centers.”
Lombardo’s campaign maintains the plan was not the result of that warning. 
“We’re going to pause those tax incentives,” says Ford, who, as a state senator, was one of the original cosponsors of 2015 legislation approving tax breaks for data centers. “That’s not to say that they will never resume. We have to be contemplative, deliberative, have conversations, and weigh the pros and cons. It’s not dogma over changing dynamics.” 
Nevada, according to experts, has one of the most regressive tax systems in the nation and is in need of an overhaul that lessens the sales tax burden on low-income residents. 
Lombardo has pledged not to raise taxes. 
Ford agrees. Nevadans, he says, “can’t afford gas, groceries or rent. People are struggling right now, and I’ve been in a circumstance where I couldn’t think beyond my circumstance, let alone to improve it.” 
Lombardo has never lost an election. In 2022 he defeated incumbent Steve Sisolak by one and a half percentage points, buoyed to victory by a bandwagon of pandemic-weary Nevadans.
Two years later, Lombardo tied his fortune to the second coming of Trump — a decision that has proved fraught with peril for the governor. His tenure has been marred by Trump’s agenda, which even the governor acknowledged benefits billionaires.
With the help of the Republican Governors Association, the Better Nevada PAC, and the Nevada Way PAC, Lombardo’s campaign amassed more than $16 million in the second quarter alone. 
Ford, as of July, had about $2.6 million on hand. Third quarter contribution and expense reports are due on Wednesday.
It’s unknown if voters, many of whom are put off by Trump’s vanity agenda and penchant for self-enrichment while in office, will view Lombardo’s multi-million dollar haul as a show of strength or of fealty.
Ford says the primary reason he ran for governor is because he knew Lombardo “wouldn’t stand up to Donald Trump. I knew he’d kowtow, capitulate and kiss up to Trump at every turn.” 
The second reason he ran is the “racist dog whistles” on the campaign trail. 
“The first message I got after I won the primary — a direct message on Facebook said, and I’m quoting, ‘Great, a f–king n—-r AG,’” Ford said. 
In his campaign for attorney general, Ford’s opponent, Sigal Chattah, suggested he should be “hanging from a f–king crane.” 
Members of Lombardo’s campaign staff, critics contend, have engaged in what some call ‘race-baiting,’ which is the practice of deliberately engendering fear or hatred based on race. 
“Nevadans deserve to know their top cop wants a promotion with an arrest record involving public intoxication, stealing tires, and failing to appear in court, in addition to trespassing a woman’s home without her permission,” Lombardo campaign spokeswoman Halee Dobbins said in a statement. 
“It’s no surprise that Joe Lombardo, who has disdain for our community in so many regards, is stooping to this level,” Ford said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: ‘Godly leadership’: Lisa Demuth’s Pentecostal faith is a driving force behind her politics
text:
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers at her campaign booth for Minnesota governor during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Lisa Demuth asked God whether she should run for Minnesota House minority leader.
On the morning Minnesota House Republicans were electing a new leader after a bitterly disappointing 2022 election, Demuth read the Bible verse 1 Peter 4:10: “God has given each of you a gift from his great variety of spiritual gifts. Use them well to serve one another.”
Demuth then had breakfast that morning with other elected officials, and one of them recommended she read a Bible verse ahead of the caucus election: the very same 1 Peter 4:10.
Demuth took this as a sign from God.
“I looked at the colleagues and said, ‘I’m running for leadership,’” Demuth recalled during a talk at a statewide Assemblies of God conference.
Demuth rarely talks about her faith publicly, but the Reformer’s review of several recorded talks she’s given at religious conferences in recent years indicate she served as her church’s worship leader for 16 years and she has frequently turned to God and her well-worn Bible to guide her legislative decisions.
Her faith is just one of many details of her life that remain largely hidden from public view, even as she asks Minnesotans to make her the state’s chief executive in command of a $66 billion, two-year budget and 50,000 public employees.
Demuth faces faces stiff political headwinds — she can’t escape her party’s association with deeply unpopular President Donald Trump and his relentless attacks on Minnesota. She’s been forced to balance an effort to separate herself from Trump on issues like trade-killing tariffs and the war in Iran, while remaining true to Republican voters’ — and perhaps her own — devotion to him.
But her greatest obstacle may be her quiet refusal, at least thus far, to share the kind of story that many Minnesota voters long for — about who she is and what’s propelled her to seek the governor’s office.
Demuth’s campaign for governor did not respond to the Reformer’s interview requests or answer an emailed list of questions.
Demuth’s unwillingness to evoke her history in her governor campaign contrasts with her Democratic-Farmer-Labor opponent, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who has written two memoirs, basked in publicity for over two decades and endured a childhood that was occasionally memorialized by her father, a Star Tribune columnist.
Lisa Demuth takes the stage at the Minnesota Republican Convention in Duluth, Saturday May 30, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)
Central Minnesota roots
Demuth, 59, was born in Paynesville, Minnesota, where her mother also grew up. Her father was an immigrant from Panama who served as a church pastor there. He died in June. Demuth’s father became a U.S. citizen in 1976 and was a Metro Transit bus driver for 30 years, according to his obituary.
Growing up biracial in mostly white central Minnesota in the early 1970s grew difficult for Demuth, she told a local radio host in 2023. Her family was supportive of her, and she never felt different until 1st grade, when a 4th grade boy in her school called her the n-word almost every day, she said.
“That’s what precipitated our move back to the metro area,” Demuth said “We just needed a bit more diversity.”
In an interview with the Star Tribune earlier this month, Demuth said her mother received welfare benefits for a short time. Asked how this lived experience shaped her view of the use of social safety net programs in Minnesota, Demuth said her story can motivate others to get off of welfare.
“I’m happy to talk about it if that can be an encouragement to someone else, that, you know what, you can have hard times and you can overcome,” Demuth said.
She graduated from Kennedy High School in Bloomington and went right into the workforce.
“I knew I wanted to work,” said Demuth, adding in the 2023 interview that “school was not my favorite.”
If elected, she would be Minnesota’s first governor without a four-year college degree since Jesse Ventura.
Demuth married in 1985 when she was 18. She moved to her husband’s hometown of Joliet, Illinois, about 40 miles southwest of Chicago. While there, Demuth worked in title insurance at the First American Title Company.
Two years later, Demuth filed for divorce, alleging that he was “guilty of extreme and repeated mental cruelty towards (Demuth) in that he assumes a morose and hostile attitude towards (her),” according to the 1987 divorce filing.
Demuth also alleged her husband refused to discuss the issues in the marriage and said he “acquired the affections and attentions of another woman.”
Demuth, whose maiden name is Pittman, has never publicly discussed that period of her life or her divorce. She would only tell the local radio host that she moved to Illinois because of a “life change.”
She met her current husband, Nick Demuth, through a local Jaycees group, a nonprofit civic and leadership organization for young adults. Demuth moved to Cold Spring — where Nick Demuth lived — and eventually became a stay-at-home mom to four children.
During her time as worship leader at her Assemblies of God church, Demuth was responsible for the church’s music program. She said this is where she learned how to work with a team.
Assemblies of God
Assemblies of God is the world’s largest Pentecostal denomination. Pentecostalism traces its origins back to the Azusa Street Revival of 1906-1909 in Los Angeles. The central figure of the revival is William J. Seymour, the son of emancipated southern slaves, who moved to L.A. and began preaching that the only way Christians can claim to be baptized by the Holy Spirit was to speak in tongues.
The idea was novel and controversial, and his preachings drew large crowds and media coverage.
“Men and women would shout, weep, dance, fall into trances, speak and sing in tongues and interpret into English,” the Assemblies of God Heritage Magazine wrote in 2005. “There was no robed choir, no hymnals, no order of service, but there was an abundance of spiritual enthusiasm.”
The revival drew even more attention because although it originated in a small Black church, the movement was welcoming of Latino, Chinese and white Americans — an unusual occurrence at the time when racial integration was uncommon, said Darrin Rodgers, director of the Flower Pentecostal Heritage Center in Missouri, in an interview. The Assemblies of God denomination was founded in 1914 and now has about 3 million adherents in the U.S., with another 89 million members worldwide, Rodgers said.
Assemblies of God is decentralized, meaning local churches largely decide their worship style. But Assemblies of God churches follow 16 fundamental truths, which declare the Bible as “the infallible, authoritative rule of faith and conduct,” and that the “baptism of believers in the Holy Spirit is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues.”
Lisa Demuth plays with Aylah, 1, the youngest of her 7 grandchildren, at the Minnesota Republican Convention in Duluth, Saturday May 30, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)
Getting into politics
Demuth’s family was not political growing up. She says she didn’t follow politics or even current events until 2007, when she read in the local newspaper that several open seats on the ROCORI School Board had no candidates.
“I couldn’t believe that somebody hadn’t stepped up. So I tore that paper out of the newspaper and left it on my husband’s place for dinner,” Demuth recalled on the 2023 radio show. “I said, ‘Hey, you need to run for the school board. This is really important.’ And he said, ‘I would never run for the school board. You do it.’”
In her telling, Demuth at first said no. When her husband asked why not, she couldn’t come up with an answer. So she made a few calls and ran as a write-in candidate for the school board, since the filing deadline had passed. She went on to serve on the school board for 11 years.
She was elected to the Minnesota House in 2018 after then-Rep. Jeff Howe, who was her representative at the time, called and asked her to run for the House since he was going to run for the Minnesota Senate.
After Howe called her, Demuth read Romans 16:23 about the disciple Paul thanking a man who worked in public works, she said in an Assemblies of God conference. Demuth took that as a sign that God wanted her to serve her community through the Legislature.
She showed the verse to her husband, Nick: “He said, ‘Well there’s your answer. You’re apparently supposed to do this,’” Demuth recalled him saying.
Demuth, the legislator
Demuth was a relatively unknown state representative from 2018 to 2022, authoring education legislation, several child protection laws and a bill to require record-keeping in the Child Care Assistance Program — one of the programs from which fraudsters have bilked money in recent years. She became the first woman and person of color to lead Minnesota House Republicans in 2022. 
Colleagues describe her as a thoughtful legislator who listens well and delegates. Demuth is not known as a policy wonk, instead bolstering other members’ ideas and letting them become the public face of an issue.
Rep. Dawn Gillman, R-Dassel, said she’s watched Demuth grow in confidence since assuming her leadership role, never shying away from hard conversations while maintaining her professionalism. Gillman described Demuth as a “Godly woman” and a “bulldog.”
“People are longing for truth and transparency, and I believe religion — or God — teaches us to show up in a way that is truthful, that is loving and kind, and that’s what (Demuth) did consistently,” Gillman said in an interview.
Demuth reflected on her time as minority leader during the 2023 Assembly of God conference, and she emphasized the importance of public service.
“The reason I believe that involvement in politics does matter is I believe that God in this day, in 2023, is stirring the hearts of believers to figure out how we can lead people through this time, and I know that there is a desperate need for godly leadership,” Demuth said.
House Republicans elected Rep. Lisa Demuth, R-Cold Spring, speaker of the House Jan. 14, 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Demuth talked about the Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta passing a law codifying abortion rights, calling it “terrible,” but she was happy that her caucus didn’t “take the bait” and engage in long-winded, unruly debates when lawmakers considered the bill, which could then hurt Republicans’ reelection prospects.
In 2023, Demuth was the chief author of a bill banning third-trimester abortions and requiring the licensing of abortion clinics.
In the conference, she discussed the bill that made Minnesota a trans refuge state and protects people from legal repercussions for traveling to Minnesota for gender-affirming healthcare.
Demuth said that bill was “devastating” because, she alleged, it would harm children.
“You know who seeks to harm our children when it comes right down to it? It is Satan. That is his goal: is to harm our children,” Demuth said, then quoting a verse from Luke.
“Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come. It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea, than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin,” said Demuth, reading the verse aloud.
“And if we are pushing trans rights on children, that is what we are accountable and responsible for,” Demuth added.
At a 2025 Assemblies of God conference, Demuth told the audience that her Bible reads like a journal because she underlines and writes notes whenever a verse resonates with her.
“As I look out over culture, over our world, over politics, the things that are changing and moving so often, I think that it is now even more important that the people of faith, that we must follow God and trust that He is going to be the one that will place us exactly where He wants us to be,” Demuth said.
Demuth’s apparent theologically inspired politics are contested by other religious leaders. While many evangelicals support President Donald Trump and his policies, he’s faced substantial resistance from Catholics and Protestant denominations.
For example, Christian faith leaders have been outspoken critics of attempts to denigrate immigrants in America, like when Minnesota Republicans sought to take undocumented people off of state-subsidized health insurance. Demuth was instrumental in the effort to strip away this benefit.
“I’m here because of my love for the immigrant brothers and sisters and (because) we need to continue to reach out and walk with them and help them,” said Bishop Kevin Kenney, an auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of St. Paul-Minneapolis at a Capitol press conference last year.
During Operation Metro Surge last winter, over 60 faith leaders openly called for changes to the immigration enforcement operation and for the protection of the “most vulnerable among us.”
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, R-Cold Spring, announced she is running in the August GOP primary election during a press conference in front of the Minnesota Capitol. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)
A rising political star
Demuth became Minnesota’s first Black House speaker in 2025 after she played a key role in Republicans toppling the DFL trifecta in 2024 by flipping three key swing districts. This brought the House to a 67-67 tie between Republicans and Democrats. After the 2024 election, a judge ruled one of the newly elected Democrats ineligible for office because he didn’t live in the district.
Republicans sought to use the temporary 67-66 advantage to win full control of the chamber, and Demuth threatened to refuse to seat a Democratic member who won a contested race.
To prevent this usurpation, Democrats boycotted the session for three weeks and then won a Supreme Court case. The two sides came to an agreement wherein the Democratic lawmaker was seated, and Demuth could claim the speakership for the whole two-year session.
She used her caucus’ power of exactly half of the House to force the DFL to roll back MinnesotaCare, the state-subsidized health insurance for undocumented immigrant adults. House Republicans also blocked numerous tax increases proposed by Democrats.
Given the sweeping progressive agenda of the 2023-24 legislative session under the DFL trifecta, Republicans were pleased that Demuth had managed to put the brakes on. They began urging her to run for governor.
She launched her race in late 2025, just as Minnesota politics was about to be hit with a tornado: National scrutiny of fraud in Minnesota’s safety-net programs was followed in quick succession by the arrival of thousands of federal officers, Walz’s departure from the race, the deaths of two American citizens at the hands of immigration agents and the launch of Klobuchar’s candidacy.
Campaign for governor
Demuth’s gubernatorial campaign has at times overcome a stiff current. She’s the first Republican since 1994 to win the primary despite losing the party endorsement. She prevailed in the primary over the better-known and Trump-endorsed Mike Lindell.
She has another asset during this campaign: money.
Demuth is the first Minnesota Republican in a statewide race in recent memory to receive the substantial backing of outside money. Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, who own a Wisconsin shipping empire and spend tens of millions of dollars on Republican campaigns, have already spent at least $14 million on an independent expenditure committee known as Restore Sanity.
A key organizer and fundraiser for the Super PAC is Tommy Merickel, the right-hand man of Star Tribune owner and Minnesota’s richest man, Glen Taylor.
She also has the unpaid help of a well-known GOP lobbyist and consultant Ben Golnik, a registered lobbyist who represents Big Pharma, the tobacco industry, a horse racing track and other clients.
Restore Sanity PAC has spent millions familiarizing Minnesotans with the until-now largely unknown Demuth and torching Klobuchar as a continuation of the policies of Walz.
Klobuchar’s campaign for governor has raised over $12.5 million since launching her campaign at the end of January and has spent $9 million, mostly on consulting and ads.
People sing and sway during the second morning service at River of Life, an Assembly of God church in Cold Spring, Minnesota Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
 River of Life

Demuth attends River of Life church in Cold Spring, a town of about 4,200 located 80 miles northwest of Minneapolis. The church was founded in 1993, and it recently completed an addition that includes a coffee shop, a stone fireplace and two levels of seating in addition to the spacious, 750-seat sanctuary.
On a recent Sunday, hundreds of parishioners attended the 10:30 a.m. service, walking into the spacious entry way with vaulted ceilings and wood beams. Demuth wasn’t in attendance. Next to the fireplace stood several volunteers encouraging people to vote in the Nov. 3 election, directing them to use a QR code that took them to a voter registration site.
Pastor Kirby St. John reiterated the message during the service: “Get out and vote. It’s our right to do that.” St. John declined to speak to the Reformer. 
That day the church invited guest speaker Martha Tennison, an 84-year-old evangelist who preached about forgiveness in dark times. She talked about her husband serving as the lead pastor at a Kentucky church in 1988 when a drunken driver crashed into a bus full of the church’s youth, killing 27 of the 67 people on board. Her son was aboard the bus and survived.
Many in the sanctuary were emotional, gasping and shaking their heads whenever Tennison shared a harrowing detail from the story, like when a boy attempted to save his brother who was burning alive in the wreckage but couldn’t or that one of the boys — prior to the bus ride — said he didn’t believe Jesus would return one day. He died in the crash.
After telling the story, Tennison encouraged all the attendees to come to the center of the room, hug and pray for one another. Parishioners grasped each other and wept.
“Church, we have no promise of tomorrow,” Tennison said.

name: California
title: School test scores up, but just a little, as progress slows in K-12 classes
text:
In summary
K-12 student test scores rose slightly last year, while enrollment numbers dropped.


California’s K-12 student test scores improved slightly in almost all categories last year, but progress slowed following a post-pandemic surge, according to state data released today.
“It’s slow but steady improvement,” said Linda Darling-Hammond, president of the State Board of Education. “It suggests we’re continuing to come out of the pandemic, and there’s still a lot of work to do.”
The percentage of students proficient in math jumped just over 1 percentage point – to 38.5% – and the number of students proficient in English language arts rose half a percentage point, 49.3%. Science scores increased 3.3% percentage points, to 36%. 
For the first time, the state released its enrollment, test score and California School Dashboard data together, making it easier for school districts to communicate with parents and the public and for policymakers to analyze gains and declines across broad categories. 
Despite the gains, though, scores were lower for some student groups, including white and Asian students, compared to 2019, before the Covid-19 pandemic forced most schools to close for in-person learning. 
Enrollment decline continues
Statewide enrollment, which has been falling for a decade, plunged to 5.7 million – a loss of 74,000 students from last year. Because the state funds schools based on the number of students who show up every day, the declining numbers will mean less revenue for many districts.
Amid the enrollment numbers, a few changes stood out. The number of students with disabilities jumped 25% over the past decade, to 850,822. And the number of English learners dropped 30% over that same time period due to a decline in immigration among other factors. 
Chronic absenteeism, which hit 30% just after the pandemic, dropped to 18% last year, a decline of more than 1 percentage point from the previous year. Prior to the pandemic, only about 12% of students were chronically absent, or gone from school at least 10% of the school year.
Test scores and just about every other academic indicator among California’s K-12 students collapsed during the Covid-19 pandemic, but rebounded significantly the first few years back to in-person learning. That progress appears to have settled, at least for now.
Darling-Hammond predicted English language arts scores will rise in the next few years, as a handful of sweeping state reforms go into effect: transitional kindergarten, dyslexia screening, literacy coaches for elementary teachers and a phonics-based reading curriculum, among others.
More grads, better prepared
Highlands charter school, the embattled Sacramento school for adults seeking high school diplomas, loomed large over the data. Last year, Highlands and its sister school, California Innovative Career Academy, had such high enrollments – 17,513 combined – and such low graduation rates – less than 2% – that they skewed graduation data for the entire state.
California Department of Education staff presented numbers with and without Highlands. Including Highlands, the state graduation rate was 87.9%, a slight increase from the previous year. Excluding Highlands, the rate was almost 2 percentage points higher – 89.7%, the highest rate in decades in California.
Highlands, under new leadership, winnowed its enrollment this year and is seeking to improve its outcomes after the State Auditor blasted it last year for alleged mismanagement.
The state’s high school graduates also showed improvements in college and career preparation. According to the dashboard, the percentage of students who completed a career pathway or the A-G classes required for admission to the state’s public universities climbed 2.2 percentage points, to 55.2%.

name: California
title: Friends who’ve fallen out feud during gritty, final LA mayoral debate
text:
Voters have been good to Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass. For the past two decades, she has won elections to the California Assembly, to Congress and to the mayoralty she now holds. She has never lost an election.
But her grip on her current job is tenuous. 
That was evident Tuesday night during a close, sometimes gritty debate with her rival, City Councilmember Nithya Raman. Bass was measured and unflappable but also biting. Polls show her trailing in her bid for re-election, but she made it clear Tuesday she has no intention of leaving quietly.
Separated from each other by a panel of questioners, the two candidates were warned at the outset to refrain from personal attacks. Both ignored that admonishment.
In the final televised debate of a close campaign, Bass was particularly assertive, several times accusing Raman of lying and misrepresenting the mayor’s record, as well as suggesting Raman would plunge the Los Angeles Police Department into “disarray” on the eve of the Olympic games and maintaining that the mayor’s office was forced to handle constituent services in Raman’s district when residents became frustrated with the council member and her staff. 
Raman shook her head in annoyance as the mayor’s accusations piled up.
Portraying Raman as naïve and slippery, Bass concluded: “Now is not the time to turn the city over to Nithya Raman.”
Those are tough words, especially for an official the mayor once favored. Raman and Bass have supported each other in prior campaigns, and Raman backed Bass in this one before jumping in herself. 
That has left Bass feeling betrayed, and some of that bitterness Raman reflected back during the debate. Raman charged the mayor with paying “lip service” to reducing red tape that bottles up housing construction and with overseeing a listless, lost administration. The Bass mayoral record, Raman insisted, was “four years of decline, of mismanagement, of excuses.”
There are no enemies in politics quite like friends who have fallen out, and that’s what this race has become. 
Substantively, their debate covered familiar ground: Raman accused the mayor of being “MIA” during and after the fire that destroyed thousands of homes in the Pacific Palisades and more broadly MIA as a manager of city services. Under Bass, the councilwoman argued, city departments have become dysfunctional, paralyzed when faced with complaints and unable to make changes that might bring down the cost of new housing.
In fact, although the two agree on the crying need for new housing construction, they managed to fight over that, too, with Bass touting the construction of 10,000 new affordable housing units during her tenure and Raman pointing out that overall apartment construction in the city is falling. Both are right.
As the two make the final turn toward Election Day, their similarities are as striking as their differences. 
Both champion affordability. Raman focuses on housing, by far the biggest expense for most L.A. residents, and Bass agrees, while also suggesting that the city should expand childcare services to provide some relief there. 
Both also support tax credits and services to the film industry as part of their effort to keep jobs in Los Angeles. But they differ over who cares more about that issue or who has done more about it so far.
And both compete for the title of being the leader who most dislikes President Donald Trump. 
Federal agents descend on MacArthur Park in Los Angeles on July 7, 2025. Photo by J.W. Hendricks for CalMatters
Bass highlights her visible role in standing against the ICE raids last summer. Raman argues the city needs to be even more forceful in refusing cooperation with federal authorities bent on turning the city into a showcase for the militarized rousting of undocumented migrants or anyone who looks like them. 
Trump and ICE are among the most hated figures and institutions in Los Angeles, so it’s hardly a surprise the top contenders for mayor would find common ground there.
In the debate, however, were glimmers of ways these candidates are different, substantively and temperamentally. 
Bass places greater confidence in police and in the current leadership of the LAPD. Raman starts from a place of greater skepticism about the department and Police Chief Jim McDonnell, who was appointed in 2024 and has a five-year term.
But Raman seems torn by the issue. During the debate, she said she would seek to remove McDonnell, but she shuffled over the questions of how and when she would do that. 
McDonnell, Raman said, had “lost the trust” of the city’s immigrant community by defending ICE against protesters and, she maintained, by sharing data with the federal government. 
Yet, when pressed on what action she would take, Raman — as she has before — equivocated, saying the chief’s removal required the agreement of the Police Commission and the involvement of City Council. 
That’s sort of true, but mostly not. The mayor appoints the Police Commission, so the mayor has no real impediment to firing a chief. And yes, an ousted chief could appeal to the council for reinstatement, but that’s never happened. It’s also hard to imagine a chief being fired, then winning reinstatement and going back to work for the mayor who fired him.
When NBC’s Conan Nolan pushed harder, asking whether Raman would get rid of McDonnell before the 2028 Olympics, she retreated further. “It will depend on these other factors.”
Bass was more sure-footed while talking about public safety, but she has her own struggles — starting with any proposal she now brings to the table. Improved childcare in city parks? Better data and transparency on police shootings? Expanded use of cameras to monitor traffic violations? 
All have merit, but why is a mayor who’s been in office for nearly four years suddenly pulling out new ideas for the future? 
It’s an exposed flank for an incumbent who both wants credit for progress and at the same time resists being accused of letting the city down. And it feeds Raman’s argument that Bass looks for excuses and only produces policies in response to the challenge she’s facing to win re-election.
Ballots are in the hands of voters, and polling in the race is frustratingly ambiguous. 
All the credible surveys suggest many voters are tired of Bass.But the mayor does better among older and most established residents, who happen to be the most likely to vote. She also has the support of most unions, and they are famous for turning out their members.
Bass’s challenge is unlike any she’s faced before. She needs to stage a comeback, to persuade voters that Raman is too extreme, too untested, “not ready for prime time,” as the mayor offered on Tuesday. 
But that’s a hard sell against the reality of Raman, who comes off as educated and careful, more nerdy than dangerous. Her eyes light up when she talks about data.
This week’s debate did not seal the deal for either candidate, but it offered a glimpse of what lies ahead: Tough disagreements between former friends who have become wary rivals, a choice of personalities and ideas, with the future of the city very much at stake.

name: California
title: Should California taxpayers chip in to fund political campaigns? Prop. 4 lets you decide
text:
In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.


In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money. 
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics. 
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued. Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races. 
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing. 
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide. 
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion, according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid. 
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office. 
“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign. 
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg, a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising. 
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising. In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, said last year on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”
Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth. 
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities. 
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program, which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.” 
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates. 
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition. 
Researchers point to the difficulty of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said. 
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

name: California
title: Inside Gavin Newsom’s taxpayer-funded team that never stops posting
text:
In summary
Gavin Newsom is preparing to leave office as one of the Democrats’ most prolific communicators. He’s transformed the governor’s press shop into a content-generating media operation.


Last month, while signing a bill to provide a tax credit for struggling local news outlets, Gov. Gavin Newsom reminisced about the days when reporters thronged around him when he was mayor of San Francisco — right around the time tech platforms swept into town and permanently disrupted the media industry. 
“There’s not a lot of you,” he said to the assembled Capitol press corps, with whom he said he had enjoyed an “awkwardly healthy” relationship over two terms as governor. “There’s not enough.”
Left unsaid was how much he’s taken advantage of the industry’s transformation in his own political rise. 
The past two decades of media contraction have allowed government officials in every town to talk less to traditional news outlets. Instead they talk directly with voters and constituents on their own platforms. 
That allows them to dodge tough questions and independent media coverage where they’re “not controlling the narrative,” said Menlo College political science professor Melissa Michelson. Politicians have sought this for decades, Michelson said, but only in recent years — when over half of U.S. adults get news through social media — have they seen it as more important than traditional media.
Newsom has exploited the trend with unique energy, and is now preparing to leave office after eight years as governor as one of the Democratic Party’s most prolific communicators. 
The potential 2028 presidential contender has been a Twitch stream guest, a Substacker and a podcast bro. He never stops posting. He picks fights, on X especially, with right-wing media, an industry he is both critical of and fascinated with. 
Some of his communications are done on campaign accounts, but much of the jousting comes from his taxpayer-funded governor’s office communications staff, who have played a major role in casting Newsom as the leading Democrat pushing back against the Trump administration in areas well beyond the boundaries of state policy. 
During his second term, the post-pandemic, post-recall election Newsom has grown his press and communications team into an around-the-clock, content-creating media operation, even as he rarely takes questions from the media in Sacramento and his agencies shun interview requests. He nearly doubled his communications staff since the pandemic, even adding a full-time photographer, making $212,000 a year, whose LinkedIn profile describes his job as focusing on the office’s “visual messaging, public perception and narrative development.”
Doing it all
Newsom has 24 taxpayer-funded employees on his official communications team who are  collectively paid at least $2.6 million a year, including staff who scout locations for events and camera operators who livestream them. That’s up from 12 in January 2020, a year into his first term. 
The only other governor with a comparable communications staff was Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, an international media sensation whose office credentialed 400 reporters in his first term and held weekly press briefings, said former spokesperson Margita Thompson. Today during one of Newsom’s rare Sacramento press conferences, between 10 and 20 reporters regularly attend. The office stopped issuing its own press credentials years ago.
Gov. Gavin Newsom addresses the media while releasing his revised 2025-26 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2025. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Newsom’s office payroll includes several spokespeople, writers and researchers who explain state policy. It also has a four-person team of Tiktok- and pop-culture-savvy Gen Z digital staff who churn out a drumbeat of social media content on official accounts. 
The size of Newsom’s communications operation reflects his “do it all” style of governing.
He won office with a long list of lofty priorities from expanding healthcare and universal preschool to fighting climate change, and created new state departments for issues previously left to other governments, like a homelessness agency and a state surgeon general’s office. He has expanded the size of the state government to an all-time high.
Newsom treats publicity as part of that public policy strategy, said Erin Mellon, a director of communications for Newsom from 2020 to 2024. 
“If you’re not actually telling people about what you’re doing, then doing it doesn’t make a difference because they can’t take advantage of that” policy or program, Mellon said of Newsom’s thinking. “When someone had a problem with the state of California, even if it was a local issue, it reflected on him, on his role and his job as governor. He would insert himself.”
Her team had the inside joke “Everything is a comms problem” printed on mugs, Mellon said.
It’s a stark contrast from the lean, budget-cutting days of his Democratic predecessor Gov. Jerry Brown, who presided over the state’s recovery from the Great Recession. Brown, gruff and unpolished, ran a famously small press shop and often eschewed weighing in on issues. The office had eight staffers at its height — including interns — and borrowed photographers from other agencies.
“He was like, ‘I don’t have to have an opinion on everything that happens and I don’t want to,’” recalled a former spokesperson, Elizabeth Ashford. “I don’t think he was that interested in new media. Newsom is.”
Bob Salladay, a former journalist and Newsom’s senior adviser for communications, said most of his staff’s time is still spent responding to traditional media inquiries and explaining state policy to national reporters and a hollowed-out state press corps. The growth of the communications staff, he said, is “responding to the volume of work that the governor is doing.” 
“You cannot overstate the difference between this governor and past governors in terms of what they’re involved in doing,” said Salladay, who makes $242,000 a year. “That generates a huge amount of inquiries into the office.”
The team also takes significant liberties beyond policy communications.
The digital staff’s output includes fan edits of Newsom set to Nicki Minaj and an X post of a pixelated image implying something tawdry about Trump’s chin flesh that got 30 million views. Newsom’s official accounts used a slew of memes and mockery last summer as they promoted both California’s resistance to Trump’s National Guard deployment in LA and Newsom’s anti-GOP gerrymandering initiative. His press office’s X account gained half a million followers last August alone, Newsom’s office said. 
There is also more overt overlap with the political side of Newsom’s operation. Izzy Gardon, the spokesperson behind much of Newsom’s more combative public image, has accompanied the governor on his political travels to red and swing states ahead of a likely 2028 presidential run. This summer, Salladay said Gardon moved into a part-time role with the office, now making half his $185,000-a-year state salary and doing political work for Newsom during his unpaid time. Other staff take personal time to volunteer for Newsom’s campaign, he said.
‘If we were Trumpian’
The relentless drumbeat of snarky posts from the governor’s official press office and Newsom’s foray into podcasting and other media known to be frequented by young men online have gotten him plenty of attention ahead of his anticipated decision. 
Celinda Lake, a Democratic strategist and pollster who has worked with other politicians considering 2028 runs, said Newsom stands out in the party for his unique comfort communicating on platforms that tend to be dominated by younger, insurgent progressives or conservatives. She called his digital operation “very effective” and “one of the best out there.”

Image via Gov. Gavin Newsom’s X account

“He has mastered being able to set the agenda and being able to get other people to respond to him,” she said. 
The strategies are not without criticism. Rob Stutzman, a Republican strategist who was once a spokesperson for Schwarzenegger, said Newsom has blurred ethical lines by using his office “to basically run a political account” in ways that mirror how the president treats his political opponents and the press.
Newsom’s office tells conservative writers they are not “real journalists.” The social media posts range from routine policy announcements to AI-generated memes boosting Newsom and sexualized taunts at Republicans. The account frequently engages in fights with the right, scorning them for their alignment with Trump, who is widely unpopular in California. In a recent flurry of posts, Newsom’s office called for California’s GOP congressmembers to condemn Trump’s declaration to “let (Iran) take out Los Angeles or San Diego.” When Republican-turned-independent Kevin Kiley responded that he criticized the comment, Newsom’s office wrote it was insufficient and replied, “You’re a weak little noodle.”
“Trump has changed the norms,” Stutzman said. “And Newsom, his operation basically adopted the Trump playbook.”
But for every alleged offense Newsom’s team points to a bigger one from the president, like his recent taxpayer-paid pro-Trump political ads. Newsom himself has attested to satirizing Trump’s rhetoric to to call attention to the president’s many disputes with California, like his withholding of federal aid in the wake of the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires.



Graphics shown during Gov. Gavin Newsom’s presentation of his revised 2026-27 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
“These last two years with Trump are different than any other moment in modern American history, so you have to deal with it in different ways,” Salladay said. He added later, “If we were Trumpian, we would have cut off the California Post by now. But we work with them every day,” referring to the Rupert Murdoch-owned offshoot of the New York Post that started publishing in January.
Countering the right
Two full-time staff members are assigned to “rapid response,” which involves fact-checking claims and misinformation about Newsom, his policies and his governance of California on four social media platforms, as well as pushing traditional media outlets to change things they deem incorrect.
The office boasts of requesting 453 corrections since 2024. Salladay said the rapid response operation grew out of narratives on right-wing media and social media about the Los Angeles fires, crime and the state’s business climate.
He denied that the effort amounts to using state funds to burnish Newsom’s political image. Misinformed notions of California, he said, could result in policy decisions that affect constituents, like the federal government withholding aid. 
“When people tell you San Francisco is a hellhole or California is driving out businesses, that’s the propaganda we have to counter,” he said. “That is a state operation. We are defending the state and we have a right to do that, because the narrative can be incredibly damaging.”
In 2025, the Public Policy Institute of California found the number of business headquarters leaving California annually increased between 2011 and 2021, but found their share of all business activity was small, as was the overall effect on jobs. 
But even as Newsom’s subordinates argue with and dismiss right-wing media outlets online, he maintains a fascination and friendliness with many of them. In 2025, in the wake of bruising election losses for the Democratic Party and young men tilting rightward hard, he shocked fellow liberals by launching a podcast, “This is Gavin Newsom,” featuring a string of conservative activists and media figures as guests. 
Pitched as a way to have friendly debate with his ideological opposites and to learn from right-wing communications successes, he launched the show with Charlie Kirk. The conservative activist put Newsom in a defensive position with a string of questionable claims about California schools, asserting their libraries contained pornography and that they were teaching “against white people.” On the show, Newsom also agreed with Kirk that it’s unfair for trans girls to play girls’ sports, and laughingly helped Kirk analyze how a 2024 campaign ad about Vice President Kamala Harris’ support for gender reassignment surgery for prisoners was bad optics for Democrats.
Gov. Gavin Newsom during a press conference in Sacramento on Aug. 21, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
It got Newsom a lot of attention and turned some heads on the right. Thompson, the former Schwarzenegger spokesperson, said she was alerted to the podcast a few months later by a conservative friend, who was surprised that in an episode with the conservative podcast host Shawn Ryan, Newsom talked of hunting and accepted a gift gun. (Earlier this year Newsom, in a financial disclosure, revealed he never took possession of the gun and his office would not say whether it’s in California.)
“I liked that he’s going places where he is unexpected,” Thompson said, though she was turned off by the “bro talk.”
Since then, the podcast, which is produced by iHeartRadio and for which Newsom is not paid, has taken a more expected liberal turn. Newsom has used it to promote Democrats, push last year for his successful gerrymandering initiative Prop. 50 and to discuss AI policy. But every few episodes, he returns to figures from the right, most recently Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy. 
Newsom spokesperson Anthony York said Newsom picks most of the guests from his personal contact list, calling the show “a reflection of who he is and his interests.”
Newsom said last month that he hopes to keep the podcast going after he leaves office in January. 
Lake, the national strategist, said Newsom will have no trouble maintaining public attention.
“The race starts Jan. 1, 2027,” she said. “He’s set up the infrastructure to keep it going.”

name: California
title: California’s ballot propositions fuel its longstanding tax-and-spending war
text:
California voters will pass judgment on 14 statewide ballot measures this year and all but two of them relate, in some manner, to financing public services.
Collectively they represent the latest version of what fiscal policy buffs call “ballot box budgeting” — persuading voters to prioritize or limit how funds are raised and spent rather than leaving those issues to elected officials.
This election’s most contentious measure, Proposition 40, typifies the underlying philosophical conflict that has raged ever since voters passed Proposition 13, the state’s iconic limit on property taxes, nearly a half-century ago.
Prop. 13 embodied the belief that high taxes undercut Californians’ ability to enhance the welfare of their own families. Prop. 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California’s billionaires, reflects the counter-contention that expansive public services better serve the well-being of all Californians.
Before Prop. 13 made the June 1978 ballot, the initiative process almost never dealt with tax and spending issues, a yearly summary from the secretary of state’s office indicates. Implicitly, voters were content to leave such money matters to elected state and local officials.
Prop. 13 reduced property taxes that had been the fundamental revenue source for local governments and school systems. It also made raising taxes of all kinds more difficult.
Prop. 13’s jolting impact also encouraged the use of ballot measures process not only to affect public finance issues but policies of all kinds. Succeeding elections saw an explosion of proposals dealing with such issues as punishment for crimes, immigration, affirmative action and same-sex marriage.
The two measures on this year’s ballot that don’t deal with taxes and spending typify that trend. Proposition 39 would require voters to show identifying documents and Proposition 45 would reduce use of the California Environmental Quality Act to block projects.
However, taxes and spending continued to dominate post-Prop. 13 elections, beginning in 1979 with a special election called by then-Gov. Jerry Brown to pass Proposition 4, a cap on state spending known as the “Gann Limit” for Paul Gann, a co-author of Prop. 13 with fellow tax gadfly Howard Jarvis.
Brown had strenuously opposed Prop. 13 but after its passage declared himself to be a “born-again tax cutter” and joined with Gann to persuade voters to approve the spending limit. It continues to be a factor in fashioning an annual state budget.
A much bigger budget factor is Proposition 98, a 1988 measure sponsored by the California Teachers Association to cushion Prop. 13’s impact on school finances. Prop. 98 contains a complex formula to guarantee a certain level of state education aid that works out to about 40% of general fund revenues.
The teachers’ union is opposing this year’s Prop. 40, the wealth tax on billionaires, which designates all but a small percentage of its revenue for healthcare, excluding Prop. 98. The conflict illustrates how ballot box budgeting pits interest groups against each other, even those on the same side in their underlying battle with anti-tax forces.
Speaking of which, anti-tax groups such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association have continued to press their cause, staving off efforts to change Prop. 13 and promoting tax limits.
This year, they are pushing Proposition 43, which would increase the vote requirement to approve some local taxes. And they’re opposing the California Teachers Association’s Proposition 3, which would make permanent a temporary tax on high-income Californians that was initially passed in 2012 at Brown’s behest during his second stint as governor.
During the 17th century, a conflict known as the 30 Years War raged in Europe. Today California’s war over taxes and spending is already 48 years old and, as this year’s array of ballot measures indicates, it shows no sign of ending.

name: Nevada Current
title: How spending $2.75 million on a campaign for a part-time job pencils out. If it does.
text:
Sandra Jauregui and Stavros Anthony are vying for the most irrelevant elected office in this or any other state. (Photos: Richard Bednarski/Nevada Current)The Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association (yes, there is such a thing) earlier this month crowed that it is spending 1.75 million American dollars in Nevada to help defeat Republican Nevada Lieutenant Gov. Stavros Anthony. 
“It is the largest investment in a Nevada Lt. Governor’s race in state history,” announced the DLGA, presumably through its Tallest Building in Kansas Division.
And in perhaps the finest typographical error of the 2026 campaign cycle, the DLGA’s spending in Nevada includes a $1.5 million “steaming” ad buy, the organization added.
Seriously? People are running for lieutenant governor? Again?

Sandra Jauregui, the Nevada Democrat who is not only running against Anthony but is also every bit as irrelevant to all this as are Anthony and the office he occupies, announced separately this week that her campaign and political action committee combined have raised more than $1 million. 
That’s “the most ever raised by a Democratic candidate for Nevada Lieutenant Governor,” Jauregui’s campaign said in a release.
Oh let’s hope so. 
Because while a million bucks ain’t what it used to be, it’s still an obscene amount of money to spend on a campaign for a part-time job with no inbox. It boggles the mind and rattles the soul to think a Democrat might have spent that much money on a prior campaign for lieutenant governor. Now, of course, it almost makes a little more sense, Trump having made life, the universe and everything so much less affordable, including presumably campaigns. (Except for Gov. Joe Lombardo’s; his campaign’s affordability problem isn’t paying for things, but explaining what he might do about them. But I digress.)
So why would so much money — $2.75 million if you combine DLGA, Jauregui’s campaign and her PAC — be spent in the hope that Juaregui is Nevada’s lieutenant governor and Anthony isn’t?
No reason at all. 
It isn’t about them. 
The Democrat in the race could be a potted plant and the Republican could be a pet rock. The DLGA would still be making its “largest investment … in state history,” and the Democratic candidate and its PAC would still be amassing “the most ever raised” by a Democrat in a lieutenant governor race. 
The money isn’t driven by the faults or virtues of the candidates. Nor is it about their positions on issues over which the Nevada lieutenant governor wields power and influence. Because there are no such issues.
Obligatory caveat: Yes, admittedly, if a serving Nevada governor were accidentally sucked into a micro black hole inadvertently created by a particle accelerator, the lieutenant governor becomes the governor. (And then whoever that person was — whatever their party —  would be tasked with earnestly explaining that now, clearly, is no time to raise the gaming tax so let’s all just tighten our belts. But again I digress).
And the freak particle accelerator contingency isn’t the only means by which an un-governoring could occur. 
For instance, a sitting governor could also be elected to the U.S. Senate.
The 2026 race for lieutenant governor is all about 2028 (if it’s about anything at all)

Democrats, history’s greatest hand wringers, worry that Lombardo will win reelection, and then immediately be the obvious Republican to run against Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto in 2028.
In case you hadn’t noticed, Cortez Masto has made no secret that she’s running for reelection.
Ah, but if the lieutenant governor is a Democrat, it would be politically impossible for Lombardo to run for U.S. Senate. 
And it’s not like there’s some other Nevada Republican on the scene whose skillset and gravitas just screams senatorial material.
For some of you all this will be reminiscent of 2014, when the Nevada Democratic Party and Harry Reid (proprietor) knew that then-popular Republican Gov. Brian Sandoval would easily win reelection, and feared he would then run against Reid in 2016. So Reid and the Democrats tried to make people pretend a race for lieutenant governor mattered. (It all turned out be preposterous, by the way).
Which brings us to the line in Jauregui’s release about a million being “the most ever raised by a Democratic candidate for Nevada Lieutenant Governor.”
In that 2014 race, the campaign of a Republican named Mark Hutchison (now a fixture in the PAC that handles the heavy lifting for Lombardo’s reelection campaign) spent $2.5 million in a successful campaign for lieutenant governor. Just in case Sandoval wanted to run against Reid, presumably. 
Sandoval didn’t.
Lombardo himself probably has no idea if he’ll be running for Senate in 2028.
But Democrats are thinking better safe than sorry.
There simply is no other explanation for the DLGA and Jauregui (and her PAC) amassing a combined $2.75 million to win a job the chief responsibility of which, by far, is breaking a tie in a state Senate that has an odd number of senators.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington AG will not pursue youth online protection legislation in wake of Meta settlement
text:
Washington's attorney general will not push a sweeping bill to limit social media for youths following a court settlement with Meta. (Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Washington Attorney General Nick Brown will not ask state lawmakers again to pass a sweeping bill to limit social media for youths, saying a recent court settlement with a social media giant is sufficient.
“The Meta settlement’s provisions go beyond the policies we were hoping to implement via legislation,” the Democrat’s office said in a statement to the Standard. “We have shown that a good path for us is through litigation and through investigation rather than trying to convince the Legislature.”
For two years in a row, a bill that aimed to rein in addictive social media feeds for under-18 users died in the state legislature because opponents said it infringed on free speech and data privacy. Last month, Brown, a Democrat in his first term, who had requested that state legislation, secured some of those provisions by going through the courts.
In the largest settlement with a major tech firm in history, Brown settled with Meta for $237 million as part of a $17.1 billion nationwide settlement. Brown’s office says it no longer plans to reintroduce the Protecting Children Online Act in light of the settlement.
Highlights of the agreement include a two-hour cap on minors’ daily use of Instagram and Facebook that will last for five years. That cap will lower to one hour per day and be extended to 10 years if other social media platforms also settle.
Push notifications will be paused during school hours and access to the app will be blocked altogether from midnight to 6 a.m. Instagram and Facebook will offer the option for minors to switch off their algorithmic feed in settings, and cosmetic filters and counts of likes will be removed.
All of these provisions hinge on age verification, which met with significant backlash in the state legislature because of concerns that it would infringe on the privacy of users. Those concerns were not resolved by the settlement.
Meta is required to adopt an age-assurance method by August 2027, and to remove under-13 users and implement the requisite design changes for under-18 users by the following year. Meta has two options: It can employ third-party age verification tools, or it can develop its own in-house age assurance method.
In the European Union, which recently adopted social media restrictions for minors, social media platforms will deploy facial-scanning technology to verify that users are over 13. Other possible methods include uploading government documents and inputting personally-identifiable information like addresses to be checked across existing databases.

“At this point in time, there’s not really a way to do age estimation or age verification without requiring some kind of data,” said Anni-Michele Jean-Pierre, the senior policy director at Children’s Alliance, a statewide advocacy group that worked closely with Brown’s office to push the Protecting Children Online Act.
Some advocates say Meta shouldn’t need to use third-party tools because they believe the company knows the ages of its users already, just based on their online behavior.
“This doesn’t mean that Meta is collecting any more data than they already have about people,” Jean-Pierre said. “What we’ve heard from folks in the industry is that they can already tell, with the existing technology that they have, how old someone is with a relative level of certainty within the first few minutes that they’re online based on their activity.”
The other sticking point for the Protecting Children Online Act was its possible unconstitutionality. The bill proposed to require social media platforms to default to a non-algorithmic feed for minors, so that users would not be fed content that they had not explicitly requested to see.
Tech industry groups testified that this violated free speech because the government was telling a corporation and its users what it could and could not say.
LGTBQ+ advocacy groups echoed this criticism late in the 2026 session, saying that a non-algorithmic feed would diminish the ability of LGBTQ+ youth to find affinity spaces online.
Under the settlement, Meta will offer users the option of switching their feeds from algorithmic to chronological, but the platforms will not default to a chronological feed as the bill had proposed.
That may assuage free speech concerns, but advocates of children’s online safety counter that kids won’t choose to turn off their algorithmic feed, which had been the crux of the bill.
“Making it an opt out rather than explicit consent, [Meta] knows the power of default,” said Danica Noble, current state house candidate and former Federal Trade Commission lawyer who worked on the FTC’s antitrust case against Meta. “This doesn’t fundamentally change the harmful product, it just gives some tools that I think are not necessarily going to be used to turn off that same potentially addictive product.”
By going through the courts rather than the legislature, Brown’s office has dodged questions of constitutionality. But that approach has left other questions unanswered that a bill may have put to rest: What happens in a decade, when the settlement’s requirements expire? Will other social media companies sign onto similar provisions? Who is the third party that will audit Meta’s compliance?
“I don’t think we should have a regime where we know you have a dangerous product and we’re just going to let you run with it, and if somebody ends up harmed, we’ll catch it on the back end,” Noble said. “I think that there are some pretty clear places that we do need legislation because right now, with the profit imperatives of corporations, their duty is to make money and value for the shareholders.”
Rep. Lisa Callan, D-Issaquah, sponsored the Protecting Children Online Act. She says she plans to pursue further legislation if other social media companies such as TikTok, SnapChat, and YouTube do not sign onto the settlement in the coming months.
“It’s excruciating to me that we couldn’t move it forward, but we have this great opportunity now with the settlement to understand the effectiveness,” Callan said. “If we can’t get it consistent across all the platforms, then we need to move forward with the legislation, some way, somehow.”
