name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ’s county clerks nudge mail voters to drop boxes for 2026 election
text:
County clerks are deemphasizing mail returns and stressing the security of drop boxes even after courts blocked President Trump's mail voting rules. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Some New Jersey county clerks are nudging voters to cast mail-in ballots by depositing them in ballot drop boxes and deemphasizing postal returns in a shift driven by the Trump administration’s stalled efforts to limit mail voting through U.S. Postal Service rules.
No clerks have urged voters not to mail their ballots back in, and none have voiced worries about fraud at the Postal Service, but the shift in their messaging has accelerated a rise in drop box returns, particularly among Democratic voters.
“I think I’ve been pushing the boxes for a while, not just this year,” said Somerset County Clerk Steve Peter, a Democrat. “It’s just this year I’ve actually been putting out more press releases and public notices because with all the stuff going on in D.C., people are more confused and concerned.”
This comes about a month after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked a Postal Service rule that would have required states to upload protected voter data to federal systems and blocked the mailing of ballots in states that refused to share the information, which the federal government has no legal right to obtain.
The rule, which was opposed by voting rights groups and secretaries of state belonging to both parties, was broadly viewed as the latest Trump bid to limit mail voting. Though he casts mail ballots himself, the president has long claimed that mail voting is rife with fraud while producing no evidence of widespread voter fraud using mail ballots.
Essex County Clerk Chris Durkin, a Democrat, said the Trump administration’s efforts to restrict mail voting had spurred worries among voters in the county that were allayed when the high court rejected the Postal Service rule, at least for this election.
“We’ve only heard concerns about people wanting to make sure their voices are heard,” Durkin said. “The vote-by-mail voters had concerns up until the Supreme Court ruled against the executive order and the USPS rule. They were concerned that they were not going to be able to vote by mail and then relieved when we were able to mail ballots.”
But New Jersey’s county clerks have continued to push drop boxes despite the legal win.
A flyer sent last month by Mercer County urges voters using vote-by-mail ballots to use drop boxes.
In a press release issued more than a week after the court’s decision, Middlesex County called drop boxes “the most secure way to return your mail-in ballot” and listed drop boxes first among the three ways to return a ballot. A similar release issued by the office last year listed postal returns first and did not opine on the security of any return method.
A mailer sent by Mercer County Clerk Paula Sollami Covello outright recommended voters return their ballot to a drop box, while a mailer from Camden County Clerk Pam Lampitt stressed drop box returns so heavily that its only reference to postal returns lay in the term “vote by mail.”
Voters have taken notice. By Wednesday morning, nearly half of the state’s 319,422 returned mail ballots, 48.3%, reached election officials after being deposited in a drop box, a New Jersey Monitor analysis showed. A similar number of voters, 47.2%, mailed their ballots back in.
The share of ballots deposited in a drop box has edged up in recent days, though the delay between a ballot being mailed and reaching election officials likely means postal returns are underreported to a degree.
The rate of drop box returns is up significantly from past years. At roughly the same point in the cycle in 2023, 26.4% of mail votes had been cast by drop box, according to archival data maintained by Rider University’s Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics. At a similar point in 2021, that number was 23.9%.
“We’ve never seen anything even approaching this level before, and it’s been a sudden difference,” said Micah Rasmussen, the Rebovich Institute’s director.
Voters can also hand-deliver their ballots to their county’s board of elections, but the method accounted for fewer than 0.6% of all mail ballots returned as of Wednesday morning. That figure may exclude some ballots hand-delivered by a bearer on another voter’s behalf.
Not all of New Jersey’s clerks have changed their messaging, nor do they all see a need to.
“I am just telling people there’s three ways to return a ballot like I always do because to me, since there’s been no change, I wouldn’t tell people to make a change,” said Monmouth County Clerk Christine Hanlon, who is also the Republican state chair.
There was no evidence of any problems, Hanlon said, and the Postal Service had successfully delivered hundreds of thousands of ballots on clerks’ behalf only weeks earlier.
“Why would you think they wouldn’t come back through the mail?” she said. “To me, it just doesn’t make sense, but that’s my personal opinion.”
Democrats were more likely than Republicans to return mail ballots using drop boxes in each of New Jersey’s 21 counties, but drop box returns among Republican voters were also elevated in most parts of the state.
They peaked in Atlantic County, where 47.7% of GOP mail votes were cast by drop box, though Republican voters in some counties, like Mercer, Union, and Monmouth, continued to use drop boxes at roughly historical levels.
Clerks stressed that drop box returns had other advantages. Ballots cast that way are collected daily and reach election officials faster than ballots returned through the post, and they can cut out postal delivery issues that plagued some counties in years past.
Counties have faced a range of postal issues over the years, from routine problems like misdelivered mail to lengthy delays due to dysfunction at specific post offices, but clerks have avoided hurling accusations of fraud at the agency even as they nudge voters away from the Postal Service.
“It’s a tough high-wire act to do because I don’t want to make false claims against the post office,” Peter said. “I just try to stick with my past experience with them, and the amount of ballots that are returned to my office that should have been delivered just leads me to wonder what’s going on at the sorting facilities, not that I think they’re doing it nefariously.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Democrats aim to break Republicans’ streak of House supermajorities
text:
Dr. Hope Tinker, left, Democratic candidate in the 48th Missouri House District, and state Rep. Tim Taylor, the Republican incumbent, on Oct. 3 look over pies entered in the Brunswick Pecan Festival pecan pie contest before they are auctioned (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Over five consecutive elections from 1974 through 1982, Missouri Democrats elected supermajorities — more than two-thirds of the 163 members — to the Missouri House.
The party drew its strength from rural voters, union households and Black-majority urban districts.
The supermajority ended as rural voters, who had developed a habit of voting Republican in national races, turned from Democrats in local contests. By the mid-1990s Democrats held only 87 seats – five more than a majority — and have been in the minority in Jefferson City since 2003.
Republicans are on a streak of their own, winning a supermajority in seven consecutive elections. But with Democrats needing to gain just three seats to break that streak, Republicans are playing defense in nearly every legislative race attracting significant attention and money.
House Majority Leader Alex Riley of Springfield, slated to become speaker, isn’t sure about extending the streak.
“I expect to be the Republican speaker with a very strong majority,” Riley said. “As far as what that looks like, I don’t know.”
House Minority Leader Ashley Aune of Kansas City said Democrats will win at least 55 seats for the first time since 2010. 
“People ask me all the time how many seats we’re gonna flip, and I always tell them we’re gonna break the supermajority and then some,” Aune said.
The national Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee is targeting 12 districts, including 11 held by Republicans.
The House Republican Campaign Committee is focused on defending 13 seats, including 10 on the Democrats’ list, while targeting a single Democrat for defeat.
Republicans entered the fall campaign with $3 million on hand at the HRCC.
The House Democratic Action Fund has less than one-tenth of those resources.
Overall, Democrats are contesting 158 seats while Republicans have candidates in 134 districts. Republicans start with five seats in unopposed districts while Democrats can count 29.
The Independent rated the remaining districts based on past results and identified 39 districts that are potentially in play. The challenge for Democrats is to break out of their current strongholds. No Democrat has won a predominantly rural district since 2010.
The Independent visited three districts — one in the Kansas City region, one in central Missouri and one in St. Louis County — where the results will test assumptions about where the parties are competitive and where they are not.
 12th District

The 12th District, which sits along the Missouri River in southern Platte County, is the only district Republicans took from Democrats in 2024, prevailing by 179 votes. 
The seat is open because incumbent Republican state Rep. Mike Jones is the GOP nominee in the 34th District state Senate race.
Tracey Steele, a commercial real estate attorney, is the Democratic nominee against Jerry Hickey, owner of an employment placement firm. Both object to the attack ads flooding the district. 
To back Steele, the union-funded Will of the People political action committee is attacking Hickey for accepting a Paycheck Protection Program loan in 2020 and later purchasing a new home.
The loans were eligible for forgiveness if recipients met federal requirements. In a social media post, Hickey said the home was purchased a year after the loan was forgiven.
Tracey Steele, right, watches his online ad, with Matt Smithmier, center, and Jess Toms, left, while campaigning for the 12th District Missouri House seat on Oct. 10 in the Thousand Oaks neighborhood of southern Platte County. Smithmier did the voiceover work on the ad (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
To back Hickey, two recently formed committees funded by the HRCC are attempting to tie Steele to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
“I’m a socialist because AOC and Mamdani are alive, apparently,” Steele said in an interview with The Independent.
In a video posted to social media, Hickey said he wants the outside groups — Republican and Democrat —  to stay out of the race. He didn’t approve the attacks on Steele and he doesn’t think Steele is responsible for the attacks on him, he said.
“I frickin’ can’t stand it,” Hickey said on social media. 
Hickey was not available for an interview for this article. His campaign website offers few specifics about his positions. On education, he says he backs school choice “when needed” and that he would address both economic and healthcare issues by “cutting red tape.”
Steele said education funding is a vital issue for the district. Property taxes for the Park Hill School District are among the highest in the Kansas City metro area and state support provides 22% of the budget.
This year’s state budget underfunds the school foundation formula by $190 million. 
Steele, like many Democrats, opposes Amendment 3, which would reinstate a near-total ban on abortion. He will also vote no on Proposition A, a referendum on the 2025 Republican gerrymandered redistricting plan. He supports Amendment 6, which would limit lawmakers’ power to alter measures enacted through the initiative process.
On a recent Saturday, Steele went door-to-door in the Thousand Oaks neighborhood.
Sonja Mosier told Steele she is upset with Republicans because they have tried so hard to block laws enacted by voters. .
“We don’t want to teach our kids that voting doesn’t matter, and that kind of teaches them that voting doesn’t matter,” Mosier said. 
Voters spoke loudly in August when they rejected, by historic margins, two Republican priorities. Amendment 4 would have made it harder to pass constitutional amendments by initiative and Amendment 5 would have allowed lawmakers to replace the income tax with increased sales tax.
Eric Munch, another voter in the district, sees those defeats differently. He blames poor campaign planning.
“The opposition to those was very motivated,” he said, “so the marketing on the opposition side was 10 times better.” 
Steele, meanwhile, argues voters should judge Republicans on their record in power.
“The Republican Party has had a supermajority in the legislature for 14 years,” Steele said. “If they had any brilliant ideas to fix the problems in the state of Missouri, they would have tried them by now.”
 48th District

The 48th District in central Missouri will test the definition of a safe Republican seat.
Incumbent state Rep. Tim Taylor of Bunceton is running for his fourth and final term. He won re-election in 2024 by a 55% margin.
His Democratic opponent, Dr. Hope Tinker of Fayette, was the treasurer for Taylor’s 2024 challenger. For this year’s race, she’s raised twice as much money as Taylor and had 15 times as much money on hand at the end of August.
“It is a different race in that the Democrats are more energized right now than they have been in a long time,” Taylor said in an interview with The Independent. “There’s no question about that.”
Tinker was a family physician in Howard and Chariton counties for 36 years. She’s better known than many first time candidates — while caring for pregnant women, she delivered many of the people now eligible to vote.
And her last name is symbolic nationally as shorthand for the free speech rights of students. Her older brother and sister were the plaintiffs in the landmark Tinker v. Des Moines decision from 1969, that found students could engage in non-disruptive political speech.
David Fortel and Hope Tinker hold homemade signs during a September 2025 protest in the Missouri Capitol rotunda (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Even with a fundraising advantage, the district’s history makes Tinker a long shot. Of the four counties in the district — Cooper and Howard with portions of Randolph and Chariton — Cooper hasn’t supported a Democrat for president since 1964 while none of the counties have been represented by a Democrat since 2015.
“Desperate times call for desperate measures,” Tinker said. “As an individual with values and a commitment to love my neighbors and do the best things I can do with my life to move our society forward, I felt I could do this.”
Campaigning in the 48th District is not really a question of money. Television time is too expensive, so advertising is mainly in the form of yard signs, direct mail and spending time at community events in the summer and fall.
On a recent weekend it was the Brunswick Pecan Festival, where the big attractions are the auction of contest pies and the Saturday afternoon parade that caps the festival.
Ennis Nieholdt of Brunswick said he will be voting for Taylor as he waited for the parade to start.
“He’s talked to some of the meetings that I’ve been at, and he seems like a real nice guy,” Nieholdt said.
Across the street, Grace Fortner of Keytesville was cooling herself with a Tinker-branded fan. She said she knows people who were patients of Tinker’s. Taylor, she said, seems unable to explain himself despite six years in office.
“He says all these things, and I feel like he doesn’t understand what he’s saying,” Fortner said.
State Rep. Tim Taylor of Bunceton, chairman of the Missouri House Special Interim Committee on Property Tax Reform, listens during testimony at a September 2025 public hearing (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
Taylor won election in 2020 after retiring as a Columbia firefighter.  His highest-profile legislative work came in 2025, when he led an interim committee through a series of hearings on property taxes across the state. The resulting legislation, which included provisions to control increases in home and business property tax bills by requiring separate tax rates on each type of property, stalled as Gov. Mike Kehoe’s call to repeal the state income tax took over legislative attention.
“At 2:30 in the morning, sometimes, I wake up with it on my brain,” Taylor said. “I think about it when I’m on my mower, just mowing the yard. I think about it when I’m doing farm chores. It has been and remains on my mind.”
He’s confident, he said, that Republican leaders will make the legislation a priority in the coming year.
Tinker sees the failure of the property tax bill as a measure of Taylor’s effectiveness. 
“I attribute the chaos and dysfunction and incompetence to the guys in Jeff City, our representatives at the state Capitol,” she said.
The state’s budget outlook is worsening as its surplus dwindles. Taylor opposes diverting money from major construction projects already underway, while Tinker says education should take precedence.
“We should look at all those options, whether that’s feasible or not,” Taylor said. “But I don’t want to cut from these capital projects and not let those that have already started get completed.”
The budget crunch, Tinker said, stems from Republican tax cuts for the wealthy.
 “If we need to take dollars out of the highway budget, do it,” Tinker said.
Taylor has been a reliable Republican vote on the big issues in the Capitol Building, rarely bucking the leadership. He voted in favor of measures that became Amendment 3, Amendment 4 and Amendment 5.
The district, like the rest of the state, overwhelmingly defeated Amendments 4 and 5.
“Even though it was a failure, I’m still proud that we have tried,” Taylor said. “I’m proud of the governor for trying to bring about some change.”
Amendments 4 and 5 were examples of misplaced priorities, Tinker said, and show how poorly the Legislature is working.
“They have failed to work collectively, in a bipartisan manner,” Tinker said. “Too many bills that were not well conceived were presented and corporate lobbyists had too much influence.”
At the Brunswick Pecan Festival, the county Republican Party did not have a booth while the Democratic Party did. 
That is notable, said Chariton County Democratic Chair Tess Jones Clay.
“The change that I’ve seen is the lack of the presence on the Republican side here compared to previous years,” she said. “The signs aren’t up here like they used to be. I don’t know if it’s just that they think they don’t need to be, or if people’s minds are changing a little bit and shifting.”
Nieholdt, the Taylor voter, said this is not a year to punish incumbents.
“It’s a year to come together,” he said. “If not, we’re going to lose our country, I’m afraid.”
 100th District

Over the past two elections, the 100th District in western St. Louis County has been one of Missouri Democrats’ most frustrating near-misses.
Incumbent Republican state Rep. Philip Oehlerking won his first term in 2022 by 181 votes. In a rematch two years later, the Democrat narrowed the gap to 143 votes.
This year’s Democratic challenger is Mary Ann Perkins, a first-time candidate who believes Oehlerking’s voting record is increasingly out of step with his constituents.
She points to the district’s support in 2024 for both Kamala Harris and a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights.
Oehlerking voted with other Republicans to put Amendment 3 on the November ballot to roll back the abortion-rights amendment.
“That’s essentially our district being silenced by a representative who doesn’t know us and doesn’t feel like he needs to vote closely in alignment with what the people here value,” Perkins said in an interview with The Independent.
Oehlerking also supported the 2025 congressional redistricting plan And he voted in favor of the legislation that became Amendments 4 and 5 in August.
Mary Ann Perkins, right, Democratic candidate in the 100th Missouri House District, speaks with Joe and Kay Wiese on Oct. 7 as they volunteer to place yard signs out for her campaign (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
But Oehlerking, who did not respond to telephone calls and texts requesting for an interview, has not always sided with his party’s leadership. He broke with Republicans over legislation providing state taxpayer support for new professional sports stadiums. 
Before winning office, Oehlerking worked at the Missouri Higher Education Loan Authority. His personal legislative agenda has focused heavily on financial matters. 
He won passage in 2025 of a bill to regulate virtual currency ATMs and allow banking customers to designate a “trusted contact” if they are suspected of being victims of suspected financial fraud. This year, Oehlerking sponsored a bill changing the regulation and licensing of paycheck advance and small loan companies.
On a recent Wednesday, Joe and Kay Wiese stopped by her Perkins’ campaign meet-up spot to get a yard sign.
This is the first year they have ever put a campaign sign in their yard, they said.
 “I’ve spread my vote around in the past,” Joe Wiese said. “In more recent years, I’m more and more leaning towards the Democratic ticket, and in the last couple of elections, absolutely straight Democratic because what’s going on with the Republican Party is extremely worrisome.”
Perkins has worked at the Brown School of Social Work at Washington University since June 2025. Prior to that, she spent 12 years as editorial consultant for UN Women, evaluating donor reports to the governments and foundations for major projects in Southeast Asia.
State Rep. Philip Oehlerking tells the House Elementary and Secondary Education Committee in January 2025 about a bill that would give parents of students with disabilities more rights (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
As she talks to voters, Perkins emphasizes the need for the state to pay its fair share of education costs. The foundation formula distribution is $190 million short of being fully funded in the current year and the State Board of Education request for the coming year would, if adopted, make the fund $300 million short.
The 100th District is part of the Parkway School District, where the state only provides 5% of the budget. Relatively modest taxes on the high property values pay the majority of costs.
“I try really hard to make the case that we need to make sure every child has a well-funded public education,” Perkins said. “We can’t just be looking only at our district saying we’re fine, then we don’t care. I think that’s ridiculous.”
Not every doorstep offered Perkins an opportunity to win over a voter.
Pat Compton had pro-Amendment 3 signs on her lawn and Perkins tried to persuade her to oppose it, describing her experience with a procedure to remove retained placental tissue after childbirth. 
Compton was unmoved. She said she would continue voting Republican.
“There is nothing about the Democratic Party that attracts me,” Compton said in an interview with The Independent.
Republicans, meanwhile, are trying to make the race less about Oehlerking’s legislative record and more about Perkins’ political identity.  
A political action committee called Missourians for Justice was organized Sept. 2. On Oct. 1, it received $130,181 from the HRCC A day later, an attack flyer was in voter mailboxes.
It features Perkins, with a mask covering her face, in a photo collage with former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush of Ferguson and Ocasio-Cortez.
“It’s weak sauce,” Perkins said.
 The big unknown

For Democrats, the August results showed that Republican voters will reject GOP-backed policies. Whether they will also reject GOP candidates remains uncertain.
The November ballot will include a referendum on Republican efforts to gerrymander the state’s congressional districts, the GOP plan to repeal abortion rights and an initiative to restrict the Legislature’s ability to alter measures passed by initiative.
Through Tuesday, committees for and against those ballot measures had, collectively, raised nearly $52 million and broadcast advertising has cost the committees more than $10 million, tracking by The Independent shows.
In previous elections, Democrats have been on the same side as voter majorities on ballot issues but haven’t seemed to benefit from that association. 
Then-House Budget Committee Chairman Dirk Deaton of Noel, left, speaks privately with Majority Leader Alex Riley of Springfield, during a May 2025 debate (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).
Voters have not connected Republicans with the unpopular side of ballot measures, Aune said. But this year, she said, Republicans must wear the brand of everything voters rejected in August and two of the three ballot questions. 
“We remind them over and over again that Republicans have been in charge,” Aune said, “and if they’re frustrated, they’re frustrated with Republicans.” 
Riley said he doesn’t think voters will reject Republicans over some unpopular ideas.
“Amendments 4 and 5 were just asking voters if they wanted to do something,” Riley said. “The question is, are they going to punish us for asking them their opinion? We’ll find out.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: For our kids’ sakes, give us innovation — not unnecessary regulation
text:
Pennsylvania and other states are scrambling to regulate AI chatbot technology even as President Donald Trump stymies state-led efforts. (Getty Images)No parent wants to receive the call I got late in the night of Jan. 28, 2025: “Ma’am, you should take your daughter to the emergency room right away.”
The good news? We were already there—because an AI chatbot had recommended the ER two hours earlier while my husband and I waited to hear back from the doctor’s office.
Thankfully, our daughter lost nothing more than her appendix.
And as her parents, we gained not only our happy, healthy daughter back, but also perspective on how modern innovation can make parenthood easier and more enjoyable for any Nebraskan—if government policy doesn’t smother it first.
Since that night last year, the positive potential for families of new technologies and breakthrough developments has only grown.
A few months ago, researchers announced that a daily oral pill can double the median overall survival of metastatic pancreatic cancer patients. Scientists showed that an experimental drug can slow cognitive and functional decline in Alzheimer’s patients by as much as 50 percent.
And how much have you heard about folks suffering from sickle cell disease recently? Probably not a lot, as new treatments can now functionally cure it.
Contrast this with so much of social media, which profits off shattering a parent’s peace of mind by making some one-in-a-million medical tragedy seem far more likely to happen to your child than it really is.
For parents, the steady drumbeat of cancer cured and debilitating conditions alleviated is a perfect excuse to enjoy our kids now rather than worry over endless what-ifs down the road.
Of course, not every improvement needs to have life-or-death consequences. My husband and I homeschool our kids when we aren’t running our own business. That means our days are full of juggling client meetings, co-op classes, work deadlines, and kids’ appointments.
Too often, it’s easy to drown in all those details. But as consumer-facing technology improves, we’re able to spend more of our time and energy teaching our kids or helping our clients while our technological tools take care of agonizing over expense reports and chore charts.
Crucially: These innovations don’t replace me as a mom. They lighten my load and make it easier for me to focus on what’s most important.
Which is why the first danger I see is not technology itself. It’s red tape—heavy-handed rules that lawmakers claim are in our best interest, but which ultimately threaten to strip families like mine of the tools we benefit from.
Earlier this year, legislators in Lincoln considered several bills aimed at regulating AI and other 21st century technologies. But virtually all of them failed to explain why bad actors shouldn’t be held accountable through laws we already have on the books.
We do not need a fresh stack of regulations that pull useful tools out of parents’ hands or threaten small startups with millions of dollars in compliance costs when irresponsible companies or individual criminals can be punished with existing statutes prohibiting discrimination, fraud, and other bad actions.
Tech-specific bills in Lincoln aren’t the only way that bad policies can strip these tools—or potential cures—from families, either.
Washington can do it with something that barely mentions AI at all: Drug pricing.
Most-favored-nation pricing, or MFN, is a perfect example. Tying U.S. government payments for pharmaceuticals to prices paid by European countries sounds like a bargain. But in practice? Importing foreign price controls can force American patients to endure less access now and fewer treatments later.
Studies show that an MFN pricing regime could cut U.S. drug-innovation revenue by nearly half, resulting in a comparable hit to research and development. Over 10 years, that points to roughly 210 fewer new drug approvals and 290 fewer post-approval indications — about 50 fewer cutting-edge treatments each year.
Those are life-improving treatments and life-saving drugs my kids might never see.
Of course, policymakers in both Lincoln and Washington do not have to choose between affordability and progress or safety and innovation.
Instead, they should lean on existing laws to hold bad actors accountable.
And health regulations should encourage new treatments, not price-control shortcuts that trade tomorrow’s cures for today’s polling boost.
American innovation is giving more kids better health prospects and more parents tools to raise them. For the sake of all Nebraskan families, our policies should encourage more of both.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s education board was designed to resist politics. Transparency is essential
text:
The Missouri State Board of Education discusses a proposed change to the state's standardized test during its meeting March 24, 2026 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Most Missourians probably could not name a member of the State Board of Education. Most could not explain why board members serve eight-year terms or why Missouri’s Constitution limits the number of members from the same political party.
That is understandable. The State Board was never intended to be a political institution that attracted significant public attention.
In fact, quite the opposite.
When Missouri’s Constitution vested supervision of public education in an independent State Board of Education, the framers deliberately created a structure designed to provide continuity, stability, and a degree of separation from day-to-day politics. Board members would serve long, staggered terms.
No more than four members could belong to the same political party. The Board, not the Governor, would appoint the Commissioner of Education. The objective was simple: public education should not rise and fall with every election cycle. Whether one agrees with that model or not, it has been Missouri’s constitutional commitment for generations.
Which is why recent developments deserve careful scrutiny.
Over the past two years, Gov. Mike Kehoe has gained the opportunity to appoint an extraordinary number of members to the State Board (seven of the board’s eight voting members). At the same time, Commissioner Karla Eslinger has departed her position, creating the need for a commissioner search and a reassessment of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education’s strategic direction.
None of this is inherently improper.
Governors have appointment authority. Commissioners resign. State boards periodically adopt new strategic plans.
The question is not whether the law has been followed.
The question is whether the constitutional purpose behind the law is being subverted.
That question became more pressing when the State Board approved arrangements to fund both the commissioner search and the development of a new strategic plan through private philanthropic contributions rather than public appropriations.
The identities of those donors are being hidden from the public. In fact, the donors are unknown to the public, to the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, and even to at least one organization engaged to help carry out the work. Board leaders have emphasized that donors will have no role in selecting the next Commissioner or influencing board decisions.
Written agreements reportedly prohibit such influence. The State Board President has stated that there can be no quid pro quo. Unfortunately, no one will ever know if a quid pro quo has occurred because the donors are unknown.
Missourians should not be asked to accept on faith that anonymous funding of a Commissioner search and statewide strategic planning process poses no concerns. Transparency exists precisely because public trust should not depend on the personal credibility of current officeholders, board members, consultants, or donors.
When citizens cannot identify the donors funding the Commissioner search, and cannot identify the donors funding the development of Missouri’s next educational roadmap, confidence in the independence of educational governance inevitably dissolves.
The issue is not whether the donors are conservative or progressive. It is not whether they support charter schools, traditional public schools, educational savings accounts, vouchers or any other particular proposed measures.  The issue is that the public does not know who they are.
And when the search for Missouri’s highest-ranking education official and the development of Missouri’s long-term educational strategy are being financed by concealed private interests, citizens have every right to ask questions.
The constitutional structure adopted by Missouri’s framers was built around the diffusion of power. Long terms. Staggered appointments. Bipartisan representation. Independence from immediate political pressures. Those safeguards were designed to ensure that educational policy would not be controlled by any single political moment, any single administration, or any single source of influence.
Today, constitutional structures can be weakened without ever being formally changed.
When one administration gains the opportunity to appoint most of a constitutionally independent board, when educational leadership changes at the same time, and when the search for new leadership is financed by funding sources hidden from the public, we should at least pause and ask whether Missouri is drifting away from the independent educational governance that the Missouri Constitution was designed to protect.
Reasonable people can disagree about the answer.
What should not be controversial is the need for transparency.
If private donors are helping fund the search for Missouri’s next Commissioner of Education and the development of Missouri’s next strategic plan for public education, their identities should be disclosed.
Missouri’s constitutional framework for public education rests on a simple principle: power should be dispersed, visible, and accountable.
Today, key donors remain unidentified. A new commissioner is being selected. A new strategic plan is being written, and Missouri’s citizens are being left in the dark.
Perhaps everything is being done appropriately.
That is exactly why transparency matters.
Public confidence should not depend on empty assurances from government officials, consultants, or anonymous benefactors. It should rest on facts that citizens can see for themselves.
The framers of Missouri’s Constitution understood that trust in public education requires more than good intentions. It requires openness and political balance.
Missourians should accept nothing less.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Hoosiers disapprove of Trump, Braun and data centers in new poll
text:
Almost 70% strongly or somewhat oppose building new data centers in Indiana with 18% in support. (Getty Images)Hoosiers largely disapprove of how President Donald Trump and Gov. Mike Braun are doing their jobs and oppose early redistricting and data centers, according to a new poll conducted by Bellwether Research.
Free Press Indiana commissioned the poll of 839 likely voters performed Oct. 8-11. It oversampled Republicans, in line with the state’s GOP lean.
Free Press is a nonprofit news organization founded in 2023 to provide free, community-based local journalism across the state. The group runs Mirror Indy, Capital B Gary and Free Press Indiana News.
When asked about Trump, 54% disapproved while 44% approved. Braun’s numbers are even lower, with 48% disapproving and 38% approving.
In three presidential runs, Trump has won Indiana easily — with 56% of the vote being his lowest win total in the state.
Christine Matthews, a longtime pollster and the president of Bellwether Research, said voters are souring on Trump all over the country and Indiana is not immune. Bellwether is considered moderate Republican polling firm.
“Indiana is not immune to what’s happening nationally. It’s not immune to rising gas prices, cost of living, the sense that the Republicans in the Trump administration are not focused on the issues that matter to them,” she said.
Matthews also said she reviewed prior polling and believes this is the highest disapproval rate for Trump in Indiana.
(Courtesy of Free Press Indiana)
The poll also included questions on top concerns for voters, with government corruption coming out on top followed by inflation or cost of living. She called the corruption result the most surprising finding of the poll.
“If I’m a Republican in Indiana, I think I would be quite concerned about that result and what it tells me about the mood of voters,” Matthews said.
One question asked about eliminating property taxes and replacing the revenue with another type of tax. Only 50% strongly or somewhat favored the move, with 27% in opposition and 24% unsure.
Matthews said it’s clear residents are interested in the idea but want to hear what the options are before jumping on board.
Hoosiers are certain how they feel about data center construction, though.
(Courtesy of Free Press Indiana)
Almost 70% strongly or somewhat opposed building new data centers in Indiana, with 18% in support.
Matthews said the opposition jumped markedly in this poll compared to a survey she ran last year in the state.
“It’s overwhelmingly negative,” she said. “So anyone associated with data centers is going to suffer for that a little bit.”
Voters were also asked about whether state lawmakers should draw new congressional boundaries in the 2027 legislative session to take effect for the 2028 election. Only 30% supported redistricting early with 56% against, aligning with previous polls in Indiana.
About 42% of those surveyed identified as Republican and 30% identified Democrat. Another 7% considered themselves independent but leaning Republican; 11% independent but leaning Democrat; and 11% independent with no lean.

name: WyoFile
title: Is gravel a mineral? The answer could decide the Casper Mountain mining controversy.
text:
The Wyoming Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday in a case concerning counties’ authority to regulate gravel and sand pit operations on some 3.4 million acres of state trust lands scattered throughout the state.
“There are 84 active solid-mineral gravel leases currently before the [State Board of Land Commissioners], so this impact is far and wide,” Cheyenne-based attorney Deborah Roden told the justices.
Roden represents Casper-based gravel operator Prism Logistics, which acquired state approval to pursue gravel mining on a cluster of state trust lands next to a rural neighborhood at the base of Casper Mountain, a popular recreation spot. The appeals case centers on whether the Natrona County Board of Land Commissioners acted within its authority when it rezoned the area back to a previous designation that prohibits heavy industrial use after a county-wide public outcry against the proposed gravel operations.
In response to the project, Coates Road area neighbors formed the Casper Mountain Preservation Alliance, which gathered more than 20,000 signatures from residents throughout the county in opposition.
Dozens of people hike a trail on state lands in the Coates Road area west of Casper, where Prism Logistics hopes to mine gravel. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
“My gosh, I just don’t think we can ignore that,” William Schwartz, an attorney for Natrona County, told the justices. 
At stake is whether counties can impose zoning regulations to protect homeowners from industrial impacts, Schwartz added, as well as activities that would disrupt recreation areas and sensitive habitats. “And this is the crown jewel of Casper, Wyoming,” he said. Counties, in his legal opinion, have the authority to impose such restrictions and, if the high court agrees, it’s highly unlikely they would shut down gravel and sand operations en masse on state lands.
“As we know, there are lots of counties in Wyoming that don’t even have zoning,” Schwartz told the justices, “and these [county-level] decisions about whether to regulate gravel pits, I think, are probably highly dependent upon their location. Counties ought to have the ability, where they do have zoning, to regulate something as sensitive as this.”
Legal wrangling


In response to the county’s rezoning, Prism asked the Natrona County District Court to review whether the county had the authority to make the change. A judge sided with Prism, and Natrona County appealed to the Wyoming Supreme Court.
Legal arguments Wednesday centered on whether Wyoming law views gravel pits narrowly as mining a mineral, or more broadly as commercial and industrial operations. Attorneys for both parties agree that counties have little authority over mineral production activities like coal, oil and natural gas operations. But they disagreed about whether state law views gravel and sand as a mineral in the classic sense of mining and processing.
The State Land Board regards gravel and sand as a mineral — a misinterpretation of the Wyoming Legislature’s intent when it comes to county authority, Schwartz said, pointing to case law.


What are state trust lands?
Upon granting statehood in 1890, the federal government bestowed some 4.2 million acres of “state trust lands” to Wyoming, which now manages about 3.4 million acres of trust land. The Wyoming Constitution prescribes that the primary use of those lands, which are scattered throughout the state in a checkerboard pattern, is to support public schools, including activities that generate revenue for schools.
The Office of State Lands and Investments commonly leases those lands — often referred to as “school sections” — for grazing and industrial development such as mining and oil and gas drilling.


“I think what the district court missed here is the really vital question of who decides whether it’s mineral or commercial or industrial,” he said. “Who decides here is the Legislature.”
Roden countered that although counties have authority to “weigh in,” or impose local zoning on industrial and commercial operations, they may not override the state’s authority regarding “mineral” extraction, which includes gravel and sand.
“Our position in this case is simple,” Roden said. “The statutes and the case law and the regulations clearly demonstrate that Prism’s state land leases are not subject to local zoning, and we would ask this court to find as such.”
Homes in the foreground are near several state land sections where a developer wants to establish a gravel pit operation. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Regardless of how the court rules, the legal wrangling has revealed a need to allow for more local input about what should happen on state-managed lands, said Carolyn Griffith, who lives near the proposed mine and chairs the Casper Mountain Preservation Alliance.
“It’s now evident that additional legislation may be needed to ensure that industrial activities on state lands align with responsible standards required of everyone else within that planning zone,” Griffith told WyoFile.
The court will issue a written decision, Chief Justice Lynne Boomgaarden said. High court decisions often come months after oral arguments.
Meantime, stakeholders await the court’s decision in a closely related case.
Under public pressure, the State Board of Land Commissioners denied a request by Prism Logistics to grant an extension for the same gravel leases in question. A subsequent Natrona County District Court ruling in January sided with the gravel miner. The state appealed to the Wyoming Supreme Court.
The post Is gravel a mineral? The answer could decide the Casper Mountain mining controversy. appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: Trump launched a federal school choice program. How will it affect Wyoming?
text:
Wyoming took another step toward expanding school choice this summer when Gov. Mark Gordon opted into President Donald Trump’s new federal tax-credit scholarships. The Wyoming Department of Education has begun to lay the groundwork for the program, which is set to launch Jan. 1.
So how will the scholarships work here, and who is eligible to benefit?
The federal program allows U.S. taxpayers who contribute to a qualified “Scholarship Granting Organization” to receive federal tax credits, creating an incentive to donate. The organizations, which must be nonprofits, will then provide scholarships to students for education-related services like tuition, tutoring and supplies.
The Wyoming Department of Education began accepting applications Monday from nonprofits seeking to participate as qualified Scholarship Granting Organizations under the program. 
This map shows the states in blue where governors have opted in to President Donald Trump’s federal school choice program. (The White House)
To participate, organizations must meet federal and state requirements and submit an official application demonstrating their ability to manage scholarship funds, maintain transparent financial reporting and effectively serve Wyoming students, according to the education department. Applications are due Dec. 1 to participate in 2027. 
Once organizations have been approved and taxpayer contributions start flowing, the idea is that families apply directly to participating nonprofits for scholarships. 
To qualify, students must be eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school and come from a household with a prior-year income at or below 300% of the area’s median gross income, adjusted for family size, according to a federal fact sheet. Eligibility does not guarantee a scholarship.
Allowable education expenses under the scholarships include private-school tuition, books, supplies, computers and tutoring for K-12 students, according to the Internal Revenue Service. 
New front
School choice has divided the education world, with critics maintaining that spending public money on private schools erodes public school funding and supporters contending it offers families necessary flexibility to meet individual needs and preferences. 
Wyoming is no stranger to the issue. The state in 2025 passed a controversial law that created a universal school-choice voucher program, the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act. 
Ten Sleep School second graders in Nikki Erickson’s class talk with partners in September 2025 during a lesson on how sand is formed. Ten Sleep is a top-performing public school in Wyoming. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Through the program, Wyoming residents can apply to receive up to $7,000 in state funds per student to pay for costs associated with private K-12 education and preschool. The money covers not only private-school tuition, but also things like admission fees to zoos or internet costs for homeschooling children not enrolled in public education. The law has traveled a rocky path, and its fate is still uncertain. A lawsuit challenging its constitutionality is tied up in court, though the Wyoming Supreme Court this summer allowed the state to begin distributing money for the program. 
While Gordon has expressed concerns about whether a state school voucher program violates Wyoming’s constitution, the governor encourages participation in the federal program. 
“Wyoming families want educational options that work for their children, whether that means additional tutoring, learning materials, or help with tuition,” Gordon said in a press release. “This program gives individuals a direct way to invest in those opportunities. I encourage qualified organizations to apply and help Wyoming families make the most of this new resource.”

name: WyoFile
title: Autumn song
text:
Opinion

Twenty-four years ago this week, the warm dry fall at the home place vanished in the night. Three inches of fresh snow blanketed the country. That same snow silenced our footfalls in the morning as we worked methodically through the high meadows, then stopped for a snack and a drink of water. That’s when we saw the elk. 
They simply appeared as if by magic, way above timberline, just little specks on a grassy shelf above a big rockslide. It was a good place to see a bighorn sheep, but it was full of elk: cows, calves, a couple of spikes and one monster of a bull. There was never any question about if we would go after them. The only question was how, and that question was swiftly put to rest as we slipped into the cover of the timber.
It was a long approach, and a tough one. We moved up through a small meadow, staying in the cover of the scattered spruce at the edges. We slipped through the lower edges of the jumbled scree, boulder-hopping and keeping one eye above us to be sure we were below their line of sight. Then we were into the dense timber on the steep slope below them. We moved slowly, steadily up the slope until we ran out of cover, sweating, huffing and puffing, straining for each painful lungful of air. 
We were naked to the world, or at least it felt like we were. There were no trees, not even a bit of stunted whitebark pine. We stashed the daypacks, the jackets and everything else we didn’t absolutely need. We were at almost 11,000 feet when we paused to catch our breath. That’s when I saw her ears. One cow had risen from her bed and walked to the edge of the grassy shelf to look down the slope. There we were, without enough cover to hide a pika. We tried to huddle up and look like rocks, but she made us in one look. She barked once, wheeled on her hind legs and it was all over. We never even heard their footfalls, but we knew they were gone. We heard the big bull bugle one time in the timber below and never saw him again. 
Elk hunting is like real life — you learn to deal with disappointment. The plan was to hit the trail in the bottom of the drainage and to drop down, maybe even head for the cabin. We were spent, and heartsick with defeat. But once we got into the timber, we began seeing elk tracks in the snow. A couple at first, then small bunches of a half dozen or so, all made that morning. All moving steadily, not hurrying, but not lingering in any one spot, either. And all headed in one direction. 
Elk are creatures of habit in our part of the Wind Rivers, and these elk were starting the same journey they made every year at about this time. They would stay in the old growth timber and skirt the shoulder of the mountain well away from the trail in the bottom of the drainage. They would timber up for a night or two. Then, if the weather didn’t clear up, they would move over into the next basin on their way to their winter range. Generations of them have successfully dodged Newe (Shoshone) hunters, mountain men, tie hacks, my grandfather and my father in this black timber tangle. And now it was our turn.
Lynn and James headed off down the drainage for the cabin, but I couldn’t quite make myself quit hunting just yet. It had been a wonderful day. The disappointment of the failed stalk had disappeared. It was eerily silent. It was still. It was perfect. There was a feeling that I still struggle to explain. The closest I can come is to borrow a term from baseball. Great batters sometimes talk about being “in the zone.” It’s that flow state where your mind, your body and your spirit come together and focus completely. Everything slows down. Your mind is focused, with no thought of anything except the moment. Your body is loose, just tired enough to be content to move slowly, but fresh enough to keep up the pace for as long as it takes. And your spirit is one with the mountain. When everything is right and I’m “in the zone” like that, it’s a feeling almost mystical in nature. I’m not invisible, but I’m not far from it. 
I felt it coming that day. I knew without a doubt that it was going to happen soon, it was only a question of when. I eased forward one slow step at a time like a coyote, feeling the ground with my feet to make sure I didn’t make a noise. Slowly, quietly, carefully around the trees. I saw him at the exact instant that he saw me. One squeal and everything erupted into chaos. He seemed to go instantly from placidly standing broadside to full-tilt, all-out run. Things happened way too fast to think about them. At times like this, there is no real thinking. Your brain is simply processing information and reacting by instinct, or it’s over. I remember thinking that he was a bull and a good one. That’s all my brain registered. I don’t remember raising the rifle, I don’t even remember firing the shot, but I remember thinking “Yes! That one was good. That was a lung shot.”
Mostly, I remember him. I remember how he watched me as he ran, not in fear but in calculated tactical retreat. I will never forget watching his left eye as it focused directly on me. I will take to my grave the way the muscles in his massive shoulders rolled and how his powerful hindquarters drove with each lunge, the way he sent great showers of snow and dirt up 10 feet in the air behind him as he sprinted for the timber. The whole thing couldn’t have taken more than a couple of seconds, but it all seems to slow down in my mind. I stood still and listened. I heard him go down in a shattering of branches behind a big granite boulder in the timber a couple hundred yards to my left. He tried to rise once, twice, and then lay still. 
He was an old bull, gray in his mane and undoubtedly on the downhill side of his life. He was a good heavy six-point, but without the long tines he probably carried a couple of years before. He had a bad gore wound between his shoulder and chest, and a collection of old scars from previous years’ battles from the nape of his neck all the way to his rump. Three of his tines were broken. He was as thin as a snake. But he had been a brawler and a commanding presence on this mountain for years, only recently beginning to feel the onset of his old age. His teeth were worn, and he looked tired as he lay there. I sat beside him in the waning light of the afternoon and gave thanks. Suddenly I was tired too, and I felt a little on the downhill side of my years. I took the tenderloins for tomorrow night’s dinner; made sure the tag was in his ear and headed down the trail as the last violet bit of alpenglow hung on the peaks behind me.
When I broke out into the big meadow, I could just make out one of the folks from a camp on the far side as he walked four horses down to the creek to water. One was belled, and I could make out the sound, clear and pure in the gathering dim. I wondered how many times I’d been in this meadow at first and last light. I wondered how many times the bull had been, and if we’d seen one another before today. We might have been old friends, I thought as I got to my feet and headed for the cabin. We would pack him out in the morning.
I am old now, and I carry a lot of scars, just like that old bull back in 2002. Kim and I are officially retired from elk hunting. But we still come back each year, and we revel in the fall as the bulls bugle and aspens turn to gold. We fish and hunt grouse and hike just for the joy of being here. My body cannot do what it once did, but I still need this experience. I need to come with my sweetheart to the cabin in the most perfect time of the year. I need to touch and hear and feel our connection to this land, these elk and this holy place.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Voting rights groups say Idaho laws from 2023 create hurdles to register and vote
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Longfellow Elementary School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)A pair of local nonprofit organizations that promote voting rights say Idaho’s voting laws make it more difficult to hold voter registration drives and make it harder for some eligible voters to vote.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
However, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said voter registration numbers for young voters between the ages of 18 to 25 have remained consistent. He also said there are multiple ways for a voter to prove identification and residency, and an Idaho judge has ruled the state’s voting laws are constitutional. 
The groups, Babe Vote and the League of Women Voters of Idaho, say Idaho’s identification and proof of residency requirements create barriers to voting that affect students and older voters alike. 
Olivia Luna, a 21-year-old Idaho college student and Babe Vote leader, said a pair of 2023 state laws that removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting hurt students and young people especially hard. 

House Bill 124 removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting. 
House Bill 340 also removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification and standardized voter registration requirements for in-person registration and online registration. House Bill 340 also required the Idaho Transportation Department to create and offer no-fee identification cards that are accepted for voting. 

Luna said many students frequently move between their parents’ house, dorms and apartments throughout their academic career, making it difficult to prove residency from a list of documents accepted by the state. 
Olivia Luna is the president of Babe Vote, a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping young people vote. (Photo courtesy of Babe Vote)
For people who don’t drive and don’t have a driver’s license, or for students who have a current out-of-state driver’s license, Luna said state voting requirements create unnecessary hurdles for young people to exercise their constitutional right to vote. 
“I would say it puts up a pretty significant road block for most students,” Luna said.  
Luna said Babe Vote paused its voter registration efforts after the laws took effect, and the laws continue to make Babe Vote’s voter registration and outreach efforts difficult. 
Luna said she appreciates the opportunities to work with McGrane’s office. But she said the technology at voteIdaho.gov can still be unreliable or tricky for some users, and she said that even though there is a free ID available, it can still be difficult to make the trip and provide a different set of state documents necessary to get the state ID.
“It’s free to get, but you still have to go in-person to the DMV, and you still need to be able to get there, which is difficult for those of us who don’t have cars,” Luna said. 
Republican state legislators who supported the 2023 laws said there was a lack of uniformity, a lack of security features and a lack of sophistication for student IDs. They said that state and federal IDs include enhanced security features to project against forgery or reproduction, which student IDs don’t have.
“At the end of the day, these laws would not be in place if it weren’t for the secretary of state, and saying that nothing has changed or it is just as easy to vote as before these laws is just factually incorrect, and I’d appreciate it if that was acknowledged,” Luna said. 
 Idaho secretary of state said voters have multiple options to meet requirements and free IDs are available

	 
McGrane said young voter registration and voting numbers have always been low, and it’s not a unique problem to Idaho or a new problem. 
After reviewing voting statistics and demographic information with his staff, McGrane said the decrease in the youngest, first time voters that Babe Vote is seeing in 2025 and 2026 is because there was not a presidential election during this year’s election or last year’s election. 
McGrane said whether or not a presidential election is taking place – not changes to voter registration and identification requirements – is the decisive factor of whether young people register and vote. McGrane said young voter registration and voting numbers peak every four years during presidential election cycles, while fewer young voters get registered for the first time and vote during years with local elections or legislative elections. 
Presidential elections drive turnout and registration among all ages and demographics, McGrane said, not just young people. 
For example, overall voter turnout was about 29% during the November 2025 election, a local election year. But overall voter turnout was almost 78% during the November 2024 election, a presidential election. 
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane at the State Capitol building on Jan. 8, 2024. Also pictured is State Controller Brandon Woolf. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“There’s an ebb and flow,” McGrane said. “So you have a presidential year, it goes up. And then it drops down, and then it goes up and it drops down again.”
McGrane said voting is important and he regularly speaks at Idaho colleges and universities to talk to young people about voting and registering. He also said his office has updated the www.voteIdaho.gov website so that eligible voters can upload a photo of their acceptable form of ID along with a selfie to register to vote without having to go anywhere in person or fill out any physical documents. He said those changes are designed to give voters options and make it convenient to register. 
The Idaho Secretary of State’s Office also mails out information voter pamphlets to every Idaho household and takes out ads designed to share election information about guide voters to the services available through www.voteidaho.gov.
McGrane also said student IDs were rarely used as a form of identification by voters in Idaho. For example, in the November 2022 election, before the laws were passed, 104 Idaho voters used a student ID to vote. That’s out of more than 400,000 voters that were checked-in on poll books across the state during that election, officials with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office said.  
State officials also pointed out that Babe Vote and the League Of Women Voters of Idaho filed a lawsuit over Idaho’s voting laws, but a judge in 2023 found that the laws were constitutional and dismissed the lawsuit. 
McGrane said he is trying to raise awareness about elections and make it easier for eligible voters to register and participate. McGrane said it has long been an issue that young voters don’t vote as frequently as older voters.
McGrane said he wrote an op-ed in 2014 saying that young people don’t vote.
“I said ‘young people don’t vote,’ and we shared a bunch of stats and I defined young people as anyone under 60,” McGrane said. “And it’s because in that cycle it was a midterm election and it wasn’t until (age) 60 that more than 50% of the voting age population showed up and voted.”
 League of Women voters says older Idahoans also have challenges meeting registration laws

Although it is not related to the changes with student IDs, Idaho’s voter registration and residency laws also create roadblocks for older Idaho voters, League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid said. 
Jean Henscheid, president of the League of Women Voters of Idaho, walks away from the lectern after testifying at a Senate Health and Welfare Committee meeting on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Henscheid and League of Women Voters of Idaho Statewide Voter Service Director Kendal Shaber said it is very difficult for older adults who don’t drive and have stopped traveling (and no longer have a passport) to meet the photo ID requirements in Idaho. 
Because voting is tied to identification requirements, Henscheid said older Idahoans who don’t have a driver’s license, state ID card or passport now need to have their certified birth certificate to get a state-issued ID that is accepted for voting. 
For older women who have married and divorced, they also need marriage licenses and divorce decrees from each marriage and divorce if their name does not match the name on their birth certificate, Henscheid said.
Henscheid said she’s helped older women voters who said the process to get all of their required documents and receive their state-issued ID for voting took six months or longer.
“Before these laws were put in place, we were able to do hundreds of voter registration support events, and we were helping hundreds of people in assisted living and nursing homes,” Henscheid said. “Now, we’ve really slowed down our outreach because it is so incredibly difficult.”
 



 Need to register to vote?

Idahoans using an Idaho driver’s license or state-issued ID card can register to vote online at VoteIdaho.gov, the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office’s elections website. Idahoans can also register to vote at their local county clerk’s office, or register to vote at their polling place on Election Day, which is Nov. 3 this year.
Idahoans can also update their voter information, check their voter registration status, find their polling place and view their sample ballot using www.VoteIdaho.gov.
 What documents do I need to register to vote?

To register, Idahoans must be a U.S. citizen who is at least 18 years old by Election Day who has lived in Idaho for at least 30 days before the election. Eligible voters need to provide photo identification from the list of acceptable forms of identification below and prove their residency using one of the documents listed below. 
Photo ID:

An Idaho driver’s license
An Idaho identification card
A U.S. passport or federal ID
A Tribal ID card
An enhanced license to carry concealed weapons issued by an Idaho sheriff’s office

Proof of residency:

Any of the acceptable photo IDs listed above, with your current address
Proof of insurance
Mortgage, lease or rental agreement  
A property tax assessment bill
A utility bill, other than a cell phone bill
A bank or credit card statement 
A paycheck or paystub
An intake document from a care facility 
An enrollment letter from an Idaho high school or university 
A letter from a social service agency 

— Source: www.VoteIdaho.gov

title: What should Wyoming’s ‘ABC’ voters do?
text:
Opinion

In August, Chuck Gray won the Republican nomination for Congress with only 25% of the vote. Roughly three of every four Wyoming Republicans who voted chose someone else, and not one of the eight Republicans he defeated has publicly endorsed him. Those voters had good reason to reject Gray. They, and others, should follow their good judgment again in November.
Gray’s partisan posturing offends most Wyomingites, but his performance as Wyoming’s chief election officer is what disqualifies him from becoming our sole representative in the U.S. House. Though voter fraud is virtually nonexistent in Wyoming, he and his Freedom Caucus friends have relentlessly trotted out that fictional bogeyman to advance partisan “election integrity” laws that do nothing but erode our most sacred right as citizens — to cast our votes in open elections free of unnecessary government conditions.
Gray made it harder for Wyoming citizens to vote.
Peddling MAGA election conspiracies, Gray pushed measures that have made Wyoming’s election code the most restrictive in the nation. We are now one of only six states requiring voters not only to show photo identification, which is reasonable, but also to prove their citizenship with paperwork many folks don’t have and can’t easily get, effectively disenfranchising them. Gray and his crowd also took away the popular freedom we had enjoyed since 1911: changing our party affiliation up to Election Day so we could make fully informed choices about which primary to vote in.
None of these laws addressed a real problem. Modern Wyoming elections have been honest and well run by our fine county clerks, and Republicans have almost always dominated regardless of any so-called “crossover” voting. But thanks to Gray and the Freedom Caucus, fewer of us can now vote, our freedom to choose our primary has been curtailed, and our voter registration, turnout and electoral competition are an embarrassment.
Gray handed our private information to the feds.
Unlike our neighboring Republican secretaries of state, Gray rushed to be the first in the nation to turn over the voter records of roughly 280,000 Wyoming citizens, including driver’s license numbers, to the Department of Justice. Our election code forbids disclosing that confidential information. No court ordered Gray to do it, and 26 federal courts have since found the federal demand unlawful. Fremont County Clerk Julie Freese, a Republican with three decades of experience, noted that state law bars clerks from giving anyone’s private information to anyone, yet our election chief handed it over without a written agreement and without telling anyone. Our clerks and voters were angry, Freese said, and she doesn’t blame them. Wyoming people are rightly suspicious of federal overreach, yet Gray opened our file cabinet to Washington anyway.
Gray turned a blind eye to federal agents intimidating our election officials.
On primary day, Justice Department agents showed up unannounced at Laramie County polling places, approaching poll workers and saying they intended to interview voters. Gray’s office had advance notice from the feds but kept it to itself, catching Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee off guard. 
“This was a poorly managed exercise and one that showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections,” Lee said. Gov. Mark Gordon called the federal conduct “aggressive” and asked for an investigation. Again, Gray — our top election official — did nothing to protect Wyoming voters or county officials.
Plainly, Chuck Gray does not deserve the support of anyone who values the right to vote and a healthy Wyoming democracy.
So, what should all the Republican “anyone but Chuck” (ABC) voters do? If we split our votes as we did in the primary, Gray wins with a minority again. This time we must unite behind a candidate from a different party who can beat him.
Crossing party lines occasionally to vote for the right person is a Wyoming tradition, not a betrayal. Republicans in Kansas and other states are doing that in numbers right now. Not so long ago, we elected Democrats Ed Herschler, Mike Sullivan and Dave Freudenthal as governor for a combined 28 years. We judged the person, not the party label, and Wyoming was well served. Since then, steadily growing one-party control has made Wyoming government more extreme and less accountable.
This November, let’s build on the encouraging wave we saw in the primary. Don’t reward a MAGA extremist like Gray just because he is the only Republican on the ballot. Your Republican friends won’t even need to know you strayed, just for a moment, from the pack.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho’s invasive quagga mussel population is ‘very small,’ state director says
text:
Jeremey Varley, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture's southern chief treatment engineer, explains the state's strategy for eradicating invasive quagga mussels during a boat tour of the infested portion of the Snake River on Oct. 3, 2025. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt told a committee of state legislators Tuesday that she believes Idaho’s population of invasive quagga mussels is very small and confined to limited sections of the Snake River. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In September 2023, state officials used water sampling to confirm the presence of quagga mussel larvae for the first time in state history.
During water sampling this year, state officials found eight veliger mussels, the larvae form of the mussels, Tewalt said during a meeting of the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Committee at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. 
Scuba divers also found what Tewalt described as “a number of adult mussels” while searching the Snake River.
The mussels, which were discovered in the Snake River near Twin Falls, can reproduce extremely rapidly, clog pipes and cover boat hulls. If left unchecked, Tewalt said the spread of quagga mussels poses serious threats to the state’s drinking and irrigation water, recreation industry, state budget and economy.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



In an effort to completely eradicate all of the invasive species, officials with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture have been administering lethal copper chemicals into the affected part of the Snake River each year since the mussels were first detected. 
Compared to previous years, the amount of mussels discovered in water sampling is lower and the affected section of the Snake River is smaller this year, Tewalt told legislators. 
“What it would signify is a very small population,” Tewalt said. 
After detecting the mussels again this summer, the ag department moved forward with another round of copper-based treatments – with scuba divers injecting the chemicals in harder to reach nooks, crannies and fissures in rock. 
Chanel Tewalt serves as the director of the Idaho Department of Agriculture. (Courtesy of Idaho State Department of Agriculture)
“Copper in the water means that reproduction cycle (for the mussels) is halted,” Tewalt said. 
Along with mussels, the copper also kills fish and other aquatic life in the river. This year, Tewalt said there have been fewer fish killed and that state officials are not stocking the sections of the river being treated with copper with new fish. 
Although the mussels were first discovered in water samples in 2023, Tewalt told legislators the mussels have likely been in the Twin Falls pool of the Snake River for longer. 
Water sampling and monitoring for quagga mussels is an ongoing, years-long process. When water temperatures warm up again next year, state officials will resume water sampling to check for more quagga mussels, state officials said.

title: ISU awarded federal grant to improve access to produce for pregnant and postpartum women
text:
Apples sit ready for purchase at a fruit and vegetable stand in Omer, Michigan. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced Tuesday a $499,465 award to Idaho State University for a new federal program, the Maternal Produce Prescription Program. (Photo by Brien Aho/USDA)Idaho State University will receive nearly $500,000 in federal funds to improve access to fruits and vegetables for pregnant and postpartum Idahoans. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced Tuesday a $499,465 award to ISU for a new federal program, the Maternal Produce Prescription Program. The federal funding is meant to serve pregnant and postpartum women and their families in low-income and medically underserved communities and increase access to healthy foods, according to a press release. 
ISU Institute of Rural Health Grant Project Coordinator Kailey Blood said the program will serve eligible women and families in Idaho Public Health District 6, which encompasses the southeastern portion of the state. 
“It aims to increase fruit and vegetable consumption among enrolled women and their families, provide nutrition education, and strengthen the relationships between healthcare providers, community organizations, and local food systems,” Blood said of the program. “Eligible pregnant and postpartum women will receive a prescription to include produce in their diet, vouchers to purchase fresh produce, and nutrition education.” 
The grant is administered nationally by the Health Resources and Services Administration, which is an agency within the HHS Department. 
“Good nutrition is foundational to good health,” Health Resources and Services Administration Administrator Tom Engels said in a press release. “Through the new Maternal Produce Prescription Program, we are helping pregnant and postpartum women and their families get fruits and vegetables. Across HRSA, we are expanding access to nutrition services in health centers, strengthening nutrition support for people with HIV, and helping make nutrition a more integrated part of healthcare, including through telehealth. These are practical steps to help Americans live healthier lives.”
