name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Bethlehem’s landfill is set to close. What happens next for residents is murky.
text:
On a rainy Tuesday, Oct. 13, Casella-branded trash and recycling bins line Agassiz Street in Bethlehem. Casella Waste Services provides free curbside waste pickup to residents of the town as part of a host-community agreement that will expire in December, when the company's Bethlehem landfill is slated to close. Transfer Station Committee members said the benefit was not worth the cost of hosting the landfill, and added they were optimistic about the town's ability to take on trash handling duties in Casella's wake. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)With Casella Waste Services’ landfill in Bethlehem slated to close at the end of this year, town officials are preparing for a post-landfill future. But with the closure arriving sooner than anticipated, those preparations have been shaded by persistent trash-related tension.
The end of operations at the landfill also marks the end of a settlement agreement between Casella and Bethlehem, under which Casella has provided curbside waste pickup and disposal services to residents. Free service will no longer be available to residents once the landfill closes, a change officials said called for the town to develop alternative, permanent systems for handling waste.
Members of the Bethlehem Transfer Station Committee, tasked with making those plans, said they were ready to distance Bethlehem from the landfill within its borders. The site has been plagued by environmental violations and concerns among some of its neighbors; the closure is the result of previous zoning decisions, voted on by residents, to prohibit further expansion at the site . But some other residents are disappointed to see the operation draw to a close, and apprehensive about the costs associated with taking on the task of managing waste for the town’s approximately 2,500 residents. 
As Bethlehem scrambles to move into a new phase at the end of this year, some long-running debates are again taking center stage.
“It’s tough. It’s a sore subject. It’s been a sore subject for a lot of years,” said select board member Casey MacDonald, speaking Tuesday night outside the Bethlehem Public Library on Main Street. “And now, it’s like, oh, we’re here — but we’re not quite there yet.”
What is changing?
Casella Waste Services announced at the beginning of October that Dec. 31 would be the last day the landfill accepts municipal solid waste.
That is earlier than the company’s previous estimates. As recently as this summer, town officials heard estimated closing dates in 2027 from Casella, Bethlehem Select Board member Nancy Strand said in a phone interview Wednesday. Casella Vice President of Communications Jeff Weld said in a Wednesday email that the company had been discussing closure timeframes with community representatives for the past year.
The announcement wasn’t too much of a surprise, Strand and other officials said.
“It’s kind of a shock, but we knew it was going to happen eventually,” said MacDonald.
Once the landfill reaches capacity, Casella must follow a closure protocol followed by ongoing environmental monitoring at the site. 
When the landfill is no longer accepting waste, the agreement that requires Casella to retrieve residents’ trash will no longer be active, Strand and Weld said. Weld also identified annual fees paid to the town, “community donations,” and an annual household hazardous waste drop-off day as among the other Casella-run programs that would end at that time. Casella also expects the amount of property taxes paid to the town to drop, he added.
The immediate result of the end of curbside pickup and residential waste drop-off at the landfill, Strand said, is that Bethlehem will need a plan in place to collect and sort waste, then transport it to another facility for final disposition.
That’s where the Transfer Station Committee comes in.
Transfer station dreaming
The Bethlehem Transfer Station Committee envisions a future municipal waste collection station for a town-owned parcel on Route 116.
Unlike most towns, with established procedures for dealing with their solid waste, Strand views Bethlehem as facing an opportunity to start “from scratch.” She hopes the facility will provide benefits to the community that go beyond fulfilling their responsibility to shepherd waste to a landfill.
“We, as a small town, can, I believe, create a really kick-ass transfer station,” she said at a June meeting of the Transfer Station Committee.
At the transfer station, the standard collection, sorting, and sendoff of trash and recycling would be a given, the committee said. (Trash will be sent to the Mount Carberry landfill in Berlin.) Other features outlined for the site include a food waste collection system, to enable residents to compost and reduce the waste that must be sent to a landfill, as well as a “free store,” where residents can exchange items they no longer want but that are not necessarily ready for the landfill. 
The station will cost about $1 million, according to the committee. Residents have funded a capital reserve account with about $300,000 for the project. The remainder of the cost, the committee and select board say, will come from a federal grant in the form of congressionally directed spending from Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, with about $750,000 earmarked for the project.
But the process of the grant’s release to the town has been slow. MacDonald said the funds were dependent on permitting reviews by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which is administering the funds.
On Wednesday, Strand said communications earlier this week from the USDA indicated the town would get the “green light” in the coming weeks. That would clear the town’s engineering firm, Concord-based Aries Engineering, to begin work on the site and issue requests for proposals for the structural work. 
But with funds not yet available to the town, and the Casella landfill’s closure likely happening sooner than planned, Bethlehem must find a way to fill the gap. Strand estimated that the permanent transfer station would be ready in summer or fall 2027; in the meantime, the town plans to operate a temporary transfer station at the town garage, with rolling dumpsters collecting materials for transport.
Funding these measures is another challenge. The Transfer Station Committee has recommended implementing a pay-as-you-throw system, in which residents must purchase specially marked trash bags to dispose of waste, to help fund the trash management system going forward. But all the same, taking on the town’s trash will have a budget impact, Strand said. 
“We have to pay the tipping fees at Mount Carberry, we have to invest in the pay-as-you-throw bags,” she said. Other costs will include staff at the transfer station: a manager, plus at least one part-time attendant. “There’s no question that taxpayers will see a change,” Strand said. “…We’re just trying to make it as minimal as possible.”
A legacy of waste troubles
The new anticipated costs of waste management have not been welcomed by all residents. The fact that curbside waste pickup is not guaranteed to continue has also been troubling to some, MacDonald said. 
The town has solicited bids from multiple companies for waste hauling, Strand said, including Casella. Though Weld confirmed that free curbside pickup would end, he did not rule out the possibility that Casella would continue to offer the service to residents for a cost — though the company has not yet said what that cost would be.
Some residents discussed putting a warrant article before voters last year to explore changing the town’s prohibition on expansion or reopening negotiations with Casella, MacDonald said. But no article was ultimately put forward last year, and though the conversations have continued this year, he said he wondered if the upcoming March 2027 town meeting would be “too late” for such a move.
“NCES has the physical space to expand and continue providing disposal capacity for Bethlehem and the more than 200 New Hampshire communities that rely on the facility. However, expansion would require a change in local zoning, which has not occurred, as well as applicable regulatory approvals,” Weld said, referring to Bethlehem’s prohibition on expansion at the site. 
Resident Daniel Noyes said he hadn’t felt positive about the closure announcement. Mostly, he said, he and others he knew were confused about the status of the town’s plans for its trash, and wished for more communication from the Transfer Station Committee. On Tuesday night, he had attempted to attend a meeting of the committee, which was ultimately canceled for lack of a quorum. Noyes said he was disappointed not to be able to ask questions.
“Everyone’s got a different story of what they think is happening,” he said. 
Even with operations drawing down, Bethlehem will not soon forget the waste pile within its borders, Strand said.
“The landfill will be there forever, you know?” she said. “That’s a giant mountain over there.”
Her hope is that the town can endure the transition ahead and overcome the trash-related disputes that have divided residents for decades. 
“Most people, I think, in our town are just tired of the fight, tired of the divisions that it creates, tired of the same old arguments, both pro and against,” Strand said. “You know, we’re just — we just want to move on.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Ballard is hoping for another once-in-a-lifetime upset
text:
Greg Ballard, a Lincoln Party candidate for secretary of state, chats with the Indiana Capital Chronicle on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)This is the second of four profiles in Indiana’s secretary of state race.
Greg Ballard has overcome the odds before.
As an unknown Republican in 2007, he forced a popular Democratic mayor out of the Indianapolis City-County Building by just 5,000 votes, despite being outspent 10-1.
Ballard widened his reelection margin in 2011, even as Democrats took control of the City-County Council. He chose not to seek a third term, leaving office at 66% approval.
He spent a decade largely outside the spotlight — including two years in North Carolina — fending off requests to run for mayor, governor, Congress and more.
Now, he’s reintroducing himself to voters, this time as an independent candidate for secretary of state. The beleaguered office leads Indiana’s elections.
“My heart is in this one. I want to do this. All the other offices I was asked to do, (for) one reason or another, just didn’t feel right to me. This one does,” Ballard told the Capital Chronicle in March, when he announced his campaign.
But he’ll have to overcome major disadvantages in money and time racked up this spring, when his campaign devoted most contributions to collecting the tens of thousands of signatures required to land Ballard’s name on the ballot without a political party’s backing.
“If we could have spent $840,000 on advertising instead of on help with signature collection, I think the race would be different today than it is right now,” Campaign Manager Nathan Gotsch said. “Now, we still have time to catch up.”
Former mayor goes statewide
Ballard was born and raised in Indianapolis, and earned a bachelor’s degree in economics from Indiana University’s flagship Bloomington campus.
Then, he joined the Marines, kicking off a two-decade career that included a master’s degree in military science, a family — his wife, Winnie, and two children — as well as service in the Gulf War.
He returned to his hometown in 2001, working for Bayer Diagnostics and as a consultant.
Ballard harnessed discontent over high property and income taxes to eke out a victory over former Mayor Bart Peterson, in what has been called Indiana’s biggest-ever political upset.
Independent/Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard listens to a question during the Indiana Secretary of State Debate hosted by the Indiana Debate Commission, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at WFYI Public Television Studios in Indianapolis. Ballard participated in the debate with Republican Max Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh and Libertarian Lauri Shillings. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)
He entered the mayor’s 25th floor as a 53-year-old political newcomer at the head of a Marion County Republican Party that was navigating an increasingly Democratic city.
“He was the ‘accidental mayor.’ But what people didn’t give him any credit for was (his) military career,” recalled Joseph Loftus, a Republican and retired attorney who led the nascent Ballard administration’s transition into office. 
“It wasn’t Republican and Democrat politics, but being successful inside the military apparatus required a lot of political skills … Ballard had what I always felt was a sort of uncanny political common sense about him,” Loftus said.
Ballard’s style often eschewed partisanship.
“This election shouldn’t be about Democrats or Republicans. To me, it’s about the future of our city,” he said in a 2007 TV ad for his first campaign, according to the Howey Political Report. “… I don’t care about the politics. I care about our city and I know you do, too.”
Although Loftus sought out rising young GOP stars to staff the administration, he noted some Democratic holdovers not only stayed, but were “critical” to some major initiatives.
“There was not a litmus test,” Loftus said. “I mean, it was all based on: Are you the right person for for the position? … Are you going to work real hard?”
A new kind of political party?
Ballard’s independent secretary of state bid prompted alarm within the Republican and Democratic parties in Indiana, including former allies and cheerleaders.
“I was the Republican mayor in a Democratic city, and they all loved me,” Ballard told the Capital Chronicle. “… I was the golden boy. (I) make one video saying I’m running as secretary of state, and now I’m the devil. I haven’t changed.”
He’s hoping to siphon off dissatisfied voters of both parties in his appeal to apolitical practicality — a contrast to the outbound, scandal-plagued GOP Secretary of State Diego Morales.
“I think I can clean that place up nicely,” Ballard said of Morales’ office.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
He has proposed banning the secretary of state from partisan actions — endorsing, fundraising for or donating to candidates — while in office.
Other goals include a similarly anti-partisan shakeup to the Indiana Recount Commission, improved election training for county election workers and a printed voter guide sent to all registered Hoosier voters. It would be customized to the precinct level and feature candidate-submitted descriptions, and come with an estimated price tag of $2.5 million to $3 million.
But underpinning his candidacy is a challenge to the two dominant political parties.
Independent candidates in Indiana must meet signature thresholds to get on the ballot. For a statewide office, that’s 2% of the total vote cast in the last secretary of state race — totaling roughly 37,000 signatures from across Indiana.
Ballard is running under a new “Lincoln Party” label in an attempt to give future independents access to the ballot sans signature requirements.
If he clears 2% of the vote in November, the party’s candidates would be on the general election ballot for the next four years. At 10%, the party would hold a state-funded primary.
Ballard has taken significant criticism — particularly from GOP nominee Max Engling — for launching a potential party without a stated ideology or structure.
“The intent in the future is to run what we call practical, problem-solving people that you’d be proud to have in office,” Ballard said. “Both parties have numerous purity tests, have extreme ideology, and they’re playing to their (bases) now because, as I mentioned, the primary is now the main election.”
The Lincoln Party this month released what it called a statement of principles, which Gotsch has said all party officials and candidates will be required to sign and uphold. They include the “ideals of American democracy,” “standards for governing in the public interest,” and “serving with integrity and humility,” with more characteristics listed under each category.
Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings knocked that as a “bare minimum standard” that serves as a code of conduct rather than a policy platform.
For Gotsch, however, the Lincoln Party will simply operate with a different perspective.
“This new party is not going to be like the current parties,” he said. “They’re really built on models from the the 1800s, and we have not had innovation in this space in, you know, hundreds of years. And the reason for that is because they get to set the rules.”
Racing to the end
Ballard has millions and months to make up in the last days before the Nov. 3 election.
“The disability of having to spend so much money … getting on the ballot and … then running a fall campaign — that is just a large agenda, and I’m sure hurt him for the fall,” said Jim Merritt, a Republican former state lawmaker who chaired Ballard’s mayoral campaign.
While other candidates with guaranteed ballot access began campaigning upon launch, Ballard’s campaign spent March through July collecting and submitting signatures, then waiting for their certification by state election officials.
“That was completely unfair, what they had us do,” Ballard said. “… It’s unfair for me to have to spend that money to go get signatures.”
The campaign’s strategy is to get Ballard in front of as many Hoosiers as possible. His first television ads went up Monday, weeks behind his major-party opponents. He also this week pledged to avoid negative campaigning.
Robert Vane, a Republican strategist, said he saw the makings of a similar “perfect storm” that heralded Ballard’s first surprise victory: “It’s very easy to believe that Greg Ballard is the right man at the right time, yet again.”
Vane, who served as a deputy mayor under Ballard, said he is in it for the “right reasons.”
“He’s not in it to build a resume to go on to bigger things — he’s already done the biggest things. He’s got an unbelievably successful marriage. He has two phenomenal kids. He’s served his country. He’s made Indianapolis a much better place,” he said. “When Greg Ballard tells you why he’s running for office and what he wants to do for secretary of state, believe him, because honesty is the foundation of his entire life.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: State auditors find widespread compliance failures in opioid treatment oversight
text:
A discarded Suboxone wrapper on a rain-soaked sidewalk in June 2025. The medication, which contains buprenorphine and naloxone, is used to treat opioid use disorder. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)A recent state audit of 100 Medicaid claims over a two-year period by all five opioid treatment providers that billed Rhode Island Medicaid during that period found at least one problem with every single claim. 
But the state agency that oversees these providers failed to flag these problems consistently, despite visiting facilities every other year, according to the Oct. 7 report by Rhode Island’s Office of the Auditor General. 
The Rhode Island Department of Behavioral Healthcare, Developmental Disabilities and Hospitals (BHDDH) regularly sends its inspectors to opioid treatment facilities. “These oversight activities were not sufficient to ensure full compliance with mandatory regulatory requirements,” the audit reads. 
The problems documented noncompliance with the regulations for medication-assisted treatment, or MAT, the more formal name for therapies like methadone and buprenorphine. The drugs are given to people who feel they can’t control their opioid use and help to reduce cravings and prevent withdrawal. 
The issues involved other medical services the federal government requires of opioid therapy covered by Medicaid, which is primarily federally funded and administered through states. To receive methadone or buprenorphine therapy, providers must ensure clients have routine counseling, annual physical exams, toxicology screenings and treatment plans. 
Documentation is also required for these services, state auditor David Bergantino said in an email to Rhode Island Current Tuesday. But his office could not always determine whether required services went undelivered, or rather if providers simply neglected to document them sometimes.
The claims did not necessarily represent patients going without their medicine or providers billing Medicaid for services that weren’t provided, Bergantino said. 
“The audit did not identify instances where providers billed but did not provide the MAT services billed to Medicaid,” Bergantino explained. 
The providers remain anonymous in the report because the audit was technically not of the providers themselves, but rather BHDDH, which enlists them to render services.
“Since the auditee is BHDDH and the audit objective was evaluating how successful their monitoring was over provider compliance, we do not identify the providers as they are not the subject of the audit,” Bergantino wrote. “It would be unfair to identify a private entity in our audit report that was not the subject of the audit.”
The audit spanned January 2023 through December 2024 and looked at five providers who operate a total of 14 treatment facilities across Rhode Island. The facilities were referred to by letters in the audit report. 
According to auditors, there were 1,729 deficiencies among the 100 sampled claims. The auditors found:

95 claims had missing or delayed assessments of patients’ medical, psychological or social circumstances.
75 claims had problems with the frequency of reviews for treatment plans, which are supposed to be reexamined every six months.
70 claims lacked required counseling sessions that are meant to accompany medication therapy.
42 claims failed to meet the annual benchmark for medical examinations — only one a year.

The 100 claims represented a sliver of the 274,412 opioid treatment claims submitted over those two years. Bergantino’s office estimated that if the rate of noncompliance held true across all of these claims, it would represent about $24.9 million in problematic claims.
The auditor’s office serves as a liaison between the state legislature and the federal government, and it regularly engages in “partnership audits” like these when the federal government has found significant noncompliance across states, Bergantino said. Historically, the feds have not sought repayment for these estimated amounts tied to noncompliant treatment.
“However, the federal government does expect that the State will take appropriate corrective actions to address the issues reported,” Bergantino added, “and the State could be subject to the issue being revisited by federal auditors in the future.” 
The purpose of the audit report was to “identify gaps in compliance that may place clients at risk for poor treatment outcomes and to support recommendations that strengthen program integrity and quality of care,” it states.
Treatment versus compliance
While the report did not mention the providers by name, one of the five providers audited shared opinions on the process with Rhode Island Current. CODAC Behavioral Healthcare runs nine facilities in the state and offers medication-assisted therapy. 
Linda Hurley, CODAC’s president and CEO, did not deny that regulatory noncompliance has occurred at her facilities. But she disputed the audit’s interpretations of its findings.
“I’m not saying that the audit was inaccurate,” Hurley offered in a phone call Wednesday. “I am saying that my interpretation of the results is different than that of the auditor general’s office.”
Hurley clarified that noncompliance with regulation does not mean subpar care.
“It does not mean that care was not competent,” she said. “The societal context wasn’t taken into consideration when they chose the time frame of the audit.”
Linda Hurley, president and CEO of CODAC Behavioral Healthcare, at the organization’s Royal Little integrated healthcare center in Providence in March 2026. CODAC was among five opioid treatment providers examined in a recent state audit. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Hurley said the audit did not adequately reflect the challenges providers have faced since the COVID-19 pandemic, such as disrupted in-person treatment options and a shortage of behavioral healthcare workers.
Hurley maintained that providers still were coping with staffing shortages and changes in treatment practices that arose during COVID. 
Hurley also pointed to problems with the regulations. “They’re not awful, but there are certain things that certainly need to be modernized,” she said. “We need to recognize the autonomy of the people that come to us for care.”
She said annual physicals can be a high hurdle to clear for some patients, who may repeatedly postpone appointments because of work or family obligations — or for the simple reason that it can absorb two hours of their day.
“They have lives, you know,” Hurley said. “Like, ‘Why do I have to do this? I’m not sick. I have kids. I have a job.’”
That can leave providers like CODAC out of compliance while they still deliver care, Hurley said. She recalled being asked by medical staff whether patients who repeatedly postponed appointments might be discharged.
Her response: “No, we can’t. Are you kidding?…We’re their safety net.”
A week after the audit’s release, Hurley said CODAC hasn’t yet made changes, although she added her organization intends to review its practices. CODAC also undergoes additional oversight, including inspections by the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities, she added.
State oversight under scrutiny
BHDDH spokesperson Randy Edgar said Tuesday in an email that the agency has met with providers, is reviewing the audit findings and is expanding its monitoring efforts.
Separately, the department’s corrective action plan, included in the audit, suggests additional unannounced inspections, internal provider audits and a centralized system to track compliance.
Also in Bergantino’s report is a separate finding of 6,347 potentially improper Medicaid claims totaling $875,696, of which $656,919 is paid with federal funds. The claims involved providers billing for daily methadone treatments, rather than bundling them together weekly as required, according to the audit report.
Bergantino said that these overpayments should be recovered from providers, and the federal government’s share returned.
In its own corrective action plan attached to Bergantino’s report, the Executive Office of Health and Human Services — the state agency which administers Medicaid — said it had already completed a review of the billing issues and was looking into the relevant claims, with “corrective action plans that include recoupments” being crafted at the time of the report.
“We are reviewing the Auditor General’s findings and will work closely together with affected providers to validate the identified billing issues and take corrective actions as outlined on page 30 of the report,” agency spokesperson Kerri White said in an email.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana opens enrollment for 274,000 Medicaid recipients who must switch plans
text:
Medicaid coverage in Louisiana through Healthy Blue will no longer be available in 2027. Its current members can join one of the state's remaining four Medicaid plans over the next month or be assigned to one by the state health department. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The Louisiana Department of Health opened a monthlong enrollment period Thursday for people in the Healthy Blue Medicaid program to switch to another plan for 2027. Enrollment will end Nov. 16. 

Healthy Blue, offered by Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana and Elevance Health, is pulling out of Louisiana’s Medicaid program at the end of the year. The plan’s 274,000 members must join one of the four remaining Medicaid plans, according to Albert Simien, who oversees the health department’s financial office. 

For Healthy Blue members who do not pick a new Medicaid plan, the state health department will assign them to one using an algorithm. The remaining options include Aetna Better Health of Louisiana, AmeriHealth Caritas, Humana Healthy Horizons and Louisiana Healthcare Connections.  

The health department’s algorithm will prioritize keeping family members in Healthy Blue on the same Medicaid plan once switched. It will also try to give Healthy Blue members a new insurer that will cover their existing medical providers, Simien said during a state Senate Health and Welfare Committee hearing this week. 
Healthy Blue members will be notified of their new Medicaid plan in late November and receive follow-up information about the plan in December. 

All prior authorizations for medical treatment given under Healthy Blue will be honored for 60 days, including prescriptions and other treatment that might not be in the participant’s network on their new plan, Simien said. 

This is the second big transition for Louisiana’s Medicaid program this year. 

In April, UnitedHealth left Louisiana’s Medicaid market when Attorney General Liz Murrill threatened to cancel its contract. 

At the time, Murrill was upset UnitedHealth, which covered 330,000 Medicaid members, refused to turn over legal documents about its prescription drug pricing she had requested as part of her lawsuit against the company. 

Approximately 1.3 million Louisiana residents participate in Medicaid, which provides health insurance to people with low incomes or who are pregnant or living with a disability.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: On CT bear hunt, Lamont and Fazio find common ground
text:
When it comes to Connecticut’s increasingly troublesome relationship with black bears, both candidates in this year’s governor’s race are in agreement on a somewhat controversial solution.
Gov. Ned Lamont, the Democratic incumbent, and his opponent, Republican Sen. Ryan Fazio, have both supported measures in recent years to allow the hunting of black bears. Those efforts have been repeatedly defeated by opponents of hunting who argue that non-lethal means can be effective at reducing conflicts with people.
Connecticut is home to between 1,000 and 1,200 black bears, with the population concentrated largely in the state’s northwest corner. Encounters with people — including home break-ins and attacks on livestock — have risen in recent years,  according to wildlife officials. 
However, Connecticut is one of only two states in the Northeast that does not allow bear hunting. The other, Rhode Island, has fewer than a dozen bears.
The state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, which tracks and helps manage the state’s bear population, has repeatedly sought support from lawmakers to establish a regulated hunting season, with Lamont’s backing. Lamont was also asked about the idea during a Democratic primary debate in July, saying he supported a hunt. His opponent in the primary, Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden, said he was opposed.
“The governor supports a limited and carefully regulated bear hunt because Connecticut’s bear population is continuing to grow and we’re seeing more and more conflicts between bears and people every year,” Lamont campaign spokesperson Lauren Gray said in a statement. “Bears are now in all 169 towns, and residents are dealing with bears getting into homes, damaging property and threatening pets and livestock. We’ve tried education, prevention and other measures, and those efforts will continue, but the governor believes we also need to have additional tools available to manage the population and keep people safe.”
Gray added, “That doesn’t mean an unlimited hunt. Any hunt should be regulated and based on the best available science, with DEEP determining the appropriate limits.” 
The most recent serious effort to enact a bear hunt came in 2025, when a bill dealing with the killing of nuisance bears was amended in the Senate to give the governor the ability to order DEEP to schedule a hunting season if the number of conflicts rise to a level that poses “a threat to public safety.” Fazio voted for the amended bill, which passed the chamber on a bipartisan vote of 34-2.
In the House, however, opponents amended the bill again in the final hours of the legislative session to remove the language permitting a hunt. The bill died upon returning to the Senate.
In an interview last week, Fazio said that having a “controlled and regulated bear hunt” is necessary to protect public safety. He specifically pointed to an incident in 2022, when a black bear attacked and injured a 12-year-old boy in Morris.
“We know the bear population is increasing at an unsustainable rate, especially in northwest and north-central and western Connecticut,” Fazio said. “Bears are smarter animals than most, and they have no fear of human beings because of our state policy currently.”
Fazio also criticized the governor’s lack of success in getting a bear hunting bill through the legislature, despite having a 2-1 majority of Democrats in both chambers.
“I think if you can’t get it done in eight years and you think it should get done, then you have a problem, and you deserve some criticism for it,” Fazio said.
In the absence of a hunt, DEEP has focused its efforts to reduce conflicts on a public awareness campaign encouraging residents to take steps such as removing bird feeders and keeping trash cans indoors between the spring and fall, when bears are most active.

In this July 25, 2014, file photo, a black bear in captivity awaits handouts at the the Maine Wildlife Park in Gray, Maine. Credit: Robert F. Bukaty / AP Photo

DEEP also hired a team of researchers from Mississippi State University this summer to conduct the first scientific survey of the state’s bear population in more than a decade. The results of that survey are expected to be released in the spring. 
Sen. Christine Cohen, D-Guilford, a former chair of the legislature’s Environment Committee who has been an outspoken opponent of bear hunting, said state officials lack the data on bear population growth they’d need to determine whether a hunt is necessary. In the meantime, she said, more can be done to condition bears to avoid humans.
“I still contend that if the problem we’re trying to solve is bears coming into neighborhoods, which is what we hear over and over again, killing them doesn’t address the underlying cause — which is really the availability of human food,” Cohen said.
In 2023, Lamont signed a measure passed by lawmakers clarifying the circumstances in which bears may be killed in self-defense and allowing DEEP to issue permits to farmers whose crops or livestock were damaged by nuisance bears. The law also made it illegal to intentionally feed “potentially dangerous animals,” including bobcats, coyotes and bears.
DEEP has since issued 21 permits stemming from agricultural damage, resulting in the lawful killing of 36 bears. 
The agency has also charged at least seven people with unauthorized killings of black bears since 2012. The majority of those cases involved claims of self-defense or defense of animals, according to a review published in CT Insider.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Republican Tom Tiffany seeks to boost turnout in Waukesha with an assist from Brett Favre
text:
Tom Tiffany throws a signed football into the crowd gathered in Stein's Aircraft Services in Waukesha for the get-out-the-vote rally hosted by Hunter Nation, a national nonprofit for hunters, anglers and outdoor enthusiasts. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Former Green Bay Packers quarterback Brett Favre spent the majority of his time on stage in Waukesha on Tuesday night talking about his time playing football. But when the conversation turned to the election, Favre was blunt about what he would say to hunters, Christians, veterans, farmers, factory workers, truck drivers and school teachers who aren’t planning to vote.
“You can’t sit it out. You can’t sit it out,” Favre, a Mississippi native, said. “You can’t bitch if you don’t vote.”
Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is running against Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, came on the stage with Favre, who signed a couple of footballs and handed them to Tiffany. The congressman threw them into the crowd gathered in Stein’s Aircraft Services in Waukesha for the get-out-the-vote rally hosted by Hunter Nation, a national nonprofit for hunters, anglers and outdoor enthusiasts.
The event also featured a presentation on delisting the grey wolf, an auction of a Ted Nugent guitar signed by Favre — claimed by the only person who bid at the starting bid of $5,000 — and a performance by Mark Mackay, a country musician. After talking about the importance of being on the “good side of this battle,” he introduced a song called “I Am Love,” saying that’s what musicians should be talking about instead of politics. 
Tiffany told the Examiner there was no “greater icon in Wisconsin” than Favre and he was glad he could be there to speak on voting and hunting issues. He expressed no concern when asked how his campaign’s accountability and anti-fraud agenda matches up with Favre’s entanglement in a fraud scandal in Mississippi. Favre has repaid the state of Mississippi over $1 million for speeches he was paid for but didn’t deliver, and he is still a defendant in a civil case filed by the Mississippi Department of Human Services to recoup millions of dollars in misspent federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families welfare funds, some of which he allegedly used to build a volleyball stadium.
“He’s appeared before Congress and talked about how requirements need to be tightened up for these various programs,” Tiffany said. “I’m going to do that as governor. I mean accountability is a big part of our agenda to make sure that all agencies are audited and make sure that no one is stealing from the taxpayers.”
Tiffany hit on a number of his campaign priorities, including rooting out fraud and auditing state government, during the rally. One of the biggest cheers he received was for saying he’d sign a bill to open a hunting season on sandhill cranes. 
“Yeah, baby!” one man yelled out in response. 
A number of people in the crowd wore Favre jerseys. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Waukesha County, one of the historically  Republican-leaning “WOW counties,” has trended a little less red in recent elections, including in the 2026 April state Supreme Court race.
Rep. Adam Neylon (R-Pewaukee), who is running for reelection to the Assembly and, simultaneously, for Waukesha County executive, said Tiffany has been putting in the work in the county to ensure people turn out and vote for Republicans there.
“He is everywhere. You would think he’s running for a local office in Waukesha County,” Neylon said. “He’s run a very aggressive campaign where he has really committed to the ground game. He’s also really strong at retail politics. He shows up, he listens and he speaks the language of Wisconsin.”
Attorney general candidate Eric Toney told the Examiner that Republicans “can’t take any area for granted.”
“Waukesha County, certainly has been crucial over the years with Republican voters or conservative voters in this area, and we just need people all across the state coming out to vote, and not just talking to folks that might live in their own city or county.” 
Rep. Jim Piwowarczyk (R-Hubertus), who is seeking reelection to his Assembly district that represents parts of Washington County, said he thinks the election will come down to turnout. Recent Marquette Law School polling has shown Crowley up slightly ahead of Tiffany. 
“We, as Republicans, if Tom Tiffany’s down three points, we actually consider that to be a good thing for our side. We think our candidates usually pull a little bit or actually end up doing a little bit better. I think it’s neck and neck right now. It’s very close. I think it’s going to come out to turnout,” Piwowarczyk said. “I’ve seen the polling myself and it’s very close.”
Piwowarczyk said the rally and other events are helping people get excited. He said he has been knocking doors in his district and has also been up to the other areas of the state, including the Green Bay area, a purple region that contains multiple competitive state legislative races.
“We have a lot of people excited to get out there. I think that they have been very frustrated by Tony Evers and the ever-increasing taxes, and they’re excited for Tiffany,” Piwowarczyk said. 
U.S. Reps. Bryan Steil and Scott Fitzgerald also attended the event and warned that Democrats want to pursue a radical agenda most voters don’t agree with. 
“When we see how radicalized the Democratic party has become, where they are going after all aspects of our culture from putting boys in girls sports to higher taxes… Their attacks on core aspects of our culture are real and substantive, and they will want to come after our hunting rights.”  
Steil told the crowd not to underestimate turnout in Milwaukee and Madison, the state’s largest cities. His own seat, long considered safe, is a target for Democrats this year and Democrat Mitchell Berman is giving him a competitive race.
“Run on the assumption that the Democrats are going to vote in full strength here in the liberal core cities in Wisconsin,” Steil said. “Every single person in the state of Wisconsin, who has a world view like those of us in this room, who stays home in three weeks from today, is effectively voting for a Democrat, and we need to get that message out to our friends, our family, our neighbors, our co-workers, folks at church.”
A number of people in the crowd wore Favre jerseys, and his presence was part of what brought out Michael Harrell, a 74-year-old New Berlin resident. He told the Examiner with a smile that he attended the rally because he “wanted to see Brett Favre.”
“I don’t know Tom Tiffany’s voting record or any of that stuff, but I vote Republican regardless,” Harrell said. He said he’s voted for the party since former President Richard Nixon was elected. 
“We’ve got God in our platform. We got common sense, and even though there are the RINOs, we got a lot of good people out there,” Harrell said. “We love America like the president does.”
President Donald Trump isn’t running this year, but in  recent weeks, he has been on the campaign trail telling people to pretend he is on the ballot.
Neylon said Trump’s absence from the ballot has been a concern for some, but he’s seen enthusiasm growing for the midterms.
“Republicans are going to turn out,” Neylon said. “Republicans are over performing in Wisconsin compared nationally, and I think part of that is because we have really good candidates, and I think Wisconsin is going to be another example of why candidates really matter.”
Tiffany shakes hands with attendees at the October rally. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Trump has been a motivator for Republicans to get out to vote in recent elections but he has also fallen in popularity in Wisconsin. Tiffany has recently distanced himself from the second-term president, despite reliably voting for the president’s agenda in Congress and receiving Trump’s strong endorsement. This week he would not say in an interview with WMTJ whether he approves of the job Trump is doing. 
“The president is doing what he believes is best for the United States of America,” Tiffany said.
Neylon said Tiffany has been able to insulate himself from Trump’s unpopularity by keeping on message and talking about lowering taxes, reducing regulations and protecting Act 10, the law passed under Gov. Scott Walker that restricted collective bargaining for public employees. 
“He’s been really consistent and focused on a message that’s different than some of the national messages you hear from federal candidates, so I don’t think people are necessarily tying them together,” Neylon said. “When you look at how each person is spending their time, there’s differences, and people see that.”
The Wisconsin state Senate and Assembly are also up for grabs this year. The Republican Assembly members said the quality of the candidates running in competitive seats will be the thing that helps Republicans hold their majorities. 
Neylon said people shouldn’t judge Wisconsin races by “national headwinds.” 
“I’m more concerned that we lose majorities at the federal level than I am at the state level,” Neylon said. 
Harrell said he thought Trump could help Tiffany get over the finish line. He said he thinks Trump has been doing a good job and that he isn’t too worried about high gas prices, which recently reached record highs.
“He’s gonna pull something here, I think, on the gas and this stuff. We’re gonna maybe see that before the election,” Harrell said. He added that he thinks Democratic candidate David Crowley has “flubbed up” Milwaukee and doesn’t want him to lead the state. 
“There’s so many crazy people nowadays, you just, you don’t know. You don’t know what’s gonna happen,” Harrell said. “I mean you hope God intervenes and has already got it planned out, but all we can do is hope — hope, and pray.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Forget the dadgum cookies. In race between Roger Marshall and Adam Hamilton, follow the money.
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Everyone was chattering about cookies late last week.
Specifically, political pundits and their online fans were discussing U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, apparently stiffing a local bakery back in 2020. A bill of $678.75 went unpaid. Marshall finally reimbursed the small business owner, no doubt hoping to make the viral story go away.
But another report emerged on Friday, a thoroughly researched and damning account by Kansas Reporter editor-in-chief Sherman Smith and MS NOW’s Matt Fuller. It might have been overshadowed by the cookie caterwauling, but it shouldn’t have been.
Sometimes bills go unpaid. But Smith and Fuller’s story suggests that Marshall’s Washington, D.C., office skirted ethical lines, blurring boundaries between taxpayer-funded official business and campaigning.
Experts contacted for comment raised alarms. Marshall’s lawyers refused to address the substance of the reporting.
If you’re looking for red flags, friends, they’re here. And not just one or two.
Here are just five alarming paragraphs selected from Smith and Fuller’s damning story. The questions raised and comments made suggest to me — at best — an operation willing to take numerous and repeated ethical shortcuts. At worst? Well, I’m not a campaign finance expert. But you can see how they reacted below.




“In a joint investigation, Kansas Reflector and MS NOW obtained audio recordings, photos, videos, screenshots of text messages and calendar items from 2020 — when Marshall first ran for his Senate seat — that appear to show the senator and his top aide repeatedly using congressional staff and government resources in ways that experts say likely crossed the line between official business and campaigning.”
“Craig Holman, a campaign finance and government ethics expert at Public Citizen — a nonprofit consumer rights and good government group founded by Ralph Nader — said these accounts of Marshall and his office’s ‘blatant disregard’ for congressional ethics rules are ‘both breathtaking and seemingly very damning of Marshall’s character.’ ”
“Both congressional and campaign staff — many using taxpayer-funded equipment like cellphones and computers — were summoned to the ‘MANDATORY ALL-STAFF CALL,’ as it appeared in their official email calendars. And video of the Oct. 14, 2020, Zoom call shows Marshall and his congressional aides discussing the status of his campaign.”

I need to break in here to note that this all-staff call raised sufficient alarm among staff that they set down their concerns for posterity. Marshall’s then-legislative director, Michael Brooks, texted a staffer: “Sending this message as a reference that we objected to this illegal (activity) and that I raised it with our superiors and noted that it is not permissible per the above ethics statute.”

Marshall flack Payton “Fuller is both a current congressional staffer — earning a taxpayer-funded salary — and an unpaid campaign volunteer spokeswoman. For that separate story involving Marshall’s Florida property, MS NOW reached out to a generic press email for the campaign. Fuller wrote back, from her campaign email, as ‘communications director for Senator Roger Marshall.’ ”
“After promising to ‘meaningfully’ respond to a detailed list of questions if Kansas Reflector and MS NOW extended its deadline for comment, Ryan Dollar, a lawyer for the Marshall campaign, sent a statement that did not address the questions.”

Ahem. On Monday, I wrote about the panoply of peculiar stories that attach themselves like so many barnacles to Marshall. This story doesn’t quite fit. It speaks to norms. It speaks to ethics. It speaks to whether the senator and his staff follow the basic rules applied across government offices.
It speaks to character.





I understand why Kansans and others across the nation fixated on the cookie story. It has all the ingredients of irresistible campaign gossip: a sympathetic protagonist, apparent hypocrisy from the candidate involved and an easy-to-understand narrative.


But more complicated stories and more challenging subjects matter too. In fact, they usually matter more.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Gov. Tony Evers tours new Milwaukee juvenile facility for 32 boys
text:
Gov. Tony Evers looks at different rooms inside the Southeast Regional Care Center for Youth. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Gov. Tony Evers toured a new Milwaukee juvenile facility on Wednesday along with Department of Corrections leaders, closing another chapter in the troubled history of the Lincoln Hills and Copper Lake youth prisons. The sleek, colorful new facility looked like  a well-resourced though highly secure school. The Southeast Regional Care Center for Youth, or SERC, will house 32 boys who are in the DOC’s custody. 
While serving their sentences the boys will have access to educational programs, a gym, a greenhouse and other opportunities to help prepare them to return to their communities. Since many of the boys will be from the Milwaukee area, the new $65.6 million facility will make it easier for their families to visit compared to Lincoln Hills, hours away in Irma, Wisconsin. 
The Southeast Regional Care Center for Youth. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“This new facility marks a historic milestone for our state and is the beginning of what I hope is a real, meaningful transformation of not only juvenile corrections in our state but of corrections in Wisconsin,” Evers said. “Not only will this new facility allow us to safely move our kids closer to their homes, their families, and their support systems, but it will give kids and families hope for a brighter future. With evidence-based strategies, this new facility will provide young people the role models, educational opportunities, and support needed so they can grow, be better, and do better, all while helping to reduce crime, prevent violence, and keep our kids, families and communities safe.”
SERC is located on Milwaukee’s North Side, tucked away a few blocks  from a busy roadway just north of Good Hope Road. At first glance the tan brick building resembles a small school, but a closer look reveals  large tinted windows and a few State Patrol vehicles parked outside. Walking through the front door, visitors come to  a metal detector station in a  front lobby with light colored walls, tiled floor and chairs. 
Wednesday’s official  tour of the new facility began with a visit to the SERC’s chapel. Next, Evers was guided by DOC Sec. Jared Hoy and DOC juvenile corrections administrator Lance Horozewski to an outside area surrounded by a high brick wall and security gate, where Evers viewed a basketball court and a large greenhouse next to  raised garden beds — one for each boy which the facility will house.
Classrooms within the Southeast Regional Care Center for Youth. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Heading back inside, Hoy and Horozewski showcased medical facilities with individual exam rooms and areas where youth can access needed dental care. There was also a large kitchen, and spaces where youth could learn welding and woodworking. Evers also looked over visiting areas complete with games and kiosks for video visits, a large indoor gym and basketball court and classrooms. Evers also checked out a creative room where the boys will be able to make and record music, and even make videos using a large green screen.
The area where the boys will be housed was  behind a door, which will be controlled by staff monitoring from an adjacent room. A common space contained couches, tables, a couple of phones and games. Down the hall were dorm rooms with wood floors and gray metal furniture, with one bed per room, a toilet, desk, and a window with a view of the outdoors, with a blind the boys can open or close. 
The design of SERC is intended to forge a new direction for juvenile incarceration in Wisconsin. For years, the Lincoln Hills and Copper Lake schools were  notorious for reports of abuse and suffering for both youth housed there and the staff responsible for their care. Earlier this year, a federal judge ended mandatory oversight of Lincoln Hills and Copper Lake after the DOC had been found to be in “substantial compliance” with reforms mandated after a 2018 class action settlement.
The garden and greenhouse area of the new juvenile facility in Milwaukee. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Lincoln Hills’ troubled history led the Legislature to spend years planning to close the 500-bed facility, convert it to an adult prison, and open up smaller and safer juvenile facilities which would also be closer to home for the youth housed there. 
Evers appeared to approve of SERC as he walked through its halls. “But our work is not over — far from it, ” he said in a statement. “Our state is decades behind in how we think about corrections, and this new facility is the first step, but it is only a step. We must continue our work to modernize our corrections system into the 21st century and close Lincoln Hills and Copper Lake schools for good.”
Hoy said that looking around SERC “you see a school, not a prison.” He went on to say in a statement that “that’s because it is a school and even more. It’s a place to learn and to heal. There’s no barbed wire. No towers. There are big windows, color, space. And it’s all secure both for the youth and for the neighborhood. The design supports what we now know about adolescent development, and the programming offered here will follow suit with staff using evidence-based techniques to help youth make better choices and support rehabilitation.”
Hoy said at the beginning of November the first group of youth will be moved into SERC, with more to come over the following months into the holidays. “We’ve been recruiting for staff starting back in the summer,” said Hoy. “And so we’ve had two graduating classes already. We’ll have more than adequate staff. Not just safety staff — so your youth counselors that are here  — but education, treatment, all of those different functions are already on board…And then we will continue to staff up. We have another class graduating, I think at the beginning of November.”
Keana Berkhalter (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Staffing shortages had long plagued Lincoln Hills and other DOC facilities. Hoy told the Wisconsin Examiner that the DOC has paid particular attention to staff-to-youth ratios for the SERC to help prevent burnout among staff, and has established staff wellness spaces. Hoy also said that “the space itself lends to a sort of feeling of wellness and calmness.”
Another Type 1 facility is being constructed in Dane County which is designed to hold 32 boys and eight girls. The DOC is also pushing for a third facility to be opened in northern Wisconsin in order to serve youth from that region of the state. Hoy told the Examiner that having multiple facilities would allow the DOC to cross-train and pull staff from one facility to another in order to help fill any gaps and prevent burnout.
Many of the staff who will work at the new facility are from the Milwaukee area, and theoretically might have an advantage in  relating with the youth there. Kashunda Brown, 37, one of SERC’s youth counselors, explained that she grew up on the North Side of Milwaukee where she learned what it’s like to experience poverty and living in a single parent home. Brown also has two boys of her own which “resonates with the youth that we encounter here,” she told the Examiner. 
Kashunda Brown (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Keana Berkhalter, 32, a licensed counselor who will be working with the facility’s Psychological Services Unit, is also from Milwaukee. “I’ve seen the complex issues and challenges that we have here, as well as the strengths that Milwaukee has,” Berkhalter told the Examiner. Berkhalter said that it’s important that youth know that the staff understand them because it helps them feel safe. “As human beings, it’s easier to connect to people that look like us, or at least that we have some sort of similar commonality.” 
The experiences the counselors share with the youth help them to connect. “I think that gives me leverage to connect to the youth, as well as help them feel safe and to talk to me and to want to trust and confide in me, to talk about things that maybe they don’t want to talk to anybody about.”
Brown said the greenhouse, raised beds, and creative spaces are especially important for the boys SERC will house. To anyone who questions whether the facility should feel more punitive, Brown says, “I think the punitive is them being away from their family.” 
Gov. Tony Evers (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
She continued, “this should be, and is, a space where they can have different things that they don’t experience on the outside. A lot of people don’t have access to a basketball court at home. A lot of people don’t have access to gardening.” These translate into coping skills the boys can take home with them to avoid getting in trouble. 
Youth who learn that they enjoy woodworking, cooking, growing food in the garden or other activities available at SERC could take that with them and become more productive members of society, Brown said. “I think all the skills that they will get here, they can use on the outside. The punitive is them being in here.”
