name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania’s attorney general accuses insulin makers, PBMs of insulin ‘pricing scheme’
text:
As drug prices increase, a number of state attorneys general have sued drug manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers over insulin prices. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)State Attorney General Dave Sunday’s office claims that more than a dozen pharmaceutical companies and pharmacy middlemen worked together to “artificially” inflate insulin prices by more than 1,000%. 
“Millions of Pennsylvanians have diabetes or prediabetes and they were all potentially harmed by this scheme to artificially inflate pricing to maximize company profits,” Sunday said in a release. “Our Antitrust Section will continue to hold accountable companies, large and small, that prioritize profits over public access to affordable life-saving medication and care.”
Pa. Attorney General Dave Sunday signs letter supporting federal PBM transparency rule

Tuesday’s lawsuit, filed in the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania, accuses manufacturers such as Eli Lilly and Company, Novo Nordisk, Inc. and Sanofi-Aventis US LLC of working with pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) such as Express Scripts, CVS Caremark and Optum RX to increase prices. 
PBMs operate as brokers between manufacturers, distributors and pharmacies, with a role under increasing scrutiny from lawmakers, regulators and critics — some of whom claim their existence adds to increasing drug prices. 
The three biggest PBMs, all parties to the lawsuit, manage roughly 80% of all prescription drug claims in addition to being owned by parent companies overseeing major insurance or pharmacy companies, setting up potential conflicts of interest. 
Sunday is the latest state attorney general to sue over insulin prices — a list that includes 2026 lawsuits filed in both Oregon and Florida. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission announced settlement agreements with Caremark and Express Scripts after the agency accused three PBMS of driving up list prices. 
The case against the third PBM, Optum, was withdrawn to consider a proposed consent agreement, according to the agency. 
In most cases, insulin costs no more than $35 per month, but many still report rationing their medication. Without insulin or proper management, people can develop kidney failure, require amputation or die.
Sunday’s lawsuit seeks injunctive relief, changes to force lower prices and restitution for harmed Pennsylvanians.

name: California
title: MyChart and a major hospital said I could opt out of sharing my health data. But they didn’t make it easy
text:
Dr. Shira Fischer, a physician who works in health policy in Boston, sought a speech pathologist for her child in 2022, when virtual appointments became the norm because of COVID-19. 
“I read their consent and they said they were going to record and use [our appointment] for training. And I said, no, my kid has a lisp. The last thing she wants is videos of her lisping to be used for training for who knows how long and who knows what database.” 
Fischer said the clinic wouldn’t change the consent, and wouldn’t proceed with the appointment if she didn’t sign it. Eventually, she found a different speech pathologist. “It ended up being better. But what is that, that they require you to allow them to record for their training?” 



Had a similar experience? Tell us
This story was originally published on The Markup, now a part of CalMatters. 
If you’ve gone to an appointment in California and have struggled with opting out of sharing your data, or if you’re a doctor or patient in California who has had challenges with AI transcription, we’d love to hear from you.

Email Alex Rosenblat, our Director of Sociotechnical Research, at arosenblat@calmatters.org.
If you’re worried about being tracked or discovered, you can send messages and files securely by using the Signal app (download it here). Reach Alex on Signal: 530-364-1838




Every day, doctor’s offices across the country tell patients that if they want to see the doctor, they must allow their health data to be accessible by tens of thousands of hospitals and clinics. Often, doctors give out overly broad consent forms, asking patients to agree to anything from hospitals using patient files for training doctors to using patient data for training AI.
Practically speaking, when a patient doesn’t agree, doctors can turn them away.
Other times, doctors’ offices tell patients they can opt-out of sharing their data later — by contacting an email address or mailing a physical letter — but in reality, opting out can be so difficult and confusing that it isn’t really a choice at all.

When I was pregnant with my child, I wondered why my gynecologists’ forms asked me to let another company, Phreesia, mine my health data for marketing. The authorization form was labeled “Required” even though it legally must be optional. I systematically opted out and kept my own records of this, but when I tried to confirm my opt-outs with Phreesia, it said I did consent. After 81 days of back and forth, Phreesia admitted I had never authorized them to use my data. But it continued to use the misleading “Required” label on the authorization form. Months later, after complaining to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and an episode of “The Indicator from Planet Money” on NPR, Phreesia changed how it labeled its forms. I found the process galling, but it spurred my curiosity, and I’ve been researching how opt-outs work ever since.
In the last year, I registered as a patient at 25 clinics and hospitals across seven states and spent hundreds of hours reviewing consent forms, privacy policies and marketing forms to see whether I could actually opt out of sharing my data.
For one hospital in Ohio, it took me 26 steps, a notary, and a flight to Las Vegas to learn how to opt out of the hospital’s many uses of my patient records. Despite my best efforts, the hospital will not follow its own policy, which ostensibly allows patients to refuse to allow the hospital to take and own photos and recordings of them.

It started last January, when I sought a second opinion on a personal health issue with a specialist at University Hospitals in Westlake, Ohio. University Hospitals is a large, nonprofit hospital system that manages its electronic health records through MyChart, a widely used patient portal across the country. MyChart is made by Epic Systems, a healthcare software company in Verona, Wisconsin, that says it has over 305 million patient charts, coming from patients in every state and more than a dozen countries. 
As I prepared for my appointment, the hospital asked me to sign its registration forms and to sign up for MyChart. In the dense terms of service, I spot three different ways that as a patient, my data is about to be used, accessed or shared:

The hospital will share my health data through Epic’s proprietary health information platform, Care Everywhere. 
The hospital will share my data with CliniSync, an Ohio-based nonprofit health information exchange that facilitates the exchange of patients’ information, like lab results, across institutions. 
The hospital will own any photos, audio, or video they take of me and may use them for any lawful purpose.

In each case, I’m told that I can opt-out or refuse, but the process felt like it was designed to keep me from doing so. Forms and websites lacked basic contact information; customer service didn’t respond; patients were required to find a notary, and hospital staff directly contradicted their own written policies and told me I wasn’t allowed to opt-out.
So I set out to see what it would truly take to say no to sharing my data, starting with Epic.
There’s no button to revoke authorization everywhere
Once a hospital makes a patient’s records available through Epic’s Care Everywhere, many clinicians who works with Epic across the country can pull up those records, with some exceptions. 
The most common way doctors use health exchanges is to get up to speed on a patient who is coming to see them. Sharing patient health records through exchanges has decreased duplicative tests on patients. It also allows emergency room doctors who have never seen a patient before to immediately get their health history and allergies, which can save a patient’s life, said Saurabh Rahurkar, a former assistant professor at Ohio State University College of Medicine.
Individual hospitals can also restrict which doctors can see a patient’s files, such as by physical distance, or by adding an extra confirmation step before doctors can see the files of patients who have received psychological services. 

“If you say to your new doctor, ‘Please go get my records at this place that’s 3,000 miles away,’ Care Everywhere can do that, but not if the system has the settings to only look for records within a 50-mile radius,” said Lucia Savage, former chief privacy officer at the federal health IT office. 
But there are clear reasons why some patients don’t want their data to show up in these searches, and hospital protections, if they exist at all, are not always effective.
For example, a patient who crosses state lines to seek an abortion treatment may not want her records to be searchable by her providers in her home state where that treatment is criminalized. 
“People who have had bad experiences with unauthorized access to their information and people who have sensitive health conditions and diagnoses for very good reasons, are just mistrusting of the healthcare system,” said Julia Adler-Milstein, a leading researcher in health IT policy and a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco. “(They) don’t feel like the healthcare system has been a good steward of them and their information.” 
For example, researchers reviewing 1,138 breach cases found that almost 10% of patient health data breaches come from unauthorized access by health care employees who forward personally identifying information to personal accounts.
Nichole Sweeney, who was recently the chief privacy officer and general counsel at CRISP Shared Services, which provides technology infrastructure to support health exchanges in more than 10 states, said she often encounters providers snooping in patient records in her job as a privacy officer: “Somebody, a provider in an office, looks up an ex, and we find that because we have monitoring software, and I have to call them and tell them not to do that anymore. They get fired sometimes.”
Cason Schmit, a health law and policy professor at Texas A&M University, warned, “We’re at a place in time where data that are being collected to help people are now being used in ways that could actively and specifically harm them.” He pointed to how Immigration and Customs Enforcement has used health data for immigration enforcement. Schmit has written about the role of state policy in fostering health information exchange and its benefits to the public, such as tracking measles outbreaks.
In my attempt to opt out of Epic’s Care Everywhere, I first looked for a way to do it with MyChart. I navigated through 40-plus menu items, including the “Sharing Hub,” where I watched videos on Care Everywhere that explained its benefits but not how to restrict its uses. In the end, I found one section under “Authorize Sharing” that said I could “request that your information no longer be shared” by sending a message to customer service. I tried that. I got no response.
Then I tried emailing and calling the hospital system’s ethics and compliance department to opt out of Care Everywhere. Crickets.
After weeks of dead-ends, I found something that worked. When I called MyChart’s patient support number, the representative said I could opt out by contacting the hospital’s medical records department. I called medical records, and they called back that day and confirmed I was opted out of Care Everywhere.
But how are patients supposed to know about this process? I couldn’t find “contact medical records” described anywhere in MyChart or on the hospital’s website.
I asked Epic for an interview, and they agreed to let me speak with Matt Doyle, who leads software development for Care Everywhere. Turns out, both of us were about to be in Las Vegas, for one of the largest healthcare tradeshow conferences in the country. I arrived early at the Epic booth, which is well-appointed among its peers in the Exhibition hall with carpets and a private meeting room. Posters proudly announced that health providers exchange approximately 22 million patient records each day through Care Everywhere.
Doyle walked over from a hub of Epic employees clicking through MyChart screens with conference attendees, and led me to the meeting room along with a colleague from public relations.
“So when you check in for your appointment, the de facto position is you’re part of Care Everywhere,” Doyle confirmed, “unless you explicitly opt out.” 
I recount for him everything I tried, and how there was nothing I could click in MyChart to opt out.
“It’s not in the MyChart enrollment process,” Doyle clarified, “but as soon as your MyChart account is set up, you can immediately go opt out.”
Doyle explained that there are two levels of opting out. 

“One is, ‘Revoke authorization, but I still want to be discoverable,’” he said. “And what that would mean is, let’s say today you’re in a car accident. You go to the emergency department. Your doctor’s office back in Ohio doesn’t have your authorization on file, but you’re discoverable.” Meaning, a doctor could see that a specific patient has a health record, and can ask the patient for his or her consent to access that record. 
The second level of opting out is to be completely undiscoverable through Care Everywhere. In this case, doctors who work in other hospital systems can’t see any record of the patient in Care Everywhere. It’s a choice only 112 patients have made since they rolled out the ability to opt out this way in August 2025, Doyle said.
There’s one extra twist. Doyle confirmed that there isn’t a single place to revoke authorization everywhere. “You have to go to each custodian of your medical records,” he clarified. A patient would revoke access to Care Everywhere “with each place that you receive care.”
“Can you show me how to opt out?” I asked. 
Doyle brought me back out to Epic’s booth, where employees have demos of MyChart on multiple screens. Doyle tried to find a demo where he can show me a new, patient-facing feature to revoke authorizations for data sharing. But the patient in the demo product had not signed any authorizations, so there was no way to show me how to revoke them.
I asked the next public relations representative who joined us if I could see it on her MyChart. She pulled it up on her phone, went to the “Sharing Hub” menu options, but we didn’t see the “Revoke authorization” button. We looked at Doyle, who then explained that only organizations that have updated their Epic software would have the opt-out methods that he described. He offered to show me on a video call the following week. 
Until a patient’s healthcare provider updates their software from Epic, Doyle confirmed that a patient’s only option is to call the medical records department and tell them “I would like to opt out of Care Everywhere.”
A week later, three Epic representatives joined my meeting with Doyle to show me how to opt out in the Sharing Hub section of MyChart. 
“There’s two different places,” explained Sean Bina, vice president of access and patient experience at Epic, as he showed me the buttons in MyChart. “One is ‘managing my record authorizations.’ And then the second is how I can prevent other organizations from requesting a record.”
After months of trying, I finally got to see actual buttons inside of MyChart that would let me opt out.
After this interview, Epic did not respond to further questions from CalMatters and The Markup about Care Everywhere, including how many current patients have the ability to see the opt out buttons inside of MyChart.

A prime example of how using health data for profit involves companies that use what expecting parents search for or watch online and what they’ve shopped for, to target them with baby ads.
Mary Ebeling, a sociologist at Drexel University who wrote the book “Healthcare and Big Data,” had just learned in March 2011 that her doctor could no longer detect a heartbeat in her 11th or 12th week of pregnancy. 
“After learning that I lost the pregnancy, literally, I came home, and my mail carrier delivered the first issue of a year’s subscription [of the now-defunct magazine American Baby] for free,” she recalled. “I had not signed up for it — to American Baby. And I was like I’m getting angry right now about it.” 
The unsolicited baby-themed marketing continued, and she eventually discovered that the data broker Experian was selling her information in a database of “new parents.”
Commercially gathered data, such as Ebeling’s online search or purchasing history, doesn’t have the same legal protections as health records at healthcare facilities, which are covered by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). But that protection isn’t bulletproof. Past Markup investigations have found that HIPAA-covered hospitals were sending sensitive patient data to Facebook through Meta’s tracking pixel.
Federal law also allows confidential substance use disorder treatment records to be shared in certain circumstances, such as with probation officers.
As a part of her work, Jacqueline Seitz, deputy director of health privacy at the Legal Action Center, frequently speaks with patients who use drugs, are in recovery, are living with HIV, and/or are in treatment for substance use disorders. She also regularly speaks with the health providers who treat them.
“When I talk to providers and I ask them what they tell patients, they say, ‘We tell patients everything is confidential.’ And that is not the right thing to say. That is not true,” Seitz said.
For patients who are mandated into treatment in order to maintain their employment, custody access or probation, when asked, their medical records must be shared with probation officers or other legal authorities, Seitz explained. It’s why she increasingly sees electronic health records as a rap sheet.
“I don’t think people are trying to trick patients,” she said, but she regularly sees examples of healthcare workers not fully understanding confidentiality rules in these cases.
Opting out of CliniSync, Ohio’s statewide nonprofit health information exchange
In addition to being asked to sign up for MyChart when I registered for my appointment at the University Hospitals in Westlake, Ohio, I was also asked to acknowledge my participation in CliniSync.
CliniSync, Ohio’s statewide nonprofit health information exchange, facilitates the exchange of patients’ information, like lab results, across institutions. CliniSync is operated by the Ohio Health Information Partnership, an independent private nonprofit founded in 2009. Ohio’s governor designated the partnership to develop the statewide exchange.
The hospital system posts many of its forms online, so I had time to research the General Consent to treatment form in advance. That alerted me to how patients are defaulted into sharing their data with CliniSync. 

A quick online search for “UH privacy policy” (UH stands for University Hospitals) brought me to the hospital system’s HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices. It says I can opt out of CliniSync if I contact their privacy officer over the phone, and it gives me an email and phone number. I emailed right away. I didn’t hear back before my appointment four days later.
I also know that CliniSync likely has its own policy, separate from the hospital system’s, so I also searched for its opt-out policy online. The instructions are simple but surprised me: CliniSync asks patients to notarize its opt-out form.
“It’s a big time suck for people. They’re going to have to spend a lot of time finding a notary. They’re going to have to pay that notary, almost certainly, unless they happen to have a friend or family member who’s a notary public,” said Lior Strahilevitz, a legal scholar at the University of Chicago who writes about privacy and teaches health law. Not only is requiring a notary burdensome, it’s also legally questionable. General guidance from the federal government states that HIPAA authorizations do not need to be notarized.
Still, I paid the $15 at UPS to get the form notarized and mailed it out.
The Ohio Health Information Partnership, which operates CliniSync, declined to respond to questions about why it requires patients to get their opt-out requests notarized.
Finally, on the day of my appointment, I tried what should have been the easiest method for patients: Asking the hospital to opt-me out in-person.
When I asked the receptionist at my appointment how I could opt out of CliniSync, she said she didn’t know, but she’d run my request up the chain while I was with the doctor. When I came back, she had an answer: Patients can’t opt-out. A colleague at the hospital told her through email that CliniSync “ensures that providers across various hospital organizations are able to request and access patient medical records, as it relates to medical need and treatment. This is not feasible to be ‘removed’ from clinisync.”
CliniSync does, in fact, have a form to let patients opt out. And clinic staff can sign the form so that patients don’t have to find a notary instead. It says so right on the CliniSync opt-out form.
But in my research into how difficult it is for patients to opt out of processes like this, multiple hospital staff have given me inaccurate information. I wasn’t surprised.
Strahilevitz described this as a common problem in any bureaucracy, a phenomenon known as “desk clerk law.” 
“Basically, there’s what the law is, and then there’s what the person at the DMV who’s actually interfacing with the consumer thinks the law is or what the person at the Secretary of State’s office is,” Strahilevitz said. “And so I would regard your experience with the receptionist as a classic instance of desk clerk law.”
University Hospitals declined to respond to questions about whether its patients can opt out of CliniSync, and did not have an expert available for an interview. 
After my appointment, I called the hospital’s compliance office and a few days later, I got a voicemail asking for more information over email, or for me to call them back. Since I know that Ohio law requires requests to opt out be written, I emailed the hospital with what they ask for. When no one responded, I called and emailed again.
Soon after my appointment, I got a hand-addressed letter from CliniSync confirming my opt-out and saying they processed it shortly after they received my notarized letter. I’m pleasantly surprised, because I’ve followed many opt-out processes in the last year, and it’s uncommon to get verification like this.
Two weeks after I saw the doctor, the hospital’s compliance office confirmed my opt-out from CliniSync over email.

Because CliniSync records a patient’s opt-out centrally, one request blocks other providers from seeing a patient’s records through CliniSync’s network, but for many health exchanges, including Epic’s Care Everywhere, patients would have to discover and follow an opt-out process at each new provider. 
Sweeney, who was the chief privacy officer and general counsel at a company that supported health exchanges in more than 10 states, estimated that a typical patient might have to opt out of data-sharing at as many as 10 different places — wherever they seek care — for their opt-out to be meaningful. 
In most states, she said, “the place to cut off the data exchange is at the provider because that’s where it starts.” 
In some rare cases, patients do not need to go through this complicated opt-out process, because their clinic refuses to share any patient data with health databases or platforms, simply because patients haven’t explicitly consented.
Dr. Keith Smith runs the Surgery Center of Oklahoma, which markets transparent pricing and cash payment. The center does not accept insurance or Medicare, and it has tried to refuse government agencies’ requests for patient data, such as from the state health department. 
“There’s no shortage of people that will claim that they have a legal right to see how many patients operated on at Surgery Center of Oklahoma had breast cancer or had inguinal hernia repairs,” he said. “And the patients haven’t consented to the release of their records.”
Because Smith’s surgery center does not accept federal dollars, he isn’t obligated to report as much information to the government. “We treat patients here as individuals. And I don’t think it’s right to violate the rights of an individual for the greater good,” he said. “All the individual cares about is that their rights have been violated.”
Refusing to let the hospital own my photos, videos or recordings
In addition to asking me to share my patient records with multiple health exchanges in order to see my doctor, University Hospitals also required me to give it complete ownership over any photos, audio or videos it takes of me. Its consent form states, “UH may, unless otherwise refused, photograph and/or audio or video record me or the Services I receive, including those in which I am identifiable. UH will own such images or recordings and may use them for any lawful purpose.”
I have rarely pondered the possibilities: If the doctor takes a picture of a rash on my child’s body for diagnostic purposes, would I want the hospital to claim ownership over or have broad rights to use that photo?
The consent form says I can refuse, but when I asked the hospital’s compliance and ethics office, they wouldn’t let me. 
“…we are not able to accept modifications or partial withdrawals of specific provisions within the General Consent for Treatment itself,” said the hospital’s email. “This includes provisions related to incidental recording that may occur as part of delivering or documenting care.”
That surprised me. In hospital systems, the compliance office is usually where staff have privacy expertise. The hospital refused to follow its own policy.
University Hospitals declined to respond to questions about whether its patients can refuse giving the hospital ownership over images and recordings it takes of patients.
“It’s misrepresentation,” said Strahilevitz, the University of Chicago expert. “So I think that’s just fraud to tell you you have a right and then telling you, ‘No, we were wrong. You don’t, in fact, have that right. And now your photograph and/or audio and/or video is going to be used.’”
Fischer, who refused to see a speech pathologist because the doctor’s office insisted on a right to record her child’s lisp treatment, said she sees health providers requiring parents to agree to clauses like this all the time.
“I can’t get a link to telehealth appointments for my kids without signing agreements that include things like ‘authorize the use of photos, videos, and/or recordings’ and ‘give permission for staff (including students) to participate and/or watch for training purposes’ or other things I don’t want to agree to,” she said. “But there is no option to not sign.”
Experts say there are practical design and regulatory solutions
Colin Gray, an assistant professor at Indiana University Bloomington and a leading expert on manipulative designs said, “You start from the position of defeat rather than starting from the position where you’re making a rational choice … the attitude is, ‘Well, if you really cared about your data, then you would go through the extra steps to turn it off.’ And in this case, it’s like, ‘That’s an hour of my time or 26 steps or whatever it is that I don’t have.’ And so it looks so onerous from the beginning, like, why would you even try?”
Experts like Stacey Tovino, a professor who teaches HIPAA privacy law at the University of Oklahoma College of Law, say there’s a clear and practical solution: “Amend these [federal] regulations to say covered entities shall not impose an undue burden on people trying to opt out.” Tovino suggested that when patients see that they can opt out in a form, the next sentence should include a link to do so.
Some states have laws that require this type of solution. Under New York law, for example, providers need explicit consent from patients to access their data from health information exchanges. I saw it firsthand when I registered my son for an appointment in upstate New York. The check-in screens showed me a form labelled “Health Exchange,” and asked for my consent for the physician group to access all of the patient’s medical records through Healthix, a health exchange. When I clicked “No,” the next form showed the detailed consent form with “I DENY CONSENT” selected as one of my two choices. But when a provider in Virginia, which doesn’t have a state law with explicit opt-in or opt-out requirements, informed me I had the choice to opt out, it refused to let me. My only option was to click “I accept” and to follow an opt-out process after the fact. 
According to Seitz, the health privacy director who works with patients going through mandated treatment, one major challenge in privacy law is that it’s difficult to put a dollar amount on the type of harm people experience, such as when intimate details about their lives are stored in recorded therapy sessions on an unsecured database, like Confidant Health did in 2024. Individuals can’t file a civil lawsuit or sue their doctor for violating HIPAA, which means that only the federal government or state attorney generals can enforce it. As a result, Seitz said that the attitude in healthcare around data breaches is: “Yeah, I’m breaking the law. What are you going to do about it?” 
To make privacy violations actionable, Seitz said, “I would want statutory damages. Like, every corporate defense attorney’s nightmare where it says, ‘Every breach equals $2,000,’ and then all the client has to do is show the breach, and then it’s money.”
At the end of the day, experts said one of the most important parts of the health data ecosystem is trust.
“Every single health data custodian that exists should be doing everything that we can to nurture and protect and foster the trust of those whose data we protect,” said Schmit, the health law and policy professor who wrote about how health exchanges can benefit the public. “And one thing that will absolutely undermine that trust are structures and processes that are opaque and difficult to follow, that make patients feel like they aren’t cared for.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: ‘Jeffrey, I forgive you’: Father of slain children supports clemency for Indiana death row inmate
text:
The Indiana Parole Board holds a clemency hearing on Monday, May 12, 2025, in Indianapolis, for death row inmate Benjamin Ritchie. (Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The father of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch is urging Gov. Mike Braun to spare Jeffrey Weisheit from execution, saying the man who murdered his children should remain in prison for life without the possibility of parole.
Steven Lynch, whose children died in a 2010 house fire set by Weisheit, signed an affidavit urging mercy ahead of Weisheit’s scheduled Nov. 5 execution. His plea comes as the Indiana Parole Board prepares to begin clemency hearings Friday.
“What good does it do the memory of my children to put this man to death?” Lynch wrote.
Death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit, currently housed at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. (Photo courtesy the Indiana Department of Correction)
His statement, provided to the Indiana Capital Chronicle by Weisheit’s attorneys, supports their request for Gov. Mike Braun to commute the death sentence to life imprisonment without parole.
“I request that Jeffrey Weisheit receive life in prison without eligibility for parole,” Lynch wrote. “With the remaining years of his life, he would be able to continue seeking the Lord’s forgiveness and redemption for his actions.”
Steven Lynch and the children’s mother, Lisa Lynch, did not respond to the Capital Chronicle’s requests for comment.
Written clemency materials are due to the Indiana Parole Board Thursday. Board members are scheduled to interview Weisheit at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City on Friday, followed by public testimony Monday in Indianapolis. The board will make a recommendation to Braun, who has the final say.
Weisheit was convicted and sentenced to death in 2013 for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb. Their mother, Lisa, was in a relationship with Weisheit and had left the children in his care while she worked.
The Indiana Supreme Court set his execution date in August. He is scheduled to die by lethal injection before sunrise Nov. 5.
Weisheit’s attorneys are seeking a two-week delay of the execution and clemency proceedings to obtain brain scans and expert analysis they want the board and governor to consider.
On Wednesday, the Indiana Supreme Court ordered the state to respond to the transportation and rescheduling requests by 4:30 p.m. Friday. Weisheit’s attorneys have until 4:30 p.m. Monday to reply.
Those deadlines fall after Friday’s scheduled prison interview and Monday’s public testimony, respectively. The order does not decide either request or change the execution date or clemency schedule. All five justices concurred.
A spokesperson for Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said only that the office “can’t comment on ongoing litigation.”
‘Jeffrey, I forgive you’
In his affidavit, Steven Lynch said executing Weisheit would cause another family to experience a loss he knows firsthand.
“Hurting Mr. Weisheit’s family by executing him is not the outcome my children would want,” he wrote. “I seek to save his family the great pain and loss from the taking of his life. I want to prevent another parent from experiencing the loss I have experienced.”
The two-page affidavit was signed by Lynch and notarized Oct. 7.
“I would like more time for Jeffrey to live,” Lynch wrote. “He knows in his heart what he did. What I want is to extend an act of mercy.”
He ended with a direct statement to Weisheit: “Jeffrey, I forgive you.”
Story continues below.
Steven Lynch - Signed
 
Joseph Perkovich, an attorney with the nonprofit law practice Phillips Black who represents Weisheit, emphasized that Lynch speaks for himself.
“From the depths of unfathomable grief, Alyssa and Caleb Lynch’s father has summoned mercy,” Perkovich said in a statement. “But it must be underscored that he simply speaks for himself, and in no way purports to speak for all the children’s family bereaved in this unspeakable tragedy. Understanding that others desire privacy, that privacy is categorically respected.”
Weisheit’s convictions stem from a fire at the Evansville home he shared with Lisa Lynch and her children.
Court documents detail how Weisheit bound Caleb with duct tape and gagged him before setting the fire with both children inside. Records also details his preparations to flee, including quitting his job and withdrawing his money before the killings.
Jurors found in 2013 that the state had proved death penalty aggravating circumstances involving multiple murders and victims younger than 12. They recommended a death sentence. Weisheit was also convicted of arson.
Dispute over brain-injury evidence
Weisheit’s attorneys argue that evidence of brain injuries, mental illness and childhood trauma was not adequately developed or presented during his trial and subsequent court proceedings.
In two emergency motions filed Monday with the Indiana Supreme Court, they requested an order directing prison officials to take Weisheit to the Franciscan Health Diagnostic Imaging Center in Michigan City for magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, and positron emission tomography, or PET, scans.
They also asked the justices to move the execution to Nov. 19, the written-materials deadline to Oct. 29 and the public clemency hearing to Nov. 2.
The attorneys contend that imaging and more detailed analysis could help establish that brain injuries affecting Weisheit’s behavior preceded the murders. He also suffered a head injury during his arrest after police used a Taser and he fell, striking his head.
Indiana death row inmate seeks execution delay for brain scans ahead of clemency hearings

But the timing and extent of earlier injuries have been disputed in court.
U.S. District Judge Sarah Evans Barker authorized funding for investigative services Sept. 16. But in an Oct. 7 order, she denied the transportation request, distinguishing her authority to approve funding from her authority to compel state officials to help gather evidence for state clemency.
Attorneys from Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita’s office opposed the federal transportation request, arguing that Weisheit’s federal case had ended and that the funding law did not authorize the requested order.
Weisheit’s lawyers then turned to the state’s highest court, which set the response deadlines Wednesday without ruling on their requests.
Braun ultimately decides
Braun said Tuesday that he wants information from the proposed testing available for consideration in Weisheit’s clemency case.
“We’re not going to dismiss it,” Braun said. “We’re not going to try to slow it down.”
The governor said the state’s legal team would review the information and advise him.
Under the current clemency schedule, the parole board will interview Weisheit at the prison Friday at 10:30 a.m. Central, or 11:30 a.m. Eastern.
Monday’s public hearings are scheduled in conference rooms 1 and 2 at the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis. Testimony supporting clemency is scheduled from 9 to 11 a.m., followed by testimony opposing it from 1 to 3 p.m.
The notice provided to Weisheit says the hearing dates will not change unless his execution is stayed or rescheduled.
Braun denied clemency to Benjamin Ritchie and Roy Lee Ward before their executions last year. Weisheit’s execution would be Indiana’s fourth since the state resumed carrying out death sentences in December 2024 after a 15-year pause.

name: California
title: Patients: All my best tips on how to opt out of data sharing
text:
In summary
Even when patients are told they can opt out, medical providers often don’t give patients instructions on how. For patients who are interested in opting out, here are my best tips on how to start.


CalMatters and The Markup’s reporting has found that opting out of data sharing is much more difficult than it needs to be because deceptive designs or “dark patterns” make it more work to say no than to say yes. Research has found that when given the choice, people prefer to have more fine-grained control over how their medical data is shared or used. 
In the last year, I registered as a patient at 25 clinics and hospitals across seven states and spent hundreds of hours reviewing consent forms, privacy policies and marketing forms to see whether I could actually opt out of sharing my data. Sometimes, opting out was simple. Other times — like in our most recent reporting on MyChart and University Hospitals in Ohio — the process was extremely convoluted. 
For patients that are interested in opting out, here are my best tips to get started: 

Get the forms in advance. A provider’s office will often send you a link 24 to 48 hours in advance of your appointment. Sometimes, you can download them off a hospital website. I usually search online for keywords like “consent forms + hospital name.” Getting the forms early means you can take many of the steps below at home, instead of under time pressure immediately before your appointment.
Nice to have: Keep a dedicated phone number and email address for health visits. It’s not always possible, but if you can, get a dedicated phone number such as through Google Voice’s free plan or the paid Burner app. Set up a new email inbox just for healthcare appointments, such as with Gmail or Proton Mail. When filling out contact information for appointments or creating a patient portal account, use your dedicated phone number and email address. This step makes it easier for you to track all the forms health providers send you, and potentially, to track your data trail in the future.
Use the screen recorder already installed on your phone, computer or tablet to record your screen as you read through the forms, so you have a copy of what you sign. Here are instructions for iPhones and tablets and Android devices. On a Mac computer, press Command + Shift + 5 and select the Record button (looks like a bullseye).
Read or skim for specific terms like opt-out, withdraw consent, restrict, refuse, responsibility, optional, authorization.
Read or skim the privacy policy for clues about what instructions to follow to opt out. Every healthcare provider should have a privacy policy. Sometimes, a privacy policy will give you the email address or phone number of who to contact to opt out of sharing your data. You can contact them ahead of your appointment to try and opt out.
Arrive early to your appointment. Like 45 minutes early. Politely request paper forms. On paper workflows, you can skip ahead without being forced to engage with voluntary forms that are bundled in with required forms. Many privacy-conscious patients also try to cross out terms they disagree with, which they date and initial. But keep in mind, some forms explicitly note that changes to those forms are not binding.
Take photos or videos of the forms you sign. And when you return the forms to a receptionist, politely ask them to provide you with a photocopy of your signed and completed forms. Keeping your own records is important, and sometimes obtaining them later can be a kafkaesque process.
If you are struggling to get a copy of a form you filled out, or if there are terms you’d like to opt out of but you can’t figure out how, try politely asking the front desk or a provider how to proceed. If they do not know, try the following:

At a smaller clinic: Ask the front desk who you can speak to about “patient administrative records” or “clinic management.” They probably aren’t on site, but you should be able to get a person or a department’s name and an email or phone number.
At a bigger clinic or hospital: Look for the “HIPAA Compliance” or ethics office or department on their website. When you find their phone number or email, call and leave a message (it is very unlikely someone will pick up the phone). By email, write to them about your concern, provide a copy of or describe what the terms are and explain that you would like to opt out, or ask them for the opt-out instructions.


If none of the above works, one more place you can try is the “medical records” department at many hospitals. That work may be outsourced to another company. Get the name and contact of the department or the company by asking at an information desk. Then ask the medical records contact how you can opt-out.
Email me if you get stuck, or have questions. I might not know the answer, but I might be able to help you strategize to get it. Or, if you figure something out that unlocks an opt-out, I’d be glad to hear about it! arosenblat@calmatters.org
If you think your rights have been violated, submit a complaint to the Office for Civil Rights at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Peter Swire, the White House coordinator for the HIPAA privacy rule under President Bill Clinton, recommends involving HIPAA enforcers to weigh in on practices. “You can bring complaints when you’re only 80% sure. A complaint is a complaint. Then, they’re supposed to look at it with their expertise,” he said. HHS can issue guidance or address enforcement concerns through their FAQ page in response.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Former Platner volunteers turn grassroots energy into independent organizing machine
text:
People Powered Maine volunteers convene in a converted barn in Cumberland after door knocking on Oct. 3, 2026. (Photo By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)One by one, people returned to a barn in Cumberland as cows wandered on a neighboring farm. But this barn, with maps of canvassing turfs and “people over party” pins covering tables inside, serves a different purpose. 
It has become one of several hubs across Maine for former volunteers of Graham Platner’s campaign. His candidacy for U.S. Senate ended in July, but the grassroots organizing he energized has not. Now operating as an independent nonprofit known as People Powered Maine, his former volunteers are still pushing for change outside the two party system. 
“Getting back to what Graham always said, ‘Win or lose in November, my objective is to create an organizing apparatus in the state of Maine,’” said Crystale Lapham, one of the lead organizers of the offshoot effort. “I was like, mission accomplished. And we cannot let that die.” 
That pitch, that Platner’s campaign had not been about him but about building an organizing effort to sustain beyond his candidacy, had drawn many Mainers in, even those who had been otherwise skeptical of the Sullivan oysterfarmer and veteran, given the litany of controversies surrounding him before the accusation of sexual assault that ultimately tanked his bid. 
The former nominee’s vow to rally against corruption, regardless of political affiliation, is another aspect that the volunteer-run independent field organization has taken to heart.
The percentage of political independents in the U.S. has increased significantly over the past 15 years, with a record high of 45% in Gallup’s 2025 poll, heavily driven by young voters. In Maine, voters not enrolled with a political party make up roughly one-third of the electorate. Even voters registered with a party are dissatisfied with the two-party system. 
“We think it is really important to have a space that doesn’t have a label of party that some people may or may not resonate with, but they do resonate with the platform,” Lapham said. 
An economy that works for regular people, healthcare as a human right, ending forever wars, and energy and climate accountability are a few of the core facets of that platform. As Lapham and seven other volunteers returned to the barn in Cumberland to regroup after a day of canvassing, the takeaways they shared were personal stories of how these issues impacted their neighbors’ daily lives. Someone struggling to pay for medication, another for gas as prices rise. 
The group does not endorse candidates but advocates for those who sign onto their platform. That includes the new Democratic U.S. Senate nominee, Troy Jackson, and Democratic nominee for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District Matt Dunlap. But as they doorknock, people are often more interested in their organizing effort than any one candidate. 
When Gioacchino Brennan explained the goal of People Powered Maine at one door, the person who answered “was less interested in Jackson and far more interested in the fact that we are an all grassroots organization and that we’re out here trying to do a year-round advocacy organizing operation,” Brennan said.
Unlike most campaign field operations, People Powered Maine does not plan to fold after the Nov. 3 election. With a goal to remain organized in order to hold elected officials accountable and push for policy change, the Maine group essentially hopes to do on the state level what the grassroots organizers behind former President Barack Obama’s campaign had tried to do, but never fully achieved, on the national level: create a permanent, mobilized network. 
“This energy that Graham tapped into and the policies he was talking about, similar to my old boss, existed before he became a thing,” said Ronnie Cho, who organized for Obama in Maine and is now advising the Maine group. “This hunger for change — for real, bold, principled stands on issues that are vitally critical to the day-to-day lives of ordinary Mainers, none of this should live and die with any one person.
“The test is whether we can sustain that.” 
Posters and pins cover a table in Cumberland at a barn used as a gathering spot for People Powered Maine volunteers. (Photo By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
How it started 
When Politico published an accusation of sexual assault against Platner on July 6, Lapham and other volunteers had been instructed by the campaign to cancel all events. Platner had weathered an array of earlier controversies, but this time, Democrats pulled their support and his top strategists behind-the-scenes urged him to drop out.
Not wanting to forgo the community the campaign built, Lapham went ahead with an event, nixing any Platner affiliation, to collect donations for Maine Needs at her house on July 8 — what ended up being the night Platner released a video announcing his intention to end his bid. 
The group watched the video together and Lapham said they recognized they still had power, both because Platner had not yet officially withdrawn and inherently as an organized group. 
They penned two letters the next morning. One to the Maine Democratic Party asking them to be transparent about the replacement process and one to the aspiring candidates asking them to pledge to the platform at the center of Platner’s campaign that 150,000 Mainers had backed in the primary. One of the candidates who signed their pledge, Jackson, eventually went on to secure the nomination at the party’s state convention later that month. 
“Maine People Powered Movement was just the name that we put on the letter. We had no intention of creating an organization,” Lapham said. “But after all of this happened, everybody was like, ‘What’s next?’”
They set up meetings across the state to crowdsource feedback to answer that question. Out of that came the idea for a 501(c)(4) organization, called People Powered Maine, and its associated political action committee, called Maine People Powered Movement.  
Roughly 2,000 people have signed up or expressed interest in the organization, according to Lapham. They are people of various ages, including recent high school graduates and retirees, with disparate political experience. 
Jim Eaton had done some organizing for his union but never a political candidate until Platner. “I was pissed off,” Eaton said. 
Many volunteers now see People Powered Maine as the most effective means to harness that frustration. Another former Platner volunteer, Robin Swearingen, moved to Maine earlier this year after leaving a job in public health in Washington, D.C., amid Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency cuts. “It really struck a nerve,” he said, “and I vowed to become a better activist.”
People Powered Maine trains new volunteers to talk to voters in much the same way Platner’s team had: build relationships first and connect on issues that matter before attempting to persuade. 
“That takes a lot of training because you’re not asking people to open a door and read a script,” Lapham said. “But it is way more effective.” 
These types of genuine, off-the-cuff conversations at doors have been gaining traction, including in Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York’s mayoral race — as has the type of relational organizing, leveraging personal connections, that People Powered Maine is also focused on.
The group prioritizes knocking doors in their own neighborhoods, Lapham said. They also send handwritten postcards to follow up. These notes — such as a stack on one of the barn tables with artwork reading, “You are not powerless” — also include basic information on how to vote.  
Not another field program 
Rather than being run by the Democratic Party, Obama’s presidential campaigns relied on an independent grassroots apparatus called Obama for America, drawing power from 2.2 million volunteers who organized their own neighborhoods during the 2008 and 2012 election cycles. 
Some saw the decision to create a separate bottom-up organizing model as redundant or wasteful. But Cho said, “Clearly this organizing wasn’t happening before. The state parties weren’t mobilizing millions of people out of the woodwork before.”
Rather than dismantle Obama’s grassroots army after the election, the team turned it into permanent, year-round infrastructure to advocate for the president’s policy agenda. However, the apparatus withered overtime and eventually folded into the National Democratic Redistricting Committee to focus on fighting partisan gerrymandering. Cho sees that outcome not as a glitch but a feature of a change-averse system. 
Gioacchino Brennan points out canvassing turfs on a map used by People Powered Maine in Cumberland on Oct. 3, 2026. (Photo By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Like Obama’s grassroots organizing operation, People Powered Maine aims to appeal to people who have been alienated by traditional party systems.  
You will not hear or see the term “progressive” when volunteers of People Powered Maine discuss their effort, Lapham said. “It puts you in a box that means you automatically don’t apply to somebody who’s unenrolled or more centrist.” Instead, Lapham summed up the group’s identity as, “We believe in an economy that works for everybody, in basic human rights.” 
Cho and his team took the same approach when they launched Obama’s organizing apparatus. 
“We wanted everyone — Republicans, unaffiliated, Democrats, everything in between — to have a home, to be civically engaged in the way that we needed to in order to win,” Cho said, “and that structure isn’t able to really thrive under traditional Democratic Party campaign infrastructure.” 
Benta Lundh, now a volunteer for People Powered Maine, has canvassed and done other work for the Democratic Party as a lifelong member. But she said she had an “aha moment” this year when she realized those efforts were often focused on mobilizing already supportive people, rather than persuading undecided voters. 
Lundh’s work now feels less affirming, she said, because she and other People Powered Maine volunteers specifically seek out people who aren’t enrolled in a political party or are likely to skip voting altogether. However, Lundh said she feels it is more impactful. 
As the group in Cumberland debriefs in the barn, they discuss upcoming plans to offer free rides to the polls and pitch ideas to build community, such as group meals. 
“One of our big founding ideas is if people are going to hold power, they have to stay organized together,” Lapham said, “and the entire way that a campaign is run around a single candidate and then a single election cycle, and then the structure dissipates — that isn’t helpful for people retaining power.”
By staying organized year-round, Lapham and other volunteers said they hope to get involved in local races, ballot questions, legislation and holding those who are elected accountable. Regardless of what comes up, Brennan said, “We’re going to be able to leverage a lot more, a lot quicker.”
Pointing to President Donald Trump’s efforts to restrict voting access, Lapham added, “Heaven forbid something actually happens with Trump refusing fair elections, there’s a network of people who know each other, who trust each other, who can, on a moment’s notice, organize.”
As Lapham described it, their effort is not just about getting a candidate elected or holding that one candidate accountable. “It’s actually about,” she started before other volunteers jumped in, “democracy.”
People Powered Maine volunteers convene in a converted barn in Cumberland after door knocking on Oct. 3, 2026. From left to right, Robin Swearingen, Sandy, Wendy, Jim Eaton, Gioacchino Brennan, Benta Lundh, Alex and Crystale Lapham. (Photo By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Increases in farm building assessments fuel calls to revisit Indiana’s property valuation system
text:
A wind turbine near a rural Indiana farm in September 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana farmers facing steep increases in building assessments are calling for changes to the state’s property valuation system, warning lawmakers Wednesday that similar structures are being assessed differently across county lines.
Indiana Farm Bureau representatives told the Interim Study Committee on Fiscal Policy that updated state cost tables have pushed up the assessed values of barns, grain bins and livestock facilities ahead of next year’s tax bills.
They urged lawmakers to address those discrepancies rather than leave individual property owners to challenge their assessments.
State officials acknowledged the concerns but cautioned that assessment changes alone would not resolve complaints about rising tax bills. They instead recommended preserving annual adjustments while improving assessment data and testing automated valuation tools.
Lawmakers also raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments climb as new or renovated houses change the surrounding market, and questioned whether new technology could help catch errors before taxpayers have to appeal.
The committee additionally heard an update on Indiana’s childcare voucher programs and proposals to finance expanded access ahead of the 2027 budget session. Discussions focused on sustaining the state’s recent voucher expansion and drawing more investment from employers, philanthropy and local governments.
Farm building increases draw concerns
Katrina Hall, Indiana Farm Bureau’s senior director of policy strategy and advocacy, said the organization commissioned Policy Analytics to examine agricultural building assessments after members began reporting large increases earlier this year.
The analysis initially showed a statewide increase of about 44% in assessed value for the agricultural buildings studied, she said. Later data, reflecting appeals and discussions with assessors, reduced that increase to 29% — still about $2 billion in additional assessed value for taxes payable in 2027.
More than half of the parcels in the later analysis had increases of at least 15%, Hall said. The figures show how much assessed values increased, not how much farmers’ tax bills will rise.
Story continues below.
attachment_6377
 
Hall said the discrepancies suggest a problem with statewide consistency. Some assessors made adjustments to the cost tables, she said, while others appeared to use them without similar changes. Identical buildings of the same age can consequently receive different values in neighboring counties.
She argued that appeals cannot substitute for correcting the underlying assessment process.
“Appeals are like a parcel at a time,” Hall said. “They are not fixing problems with assessing in the tax base.”
Farm Bureau wants the state to consider a nationally recognized valuation system, like Marshall & Swift, and examine outdated depreciation schedules. Hall said taxpayers seeking to challenge assessments often get appraisals using that system, creating a mismatch with the state’s tools.
The organization also proposed moving agricultural improvements from the 3% property tax cap category to the 2% category. Hall said its analysis estimated about $44 million in savings across agricultural properties.
That would be a tax relief change separate from revisions to assessment methods.
The proposals follow Indiana’s 2025 property tax overhaul, which changed homeowner deductions and credits, business personal property taxation and local government revenue rules.
A subsequent Indiana Fiscal Policy Institute analysis found that most homeowners would likely receive relief, but owners of low-value homes could face increases while more expensive homes received larger breaks.
State defends annual adjustments
Tim Rushenberg, general counsel for the Department of Local Government Finance, said Indiana can change its assessment tools, but the results must still meet constitutional requirements for uniform, equal and just valuations.
The department’s report explains that assessed value is only one part of a property tax bill, which also depends on local budgets, tax levies, deductions, credits and caps.
“An individual parcel can see a higher bill even when the district rate falls, or a lower bill despite increasing gross assessed value,” Rushenberg said. “There’s a lot of moving parts, so there is no reliable shortcut from gross assessed value to taxpayer impact.”
Annual adjustments, commonly called trending, help keep assessments aligned with market evidence between physical reassessments, he said.
Story continues below.
attachment_6376
 
Less frequent updates could reduce annual changes but allow inequities to accumulate and produce larger increases when properties are eventually reassessed. Limits tied to purchase prices or annual assessment growth could also raise constitutional questions if comparable properties receive different treatment.
Cost tables provide a common starting point for estimating property values, Rushenberg continued, but their results must remain open to challenge using credible evidence.
Barry Wood, the department’s assessment division director, said the state previously updated cost schedules once every four years. It’s moving toward annual review of the schedules or a related adjustment factor to help limit large fluctuations.
Rushenberg said the department wants construction costs, appraisals and other evidence to evaluate whether particular agricultural building schedules need correction. Public comments on readoption of the state’s real property assessment rule close Oct. 23.
“We want to look at the data,” Rushenberg said. “We’ve asked for data to see where, maybe in the cost schedule, something isn’t adding up there. But we certainly don’t want to make a general assumption that an entire schedule is is incorrect.”
Homeowners face hurdles, too
Rep. Cherrish Pryor, D-Indianapolis, raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments rise as new or renovated houses elevate housing prices, even when they have made no improvements themselves.
She urged officials to make the process easier to understand and reduce the need for homeowners to challenge inaccurate values.
“We live it, and so it’s easy for us, but it’s not easy for the average person, particularly if you’re an older individual,” Pryor said.
Wood said assessors can distinguish between different types and ages of homes within a neighborhood when applying adjustments.



Quotation







Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences.


– Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis


Automated valuation models could help identify inconsistencies requiring closer review, said Hamilton County Assessor Kevin Poore. An assessor-led pilot is underway in Hendricks, Clark, Lake, Vanderburgh, LaPorte and Allen counties.
The department recommended beginning with an advisory or quality-control pilot, retaining local assessor judgment and taxpayers’ notice and appeal rights.
Still, Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis, pressed for clear error measures and analysis of who would pay more or less before broader implementation.
“Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences,” Qaddoura said.
Childcare funding debate continues
Also Wednesday, Adam Alson, director of the Office of Early Childhood and Out-of-School Learning, said Gov. Mike Braun intends to continue the voucher expansion supported by a one-time $200 million infusion announced this spring.
“The additional 14,000 CCDF vouchers are funded solely with state dollars and for one fiscal year,” Alson said. “The governor is committed to continuing this increase in enrollment, and as such, this additional investment and allocation will be reflected in its upcoming budget.”
September figures presented to the committee showed 46,579 children enrolled across the Child Care and Development Fund and On My Way Pre-K programs, with 17,732 on their combined waitlists.
Story continues below.
attachment_6393
 
Regulated childcare capacity nevertheless fell about 3.3% from a year earlier, to 156,151 seats.
Alson said the administration is pursuing regulatory changes and additional ways for employers, philanthropy and local governments to invest.
Whitney Coake, a Taft public affairs director speaking on her own behalf, proposed a “QuadShare” framework combining employer, taxpayer, state and philanthropic contributions. It would fund expanded childcare assistance, 12 weeks of paid parental leave and an early care trust fund.
Her model estimated about $1.74 billion in annual operating expenses, separate from proposed trust fund deposits. Financing would include a 0.3% employer payroll contribution and a 0.15 percentage-point increase in the individual income tax rate. Philanthropic contributions and investment returns remain proposed or illustrative.
Alson emphasized that communities need flexibility to develop approaches suited to their families and employers.
“There are places throughout the state that are saying this is important,” he said. “How do we figure out how we do it?”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawsuit alleges MDOC staff filmed incarcerated woman while giving birth, violating privacy statute
text:
Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA new lawsuit filed Oct. 8 in federal court against eight employees of the Michigan Department of Corrections, alleges that the right to privacy of Natalie Forrest, who was incarcerated at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility at the time, when officers recorded her on their body cameras while she was giving birth to her son. 
“It was hard to be able to even try to connect with my newborn son, just for the simple fact that they were sitting there recording everything,” Forrest said in an interview. “I can’t even put into words how uncomfortable I felt. I felt degraded. I just felt like I couldn’t even actually enjoy the moment of my son being born.”
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Michigan, argues that filming Forrest while giving birth on March 8, 2025, violated Michigan’s criminal voyeurism statute — and that the Department of Corrections was notified on Feb. 17, 2025, nearly a month before Forrest delivered her baby that the policy in place allowing that filming to happen was illegal. Changes to the policy, which had also allowed correctional officers to record on their body cameras during strip searches, did not go into effect until March 24, 2025.
A spokesperson for the Department of Corrections did not respond to multiple requests for comment by Michigan Advance on the lawsuit. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Forrest described the practice of recording, up until she gave birth, as a pattern, adding that “There were multiple times where I was strip searched due to the simple fact that I had to leave the prison to go to doctor’s appointments for the baby, seeing that I was high risk. Every time that I had to leave the prison to go to a doctor’s appointment, they would strip search me, pregnant at all.”
Complaint ECF 1
According to the complaint, two correctional officers, one of them male, remained inside the delivery room with Forrest through cervical exams, labor and delivery, not outside the door or behind the privacy curtain, with chest-mounted cameras facing her bed. 
Maura Battersby, an attorney with Flood Law representing Forrest along with her minor son and her mother, who was present at the time of Forrest giving birth, described the situation in the lawsuit as “treating these women like they’re subhuman.”
Battersby emphasized that, even though incarcerated individuals have a lower expectation of privacy than non-incarcerated individuals, and some recording is necessary for the safety of guards and others in custody, she does not believe that there is a justification for recording during strip searches or similar nude settings.
“When you are incarcerated, you have a much lesser expectation of privacy than a citizen out in the world, not in custody,” she explained. “But as far as the standards go, and where it is more important, nude is top of the list as far as your expectation of privacy, even as an incarcerated individual.”
Recording during strip searches at Women’s Huron Valley was the subject of an earlier lawsuit from Flood Law against department leadership — and though a state circuit court dismissed that lawsuit, an appeal remains open according to online court records. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You’re not supposed to follow an illegal order if you know that to be wrong. You are not supposed to do that. So I don’t think that absolves even just the corrections officers from doing that,” Battersby said of the recording policy. “From the top all the way down, there’s blame to be had all around there. They knew for a very long time this is what was happening. They were told by lawmakers … Part of our complaint in the exhibits shows the emails with the lawmakers saying this is illegal. You have to stop doing this immediately.”
Forrest emphasized that having officers who she did not know made her feel uncomfortable communicating with both her mother, who was present as her support person while giving birth, and her doctors. She also said that it made it harder for her to connect with her newborn son — something that was already difficult for her because she was incarcerated for the first months of his life. 
“I got less than 48 hours with him. They took my baby. My mom had to take my baby. I didn’t get to actually physically hold him, connect with him, see him,” she said. “And the simple fact that I’m sitting here thinking about the moment I gave birth to my son. It’s all recorded. Who knows where those recordings are? Who knows who has access to those recordings? Who knows what they could do with them?”
Forrest said that the whole experience continues to take a toll on her mental health, saying, “I still think about it every single day.”
The lawsuit alleges that after Forrest’s son was born, a corrections officer told her mother, who is also a plaintiff, that two years would be added to Forrest’s sentence if she took a picture of her newborn grandson in the hospital. 
Battersby said she was unaware of any mechanism for an individual officer to do that, adding, “What’s important is that it was meant to intimidate and meant to control, whether true or not. I would be interested to see what that complaint was or what any additional charge was for that.”
On March 14, 2025, eight days after her son’s birth, Forrest filed an internal grievance with the department, describing her experience which, the lawsuit claims, “described conduct constituting
sexual abuse as defined by the Prison Rape Elimination Act and MDOC’s own policy directives governing sexual abuse and the mandatory referral of such allegations to the facility’s PREA Coordinator rather than the ordinary grievance process.” 
Instead of referring the grievance to the Prison Rape Elimination Act coordinator, the lawsuit says that it was thrown out for being “Untimely,” despite Forrest’s arguments that, in her recovery from pregnancy, she submitted the grievance as quickly as was reasonable. An appeal of the grievance was also denied.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: A plan to introduce competitive bidding for these medical products will hurt patients
text:
Scheduled to take effect no later than Jan. 1, 2028, The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) says competitive bidding for ostomy supplies will lower costs for beneficiaries and reduce fraud, waste and abuse. But patients worry their choices will be limited in an effort to save money that could cause them harm. (Getty Images Creative)Do you know someone with an ostomy? I bet you do, but you might not know it.
The public often refers to an ostomy as a “colostomy bag.” But that’s an oversimplification.  An ostomy is a surgery that creates a new opening (stoma) on the abdomen for an individual to eliminate waste.
When the fit is right, most people get on with their lives. When it is wrong, the consequences can be immediate and deeply disruptive. It is this precise reason why Medicare’s decision to bring ostomy supplies into competitive bidding is bad policy.
Scheduled to take effect no later than Jan. 1, 2028, The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) says competitive bidding will lower costs for beneficiaries and reduce fraud, waste and abuse. These are both worthy goals. But saving money on an ostomy product is not necessarily saving money on healthcare—and fighting bad actors at the expense of patients’ access and choice is the wrong strategy.
As a patient, I know where the real cost can show up.
It shows up when my pouch leaks and effluent damages my skin.
It shows up when I cannot leave the house because I am worried about an accident, or when I lose sleep because I fear missing work.
And, in more serious cases, it shows up as a trip to the emergency room.
The fundamental problem with competitive bidding is that it treats products as though they are interchangeable, like a walker or knee brace. Ostomy supplies are not one-size-fits-all. They are prescribed to meet each person’s unique needs — stoma type and size, skin condition, body shape and lifestyle. I went through three different brands of skin barriers and bags before I found a combination that fit my body, and provided me with a sense of security.
Consider eyeglasses. A prescription that works for one person would not work for everyone. Ostomy supplies are no different.
Two products may look similar while behaving completely differently on an individual’s body. One person may need a particular adhesive because of their skin type. Someone else may require a specific pouching configuration for their body or lifestyle.
The federal government points to safeguards, saying that when a physician specifically prescribes a particular brand to avoid an adverse medical outcome, contract suppliers must provide it or help the beneficiary find a supplier that can. This all sounds reassuring on paper. But patients should not have to become medical advocates, insurance experts and supply negotiators every time they reorder the products that allow them to function normally. Nor should they have to wait until a problem becomes a documented “adverse medical outcome” before getting access to what works. Preventing complications is the whole point of good ostomy care.
I am not opposed to controlling Medicare spending. I want to eliminate unnecessary costs just like any taxpayer. But there is a difference between eliminating waste and creating incentives to substitute products that are cheaper but less appropriate for a particular patient. 
If a lower-priced product works perfectly for me, great. But the determination should be based on whether it works for me — not simply whether it won a bidding process.
An ostomy is already a profound adjustment. Many of us have had this life-saving surgery because of birth defects, cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, trauma or other serious medical conditions. We have learned to care for a part of our body in a way we never expected. We have adapted our routines and our sense of self. The least our healthcare system can do is recognize that the products we depend on are not interchangeable widgets.
The question should never be, “How cheaply can Medicare buy this pouch?” but rather, “What does this patient need to stay healthy, independent and out of the hospital?
I am reminded daily that when it comes to something as essential as managing my own body safely and with dignity, the lowest bid should never be more important than the right fit.
