name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Judge orders Oklahoma board to reconsider former Norman teacher’s license revocation
text:
Former Norman High School teacher Summer Boismier, far right, sits next to her attorneys, Iris Halpern, center, and Neil Sandhu, left, before a hearing in Oklahoma County District Court on Wednesday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s top school board has been ordered to reconsider its decision to revoke the teaching license of a former Norman High School teacher who posted a QR code in her classroom linking to a library catalogue containing banned books.
Oklahoma County District Judge Richard Ogden decided Wednesday the original 2024 revocation proceedings against Summer Boismier were flawed by former state Superintendent Ryan Walters’ participation. 
Boismier had a pending defamation lawsuit against Walters at the time that he led the Oklahoma State Board of Education in revoking her teaching certification, and “there is indication Mr. Walters had certain biases” affecting his decision-making, the judge said.
“Significant is that if someone has active litigation against you, that is a conflict of interest that cannot be set aside,” Ogden said while making a ruling from the bench.
Former state Superintendent Ryan Walters, left, sits with his attorney, Andy Lester, right, before a hearing in Oklahoma County District Court on Wednesday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The state board never formally considered a request from Boismier to disqualify Walters from taking part in the revocation proceedings, Ogden said. Instead, he participated in multiple votes concerning her license revocation and “carried a great deal of influence” in the process, the judge said.
After losing her certification, she appealed the decision in Oklahoma County District Court. 
Boismier said the decision Wednesday was “validating.”
“I have no apologies for anything to anyone,” she said after the hearing. “It’s just always been about doing what’s best for the students in our classrooms and my colleagues who help facilitate that education. That’s really what all this has been about the entire time, and I feel like it’s validating not just for me but for them, as well.”
In a statement through its communications office, the Oklahoma State Department of Education said it was “surprised by today’s ruling and the deviation from judicial procedures.”
“The board general counsel and OSDE general counsel will now present the State Board members with their options regarding next steps,” the agency said.
The judge made his decision after hearing testimony from Walters and Boismier in his courtroom Wednesday. 
Walters, who stepped down from office last year, testified that his goal was to “rid the classroom of indoctrination” and carry out a state law that bans certain race and gender topics from being taught in public schools. 
That law, known as House Bill 1775, requires action against teachers’ certifications if they are found in violation, he said.
“I believe that was my duty as an elected official,” Walters said on the witness stand.
He first called for Boismier to lose her teaching license before he took office. 
Walters was a Republican candidate running for state superintendent in August 2022 when Boismier made national news for resigning from her teaching job in protest of HB 1775.
Shortly before her resignation, Boismier had covered the bookshelves in her English classroom with red butcher paper that read “books the state doesn’t want you to read.” Norman Public Schools had asked teachers to remove their classroom books until each title could be reviewed, following the enactment of HB 1775.
During her testimony Wednesday, Boismier called the law an “educational gag order” and “poorly disguised bigotry” that prevented her from properly doing her job.
Former Norman High School teacher Summer Boismier sits with her attorney before a hearing in Oklahoma County District Court on Monday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Her classroom display also included a QR code next to the words “definitely don’t scan.” The code linked to the Brooklyn Public Library’s Books Unbanned initiative, which gives students in any part of the country access to its catalogue. The library collection includes some books that have been banned in some schools.
After taking office as the head of the state Education Department, Walters directed the agency to file a motion to revoke Boismier’s teaching license. The agency contended she violated teacher code of conduct standards by posting the QR code. 
Walters’ administration singled out a few books in the library catalogue that it argued had sexually inappropriate content or contained topics that would violate HB 1775. 
Boismier said she never recommended a specific book from the Brooklyn library that students should read.
“I believe it is important for students not only to choose what they read but also to form their own opinions,” she said while testifying Wednesday.
The agency presented its case for revocation in a June 2023 hearing before an administrative law judge, who then recommended Boismier not have her teaching license taken away. 
The state Board of Education, with Walters at the helm, took the unusual step of rejecting that recommendation. Instead, it voted in August 2024 to revoke Boismier’s certification, preventing her from teaching in any Oklahoma public school.
All the while, she said, Walters “was both my adjudicator and my accuser.” After leaving her teaching job, Boismier moved to New York City to work for the Brooklyn library but said she has since returned to Oklahoma.
Walters had only one vote on a board that agreed unanimously to revoke her license, said Heidi Long, an attorney representing the state board.
“We heard evidence today that Ms. Boismier was biased against Ryan Walters, that she violated HB 1775, that she does not regret it and that she would do it again,” Long said during Wednesday’s hearing.
Boismier’s attorneys spent much of Wednesday’s hearing showing several social media posts, public statements and a political campaign advertisement from Walters in which he said he opposed “woke indoctrination,” liberal political views and “transgender ideology.” 
Former state Superintendent Ryan Walters, left, walks toward a courtroom with his attorney, Andy Lester, center, before testifying in a hearing in Oklahoma County District Court on Wednesday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Even before he took office, he publicly stated “there is no place for a teacher with a liberal political agenda” like Boismier.
Boismier testified she was an advocate for racial minorities and the LGBTQ+ community. She was the faculty sponsor of a school Gender-Sexuality Alliance club and displayed an LGBTQ+ rainbow flag in her classroom.
Ogden agreed the language Walters used in his public comments and posts could indicate bias against people with certain political beliefs.
He ordered the state Board of Education to decide whether to accept the findings of Boismier’s original revocation hearing or to schedule a new hearing.
“There needs to be a decision by the state Board of Education free from any bias that may have come from Mr. Walters,” Ogden said in court.
Boismier still has an active federal lawsuit pending against the state board, the Education Department and the state superintendent, though her initial defamation case against Walters was thrown out. 
She argued in her pending case that the state violated her constitutional rights to equal protection, due process and free speech, among other allegations.
Her attorney, Iris Halpern, said Boismier’s legal team will look into whether that ongoing case could complicate the state board’s ability to fairly vote on her license revocation. However, she said the board, which now has entirely new members, should move on and “make the right decision.”
“This is someone’s life and career that the state is messing with,” Halpern said after the hearing. “They know they should not have revoked her license in the first place. I think that’s very clear. It was infected with bias and prejudice, and it was a political stand at that time, and it continues to be a similar stand now.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: One year after ex-Typhoon Halong, Western Alaska’s recovery is ongoing and uncertain
text:
Pollution response teams from the U.S. Coast Guard conduct post-storm assessments in Kipnuk on Oct. 22, 2025, after the community was impacted by severe flooding from ex-Typhoon Halong. (Photo by Petty Officer 1st Class Shannon Kearney/U.S. Coast Guard)One year since the remnants of Typhoon Halong ripped through coastal communities of Western Alaska, displacing an estimated 1,600 residents and prompting the largest mass evacuation of the region in state history, the recovery effort is ongoing and uncertain.
Today there is no official tally of how many residents are still displaced from their homes. But nearly 200 households continue to receive federal temporary housing assistance, according to state officials. 
Hurricane force winds and floodwaters damaged more than 45 communities, from Kotzebue down the coast to the hardest-hit Yukon-Kuskowkwim Delta region, the majority of whom are Alaska Native. Evacuated residents were displaced to the nearby hub of Bethel, or to Anchorage and other communities throughout Alaska.  

A drifted home on the outskirts of Kipnuk after Typhoon Halong flooded the Western Alaska village, underscoring the scale of erosion and storm damage facing climate-threatened communities. October 22, 2025. (Photo by Jenni Monet/Alaska Beacon)
 

Over the last year, local and state crews have made significant progress in repairing some homes and essential infrastructure in the region. That has included moving back more than 125 homes that were ripped off foundations — some floated miles away in the storm — according to officials with the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities. 
Emergency infrastructure work is “mostly complete” in 30 communities, a DOT spokesperson said by email, including repairing critical community systems such as water, wastewater and power to restore basic functionality. But repairs, recovery and environmental and debris clean up is ongoing. 
More than 2,500 people received some kind of federal assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency over the last year, with FEMA reporting over $100 million in aid spent on individual, household or other needs assistance.

In October of last year, Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the Trump administration would fully reimburse the state for the first 90 days of immediate disaster relief and recovery efforts. But when the state made that request it was denied, as well as an appeal for a 90-10 cost share with the state. That leaves FEMA covering 75% of disaster relief costs and the state covering 25%. 
On the state side, legislators approved an additional $75 million for the state’s disaster relief fund last fiscal year, with nearly $28 million spent on the Halong response, according to officials with the state’s legislative finance division this week. More than 2,300 people applied for state disaster assistance, which covered additional repairs not covered by FEMA assistance such as damage to subsistence camps. The state has allocated $2.65 million in that state aid, but the number of people who received state assistance was not immediately available, according to Jeremy Zidek, public information officer with the Alaska Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. 
Local and regional Tribal governments and organizations, municipalities and non-profits have also provided assistance and donations to storm affected residents and the recovery effort. 
Funding for rebuilding homes uncertain
But repairing and rebuilding homes, which would allow displaced residents to return, is largely at a standstill — particularly in the hardest-hit communities of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok. 
In August, FEMA denied Alaska’s request for permanent housing construction assistance. The state is planning an appeal, according to state officials.
State officials say Dunleavy was in Washington D.C. on Monday to meet with FEMA officials and urge their reconsideration of the agency’s denial of the housing funding. The funds would enable repairs and rebuilding of hundreds of homes, beyond the $44,800 per household in assistance provided by FEMA.
Dunleavy officials did not offer details about the trip or respond to a request for comment about broader recovery efforts on Monday.
Bryan Fisher, commissioner with the Alaska Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, told Alaska’s News Source that housing is a huge concern on the state level in an interview on Monday. 
“There’s still not sufficient resources to rebuild and repair the homes that were either destroyed or catastrophically damaged,” he said.     

Alaska Organized Militia members assigned to Task Force Bethel continue removing debris and waterlogged insulation from buildings at Tuntutuliak after ex-Typhoon Halong on Oct. 25, 2025. (Alaska National Guard photo by Capt. Balinda O’Neal)
 

Fisher said FEMA is estimating a cost of $200 million for the disaster recovery, but he has doubts. “I expect that to double. I think it’s going to be more around $400 million dollars when all’s said and done,” he said. 
Rising costs of fuel and construction materials, combined with weather and logistical challenges to barge in supplies and remove storm debris presents ongoing challenges, he said. 
For Kipnuk and Kwigillingok, tribal leadership have issued no-return orders for residents while repairs are ongoing. Both communities have also voted to relocate, with Kwigillingok voting to do so before Halong hit, with potential sites selected on higher ground, according to KYUK. But how and when funding and state and federal support would assist in relocation has yet to be determined. 
“A huge cleanup effort still needs to be accomplished, and homes need to be rebuilt,” Fisher said. “The infrastructure is there, power and water is available, but there isn’t housing available for folks to return to. So until that happens, it’s really not safe or appropriate for folks to return to the communities.”
Fisher said there is only government support to stabilize and rebuild storm-damaged communities, not for permanent relocation. 
“So the disaster recovery programs, both at the state and federal level, can’t facilitate the entire relocation of a community,” he said. “There is no one federal agency. There is no one source of funding.”
Fisher said the goal is to rebuild to allow people to return to their communities, their subsistence lifestyle and culture. “So our goal is to get them home as soon as we can,” he said. “And then work with them and all the partners necessary to look at long-term relocation and whole community relocation.”
Building back stronger 
Fall storms have become more frequent in Western Alaska in recent years, and Fisher acknowledged the dilemma of building back in a region still at risk for future storm disasters.     

Residents of Nightmute, Alaska, make their way to a Bethel-bound Alaska Army National Guard HH-60M Black Hawk helicopter during Operation Halong Response, Oct. 17, 2025. (Alaska National Guard photo by Staff Sgt. Joseph Moon)
 

“So we spend more money repairing damage caused from storms as opposed to saving money on the front end and looking at real mitigation,” he said. “So it’s a challenge, and we’ve had lots of conversations with many, many administrations about more funding for that — to be able to protect folks and have them not be impacted by storms.”
In the meantime, he said the state’s focus is on rebuilding. “Our commitment is to rebuild stronger, higher, more resilient, so the communities can survive future storms,” he added. 
That involves additional engineering to stabilize structures, he said, fortifying homes and boardwalks against future storm surges and thawing permafrost, using steel helical pilings.
“Most of those boardwalks were destroyed during the storm, those that were installed with these pilings survived. So this winter, we made a huge effort to rebuild all of that boardwalk. You know, transportation through the communities is critical to facilitate the rebuilding, and we put all the new boardwalks on piling so they’ll be more survivable in the future.” 
Officials with DOT reported that over the past year local and state crews installed more than 25,000 feet of boardwalk and 11,000 helical piles, and 19 million pounds of cargo transported as part of relief efforts. 
Looking ahead, repair work is continuing and preparations for winter are underway, even as funding and prospects for many to return home are uncertain. 
In a social media post on Monday, Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski acknowledged the devastation of Halong and the uncertainty communities still face, and pledged to continue advocating for federal support. “I will continue working to improve disaster preparedness and recovery for communities across our state,” she said.
“One year later, we cannot look away. I remain committed to standing with affected communities, listening to their voices, and ensuring they have the opportunity to shape their path toward healing and long-term recovery.”
The remnants of Typhoon Halong that hit Western Alaska in October of 2025 impacted more than 45 communities. (Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities map)

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn reignites talks of 3rd District debate as early voting begins
text:
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn held a news conference after casting his ballot on the first day of early voting in Iowa at the Polk County Election Office Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Candidates in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District — one of the nation’s most competitive U.S. House districts in the country — were unable to agree to a debate before early voting started in the 2026 midterm elections. But discussions may have restarted as U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn told reporters Wednesday he was accepting a debate request for Oct. 27 against Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott.
After going to cast his ballot at the Polk County Election Office on the first day of early voting, Nunn held a news conference encouraging Iowans to go to the polls — and he criticized his Democratic opponent for not agreeing to debate on a day before Iowans could begin casting their ballots.
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, holding his daughter, Olympia, filled out his ballot alongside daughters Jayna and Aliya on the first day of early voting in Iowa at the Polk County Election Office Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The 3rd District is the only congressional race in Iowa where a debate has not been scheduled. The two campaigns failed to agree on a date with the news channel KCCI by Oct. 1, with Nunn’s campaign advocating for dates before or shortly after early voting began, and Trone Garriott’s campaign agreeing to dates in late October because of scheduling conflicts earlier in the month.
Iowa Field Report, a conservative-aligned news organization, published an audio recording of an interaction between Nunn and Trone Garriott’s campaign staff and KCCI staff — a 20-minute conversation in which the parties were unable to find a compromise on a date, which included discussion on the date of Oct. 27.
But Nunn told reporters, “just said yes again to KCCI to do this on the 27th of October” on Wednesday in order to ensure Iowans in the 3rd District hear from the candidates on the debate stage.
“I think it’s important, most of all, for Iowans to know that they have an opportunity to hear from both candidates on the stage,” Nunn said. “We have always debated in every race I’ve ever run, including in my primaries. It’s important too, because this is an opportunity for Iowans to ask the questions, but also to hear from the candidate — not just in the campaign rallies, but on the debate stage. So again, I will say, I’m ready to debate my opponent.”
Nunn also said in addition to the discussions with KCCI, he had agreed to participate in debates before the start of early voting with WHO-13, Iowa Public Television and WHO-AM. These dates were not agreed to by both parties and the media organizations. Nunn said though his campaign wanted to hold a debate before the start of early voting, the proposed Oct. 27 event “is an opportunity for us to come to the debate stage” before Election Day Nov. 3.
“Every other race has done this,” Nunn said. “There is no reason that the 3rd District should be any different. We stand ready. I wish we would have done this before early voting started, but as we turn out here today as one of the first candidates to vote, it’s important Iowans of all stripes get to hear from their candidates.”
In a statement to Iowa Capital Dispatch, Trone Garriott said she accepted a debate on Oct. 27 “weeks ago,” and was supportive of facing Nunn on the debate stage.
“I’ve been looking forward to a debate from the beginning,” Trone Garriott said. “Iowans deserve to hear from both candidates side by side before they vote.
“Unfortunately, Zach Nunn continues to play games rather than being honest with voters. I accepted a debate on October 27th with KCCI weeks ago, and I remain ready to debate. Our campaign has been working with KCCI today, and we hope this date still works for them.”
It is unclear if KCCI will be able to host the debate Oct. 27 — a day two weeks away, that will be one week before Election Day. Iowa Capital Dispatch reached out to the TV news station but did not receive a response by the time of this article’s publishing.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Northwest Arkansas candidates tackle AI, affordability in US House debate
text:
U.S. Congressional District 3 candidates for Arkansas Rep. Steve Womack (R), and Robb Ryerse (D), debate their positions at the Arkansas TV debate held on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. Bobby Wilson (L), also participated in the debate. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Candidates seeking to represent the state’s 3rd Congressional District generally agreed on the need to regulate artificial intelligence during an Arkansas TV debate Wednesday, but split on the use of the technology for warfare. 
Democrat Robb Ryerse and Libertarian Bobby Wilson are challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack as he runs for a ninth term in Congress. 
All three candidates agreed AI can be a useful tool and that lawmakers can help protect people from the negative consequences of the rapidly evolving technology. 
Womack, an Army veteran who was first elected to Congress in 2010, said “AI is here to stay” and it’s important to have guardrails for the technology and the data centers that power them. 
“But I think we got to be careful that we don’t go too far to where we cede a lot of that technology to adversaries that have nefarious intentions for our country,” he said.
Concerns that rapidly developing AI models could hurt humanity have prompted calls for more federal guardrails, though President Donald Trump has pushed back against slowing its development. Data centers needed to power the technology have also faced bipartisan pushback, with several Arkansas communities enacting new restrictions on them.



Ryerse, a pastor of a nondenominational church, said he’s pro-technology, but history has shown how quickly advancing tech can have environmental and human consequences. 
“There needs to be a moratorium on data centers until data centers are energy independent, they don’t pollute the environment and they aren’t a nuisance to the neighborhoods that they are put in,” he said. 
Wilson, chief operations officer of a trim and door company, said the United States needs to be first in developing AI technology. Congress could play a role by addressing privacy concerns, he said.
Wilson also said data centers should meet standards for things like sound or zoning, but didn’t specify if the standards should be set at the federal level.
“We do have a lot of abuses going on with data centers, and so there needs to be some type of standardization to make sure that localities are protected,” he said. 
Advancing technology is being used by companies in the 3rd District to produce equipment used in conflicts. Swarm Aero, a California-based company that manufactures large unmanned drones, opened in Fayetteville this year, despite pushback from local residents. The company secured more than $10 million in contracts with the Air Force Research Laboratory. 
Womack praised the company for creating jobs and saving lives in combat through its unmanned drones. 
“We are participating in this idea of provide for the common defense with these kinds of advancements in Arkansas’ 3rd District, and I’m proud of that,” he said.

(Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Robb Ryerse (D), answered questions at the press conference directly following the debate between U.S. Congressional District 3 candidates on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026 as part of the Arkansas TV debate in Conway, Arkansas. Other candidates include incumbant Rep. Steve Womack (R), and Bobby Wilson (L). (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Ryerse expressed concern about the proliferation of war and Arkansas becoming an international target because Womack has “bent the knee to the military industrial complex.” 
Arkansas is home to several defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin, L3Harris and Raytheon.
“I think Arkansas ought to be leading the way in making the world a better place, not making it more dangerous,” Ryerse said. 
Wilson said he opposes all military interventions, and that technology could be used to make life better for people. 
“I think drones are a massive win for society, whether it comes from making sure that we don’t have forest fires or getting medical help to people that are outside of any type of areas,” he said. “And it’s kind of sad to see that we’ve decided to put our focus on using it to bomb other people or sell it to bomb other people.”  
The Iran war has increased the cost of gas and other goods for Arkansans, as has the president’s “chaotic tariff war,” Ryerse said.
Northwest Arkansas candidates consider Iran war, immigration in US House race

“Congress has not acted like it should, and you are the ones paying the price,” he said.
Wilson said everything costs so much because the country is running “massive deficits.”  When there’s a deficit, it’s made up through inflation, so everything costs more because Congress can’t pass a budget, he said.
“They just do reconciliation bill after reconciliation bill,” Wilson said. “And if you want to get costs down, the government just needs to quit spending and get the budget in order.”
Congress approved a short-term funding bill last month to keep the government funded through Dec. 11. 
Womack, who has been critical of Congress’ budgeting process, voted for last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act tax and spending cut legislation, which he said saved people “a massive tax hike” by making 2017 tax cuts permanent. He said lawmakers also took action to save on taxes for tips, overtime and certain Social Security recipients. 
The bill is expected to reduce federal spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion during the next decade to help pay for tax cuts that disproportionately benefit the wealthy. 
Womack acknowledged the high price of gas and homes, and said the country could do a better job if “we can unleash the potential of the American energy supply system.”
“Build more refineries and then be able to handle energy in a much more cost-effective way right here at home,” he said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Former Rep. Ken Buck tops list of Colorado Republicans endorsing Weiser for governor
text:
Phil Weiser, the Colorado attorney general, speaks to supporters during his primary election night watch party for his campaign for governor, in Denver at Ace Eat Serve on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Ken Buck, the former five-term Republican member of Congress from Colorado and onetime chair of the state GOP, endorsed Democrat Phil Weiser for governor Wednesday alongside more than a dozen other state and local GOP officials.
“I’m supporting Phil Weiser because I know Phil,” Buck said in a video released by the Weiser campaign. “I’ve worked with Phil. He’s an honest person. He’s hard-working, and he cares for all the people of Colorado and he will be inclusive as governor to make sure all views are represented in his administration.”
Weiser, who has served as Colorado’s attorney general since 2019, is favored in the race to succeed outgoing Democratic Gov. Jared Polis, who is term-limited. He faces Victor Marx, a first-time candidate and ministry leader from Colorado Springs who has largely eschewed debates and other traditional campaign events as he faces scrutiny over his personal history in the run-up to Election Day.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Buck entered politics when he was elected Weld County district attorney in 2004. He ran for U.S. Senate in 2010, aligning himself with that year’s Tea Party movement and upsetting Jane Norton, the choice of the Republican Party establishment, in a head-to-head primary, before narrowly losing to incumbent Democratic U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet.
Elected to the House of Representatives in 2014, he represented the deep-red 4th District and joined the far-right House Freedom Caucus, consistently ranking as the most conservative member of Colorado’s congressional delegation. He abruptly announced his retirement after becoming disillusioned with his party in late 2023, saying that “too many Republican leaders are lying to America,” including by “claiming that the 2020 election was stolen.”
Colorado has elected only one Republican governor in the last 56 years. Weiser defeated Bennet in the June Democratic primary, while Marx won a narrow victory over state Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer and state Rep. Scott Bottoms, who blasted Marx as a “con man” and “grifter” and have declined to endorse him in the general election.
Marx, a self-described “high-risk missionary,” became a target of national ridicule in the final weeks of the GOP primary when he struggled in interviews and debates to answer questions about his overseas ministry work, including how many people he has killed. He has since faced scrutiny over multiple alleged campaign finance violations, his ministry’s practice of performing exorcisms, his views on abortion and past comments in which he recalled “grabbing (his wife) and slamming her into our front door.”
Other Republicans endorsing Weiser’s campaign Wednesday included Cynthia Coffman, a former Colorado attorney general; Russ George, a former speaker of the state House of Representatives; and former state lawmakers Don Coram, Cole Wist and Rob Witwer.
In a statement, Weiser said he was “deeply honored” by the endorsements.
“As attorney general, I’ve worked with all Coloradans to deliver results – and I look forward to building a broad, diverse coalition of Coloradans from across the state to deliver housing and health care we can afford, build a stronger economy and brighter future for the next generation, and protect our rights and freedoms,”  he said. “All of us need all of us — and I’m ready to get to work for all Coloradans.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Early voting is underway in Georgia. Here’s where you can cast a ballot in your county.
text:
Georgia "I voted" stickers line a table at a Fulton County polling place on the first day of early voting. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderElection Day is still weeks away, but Georgia voters are already starting to cast their ballots.
That’s because state law mandates that counties offer three weeks of early voting before every major election. Each of Georgia’s 159 counties offers at least one early voting location, and unlike with Election Day voting, where residents are assigned a specific precinct, early voters can choose to cast their ballot at any location in their county.
Early voting is offered during the week and on Saturdays at most locations. Polls will also be open on Sundays in some counties.
Tuesday was the first day of early voting for this year’s midterms, which saw a record-setting 189,000 Georgians turn out. Early voting will conclude on Oct. 30. 
Georgia residents can check the secretary of state’s My Voter Page to view their voter registration status, sample ballots and other election information. A full list of early voting locations across the state is available below.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Sen. Raphael Warnock says Scott Colom could flip Senate seat Democratic like his Georgia upset
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Raphael Warnock knows something about winning a Senate seat in the Deep South, and he says Mississippi’s race looks awfully familiar to his Georgia election five years ago.
That’s what he said at a meeting with faith leaders and to an electrified crowd in Jackson on Wednesday, urging voters to unseat Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and replicate his successful Georgia election that sent a Black Democrat to the Senate from a Southern state and delivered a Democratic majority to the U.S. Senate. 
“I’m here because I’m tired of the South being overlooked or diminished in terms of its electoral importance,” Warnock told reporters. “We ignore the South at our own peril. Democrats are investing here. I would like to see more, for the sake of the country.”

Warnock shares similarities with Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Mississippi. Both faced steep electoral odds and several national Democratic figures believed victory in a reliably red state impossible. 
U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., speaks with members of the media alongside Scott Colom, Mississippi’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since the 1980s, and the electorate has consistently aligned itself with the national Republican Party. 
But Warnock said Mississippi, the state with the highest concentration of Black voters in the nation, is ripe for the Democratic Party to flip the Senate seat if only they’ll consistently spend money in the Deep South state and keep working to register voters. 
“We lose elections by the margins of our disengagement,” Warnock said. “Mississippi is a blue state. It just doesn’t know it yet.”  
Warnock said he spent years working to register and mobilize voters across his state alongside Stacey Abrams, who was raised in Gulfport before moving to Georgia, where she would later run for governor. 
Abrams lost both of her gubernatorial bids, but many leading Democrats believe she built the organizing infrastructure that Warnock and fellow Georgia U.S. Senator Sen. Jon Ossoff ultimately used to flip what had been a deep-red state. 
He said Colom is capable of replicating his success in Mississippi, which will require amping up Democratic voter turnout. In Mississippi and across the Deep South, churches have long been an engine of political organizing for Black voters and the Democratic Party.
Warnock, who was elected to the Senate after serving as the senior pastor of Atlanta’s famed Ebenezer Baptist Church, and Colom met with faith leaders for a discussion about how pastors can use their pulpits to connect their congregations to the polls. 
The Rev. Jerry Young, senior pastor at New Hope Baptist Church in Jackson and former president of the National Baptist Convention, spoke about how he believes America is currently at a moral crossroads because the government is allowing the affluent to become richer while cutting benefits for the poor. 
“There is an attitude in this country, I think, that is antithetical to everything that the barefoot boy from Nazareth preached and talked about,” Young said. “And I just think it’s not Black or white or Republican or Democratic. It’s what is right versus wrong.”  
Pastor Stephen Cook of Anderson United Methodist Church in Jackson said his congregants were coming for guidance on how to deal with everyday struggles such as the rising cost of healthcare and groceries. 
“Every pastor, every faith leader in this room knows someone who is struggling to afford medication, worried about losing a hospital or working hard and still falling behind,” Cook said. “How do we help our congregation connect those everyday struggles to the decisions being made in Washington?” 
Colom said Hyde-Smith’s failure to address those issues puts her at odds with Christian teachings. 
Supporters cheer during a rally for Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Mississippi, at his campaign headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“She has forgotten about the working people of Mississippi,” Colom said. “She’s forgotten about the teachings of Jesus Christ. And she’s not living the values that actually make our country great.” 
Warnock’s visit is the latest in a string of appearances by national Democrats as the race enters its homestretch. Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey have already campaigned in Mississippi for Colom, the Democratic nominee.
Former President Barack Obama recorded an ad for Colom that began running this week. “Mississippi, it’s time for a change,” Obama says in the ad.
More are coming. Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign with Colom in Columbus on Oct. 22, and former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will visit cities along the Gulf Coast on Oct. 27 before the Nov. 3 election.
Hyde-Smith has criticized Colom for his ties to the national party and for using national Democratic surrogates.
Her campaign manager, Jake Monssen, said in a statement that Colom “will suffer the same fate as the last two candidates President Obama endorsed in Mississippi,” referring to Obama’s endorsements of Mike Espy in the 2020 Senate race against Hyde-Smith and Jim Hood in the 2019 governor’s race. 
President Donald Trump has again endorsed Hyde-Smith.
Colom has countered that Hyde-Smith is out of touch with average Mississippians and afraid to face voters in town halls or debate him. He has said he is focused on lowering costs for Mississippi families, raising the minimum wage and protecting health care and rural hospitals.
Colom and Hyde-Smith are also competing against independent candidate Ty Pinkins.
Earlier on Wednesday, Warnock said he visited the Jackson home of the late Medgar Evers, the civil rights legend who was assassinated in his driveway after he spent years registering Black voters. 
The Democratic senator spoke about the central role that Mississippi civil rights heroes such as James Meredith and Fannie Lou Hamer played in reshaping American politics by fighting for the right to vote. 
Warnock said the political stakes are always higher in the South, where “bloodstained ballots” mark the sacrifices made by legends such as Evers, James Meredith and Fannie Lou Hamer. 
“This is our moment,” Warnock said. “It is a moral moment. Don’t count out the South because as goes the South, so goes the rest of the nation.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: China takes center stage in SC’s US Senate contest
text:
(Photo by Getty images)The Democrat trying to flip South Carolina’s U.S. Senate seat called Wednesday for Sen. Darline Graham to recuse herself from all trade and military votes involving China.
Annie Andrews also asked Graham to “cut her family’s business ties” with the country, emphasizing a Washington Post report that the Republican senator’s husband works for two companies that import products from China.
Responding on social media, a Graham campaign spokesman called the demands “desperate,” while Graham called the criticisms a “weak attack” on her family.
Democrat Annie Andrews, who is running for U.S. Senate in South Carolina, speaks at a news conference in Mount Pleasant on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Andrews campaign)
Andrews’ public demands were her latest step in highlighting the report, which she also raised on the debate stage Sunday.
Graham’s response Wednesday on social media echoed her response during the debate: “The company my husband works for sells toys for children. He doesn’t own the company nor does he have any equity stake,” she wrote.
Most toys are made in China, wrote her spokesman T.W. Arrighi. “Just look on Amazon.”
Graham, who was appointed to the seat in July following the death of her late brother Lindsey Graham, has advocated for manufacturing more in the United States instead of China as she seeks the next full term.
But Andrews says Graham’s husband’s paycheck relies on trade with the communist nation.
“It’s inappropriate for a senator to profit from business with China. It’s even worse to conceal those ties from the public,” Andrews said at a news conference Wednesday in Mount Pleasant with the USS Yorktown as a backdrop.
On her financial disclosure, Graham lists her husband’s employer as Birchwood Trading, which sells gift products. But he also works for Cosmox North America, which sells guns and toy guns. The two businesses share an address in Columbia.
Cosmox isn’t included on the form, filed Aug. 7, because Larry Nordone’s paychecks come only from Birchwood Trading, said Graham spokesman T.W. Arrighi. The two small businesses are owned by the same person, who employs Nordone, he told the SC Daily Gazette.
The Washington Post reported Saturday that Cosmox imports gel blaster toy guns from China. The newspaper also linked Cosmox’s New York-based parent company, Coxmox Outdoors, to a Chinese weapons supplier.
Social Security, data centers and healthcare: Senate candidates exchange jabs while talking policy

Andrews initially brought it up Sunday, after Graham called the Democrat’s proposal of a two-year moratorium on data centers dangerous, saying it would put China “so far ahead.”
“So it’s interesting that Darline brought up China because the Washington Post just yesterday uncovered that Darline is hiding her family’s business interests in China,” she said. “I don’t think it’s appropriate for a sitting senator to be lining her pockets with money from China.”
Allowed a 30-second rebuttal, Graham said, “So you’re bringing up my husband. You’re sinking pretty low. My husband is employed by the company. He doesn’t own the company or have any interest in the company. They buy toy guns from China. If y’all didn’t regulate everybody to death, maybe some of the manufacturers would actually stay in this country.”
The back-and-forth comes as polls show Andrews and Graham in a closer-than-expected contest in a state that President Donald Trump won two years ago by nearly 18 percentage points.
Trump encouraged Graham, appointed to complete the term that ends in January, to jump into the special GOP primary to replace her late brother on the Nov. 3 ballot. She ultimately won the 10-way GOP contest with Trump’s endorsement, to include a rally in Myrtle Beach ahead of the runoff.
Trump is expected to return to South Carolina next week in what’s seen as an effort to boost Graham’s bid.
MS NOW reported he’s coming to Greenville on Wednesday.
Greenville County, the state’s largest, is among the counties Graham lost in the GOP runoff.
Details are still in the works, Greenville County GOP Chairman Jeff Davis said in a release.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore, lawmakers back proposal to tie prescription drug costs to federally negotiated prices
text:
Vincent DeMarco, president of Maryland Health Care for All, celebrates the governor's approval of  2025 legislation that could help Marylanders save on prescription drug costs. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore offered his “public and loud” support for proposed legislation that would allow the state to more quickly reduce the price of some expensive drugs for non-Medicare recipients by piggybacking on the federally negotiated price limits under Medicare. 
And at a press conference Thursday announcing the legislation, he promised to sign the bill, assuming it survives the 2027 legislative session. The current odds look promising.
The Maryland Healthcare for All Coalition, the organization driving the measure, recently sent letters to House and Senate candidates in the upcoming midterm elections asking for their stance on the measure.
The coalition received support from 29 Senate candidates with 26 incumbents backing the measure, along with 98 House candidates, of whom 79 are incumbents.
To pass a typical bill, 24 senators and 71 House members need to approve the measure. With Moore’s public support, coalition president Vincent DeMarco said “we’re in pretty good shape.”
Board votes to cap how much state, local governments spend on Ozempic

“It takes a while for the board to set up these upper payment limits,” DeMarco said. “Naturally, the legislature wanted them to go through a process … and that takes a while. But what we’ve come to conclude is that there is a way to make it happen more quickly.”
The proposed legislation would allow the Maryland Prescription Drug Affordability Board to set “upper payment limits” for prescription drugs based on the Maximum Fair Price, which were negotiated between federal officials and pharmaceutical companies to offer lower prescription drug costs for those on Medicare.
“If the federal government sets a Maximum Fair Price for a drug under the Medicare negotiation, our board doesn’t have to go through this months of process, and could right away, if they deem it right, set that same upper payment limit for Marylanders,” DeMarco said.
The lengthy cost review process to determine if a prescription drug is unaffordable has been a sore spot for the board members as well as opponents of the board’s efforts.
The board’s current authority only applies to those on state healthcare plans, meaning state employees and incarcerated individuals.
The cost review process has taken months, as the Prescription Drug Affordability Board staff collect data and speak with drug manufacturers to learn more about how and why some drugs are more expensive. 
Once board members determine that a drug likely “poses an affordability challenge,” the board then must investigate routes to lower those costs, which includes but is not limited to setting upper payment limits that create a ceiling for how much the state is willing to pay for a prescription drug.
The Affordability Board staff say that future evaluations should run more smoothly now that the process has been established, but the board is also looking for ways to streamline the cost review process even further.
The bill as proposed Thursday would at least trim the evaluation process for the 25 drugs that have already been negotiated by federal officials, as well as the 15 drugs currently in negotiations and any future negotiated prices.
“Under this bill, when Medicare negotiates what it pays for a drug, Maryland can pay the same once our board signs off. No more starting over, no more starting from scratch,” Moore said. “No more months of review to reach an answer for something that we already have, where we can save Marylanders 10s of millions of dollars a year and make life affordable for people in this state.”
Del. Jennifer White Holland (D-Baltimore County), is the anticipated bill sponsor in the House and Sen. Dawn Gile (D-Anne Arundel) is the expected Senate sponsor.
While Gile was not in attendance at the Thursday press conference, White Holland said the high cost of drugs are challenging for families facing tight budgets, who may go without or ration their pills when faced with unaffordable medications.
“Our friends, our neighbors — we are all hurt by this runaway greed,” White Holland said. “Whether it’s at the pharmacy counter … through our insurance premiums or with our taxpayer dollars, we all pay the high cost of prescription drugs.”
But drug manufacturers, some advocates of patients with rare diseases and other opponents of the proposal say that the efforts of the Prescription Drug Affordability Board to lower prescription drug costs could threaten access to life-saving drugs. They’re also skeptical over whether the board’s efforts will even result in lower out-of-pocket costs for Marylanders.
State officials approve 14.6% rate increase for individual premiums on ACA marketplace

“Government price-setting creates uncertainty for patients and risks limiting access to medicines,” said Will May, a spokesman for PhRMA, a powerful lobbying group representing pharmacy manufacturers. “Medicines may not be available if a pharmacy, hospital or physician cannot purchase them at the capped price. In countries that rely on government price-setting policies, patients often have access to fewer new medicines and wait longer for breakthrough treatments.”
Expanding to the private insurance market
Those potential consequences are yet to be seen, because in the years since the board’s formation from 2019 legislation, it has not lowered the price of any prescription drugs in the state.
Created by the General Assembly in 2019, the board had a hard time getting off the ground. It was slow to launch in part because if a veto from then-Gov. Larry Hogan (R) amid pandemic-induced economic uncertainty in 2020 that delayed the board’s formation.
After Moore allocated funding for the board’s operation in 2023, the entity went through lengthy rulemaking to create the “cost review” process for targeted drugs. The board finally picked its first six drugs for cost review in May 2024.
This year, board members determined Jardiance, the brand name for drug to treat Type 2 diabetes and other conditions, and Ozempic, another popular diabetes treatment and weight-loss drug, posed an affordability challenge and agreed to set upper payment limits based on their negotiated costs under the Maximum Fair Price.
The board’s authority is currently limited to just lowering costs for people  with state health insurance, which includes state employees as well as incarcerated individuals.
Its authority is set to expand to the private insurance market in 2028. Because the board has not yet lowered costs on any drugs, a 2025 law granting the board’s extended authority will not activate until one year after it has set upper payment limits on two prescription drugs with its current authority.
The upper payment limits Jardiance and Ozempic limit go into effect in January 2027, meaning the expanded authority will not be in play until 2028 at the earliest.
That said, the upper payment limit for Jardiance is estimated to save the state around $320,000 a year, which could balloon to between $9 million and $16 million a year if expanded out to all Maryland health plans.
Savings for Ozempic would be greater. The projected Ozempic savings would go from $5.8 million a year for just the state health plan, to somewhere between $113 million and $165 million a year when expanded.
DeMarco said that there will be an analysis in the works to estimate savings if prescription drug costs in Maryland were tied to 25 prescription drugs currently on the Maximum Fair Price list. He expects those estimates to reveal hundreds of millions in savings for the state, if not over a billion.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Podcast: Pros and cons on a ballot question that could repeal SD’s Medicaid expansion requirement
text:
An economic assistance application for the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




In the Nov. 3 election, South Dakota voters are considering four proposed amendments to the state’s constitution, all placed on the ballot by the Legislature. One of the questions, Amendment I, would repeal the expanded Medicaid eligibility requirement in the state constitution if the federal government’s share of funding for the expansion drops below 90%.
There’s a dispute about whether the amendment would trigger an immediate termination of expanded Medicaid if federal funding declines, or whether the amendment would merely give lawmakers the opportunity to consider eliminating the expansion in the event of reduced federal funding.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Medicaid is a federal-state healthcare insurance program for people with low incomes. In 2022, South Dakota voters expanded Medicaid eligibility to adults with incomes up to 138% of the poverty level, to capitalize on a federal funding match included in the Obama-era Affordable Care Act. The expansion is part of the state constitution and can only be altered by voters. The state Department of Social Services reported in August that about 143,000 South Dakotans were enrolled in Medicaid, including 31,000 who were enrolled through expanded eligibility.
A yes vote approves the amendment and repeals the Medicaid expansion requirement from the constitution if federal support declines. A no vote leaves the constitution as it is.
Supporters of the measure, including state Rep. Will Mortenson, R-Fort Pierre, say it’s fiscally responsible. Opponents, including Deb Fischer-Clemens, a nurse and Democratic former state lawmaker, worry it could leave thousands of people without health insurance.
In this episode, Mortenson and Fischer-Clemens explain their positions to Searchlight Report host Meghan O’Brien, who also speaks with Attorney General Marty Jackley about the dispute over the amendment’s meaning.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Some people are just like that
text:
It was a visit from Archbishop Desmond Tutu, pictured here, that helped columnist Doug James better understand his father and Great Falls, the community in which he was raised. (Photo by Getty Images)“Agent 86 reporting, sir.”
“What do you have to report, 86?”
I listened as 86 reported.
My father replied, “Thank you, 86. Carry on.”
It felt awkward.  I knew that 86 was no agent.
I was walking down Central Avenue in Great Falls with my father.  A middle-aged man approached. I recognized his coat. It had been my father’s. My father had given it to him. The man thought my father was still the Cascade County Attorney. He wanted to be helpful. My father was long removed from that job.
“Agent 86” and my father had a decades-long relationship.
I asked what was wrong with him.
My father replied, “Some people are just like that.”
No label. No judgment. Acceptance.  “Some people are just like that.”
My father’s community extended well beyond our family and neighbors. It included Agent 86, whose perception of the world was different.
After that day, I always looked for 86 when I went downtown. I didn’t see him often, but I always felt better when I did.
My father was a lawyer, a former county attorney and a former member of the Board of Pardons and Parole.
I was home alone for a few days. I was 16. No, I didn’t party. My Dad suggested I have dinner with a man who had done serious time in Deer Lodge. He was a great chef. My father didn’t want me to be alone. He thought I should spend time with the chef.  So, I had dinner with him and his wife.  It was a memorable evening with amazing food and wonderful company.
At the time, this seemed ordinary. Normal.
Later, I understood that a person is more than the decision they made on the worst day of their life.
The labels society likes to use are another kind of incarceration. Labels are harmful. People have names. There is power in speaking a person’s name. It is affirming. It is not a label or a judgment.  Speaking a person’s name creates connection.
In college, I spent time studying African history. It taught me something about my father. Yes, from African history.
I learned about an ancient southern African philosophy of our shared humanity, Ubuntu. It means that I am because we are. We are connected. Our humanity comes from our relationships; how we treat each other.
I am sure my father never heard about Ubuntu, but his life embodied the principle. All people matter.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu embodied that philosophy. He even came to Montana in 1990. He raised money in Helena for student scholarships. People paid to be there. During the dinner,  Tutu walked around the room and thanked the wait staff. He went into the kitchen and thanked the cooks. He made a special effort to thank everyone who served; those whose labor made the evening enjoyable.
Through Tutu’s example, I better understood my father.
He made a point of thanking those whose labor made our lives better. The wait staff. The piano player. The host. The cook. Everyone who labored.
My study of African history gave me a word to explain what my father had been teaching me.
My father was a part of the criminal justice system. The people he met through his work were part of his community and part of his humanity.
Thousands of Montanans carry felony convictions, long after serving time.  Today, more than 14,000 are under the supervision of the Department of Corrections. People in prison, on parole or probation, in a residential treatment center, an assessment center, or a pre-release center.  They are part of our community. Part of our humanity.
When I walk around today, I still look for Agent 86.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska needs farmers. Farmers need farmland.
text:
Sun Circle Farm is a 2.5-acre organic farm that produces vegetables, fruits and flowers for farmers markets and for a CSA service in Palmer, Alaska. (NRCS Alaska photo)This summer, I stood with a landowner at the edge of a hayfield her parents cleared more than 60 years ago. Wisps of her grey hair caught in the wind, and her eyes narrowed as she looked out over her farmland ground, thinking about so many neighboring farms that have been converted to gravel pits and subdivisions.
“Converting this should be considered a sin,” she told me. “My parents would be sick to know what has happened to this valley. We need our farmers. We need our farmland.”
She’s right, and she’s only saying out loud what a lot of Alaskans feel. When we talk about strengthening our food system, we usually talk about farmers: getting more people into agriculture and making sure they have greenhouses, equipment, markets and workers. All of that matters. But every farmer needs one thing before any of it can matter, and that is land. Alaska has a limited supply of soil capable of reliably producing food, and once that land is fragmented or converted to other uses, we cannot create more of it. That should matter to every Alaskan, not just farmers.
 Farmland is economic infrastructure

We tend to think of infrastructure as roads, ports, power systems and broadband. Productive agricultural land belongs on that list too, because it is the physical foundation an agricultural economy is built on. A farm doesn’t operate in isolation. Farmers buy fuel, seed, fertilizer and equipment. They hire contractors, accountants and employees. They sell to families, restaurants and institutions. When food is produced here, more of those dollars circulate here, and each working farm creates an opening for the next farmer and the next generation of Alaskans who want to make a living from the land.
 Food security starts with land

Alaska imports the majority of the food we eat, which leaves us vulnerable to transportation and supply disruptions thousands of miles away. No one is suggesting Alaska needs to grow everything. We don’t. But if we want more Alaska grown food, we need somewhere to grow it, and that means treating farmland as part of our state’s long-term food infrastructure.
A parcel farmed today, like that hayfield, may eventually be developed. That is a legitimate choice for a landowner to make. But when enough productive land disappears, the cumulative effect is one we all feel: fewer opportunities for farmers, less agricultural production and a smaller foundation for a local food economy.
 What role does government play?

State and local governments don’t farm the land, but they make decisions that either support or undermine the conditions agriculture needs to succeed. The state owns and manages agricultural land, decides how it is made available and shapes the policy environment farmers work in. Boroughs and municipalities influence the same outcome through comprehensive plans and subdivision rules.
None of this means the government should tell private landowners what to do with their property. It means recognizing that productive agricultural soil deserves weight when we make decisions about growth, the same way we have always weighed oil, minerals, timber and fisheries.
 The questions that matter

That is why the conversation about Alaska agriculture needs to go beyond whether our leaders support farmers. The more revealing questions are about farmland. What is the long-term vision for Alaska’s agricultural economy? How will beginning farmers gain access to land they can afford? And will an Alaskan who wants to farm 20 years from now be able to find ground to do it on?
These aren’t questions about stopping development. Alaska will grow, and land will be developed. But we have choices about how we grow and whether agriculture has a place in that future. At the Alaska Farmland Trust, we believe it should.
I think about that landowner often now. I think about her parents, that hayfield and that farm’s future. I think about the young Alaskan who wants to start a farm someday and doesn’t know it yet, and the family that will want locally grown food in ten years and hasn’t found the farmers market yet. All of them will need land.
This land is your land. It is also the foundation of Alaska’s agricultural future.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Coach who recorded young gymnasts undressing is sentenced to 90 years in prison
authors: By Ryan J. Foley, Associated Press
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A once prominent youth gymnastics coach was sentenced to 90 years in prison Wednesday for secretly recording his young female students undressing and using the bathroom at a Mississippi gym, in a case that rocked the sport.
This booking photo provided by the Des Moines, Iowa, Polk County Sheriff’s Office shows Sean Gardner on Aug. 14, 2025.  Credit: Polk County Sheriff's Office via AP, File
Sean Gardner, 39, received the maximum sentence possible. U.S. District Judge Kristi Johnson ordered that he serve 30 years in prison for each of the three federal child pornography production charges to which he pleaded guilty. The sentence likely amounts to life in prison for Gardner.
READ MORE: Ex-Mississippi gymnastics coach plans guilty plea in child pornography case
Gardner’s arrest last summer by the FBI, first reported by The Associated Press, renewed questions about whether U.S. gymnastics authorities had done enough to protect athletes from sexual abuse at the hands of an influential coach.
Gardner pleaded guilty to placing a hidden camera in a bathroom at a gymnastics studio in Purvis, Mississippi, between December 2017 and April 2018 to record his students. Investigators say he created videos showing close-up images of at least 10 minors naked or undressing, which they recovered from his computers years later while investigating claims that he sexually abused gymnasts in Iowa.
Several of his former students at Chow’s Gymnastics and Dance Institute in West Des Moines, Iowa, have alleged to police and in civil lawsuits that he used his position to prey on them. The institute was founded by prominent coach Liang “Chow” Qiao, who is known for producing Olympic champions. Gardner coached several youth prospects and served as director of an annual winter meet that drew hundreds of gymnasts to Iowa.
Chow’s Gymnastics & Dance Institute is seen Aug. 4, 2025, in West Des Moines, Iowa. Credit: AP Photo/Scott McFetridge
Gardner has not been charged in connection with any of the Iowa allegations, and police have said they would wait to determine how to proceed after the federal case concludes.
The lawsuits have also alleged the sport’s oversight bodies, USA Gymnastics and the U.S. Center for SafeSport, were told about inappropriate behavior by Gardner in 2017 but failed to take action to remove him from the sport for years. SafeSport temporarily suspended Gardner in 2022 after a Chow’s gymnast alleged sexual abuse, and Chow’s fired him then.
SafeSport has said it learned during its investigation that Chow and other coaches had been aware of allegations of sexual misconduct against Gardner but failed to report them to the center as required by its policy.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG finds ‘substantial share’ of Project Jupiter public comments raise concerns
text:
A rendering of Project Jupiter with a public comment in which an Albuquerque resident writes that prior comments in favor of the development made under her name were submitted without her knowledge or consent. (Rendering courtesy of STACK Infrastructure)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a Wednesday letter to New Mexico Environment Department Secretary James Kenney said that a “substantial share” of public comments on the pending air quality permit application for the Project Jupiter data center were “not sent by members of the public acting on their own.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Source NM in June revealed how residents in New Mexico’s three largest cities said their names falsely appeared on pro-Project Jupiter comments after they were approached by canvassers representing the Oracle and OpenAI data center. Several elected officials — in the state Legislature and on city councils across the state — subsequently said their names were similarly misused, prompting Torrez to open an investigation.
Torrez’s Wednesday letter to Kenney said the New Mexico Department of Justice’s review is “ongoing.”
“As it proceeds, we will evaluate whether the conduct described in this letter may also violate New Mexico criminal laws, and we will expand the inquiry accordingly,” Torrez wrote.
In his letter, Torrez said his office analyzed all 17,419 comments submitted during the public comment period for the data center’s air quality permit application.
If approved, the air quality permit would enable developers to use a natural-gas powered fuel cell system to power Project Jupiter. Projections show it could emit as many greenhouse gases annually as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
Torrez said that about 60% of the public comments — between 10,000 and 10,600 — contained the same pro-Project Jupiter form letter and came from 9,000 internet addresses, most of which submitted one comment apiece. Most listed out-of-state phone numbers even though the public comment portal didn’t require a portal, Torrez said.
He added that many of the form letters matched the supporter list associated with Project Jupiter’s website, projectjupitertogether.com, which hosts an interactive form letter titled “Send a comment to NMED.”
About 4,700 comments, most of which opposed the permit application, came from just 17 internet addresses, Torrez said.
Torrez wrote that he wanted “to be precise about the limits of what we know.”
“This letter does not establish who is responsible for any particular comment, and it does not characterize anyone’s intent,” he continued. “It does establish that a number of comments cannot be read as a measure of public opinion until the record has been verified.”
The NMDOJ review also turned up 22 comments bearing the names of public officials, local governments and organizations that all came from one computer, Torrez wrote, adding that “several of the officials named in those filings have informed my office that they did not write or authorize the submissions made in their names.”
“Taken together, these patterns mean that a substantial share of the comments was not sent by members of the public acting on their own,” he wrote.
Torrez asked NMED to preserve records including IP addresses and submission timestamps, to set aside the comments he’s flagged and to mark them as unverified. He also asked NMED officials to seek a ruling from the hearing officer presiding over the air quality permit application as to whether the flagged comments should be “considered in determining significant public interest.”
If the records can’t be verified, Torrez advised NMED to consider reopening its public comment period.
Torrez added that his office is asking Project Jupiter’s developers, its consultants and vendors to preserve corresponding records.
In a statement to Source NM, NMED spokesperson Drew Goretzka said that Kenney and Torrez met Wednesday morning to discuss the ongoing investigation.
“Secretary Kenney appreciates Attorney General Torrez’s investigation of this matter, and the New Mexico Environment Department will continue to preserve records in support of the New Mexico Department of Justice’s investigation,” Goretzka said. “While NMED has strengthened security measures in its public comment system, any person or organization that attempts to misuse the public comment process to steer a permit decision should be held accountable. NMED looks forward to continuing to work with the NMDOJ as the investigation proceeds, including helping in any resulting civil or criminal proceedings, as appropriate.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador sues OpenAI for alleged harms of ChatGPT
text:
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador addresses attendees during the Idaho National Guard's Cyber Discovery 2026 conference at the state's Chinden campus in Boise on June 9, 2026. (Photo by Sgt. Rusty Rehl/U.S. Army National Guard)Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador on Wednesday joined seven other states in announcing separate lawsuits against OpenAI, alleging the company’s chatbot ChatGPT harm. 
The 107-page lawsuit filed in Ada County Fourth Judicial District Court alleges that the company has harmed Idaho children and deceived adults in violation of the Idaho Consumer Protection Act. 
“We have watched technology giants experience tremendous growth and gains while putting consumers, especially children, at significant risk,” Labrador said in a press release. “The safety of Idaho’s children cannot be an afterthought to runaway profit or technological advancements. We will hold OpenAI accountable for their reckless priorities.”
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that the company continues to improve its safeguards and respond to “misalignment.” 
“We’ve built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack,” Pusateri wrote. “While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry —  not just one company.” 
Attorneys general in Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona filed similar lawsuits in their state courts Wednesday, Reuters reported. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What’s in Idaho’s OpenAI lawsuit? 

Labrador, deputy attorneys general Matthew Maurer and Stephanie Guyon, and private attorneys from the Los Angeles and New York City offices of Kibler Fowler & Cave LLP brought Idaho’s lawsuit. 
The complaint alleges that OpenAI misled the public “into believing that OpenAI is a responsible actor and that ChatGPT was and is a safe, teen-appropriate tool that puts safety first.” 
“Designed to be overly agreeable and feign human compassion, ChatGPT has proven that it can be incredibly dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and the public,” the lawsuit states.
The attorneys argue the company falsely represented the safety, reliability and accuracy of ChatCPT. It also argues the company failed to disclose personal data was collected from children under 13, and failed to warn users of risk of self-harm, violence and suicide. 
“Given these accelerating threats, Attorney General Labrador is suing to compel OpenAI’s compliance with the Idaho Consumer Protection Act and to cease its dangerous activities that have put Idahoans in harm’s way with willfully reckless and unlawful conduct,” the press release said. 
The state’s attorneys are asking the court to declare OpenAI violated Idaho law, order the company to pay $5,000 to the state for each violation of the law, and pay actual damages and restitution. The complaint also asks the court to stop the company from testing advanced AI models “outside of a secured, independently verified testing environment,” and to require the company to adopt additional safety measures and protocols. 
The lawsuit cites examples from other lawsuits and national reporting of cases in which the chatbot fueled delusions, coached users to commit violent acts, or encouraged self-harm and suicide. The court documents also cite a recent case in which OpenAI said some of its advanced AI models “went rogue,” and hacked the startup Hugging Face. None of the cases originated in Idaho. 
Pusateri, the OpenAI spokesperson, said the company will “continue sharing information about the extensive steps we’ve taken in response to incidents of misalignment. We’ve strengthened safeguards across our research systems, continued a broader review of model activity, provided notifications to affected organizations, and published our findings.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho lawmakers tee up bill to reform prior authorization, and more health insurance issues
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care.
The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior authorization, a cost-control measure that health insurers use to deny covering certain treatments, and to target several other issues that the interim legislative committee heard about in its meetings in the last few months and through surveys it sent to insurers and health care providers.
In a series of votes, the interim committee teed up a series of bills focused on health insurance that could be considered by the Legislature when it returns next January. Some of the other bills that could be drafted could address:

Reducing delayed payments to providers, by setting standards for providers and insurers;
Establishing uniform standards to credential health care providers through insurers; and
Requiring the Idaho Department of Insurance, which regulates health insurers, to collect and present to the Legislature data about the timeliness of payments, and healthcare denial rates. That might also include information on one arbitration tool created by Congress that the state’s largest insurer, Blue Cross of Idaho, claims that a North Idaho microhospital heavily relies upon. Blue Cross argues the practice could drive up the cost of healthcare, and Congress is considering overhauling the tool.

The potential prior authorization reform bill wouldn’t be the Legislature’s first attempt to address the issue, which some patients say can delay access to healthcare through drawn out timelines to issue decisions. Earlier this year, a bill, House Bill 611, set out to require more transparency and establish timelines in the process, but it never received a committee hearing. 
Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, listens to proceedings during the Jan. 12, 2026, Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Prior authorization also impacts healthcare providers. Providers in Idaho reported spending more time on administrative work to respond to prior authorization requests in recent years, according to data that committee co-chairman Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, summarized. In 2025, an American Medical Association survey found that 92% of physicians reported negative patient impacts caused by prior authorization processes. 
The committee was formed after a now-resolved contract fallout between a hospital in East Idaho, Portneuf Medical Center, and the insurer that runs the health plan for state employees, Regence BlueShield of Idaho. 
In the coming years, the state plans to transition Medicaid, a health insurance public assistance program for people who have disabilities or earn low-incomes, from being state-run to being managed by private health insurance companies.
