name: Maryland Matters
title: Malcolm X Monument rises in Anne Arundel County
text:
One side of the two-sided Malcolm X Monument near the Michael E. Busch Annapolis Library. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)A double-sided monument sharing quotes and photos of civil rights activist Malcolm X was unveiled Wednesday at the Michael E. Busch Annapolis Library.
More than 100 people came for the unveiling and to hear from various federal, state and local officials.
Malcolm X, who died at the age of 39 in 1965, had no direct connection to Maryland, but that was not a deterrent to honoring him, said Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel).
“Why not Malcom X?” Henson said. “When you think of Malcolm X and you think of a library, Malcolm X was a storyteller. The value of his work has been captured for history … that’s how they were able to make a movie [about Malcolm X]. That’s how we were able to inspire generations because we were able to tell his story.”
 The Caucus of African American Leaders began its push to install a memorial in the county in May 2025. Carl O. Snowden, convener of the caucus, said the memorial project cost $350,000, which included $70,000 from the county. The remaining amount was raised by the caucus, the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Committee, among others.
Carl O. Snowden, convener of the Caucus of African American Leaders, served as master of ceremonies  at the dedication of the  Malcolm X Monument on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. The memorial is near the Michael E. Busch Annapolis Library. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The memorial, he said, represents the first in the state dedicated to a Muslim American.
Snowden said he was 15 when he read “The Autobiography of Malcolm X: As Told to Alex Haley,” which was published several months after Malcolm X’s death in October 1965.
“This is not by accident. It’s not by coincidence. It’s not by happenstance. It’s by providence,” Snowden said after the nearly 90-minute ceremony. “And I’m so pleased on this day that we’re honoring Malcolm X.”
‘Open their minds’
Malcolm X was born Malcolm Little in May 1925 in Omaha, Nebraska. His parents were activists — his mother served as the national recording secretary for the Marcus Garvey Movement and his father a Baptist minister and chapter president of the Universal Negro Improvement Association.
His father died when he was 6 and his mother was later committed to a mental institution when he was 13. In 1946, at age 20, he was sent to prison for larceny.
In prison, he became an avid reader, learned about the Nation of Islam and adopted the surname “X.” After his release from prison in the early 1950s, he became a minister and spokesperson for the Nation of Islam and helped increase membership from 500 people in 1952 to 30,000 in 1963.
One year later, Malcolm X left the Nation of Islam and went on a pilgrimage to Mecca. He changed his name to El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz and broadened his views that all races can work together to fight injustice.
The memorial in Annapolis summarizes his life and includes photos of Malcolm X with the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., and former heavyweight boxing champion Muhammad Ali, as well as of Malcolm X on a stretcher after being shot at a rally in New York City in February 1965.
From left to right: Anne Arundel County Superintendent Mark Bedell, Annapolis Mayor Jared Littmann, Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman and Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) listen to remarks Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, before the unveiling of a Malcolm X Monument near the Michael E. Busch Annapolis Library. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Snowden and others said that they know some people may not like having a memorial outside a library to honor Malcolm X. While the human rights activist championed self-determination and cultural pride for Black people, he also angered those in the Jewish community with antisemitic statements.
But on Wednesday, those who celebrated Malcom X’s life simplified it with this phrase: People grow and change.
Steuart Pittman, the Anne Arundel County Executive, said he was raised to believe King was good, “Malcolm X, a little scary.”
Pittman added, “my thinking evolved over time, and I started to see some nuances” in reading about the life of Malcolm X, and how Jewish and Black Americans worked together during the civil rights movement.
“There are people out there from Anne Arundel County who are going to see in the news that we just put up this Malcolm X memorial [near the] library, and they’re going to be angry about it,” he said. But “they’re going to learn from it … and it’s going to open their minds.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Pilot error was the reason for Tiffany plane crash, according to preliminary report
text:
Tiffany was flying with Boltz from La Crosse to Wausau in September when Boltz’s plane suffered what was subsequently described as a “mechanical failure.” Tiffany speaks to reporters after his launch event in Wausau in September 2025. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)A preliminary National Transportation Safety Board report released on Oct. 13 found that an error by pilot Leonard Boltz was the cause of the plane crash with Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany.
Last month, Tiffany was flying with Boltz from La Crosse to Wausau when Boltz’s plane suffered what was subsequently described as a “mechanical failure.” Boltz crash landed the plane into Lake Wausau and the pair swam to a shallow area where they were rescued. Both sustained minor injuries. 
Tiffany, who had taken at least 12 flights with Boltz over the course of his campaign, praised Boltz during a press conference the day after the crash.
“It took some real expertise to be able to land that plane as he did,” Tiffany said.
The investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board remains ongoing, but the preliminary report stated Boltz told his aviation mechanic after the crash that the loss of engine power was due to his delay in switching fuel tanks and not turning on the electric fuel boost pump.
According to the report, Boltz had flown throughout the day, first flying from Langlade County, where he chairs a local Republican party, with a full load of 70 gallons of fuel. While flying from La Crosse to Wausau and preparing to land, the report states that Boltz “observed a higher-than-normal engine exhaust gas temperature.”
According to the report, Boltz did not refuel the airplane at La Crosse before the flight departed for Wausau, and he stated that he had selected the left main fuel tank for both flight legs except for when he briefly selected the auxiliary tanks while in cruise flight before switching back to the left tank.
The report states that all the fuel tank caps were found secure in a postaccident examination. The left main tank had no fuel while the right main tank and both auxiliary tanks were full of fuel.
The report states that the Beech K35 plane was “substantially damaged” in the crash into Lake Wausau.

name: California
title: Decenas de presas de California necesitan reparaciones ante la inminente llegada del invierno de El Niño
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Ante la amenaza de fuertes lluvias durante el invierno debido al fenómeno de El Niño, el Auditor Estatal advierte que las represas envejecidas de California “siguen representando un riesgo para la seguridad pública”, especialmente en las áreas de la Bahía de San Francisco, San Diego y Los Ángeles.
En 2017, los legisladores otorgaron al estado la facultad de sancionar a los propietarios de represas que infrinjan las normas de seguridad, después de que el fallo del aliviadero de Oroville obligara a la evacuación de casi 200,000 personas . La auditoría reveló que los gestores del agua aún no han utilizado esa facultad.
 Aunque los responsables estatales de la gestión del agua hubieran ejercido sus facultades coercitivas, es probable que los propietarios de las presas no hubieran podido costear las reparaciones.
 Una auditoría publicada el lunes reveló que, a fecha de mayo, 57 represas se encontraban en mal estado o en condiciones insatisfactorias, una cifra superior a la de recuentos anteriores. Es probable que este número siga aumentando, a medida que los funcionarios estatales de recursos hídricos reevalúen las represas más antiguas.
 Las 40 represas más riesgosas —clasificadas como de alto o extremadamente alto riesgo— están ubicadas en todo el estado, pero se agrupan cerca de ciudades costeras densamente pobladas.
Según el informe del auditor, si estas represas fallaran, “podrían poner en peligro a hasta 1.5 millones de personas y causar daños económicos por más de 265 mil millones de dólares”.
 Hace casi una década, los legisladores reforzaron la autoridad del Departamento de Recursos Hídricos de California para imponer sanciones como restricciones en los embalses, embargos de propiedades y multas cuando los propietarios de presas infrinjan las leyes estatales de seguridad y otros requisitos.
 Hasta abril, los ingenieros estatales habían remitido a los propietarios de 44 represas para que se tomaran medidas coercitivas. Sin embargo, según escribió el auditor, el departamento de recursos hídricos “nunca ha tomado medidas coercitivas punitivas contra los propietarios de represas que no subsanan sus infracciones”. 
 Presas envejecidas, fondos limitados
 El problema es que las represas están envejeciendo. Muchas se construyeron cuando las normas de seguridad eran menos estrictas. Las leyes estatales nunca obligaron a los propietarios de represas a reservar fondos para su mantenimiento, por lo que cuando el hormigón se desmorona, se acumulan sedimentos y los aliviaderos amenazan con erosionarse bajo las aguas de las inundaciones, la mayoría de los propietarios carecen del dinero necesario para las reparaciones.
El departamento de recursos hídricos del estado supervisa la seguridad de más de 1,220 represas, la mayoría en buen estado. La responsabilidad del mantenimiento de las represas recae en los gobiernos locales, las empresas de servicios públicos, las agencias de agua y los propietarios privados de terrenos y empresas que las poseen. Algunas de las represas clasificadas como en mal estado pertenecen a agencias estatales.
 Los desastres son extremadamente raros. Pero cuando ocurren, como en Oroville o el colapso en 1928 de la presa de St. Francis, prácticamente nueva, al noroeste de Los Ángeles, pueden ser catastróficos. 
 La presa del lago Hodges de San Diego en reparación durante el otoño de 2022. Se prevé que la presa sea reemplazada en la próxima década. Construida con un diseño de arcos múltiples, la presa se terminó en 1918 y fue adquirida por la ciudad de San Diego en 1925. Fotografía de John Gastaldo para CalMatters.
 El auditor elogió el programa de inspección del departamento de recursos hídricos, pero criticó duramente su inacción ante los propietarios de represas que no cumplen con los requisitos estatales de planificación, seguridad u otros, “permitiendo así que persistan graves deficiencias”.
 Uno de los casos involucró una presa con un agujero de 14 metros de ancho en su aliviadero que ha permanecido sin reparar durante más de 30 años, lo que, según la auditoría, podría causar inundaciones que afectarían a casi 300 personas y daños por más de 88 millones de dólares.
 La auditoría no menciona el nombre de la presa. Los administradores estatales del agua dijeron que dar más detalles podría plantear problemas de seguridad, aunque el departamento hace público el potencial de riesgo y el estado de cada presa en un informe anual.
 Los responsables estatales de la gestión del agua finalizaron las normas de aplicación en 2022. Sin embargo, comunicaron al auditor que no han podido dotar de personal suficiente a un departamento de control y que no confían en poder costear la defensa de sus acciones en una audiencia.
 Aun con personal y recursos económicos, concluye el auditor, si el propietario de una represa sigue sin cumplir con la normativa, el estado “no puede actuar antes de que la represa represente un peligro de nivel de emergencia. Esto deja un vacío en la legislación estatal que pone en riesgo la seguridad pública”. 
 Una gota en el océano
 Hace cuatro años, el gobernador Gavin Newsom promovió la reparación de represas en su estrategia de suministro de agua durante la sequía, como una forma de reforzar las reservas hídricas. Dos años después, en 2024, Newsom y los legisladores recortaron drásticamente la financiación de un programa de subvenciones para la reparación de represas.
Desde entonces, una propuesta electoral de 2024 proporcionó una inyección de 464 millones de dólares para el programa. Una subvención de la Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias también otorgó a California 629,198 dólares este septiembre, según Jason Ince, portavoz del Departamento de Recursos Hídricos.
Sin embargo, la auditoría citó estimaciones que indican que reparar las represas del estado, que dejan mucho que desear, podría costar alrededor de 28 mil millones de dólares, lo que convierte los fondos disponibles en una cantidad insignificante.
 El informe instó a los legisladores estatales a establecer plazos y exigir a los propietarios de presas de alto y muy alto riesgo —es decir, aquellas que podrían causar la muerte de personas si fallan— que presenten planes de mantenimiento y reparación a las agencias estatales.
 También pidió a los legisladores que ampliaran la autoridad de los administradores estatales del agua para hacer cumplir la ley, y que la agencia utilizara toda la fuerza de sus poderes.
 “Para garantizar que se aborde la seguridad pública antes de que el estado de una presa provoque una emergencia”, señala la auditoría, “la Legislatura debería modificar la ley estatal para permitir que el Departamento de Recursos Hídricos ordene la expropiación y el desmantelamiento de una presa cuando otros medios de aplicación de la ley por parte del Departamento de Recursos Hídricos no tengan éxito”.
 Laura Hollender, subdirectora de gestión de inundaciones y seguridad del Departamento de Recursos Hídricos, afirmó que el departamento trabajó en estrecha colaboración con el Auditor Estatal, pero discrepa con algunas de las conclusiones y recomendaciones del informe.
 Sin embargo, afirmó en un comunicado que están revisando cuidadosamente las recomendaciones y preparándose para lo que traiga El Niño. «Proteger la seguridad pública es la máxima prioridad del DWR, y reconocemos el papel fundamental que desempeñan la seguridad de las presas y el mantenimiento de los diques para reducir el riesgo de inundaciones en las comunidades de California».
 Con la llegada de la temporada de lluvias, el auditor también destacó que la planificación de la seguridad de las represas en todo el estado está incompleta.
 La Oficina de Servicios de Emergencia del Gobernador aún no ha aprobado los planes de emergencia para 245 represas, los cuales describen las medidas que sus propietarios tomarían para proteger a las personas y los bienes en caso de una falla en la represa. Los funcionarios informaron a la oficina del auditor que los propietarios de las represas no han completado las revisiones requeridas y que la ley estatal no establece plazos.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Omaha’s planned $80M public market sprouts from old roots
text:
Terrace view of the public market set to rise in downtown Omaha, creating another attraction for tourists and Nebraskans in the riverfront area. Heritage Omaha said it has raised private donations to cover the cost, including a cushion for early operating expenses. (Courtesy of Alley Poyner Macchietto Architecture and OJB)OMAHA — The $80 million indoor public market being built along downtown Omaha’s riverfront is envisioned as a year-round draw for tourists as well as statewide farmers and locals seeking to sell and buy specialty and Nebraska-centric goods.
The three-level glass structure will span 50,000 square feet featuring an upper mezzanine and a main market floor that holds dozens of vendors and spills into a courtyard and lawn suited for community events.
East aerial view of the public market set to rise in downtown Omaha, creating another attraction for tourists and Nebraskans. Heritage Omaha is leading the project and has raised  private donations to cover its cost. (Courtesy of Alley Poyner Macchietto Architecture and OJB)
Expected to open in summer 2028, organizers say the market is funded entirely by private funds raised by Heritage Omaha and structured as a nonprofit. 
 To Vic Gutman —  who advised Heritage after spending decades shaping the modern landscape of seasonal farmers and arts markets — the venture is the fruition of a 40-year dream.
“Finally it’s now going to happen,” said Gutman, who soon turns 75. “I’ve worked on a lot of projects over the years, and this is going to make a great community gathering place. I’m very excited.”
Fizzled efforts of past
Gutman, in an interview with the Nebraska Examiner, reflected on past efforts to establish a public marketplace in the state’s most populous city.
Vic Gutman with his dog in 2024 at the Sunday Market at Aksarben Village. (Courtesy of Maggie Winton)
He said his idea was grand and he started smaller: He founded a summer farmers market in 1994 that expanded to Aksarben Village in 2012.
In 2015, a key donor helped buy a cavernous postal annex, which previously stored street cars, just south of downtown Omaha in the resurging Little Italy neighborhood. That “Tenth Street Market” had been anticipated to open in 2017 as a year-round indoor marketplace, but fundraising fell short. Gutman, who spearheaded it, said some philanthropic doubters wanted the market to be in downtown. 
“In many ways it was a blessing in disguise that it didn’t work out then,” Gutman said. He said the COVID-19 pandemic would have set back the operation and vulnerable small businesses and vendors.
While Gutman had envisioned a public market in a retrofitted vintage warehouse, he said he sees an advantage in the custom-made structure that Heritage is building new into a hill overlooking The RiverFront’s Heartland of America Park near Eighth and Farnam streets.
The design provides space for about 30 permanent vendors, he said. Those locally owned and operated small businesses are yet to be selected, but Gutman said a sampling of staple tenants would include a butcher, a fishmonger, bakers, beer and wine makers and an ice cream shop. Prepared food will be offered.
Site plan for a public market set to rise in downtown Omaha. A goal is to expand access to nourishing foods and community experiences while uplifting local producers. (Courtesy of Alley Poyner Macchietto Architecture and OJB)
He said the entrance area will allow for dozens of additional pop-up vendor booths, including flowers and crafts. Fresh foods, fruit and produce are integral as a stated goal is to expand access to nourishing food and community experiences while uplifting local producers.
Spaces will be rented for weddings, conferences and other events. There will be a teaching and demonstration kitchen, flexible programming areas, outdoor seating. 
Prior to the fizzled Tenth Street Market, the nearby Burlington Station had been eyed as a market site by a different entity. That plan, which was publicized in 1994 but never materialized, envisioned artists, musicians, craftsmen, merchants and others populating two outdoor levels and part of the former train station’s rotunda on the weekends. The structure now is the headquarters of KETV.
Hark back to 1903
Even farther back — around 1903 — an Omaha “market house” was built and opened downtown near Capital Avenue and 14th Street. Gutman said his research reflects that the building’s use as a public market was only fleeting. 
Vic Gutman said he has used this historical image of the Omaha Market House, built around 1903, in presentations about markets. (Courtesy of Vic Gutman & Associates)
Morning World-Herald coverage of that era said vendor stalls in the new building were nearly full for a few weeks, following “insistent demand” for an indoor public market.
“But an organization of grocers proceeded to choke the life out of the new project in its infancy and succeeded,” the newspaper reported. 
The structure was leased for a time, then Mayor Jim Dahlman sought to shift its use to public baths, but it was ultimately torn down. 
Tourism and Heritage officials believe the modern-day Heritage-led project will be Nebraska’s first to rival public markets such as Seattle’s iconic Pike Place, Philadelphia’s Reading Terminal or Milwaukee’s Public Market.
Overseeing the local operation is the nonprofit Omaha Market Trust, which has a board of directors. The group hired Jerrica Marshall as the market’s inaugural executive director. She is former manager of the Downtown Des Moines Farmer Market and has 10 years of community development and public markets experience.
Entrance of the public market poised to rise in downtown Omaha. Site preparation and groundwork have started, with opening expected in 2028. (Courtesy of Alley Poyner Macchietto Architecture and OJB)
Heritage representatives introduced Marshall and unveiled site renderings during an event earlier this month.
They said that while Gutman laid the groundwork with earlier ventures, Mogens Bay, board chair of Valmont Industries and vice chair of the Heritage board, propelled this public market forward. The global Project for Public Spaces is a partner in planning and design.
‘Different type of energy’
Tina Cherica, Heritage president, told the Examiner that public markets usher a “different type of energy” into a community and draw people from all parts to “experience something uniquely Omaha and uniquely Nebraska.”
Tina Cherica, Heritage Omaha president. (Courtesy of Heritage Omaha)
Cherica, who has a family farm background, said a goal is to engage producers and farmers from across the state to showcase their goods, incubate their businesses and engage entrepreneurial skills. She said the $80 million investment and campaign goal is covered by philanthropic donations. That amount includes a cushion to help sustain market operations as the project launches. 
Eventually, founders expect the market to be self-sustaining through fees and rental agreements.
Those interviewed touted the anticipated tourism boost.
Jenn Gjerde, executive director of the Nebraska Tourism Commission, said the added attraction to a developing downtown strengthens Omaha’s position as a competitive market for business conferences, sporting and other events.
“It further activates the riverfront, which already is a huge draw for out-of-town visitors,” said Jasmyn Goodwin, executive director of Visit Omaha, which promotes tourism for Douglas County.
 
 Heritage Omaha 
Over the past 30 years, Heritage Omaha has leveraged more than $800 million in donations to create $1.7 billion in civic projects for Omaha, its leaders say. Site preparation has begun on its latest undertaking, the downtown public market.
Heritage-led fundraising campaigns built or transformed multiple other venues including Omaha Central Library, Kiewit Luminarium, Charles Schwab Field and Holland Performing Arts Center and Orpheum Theater.



Dramatic changes to the downtown riverfront area have occurred in recent years, including a roughly $400 million overhaul of parks and amenities, collectively called “The RiverFront.” Other developments include various new apartments, the $600 million Mutual of Omaha office tower and the controversial streetcar project that tops $400 million.
The latest countywide figures showed 14.8 million annual visitors directly spending $1.6 billion on food, lodging, entertainment and merchandise in the county, Goodwin said.
She said travelers want to experience a “taste of the local area” they are in, and that is an allure of a public market. Meanwhile, locals can showcase goods in front of a larger audience.
Plans for the market were informed by thousands of metro-area residents, food entrepreneurs, farmers and makers, organizers said. Gutman said on-site parking for about 75 cars is to be supplemented with a city parking structure across the street.
“I just want to see it happen,” Gutman said. “It’s in good hands.”
West aerial view of the public market under construction in downtown Omaha. Organizers said about 75 on-site parking spaces will be supplemented with more parking in a nearby city garage. (Courtesy of Alley Poyner Macchietto Architecture and OJB)

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas wildlife refuge important for duck migration to expand
text:
Bayou DeView in the Cache River National Wildlife Refuge, Arkansas (Photo courtesy of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is expanding one of its wildlife refuges in Arkansas, said the nonprofit partnering with the federal government on the project said Wednesday.
The Trust for Public Land, an outdoors nonprofit, said 435 acres would be added to the Cache River National Wildlife Refuge in east Arkansas. That’s on top of 73,000 existing acres in Jackson, Monroe, Prairie and Woodruff counties.
The new addition to the refuge will provide new entry points to the public land and add 1.2 new miles of protected riverfront. 
The refuge is one of the most important wintering spots for ducks, and is the largest remaining tract of contiguous bottomland hardwood forest in North America.
Like the Buffalo National River in north Arkansas in the decades before, the Cache River found itself under threat in the 1970s by the Army Corps of Engineers, which proposed altering the river to reduce flooding. 
Arkansas permanently bans large-scale swine operations from the Buffalo River watershed

Community organizing and lawsuits prevented the proposal until the refuge was established by Congress in 1986, and it is now one of the only waterways in the Lower Mississippi River Valley that hasn’t been drastically altered.
More than 200,000 people visit the refuge each year, according to the Trust for Public Land.
“This addition to the Refuge is significant not only for conservation of incredible wildlife habitat, but for creating needed access to these cherished wildlands along Cache River,” Stacey Shankle, program director of the mid-South region for Trust for Public Land, said in a press release.
“Adding these 435 acres to Cache River National Wildlife Refuge protects important habitat along the Mississippi Flyway and gives people more opportunities to enjoy Arkansas’s outdoors,” Holly Gaboriault, southeast regional chief of the National Wildlife Refuge System, said in a press release.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Ten endangered red wolves exchanged between NC and NY in conservation effort
text:
Endangered red wolf pups Cane, Champ, Puck, Stormy and Whaler prepare for transport from Durham to a new conservation center in New York. (Photo: Museum of Life and Science)Ten endangered red wolves were transported between North Carolina and New York Tuesday as part of a coordinated effort to preserve the critically endangered species.
Pilots to the Rescue — a nonprofit that uses volunteer pilots to transport animals — flew three red wolves from the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York, to Raleigh Regional Airport in Person County. 
One of those wolves, Sassafras, was heading to another North Carolina facility. The other two, Mac and Sabine, were brought to the Museum of Life and Science in Durham.
Volunteer pilots and museum staff load the plane on the tarmac at Raleigh Regional Airport Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo: Museum of Life and Science)
The team then returned with a breeding pair of wolves and their five young pups from the museum. The seven wolves were transported by ground from New Jersey to the conservation center in New York. 
The family includes first-time parents Carolina and Jacques and their five pups, who were born in May. The exchange is part of a breeding program designed to maintain genetic diversity among red wolves living in human care.
Museum officials said the move will allow the family to stay together while giving the growing wolves more space. Carolina and Jacques could have another litter in 2027.
The Museum of Life and Science has participated in red wolf conservation for decades. The exchange allows the museum to coordinate breeding and family groups as part of the recovery effort. 
Sherry Samuels, senior director of animal care, said the transfers are a routine part of conservation work. She said she hopes the new wolf pair will produce pups, though there is no guarantee. 
“We’re just temporary housing,” she said. “They’re not here forever, so I always know they’re going to head on.” 
Endangered red wolves rebound in NC with four litters of pups born this year

The red wolf is one of the world’s most endangered animals. Once found across much of the Southeast, the species was driven to the brink of extinction by habitat loss and human predation. 
Today, eastern North Carolina is home to the only remaining wild population. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimates that 21 adult red wolves remained in the wild, along with about 14 pups. 
Samuels said the museum’s conservation program has pioneered new techniques such as fostering captive-born pups with wild red wolf mothers, helping to support the recovery of the wild population. 
“We’re better because of having animals like this around,” Samuels said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, other AGs move to sue OpenAI in state courts
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, joined by, from left, fellow state attorneys Kris Kobach of Kansas, JB McCuskey of West Virginia and Mike Hilgers of Nebraska, held a news conference Oct. 14, 2026 at the Iowa State Capitol on state AGs pursuing litigation against OpenAI. (Photo via Iowa Attorney General's Office's Facebook page)Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird and counterparts from three other states announced plans Wednesday to sue OpenAI in state courts, alleging ChatGPT harmed children and violated each state’s consumer fraud act.
Bird was joined by attorneys general Kris Kobach of Kansas, Mike Hilgers of Nebraska, and JB McCuskey of West Virginia at the Iowa Capitol to announce their planned litigation against the generative artificial intelligence company. Bird quoted OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who recently told Politico, “we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”
Bird said as attorneys general, “we refuse to accept that.”
“We will not just accept that any big tech company can make money by hurting Iowa’s kids and use them as lab rats, you know, in a race to be the first or the biggest or to have the most users,” Bird said. “When a big company does that, it’s time for me, as attorney general, to step in and … hold them accountable to our law and take them to court.”
The lawsuit filed in Iowa district court accuses OpenAI of failing to provide proper warnings or restrictions on the use of ChatGPT — particularly by minors — amid reports that the chatbot has issued responses that include false medical advice and that encourage violence or self-harm. The petition cites other lawsuits filed against OpenAI by parents who allege ChatGPT encouraged their minor child to commit suicide, and parents who say ChatGPT advised their teenage son it was safe to take a combination of drugs which ultimately led to his death.
Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana are also suing OpenAI in their respective state courts, alleging the company provided misleading statements about the safety of ChatGPT.
Kobach said many people may be used to attorneys general coordinating on litigation, pointing to lawsuits regarding the opioid crisis or tobacco.
“But usually, you don’t see us getting together to announce the lawsuit unless it’s really, really important,” Kobach said. “This is one of those lawsuits that’s really, really important, which is why I did the three-and-a-half hour drive (from Kansas) and Mike did a two-and-a-half hour drive from Lincoln.”
He said the litigation was a way to address ongoing safety concerns about the use of ChatGPT in states like Iowa and Kansas without needing to wait for Congress to take action on the federal level. Kobach said the lawsuits were filed because it would be “foolish” to wait for federal action to address this problem.
“Congress has been deliberating on this and holding hearings for more than a year,” Kobach said. “There are over 150 bills that have been submitted in Congress, and the vast majority of them have not even gotten a committee vote yet. The notion that we should wait for Congress to develop a universal solution, covers the entire country, and then apply that solution or apply those standards is foolish. We absolutely need to take action, because in the intervening year and a half or so, these harms that Attorney General Bird mentioned, have already occurred. And there will be more people … harmed by OpenAI if we continue to wait.”
The Kansas Republican added, “you also have the problem that many in Congress appear not particularly willing to oppose any significant restraint on the corporations engaged in AI.”
McCuskey said the lawsuits are not meant to be an impediment to the advancement of AI technology, “because there are so many remarkable things that AI is gonna do for us — It’s gonna cure cancer, it’s gonna help our military. it’s gonna make sure that we have the best processes for energy development that any other country in the world has.”
“But it can’t hurt our children,” McCuskey said. “And what we know is that it does. It is harming our children in real time, and what we’re doing today is we’re standing up and saying, ‘We believe that American exceptionalism is going to create an AI world that’s better than China, it’s better than Russia, it’s better than Iran, it’s better than our adversaries. But it’s going be safe for our children at the exact same time.”
Bird said the bipartisan group decided to pursue litigation on a state-by-state basis instead of as a group because it allows the attorneys general to sue OpenAI under their respective state’s laws, including state consumer fraud acts.
“The way the Iowa law works, it allows me, as attorney general, to step in on behalf of the whole group of Iowans who have been hurt under our consumer protection laws — and that is a state law, and so that is why we file it in our state court,” Bird said. “… We also know that there is power in numbers, and that OpenAI is a huge company, massive company. And so we know there is power in this bipartisan group of attorneys general coming together to stand up for their states, to stand up for the citizens of their state.”
Hilgers said filing separate state lawsuits allows each state to pursue action against the company on the basis of harm to their state’s citizens.
“I want to make sure that Nebraska parents are on a Nebraska jury to be able to determine what the Nebraska harm was, to hold them liable,” Hilgers said.

name: VTDigger
title: Robert A. Burley, FAIA
text:
Born: 12/11/1927
Buffalo, New York
Died: 09/23/2026
Shelburne, Vermont
Details of service:
There will be a memorial event to honor Bob’s life at the Mad River Glen Basebox on Saturday, October 24, at 2:00 p.m. All are welcome. Please bring memories and stories to share.

Bob Burley read The New York Times nearly every day of his adult life, and would have appreciated us starting in Times style:
Robert A. “Bob” Burley, a longtime resident of Waitsfield, who started his brilliant 60-year architectural career working with Eero Saarinen on the St. Louis Arch, left his imprint on iconic landmarks in Vermont and beyond. His dedication to historic preservation, natural site design and client collaboration earned him a national reputation. He died at his home in Shelburne on September 23, 2026, his daughter Jill at his side. He was 98.
Born December 11, 1927, to Alan and Mildred Burley, Bob grew up in Kenmore, New York, a planned community north of Buffalo. His natural talents for drawing, problem-solving and both creative and practical thinking carried him through a successful career and a fulfilling life. His confident yet humble nature was always friendly and positive. Bob rarely said “no”; rather, he would persist to find the best solution, often an innovation rather than a compromise.
He earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts from Columbia College in 1950, and a Bachelor of Architecture from Columbia University in 1953. His gift for architecture was recognized early; he received six major awards upon graduation, including a fellowship and stipend to travel through Europe for a year. Bob married Pat, whom he had dated through college, following graduation, beginning their lifelong collaboration in adventure, work and family.
His fellowship took them through Europe, the Middle East and into Egypt. Their adventures were many, including driving their two-seater Porsche through the desert along the Nile to visit the Valley of the Kings. Imagine: no cellphones or internet, no roadmaps, few gas stations, just good sense, good luck and Bob’s easy way with people, even in other languages and cultures.
On return to the U.S., Bob began his career with Eero Saarinen and Associates, at the height of its influence on architecture and design internationally. Bob later said the seven years he spent under Saarinen’s mentorship were key to his perspective and method. It was there he learned to listen to and analyze a client’s needs, before beginning a design.
While at Saarinen’s office, Bob led the design team for construction of the new U.S. Embassy in London, moving there for a year with his young family. When they returned to the U.S., Bob led the design team for the St. Louis Gateway Arch, charged with ensuring every detail of a beautiful and complicated structure.
While still in school, Bob had organized some of the first weekend ski trips by bus from New York City to Vermont, where both he and Pat had skied earlier as members of a Buffalo ski club. With a connection to the Mad River Valley, Bob and Pat built a ski chalet on Bragg Hill, commuting on weekends, from New Haven and then Manhattan to ski and vacation, always with their eyes on settling there. They moved to Fayston in 1964 and started Robert Burley Associates (later The Burley Partnership), joined by friend and fellow architect Malcolm Appleton. Pat was an integral part of the business from the start.
Bob’s impact on Vermont’s built and natural environments was profound, prolonged and widespread. From the historic Number Nine Schoolhouse on Route 17 in Fayston, he helped shape the look of the state from the 1960s well into the current century.
Bob’s firm was selected in the mid-1960s to create a master plan for the Capitol Complex in Montpelier, a task he stayed with for more than two decades and that included designs for the historic Pavilion Hotel and a modern yet seamless addition to the Vermont Statehouse. Bob was forward thinking and masterful at attaining consensus; the results were routinely lauded as exemplary historic preservation for new uses.
In 1985, the Barre-Montpelier Times Argus dubbed Bob “Vermont’s Master Architect” citing his work on the capitol as well as the new Trapp Family Lodge, Maple Tree Place, the addition to the UVM Library, expansion of the Woodstock Inn, Timberlane Medical Building and many award-winning residences from Maine to Florida. He was a potent force in the discussions that led to both Act 250 and Vermont’s prohibition on billboards and worked on other statewide initiatives such as Vermont’s Scenic Byways and the 1976 Bicentennial Steam Train.
Bob had high-profile and successful national assignments and awards in historic preservation. He was a long-term member of the advisory panel guiding the restoration of Thomas Jefferson’s Poplar Forest Retreat in Virginia. He was the executive director of the Taliesin Preservation Commission, a four-year commitment to begin the restoration of Frank Lloyd Wright’s home and studio in Spring Green, Wisconsin, a National Historic Landmark. He led the American Institute of Architects (AIA) task force to preserve the West Front of the U.S. Capitol. His clever reuse of two cow barns into a library at Colby-Sawyer College earned awards from both the AIA and the American Library Association.
Even as he saw the economic benefits of historic preservation, he was not bound by that as a mandate. He designed award-winning Modernist buildings and was as familiar and versatile with that vernacular as he was with others.
Bob did not have a signature “Burley” look. Rather, his work process was characterized by a deep understanding of a client’s needs and budget, the site, and the context. He put functionality before aesthetics, which resulted in excellent designs that exceeded client expectations.
He was named a Fellow of the AIA in 1979, a rare distinction offered for exceptional contributions to the profession. Bob served two terms as president of the Vermont chapter of the AIA; Mad River Valley residents may remember his personalized “AIA” license plate from those years.
Bob was committed to public service, offering his time to initiatives that he thought would help his town, state or country have a more hospitable environment. Whether it was service on Vermont’s Committee for Scenery Preservation, the Waitsfield Historical Society or the many other public dialogues he engaged in, he was a leader and an advocate. Many saw him as a mentor.
Bob’s passions extended beyond architecture. He was a dedicated Mad River Glen skier well into his 80s. He was a sailor for as many years, learning as a youngster on Lake Erie. The family graduated from a 17-foot fiberglass daysailer to a 44-foot 1939 classic wooden sloop! Together, Bob and Pat were fearless in their endeavors. In their late 70s, as a segue to retirement, the couple bought a 45-foot trawler and headed south down the Intercoastal Waterway — Pat at the helm, Bob on deck, Skipper their cat sleeping in the fo’c’sle.
He was an avid reader of The New York Times, a habit he developed as a young man. Well into his 90s, he would drive 40 miles roundtrip to get his newspaper. His daughter used that as enticement to move closer to her: “You can have the Times delivered to your door every morning, Dad!”
Leaving his home and friends in the Mad River Valley was eased by all the friends that Bob quickly made at The Residence at Shelburne Bay. He will be missed by many in Shelburne, the Valley, the architectural community, and others far and wide, for his interest, his gentleness of spirit, and his passion for his work and life. To the end, he offered to all a compliment, a word of encouragement, a funny line, and a beaming smile.
He was predeceased by his dear wife of 70 years, Pat; his beloved son, Todd; and his brother, Elliott. He is survived by his beloved daughter Jill, her spouse Elizabeth, nieces, nephews, extended family, and many friends.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Robert A. Burley, FAIA.

name: Washington State Standard
title: New ad fires up debate in closely-watched WA congressional race
text:
State Senate Republican Leader John Braun and Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez are dueling in southwest Washington’s 3rd Congressional District. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican state Sen. John Braun faced off for their final debate Tuesday, each looking to more clearly mark their turf on federal policies and social issues with voters beginning to cast ballots in their nationally-watched contest.
They parried on an array of subjects for the better part of an hour, with some exchanges exposing clear differences, others few degrees of separation.
In the waning moments, Gluesenkamp Perez got personal, questioning Braun’s lack of outreach to the family of a man killed in an accident at Braun’s company two years ago. She raised the matter hours after launching a campaign ad featuring a son of the man who died in that workplace incident who says that Braun “never called.” The son worked for the company at the time.
“You owe that family an apology,” she said in the debate.
Braun responded curtly. “This is a new low for Marie,” he said. “Here’s the reality. I talked to the son twice that day. I didn’t call him. I talked to him in person.”
Moments later when the debate concluded, Braun approached and spoke briefly to the two-term incumbent before they exited the studio of Portland television station KATU.
“I said I didn’t think she had a soul,” Braun told the Standard on Wednesday. 
“This is a character attack,” he continued. “This was a terrible tragic accident. We did everything we could to do this right. To say we didn’t try, it’s heartless.”
Gluesenkamp Perez did not reply to Braun’s post-debate comment, her campaign manager said Wednesday.
The man’s son “came to us because he believed voters deserved to hear what happened to him, despite knowing it could cost him personally. It’s disappointing that Braun has resorted to personal attacks,” campaign manager Tim Gowen wrote in email.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The ad-fueled tension is the latest flashpoint in this match-up in the 3rd Congressional District seat in southwest Washington. It is among a handful of competitive congressional races nationwide, the outcome of which could help determine which party holds the majority in the House next year. 
Gluesenkamp Perez is seeking a third term against Braun, the Republican leader in the state Senate. The district encompasses Clark, Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Wahkiakum, and Skamania counties and a small part of Thurston County. 
President Donald Trump won it three times, evidence of its Republican lean. But the GOP lost the congressional seat in 2022 when Gluesenkamp Perez, co-owner of an auto repair and machine shop and a Democratic newcomer, beat Republican Joe Kent, a former Army Special Forces soldier who Trump backed.
She defeated him in their rematch in 2024 by a wider margin while in the presidential race, Trump soundly beat Democrat Kamala Harris in the congressional district.
Braun, a Centralia resident in his fourth term as a state senator, brings legislative experience, electoral know-how and a brand of Republicanism he hopes will appeal to independent and moderate GOP voters who shunned Kent, who promoted conspiracy theories and asserted that the 2020 election results were fraudulent.
On Tuesday, each candidate stuck to their general talking points as they worked through an array of topics.
On tariffs, both frowned on the Trump administration approach.
Gluesenkamp Perez said they “are a tool that can be used recklessly or productively” and the administration has done “a terrible job” of carrying out “a strategic, thoughtful” policy that will help restore manufacturing.
Braun, owner of Braun Northwest Inc., an emergency response vehicle manufacturer, said tariffs are not a means to revitalize the manufacturing sector. “With our allies, indiscriminate use of tariffs is not helpful and ultimately leads to an increase of prices for manufacturers and consumers,” he said.
On a question about the Iran war, Gluesenkamp Perez said she had voted against U.S. military action and pushed for Congress to exercise its oversight under the war powers resolution. The president “has gone into this war recklessly, with no clear objectives and no strategy to achieve them,” she said. 
Braun, in his response, said Iran cannot be allowed to build nuclear weapons and long-range ballistic missiles. But, he sounded ready to buck Trump – who has endorsed him. “I will not, and I do not support a war without clear objectives and without a clear ending point. I think Congress has a very important role here, one they should exercise,” he said.
On data centers, Braun says they can be “enormously positive” if companies “build trust” with communities and assure promised benefits are delivered. Each “absolutely should either provide power or work with the local utility to make sure they’re investing in infrastructure that will bring down the cost of power for everyone,” he said.
Gluesenkamp Perez said communities surrounding data centers “need to be held harmless” from effects of noise pollution and rising energy costs. There should be thresholds for how much power a center is allowed to consume or a different rate set for their energy usage, she said. 
On the subject of allowing trans girls to play in girls’ sports, they both said it is unfair. 
Braun would ban their participation. “For decades, we fought for a fair playing field for women. Now, for reasons I can’t fully explain, here in 2026, we want to undo all that. I think it’s unfair. I think it’s unsafe, and it’s the wrong path for our state and our country,” he said.
Gluesenkamp Perez described herself as “libertarian on this issue.” Continuing, she said, “fundamentally, I agree it’s not fair for boys to compete in girls’ sports” but the final decisions on competition “are best made by local stakeholders.”SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sierra Club calls for renewable energy to be part of Iowa steel mill deal
text:
Sierra Club Iowa Chapter is calling for renewable energy and local job requirements in tax incentives offered to a massive steel plant slated for Iowa. Pictured is a steel plant in Pennsylvania. (Photo by Jeff Swensen/Getty Images)The Sierra Club Iowa Chapter urged Iowa leaders Wednesday to require provisions including renewable energy infrastructure, air pollution controls and commitments to work with the local community when authorizing incentives to a massive steel plant slated for southeast Iowa.
The environmental group sent a letter Wednesday to Iowa Economic Development Authority Director Debi Durham with a list of recommendations to include as the department intends to issue a tax credit to a $15 billion steel plant project. 
President Donald Trump announced in late September that the steel company Mesabi Metallics planned to build a $15 billion steel mill in southeast Iowa. 
Lawmakers responded by swiftly returning to the Iowa Capitol for a special session, where they passed and Gov. Kim Reynolds signed a bill allowing IEDA to authorize a tax credit to a business for up to 10% of its qualifying investment in a rural county. The bill doubled the previous tax credit cap IEDA could issue under the Major Economic Growth Attraction, or MEGA, program. 
The letter from Sierra Club said the mill could be “among the cleanest and most modern in the country” if the group’s ideas are included in negotiations on the terms of an incentive package for the plant. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Failure to adequately enforce the below items jeopardizes this prospect as dirtier steel and iron is priced out of international markets, fossil fuel prices create uncertainty for primary manufacturers, and communities and workers organize to oppose projects that increase local burdens,” the group said in the letter. 
Sierra Club supports an end to coal-fired power plants and each year issues its “Dirty Truth” report, which rates utilities across the country on their plans to retire coal plants and to build renewable energy infrastructure. 
The Iowa chapter of the group urged IEDA to include a provision in the tax incentive deal that Mesabi Metallics must either procure or produce “new renewable energy generated from wind, solar, geothermal, and/or batteries for its operations’ electricity and heat needs.” They also said the company should work with Iowa utilities to ensure the cost of new electricity generation or infrastructure upgrades are not passed along to ratepayers.
Sierra Club said the mill, which would use iron ore mined in Minnesota, should implement “as much electric equipment as possible” at the mill. 
In a news release from the company, Mesabi Metallics said the plant would “be one of the most efficient and environmentally friendly facilities in the world.” 
The company plans to utilize hot direct-reduced iron technology to take the iron ore and convert it into solid metallic iron and electric arc furnace technology to recycle materials and produce the steel. Keeping the materials hot and using an electric furnace with these technologies will “significantly lower energy usage and reduce emissions” according to Mesabi. 
Sierra Club also suggested Iowa’s incentives require the plant to use “covered- and zero-emissions trucks,” implement best available control technologies for air pollutants and to develop a “credible path” to procuring and using green or geologic hydrogen. 
Trump said the plant would be the largest in the U.S. and one of the largest steel mills in the world. Once fully operational, the company has said it will employ at least 1,750 full-time employees. The company anticipates over 6,000 jobs during the construction of the plant. 
The list of recommendations from Sierra Club also called for a commitment from Mesabi for a minimum number of local hires and a commitment to not interfere with union organizing activities. 
Mesabi Metallics has said it plans to utilize “local vendors” during construction “to support additional job growth throughout the area.”
The Iowa Economic Development Authority did not respond Wednesday to a request for comment on the letter. 
In a news release about the club’s demands, Sierra Club Iowa Chapter Director Pam Mackey Taylor said Iowans deserve “enforceable commitments that protect their health, lower pollution, support good union jobs, and deliver lasting benefits to local communities.” 
“These commitments must be credible, put in writing and backed by real consequences if the company fails to deliver,” Mackey Taylor said. “We know Iowa can attract businesses on the cutting edge of clean American manufacturing, and while we can offer incentives to ensure these companies build here, we can also not sacrifice healthy communities and a just economic future in the process.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Ayotte proposes tuition assistance program for community college students
text:
Manchester Community College, where Gov. Kelly Ayotte announced a proposal for a free community college tuition program she wants to request in the budget, Wednesday Oct 14. 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)Gov. Kelly Ayotte called for a program Wednesday to provide free tuition for New Hampshire community college students with a total family income of up to $100,000, and said she would add such a proposal in her budget if reelected.
The announcement, made at an event at Manchester Community College, comes on the heels of a recent decision by the University System of New Hampshire to offer a similar free tuition program to New Hampshire residents starting in the 2027-2028 school year.
But unlike the university system’s program, which was approved by the board of trustees and will take effect next year, Ayotte’s program would require the approval and funding of the Legislature next year. 
Ayotte called the state’s community colleges “critical to growing our economy.”
“They’re really the backbone of the training that we need for our workforce,” she said. 
Ayotte’s proposal would allow New Hampshire residents with a total family income of up to $100,000 to get tuition covered by the state — provided they had already signed up for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) financial aid program and any available state financial aid programs. The governor’s proposed program would provide reimbursement to those students for any remaining tuition costs not already covered by those prior programs, known as a “last-dollar” approach.
To receive the money, students would be required to maintain a 2.0 GPA and be enrolled in at least six credits per semester at a state community college, Ayotte announced Wednesday.
New Hampshire community colleges currently charge $238 per credit for New Hampshire residents; a full academic year consisting of 30 credits would cost $7,140 in tuition. But when adding in fees, housing, books, transportation and personal expenses, the full cost per year can be between $22,000 and $28,000 per year, depending on housing and transportation arrangements, CCSNH estimates. 
Ayotte’s proposed program would cover only the remainder of the $7,140 of tuition — and only the remainder not already covered by other financial aid programs. 
The program would be funded via the state’s General Fund; the Community College System of New Hampshire has estimated that it could cost the state about $5.5 million per year. 
Should Ayotte win reelection, her community college tuition proposal would need approval in the two-year budget in 2027. Ayotte could include the program in her proposed gubernatorial budget in February, but would need to win ultimate approval in the state House and Senate. 
If Ayotte were reelected, the success of a tuition program could be affected by the make-up of the state House and Senate, which Republicans currently control. 
New Hampshire’s revenues have come in higher than expected since the last budget was enacted in July 2025; from July to September 2026, the first quarter of the 2027 state fiscal year, revenues were 12.5% above budget expectations. That trend, if it continues, could give the next governor and Legislature some leeway to increase spending or reverse previous cuts to programs during the 2027 budget process. 
Ayotte announced the proposed community college tuition assistance program weeks after the university system launched its “New Hampshire Promise” program, which will allow first-year, full-time students who are New Hampshire residents, have a 2.7 high school GPA or higher, and whose total family income is $100,000 or less to receive free tuition, provided they have already filed for the FAFSA. The university system plans to finance that program by transferring existing financial aid programs for Pell Grant recipients. 
CCSNH Chancellor Chuck Lloyd, appointed to the role in July, said the proposed program is modeled off a $3 million pilot program in 2023 targeted at New Hampshire community college students receiving Pell Grants. He called that two-year program a success for recruiting more students. “We saw a significant uptick,” he said in an interview. 
The proposed tuition assistance program would cover more students; the $100,000 income limit is higher than the typical income limits for Pell Grant recipients. 
Lloyd characterized tuition assistance as a tool to address the state’s workforce shortage by incentivizing more students to seek additional education.
“If we can open up the front end of the funnel, we get more folks into career paths, and then we can solve the workforce,” he said. “It’s thinking holistically about supporting students who maybe weren’t thinking about post-secondary education. Now it’s an option.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Stealing Elections, American Style: Voting rights attorney David Walbert on how the 2026 election could be hijacked — and saved
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Author David Walbert and his latest book, “Stealing Elections, American Style.” Courtesy photo
Election deniers, egged on by President Donald Trump, are now running elections in numerous locales across the country. The playbook for stealing elections has remained the same for over a century: “control who votes, control how votes are counted, and control who decides when the counting stops.”
That’s the argument by veteran voting rights lawyer David Walbert in his new book, “Stealing Elections, American Style.” He recounts stories of voter suppression and stolen elections dating back 150 years.
Walbert says these time-tested strategies could be deployed to thwart the will of the people in the 2026 election. He warns that there could be an unprecedented new tactic: If House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Trump loyalist, refuses to seat new members of Congress in January 2027, the country could be plunged into an uncharted constitutional crisis.
“One of the lessons that the election deniers learned in 2020 was it’s good to control the people that count,” Walbert told me. He quoted an elections official from Louisiana who helped flip the outcome of the 1876 presidential election, which was won – or stolen — by Rutherford B. Hayes.
“They may have us in the vote, but we got them in the count,” said the official.
Walbert explained that the current 435 House members’ terms end at noon on January 3, 2027. The House clerk’s list of representatives-elect would determine who is initially seated, potentially affecting control of election contests.
“If the Republicans can finagle that to have a majority of one in that first group that is seated, then they’ve got a big leg up on cheating,” he said.
Walbert said he is also “very worried about deployment of people to intimidate voters. The position of ICE on this — they keep waffling on what they’re going to do.” 
David Walbert has litigated dozens of election cases in his five decades as an attorney in Georgia. He argued a landmark election case in the U.S. Supreme Court and has taught constitutional law and testified before Congress as an expert on voting rights legislation. He holds degrees from Stanford, the University of Michigan, and Case Western Reserve Law School.
Walbert said that a key lesson from the Jan. 6 insurrection by Trump supporters is to anticipate and prepare for how to counter every scenario for how the 2026 election could be hijacked.
Walbert said there is one way to pre-empt cheating. “If the Democrats win overwhelmingly in November, I see no danger of this happening.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Stealing Elections, American Style: Voting rights attorney David Walbert on how the 2026 election could be hijacked — and saved.

name: WyoFile
title: Judge halts sweeping plan to move Forest Service headquarters west, including state office in Cheyenne
text:
The Trump administration’s plan for the most sweeping U.S. Forest Service reorganization in history has been at least temporarily halted by a federal judge who ruled such changes require congressional approval. 
U.S. District Court Judge Vince Chhabria filed a written ruling on Tuesday out of the Northern District of California, agreeing to relief sought by labor unions, retirees, counties and environmental advocacy groups that have a presence in Wyoming. The order prevents the Forest Service from closing or eliminating offices or reassigning employees to new locations, which are activities that Chhabria described as “reprogramming” requiring congressional approval. 
“[P]reliminary relief is necessary to protect the congressional prerogative, prevent irreparable harm to federal employees, and vindicate the public interest,” Chhabria wrote in his 40-page order. 
The federal judge is requiring the U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to notify all employees of the order within two days, and also post it to the Forest Service’s reorganization website. Within seven business days, the Trump administration must file a declaration verifying that they have complied with the order that outlines the steps they’re taking. 
The reorganization would have been the largest in Forest Service history. It called for dissolving nine regional offices the agency’s first chief, Gifford Pinchot, created nearly 120 years ago. Instead, there’d be 15 state offices — including a Wyoming office in Cheyenne — and a network of operational service centers. Led by Chief Tom Schultz, Forest Service leadership was in the process of relocating their headquarters in Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City. Additionally, the plan called for closing 23 research and development facilities and consolidating them in a single complex based in Fort Collins. 
U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz delivers the keynote address at the Western Governor’s Association conference in Park City, Utah, on June 30, 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
The Forest Service’s national media team on Wednesday sent a statement in response to WyoFile’s inquiry. 
“The Department is reviewing the Judge’s decision and will file its response with the Court,” a USDA spokesman wrote in an email.
Earlier this summer, WyoFile sat down with Schultz, who detailed and defended the reorganization, which he signaled was happening soon. 
“Sometimes toward the end of October, early November is when we’d be looking at getting [state] offices operational,” the Forest Service chief said.
Plaintiffs that brought the case include the American Federation of Government Employees and three other union groups that speak for Forest Service employees. Counties on both coasts also signed on, and so did the American Geophysical Union, Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, Natural Resources Defense Council and Western Watersheds Project.
“USDA employees that were surveyed writ large … 90% of the workers facing involuntary translocations would quit instead of move,” Western Watersheds Project Executive Director Erik Molvar told WyoFile. “This is really about getting rid of federal agency personnel, which is bad for the land, bad for the wildlife, and it’s bad for responsible management of our national forests.” 
There was strong support for the Forest Service reorganization and state-based model in some circles. The bipartisan Western Governor’s Association, for example, was in favor of the plans. But Molvar perceived some pitfalls for the broader public good. 
“Certainly the state of Wyoming would love to meddle in federal land management, and pretend that only the interests of Wyoming residents should matter in federal land management issues,” Molvar said. “But the reality is that the federal lands belong equally to all Americans, and Wyoming locals shouldn’t have any greater or lesser influence on these decisions than members of the public from other states.”
