title: NC’s Duke Health and CaroMont Health propose expansion into Mecklenburg County
text:
Duke University Hospital in Durham, NC on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)Duke Health and CaroMont Health are planning to work together to open two hospitals in Mecklenburg, health system officials said, adding 200 hospital beds to the state’s second-most populous county. 
The two hospitals would be owned by a new company that the health systems would equally own and operate. The partnership would mean an expansion into Mecklenburg for Duke and CaroMont. 
“This is a true partnership,” Dr. David Zaas, Duke University Health System CEO, told reporters.  “This is a 50-50 joint venture with shared governance, shared leadership of two organizations committed to improving the health of the communities we serve
Under the state’s certificate of need law, health systems must ask the state Department of Health and Human Services for permission to build hospitals. The applications will be submitted on Wednesday, the health system leaders said. 
Atrium Health and Novant Health dominate the county’s healthcare market. Those two health systems currently compete for permission to add hospital beds in Mecklenburg.
New NC State Health Plan agreement will avoid big cost hikes for using some Atrium hospitals

The NC State Medical Facilities Plan forecasts the need for hundreds of additional hospital beds in Mecklenburg. 
Duke and CaroMont plan to build the hospitals outside Charlotte city center. One is planned for a district near Charlotte Douglas International Airport, and the other in northeast Charlotte.
The plan is “to really try to get advanced care closer to home,” said Chris Peek, CaroMont president and CEO. Many patients in the area who require advanced care must drive into central Charlotte, he said. 
“These facilities will allow us to provide that same advanced care around the perimeter and closer to where people live,” he said.  
CaroMont Health has two hospitals and a free-standing emergency department in neighboring Gaston County, Duke Health owns Duke Health Lake Norman Hospital in nearby Iredell.
Duke and CaroMont will submit two certificate of need applications seeking approval to build the hospitals. Duke Health and CaroMont Health anticipate decisions on the applications by March 2027. The hospitals could open by the end of 2031.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Ethics lawyers: Search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home may have violated Hatch Act
authors: Norm Eisen, Virginia Canter, Richard W. Painter, Christopher Swartz
text:
President Donald Trump shakes hands with newly sworn in Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin during a ceremony in the Oval Office on March 24, 2026. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)Editor’s note: Below is an except of a letter written by a group of ethics lawyers to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel calling for an investigation into whether the recent raid on the Washington, D.C. home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar violated the Hatch Act, which prevents the use of official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election.
Dear Special Counsel Baldis:
We respectfully request that your office investigate whether Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Director Joseph Edlow, Attorney General Todd Blanche, or any other employee of the Department of Justice or Department of Homeland Security, violated the Hatch Act by orchestrating a predawn raid of Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C. home on October 12, 2026. 
This unprecedented raid occurred a mere four days before general early voting begins in Minnesota and appears to be timed to influence voters in the upcoming midterm election, in violation of 5 U.S.C. § 7323(a). 
DOJ’s Justice Manual advises prosecutors and agents that they “may never select the timing of any action, including investigative steps, criminal charges, or statements, for the purpose of affecting any election, or for the purpose of giving an advantage or disadvantage to any candidate or political party.” 
That direction is not a simple policy directive: choosing to investigate or prosecute someone for the purpose of affecting an election violates the Hatch Act, 5 U.S.C. § 7323(a)(1), which prohibits any officer or employee of the executive branch from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election.” DOJ has further instituted a longstanding “rule of forbearance” that dictates that DOJ will not take overt investigative steps against a candidate in the run up to an election for fear of affecting or influencing election results.
…
The Department of Justice secured a warrant to allow the Department of Homeland Security to raid Omar’s home just weeks before the election, purportedly based on accusations that her father made misrepresentations on her asylum paperwork over 30 years ago when she was 12 years old. DOJ and DHS’s decision to instigate this raid at this very moment and for these alleged reasons is unexplainable — except for as a politically motivated use of power to influence the Minnesota congressional election in violation of the Hatch Act. A review of this matter is therefore immediately necessary.
…
The Hatch Act places restrictions on the political activities of all federal executive branch employees, excluding the president and vice president. The Hatch Act was enacted to prevent the government from becoming a “corrupt political machine” and to ensure against both the practice of “political justice” but also the appearance of political justice. As the Supreme Court said in the seminal case Civil Service Commission v. National Association of Letter Carriers:
“It seems fundamental in the first place that employees in the Executive Branch of the Government, or those working for any of its agencies, should administer the law in accordance with the will of Congress, rather than in accordance with their own or the will of a political party. They are expected to enforce the law and execute the programs of the Government without bias or favoritism for or against any political party or group or the members thereof.”
…
DOJ has long recognized that investigations of political candidates during an election year, particularly close in time to an election, can affect voter behavior. That is why DOJ has traditionally abided by an internal “rule of forbearance” against engaging in overt investigative or prosecutorial steps in the immediate 60 to 90 days prior to an election. That unwritten rule has been respected across administrations.
For example, on October 16, 1992, Charles Banks, the Republican-appointed U.S. attorney for Little Rock, Arkansas, refused to open a grand jury investigation that could implicate presidential candidate Bill Clinton in the Whitewater scandal. As he said at the time: 
“[T]he insistence for urgency in this case appears to suggest an intentional or unintentional attempt to intervene into the political process of the upcoming election…. For me personally to participate in an investigation that I know will or could easily lead to the above scenario… is inappropriate. I believe it amounts to prosecutorial misconduct and violates the most basic fundamental rule of Department of Justice Policy.”
The administration’s raid of Omar’s home has many of the earmarks of official action that is scheduled and designed to influence the current midterm election — the exact concern that longstanding DOJ policy was instituted to protect. Departure from this longstanding norm itself raises serious concerns that the investigation was politically motivated.
Further, there appears to be no non-electoral reason why DOJ or DHS would have instituted this search right as Minnesotans are heading to the polls. There is certainly no evidence that DOJ or DHS had a compelling, exigent circumstance supporting the need to search Omar’s home. There was no emergency at hand, no imminent risk of physical harm was to befall any person, and there is no indication that the failure to wait a mere three weeks would result in spoliation of evidence. Nor is there apparently a pressing deadline to meet the statute of limitations. If, as reported, the warrant is focused on documents signed when Omar entered the country, the statute of limitations appears to have long passed. Neither 18 U.S.C. § 1015 or 18 U.S.C. § 1546 provide a statute of limitations that would cover actions that occurred 30 years ago.
Notwithstanding the lack of urgency, the decision was made to initiate this raid after absentee ballots had been sent out and mere days before general early voting begins in Minnesota, when it would have the greatest impact on voter behavior. As one of us said in a complaint to OSC raising concerns about former FBI James Comey’s communication of information to Congress related to the investigation of Hillary Clinton’s investigation ahead of the 2020 election: “A public communication about a pending FBI investigation involving a candidate for public office that is made on the eve of an election, or as in this case, while voting is in progress, is very likely to be a violation of the Hatch Act.” 
That is doubly so for initiating overt investigatory acts, like the raid of a candidate’s home.
Finally, these facts cannot be taken outside of the greater context of the administration’s ramp-up of questionable activity in the past few weeks. Three weeks ago, the administration began airing propaganda ads using Department of Homeland Security appropriations. Those ads were the basis of several Hatch Act complaints, as well as subject to two lawsuits. 
The administration is temporarily enjoined from airing those advertisements, which a court determined the plaintiffs were likely to prove were “purely partisan” propaganda.
As the Supreme Court wrote over 50 years ago, “the impartial execution of the laws” is the ‘great end of Government.’”
DOJ and DHS’s decision to push forward with an invasive, multi-hour search of a sitting member of Congress and political candidate’s home in the very throes of election season, purportedly related to allegations concerning conduct that purportedly occurred 30 years ago, has all the hallmarks of the type of “political justice” prohibited by the Hatch Act.
The use of any employee’s “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election” is a serious offense in violation of 5 U.S.C. §7323(a)(1). But potential manipulation of the law enforcement system for political gain strikes at the very core of our system of representative democracy. For that reason, it is imperative that your office open an investigation into the timing of this investigation as soon as possible.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Advocates, Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission continue to clash over agency’s  direction
text:
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The tension between voters and the appointed members of the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission has not faded in the year since the commission issued its first licenses.
A public hearing on the commission’s latest proposed changes to its rules and regulations is Thursday. However, some concern extends further, into the role of the Nebraska Legislature and how far lawmakers should step in regarding the voter-approved medical cannabis laws, such as around testing.
The commission first began its work in June 2025 and licensed the first cultivators in October 2025. Now, the first cultivator is close to harvest: MahāMotā Cultivation near Raymond.
‘Don’t want to be sitting on our hands’
Garrett Elting, a cultivation systems manager at MahāMotā, told the commissioners last month that the company was roughly four to six weeks away from harvest. However, Elting said, the organization has no pathway to lab testing, and no product manufacturers or transporters are licensed in the state.
Elting said storage could be needed for months, which also has drawbacks.
“With the storage we have degradation of the biomass, and we’re going to be losing terpenes and cannabinoids the longer it is stored,” Elting told the commission. “We’re kind of wondering: What happens there?”
He added that MahāMotā didn’t want to lose out on the quality of product for future use.
“Since we are so close to harvest and so close to these storage timeframes, we don’t want to be sitting on our hands,” Elting said.
Public can weigh in on Nebraska medical cannabis regulations Thursday

Under state law, the commission has no authority to license or oversee state testing facilities. Though the Nebraska Legislature had the opportunity in two legislative sessions to step in since the 2024 public vote to legalize and regulate medical cannabis, it so far hasn’t. The delay in 2025 also delayed legislation to authorize fees until new legislation passed in April.
Part of the delay, too, was over the continued legal fight over the validity of the laws voters approved. Those two cases played out in Lancaster County District Court, and advocates won both times, but opponents, including Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office, appealed.
The Nebraska Supreme Court unanimously upheld the advocates’ success in early September.
A hearing on the commission’s proposal to add fees is Thursday, beginning at 1 p.m. in Lincoln. Commissioners have said they won’t proceed with more licensing until they can assess fees.
‘Far too long’
Crista Eggers, the leader of Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana, which led the 2024 ballot measures, told commissioners it’s been about 10 years since she started showing up at the Legislature and more than 2,500 days since advocates first began petitioning for the ballot in 2020.
Crista Eggers of Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana, center, leads a news conference urging legislative support for bills to help implement a safe, fully regulated medical cannabis system. March 3, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Eggers, whose 11-year-old son, Colton, has had “thousands upon thousands upon thousands of seizures” in that time, said the delays are “horrific,” especially for the children impacted. At this point, she said, the delays feel intentional.
“Those parents have spent countless nights, over and over and over, praying as their children lay before them, hoping they will wake up,” Eggers said.
“My God, 10 years of my life I have shown up. That is far too long,” Eggers continued. “I would not wish one moment of any of these patients’ or parents’ or caregivers’ lives to be part of yours for a moment. I am begging you to think about what it feels like month after month that we wait.”
‘We’re making progress’
Eggers and other longtime advocates have repeatedly criticized the commissioners for not moving faster to get medicine into patients’ hands. The consistent criticism led two commissioners, Commissioner Jim Elworth of Nebraska City and Commissioner J. Michael Coffey of Omaha, to defend their positions and timing of work last month.
Elworth noted no commission meeting happened until June 2025, shortly before Coffey was appointed. Then, the commission was “blown up” when two commissioners were forced to resign in September 2025 over federal indictment of the former director of the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. The commissioners were not implicated, but they had split duties between both commissions, as dictated by state law.
“We’re starting at square one at that point,” Elworth said. “Nothing had gotten done. We were the first to admit it.”
Commissioner Jim Elworth, who serves on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission and Nebraska Liquor Control Commission, listens to public comment during a hearing on proposed medical cannabis rules and regulations set by the overarching commission. Feb. 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
By then, the commission had already approved an initial set of regulations and, in early October 2025, they licensed their first cultivators. In November, Elworth and Commissioner Bud Synhorst of Lincoln filled the two vacancies from months before.
The chair of the commission, Dr. Monica Oldenburg of Lincoln, then resigned in February 2026. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen has not replaced her.
Elworth said it was finally in April that the Legislature gave the commission more funding. Pillen and state lawmakers had said they could free up funds last year. It wasn’t enough.
“It was only then that we were able to hire staff, procure office space — for goodness’ sake, to buy a printer, or a chair,” Elworth said last month. “At that point, despite all this upheaval, all this uncertainty, throughout that time period we have promulgated temporary regulations that are now permanent.”
He added: “We are protecting this process. It’s going to be a good process. We have dealt with major issues. We’re making progress; we continue to make progress.”
Last month, the commission also hired Brett Long as its first executive director. Long brings experience from the Nebraska Department of Revenue, particularly in charitable gaming and skilled gaming regulated services. He also previously worked in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, including behavioral health and substance use initiatives.
“We believe this combination of regulatory compliance data and state government experience makes him a strong fit to help the commission continue developing and implementing Nebraska’s medical cannabis regulatory program,” Commissioner Lorelle Mueting of Gretna, interim commission chair, said last month.
Mueting this summer had described building a new regulatory agency as “much like constructing a house.”
‘We’re trying to do our best’
Coffey, a retired Douglas County District Court judge, said last month that he takes oaths “very seriously,” including his time in the U.S. Army before being deployed to Vietnam, when he passed the state bar, his service as a district judge between 1998 and 2023, and now on state regulatory commissions.
“I truly believe I’ve tried to live up to those oaths,” Coffey said.
The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission meets for a second time. Commissioners adopted emergency regulations. Commissioners at the time, from left: Lorelle Mueting of Gretna, Dr. Monica Oldenburg of Lincoln (chair), Bruce Bailey of Lincoln and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. June 26, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Other than meeting with Pillen for the interview, Coffey said he doesn’t know the governor. And of Hilgers, Coffey said he “wouldn’t know him if he walked in here.” 
Coffey said he’s never received directives or orders from anyone.
“Whatever you want to hold against us in the way we’re conducting this commission’s business, is us. It’s not anybody else, and I wanted to make that clear,” Coffey said. “We continually hear that we’re taking orders from the governor, the AG, and that’s just not true.”

He added: “I just want people to understand that I think we’re trying to do our best.”
The commission’s next regular meeting is 1 p.m. Oct. 19 at the State Office Building in Lincoln.

title: Former Vermont Rep. Noel Neely died two days before being found, documents show
text:
A street sign for Douglas Hill Road in Norwich near the Neely residence. Photo courtesy of Valley News

This story by Alex Ebrahimi was first published in the Valley News on Oct. 13, 2026.NORWICH — Former Vermont Rep. Noel Neely died two days before police found her body, according to details from search warrant applications.
The investigation, Vermont State Police wrote in an affidavit establishing probable cause to search her residence and a vehicle on the property, concerned “the suspected homicide of Noel Neely.”
First responders discovered the body of Neely, 82, on the morning of May 9 in a bedroom of her Douglas Hill Road residence in Norwich, Vermont State Police Detective Sergeant Zachary Van Valkenburgh stated in the affidavit.
Neely was lying on a neatly made bed with a white bag around her head and a plastic tube attached to a gas cylinder feeding into the bag, according to the affidavit.
The Vermont Chief Medical Examiner’s Office noted that Neely’s cause of death was asphyxia due to nitrogen gas exposure, but her manner of death “could not be determined” and she died at an “unknown time,” according to her July death certificate.
However, the family physician, Dr. Adam Schwarz, informed police on May 9 that Neely’s husband, Donald Neely, texted him that his wife died two days prior, according to the affidavit.
On May 9, at around 10 a.m., Vermont State Police had been requested by the Hanover Rescue Squad for assistance at the Neely residence, “where a female was reported deceased, and had been deceased for a few days,” the affidavit stated.
Vermont State Police responded as the primary agency due to staffing issues with the Norwich Police Department, the affidavit explained.
Upon arrival, police knocked on the door and announced their presence, receiving no response.
VSP Sergeant Max Trenosky then located a ladder and used it to climb to a second-story balcony, where he observed a bedroom. Inside, he could see the body of Neely on the “neatly made bed” with a “white bag” around her head, according to the affidavit.
Entering the bedroom, “he observed that the bag was tight around the head and that a plastic tube fed into the bag,” the affidavit described. “At the other end, that plastic tubing was attached to a gas cylinder via a regulator. This tank resembles a tank that holds pressurized gas.”
The affidavit stated that Trenosky also found “a pink/red towel blocking the threshold/seam, placed along the seam from the outside hallway into the bedroom.”
While police were awaiting additional resources, Donald Neely drove up to the house in a blue Tesla, the affidavit said. Troopers did not allow him inside.
Law enforcement noticed white bags inside the Tesla he was driving “that resembled the bag on the deceased’s body,” according to the affidavit.

READ MORE

Neely informed troopers “that there was a long document that would explain the situation, including ‘exculpatory information,’” the affidavit stated.
“D. Neely explained that this document had been emailed to his lawyer and that he did not have it,” the affidavit continued. “He made a reference that he wanted to speak with his attorney before talking with the police.”
Neely had texted the family physician, Dr. Adam Schwarz, that day at around 9:30 a.m., informing him that his wife had died two days prior, on May 7 at around 8 p.m., Schwarz told Medicolegal Death Investigator Doug Jasmin in the affidavit.
“D. Neely also told Dr. Schwarz that she (N. Neely) was in bed, and that he needed a death certificate before calling the police,” the affidavit stated.
Schwarz also told Jasmin that he had not seen Noel Neely for care in approximately one year.
“Jasmin obtained a brief medical history for N. Neely, which included insomnia, stomach issues, hernia and hyperthyroid issues,” the affidavit said. “However, he could not see supporting documentation.”
A voicemail left for Schwarz was not immediately returned on Tuesday.
“Dr. Schwarz also mentioned that the last time he had seen N. Neely, she was under duress due to D. Neely’s failing business,” the affidavit added.
On Tuesday, the third-floor office space at 7 Allen St. in Hanover was locked, dark and stripped of Donald Neely’s orthodontic practice, Hanover Orthodontics.
The practice has been closed intermittently since May due to Neely’s death. Social media posts indicate that issues with the practice, including scheduling struggles and incomplete prepaid treatments, date back further than the spring, the Valley News previously reported.
Phone and email efforts to reach Neely were unsuccessful.
Noel Neely worked as the office manager in her husband’s orthodontics practice, the Valley News previously reported.
Following the news of her death, Vermont legislators in Montpelier held a moment of silence in memory of Neely, who served as a Republican representative from Pomfret from 1977 to 1982. At the time, her district also included Sharon and Royalton.
“Specifically regarding this case, the investigation into Noel Neely’s death remains open and active,” Adam Silverman, spokesperson for Vermont State Police, said in an email. “To avoid compromising that investigation, we don’t have any further details to share with the public at this time.”
Vermont State Police Detective Sergeant Zachary Van Valkenburgh submitted the affidavit in support of the search warrant applications on May 9 “for the limited purpose of establishing probable cause” to search the Douglas Hill Rd. residence and the blue Tesla Neely was driving, he stated in the affidavit.
That day, Windsor Superior Court Judge Elizabeth Mann approved the search warrants.
From the house, police seized numerous pieces of property, including plastic tubing, adhesive tape, a nitrogen tank, “Teva” pills, a towel and DNA, according to a search warrant return and inventory dated May 10.
Plastic bags, paperwork and folders were seized from the Tesla two days later.
“Speaking generally, the issuance of a search warrant means a judge has granted the police the ability to search a location, person, etc., for potential evidence of a crime,” Silverman said. “It does not mean that a crime has occurred.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Public can weigh in on Nebraska medical cannabis regulations Thursday
text:
Advocates for medical cannabis join together before a public hearing at the Nebraska State Office Building in Lincoln, Nebraska, on state-drafted regulations for the new medicine approved by Nebraska voters in November 2024. Oct. 15, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — People wishing to weigh in on the latest regulations for the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission can do so in person Thursday or by sending in written comments by the end of the day.
The public hearing begins at 1 p.m. Thursday at the State Office Building in downtown Lincoln. It will run for up to three hours, or until there are no additional speakers, whichever comes first. Speakers will be limited to three minutes, or two minutes if many people wish to speak.
Written comments can be sent by email (mcc.contact@nebraska.gov) or mail (Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission, PO Box 95046, Lincoln, Nebraska 68509-5046) by 11:59 p.m. Thursday. In-person speakers are strongly encouraged to bring written copies, too.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, left, and Gov. Jim Pillen. Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Gov. Jim Pillen and Attorney General Mike Hilgers signed off on the commission’s previous regulations this summer. They took permanent effect July 6.
“Participants are encouraged to review the proposed amendments before the hearing and focus their comments on specific provisions they would like the commission to consider changing, clarifying, adding or removing,” the commission website states. “Comments regarding the proposed fee schedule are also welcome.”
All comments must be reviewed before the commission can sign off on the regulations and forward them to the governor and attorney general, which delays the process into 2027.
The commission has said it won’t license more establishments until the next round of regulations is approved, which again will require approval from the executive branch officials. Both Pillen and Hilgers are up for reelection next month.
Proposed amendments
The latest proposal offers a few distinct changes, the largest of which is a proposed fee structure for applicants — a $5,000 application fee, annual license and renewal fees based on type (between $10,000 and $28,500), a $1,500 relocation fee and a $13,000 fee for participation in the state’s seed-to-sale inventory tracking system. Dispensaries would also need to pay a $250 fee to license a new product, plus a $100 renewal fee. 
Currently, there are no fees under the program. Sales taxes are currently prohibited.
The latest amendments would also merge transporter licenses with product manufacturers, so transportation would be an optional certification.
Advocates, Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission continue to clash over agency’s  direction

Other notable changes:

Removing a label that would list medical cannabis as a “Schedule I” controlled substance. In May, the federal government downgraded state-licensed medical cannabis from a Schedule I drug to a Schedule III drug.
Allowing disenrollment of healthcare practitioners who voluntarily choose to participate in the program if the practitioner fails to maintain a medical license in good standing.
Requiring healthcare practitioners to attest when an in-person appointment occurs before they issue a recommendation for medical cannabis. 
Attesting whether a provider knows whether a patient is pregnant before recommending medical cannabis. If the provider in the future learns a patient is pregnant, they must alert the commission.

At the commission’s August meeting, Commissioner Jim Elworth of Nebraska City called the changes as a whole “significant” because they would help “streamline” the process. He cited a small change to the definition of cultivator and the potential expanded responsibilities of manufacturers. He had said that despite “insinuations” and, “frankly, the rudeness during the public comment period,” commissioners had visited a potential manufacturer, “taken his recommendations to heart” and made certain changes based on conversations,
“These regulations are 70-some pages, and they’re tight at this point,” Elworth said. “We are hoping that they will be approved as soon as possible and you will see that they make a difference in how this process works.”
Current state of regulations
The current medical cannabis regulations call for the state to:

Establish a “Recommending Health Care Practitioner” directory and require patients who want to access Nebraska-licensed dispensaries to go through one of the in-state providers.
Cap cultivators at no more than 1,250 flowering plants at one time.
Restrict purchases of medical cannabis to 5 ounces of medical cannabis in 30 days, of which no more than 5 grams can be delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) from the same dispensary. Delta-9 THC is the part of cannabis most associated with a “high.”
Allow no more than 12 medical cannabis dispensaries statewide, arranged by judicial district. That would mean one dispensary each in Douglas County (584,526 residents), Lancaster County (322,608 residents), Sarpy/Cass counties (217,202 residents) and Buffalo/Hall counties (112,979 residents), according to 2020 census data.
Prohibit the sale of smoking or vaping products and edibles of any kind.

Current state law allows possession of up to 5 ounces of medical cannabis with the written recommendation of any healthcare practitioner.
Advocates have repeatedly expressed concern that the regulations could hurt the program’s ultimate success. This includes the Legislature’s failure this spring  to pass protections for health care providers who wish to recommend medical cannabis.
The commission’s next regular meeting is 1 p.m. Oct. 19 at the State Office Building in Lincoln.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Democratic Governors Association expands its map, but not yet to Florida
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly in  Tallahassee on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The Democratic Governors Association (DGA) is “aggressively going on offense” and expanding its financial contributions governor’s races, but none of that money is going to boost David Jolly’s efforts to win Florida’s Governor’s Mansion.
DGA executive director Meghan Meehan-Draper says in a memo that the organization has invested at least $10 million each in Arizona, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio, and Wisconsin.
And Florida?
The only mention of the Sunshine State in the memo is that “[t]here are increasingly competitive races in states like Texas, Florida, Oklahoma, and Nebraska.”
The memo was first published Tuesday in Politico.
The DGA’s announcement came weeks after Jolly said he needs the national party “to come into Florida and start spending money.” No Democrat has won Florida’s governorship in 27 years.
Speaking at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club on Sept. 26, Jolly quoted someone he described as a top Tallahassee-based Republican consultant who said the only way he could lose is “if the national Democrats choose to take a pass on Florida like they have in the past 10 years.”
A series of public opinion polls have been released recently in the governor’s race. The RealClearPolitics average shows Donalds ahead of Jolly by 5 percentage points. Some polls show the race in a statistical tie.
Jolly has raised around $20 million in his two campaign accounts. That pales in comparison to the more than $140 million that Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has raised to date.
“In terms of the national party, they’ll continue to rack and stack their races. … Everybody understands what’s happening in Florida and they’ll have to make some decisions,” Jolly told reporters in Tallahassee on Monday. He added that he had seen his fundraising “improve dramatically” in recent weeks through small donors.
Jolly did receive $241,431 in public financing in the week ending Oct. 9. Donalds took in $38,888.
Florida’s public campaign financing matching funds program provides state taxpayer dollars to match individual campaign contributions of $250 or less for statewide candidates.
Jolly said he might have roughly $15 million to spend in the final three weeks of the campaign for communications and field operations, while Donalds may have between $30 million and $35 million.
Other Florida Democrats running statewide have recently received financial boosts from national groups.
The Democratic Attorneys General Association last week announced a $5 million investment in José Javier Rodríguez in his bid to defeat Republican James Uthmeier in the race for Florida attorney general.
And the Florida Democratic Party said in a press release this week that the Democratic super PAC American Bridge has spent $2.5 million in Florida’s U.S. Senate race on behalf of Angie Nixon.
The Phoenix reached out to the DGA but did not receive an immediate response.
With additional reporting by Jay Waagmeester.

name: VTDigger
title: Tuition free college or training? Yes!
text:
As seasons change, it’s always a good time to think about what’s next and evaluate options. And when it comes to college, training, and career changes, there’s truly no better time than the present to go back to school, finish a degree, or start something new. 
Education unlocks economic opportunity. The cost of education is also a huge factor—but did you know VSAC and our partners offer many opportunities to earn a degree, tuition free?
These programs are available to students of all ages and at all stages of their lives, for people who want to study full-time or part-time. And there are so many careers and job pathways to choose from, with classes offered in person, online, or in hybrid formats. VSAC’s pathways to a tuition free education include:

802Opportunity: Free tuition at Community College of Vermont
Freedom & Unity: Free general tuition at Vermont State University
Workforce Development Funding for Trades: Support for training in high-demand trades
Vermont Rural Health Transformation Tuition Benefit: Free tuition in 14 healthcare careers 
Vermont National Guard Tuition Benefit: Tuition assistance in skilled fields

Each of these programs has its own guidelines and eligibility requirements. Let’s dig in. And if you have questions, VSAC can help!

For classes at Community College of Vermont, students may be eligible for 802Opportunity 

Available to Vermont residents with a family income of $100,000 or less who don’t have a bachelor’s degree, 802Opportunity provides up to the full cost of tuition at Community College of Vermont (CCV). 
“802Opportunity has been enormously impactful, because it has enabled me to further my professional goals in a way that I would not have been able to do without it,” said CCV student John LaLonde. “This program has helped me overcome the biggest obstacle to finishing my education: financial insecurity. It has also rekindled my love of learning.” 
With opportunities for certificates and associate degrees, and with transfer agreements with many of Vermont’s colleges and universities, students can look to CCV for an affordable, accessible education in programs like education, business, and IT and cybersecurity. 

At Vermont State University, students may be able to access Freedom & Unity

Available to Vermont residents with a family income of $85,000 or less who don’t have a bachelor’s degree, Freedom & Unity offers students the opportunity to earn an associate or bachelor’s degree, tuition free. 
Vermont State alumna Kaitlyn Dingman received Freedom & Unity to complete her nursing coursework and is now an RN at a long-term care and rehab facility in Brattleboro. She said, “Without Freedom & Unity, becoming a nurse would not have been possible for me. It gave me the chance to attend Vermont State University, focus on my education instead of worrying about tuition, and prepare for a career where I can give back to my community. Knowing that I am able to care for patients here in Vermont makes me proud to have been part of a program that’s helping students while supporting the future of healthcare in our state.” 
Students can pursue degrees in programs like education, engineering, athletic training, and more. 

For students interested in careers in the trades, there is Workforce Development Funding

Workforce Development Funding can be applied to programs that lead to careers in building trades, mechanical or industrial careers, transportation, energy, and other high-demand sectors. It covers training for certificates or non-degree programs. Following program completion, students commit to working in Vermont for one year for each year of assistance received. 
For one student, VSAC’s Vermont Trades Tuition Benefit Program covered tuition at Stafford Technical Center. “The financial aid from VSAC was what made it so I could take the class and get my Class A CDL,” Parker Hoblin shared. 

Funding for health-related careers is available via the Vermont Rural Health Transformation Tuition Benefit

The Vermont Rural Health Transformation Tuition Benefit*1 provides financial support for students to pursue education in 14 eligible undergraduate or graduate health-related fields. In exchange, students commit to working as a healthcare professional in a Vermont healthcare setting that serves a rural Vermont community for five years, following the completion of their degree and licensure.
Stacy Emerson received the Vermont Rural Health Transformation Tuition Benefit. She shared, “I grew up in Newport and went to North Country Union High School. I’m planning to stay and live and work in this area. To achieve my goal and to have the support to do it means a lot to me.” 
This funding is available for students to pursue careers in nursing, radiology, respiratory therapy, mental health counseling, dental hygiene, and more. 

Enlist in the Vermont National Guard for tuition benefits, training, and more

The Vermont National Guard Tuition Benefit Program provides tuition assistance to members pursuing training in various fields, from engineering to medical support. Support under this program is available for undergraduate, graduate, non-degree training, certificate training, or continuing education.
Students can train in key roles such as aviation maintenance, cybersecurity, combat medic, engineering and construction, logistics, and communications, while attending school. To qualify for the Vermont National Guard Tuition Benefit, members must be active and in good standing, and generally complete two years of service for each academic year the award is disbursed.
There are many other opportunities available through VSAC and our partners
Beyond these five programs, there are other opportunities to find a custom fit for your education! The Vermont Grant and the Advancement Grant, and the many scholarships available through VSAC, provide additional support for students of all ages. Whether you have just a tiny idea for a career or job, or you know exactly what you need to realize your dream, reach out to VSAC. We’ve been there—and we can help.

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Kamala Harris to campaign in Columbus for Scott Colom
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris will travel to Mississippi to campaign for Scott Colom, Mississippi’s Democratic Senate nominee, in Columbus on Oct. 22, a campaign spokesperson told Mississippi Today. 
Harris’s stop in east Mississippi will mark the second day of her final fall campaign blitz on behalf of other Democrats ahead of the midterms. The former vice president is the latest in a string of national Democratic figures to  campaign for Colom, or announce that they will, as the Nov. 3 election nears.
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has blasted Colom for his ties to the national party and use of national Democratic surrogates in his campaign in what has become a negative race in the home stretch before Nov. 3. Colom has countered Hyde-Smith is out of touch with average Mississippians and afraid to face her constituents at-large in town halls or to debate him.

“I am honored to have Vice President Harris join me on the campaign trail as we fight to lower costs for Mississippi families, raise the minimum wage, and save healthcare and our rural hospitals,” Colom said in a statement. 
More details about where the campaign event would take place in Columbus were not yet available on Wednesday.  
Colom, competing against Hyde-Smith and independent candidate Ty Pinkins, has in recent weeks seen a flurry of support from national Democratic leaders. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Colom in an ad that started running this week, and former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg announced plans to campaign in Mississippi along the Gulf Coast on Oct. 27.
Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia will host a fundraiser, conduct a conversation with faith leaders and headline a campaign rally on behalf of Colom in Jackson on Wednesday.
Those who have already visited Mississippi for Colom include Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey. 
Harris’s trip marks her second visit to Mississippi in the past year. She came to Jackson in January for her book tour and spoke before a packed crowd at the newly reopened Thalia Mara Hall.
Harris has said in multiple recent interviews that she’s focused on helping Democrats win in November. But she’s not ruled out another presidential campaign after losing the 2024 general election to Donald Trump.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: 2 independent candidates for Kansas House try to capitalize on ‘hunger’ for alternatives
text:
Jack Geiger, left, and Lex Goff are running as independents to serve their districts in rural Kansas. (Submitted photos)TOPEKA — The November election will determine whether two independent candidates’ refusal to stand with Democrats or Republicans earns them a Kansas House seat.
Jack Geiger, an organic farmer and self-described former “conservative Democrat” from Brown County, is running against incumbent Republican Rep. Sean Willcott to represent a north-central district that includes Brown and Nemaha counties, and portions of Jackson and Atchison counties.
Lex Goff, a Wellington resident who graduated high school in May, is running against four-term incumbent Republican Rep. Bill Rhiley to represent the district south of Wichita in Sumner County and part of Cowley County.
There is no Democrat in either race.
Both Geiger and Goff found their way to an independent ticket after local issues pulled at them to get more involved, and they didn’t like what they saw from the two-party system.
Geiger said he is receiving support from people from multiple generations, Democrats and Republicans alike. 
“This is not a hungry-for-power game,” he said. “I view myself as a bridge for the political realignment that is coming, and it’s inevitable. I can see it, and I think the guys and the gals that I fight for, I think they see it and they hunger for it.”
Goff’s interest in politics increased after he jumped into a fight to pass a bond issue at his high school during his senior year. It was surrounded by “negative stigma” with the idea of a mill levy increase, he said. 
“I did my best as a student to have some smaller rallies, put out the right information, and it felt good doing something like that, even though it was so small,” he said. 
After graduation, he toyed with joining the military to help pay for college, where he planned to major in political science and finance, Goff said. His desire to help people and accomplish goals instead shifted him toward running against Rhiley, he said. 
Goff said he wanted to do so in a way that “isn’t partisan.”
Geiger, who follows politics like some people follow football, said he was led toward the idea after a strong local candidate was obliterated in a race when PAC money got involved a couple of years ago. 
“The parties, the powers that be, if you will, put their finger on the scale,” he said. 
Then, Flock Safety cameras, which automatically read license plates, went up in the area and Geiger began digging into a proposed data center. He also started following Willcott and what the Legislature was doing. 
“Every time that I asked a question or did a little bit of research, I became more unsettled, and I became a little more disenfranchised with what was going on,” he said. 
Everyone keeps asking him why he is running as an independent, Geiger said, except for his local neighbors who know his politics well after an eight-year term as a township trustee.
“My local neighbors knew that I was a Democrat. They also know that I’m not extreme, that I am conservative,” Geiger said.
But he saw his way forward in Kansas as an independent, especially after looking closely at the Legislature’s record in 2026. 
“There comes a point in time where you have to speak truth to power, call a spade a spade,” he said. “I did follow the last legislative session, and I honestly cannot give them credit for any single piece of legislation. That legislative session was an insult to the people, and that is why when I went out to get my petition signed, we did not go by party affiliation.”
Independent candidates in Kansas must get 5,000 signatures on a petition to be added to the ballot. 
Goff and Geiger said going door to door was a good way to understand what people in their districts want. 
Geiger laughed as he recalled that because he is so well-known in the community, he was getting yeses when he asked Republicans or Democrats to sign the petition, with just two exceptions. One of those was when he and his wife targeted the independents in the area and got their first “no,” he said. 
“The reality is that we’re perceived to be Republican, if you will, but yet there is a lot of unrest out here,” Geiger said of rural Kansas. 
Willcott, Geiger’s opponent, is serving his first term after becoming interested in politics when he worked to change a state law that affected his business, a brewing company. He said he isn’t focusing on Geiger but on issues that concern people in his district. 
“We agree that government’s too big. We agree that there’s too much regulation for small businesses,” Willcott said. “The cost of living’s high, property taxes are climbing. Those are kind of the discussions that I have and I engage with, and I think it represents the district pretty closely, east to west, north to south.”
Goff’s top three issues are education, healthcare, and agriculture, he said. Farmers are struggling, he said, adding that he summarizes the need for action by saying, “no more next year.”
Although he understands agricultural issues are primarily affected by federal actions, Goff said he believes the state can be more proactive, such as addressing property tax concerns. 
Other concerning issues are the $200 million special education funding gap and Kansas hospitals at risk of closing, he said.
Rhiley, Goff’s opponent, didn’t return an email or phone call from Kansas Reflector.
Geiger said he supports term limits; rural economic development with a focus on vocational education, hospitals, schools and infrastructure; and fair and transparent taxation. He said he wants to “end state budgeting shenanigans.”
He doesn’t like the pay raise legislators gave themselves, the way Kansans are being hit by inflation, diesel prices and difficulties buying a home. 
“We raise cattle, and a bunch of my stories are not only the farm ethic, but they’re the cattle ethic in Kansas,” he said. “But the brand that I write for is the state of Kansas. If you’re going to try and bend me to a party platform or this or that, well, it just ain’t going to happen.”

name: WyoFile
title: University of Wyoming grad student accused of poisoning colleague has been arrested fleeing to China
authors: By Mead Gruver, Matthew Brown and Safiyah Riddle, The Associated Press
text:
CHEYENNE—A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she didn’t get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work she’d done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
U.S. officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student’s life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told The Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The university is following all normal processes in a student conduct proceeding, according to a UW statement. College officials are working with authorities, it said.
“The university takes matters involving the health and safety of the campus community seriously and remains committed to providing a safe and secure environment for students, faculty, staff and visitors,” UW President Shane Reeves said in the statement.
Amateur sleuthing helps campus cops develop case
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “K.T.,” began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through the alleged victim’s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she “had not used acrylamide in years.” A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of “multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials,” according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to “significantly increase” her $200,000 bond upon extradition.
Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved “new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment,” according to the affidavit.
Wang “was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.,” the affidavit alleges.
A high-achieving student from Vietnam
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.
Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague’s success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang had not been doing lab work since June while she worked on her dissertation, he said.
Suspect faces return to Wyoming to face charges
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5 million cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.
Best known as a carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide can be acutely toxic in high doses. It’s used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is “not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere,” Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on “a pretty promising cancer therapy method,” Sumaya said. Wang, Sumaya added, took photos of every page of a notebook the alleged victim left on his desk.
“You wouldn’t do that with like your office or lab mate’s notebook unless there’s a really good reason, and there wasn’t,” Sumaya said.
Professor says the victim is still experiencing symptoms
The alleged victim went to the campus health clinic in August with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness. Suspicion led his wife and others to boil away coffee maker water from the shared office to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit.
The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.
The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
“Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it’s unclear if he’ll fully recover or not,” the professor said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG, Secretary of State issue voter advisory for Nov. 3 general election
text:
Teresa Vigil fills out her ballot on June 2, 2026, at the Doña Ana County Government Center. (Leah Romero for Source NM)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver on Tuesday issued a voter advisory in advance of the Nov. 3 general election reinforcing practical information and voter rights.
“Every eligible voter in New Mexico has the right to cast their ballot safely and freely, without being intimidated, threatened, or coerced,” the advisory reads. “Voting is our most fundamental right and New Mexico’s laws protect voters, poll workers, and election officials to maintain safety and order in and around the polling place. Voter intimidation and discriminatory conduct, as well as obstruction or interference at the polls, is illegal under federal and New Mexico law.”
[Voter Guide: New Mexico Primary Election 2026 Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The advisory follows the Trump administration’s failed efforts to obtain voter rolls from New Mexico and other states; thwarted bids by Trump to restrict mail-in ballots; and amid ongoing concerns by states about federal interference during the midterm elections. Earlier this year, the Legislature passed and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed legislation intended to prevent troops or other law enforcement from interfering in the state’s elections.
New Mexico’s advisory includes key dates and information about voting, as well as information about law enforcement’s role at polling places and prohibited activities and people at both polling and drop-box locations. 
“This joint advisory is an essential tool in helping New Mexico’s voters make a plan to cast a ballot,” Toulouse Oliver said in a statement. “Now more than ever, New Mexicans are being bombarded with misinformation about how to participate in our elections and about the security of the process.”
The Secretary of State’s Office also launched a “good questions” campaign in September aimed at countering election misinformation, and has an election fact-checking site online.
“The right to vote is a fundamental right at the heart of our democracy, and every American must be able to exercise that right without intimidation, interference, or coercion,” Torrez said in a statement accompanying the new advisory. “The New Mexico Department of Justice has worked to protect voters and uphold the integrity of our elections, and we will continue to enforce the law when those rights are threatened.”
A news release about the advisory notes that it “underscores the fact that all registered voters have a right to cast a secret ballot without anyone bothering them or telling them how to vote” and advises those experiencing or observing interference should notify the presiding job at the polling location or call NMDOJ at 1-800-477-3632.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Upstate car parts manufacturers investing $82M to supply Scout Motors
text:
Scout Motors announced investments Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, by seven South Carolina companies that will expand to supply parts for electric and hybrid-like models of the Traveler SUV and the Terra pickup to be made at its $2 billion electric vehicle assembly plant near Columbia. (Provided by Scout Motors)Seven Upstate auto parts makers pledge to hire 200 South Carolinians as they expand production to meet the needs of Scout Motors.
The companies — Spartanburg Steel, Magna DRIVE, KV Final, Röchling Automotive, Magna Mirrors, Cooper Standard and Bant Boru — announced Wednesday they would invest a total of $82 million in their existing facilities across Spartanburg, Duncan and Piedmont.
“Building Scout vehicles in South Carolina means building more of our supply chain here, too,” Scout Motors CEO Scott Keogh, said in a statement. “These supplier expansions are another step toward reshoring American manufacturing, creating good jobs, and developing the domestic capabilities needed to support production for decades to come.”
Hands-on training begins for first assembly workers at Scout Motor’s SC assembly plant

The companies, which already supply parts to other South Carolina-based automakers, such as BMW, also will manufacture for and deliver to the Volkswagen subsidiary’s electric vehicle assembly plant under construction in Blythewood.
It is unclear whether any of the companies plan to seek state tax credits as part of their expansions.
“The Upstate has spent decades building a world-class manufacturing base, and Scout Motors took notice,” Allen Smith, president of OneSpartanburg, Inc., the city’s chamber of commerce organization, said in a statement. “These supplier expansions reflect the talent, infrastructure, and momentum driving our region’s growth. We are proud to see Spartanburg County companies play an important role in the next chapter of automotive manufacturing in South Carolina.”
The Upstate expansions follow an announcement last year by Sodecia Aapico for a $120 million Orangeburg County plant to build vehicle frames for use in electric SUVs and trucks assembled at the Scout campus.
All of this is in addition to the $2 billion investment and 4,000 workers Scout has pledged to hire directly.
Auto suppliers for Scout Motors to jointly open $120M Orangeburg factory

The electric vehicle maker is on schedule to roll its first round of test vehicles off the line by the end of the year. Testing will continue in phases throughout 2027. Vehicles are now expected to hit the market in 2028.
At full capacity, Scout plans to produce 200,000 vehicles annually. That will include a mix of fully electric and hybrid-like models.
State Secretary of Commerce Harry Lightsey touted this latest round of investments as a byproduct of “the powerful momentum created by Scout Motors and the transformational impact already taking place across South Carolina.”
“And the reality is that we are witnessing only the beginning,” he added.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Ole Miss employee disputes university’s claims of disruption in latest court filing
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A former University of Mississippi employee argues in a new court filing that Chancellor Glenn Boyce bowed to public pressure when he fired her because of backlash from a social media post about the killing of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk. 
In a brief filed with the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week, Lauren Stokes, former executive assistant in the university’s development office, challenged Boyce’s claims that her post – or the resulting public outcry over it – disrupted the university operations, including a fundraising event and its social media channels.  
Chancellor of the University of Mississippi Glenn Boyce, center, speaks during a Institutions of Higher Learning meeting Thursday, Jan. 16, 2020. 
Instead, she said, Boyce and the university gave in to what she called a “heckler’s veto.” That’s when a speaker is drowned out by hecklers. Stokes asserts that the university, when it fired her, did the bidding of Kirk’s supporters who wanted her silenced.
The latest court filing is part of an appeal Stokes filed in July, after a U.S. district court judge dismissed her initial lawsuit claiming that she was wrongly terminated. The judge ruled that Boyce, as chancellor of the university, was entitled to qualified immunity and did not violate her First Amendment rights. 
At the root of the dispute is a post she shared on her private Instagram account following Kirk’s assasination. The post criticized Kirk views on guns, abortion and race and described those like him as “yt supremacist and reimagined Klan members” who had “wreaked havoc on our communities, condemning children and the populace at large to mass death for the sake of keeping their automatic guns,” the online statement said. Stokes later deleted the post and apologized. 
The post received immediate backlash from conservative activists and state leaders, including Mississippi State Auditor Shad White, a vocal critic of what he calls “woke” initiatives in higher education. He shared a screenshot of Stokes’ post on X, formerly known as Twitter, and tagged the university.
Alysson Mills, Stokes’ attorney, declined to comment. Jacob Batte, a spokesperson for the university, said its position is laid out in court filings. Cal Mayo Jr., an attorney for Boyce, did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Trump administration seeks to rescind approval for Revolution Wind
text:
Turbine installation for Revolution Wind is shown. The Trump administration had ordered construction stopped. A court ordered work resumed while the full case plays out in court. (Photo courtesy of Ørsted)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
The Trump administration is once again seeking to interrupt the development of Connecticut’s first offshore wind project, Revolution Wind.
In a federal court filing on Friday, attorneys representing the U.S. Department of the Interior sought permission to rescind the agency’s three-year-old approval for the construction of the Revolution Wind project, which is now nearing completion.
The filing was made in a lawsuit filed in 2024 by Green Oceans, an anti-wind energy group, challenging the federal government’s approval of permits for Revolution Wind and its sister project, South Fork Wind.
“The Department of the Interior agrees that remand of its prior approval of the construction and operations plan (“COP”) for the Revolution Wind Project is warranted so that the agency can reevaluate its compliance with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act,” the filing states. “Given that remand, the Court need not reach Plaintiffs’ other claims challenging Interior’s COP approval.”
A spokesperson for the project’s developer, Ørsted, declined to comment on the filing Monday.
The Department of Interior issued a statement Tuesday evening in response to a request for comment.
“The Department of the Interior is complying with a briefing schedule, not announcing a policy change. Our position has remained consistent throughout this administration and this filing should not be misconstrued as a shift in the Department’s approach to offshore wind,” the statement said.
Revolution Wind’s 65th and final turbine was installed in September, and developers say the project is on track to begin producing its full, 704-megawatt output by the end of this year.
The project is located off the coast of Rhode Island, with onshore assembly taking place at the State Pier in New London. The project began supplying power to the New England electric grid in March, and is supported by contracts with utilities in Connecticut and Rhode Island. (South Fork Wind, which was not mentioned in the filing, was completed in 2024).
The move also comes as Congress is mulling bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects, including offshore wind farms. A vote on that bill is not expected until after the midterm elections.
National Ocean Industries Association President Erik Milito released a statement on Monday calling for Congress to vote on that legislation in response to the Trump administration’s latest efforts to interfere with Revolution Wind. The NOIA represents companies involved in offshore energy development for the wind, oil and gas industries.
“Predictable regulatory processes and timely decisions are important for offshore energy development of all kinds,” Milito said. “We recognize the federal government’s responsibility to review projects and ensure compliance with applicable requirements, and we hope the remaining process can move forward efficiently while Revolution Wind continues progressing toward full operations. The second-guessing of federal approvals that have already gone through a lengthy review process is precisely why Congress must pass comprehensive permitting reform legislation, specifically the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.”
Friday’s filing did not cite any specific concerns that prompted officials to reverse their stance on the Revolution Wind project. However, the filing criticized the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management’s original 2023 record of decision for failing to “adequately explain” how potential impacts fit within the agency’s mission to provide for other uses within U.S. waters, including fishing and recreation.
Previously, the Department of Interior has cited concerns about the impact turbine blades can have on military radar in its efforts to halt offshore wind development.
Those arguments, however, have failed to gain much traction within the courts. The judge overseeing the Green Oceans case, Royce C. Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, has twice sided with the developers of Revolution Wind in blocking the Trump administration’s efforts to halt work on the project.
Lamberth has yet to rule on Interior’s latest request to reconsider the project’s construction permit.
The Trump administration has had greater success stopping wind projects that have yet to begin construction. On the first day of his second term, Trump issued an executive order withdrawing all areas of the outer continental shelf from further leasing to wind developers, while also pausing permiting on any new projects.
Since then, several wind developers have reached agreements to relinquish their leases for areas of the U.S. coast, in exchange for billions in refunds and promises to develop oil and gas projects instead. Those agreements have prompted lawsuits from several state attorneys general, including Connecticut’s William Tong.
