name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Public parks aren’t development opportunities
text:
Stansbury Park in Louisville was designed by fames landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted. It sits near the University of Louisville campus. (Photo by Bonnie Jean Feldkamp for the Kentucky Lantern.)I thought the University of Louisville had listened.
Two years ago, the university hosted public meetings about the prospect of developing Stansbury Park, a historic Olmsted-designed park at the edge of campus. The community pushed back and the idea seemed to disappear.
Then, in August, UofL President Gerry Bradley listed Stansbury Park development among his fiscal year 2027 priorities.
So here we are again, asking the question: Shouldn’t the community have input when it comes to the fate of a public park?
Let’s be clear. The university does not own this park, but its interest in acquiring it is well documented. They’ve been eyeing it for years. An internal campus plan I obtained in 2024 even included a drawing labeled “Intramural Fields at Stansbury Park.”
The park is a seven-acre triangle at the edge of UofL’s campus and it is the linchpin of Louisville’s Olmsted Park System.
Frederick Law Olmsted envisioned park systems instead of stand-alone parks. His designs treated them as civic infrastructure, not decorative leftovers. He intentionally designed parks to improve the lives of the entire community. “Parkway” is a term that Olmsted coined, meaning wide urban greenways that connected the parks.
Not every city Olmsted worked with implemented this vision, but four cities did: Rochester and Buffalo, New York; Boston, Massachusetts; and Louisville, Kentucky.
Stansbury Park is the connecting hub for the Olmsted parkways in Louisville. It is green infrastructure and the park system is on the National Register of Historic Places. Stansbury Park deserves to be showcased in a way that demonstrates its significance.
After reading UofL’s 2027 intentions, I submitted an open records request with both the university and the city. What I received in return was pages of heavily redacted emails citing the  Kentucky statute that permits such redaction if the records are “preliminary recommendations, and preliminary memoranda in which opinions are expressed or policies formulated or recommended.”
Stansbury Park in Louisville (Photo by Bonnie Jean Feldkamp for Kentucky Lantern)
That statute means some of the preliminary discussions and recommendations about this park can happen behind closed doors and remain shielded from public view. I understand that we elect public officials to work on our behalf, and every action cannot be open to public debate. But a historic park that the community has already spoken out about feels like the right time to be transparent. Especially since the city has a history of leasing park space to UofLouisville. In 2017, the city leased Churchill Park, which was also an Olmsted park, to the University of Louisville for the development of soccer fields, putting it off limits for public use.
In the heavily redacted emails I received, one sentence stood out. U of L President Gerry Bradley wrote this regarding Stansbury Park: “University Ownership is the best and only feasible option for the University to provide the financial investment necessary to achieve our shared goal.”
When I asked if the university would like to comment on this they responded, “We look forward to sharing details at the appropriate time.”
When I asked the Louisville city officials if they plan to sell this park to the university, Matt Mudd, Mayor Craig Greenberg’s press secretary responded,  “No. Stansbury Park is an important city park. It is also in need of significant improvements.”
Both the university and the city say they are discussing ways to work together to significantly improve the park. But if the city isn’t selling the park and the university is saying ownership is the only way they’ll invest, does this mean there’s another long-term lease in the works that basically hands control of the park over to the university?
Forgive me if I sound suspicious. I’ve seen this play out before. Louisville has watched its mayor waste time and resources planning for park improvements only to learn he was completely tone deaf about what the public wanted. I’m looking at you, Creason Park.
Louisville isn’t unique. Across the country, cities are being asked to balance aging parks and limited public budgets against developers, universities, sports organizations and other institutions with money to invest. The temptation is understandable: If someone else is willing to pay for improvements, why not let them?
Because the question isn’t simply who can afford to improve a park. It’s who gets to decide what that park space is used for. A city park isn’t the city’s private real estate. The city holds the land for the public’s benefit and the public deserves a voice before any ribbon-cutting press conference.
Thoughtful planning means listening to the community you claim to serve while protecting the public spaces entrusted to you. Once parks are lost, they are rarely reclaimed. Louisville is lucky to have one of the four complete historic Olmsted park systems in the country, and its significance is not only local but national. If Stansbury Park needs “significant improvements,” as the mayor’s office says, that’s on the city. Prioritize funding for it. Make it a place that visitors, residents and UofL students alike can be proud of. But don’t trade away public control simply because someone else is willing to pay for the improvements.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY senator hits the road to shore up support for amendment to curb governors’ pardon power
text:
Sen. Chris McDaniel, chair of the Senate Appropriations and Revenue Committee, has tried to get a constitutional amendment to curb the governor's pardon powers passed for seven years. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)Sen. Chris McDaniel is on the road this week, crossing Kentucky to urge voters to support a constitutional amendment aimed at curbing governors’ pardon powers around elections. 
The Ryland Heights Republican repeatedly proposed the amendment in the Kentucky General Assembly for seven years following a flurry of controversial pardons issued by former Republican Gov. Matt Bevin after he lost the 2019 election to Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Earlier this year, the legislation finally made it through the Senate and House. 
No issue committees have filed to campaign on the issue, but at least one banner says “Paid for by Chris McDaniel,” he said in a Tuesday phone interview. He had upcoming stops in Corbin, Somerset and Bowling Green to discuss the amendment. 
“This is just a fundamental issue of justice. It’s one that I’ve been honored to champion for a long time,” McDaniel said. 
If enacted during the Nov. 3 election, the amendment would limit Kentucky governors’ power to grant pardons and sentence commutations around elections by blocking them 60 days before their election through their successor’s inauguration in December. McDaniel’s bill this year had support from both Republicans and Democrats, and he said he’s continued to see bipartisan backing on the campaign trail. 
The “basic amendment” is about allowing voters to have more accountability to candidates using the power, McDaniel said. 
“Once I go through it, across party lines, people realize what’s gone wrong in the past, and they realize the need for a fix,” he added. 
Pardon controversy
In recent state history, Bevin’s pardons were widely criticized. He issued pardons to people convicted of crimes including rape, murder and child abuse. One was for a Northern Kentucky man who had been convicted of raping a nine-year-old the year before. Another was for a convicted killer whose family raised money for Bevin’s campaign. 
McDaniel said one example that sticks out for its egregiousness is Bevin reducing the sentence of Gregory Wilson, who was sentenced to death after being convicted in 1988 for kidnapping, raping and killing Deborah Pooley of Covington. Wilson had been eligible for parole in 2024, but the Kentucky Parole Board decided he must serve out the remainder of his life in prison. 
The senator said he became aware of the situation because of Joe Heil, who employed Pooley at Barleycorn’s sports bar in Newport. 
“Joe went to the parole hearing and stood there and said he should never walk free again,” McDaniel said. “And he’s a passionate advocate for the amendment and for the idea that these pardons shouldn’t exist.” 
However, some are wary of changing the state’s constitution, which has been in place for over a century. 
“There is no question that Gov. Bevin abused the pardon authority and let violent criminals out of prison, some of whom then committed additional crimes,” said Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for Beshear, told the Lantern in June. “The solution should not be to limit a governor’s pardon powers but to ensure we elect good governors.”
McDaniel said that while many hope “they will find the better angels amongst us,” governors of both parties have issued “these pardons that occur in the darkness.” 
“While that is an excellent talking point, the practical reality is that governors still issue these pardons, and the power has got to be reined in,” McDaniel added. “It’s not about people; it’s about systems, and the system that’s in place is broken, and the system needs to be fixed.” 
Within the last few years, constitutional amendments from the General Assembly have had trouble getting passed by voters. They include a 2022 amendment that would have allowed the legislature to call itself into special session without the governor’s say and another that said the state constitution did not protect abortion rights. A 2024 effort to allow the Kentucky General Assembly to fund private schools also failed. 
However, a 2024 amendment further prohibiting people who are not U.S. citizens from voting in Kentucky election did pass with 64% of the vote. 
McDaniel hopes the amendment’s simplicity will gain support from voters in about three weeks as it is “a basic issue of how does power flow.” 
“There is no check on the power to pardon, and so we’ve got to get ourselves to the point where there is a check,” he said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Warner seeks a final term as Mizusawa makes his case for change
text:
Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Warner (left) faces Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa in his bid for a fourth term in the Senate. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)U.S. Sen. Mark Warner says he wants one final term to help undo the damage he believes President Donald Trump has caused. His Republican challenger, Bert Mizusawa, argues Virginia would be better served with a senator Trump will actually listen to. 
The two candidates made their cases in two separate phone interviews with the Virginia Mercury on Monday, three weeks before the Nov. 3 election.
Warner, a three-term Democrat, is seeking a fourth term against a retired U.S. Army major general who has extensive national security experience but little money to compete with the incumbent. 
Warner won 56% of the vote against Republican Daniel Gade in 2020, six years after narrowly defeating Ed Gillespie. No Republican has won a U.S. Senate election in Virginia since John Warner in 2002. 
The Democrat holds a commanding fundraising advantage. According to the Virginia Public Access Project, Warner has raised more than $25.1 million through July 15, the most recent reporting period, and had $16.1 million remaining. Mizusawa had raised just over $376,000, with about $53,000 on hand. 
“Republicans have not made this race a priority,” said Stephen Farnsworth, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Mary Washington. 
Warner’s reputation as a centrist works in his favor, Farnsworth said, but Trump’s unpopularity and voters’ frustration over high prices would likely benefit almost every Democrat. 
 Warner focuses on healthcare and AI

An Alexandria resident and former technology entrepreneur, Warner served as Virginia’s governor from 2002 to 2006. He was elected to the Senate in 2008 and now serves as vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. 
During his unsuccessful first Senate campaign in 1996, Warner pledged to serve only two terms if elected. 
Asked why he is now seeking a fourth, he pointed to the Trump administration, the challenges posed by artificial intelligence and his growing conviction that the country needs universal healthcare coverage. 
Warner also said that his experience and relationships with Republicans would help restore bipartisan negotiations. He cited his work on infrastructure legislation, broadband expansion, semiconductor manufacturing and funding for a second passenger rail bridge across the Potomac River. 
“I know what I said in 1996, and that was kind of my intent then, but I believe very much that I’m a much better senator today than I was on day one,” Warner said in the interview. 
On the economy, Warner said ending the war with Iran and reversing Trump’s tariffs would offer the quickest relief from high prices. “I think the president needs to declare victory and get out,” he said. 
Healthcare is another priority of the Democrat’s reelection bid. A bill Warner introduced last month would establish a public insurance option, restore enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse healthcare provisions of the 2025 Republican tax-and-spending plan. 
“On the public option piece, that is a place to start the debate,” Warner said. “I think we need to move to universal coverage so there is a requirement for coverage.” 
Warner also acknowledged that policymakers underestimate the consequences of rapid data center development. 
He wants federal standards addressing energy and water consumption, setbacks from residential neighborhoods and public disclosure requirements. Companies would have to comply with those standards to qualify for certain tax benefits. 
As AI changes the workforce, Warner said technology companies should help pay for programs that prepare displaced workers for other careers. 
“I’ve never seen a technology that could be more transformative and less popular,” he said. 
Warner acknowledged that he wished he had done more to prevent federal workforce cuts carried out through Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency last year. However, he cautioned against simply restoring the previous staffing levels. 
Relations between Republicans and Democrats have deteriorated under Trump, Warner said, with many of his GOP colleagues reluctant to challenge the president publicly. 
“I’m making the bet that after the midterms there’s going to be a much greater willingness to come to the table and get things done,” he said. 
On election security, Warner expressed confidence in Virginia’s bipartisan election administration. But he also warned that Trump or his allies could attempt to justify interference by relying on flawed intelligence. 
“I’m asking people to rehire me, and I think I’ve got a strong record of results,” he said. 
 Mizusawa argues military experience gives him an advantage

Mizusawa, a West Point graduate who earned law and public policy degrees from Harvard, served on the Senate Armed Services Committee staff and as a deputy undersecretary of the Army. He advised Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and later served as a CIA adviser. 
He argues those connections would give him influence with Trump that Warner lacks, particularly on the war with Iran. 
“If there’s anybody he’ll listen to, it would be me, especially compared to my opponent,” Mizusawa said. 
He defended Trump’s decision to attack Iran, saying the president has access to classified information unavailable to the public. 
Mizusawa would not rule out deploying American ground troops and declined to make a firm commitment to require congressional authorization before providing further funding for the conflict. 
“I basically will tell you that I would disagree with (Trump) in private before I would disagree with him in public,” he said. “I would want to give him the benefit of my input.”
To address rising energy costs, Mizusawa called for more domestic oil, natural gas and nuclear production, including small modular reactors. Renewable energy should also be part of the mix, he said.
Data center developers should pay the full cost of the infrastructure their projects require, he said, rather than shifting those expenses to other utility customers. 
Mizusawa also proposed eliminating the capital gains tax on sales of primary residencies. He argued that encouraging more homeowners to sell would increase housing supply and help bring down home prices and rents. 
On healthcare, he called for tying federal Medicaid funding to states’ ability to account for how the money is spent. States that demonstrate responsible spending should be rewarded, and those that cannot adequately audit their expenditures should receive less funding. 
“It’s not just illegal aliens, but it’s people that are stealing from our government, from our U.S. taxpayers,” Mizusawa said. 
He also promoted telemedicine and artificial intelligence as ways to improve access to healthcare in rural communities. 
On election security, Mizusawa supports requiring photo identification to vote. He acknowledged that he did not know whether voter fraud was widespread enough to change election outcomes. 
When asked whether he would concede if certified results showed Warner had won and any recounts or court challenges had concluded without changing the outcome, he answered: “Yes.”
Mizusawa defended tariffs against countries he considered unfair trading partners but opposed imposing blanket tariffs on every nation. 
Virginia’s extensive military presence makes his experience particularly relevant, Mizusawa argued. He said the state would benefit from having both a veteran and a Republican in the Senate. 
Neither Warner nor Virginia’s other Democratic senator, Tim Kaine, are veterans. 
“I think it’s time we get a new senator in there who can work with both parties, Republicans and Democrats, with my proven record,” he said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Chesapeake Bay gets a C+ in overall health, Va. and Md. leaders say work to protect it must continue
text:
Heath Kelsey with the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences presents the 2026 Chesapeake Bay Watershed Report Card in Woodbridge, Virginia. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The Chesapeake Bay earned a C+ on the annual report card that calculates improvements or losses in key indicators of health and conditions in the estuary and surrounding areas. This is the highest the Bay has ever scored since the record-keeping began in 2006. 
At the announcement in Woodbridge on Tuesday, Virginia leaders said the score reflects the impact continuous clean up efforts have in the Bay, however slow the progress may be.
“We are taking this as an opportunity to acknowledge that what we are doing is working, and that we have momentum moving forward,” Virginia’s Secretary of Natural and Historic Resources David Bulova said.
A map of the Chesapeake Bay Watershed shows areas in 2026 that have improved in water quality over the last year. (Map courtesy University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences)
Of Virginia’s watershed regions, the lower James and lower Eastern Shore are the only areas whose quality ratings decreased. 
The York, Elizabeth, James, and Rappahannock Rivers all saw boosted scores when it came to dissolved oxygen levels, aquatic grasses and reductions in the amount of phosphorus and nitrogen in the water. 
However, all those waterways’ health trends rank in the D or C range – which is barely passing in some cases.
The highest-scoring area was the lower Bay region, with a B+. This part of the Bay, stretching between Cape Henry and Cape Charles in the commonwealth, is aided with water from the Atlantic Ocean.
A map of the Chesapeake Bay Watershed shows areas in 2026 that have improved in water quality over the last year. (Map courtesy University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences)
The yearly report is conducted by the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science (UMCES). 
Researchers found that the level of pollutants in Virginia waterways that feed into the Bay have held steady or decreased. However the amounts of chlorophyll a, which causes harmful algae blooms, and the water clarity levels both worsened since last year.
A recent algae bloom in the Eastern Shore had devastating impacts on oyster farms in the area. The bloom is also reported to be connected to recent reports of fish kills, according to the Chesapeake Bay Foundation.
“This type of water quality data does take a long time to improve, and especially with the population pressure, development pressure that we have in our region, with large cities, large population centers, and also agriculture, and other types of pressures on the system like tourism,” said Alexandra Fries, program manager for UMCES. 
“Even though we are managing and trying to restore, there’s still a lot of threats. And so, the fact that we are seeing significantly improving trends is really promising.”
The progress in managing the Bay’s pollution levels is partly due to the Chesapeake Bay Watershed agreement that was first established in the late 1980’s as a partnership between the six states and Washington D.C. whose waterways feed into the estuary.
The agreement set goals to reduce sediment and nutrients that end up in the Bay, make infrastructure improvements and follow agricultural best practices. The latest version of the agreement was signed in 2025, outlining new goals to meet by 2040.
“When you’re improving, when you’re on an upward trajectory, you don’t stop,” said UMCES President Fernando Miralles-Wilhelm. “You don’t cut funding, right? You double down on investments. And that’s what we need to continue to be doing.”
Earlier this month, The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced $37 million in grant funding, which would be matched by additional $53 million, for specific watershed and nutrient projects across the watershed. 
Bulova highlighted millions in recent investments Virginia has made to enact pollution prevention methods in the Bay. 
“I was especially proud that this year in Virginia, we invested a record $304 million for agricultural best management practices,” Bulova said. “We also invested $329 million for wastewater treatment plant upgrades, and $43 million to clean up our polluted stormwater runoff.” 
The report indicated some improvements manifested because much of the watershed experienced a very dry year, with many regions recording droughts.
This means less water was running off of agricultural land and out of stormwater systems that might have otherwise carried pollutants into the Bay and connected waterways.
But scientists who compiled the report emphasized that other factors weighed heavily in the Bay’s progress. 
“The score overall went up 6%. So having such a large increase, to me, is not just due to less precipitation,” Fries said. ”I think it’s also due to some of the restoration actions and best management practices that we’ve been putting in throughout the watershed.”
Key restoration wins that may have contributed to the improving scores include major investments in oyster habitat restoration. 
The hard-shelled mollusks are natural filters for water. Combined, Virginia and Maryland restored and protected about 2400 acres of oyster reefs since the 2014 signing of the watershed agreement. Over 7.5 billion oysters were planted as part of the effort and more are planned for in the latest iteration of the agreement.
The report card also outlined grave threats to water quality over the past year, including the sewage pipe that burst near Cabin John in Maryland sent an estimated 243 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. 
The disaster led to oyster harvest closures in some areas and demands from elected officials for more testing to be conducted.
The report card mirrors the continued efforts of state and local officials, scientists and communities to preserve and protect the Bay, the largest estuary in America and the third largest in the world. 
“I actually get a question all the time: ‘Why are you all investing so much money and restoring the Chesapeake Bay?’” Serena Mcllwain, Maryland’s Secretary of the Department of the Environment, said at the announcement event. 
“I just tell them, imagine if we didn’t spend any money. We wouldn’t progress, and we wouldn’t have the clean, beautiful Bay that we have today. Yes, it’s going to take continued investment. No, it’s not going to be solved tomorrow.  It means that we must continue to work in partnership.” 
More details of the Chesapeake Bay report card can be read here.

title: Loudoun superintendent pushes back after Va. delegate slams LGBTQ+ history acknowledgment
text:
Loudoun County Public Schools Superintendent Aaron Spence testifies during a June 10, 2026 congressional hearing. (Photo courtesy of House Committee on Education and Workforce)Loudoun County Schools Superintendent Aaron Spence defended his school board’s recent LGBTQ+ History Month proclamation, after Republican Del. Tim Griffin, R-Bedford, called the board’s decision “despicable” on social media and suggested the school system influences students’ sexual identities.
Spence joined the division in 2023 and has led the state’s third-largest school division through a series of federal investigations and disputes over transgender students’ access to school facilities, parental concerns and administrators’ handling of complaints.
Griffin said in an Oct. 6 Instagram post that he “hates” to see the board’s decision to acknowledge LGBTQ+ history, calling it “despicable, disgusting,” and telling the board to “leave children alone.” 
Griffin said the proclamation followed Loudoun schools’ attempt to “get as many kids into their ‘transing’ program” as possible during Pride Month in June.
In a recently published three-page letter to Griffin entitled “Enough is Enough,” Spence upheld the board’s decision, affirmed LGBTQ+ Americans’ place in history and condemned unsubstantiated accusations against public schools and educators.
“We cannot build trust by manufacturing fear, and we cannot model civility for children while treating entire communities of Americans with contempt,” Spence wrote, challenging Griffin’s rhetoric and stressing respectful public discourse.
The school division said it mailed the letter to Griffin’s office and sent another copy by email on Monday.
In reply to a request for comment, Griffin said in an emailed statement: “Taxpayers should never fund the extreme and despicable sexualization of students in schools. Ever.”
Griffin represents the 53rd District, which excludes Loudoun County and is over 150 miles away.
Beginning in 1994 with Rodney Wilson, a Missouri high school teacher, the U.S. began celebrating contributors to gay and lesbian history during October, highlighted by Coming Out Day, first celebrated on Oct. 11, 1988. 
Pride Month, observed in June, celebrates the LGBTQ+ community, recognizes its contributions and highlights ongoing efforts toward equality. LGBTQ+ History Month, observed in October, focuses on learning about and honoring the community’s history, achievements, and the stories of the people who shaped it.
Since then, several organizations have endorsed the celebration, including GLAAD, the Human Rights Campaign, the National Gay and Lesbian Task Force and the National Education Association.
Spence is no stranger to defending the school division on the national stage. Four months ago, he supported Loudoun school before a U.S. House Committee, as Republican lawmakers grilled him about how the district manages sensitive educational content, student safety and the extent of parental control in classrooms. 
Spence’s letter criticized Griffin for describing the recognition of LGBTQ+ History Month as “despicable” and “disgusting” and for making unsupported claims about schools influencing children’s sexuality.
He also said inclusive history education is important, emphasized that public schools must ensure all students feel safe, respected, and valued, and urged elected officials to engage in respectful, evidence-based discussion rather than spreading fear and misinformation.
Spence emphasized supporting students’ identities, dignity, and well-being, as well as teaching an inclusive and accurate account of American history.
“Our children deserve better than this,” Spence wrote. “Our educators deserve better than this. And frankly, our democracy deserves better than this.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Should a Virginia jail be exempt from state standards just because it contracts with ICE?
text:
Located near Bowling Green, the Caroline Detention Facility began operations in the 1990s as a legal entity known as the Peumansend Creek Regional Jail Authority. It is now used as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility. (Photo by Keith Gardner/Defense Visual Information Distribution Service)Harsh practices used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) continue to make news across the country, with detainees including U.S. citizens describing agents kneeling on their necks, holding them in isolation and more. 
Records show that the majority of detainees have no criminal convictions and a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll earlier this year found a majority of citizens say “ICE is making Americans less safe,” while “a growing number believe the agency’s actions have gone too far.”
How should Virginians who share those sentiments respond? One could start by demanding  our local and state institutions use the power they already have.
The Caroline Detention Facility, one of two main immigrant detention centers used by ICE in Virginia, is a case in point. Virginia  law gives a state regulator, the Board of Local and Regional Jails, authority to inspect and oversee the facility. The Board has largely abdicated its responsibility to do so. 
 Origins of the jail

Located near Bowling Green, the Caroline Detention Facility began operations in the 1990s as a legal entity known as the Peumansend Creek Regional Jail Authority. It was a joint project between Caroline County and Northern Virginia localities to deal with overflowing jail populations.
Thankfully, incarceration rates have since declined and counties set up successful programs to divert low-level drug offenders away from incarceration Consequently, in 2017 the facility was no longer needed by Caroline’s regional partners, who withdrew from the authority, leaving an empty jail with no clear public safety mission.
Three young immigrants ordered freed as Virginia lawsuit tests ICE detention policy

The state and Caroline County explored different uses for the jail, including converting the facility into a state mental health hospital. Instead, in 2018 under the first administration of President Donald Trump, the County opted to use the facility and its staff for immigration enforcement through a contract with ICE. 
 Humanitarian concerns

Since Trump took office a second time and made mass deportation a federal priority, the Caroline Detention Facility has routinely exceeded its rated capacity. The large majority of people held at the facility have no criminal record. 
Despite its nonviolent population, the jail was highlighted in a national report by Physicians for Human Rights for improper and excessive use of solitary confinement. 
Nationally, human rights organizations have credibly reported unsanitary conditions at ICE detention facilities and the physical abuse of people being held there (see here or here).
Given this context, the state of Virginia should be doing all it can to ensure safe and humane treatment of people being held at the Caroline Detention Facility. Instead, the state regulator of regional jails has largely given it a free pass.
 Continued inaction

The Virginia state code that gave local governments the ability to create regional jails also requires that they abide by certain basic standards. In 2020, the General Assembly passed legislation to confirm that a jail like the Caroline Detention Facility, which incarcerates people on behalf of the federal government, is still considered a local correctional facility subject to state standards.
Despite the clear letter of the law, the Board of Local and Regional Jails stated in its annual inspection report released last December that it is not “authorized to inspect or audit United States prisons or federal corrections institutes” and therefore can only conduct a minimal sanitation inspection of the Caroline Detention Facility. 
Based on this incomplete and erroneous reading of the law, the Board forgoes a comprehensive inspection of the facility that would also assess the wellbeing and humane treatment of inmates.
State administrative code also requires local and regional jails to produce a “written annual report of the availability of services and programs to inmates…” 
However, when I asked the Superintendent of the Caroline Detention Facility (CDF) for its annual reports from the last few years, he said “the CDF does not provide an end of year report to the Peumansend Creek Jail Authority. We have Authority meeting minutes available on our website.” 
Clearly, meeting minutes are no substitute for a report required by state code.
More troubling, Virginia code requires that all local and regional jails notify the state in the event of a serious incident or death at the facility. When I asked for any such past notification submitted by the Caroline Detention Facility to the state over the past five years, I was told that there were none. 
The explanation I was given: “The Caroline Detention Facility does not house or hold any Virginia State or Local inmates; only detainees who are held under federal authority.” But again, Virginia state law does not exempt local jails from state standards on reporting if they are contracting with ICE.
 Asserting state authority, rethinking the future of the facility

When the Virginia General Assembly gave localities the ability to create local and regional jails, its members did not anticipate that one of those counties would use that authority, in effect, as a legal shell to contract with ICE. 
This, however, is exactly what Caroline County has done. While the jail gets benefits from the law like authorization to detain people, tax exempt status, and state employee retirement benefits, it also claims that it does not have to comply with the same state rules and regulations applicable to all other regional jails.
The Board of Local and Regional Jails should uphold the law and apply it equally across all the correctional institutions that it regulates. Its evident failure to do so means it might need to be reminded of its responsibilities by Virginia’s governor or attorney general.
In its upcoming session, the General Assembly may want to consider the future of the Caroline Detention Facility. 
The Peumansend Regional Jail Authority was created as a shared project between counties in the state with a clear criminal justice mission. But now that the regional nature and its public safety objective have ended, it is time to ask if the jail authority should be dissolved and the facility put to some other beneficial use.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Alabama coastal restoration project could inform Louisiana work on lower insurance rates
text:
A partially flooded road in Venice, Louisiana. A new report looks at how coastal restoration can be connected to lower flood insurance rates and risk. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana IlluminatorA flood reduction project on an island off Alabama’s coast is helping Louisiana researchers understand how coastal restoration can decrease both risk and insurance prices in other Gulf Coast communities. 
The report from The Water Institute, a Baton Rouge-based research and policy group, shows that while coastal restoration reduces the risk of flooding for nearby homes and businesses, more policy work is needed to better reflect that lower risk in insurance prices. 
The Water Institute worked on a pilot marsh restoration project on the north side of Dauphin Island in partnership with Munich Reinsurance America Inc., a New Jersey company that covers risk for insurance policy issuers, and Moffatt & Nichol, a Baton Rouge engineering firm. 
The Graveline Bay marsh restoration project rebuilt 60 acres of marsh habitat, measurably reduced the wave heights during major and minor flood events across the island and lowered overall still water levels, according to the report.
“I think it’s exciting that we’re able to see this measurable impact,” said Renee Collini, the Water Institute’s Community Resilience Center director and primary investigator on the report. Her work focuses on navigating federal, state and local governments to help Gulf Coast communities support climate resilience planning and action. 
Another goal of the Dauphin Island pilot project was to see if the project could be replicated in other areas such as Louisiana, where the need for coastal restoration and insurance cost relief are also acute, according to Collini. 
“When marshes are implemented, one of their benefits is that they reduce flood risk,” she said. “This is us working to help find sustainable ways to connect risk mitigation to risk pricing.”
A “consistent” decrease in wave heights after the Graveline Bay marsh was rebuilt translated to a lower risk of flooding for nearby homes and businesses, with the reduction ranging from 9% to 18%, the report found. But while the flood risk decreased, insurance prices didn’t always reflect the reduction. 
The federal-government backed National Flood Insurance Program is often the only option on the market for home and business coverage in flood-prone areas. The Federal Emergency Management Agency uses the program’s disaster risk rating system to set insurance rates for policy holders. 
Its latest version, known as Risk Rating 2.0, has been widely criticized as not fully reflecting efforts local governments and communities have taken to reduce flood vulnerability, such as home elevation, roof upgrades and coastal restoration projects.
Collini said the Dauphin Island project is a “first step” in connecting coastal restoration work to consistently lower insurance prices.
“(We’re) trying to move forward in a way where we don’t ignore that things are risky, but we are also not ignoring when we do work to make it less risky,” she said.
Collini said the Water Institute is “actively working with partners in Louisiana” to choose areas in state where a similar project can help local communities better understand how nearby coastal restoration has reduced flood risk — and if it can be carried over to decreased insurance prices. 
“For Alabama, 60 acres is a big restoration, but that’s not a big restoration in Louisiana,” she said. “There are much bigger projects, and so it’s exciting to think about the kind of impact they could be having.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson: Economic opportunity is the unfinished work of the Civil Rights movement
text:
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson kicks off her general election campaign for governor in a roundtable with small business owners at Good Cakes and Bakes in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Jocelyn Benson has been Michigan’s Secretary of State since the start of 2019. But before that, she was, as she describes, “a student of the Civil Rights movement,” moving to Montgomery, Alabama after college to volunteer with civil rights organizations investigating hate groups. After graduating from law school, she worked at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and clerked with Judge Damon Keith, a notable federal judge and civil rights champion in Detroit. She went on to teach at and eventually serve as the dean of Wayne State University Law School prior to serving as Secretary of State. 
Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor facing off against Republican nominee John James, sat down with Michigan Advance to discuss how her civil rights background would shape her approach to the office if elected on Nov. 3.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Michigan Advance: How does your background inform how you’ve both tackled your current role the last eight years, and how you plan to tackle the role of governor?
Jocelyn Benson: The heart of it is what can we learn from those who came before us and fought similar battles, and also what responsibility do we have to continue on that work, and what’s the unfinished business of that work? The evolution of that is realizing that the unfinished work is not just protecting democracy, which very much still is the fight today, but also continuing to expand that to ensure educational quality and economic justice. That is all tied up in improving our schools, as not just necessary to the future of our state and economy, but the unfinished work of the Civil Rights movement, growing wealth, particularly in communities that have been left out of that opportunity, ensuring we’re working to eradicate poverty in partnership with mayors. That’s going to be what you see a lot of me as governor trying to say, where is that injustice that needs to be tackled, and what can we do to really show up for communities that have often been left out of access to opportunity for far too long. We have a moral responsibility to each other to ensure that everyone has access to real opportunity economically, educationally, and otherwise.
 
MA: What do you see as the role of the governor in enforcing civil rights law and in improving civil rights in Michigan compared to the attorney general, secretary of state, the courts, the Legislature or local officials?
JB: Every single position has a role to play. The governor is the opportunity to set the tone and the expectation for everyone else to say this is our job, and I, as the CEO of the state of Michigan, am going to demand and hold all public officials to the expectation that we stand up for justice and that we stand up for marginalized communities and those who have been left out of opportunity, because our state does not grow and thrive, we do not become an economic engine if anyone is left out of that opportunity. For me, as governor, my first act will be signing a Voting Rights Act for the state of Michigan to restore the federal protections that were taken away in the recent Supreme Court decision. That’s how I also expect to set the tone. If folks want my support for things, they’re going to have to show me that they’re also working to promote equality of opportunity for every community in the state.
Voter Guide: 2026 Michigan General Election

 
MA: In terms of ICE and rights of immigrants in Michigan, how do you think your approach to that, in terms of gubernatorial responsibility, will differ from Gov. Whitmer’s? 
JB: I think you can look to how I’ve operated as secretary of state, where I’ve been unafraid to stand up to the president when he tramples on our rights, and particularly when he violates the Constitution. In alignment with what Gov. Walz has done and others, to say, ‘I’ll see you in court if you try to violate the law’ — that’s my approach. Obviously, I want to have good relations with everyone that I work with, but at the same time, when anyone is violating the law, when anyone is trampling on the rights of residents of the state, my duty and responsibility is to fight for them. As governor, you have to use every tool in your toolbox to protect the communities of the state, whether it’s the bully pulpit or the legal processes, but also finding ways that we can stand up to the growth of detention facilities in the state, especially when there’s no transparency about what’s happening in them. As governor, finding ways to both implicitly and explicitly, directly and indirectly, identify ways to promote transparency in those facilities, so that we can empower others to seek accountability where they may have the legal ability to do so. It’s looking through the lens of a moral responsibility to all of the people of Michigan to keep them safe.
 
MA: With that legal element, how do you think your background in civil rights law sets you up to use that wide range of tools? 
JB: I understand how the law has been used both to hurt and oppress, and also empower and provide opportunity. And I’m squarely someone who got into public service and became a lawyer because I wanted to ensure the law was used to promote and inspire and uplift and empower, as opposed to divide or suppress or disempower. As someone who’s taken an oath to not just uphold and defend the Constitution, but also as an attorney to ensure the law is followed, that provides me I think with a unique responsibility and understanding and about how to stand up to those who may try to skirt the law.
 
MA: When it comes to the rollback of civil rights for LGBTQ+ people and specifically the transgender community, where do you see the role of the governor on these civil rights questions, especially trans kids in Michigan?
JB: I am someone who will always fight for civil rights. That is the core of who I am in recognizing the importance of whether it’s fair housing or fair employment or access to justice or access to opportunity. It is a non-negotiable for me to ensure all communities are safe and that rights are protected. What I’ve also seen as one of the most effective ways to do that, as someone who’s worked in sports, is in partnership with folks in the schools, coaches and others who oftentimes really can get to the right decision for the community without the interference of a governor. I look at this as someone who was a female athlete and worked in sports. Coaches often know best about what’s best for the particular community, and so allowing them to be in the driver’s seat for this is important to me. You’ll see it in my approach to educational policy as well. You need to sometimes just allow the teachers in the room to be empowered to make the right decision on the front lines beyond what a politician in Lansing might think is best. The bottom line for me, and you’ve seen this for me as secretary of state, is I’ll always use every tool in my toolbox to keep communities safe and make sure folks aren’t marginalized. That’s why I was proud to ensure our licensing policies also reflect the needs of the community, because that’s a very clear administrative process where past secretaries created more burdens, and I was able to alleviate them. My approach, because this is one issue in this moment, but there will be others, is just always involving the community as sort of part of what democracy is supposed to be.
Benson, James tackle affordability, federal relations at first gubernatorial debate

 
MA: This is another issue where the federal government has really taken a strong stance. How do you manage dynamics with elected officials on any level who have policies that you just staunchly disagree with?
JB: We have a core set of values, and when those values are threatened, and the law or the constitutional protections that I am charged with enforcing are violated, that gives you all the fuel you need to stand up to anyone, and that has been what I’ve seen as secretary of state. I told my team, ‘The truth is on our side, history is on our side, and the law and the Constitution are on our side.’ I’ll go into battle every day with those in my pocket, and so I think when it comes to any issue, economic growth, development, bringing jobs to Michigan, I’ll always work with anyone to get that done, but I’ll be unafraid to stand up to anyone who would trample on the freedoms of Michiganders, especially to further their own power grabs and abuse of authority. 
 
MA: The Southern Poverty Law Center has come under fire from the Trump administration and from the GOP. What do you make of these kinds of attacks on a civil rights group like that, especially one that you’ve worked so closely with on their board?
JB: It’s not lost on me that a tactic of oppressive governments is to attack civil rights organizations. We’ve seen it in the 1960s in the Civil Rights movement, especially some of the most effective ones. But that said, my interaction with the organization was primarily in the late 90s, long before any of these allegations came to fruition, and it was as a volunteer in investigating hate crimes. I think you can’t deny the very clear work that many civil rights organizations, including this one, have done to contribute to advancing the cause of social justice today. I think you have to see this in particular as an effort by the Trump administration not just to attack that work, but to also distract from its failed economic policies.
 
MA: What do you hope is the future of developing civil rights in Michigan?
JB: Economic justice and opportunity. Full stop. More jobs, better-paying jobs, costs going down, wages going up. That is something that’s particularly affecting communities that have been left out of the opportunity to create wealth for generations, even more than anyone else. Economic growth power is the unfinished work of the Civil Rights movement, tied with educational opportunity. Making sure every public school and every ZIP code is providing a quality education for their kids with wraparound services to address any specific needs of that locality, community or ZIP code, and ensuring that well-paying jobs are waiting for everyone on the other side of that public school system, and that if you want to start and grow your small business, you have access to capital and support to do that. The future of civil rights to me in Michigan is economic opportunity for all, tied with educational excellence for all, and continuing to protect democracy. Those three pillars of the Civil Rights movement still hold true today.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Northeast Indiana voters to decide potential casino’s fate
text:
Indiana voters in three counties can block a casino development on Nov. 3. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Voters in three northeast Indiana counties have the rare chance to directly decide the fate of a potential $500 million development with a question waiting near the end of their ballots.
“Shall inland casino gambling be permitted in (your) county?” is Public Question No. 3 on the ballots of Allen, DeKalb and Steuben county voters, after questions on bail and judge residency.
Groups mobilizing to sway their votes for or against the casino possibility disagree on whether one will bring growth or decay.
“We’ve been on a really, really nice run for about eight to 10 years,” said Tom Borne, a retired advertising executive involved with Advance Fort Wayne Allen County’s “Yes for Allen” initiative. 
“If we can’t find ways to generate additional revenue to keep this moving, then … we can take the little bites out of the apple,” he continued. “But I’m of the philosophy: let’s take a big bite of the apple, and keep this coming through and making our community even better and stronger.”
Others point to potential costs.
“The casino industry is predatory in nature,” said Kristen Bissontz, vice president of the Coalition for a Better Indiana’s volunteer board. The grassroots group is pushing a “No casiNO” campaign.
The industry, Bissontz added, “preys on the most vulnerable and the weakest and the ones that really can’t afford (it). … It’s a bad bet because the house always wins.”
Failing casino kicks off license relocation turned addition
House Enrolled Act 1038, approved earlier this year, authorizes a new license for an inland casino in one of the three northeast counties and knocks off one unused “racino” license for horse-racing wagering with slot machines.
If voters in a county agree to allow a casino, prospective developers can submit their applications for that specific county to the Indiana Gaming Commission by Dec. 1. If they reject the casino idea, the law provides, “a second public question under this section may not be held in that county.”
Voters will have say on Fort Wayne-area casino under plan backed by lawmakers

Whichever developer is selected would be required to invest at least $500 million across the prospective casino and non-gambling amenities, with at least 60% spent within two years of the license authorization.  The rest must be invested — and the development completed — within five years of when operations begin.
They’d also pay a fee to the state: $100 million for the license and $50 million to support former host communities hurt by casino closures. Additional payments to the host community or state could be part of the deal, too.
Lawmakers initially attempted to set up a process for relocating Indiana’s worst-performing casino from Rising Sun, located along the Ohio River, without establishing a new casino license.
The final version, however, leaves that casino in place. Ohio County and Rising Sun officials raised concerns about how their local governments could be compensated if the community lost the casino that is its largest employer and taxpayer.
Rising Star generates about $42 million a year in gross revenue and paid $3.6 million in state gaming taxes last year. A 2025 Indiana Gaming Commission study projected that an Allen County casino could generate $204 million in revenue and $61 million in annual state taxes. Steuben County Economic Development Corp. released a feasibility study in April with its own case for a casino there.
Supporters hope to boost economy, replace lost revenue
Steve Corona is the Fort Wayne Community Schools’ Board of Trustees longest-serving member at 46 years and counting. When Borne and other businesspeople approached him for marketing help on the “Yes for Allen” campaign, he initially told them he might be the “wrong guy.”
“I don’t gamble and I don’t like Las Vegas,” Corona said. 
Then he learned of the revenue boost a casino could bring the school district. Units of local government have taken in less property tax revenue under 2025’s controversial Senate Enrolled Act 1 than they otherwise would have.
“Our school district is just getting killed. We lost $10 million last year. We’re losing $11 million — yeah, I mean, we’re the largest district in the state, and we are getting our (butt) kicked,” Corona said. 
Borne is also agnostic on commercial gambling.

“I’m not here to say they’re right or wrong, quite frankly,” he said of opponents. “… I’m not a person that goes to casinos, but I am a person who likes to see growth, and I’m a person who likes to see jobs.”
His organization estimates the development will require about 5,500 temporary construction jobs and an additional 2,000 jobs to run the place. Casino foes contest those figures, but Borne shrugged them off: “I guess there’s always ways to shoot holes through any numbers, but nobody has a better answer.”

The campaign is supported by the Greater Fort Wayne chamber of commerce, the business “community” and several labor unions. It has advertised through TV, social media, mailers and even a text campaign.
Asked how much money the group had spent, Borne said, “The only way I can answer that … is I’m always looking for more.”
In Steuben County, a “privately funded group of citizens” have joined forces with the county’s government, economic development agency and tourism bureau to launch the Where Fun Wins political action committee, according to the group’s website. The PAC was unable to accommodate an interview before deadline.
Opponents warn of consequences
While some state lawmakers representing the area led the state legislative charge to bring northeast Indiana into the casino discussion, others voted against it. The issue has risen to Indiana’s congressional delegation as well, with Third District Rep. Marlin Stutzman speaking in opposition last week.
A yard sign urges a “no” vote on a casino referendum in northeast Indiana. (Photo courtesy of the Coalition for a Better Indiana)
“While many enjoy gambling as entertainment, several of our neighbors will eventually fall victim to the proposed casino as it seeks to generate profit off the backs of hard-working Hoosiers,” Stutzman said in a news release. “Business development is a top priority of mine, but gambling is the opposite.”
“Expanding addictive gaming into our untapped territory will upset the favorable economic development our community has fostered,” he added. “The values Hoosiers hold in Northeast Indiana simply do not align with the moral decay casinos represent.”
Bissontz fears for her neighbors.
When she first moved to Fort Wayne at 21 she didn’t really think about it being a good place to raise a family. More than three decades and a family of her own later, she wholeheartedly agrees.
A casino, to Bissontz, is “contrary to that morally.”
“The frequency of the bells and the lights and the fast pace, it’s designed to hook you in, to get you that dopamine and to keep you there until you can no longer play because you’re completely out of money,” she said. 
Her coalition has sent out mailers and organized meet-and-greet forums to get that message out, supported by the small donations from similarly concerned residents and small businesses.
“I’ve literally taken a handful of tens and twenties to our bank,” Bissontz said. “Going up against a multi-billion-dollar industry, it can be intimidating. But we’ve always had the mantra of: you just do the next right thing.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Bonds. More bonds.
text:
A 'Vote Yes on 4' sign supports a $50 million bond question on the Nov. 3 ballot seeking to build a new Rhode Island State History Center in Providence and fund grants to preserve historic and cultural properties. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) One thing is true of Rhode Islanders: we love a good general obligation bond. We’ve approved 34 of the 35 put to us by the General Assembly in the last 20 years — upwards of $2.26 billion in taxpayer-backed debt. We haven’t just approved them. We’ve APPROVED them by a median margin of 66%. The last time we said no was 2006: $4 million for Fort Adams, which might qualify as one of those “penny-wise and pound-foolish” moments in the grand scheme of things.
Our penchant for laying the full faith and credit of the state on the line has earned us the nation’s highest per capita debt: $10,259. Yet, since 2025 Fitch has upgraded and affirmed Rhode Island’s credit rating at AA+, and S&P Global Ratings and Moody’s Ratings have followed suit at AA and Aa2. We may not enjoy Utah’s AAA, AAA, and Aaa ratings, but our creditworthiness is stable and respectable, depreciated primarily by our unfunded pension liabilities. How do we manage this with substantial public debt? The answer might surprise you: our middling General Assembly.
Rhode Island election rules crush the competition. Here’s what can be done about it.

That isn’t just a cheap shot at Smith Hill. It’s the conclusion of a 2018 study by political scientists David Fortunato and Ian R. Turner, who compared the bond ratings of the 40 states issuing general obligation debt from 1995 to 2010 with how “professional” each state’s legislature is: what lawmakers are paid, how many days they meet, and how much staff they have. Counterintuitively, the more capable the legislature, the riskier lenders judge the state. A well-staffed, full-time legislature can rewrite tax rates, spending priorities, and regulations faster than a bond analyst can update a spreadsheet, and markets don’t like what they can’t predict. A part-time legislature like ours can’t do much quickly; it is, in the authors’ words, “an institutional commitment to the status quo.” The effect is significant: raising legislative capacity by one standard deviation effectively doubled a state’s estimated credit risk — a bigger effect than revenue limits, spending caps, or debt restrictions. Lenders give Rhode Island good marks not because our lawmakers manage our money brilliantly, but because they’re too under-resourced to mess with it much.



Quotation







The last time we said no was 2006: $4 million for Fort Adams, which might qualify as one of those “penny-wise and pound-foolish” moments in the grand scheme of things.


“Middling” isn’t an insult; it’s a ranking. Fortunato and Turner’s yardstick, the Squire Index, measures how closely a legislature resembles Congress in pay, session length, and staff. In Peverill Squire’s latest update, based on 2015 data, Rhode Island scored .200 (Congress equals 1), ranking 28th of 50 — well behind California (.629) and Massachusetts (.431), far ahead of New Hampshire (.048). And triple-A Utah? It ranks 46th, at .115. If Fortunato and Turner are right, that’s no coincidence.
Part-time doesn’t mean clueless. Studying 20th century state legislatures, Nancy Burns and her colleagues found that most were neither purely amateur nor purely professional, and that even amateur bodies built “pockets of expertise” where the money is. In citizen-run Vermont, not a single first-term member sat on the House Appropriations Committee in 1981 or 1997. A middling legislature doesn’t leave the budget to amateurs; it hands the purse strings to a few veterans and leaves everyone else without the time or staff to second-guess them. Anyone who follows our state budget through the General Assembly each year will recognize the pattern.
How a legislature is built shapes that pattern. Peter Bucchianeri, Craig Volden, and Alan Wiseman looked at lawmaking effectiveness in 97 state legislative chambers. They found that generous staff support spreads effectiveness to rank-and-file members, but where staff is thin, committee chairs “can often exploit expertise advantages.” A lean legislature funnels policymaking through a handful of chairs and leaders. To a bond analyst, that’s a feature, not a bug: fewer hands on the levers, fewer surprises.
Nor do citizen legislatures earn their good grades by being cheap. Neil Malhotra found that professional legislatures appear to spend more: States classified as professional spent about 5% more per capita than those with citizen legislatures, and states that cap their session lengths spent about 7% less. But once he compared states equally likely to professionalize, the gap disappeared: Big-spending states build professional legislatures to manage big governments, not the other way around. Rhode Island’s bond record proves a part-time legislature can borrow with the best of them because lenders reward predictability, not thrift.
There is a catch. Squire’s review of the research notes that more professional legislatures are associated with “better funded state pension systems” — the very liability that keeps Rhode Island from a higher rating. But that’s a commentary for another day.
In the next few weeks, Rhode Islanders will be asked to approve another $600 million in general obligation bonds. History suggests these will pass, and by comfortable margins. The evidence suggests Rhode Island’s creditworthiness will remain unscathed — because of how little our middling General Assembly is equipped to change.
