name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawsuit alleges MDOC staff filmed incarcerated woman while giving birth, violating privacy statute
text:
Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA new lawsuit filed Oct. 8 in federal court against eight employees of the Michigan Department of Corrections, alleges that the right to privacy of Natalie Forrest, who was incarcerated at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility at the time, when officers recorded her on their body cameras while she was giving birth to her son. 
“It was hard to be able to even try to connect with my newborn son, just for the simple fact that they were sitting there recording everything,” Forrest said in an interview. “I can’t even put into words how uncomfortable I felt. I felt degraded. I just felt like I couldn’t even actually enjoy the moment of my son being born.”
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Michigan, argues that filming Forrest while giving birth on March 8, 2025, violated Michigan’s criminal voyeurism statute — and that the Department of Corrections was notified on Feb. 17, 2025, nearly a month before Forrest delivered her baby that the policy in place allowing that filming to happen was illegal. Changes to the policy, which had also allowed correctional officers to record on their body cameras during strip searches, did not go into effect until March 24, 2025.
A spokesperson for the Department of Corrections did not respond to multiple requests for comment by Michigan Advance on the lawsuit. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Forrest described the practice of recording, up until she gave birth, as a pattern, adding that “There were multiple times where I was strip searched due to the simple fact that I had to leave the prison to go to doctor’s appointments for the baby, seeing that I was high risk. Every time that I had to leave the prison to go to a doctor’s appointment, they would strip search me, pregnant at all.”
Complaint ECF 1
According to the complaint, two correctional officers, one of them male, remained inside the delivery room with Forrest through cervical exams, labor and delivery, not outside the door or behind the privacy curtain, with chest-mounted cameras facing her bed. 
Maura Battersby, an attorney with Flood Law representing Forrest along with her minor son and her mother, who was present at the time of Forrest giving birth, described the situation in the lawsuit as “treating these women like they’re subhuman.”
Battersby emphasized that, even though incarcerated individuals have a lower expectation of privacy than non-incarcerated individuals, and some recording is necessary for the safety of guards and others in custody, she does not believe that there is a justification for recording during strip searches or similar nude settings.
“When you are incarcerated, you have a much lesser expectation of privacy than a citizen out in the world, not in custody,” she explained. “But as far as the standards go, and where it is more important, nude is top of the list as far as your expectation of privacy, even as an incarcerated individual.”
Recording during strip searches at Women’s Huron Valley was the subject of an earlier lawsuit from Flood Law against department leadership — and though a state circuit court dismissed that lawsuit, an appeal remains open according to online court records. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You’re not supposed to follow an illegal order if you know that to be wrong. You are not supposed to do that. So I don’t think that absolves even just the corrections officers from doing that,” Battersby said of the recording policy. “From the top all the way down, there’s blame to be had all around there. They knew for a very long time this is what was happening. They were told by lawmakers … Part of our complaint in the exhibits shows the emails with the lawmakers saying this is illegal. You have to stop doing this immediately.”
Forrest emphasized that having officers who she did not know made her feel uncomfortable communicating with both her mother, who was present as her support person while giving birth, and her doctors. She also said that it made it harder for her to connect with her newborn son — something that was already difficult for her because she was incarcerated for the first months of his life. 
“I got less than 48 hours with him. They took my baby. My mom had to take my baby. I didn’t get to actually physically hold him, connect with him, see him,” she said. “And the simple fact that I’m sitting here thinking about the moment I gave birth to my son. It’s all recorded. Who knows where those recordings are? Who knows who has access to those recordings? Who knows what they could do with them?”
Forrest said that the whole experience continues to take a toll on her mental health, saying, “I still think about it every single day.”
The lawsuit alleges that after Forrest’s son was born, a corrections officer told her mother, who is also a plaintiff, that two years would be added to Forrest’s sentence if she took a picture of her newborn grandson in the hospital. 
Battersby said she was unaware of any mechanism for an individual officer to do that, adding, “What’s important is that it was meant to intimidate and meant to control, whether true or not. I would be interested to see what that complaint was or what any additional charge was for that.”
On March 14, 2025, eight days after her son’s birth, Forrest filed an internal grievance with the department, describing her experience which, the lawsuit claims, “described conduct constituting
sexual abuse as defined by the Prison Rape Elimination Act and MDOC’s own policy directives governing sexual abuse and the mandatory referral of such allegations to the facility’s PREA Coordinator rather than the ordinary grievance process.” 
Instead of referring the grievance to the Prison Rape Elimination Act coordinator, the lawsuit says that it was thrown out for being “Untimely,” despite Forrest’s arguments that, in her recovery from pregnancy, she submitted the grievance as quickly as was reasonable. An appeal of the grievance was also denied.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Cincinnati Public Schools has served hundreds with first-in-the-nation sleep lot for families
text:
The modular unit and playground at Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot at William Howard Taft Elementary School. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Cincinnati Public Schools is the first school district in the nation to own and operate a parking lot where families experiencing homelessness can go to at night and sleep in their cars. 
Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot opened April 30 at William Howard Taft Elementary School and more than 300 people have slept in the lot so far, said Megan Rahill, shelter and housing specialist with Project Connect. 
“A lot of times, when you’re sleeping in your car, it’s because you’ve exhausted all your social avenues of people you can stay with, and so they’re often feeling so isolated and like nobody cares anymore, and they’re on their own,” Rahill said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“If they’ve already been sleeping in their car, it’s just on a dead-end street and it’s scary, so we’ve got a space you can come to where other people and other kids are there, there’s food and you don’t have to worry about where you’re going to the restroom.”
Project Connect is a program that provides support to students in the district experiencing homelessness under the federal McKinney-Vento Act that supports the enrollment and education of homeless students by making sure homeless youth have access to a public education.
Nearly 8% of Cincinnati Public School students — about 2,650 — experienced homelessness during the 2025-26 school year, according to data from the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce. 
The number of students experiencing homelessness in the district has mostly been on the rise in the last five years — up from about 2,000 students experiencing homelessness during the 2021-22 school year, according to ODEW data. 
The district also noticed a “pretty significant increase” of families experiencing homelessness sleeping in their cars, said Project Connect Manager Rebeka Beach. 
Families sleeping in their cars often do not know where to safely park their car overnight. Sometimes, they would park somewhere and feel unsafe or the police would ask them to move, Rahill said.  
“It was hard to have a consistent spot or they’re parked in the Kroger parking lot, but then you’re worried maybe someone I know will see me,” she said.
People staying in their cars often don’t have a place to go to the bathroom, shower, access water, or cook food. 
“I had a parent tell me ‘We feel like we’re just like animals. We don’t have facilities that we can use. We’re trapped in this little vehicle,” Rahill said.
A street outreach worker from Greater Cincinnati Behavioral Health Services has to see someone sleeping in their car in order to have them verified to be put on a homeless shelter waiting list. 
Megan Rahill, housing and shelter specialist with Project Connect, (left) and Rebeka Beach, the manager of Project Connect (right). (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
“We were hearing so often from parents that it was taking so long to get verified just to get on the waiting list for shelter because they moved so much throughout the night they couldn’t connect with the street outreach worker,” said Beach, who has been working for the district for nearly twenty years.  
“In one week we had two parents who came in and said they had lost their employment because they’d fallen asleep just because they were up watching their children during the night and couldn’t sleep.” 
That’s when the district started looking into some ideas to help families. 
Project Connect discovered San Diego’s Safe Sleeping Program and Long Beach City College’s Safe Parking Program, so they went on a research trip to California. 
“We decided we wanted to open our own safe sleep lot,” Beach said.
Once Project Connect had the idea for the Safe Sleep Lot, it took just under a year for the lot to open. 
“One of the reasons that we created the lot was that that the process (to get verified) can be quite cumbersome for a family,” Rahill said. 
“It’s so early in the morning that they’re coming. Oftentimes our families are going to work, they’re taking the kids to school, they’ve been ships passing in the night.” 
When a family spends a night in the Safe Sleep Lot, they are automatically verified and added to a shelter waiting list. 
“The Safe Sleep Lot serves as a bridge to shelter, so families sleep in the lot, they’re verified within 24 hours,” Beach said. 
How the Safe Sleep Lot operates
The Safe Sleep Lot has 12 spaces and is open daily from 9:30 p.m. to 6:30 a.m. There are typically between three to eight families that stay in the lot every night. 
A family gets referred to the Safe Sleep Lot and then Project Connect does an intake appointment. Once they are accepted, families receive a bag with pillows, towels, blankets, and laundry pods. The kids also get to pick out a stuffed animal. 
Each family that stays in the lot gets a parking pass with a unique code that security scans when they arrive for the night to help keep track of who is staying in the lot. 
After a family spends a night in the Safe Sleep Lot, Rahill is able to get them on the shelter waiting list. She also gets the family a hotel stay. 
Project Connect can put a family in a hotel for up to two weeks if they have CareSource as their health insurance provider. A family will still get a hotel stay if they don’t have CareSource, but instead it’s for four to six nights. 
“We are quite transparent with them that it’s unlikely that the shelter placement will come through while you’re in the hotel,” Rahill said. 
Cincinnati’s Safe Sleep Lot at William Howard Taft Elementary School. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
She encourages families to use that time in the hotel to try to find somewhere to stay. 
“Most of the families are on that trajectory of Safe Sleep Lot, emergency hotel stay back to the Safe Sleep Lot on a waiting list,” Beach said. 
There is no limit on how many nights a family can stay at the Safe Sleep Lot and the average wait time to get into a shelter typically ranges from one to two months, Beach said. 
The Safe Sleep Lot has security, a library, wifi and a tutoring program will soon be available to families on Wednesday nights.
The Safe Sleep Lot is open March through November. 
“We’re not really comfortable having people there when it’s really cold,” Rahill said. 
Christ Church Cathedral will be able to host families during the winter months. 
Project Connect built a modular unit through grant funds complete with a kitchen area, showers, bathrooms, and room for security. There are frozen meals, snacks, breakfast items, and hygiene items. A local nonprofit has also partnered with the Safe Sleep Lot to provide laundry services to families.

Project Connect is going to build a pergola so families can have a place to sit and stretch their legs. 
The Safe Sleep Lot has led to more students being enrolled in school and some students are now enrolled at Taft Elementary School. 
“We do have quite a few students who now go to (Taft Elementary) because we were able to use the address of the Safe Sleep Lot,” Rahill said. “They’re just taking their kids to school in the morning from the Safe Sleep Lot.”
“Once they get into shelter or to a more stable address, then the next step is we we set up transportation for them, so that they can stay at the same school. The closer we get to that really stable point, the attendance starts to rise.”
For students experiencing homelessness, Beach likened it to Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. 
“If your basic needs are not being met, you’re not positioned to learn,” she said. 
“Our goal is for families to be able to sustain jobs that provide for livable wages and be able to sustain housing and exit shelter.” 
She hopes other school districts will be able to create their own version of the Safe Sleep Lot and was, at one point, receiving calls daily asking how the district made the lot. 
“I really want to build a blueprint out of how we did it, so that it’s replicable,” Beach said.

title: Poll shows Ohio voters are mad at Trump as Dems maintain small leads
text:
(Photo by Getty images)President Donald Trump is trying to salvage the Midterm elections by making them about himself with campaign swings in Ohio and elsewhere, but in Ohio at least, new polling shows 57% of Ohioans disapprove of Trump’s performance as president.
Consumer prices have been persistently high with Trump’s Iran war choking energy flows out of the Middle East, and because of sweeping tariffs. 
Trump has embraced several other highly unpopular measures such as cutting rich people’s taxes, slashing Medicaid and federal food assistance, and saying Big Tech should have a free hand to build data centers and develop artificial intelligence.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Independent election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 76% chance of winning the U.S. House and a 56% chance of winning the U.S. Senate despite having an unfavorable map this year for the latter body. 
Online prediction platform Polymarket gives Democrats an 89% chance of winning the House and a 60% chance of winning the Senate. It also gives the party a 70% chance of controlling most governorships.
To help Republicans’ chances, Trump is going on a campaign blitz. Trump held a midterm convention in Dallas in September that was promoted as “Trump-a-Palooza.” He also has recently held two separate rallies in Ohio.
Controversially, Trump also used $20 million in taxpayer money to air commercials about himself — including one his campaign already paid to air in 2024. 
But Republican candidates in Ohio’s closely contested elections for governor and U.S. Senate may not be happy that Trump is so insistently making himself the face of the party.
In Ohio’s two nationally-watched contests, for governor and U.S. Senate, both races are close.
The Silver Bulletin, public opinion expert Nate Silver’s poll aggregator, has former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, up 3.8 percentage points over incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican. 
The aggregation has had Brown narrowly in the lead since late May, with it beginning to widen in mid-August.
Importantly, however, Brown only briefly hit 50% in June and now stands at 48% approval compared to Husted’s 44.2%. Historically, political professionals want to see their candidates at 50% or better in the polls.
Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic candidate for governor, is four percentage points ahead over her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy — 48.5% to 44.5%. The candidates were essentially tied from mid-August to mid-September, when Acton began to open up her lead. 
With early voting underway and some Ohioans still undecided, Husted and Ramaswamy are still in the fight. 
A YouGov poll published last week indicates they’re being dragged down by the man in the White House.

It had Brown up on Husted 49% to 45% and Acton up on Ramaswamy 48% to 44%.
Both results were outside the 2.5% margin of error in the survey of 3,780 likely voters. Most respondents described themselves as moderate or conservative, and 41% identified as Republicans, 33% as Democrats and 22% as independent.
Most didn’t think very highly of either party. Fifty seven percent had a very or somewhat unfavorable view of the Democratic Party, while 55% held the same view of the Republican Party.
Asked about the job Trump is doing as president, 43% of Ohio likely voters said they strongly or somewhat approve — 27% and 16%, respectively. That compares to 57% who said they disapprove. 
Hidden in that number is the intensity with which most Ohioan voters dislike Trump. A full 51% said they strongly disapprove of the president while another 6% said they somewhat disapprove.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee County covers Flock cameras, moves away from controversial tech
text:
A Flock camera in Milwaukee County covered after local officials decide to remove them from county parks. (Photo courtesy of Milwaukee County)Milwaukee County is a step closer to getting rid of Flock automatic license plate reader cameras. On Monday, joined by county board members, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley signed a resolution directing the removal of Flock cameras from county parks.
“Today is about our commitment to protecting the rights and privacy of our residents,” said Crowley, who is running for governor against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany.  “Across the country, the use of Flock cameras and automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, has sparked a fierce backlash that defies traditional partisan lines. Residents and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are asking whether the convenience of this technology is worth the cost to our privacy, and who is accountable for how it is used.”
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Flock cameras store images of traveling vehicles and their license plates in a database which can be searched by law enforcement using license plate numbers or vehicle descriptions. 
Although police can use the AI-powered cameras to investigate crimes such as homicide, kidnapping and theft, they have also been used to track protesters and women suspected of crossing state lines to seek an abortion. There have also been numerous cases in Wisconsin and elsewhere of officers or police staff using Flock to track romantic partners and exes. In some areas, local police chiefs and elected officials have expressed a distrust of Flock Safety, the multi-billion dollar company behind the cameras. 
Both Crowley and Tiffany have criticized Flock, though Tiffany said just months ago that he did not know what the cameras were. Since then Tiffany has proposed prohibiting shared revenue funds from being used for Flock cameras, and has labeled Crowley as an advocate of constant surveillance. Police surveillance cameras were  adopted in Milwaukee as the city and county sought to tamp down reckless driving and car theft with the support of  Republican lawmakers. 
Crowley said that in Wisconsin, “Flock executives have shown a pattern of misleading the public about their business practices, their safety record, their commitment to privacy, and their efforts to protect vulnerable populations.” He added that, “nationwide, we have seen documented cases of law enforcement officials misusing this data for personal and often malicious reasons.”

Though Crowley said that none of those cases involved Milwaukee County employees, but two officers with the city’s police department have been charged or sentenced for misusing Flock. 
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley signs a resolution removing Flock cameras from county park property. (Photo courtesy of Milwaukee County)
Crowley said that while he appreciated the sheriff’s office work on a policy framework to address concerns about Flock, “even the strongest policy framework is only as trustworthy as the company behind the technology, and a good relationship with the vendor does not safeguard our residents’ data.” 
“‘It hasn’t happened here yet’ is not a good enough reason to keep this technology in place,” he said. “We cannot wait until data is breached, privacy is compromised, or information is misused before we act. When it comes to our residents’ rights and safety, we must be proactive.”
Milwaukee County’s contract with Flock expires in December, and the proposed 2027 budget does not include funding for Flock. Last week, teams of Milwaukee County Park workers began covering the cameras to prevent them from collecting data. In recent public meetings, the sheriff’s office pushed against the cancellation of Flock, attributing a 43% decline in certain crimes within county parks to the camera’s arrival, and warning that crime will rise should they be removed. Recently, the Milwaukee Police Department signaled that it would renew its own contract with Flock while also employing new auditing and other guardrails to detect further signs of misuse.
“Our residents should be able to enjoy our beautiful parks without wondering whether their presence is being logged in an AI-powered surveillance system run by a company that has already lost the trust of local governments and law enforcement agencies across the country,” Crowley said. “Today, Milwaukee County is choosing to put our residents first. And I will keep making that choice, every day, in every decision.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s state supreme court races could decide limits on abortion rights amendment passed by voters
text:
The Gavel outside the Supreme Court of the State of Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)
In the heated news coverage of what’s at stake in the 2026 midterms, state supreme court races are drawing relatively little attention. Yet these are highly significant elections.
Thirty-one states are holding supreme court elections in 2026, with voters nationwide picking judges to fill more than 60 open seats.
As a law professor whose research and writing focuses on reproductive health, I’m watching these races closely. That’s because in the coming years these courts will have the final word on many consequential legal fights around abortion and trans healthcare.
 State supreme court judges make high-stakes decisions

When the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, ending a half-century of federal constitutional protection for abortion, it handed this major issue back to the states. As a result, in addition to prompting ballot initiatives, the court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization has also spurred litigation in state courts.
These cases ask judges to discern, for example, whether state constitutions create a right to abortion – or, at least, prohibit restrictions on abortion access.
Moreover, in weighing the legality of abortion bans, state judges must determine specific issues of abortion access. Idaho’s high court recently approved Republican officials’ rewritten wording for a ballot initiative that would repeal the state’s abortion ban; advocates for the initiative argue that the language misrepresents Idaho’s abortion law.
In Indiana, the state Supreme Court recently heard arguments over whether a religious freedom law creates an exception to the state’s near-total abortion ban. The plaintiffs in that case argued that their faiths allowed or required the procedure in circumstances the ban currently forbids.
Increasingly, the U.S. Supreme Court has been handing questions concerning transgender rights back to states, too.
In June 2025, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in United States v. Skrmetti that Tennessee’s ban on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for transgender minors does not count as sex discrimination under the U.S. Constitution. Consequently, that and similar bans only need to pass the lowest level of judicial review; they no longer have to pass the higher bar of “strict scrutiny.”
This means lower courts can essentially rubber-stamp the bans that state legislatures have passed. In fact, the Skrmetti decision cleared the way for the roughly two dozen states with similar bans to keep enforcing them.
Skrmetti did not, however, require any state to pass such a law. And it does not address how far the ruling extends to adults or whether it applies to other related aspects of gender-affirming care, such as insurance coverage.
In other words, the people who now decide whether abortion restrictions stay on the books or whether a minor can get gender-affirming care are, in many cases, not justices sitting on the U.S. Supreme Court. In many cases, they will be state supreme court judges.
 North Carolina, Georgia, Michigan, Montana have races to watch

In Montana, judicial races could change the ideological bent of the state’s top court. Judicial elections in the state are technically nonpartisan, but Republicans see a chance to retake the state Supreme Court with judges they endorse.
In 2023, its Democrat-endorsed majority ruled that the state constitution protects abortion rights. It also determined that attempts to stop one class of health providers – advanced practice registered nurses – from performing abortions violated those rights.
Judges who upheld restrictions affecting residents’ reproductive rights will face voters this fall in Alabama, Arizona, Florida, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Texas. In some of these races, abortion is a live – and legally dynamic – issue.
North Carolina’s high court also leans heavily conservative. This year one of just two Democrats on the seven-judge panel – incumbent Democrat Anita Earls – is up for reelection. If she loses, the GOP would gain a near-total supermajority on North Carolina’s Supreme Court. That outcome would likely cement the party’s edge on key political matters for years to come.
Michigan looks like the mirror image of North Carolina. All justices there are officially nonpartisan, but Democrat-backed justices hold a 6-1 majority on the seven-member court. Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Justice Noah Hood – both Democrats – are up for reelection this fall.
Democrats are hoping to retain their edge, in part to keep abortion protected. Voters enshrined abortion rights directly into Michigan’s Constitution in 2022, and the state’s highest court has already interpreted that amendment to dismiss abortion-related restrictions.
 Ohio protects abortion, but courts will decide how much

Ohio is a powerful example of what is at stake in this year’s state supreme court races. Republicans hold a 6-1 majority on the state’s high court, a dominant position built over successive election cycles in 2022 and 2024.
In the 2026 midterms, Ohio’s only Democratic state Supreme Court justice, Jennifer Brunner, is defending her seat against a Republican challenger. If Brunner loses, Ohio’s highest court could become a unanimous conservative bench – one that will likely determine the outcome of high-profile cases related to both abortion access and gender-affirming care.
Ohio voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2023 protecting abortion access. The amendment establishes that individuals have the right to make their own reproductive decisions. The language covers contraception, fertility treatment, continuing a pregnancy, miscarriage care and abortion up to fetal viability. It also asserts that the state generally cannot interfere with these decisions.
Now, lower courts are litigating whether restrictions on abortion access – for instance, the state’s 24-hour waiting period and ban on telehealth for medication abortion – can survive scrutiny under that amendment.
The Ohio Supreme Court may eventually decide that case. In my assessment, an even more conservative Ohio court might be inclined to read the voter-approved abortion amendment as narrowly as possible.
Ohio’s Supreme Court is similarly poised to make big decisions on trans rights. For example, it could uphold the state’s ban on gender-affirming care for transgender minors. That would reverse a 2025 appellate ruling that had struck down the law, which was passed over the veto of Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.
Even if they don’t change the partisan makeup of these courts, elections for state supreme court seats in places such as Ohio may matter for the scope and breadth of rulings that claw back individual rights. Or they may foretell how a conservative near-supermajority might lock in abortion and trans restrictions for a generation.
Whoever wins these judicial races in November will not just be interpreting the law. In a real sense, they will be writing the next chapter of it.
This story was produced in collaboration with Rewire News Group, a nonprofit newsroom that covers reproductive health.
Rachel Rebouché, Professor of Law, The University of Texas at Austin

Ohio electricity customers could pay an extra $16 billion over the next eight years because of the state’s booming data center industry, according to a new economic analysis.
Scioto Analysis, a Columbus-based public policy research firm, found that data centers have brought Ohio billions of dollars in economic benefits, but the next wave of development could cost nearly as much as it delivers.
• Elon Musk’s election spending. The New York Times reports, “Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans.”
Elon Musk has quietly funneled more than $276 million into Republican groups and his super PAC since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.
The staggering amount of money makes Mr. Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Mr. Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Thursday.
In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, he gave a total of $158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team. In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.
• Elon Musk’s disinformation campaign. Mother Jones reports, “Elon Musk Is the Midterms’ Biggest Disinformation Risk.”
With the midterm elections just weeks away, Musk is pouring money into GOP Senate candidates’ coffers and involving himself in the spread of literal fake news about a Democratic candidate, at a time when basically every true trust and safety guardrail has long been erased from his site. Given that he and his companies stand to profit handsomely from a Republican victory, the pattern is clear: the biggest election disinformation risk in the next few weeks is Elon Musk.
• Elon Musk’s DOGE workers now profiting off government. The Washington Post reports, “They came to Washington to dismantle government. Now, they’re profiting from it.”
Last year, billionaire Elon Musk unleashed a small army of Silicon Valley techies to drain what he called the “swamp” of Washington — wielding the U.S. DOGE Service to slash at a bureaucracy they argued was bloated and corrupt.
But today, many of his former DOGE foot soldiers have leveraged their government stints to fuel private-sector ambitions: building companies that tap government largesse or that deploy knowledge they garnered during their brief tenures in Washington.
A Washington Post analysis found that roughly two dozen former DOGE staffers have parlayed their government experience into relevant private-sector jobs or investments — becoming founders, securing CEO positions or senior executive roles, amassing large stakes in start-ups looking to win government contracts or approvals, or taking the skills developed at DOGE to the private sector. Though several of the businesses are only months old, with little public activity, at least six DOGE alumni have registered on Sam.gov, a government contracting portal examined by The Post.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Flint, Forstag trade barbs during debate for Montana’s open Congressional seat
text:
Democrat Sam Forstag and Republican Aaron Flint debated each other in a closed studio the morning of Oct. 13, 2026.  (screenshot via NonStopLocal(As many Montanans were still on their first cup of coffee Tuesday, two candidates in a tightening race for federal office traded full blows in a debate, one attacked for being too crazy and the other for already being too much of a politician. 
Republican Aaron Flint and Democrat Sam Forstag are vying to replace U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke, a Republican, representing the western part of Montana
Hosted by NonStop Local’s Ben Wineman, the closed door debate moderated by Montana Free Press reporter Tom Lutey and NonStop Local anchor Bradley Warren. 
For an hour, candidates took questions on a variety of topics, but didn’t give  many straightforward answers. The debate can be viewed in its entirety here. 
 Flint’s background as a radio host showed. 

For much of the debate, Flint showed the skills he used during his years as the host of the conservative talk radio show, “Montana Talks.” He spoke faster, was quicker to throw out accusations and leaned into the same aggressively conservative messaging that made him popular among Republicans on the airwaves. 
On the other hand, Forstag, a former wildland smokejumper, often seemed annoyed during the debate with sighs and eye rolling. 
 Sparks flew often

By the time the moderators paused for a few-minute break halfway through the debate, both candidates were talking over one another. 
Forstag repeatedly jabbed at Flint for talking like a seasoned politician and for being angry. 
“It is amazing how many words a politician can say without saying a single thing at all,” Forstag said after one of Flint’s answers.
Forstag said Flint was showing the main issue of politics — “angry rhetoric” from both sides of the aisle — rather than solving problems, and said that Flint lacked professionalism. 
Flint rolled off a litany of attacks painting Forstag as an out-of-touch, out-of-state liberal lobbyist (he said lobbyist more than 25 times), called him “phony Forstag,” and invoked New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar at least 18 times. Forstag has endorsements from Ocasio Cortez and Sanders, and Ocasio Cortez held a rally for him in Missoula ahead of the primary. 
“Phony Forstag, unfortunately he pretends to be this poor, blue-collar working-class guy,” Flint said. “He was a high-paid LGBTQ lobbyist from Portland who lobbied for all the crazy stuff.”
Forstag was registered as a lobbyist at the state legislature in 2021 and 2023, on behalf of the Montana American Civil Liberties Union, and various clients of a lobbying firm including the cities of Missoula and Bozeman. 
Flint said the race was about “common sense versus crazy,” and found many things crazy — “crazy leftists,” “crazy trans agenda,” “crazy climate alarmist agenda.” 
Going into the break, the moderator had to interject seven times before the candidates stopped speaking. 
“We’re having a lot of fun this morning,” Wineman said. “Hope you are as well across the Western Congressional District.”
 They agree on a lot of broad ideas, but with different solutions

From Montana being unaffordable for many, to wanting to help working people and the idea of protecting public lands, the candidates had similar opinions on issues facing Montana, but took different stances on how to address them. 
Both candidates agreed that Montanans face affordability issues, but clashed over where the answers lie. 
Flint said he supports President Donald Trump’s plan to ban Wall Street firms from buying up family housing, but said ultimately the cause of housing costs in Montana are due to inflation and price increases from the previous Democratic administration. 
“Big government created this crisis. Thirty percent of the price of a home is due to big government regulations and red tape,” he said. “It’s also why we got to make our timber industry great again here in Montana, and that’s why I’ve got support from folks in the industry.”
Forstag said getting housing costs down is his No. 1 priority, and also said banning corporate ownership would be critical. 
He said private equity firms shouldn’t be allowed to buy mobile home parks, which has happened across the state and led to spiking prices. 
“Let’s invest to build homes that people can actually afford on the back end, and let’s make the reforms to make it easier to build them right in the center of town where people need it,” he said. “That’s how we start tackling a crisis.”
The candidates agreed on a few key issues, saying they would vote to ban congressional stock trading; both agree with banning corporate ownership of family homes; and trains. 
A question from a voter about whether they support restoring passenger rail service from Glendive to Missoula drew enthusiastic support from both sides.  
Flint said he grew up with family on both sides of the Continental Divide, and often took the Amtrak from Glasgow to Whitefish. Currently, passenger train service is limited to just the Hi-Line, and excludes most large Montana cities.
“I’m very excited about the opportunity for a southern route for the Big Sky passenger rail,” he said. “But we also have to make sure that the Hi-Line Empire Builder route is protected as well.”
Forstag said he supports the rail project, and said it represents a bigger-picture idea — projects like the southern Montana passenger rail line are “precisely” the kind of large-scale projects the federal government could tackle. 
“The role of government is not to impose a worldview on us one way or the other. It’s to actually improve our lives,” he said. “We should be stepping in to make sure that Montanans are able to get to where they need to go without going broke because they’re paying six bucks a gallon for diesel as a result of another needless, endless war.”
 ‘Us and them’ mentality was prevalent — just defined differently. 

Forstag painted the current state as “working people” against the rest — including both major parties. 
“We need to come together as working people and say that whatever the political pundits and party bosses might say: The working person beside you is not your enemy,” Forstag said. “We need a congressperson who answers to working people in this state, not to corporate donors, not to AI super PACs, not to political party bosses who pull their strings.”
Forstag also pointed to having endorsements from multiple Republican former officeholders, and said he would work across the aisle to tackle problems. 
Flint, on the other hand, pointed to the clear split between Democratic and Republican branded ideology, telling Forstag he attributed many problems in the country to “your side.”
“I’ve also met a lot of folks who fled these failed cities on the West Coast, like Portland and Seattle and San Francisco, and they fled the tyranny on the West Coast, and they came to Montana so they could raise their kids in faith and in freedom,” Flint said. “They were told to shut down their churches and wear the stupid masks and abide by all these mandates while their Democrat politicians were wining and dining at the French Laundry.”
 The national scene

Tuesday’s debate came one day before President Trump will touch down in Kalispell for a midterm rally in support of Flint. He will be speaking at Majestic Valley Arena on Wednesday evening. 
The president is making a swing through 10 states, stopping in Alaska, Arizona, Montana and Georgia this week. Many states he’s visiting have competitive Senate or House races. 
Montana’s western congressional district is the most competitive of the three federal seats on November’s ballot, with Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Cook Political Report rating it as “lean Republican.”
But on Tuesday, Fox News released new “power rankings” that shifted Montana’s western district into the toss-up category. 
Both national party congressional committees released statements on the “decisive” debate victories by their respective candidates. 
National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Christian Martinez called Forstag a “mouthpiece for Bernie Sanders and AOC’s socialist agenda that would jack up costs, crush Montana jobs, and put Washington bureaucrats in charge of Montanans’ lives.”
“Aaron Flint is an Army veteran fighting to lower costs, strengthen Montana’s mining and timber industries, and protect good-paying jobs,” he said. “Forstag can slap a Montana label on his socialist garbage, but Montanans know a con job when they see one.”
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said Montanans saw a clear contrast in the debate between “an independent, Montana-first leader in smokejumper and union leader Sam Forstag, versus political insider Aaron Flint who fights for the corrupt, out-of-state special interests.”
“Once again, Forstag proved he is focused on the issues that matter to voters, like lowering costs, ending corruption, and working across the aisle to get things done for Montanans,” spokesperson Lindsay Reilly said. “While Flint shouts into a void defending his reckless, cost-hiking agenda that’s crushing working families, Forstag is making it clear that he is the leader western Montana deserves.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: In heated debate, Harris-Schwartz clash over diesel, agree on redistricting
text:
Democratic candidate Dan Schwartz focuses on the affordability challenges Eastern Shore families face during the candidate debate in Cambridge, Maryland, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)CAMBRIDGE, MD. — The debate between U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, the Republican incumbent of Maryland’s 1st District, and Dan Schwartz, the Democrat trying to unseat him, was frequently interrupted Tuesday night by outbursts from the audience.
More than 150 Eastern Shore residents were gathered in Cambridge to hear the candidates answer the questions they had submitted to the League of Women Voters, the hosts of the debate.
Their questions covered topics that hit home in the district: how increased deportation efforts have impacted the poultry industry, what to do about aging bridge infrastructure, and whether the state’s energy needs should be met with offshore wind projects.
Interjections from the audience members, largely in opposition to Harris’s statements, interrupted the debate several times but tensions in the room boiled over when the candidates were asked about the Trump administration making a deal with Russian leadership for diesel.
“Making a deal with Russia to lift sanctions on their diesel when they are actively working with Iranian forces to kill our troops is not only wrong; it’s disgusting,” Schwartz responded, “and it follows the pattern of this administration pardoning criminals.”
No one in the audience interrupted Schwartz, but that was not the case for Harris.
U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (MD-1) responds to outbursts from the audience at a candidate forum in Cambridge, Maryland, on Oct. 13, 2026. Also pictured is Glenna Heckathorn, president of the League of Women Voters of the Mid-Shore. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
“The facts are diesel prices have gone up. There’s no question about it. Why has it gone up? Because the Democrats have environmental regulations –” Harris said before getting interrupted by laughter, groans and shouting.
“See this is the problem,” Harris said to the audience. “You say you all believe in the First Amendment but only if you agree with me … you’re rude.”
Glenna Heckathorn, president of the League of Women Voters of the Mid-Shore, asked Schwartz and Harris to urge their supporters to remain civil.
Schwartz did just that.
“It’s very important that you guys are able to hear from both of us tonight,” he said.
Harris asserted that he didn’t need to address his supporters.
“My people aren’t interfering with Mr. Schwartz. It’s only one way,” he said.
While smaller flare-ups occurred, Harris also took heat from Schwartz, who lambasted his role in steep cuts to healthcare, food assistance programs and funding for the Chesapeake Bay.
“He does not care about the fact that there are so many hungry kids across our 11 counties. He has presided over a farm bill that cuts billions of dollars of aid from those hungry kids,” Schwartz said.
“I think that’s a scam,” he added, noting his 14 years of experience with a national organization of state financial regulators. “The Representative you vote for should work for the people of this congressional district — not for the President or his billionaire friends.”
Harris, seeking a ninth term to represent the Eastern Shore said his over two decades of experience speaks for itself.
“Experience counts — experience in the 1st District and experience in Congress,” Harris said. “I’ve delivered for the 1st District. Whether it’s the fire companies, for the water towers … waste systems, the hospital. I’ve delivered for them, because I’m experienced.”
Despite their many differences, the candidates found areas of common ground. They both agreed that death penalties should not be live streamed, which Trump officials are considering for the execution of Nidal Hasan, the man convicted of killing 13 people in Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
They also aligned in rejecting the state’s Democratic-controlled General Assembly’s effort to redraw congressional maps through a Constitutional amendment on the November ballots.
Question 3 carries the proposed constitutional amendment that would set new, looser standards for the way congressional maps are drawn in the state.
But the measure is unpopular on the Eastern Shore, where critics see it as an attempt to gerrymander Harris, the sole Republican in the state’s congressional delegation, out of office.
Schwartz said Democrats have to win the seat “fair and square” and believes he can overcome the odds by continuing to talk with constituents about cost of living challenges and growing uncertainty on the Trump administration due to steep federal cuts.
“If we’re going to win the seat here in the first Congressional district, and represent the people, you have to represent the people regardless of what party they’re in,” Schwartz told reporters after the forum.
“We cannot just take away this seat by redrawing the lines two years before a census. We have to win this seat. And we can.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The 169 Problem: Why CT is more expensive than it needs to be
text:
Connecticut loves its towns, and for good reason. Our local identities are part of what makes this state special. Old Saybrook feels different from Hartford. New Haven feels different from Shelton. Nobody is suggesting otherwise.
But here’s a question we don’t ask nearly enough: Does Connecticut’s economy still operate the way Connecticut’s government is organized?

Paul Lavoie

I don’t think it does. And nowhere is that disconnect more obvious than property taxes.
Let’s do a simple thought experiment. Imagine a manufacturer is considering a $10 million facility somewhere in Connecticut. Same company. Same building. Same products. Same employees. Same customers.
The only thing we’ll change is the town where the facility is located.
Using Connecticut’s standard assessment methodology, the property would have an assessed value of approximately $7 million. Apply current municipal mill rates and the annual property-tax bill changes dramatically.
In Shelton, the tax might be about $132,000. In Hartford, nearly $483,000.
Nothing about the company changed. Nothing about the business changed. We changed the ZIP code. The difference is roughly $351,000 every year, or about $3.5 million over a decade. Same factory. Same state. Very different economics.
That’s what I call the 169 Problem.
The challenge is that policymakers often talk about taxes in separate buckets: state taxes, local taxes, corporate taxes, sales taxes, property taxes. Businesses don’t see it that way.
A CEO or CFO looks at one number: What does it cost to operate here?
Taxes are part of that calculation, but so are energy costs, workforce availability, housing, transportation, permitting, healthcare, and infrastructure. Increasingly, another cost belongs on that list as well: Fragmentation.
Think about how we actually live today. Someone may live in Manchester, work in Windsor, shop in West Hartford, visit a doctor in Farmington, and attend an event in Hartford. A company’s workforce, suppliers, and customers rarely stop at municipal boundaries.
Our economy is regional. Yet much of our tax structure remains intensely local. The result is that towns often end up competing for tax base instead of collaborating on regional growth.
Instead of asking, “How do we grow Connecticut’s economy?” we can end up asking, “How do we grow our grand list?” Those aren’t always the same thing.
There is another side of the 169 Problem that deserves attention.
Every municipality performs many of the same functions: purchasing, finance, technology, assessment, human resources, planning, economic development, and administration.
Some of those functions should absolutely remain local. But do all of them need to be performed independently 169 times? [
Connecticut businesses figured out long ago that duplication is expensive. They share services, centralize purchasing, deploy common technology, automate routine work, and continuously improve operations.
Not because it’s fashionable. Because scale matters.
So here’s a modest proposal.
Forget municipal consolidation. Forget redrawing maps. Forget eliminating local government. Instead, start with a simple question: Could Connecticut find 5%?
Could regional purchasing, shared technology platforms, cooperative public works, or joint administrative services reduce costs by even 5%? If the answer is yes, return the savings to taxpayers through lower property taxes. If 5% isn’t achievable, prove it. If 10% is achievable, pursue it.
But let’s measure it.
This isn’t about eliminating towns. It isn’t about forcing regionalization. Connecticut can preserve local identity while embracing regional systems where they make sense. Those ideas are not mutually exclusive.
More importantly, Connecticut towns aren’t really competing with one another. Connecticut is competing with Massachusetts, North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Florida, and increasingly the rest of the world. When a company chooses one Connecticut town over another, Connecticut hasn’t necessarily won.
Connecticut wins when that company chooses Connecticut.
Maybe we’ve been asking the wrong question. Instead of debating whether Connecticut’s business taxes are too high, perhaps we should be asking why Connecticut remains so expensive in the first place. That question forces us to look beyond tax rates and examine the system itself
Because our workforce is regional. Our housing markets are regional. Our supply chains are regional. Our transportation systems are regional. Yet much of the government supporting that economy remains organized locally.
Our economy is regional. Our tax structure is local. And that mismatch is costing us.
Connecticut doesn’t need 169 economic-development strategies. It needs one growth strategy supported by strong communities and strong regions. And the most important competitiveness initiative we can pursue may not be another incentive program.
It may be redesigning the system that makes Connecticut expensive in the first place.
Paul Lavoie is Vice President of Corporate Partnerships & Innovation and Executive Director of The Elevation Center at the University of New Haven. He previously served as Connecticut’s Chief Manufacturing Officer, where he led statewide efforts to strengthen the state’s manufacturing sector and workforce pipeline.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hinson, Turek share views on U.S.-Iran, Russia-Ukraine wars amid high fuel prices
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek will compete in the Nov. 3, 2026 election to become Iowa's next U.S. senator. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)As U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek met for the second — and final — U.S. Senate debate Tuesday, both candidates said they did not support President Donald Trump’s move to lift sanctions against the “import sale, delivery, offloading, or importation” of Russian diesel in response to high fuel costs.
Trump’s order, which followed his Oct. 9 call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, spurred the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as American fuel costs have risen dramatically in recent months due to the ongoing war in Iran. A bipartisan group of U.S. senators criticized this move because it violates a 2022 law to ban Russian energy imports while the country continues its war with Ukraine, a NATO ally.
During the debate hosted by WHO-13, both Hinson and Turek said they do not support the president’s deal with Russia.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” Hinson said. “I think we should be doing it by lowering the gas tax temporarily, making sure we’re actually looking at potentially a diesel rebate program for our producers, investing in America’s biofuels, which is the homegrown answer that we have right here in Iowa … But again, I am proud to have voted for sanctions against Russia. I’m banned from Russia because of my stance on being tough on them and supporting Ukraine, and we cannot allow Vladimir Putin to win that war.”
Turek also said he does not support the deal, though he agrees high fuel costs are a major concern for Iowans.
“I’m hearing from Iowans talking about gas prices and diesel prices, but I don’t think it should be at the expense of benefiting the economy of someone like a Vladimir Putin, who we clearly cannot trust,” Turek said.
Turek also pointed to his own policy proposals to temporarily suspend the federal and state gas tax, suspend diesel exports and to open the Strategic Oil Reserves as a way to address high costs. But he said the key to lowering gas costs is ending the war with Iran.
“We are in this situation because of this unnecessary war in Iran, that actually Hinson voted in favor of continuing seven times,” Turek said. “This has led to gas prices going up in Iowa, more than almost any other state. Diesel prices (are at) an all-time high as our farmers are going into harvest, and it’s leading into an increase into fertilizer input prices to our farmers. It has disproportionately hurt Iowa, we need to end this war in Iran.”
While the two candidates agreed there were other methods available to address high fuel costs, the candidates gave different answers when asked if they would support the president’s deal if Putin would have to agree to a ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine conflict in order to trigger sanctions relief.
Turek said, “I think that there are other ways that we can go about this without benefiting the economy or trusting someone like Vladimir Putin.”
But Hinson said she would “absolutely” support a sanctions-related deal to bring the end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
“I think we need to bring an end to the war in Ukraine, and we need to bring an end to the war in Iran,” Hinson said. “It’s why I’ve called for an immediate and successful end. I do not think Iran should be allowed to get a nuclear weapon, so I think we do need to bring it to an end as quickly as possible, and I’ve been working directly with farmers to figure out ways where we can provide them relief.”
Both candidates brought up the U.S. war against Iran during their statements on the Russian diesel fuel deal. When talking about the Iran conflict — and her votes in Congress not to support a war powers resolution to curb Trump’s ability to continue the war with Iran — Hinson said, “I don’t think we can trust Iran,” particularly about nuclear capabilities.
“So ‘successful end,’ to me, means we have to have assurances that there will never be a nuclear program in Iran,” Hinson said. “I trust the U.S. military to achieve that objective, whatever that looks like. I’ve met with our generals, had those conversations, but I’ve also met with the families. … I don’t want to see that happen to another family, and nobody wants a forever war. … I want it to come to a close as soon as possible.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 3 debate highlights disagreements over fixing the lack of competition in Mass. elections
text:
PERHAPS THE MOST controversial of the nine ballot questions that will appear before Massachusetts voters in November is Question 3, which would replace partisan primaries with all-party primaries for most state, federal, county, and district offices, allowing the two candidates receiving the most votes to advance to the general election.
CommonWealth Beacon hosted a debate Tuesday night at Northern Essex Community College in Haverhill between Danielle Allen, a Harvard University professor who founded the group advancing the ballot initiative, and Jordan Berg Powers, chair of Voting Rights MA, which is opposing the ballot question.
The debate comes as election day nears, and the question draws high-profile supporters and opponents. Former Republican Gov. Charlie Baker and former Democratic Gov. Deval Patrick recently united in favor of the question, while other high-profile figures, including US Rep. Ayanna Pressley and Sen. Ed Markey, have lined up to oppose all-party primaries.
A recent CommonWealth Beacon survey conducted by the MassINC Polling Group found that Question 3 had the support of 43 percent of likely voters, with 36 percent opposed and 20 percent undecided.
Given the election dynamics of deep-blue Massachusetts, the state has long had uncompetitive elections. In fact, Ballotpedia has dubbed the Bay State home to the least competitive state legislative races in the country for the last five cycles in a row. This cycle, about three in five House and Senate districts will have a single candidate on the ballot. In her opening remarks, Allen argued that the change to primary elections would send a message to a notoriously unproductive and unresponsive state Legislature. 
“We have the fewest competitive elections in Massachusetts of any state in the country. Without competition, elected officials don’t have to listen to voters,” Allen said.
Berg Powers, pointing to outside spending and money in politics, argued that while election system reform is necessary to remove barriers and encouraged more people to run for office, all-party primaries would do “the opposite.”
“You’re actually going to see fewer people run for office, and when they do, it’s going to be more expensive and more ugly,” he said. “I agree there isn’t enough choice, and there aren’t enough candidates running for office. Let’s actually make it easier for people to run for office.”
He pointed to other solutions, such as changing the date of primary elections, implementing ranked-choice voting, lowering the signature collection requirements for those running for office, and establishing public financing of campaigns.
“I 100 percent agree that we need public financing for candidates, and indeed we voted for that here in Massachusetts, but the Legislature repealed it,” Allen responded, referencing a 1998 ballot question passed by voters that created a voluntary system of public financing for candidates. “This is our problem. We often do things that are good for democracy in this state. We tell the Legislature what we want — the audit, for example — and then the Legislature does not follow through.” 
Berg Powers said that an all-party primary system would only benefit wealthier candidates and would make candidates more reliant on donors.
“In this system, you can’t risk one of your two possible top twos going to somebody who doesn’t have a chance to win. How do we determine who has a chance to win? That’s money,” he said. “It shortcuts to the types of people who are able to run for office, which is people who have access to the funds to compete in the system.”
Allen pushed back, arguing that an all-party primary would ultimately increase the number of candidacies in an election and reduce the rate at which incumbents are retained in office, pointing to Washington and California, which both have all-party primary systems, as examples.
Republicans do not hold a single statewide or congressional seat in Massachusetts, and they are outnumbered in the Legislature by more than six to one. When asked whether the adoption of Question 3 would disadvantage Republicans specifically, Allen responded by saying an all-party primary would benefit both parties in Massachusetts by no longer gatekeeping who can run for office on party lines.
“The entire point is that the general electorate — the bigger electorate — gets the decisive vote,” she said. “The Republicans should have the chance of seeing better, stronger candidacies — people who actually have the potential to win in the general election. Currently, the way the MassGOP operates is they’re routinely nominating people who have no chance of winning in the general election. This gives them incentives to open up a different pipeline of candidates.”
Question 3 has been wholeheartedly embraced by a group of private equity backers and donors — a sign that wealthy interests see something to gain under an all-party primary, Berg Powers argued.
“These people are not bastions of trying to make the world more just. They are in it to make themselves a little bit richer and keep the Gilded Age going. That’s why they’re investing so much money in this system,” Berg Powers said.
Question 3 would also eliminate the rules that require statewide office seekers to secure at least 15 percent of delegate votes at party conventions, effectively reducing the role of political parties in the nominating process. The Massachusetts Democratic Party and the Massachusetts Republican Party both oppose Question 3.
Other opponents of the initiative include organized labor groups like the Massachusetts AFL-CIO and progressive activists such as Act on Mass, while other notable supporters include Auditor Diana DiZoglio and the NAACP New England Area Conference.
“I don’t want to open my ballot the way we all have and look down the line and see just one name per office,” Allen said in her closing remarks. “I want meaningful choice in November, and I want a legislature that listens.”
Berg Powers ended by saying he knows what it’s like to try to get new candidates to run for office in Massachusetts, and “not a single one of them has ever said it would be easier to run for office if it costed more and took longer.”
“We’re not opposing this initiative because we love what’s happening. We’re worried that all the problems that we have will get worse,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Delayed by investigation, Fazio spent $9.6M over summer challenging Lamont
text:
Republican gubernatorial challenger Ryan Fazio’s campaign spent $9.6 million from July 1 through September 30 as he worked furiously to raise his name recognition and sow doubt about Gov. Ned Lamont with a publicly financed outreach on television, the internet and directly to the phones of Connecticut voters.
A new quarterly campaign finance report shows that Fazio did not get his Citizens’ Election Program grant of $18 million until July 15, surprisingly late given that his application for public financing was approved Feb. 18 by the State Elections Enforcement Commission.
A Fazio spokeswoman said the grant was delayed while the commission investigated a complaint filed before the GOP nominating convention in May that an independent-expenditure group, Hands Off Our Schools, and the Fazio campaign appeared to share a consultant. 
No wrongdoing was found, and the grant was paid, said the spokeswoman, Hannah, Lemek. 
The delay could have been fatal had Fazio faced a primary challenge for the Republican nomination, as did Lamont for the Democratic nomination. Fazio’s rival for the GOP nomination, Erin Stewart, quit the race a day before the convention opened over disclosures of financial improprieties, including the misuse of a city credit card, during her tenure as mayor of New Britain.
Fazio’s campaign finance report for the quarter ending Sept. 30 was filed Monday; Lamont’s was filed Tuesday night, just four hours ahead of the midnight deadline.
Over the same three month period when Fazio spent $9.6 million, Lamont spent $10.6 million: $7.4 million in July and August, and another $3.2 million in September. Counting all money spent since both campaigns opened last year, Lamont has outspent Fazio, $13.6 million to $10.6 million.
Fazio spent $7.2 million to advertise on broadcast, cable or streaming television and more than $400,000 on text messages since July 1. He paid $344,525 for texting services to Grand Old Victory, a company owned by his campaign strategist, Tyler Flanigan, and $90,000 to a second vendor, Grassroots Targeting.
Fazio, who faces a spending limit as a participant in the Citizens’s Election Program, began October with $8.4 million to spend over the last five weeks of the campaign.
The wealthy Democratic governor opted out of public financing and has largely self-funded his campaign, as he did in his two successful runs for governor in 2018 and 2022 and in his loss in the 2010 Democratic gubernatorial  primary. 
His campaign had nearly $2.2 million cash on hand at the end of September, compared to $8.4 million for Fazio. One difference: Lamont is free to make more contributions to his own campaign in October. Twice last month, he gave his campaign donations of $2.6 million.

Gov. Ned Lamont greets House Speaker Matt Ritter, right, and Treasurer Erick Russell at Democratic rally on Pratt Street in Hartford. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org

Even after facing a primary, Lamont actually is spending $1.2 million less this cycle than in 2022. At the same point four years ago, Lamont had spent $14.8 million to Republican Bob Stefanowski’s $9.2 million.
Like Fazio, Lamont has spent about $7 million on television ads, including $1.9 million last month. Fazio is the first gubernatorial nominee since 2014 to use public financing. The general-election grant was raised from $7.7 million in 2022 to $18 million this year, making the option more attractive.
Lamont, who has enjoyed double-digit leads in most public polling, has not said how much he intends to spend on the rest of the campaign. With a heavy advertising blitz to close the campaign, he ultimately spent $25.7 million on the 2022 campaign.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Collins, Ossoff clash in a second heated debate as early voting begins in Georgia
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins debates incumbent Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff during the Loudermilk-Young Senate Debate Series at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Tuesday, October 13, 2026.  (Pool photo via Miguel Martinez/AJC)Democratic U.S. Sen Jon Ossoff and Republican Congressman Mike Collins met face to face on the debate stage Tuesday for their second and likely final confrontation before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The two candidates for Georgia’s U.S. Senate seat clashed over issues including immigration, the war in Iran and the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at Georgia Public Broadcasting’s Atlanta studio in a fiery debate that again veered into personal attacks.
Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins speaks at the Loudermilk-Young Senate Debate Series at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. (Pool photo via Miguel Martinez/AJC)
Collins, who has represented Georgia’s 10th Congressional District in the northeastern part of the state since 2023, attempted to paint Ossoff as an out-of-touch elite who is more aligned  with Hollywood than Georgia.
“This is a race between Georgia and Georgetown,” Collins said. “Somebody that’s created jobs and opportunities right here in Georgia on this red clay versus a globe-trotting trust fund kid who got to the Senate and then at every turn has voted to make our life less safe, more expensive and worse off.”
Ossoff took office in 2021, flipping the seat blue after a close runoff. He targeted Collins as a “puppet” of President Donald Trump and bashed Collins for his support of the president’s tariff policy and war in Iran. Ossoff also hammered Collins over a House ethics investigation into government funds allegedly used to pay a longtime advisor’s girlfriend for work she did not do and a series of scandals involving bizarre and racist online posts from family members and former campaign staff.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff debates with Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins during the Loudermilk-Young Senate Debate Series at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. (Pool photo via Miguel Martinez/AJC)
Ossoff repeatedly pressed Collins to denounce his son-in-law, an online influencer who has posted antisemitic material from Collins’ property, according to the campaign.
“You stand here and say you’re going to be a champion for Black Georgians when you elevate to positions of leadership in your political organization people with ties to the Ku Klux Klan,” Ossoff said. “You want to explain that to folks across Georgia? Did you accidentally put people with Klan ties in your political organization?”
Collins has called the ethics investigation a politically motivated “nothingburger” and said he denounces all forms of hate.
Ossoff is the only incumbent Democratic senator up for reelection in a state Trump won in 2024. Bolstered by that win, some Republicans were optimistic that he could be easily defeated and his seat would help protect their Senate majority. Instead, Ossoff has maintained a steady lead in the polls, to the point where the GOP has reportedly considered moving resources to other states they feel more optimistic about. The Collins campaign denies this, pointing to million dollar-plus ad buys from Senate Republicans.
Early voting is underway for the Nov. 3 election, where voters will determine Georgia’s next U.S. senator, governor, constitutional officers like lieutenant governor and secretary of state and other down-ballot seats.
Immigration
Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins delivers his opening remarks at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of The Atlanta Press Club’s Loudermilk-Young Senate Debate Series. (Pool photo via Miguel Martinez/AJC)
Collins was the primary author of the Laken Riley Act, which expanded requirements for the detention of immigrants charged with property crimes. The first bill signed by Trump in his second term, it was named for a 22-year-old nursing student who was killed in Collins’ district by a man who had entered the country illegally.
Collins, who has supported strict border security and deportation policies, characterized Ossoff as weak on the border and responsible for allowing criminals to enter the country, and for Riley’s death.
“If he’d have been in the private sector, he’d have been fired because he was responsible for that young woman’s death,” Collins said. “He allowed that border to stay open. He knew that border was open. He knew that criminals were flooding across that border down there, killing and harming Americans. He didn’t lift a finger on that bill. He only voted for it when it was politically convenient and he knew it was going to pass.”
Ossoff was one of 12 Senate Democrats who voted for the act and disagreed with Collins’ characterization.
“Mike, you know I voted for the bill,” he said. “You’re not just lying about my record. You’re lying about a young woman’s death because your campaign is in collapse.”
Ossoff indicated he did not regret the vote but he said he did find fault with President Donald Trump’s heavy-handed immigration tactics.
“It is right that immigration enforcement should focus on those who are convicted of or wanted for crimes,” he said. “If you’re in the United States illegally and you commit a crime, you’ve got to leave. It is also right that provisions of that law were overbroad, and we need to address that. But look at what Mike Collins and Donald Trump have been doing. They’ve been rounding up people with no criminal history, with no criminal record. They’ve been separating children from their parents. They’ve unleashed masked federal agents on the streets of our cities who have killed American citizens with impunity.”
War in Iran
Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff delivers his opening remarks at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of The Atlanta Press Club’s Loudermilk-Young Senate Debate Series. (Pool photo via Miguel Martinez/AJC)
Ossoff sought to press Collins on the war in Iran, now nearly in its eighth month and a key driver of rising fuel prices. Collins argued the war had made Americans safer by preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. According to the Pentagon, 21 service members have died during the war.
“We have been at war with this Islamic terrorist regime for over 47 years,” Collins said. “They’ve been killing Americans ever since. And they were this close to getting a nuclear weapon. And thank goodness we had the leadership to send people over there to take care of those nuclear weapons that they were trying to create.”
In response to a reporter’s question during the debate, Ossoff expressed skepticism that Iran was close to obtaining a nuke. He also indicated he regretted voting to approve the nomination of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was previously a Republican senator from Florida. The Senate vote to confirm Rubio was unanimous.
“Secretary Rubio has been a deep disappointment, but not as deep a disappointment as Secretary (of defense Pete) Hegseth, who has lied repeatedly about the war in Iran, I want everybody to remember that they told us last year that they’d obliterated Iran’s nuclear program, and then they told us this year that it posed an imminent threat and they had to take us to war. Both times they were lying.”
