name: Maine Morning Star
title: Charles, Pingree spend third debate blaming each other for Mainers’ woes
text:
Republican nominee Bobby Charles and Democrat Hannah Pingree during the third gubernatorial debate on Oct. 13, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of WGME)Republican Bobby Charles and Democrat Hannah Pingree punctuated every answer by blaming each other for Mainers’ troubles during their third televised debate on Thursday night.
During the hourlong conversation hosted by WGME, Charles repeatedly accused what he dubbed the “Mills-Pingree administration” for worsening every challenge he was asked about. Pingree pushed back by attributing Mainers’ hardships to a lack of affordability due to President Donald Trump’s policies. 
The finger-pointing resulted in a less substantive debate than the candidates’ previous appearances. 
“This debate here, if you want to call it that, is exactly why we need independent leadership again in this state,” said independent candidate Rick Bennett, who throughout the evening avoided taking sides. “The two parties aren’t getting it done. They’re good at doing what you just heard: fighting with each other, name calling, and all of that.”
The candidates were asked about healthcare, housing and energy costs — all issues they discussed during the first two debates. But they also spoke about education and Medicaid fraud, highlighting their different views on the subjects.
One of the most contentious questions was about the projected $1.3 billion budget shortfall the next governor will have to address. Charles blamed eight years of Democratic control in Augusta for the state budget increases, and directly tied that to Pingree’s work in Gov. Janet Mills’ administration as former head of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. 
“This is like someone who takes your credit card, runs it all the way up, doesn’t pay the bills, puts it back on you, and says, ‘Hey, can I have another credit card? I’m ready to go help and fix the problem,’” he said.
Pingree pointed out that the increase in spending was largely due to rising healthcare costs, the state finally meeting its 55% share of public education funding and revenue sharing with towns.
“We need to find a way to sustain those programs, but also tighten our belt during a very difficult time,” she said. “So again, Bobby is selling a lot of snake oil, but the reality is the next governor is going to have to actually get it done.”
Medicaid fraud
Charles and Bennett both said that there was evidence of fraud within the MaineCare system, again blaming it on the state’s Democratic leadership. Charles went much further, however, calling Pingree “the poster child for fraud.”
“The reason that we’re facing a lot of this fraud — and it relates again to mismanagement — is that the Pingree-Mills team accepted Medicaid expansion without funding it,” Charles said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He has previously blamed the expansion — which allowed 100,000 more low-income Mainers to have health coverage — for the fraud that state and federal Republicans have alleged. While the Department of Health and Human Services has found five providers guilty of fraudulent billing and suspended their contracts, Republicans claim the problem is much more rampant. 
Charles also echoed the GOP refrain that the $46 million the federal government found in improper payments for autism services is evidence of fraud, though that is not what the audit found —a point that debate moderator Gregg Lagerquist clarified.
Bennett proposed the state hire an inspector general to work under the next governor to ensure every complaint of fraud is investigated. 
“What we’ve done in the Legislature is wait every two years for the state auditor to show up and make a report about what’s working, what isn’t working,” he said. “We can’t wait. Maine voters, Maine taxpayers deserve to know that their hard-earned money is being spent well.”
Pingree said she would do everything in her power to ensure “that every healthcare dollar is being spent on healthcare.” But she also blamed Trump and Vice President JD Vance for making baseless allegations about fraud in Maine.
While the Trump administration has targeted Maine for alleged Medicidad fraud, announcing a new audit Friday, the Bangor Daily News reported that federal delays are holding up two cases involving nearly $2 million in potential losses to taxpayers.
Public education 
The three candidates had a rare moment of agreement expressing concern about Maine students’ low test scores. Bennett and Pingree both said if elected, they would rely on evidence-based curriculums including the science of reading. 
“We know that in some school districts they are delivering, and in other school districts they are not,” Pingree said. “We need to ensure that every young person in the state of Maine is getting access to those skills.”
Maine’s current laws do not allow the state to impose mandates, such as requiring districts to use evidence-based curriculum. Other states have shown that state-level guidance has improved academic outcomes that tanked nationwide during the pandemic.
Pingree also criticized Charles for his support of charter schools.
“I believe that every kid deserves equal access to education, and by taking money out of public schools, that is a way to dilute every kid’s ability to learn,” she said. “There are many issues where I disagree with Gov. Mills and her administration, and this is an issue where I do think we need to do much better.”
Charles pushed back on her statement with his own criticism of the Democratic nominee. 
“I find it fascinating that Hannah talks here tonight about public education,” Charles said when asked about his plan. “You had six and a half years to fix it, and you didn’t fix it.”
He said he would overhaul education, including restructuring the curriculum. He also indicated that he would make changes to the broader school environment that would “restore academics and discipline” and “comply with Title IX so that our girls don’t have to worry,” referring to the ongoing dispute over Maine’s inclusive policies regarding transgender athletes.
Of all three candidates, Bennett has released the most comprehensive education plan. He said Tuesday he would ensure every child can read and do math proficiently by the fourth grade. According to latest national test scores, less than a third have reached this benchmark.
He also discussed Maine’s aging school buildings, which are estimated to cost $11 billion to fix, according to a report by the governor’s commission on school construction.
“We’re not rewarding our school districts for keeping the buildings up to date and repaired, and that’s a problem,” Bennett said. “Deferred maintenance is always the place people go when they’re trying to save money, and particularly property tax money. So we do need to listen to the commission’s report on this, but we also need to take action.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Jahana Hayes, Chris Shea square off in CT 5th District debate
text:
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, and her Republican challenger Chris Shea squared off in a Tuesday night debate that featured contrasting views and occasional sharp exchanges over Trump administration policies, immigration and the war in Iran.
The forum hosted by the League of Women Voters of Litchfield County was the first and likely only debate between Hayes and Shea ahead of the Nov. 3 election. They are running for Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District, which remains one of the state’s only competitive races for federal office.
One of the biggest contrasts between the candidates during the debate was over H.R. 1, Republicans’ party-line tax legislation that passed last year and was dubbed by President Donald Trump as the “big beautiful bill.”
Hayes said she would prioritize trying to rescind some of the cuts to programs like Medicaid and the federal nutrition program known as SNAP that the law will enact through changes to the programs like new work requirements. Nearly 63,000 residents in Connecticut already lost SNAP benefits since eligibility rules changed as a result of H.R. 1.
Shea, on the other hand, said he wants to see the bill’s  tax relief measures strengthened or made permanent. He noted his opponent’s opposition to the bill, which also included new federal deductions for overtime pay or tips, as well as an increase on the cap for state and local tax (SALT) deductions.
Hayes said she supports tax relief provisions like those, but noted that many of them expire in 2028 when Trump’s term ends. She called those temporary tax breaks “crumbs on the table,” while wealthier people and corporations benefit from permanent tax cuts.
The two candidates also disagreed over the authority of the executive and the legislative branches in relation to the president’s tariff agenda and a war in Iran that has stretched into its eighth month.
On tariffs, Shea acknowledged people in Connecticut and around the country have been affected in “multiple ways” and said he’s “not a fan either” of the higher costs of goods. But he defended Trump’s ability to impose tariffs by arguing that it can be helpful in negotiating trade deals and as a mechanism for spurring more manufacturing.

Republican challenger Chris Shea is running against U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes in the race for Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District. Credit: Screenshot via Vimeo

“With tariffs, though, I think the thing that we need to look at is, as most things, we need to look at things eyes wide open,” Shea said. “And the executive branch and the State Department need to have tools to bargain with, and that’s one of them.”
“But if he can’t use, or any administration can’t use that as a tool to negotiate with, I don’t think we’re putting them in the right position to negotiate on our behalf,” he said.
Hayes pushed back, saying it’s the job of Congress to negotiate trade law, not the executive branch. She specifically cited the farmers in the 5th District who have been hurt by such policies, including higher costs that are a result of the war in the Middle East.
“I don’t believe it’s the president’s prerogative to just wield tariffs as he pleases,” Hayes said. “The president should not have the power to unilaterally impose tariffs on behalf of our nation.”
“I want to go back to Congress so that we can put a check on this administration so that we can make sure we are doing the will of the people, not the will of the president,” she added.
The candidates also debated the ongoing war with Iran, which led to a back-and-forth over which branch of government holds the authority to engage in war. They were specifically asked how Congress can ensure the administration seeks congressional authorization before ordering more military strikes.
Shea, who served as a Navy SEAL for more than three decades, said he “vehemently disagrees” with the characterization that military action against Iran was a war of choice, arguing that Iran continues to pose a threat to the U.S. 
“If we’re going to go to full war with them, then yeah, Congress has to authorize it. That’s what the rules are,” Shea said. “But the president is the commander-in-chief and has the ability to make decisions based on intelligence that is timely and get after those target sets that are necessary.”
Hayes said she’s already voted five times in the House for war powers resolutions that would rein in military action until the president seeks congressional approval. She argued that Congress recessed early because House GOP leaders wanted to stop a vote on impeaching Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth — something Hayes said she supports.
“Our Defense Department is on the wrong track, and Congress has to exert our oversight authorities and our Article 1 authorities,” she said. “This president is not a king.”

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes faces Republican challenger Chris Shea as she seeks reelection to Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District. Credit: Screenshot via Vimeo

The forum also touched on immigration policy, which comes at a fraught time in the 5th District given recent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in Danbury that led to the arrest of 118 people. While the Department of Homeland Security disputes it happened, video released by Danbury United for Immigrants on social media appears to show ICE officers arresting someone at a school bus stop.
Both candidates agreed that Congress needs to tackle more comprehensive immigration reform and border security, but their views diverged from there.
Hayes called the current policies surrounding deportations and ICE “lawlessness,” and noted that it’s “peculiar” that Black and Brown communities are specifically targeted. She pointed to the recent decision to end Temporary Protected Status that was affirmed over the summer by the U.S. Supreme Court.
Shea appeared to take issue with Connecticut’s Trust Act, arguing the state has “gone in the wrong direction with interfering in federal law enforcement.”
“I think the cases that the congresswoman brought up of people being grabbed in less than desirable locations is a forcing function of what the government here has done,” Shea said. “The safest place for someone to get detained by ICE is in a courtroom, is in a jail, is in one of these public places, not in neighborhoods, not in churches.”
While they ultimately disagreed on most issues, there were a few areas of agreement.
On data centers, Hayes said the companies need to “pay their fair share” when it comes to the energy these large facilities consume and that Congress should consider federal oversight.
Shea largely agreed with the need for oversight, saying that local zoning needs to be respected while also noting that the U.S. remains in an artificial intelligence race with China.
The candidates were also asked how they envision their priorities and committee work in the next session of Congress.
Shea said he’d like to serve on a committee with jurisdiction over veterans and defense issues. He also signaled interest regarding agriculture.
Hayes hopes to continue serving on her current assignments: the House Agriculture Committee and the House Education and Workforce Committee. She recently announced she will run for the top spot on the latter, facing a few other Democrats.
“I plan to run as chairman of this committee because I will not sit in Congress and do nothing while the doors of the Department of Education close,” Hayes said, citing both her work on education and labor issues.
She used that moment in the debate to take a jab at her opponent, pointing out that “Shea’s own union didn’t even endorse him,” referring to her endorsement from the Uniformed Professional Fire Fighters Association of Connecticut.
Shea works as a firefighter in North Haven. He appeared unbothered by the union’s endorsement of the congresswoman.
“It’s like calling the sky blue. The union endorsed the Democrats — surprise, surprise,” Shea said. “The boys will be voting for me.”
Hayes is seeking her fifth term to represent the sprawling district in the western part of the state, which is viewed as the most competitive congressional race in Connecticut.
In addition to his work as a firefighter and a Navy SEAL, Shea founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders.
Hayes, a former teacher who won National Teacher of the Year in 2016, faced Republican George Logan in her last two reelection races. Both received national attention and resources but her 2024 race was not as close as the one in 2022.
The district is viewed as Connecticut’s most competitive congressional race. But this cycle, election analysts who rate federal races moved Connecticut’s 5th District closer to Democrats. And historically, the party in power faces headwinds in a midterm election. 
The League of Women Voters’ forum comes less than a week before in-person early voting, which begins Oct. 19 and runs through Nov. 1. Voters can also vote absentee by mail; The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2. Those ballots must arrive before polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump rally puts Wasilla in national campaign spotlight
text:
Protestors line the Parks Highway in Wasilla on Oct. 13, 2026, in the afternoon of a campaign rally by President Donald Trump in the city. Trump was in Wasilla to stump for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The bedroom community made famous during former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin’s 2008 vice presidential run took center stage on Monday in the national fight for control of Congress.
President Donald Trump came to Wasilla to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican facing a stiff challenge from former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat. The outcome could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.
The venue for Trump’s campaign rally, which followed a similar rally last week in Fairbanks that was headlined by Vice President JD Vance, was the Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center. The facility can hold up to 5,000 people.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

For Wasilla, a city of 10,000 people located about 40 miles north of Anchorage, the presidential visit was a major event that spurred coordinated preparations.
The Wasilla Police Department and Alaska State Troopers cautioned residents and motorists about road closures and limited pedestrian access around the Menard Center, likely traffic delays around the city, heightened law-enforcement presence and other possible inconveniences.
A banner hanging on the outside wall of Tailgaters Sports Bar & Grill in Wasilla on Oct. 13, 2026, welcomes President Donald Trump to city. Trump came to Wasilla to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
“We appreciate the public’s patience and cooperation as we work to ensure a safe event,” the troopers said in a statement.
As of midafternoon Monday, traffic was moving normally in Wasilla, despite the presidential visit.
Ticketed attendees were directed to park at the Church on the Rock, a large house of worship north of the Menard Center on the George Parks Highway, the main thoroughfare through Wasilla. The church served as a shuttle stop for attendees, though many wound up parking along the roads near the sports arena and walking to the rally.
Particularly happy with Trump’s visit was Republican gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson, who won the president’s endorsement on Tuesday.
“Thank you President President Donald J. Trump! I am incredibly honored to have your support and look forward to partnering with your Administration to bring lasting prosperity to Alaska! Alaska conservatives are united to win this race!” she said on her Facebook page.
 

Alaska Democratic Party chair Eric Croft speaks at a news conference at Newcomb Park in Wasilla on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	South of the Menard Center, the overwhelming evidence along the Parks Highway of Trump’s presence in town came in the form of protests.
Two progressive groups, Mat-Su United for Progress and Stand Up Alaska, staged the major protest in town, an event at Newcomb Park that drew hundreds of sign-waving critics of Trump, Sullivan and U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, another incumbent up for reelection.
Nearby, The Alaska Democratic Party, which held a news conference in the park at shoreline of Wasilla Lake, delivered a similar critical message, complete with cardboard cutouts of Sullivan and other props.
Eric Croft, chair of the state Democratic party, said Trump’s visit is a sign of that the Republican incumbents are fearing defeat.
“We’re here today because in 23 short days, we’re going to be voting both Nick Begich and Dan Sullivan out of office, and they richly deserve it,” Croft said at the news conference. “They are self-serving, self-dealing DC politicians who’ve repeatedly voted to make life harder. It’s this record that’s going to cost them in November, and it’s this record that’s made them deeply unpopular in Alaska, so unpopular that they had to call Daddy and ask for reinforcements.”
 

Campaign signs for U.S. Sen Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, line a packed parking area near the Church on the Rock in Wasilla on Oct. 13, 2026. The church was used as a bus shuttle site for people attending a campaign rally headlined by President Donald Trump. Trump was in town to stump for Sullivan. The rally was held at the nearby Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	In the Aug. 18 primary election, an open, nonpartisan contest in Alaska, Peltola got 49.5% of the vote, while Sullivan received 41.4%. In the U.S. House race, Begich took 44.6% to 32.5% for independent Bill Hill.
Croft said Wasilla was probably selected deliberately for the rally because it is one of the most conservative spots in Alaska. He called that choice a sign of desperation.
Prior to the Wasilla protest, Hill, Begich’s main challenger, headlined a morning rally on the Delany Park Strip in downtown Anchorage. At the “Gas Prices are Too Damn High” rally, Hill and others repeatedly spoke about the effects of high fuel prices in Alaska.
In a brief interview, Hill referred to the Trump and Vance rallies, as well as an August visit to Alaska by U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana.
 

Gretchen Manning-Hopping is among the protestors lining the Parks Highway in Wasilla on Oct. 13, 2026, in the afternoon of a campaign rally by President Donald Trump in the city. Trump was in Wasilla to stump for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“They’re here because they’re worried about losing this seat, and that they’re frightened,” he said. “They’re pulling out all the stops.”
Trump’s approval rate is cratering, according to national polls. That is the case even in Alaska, according to recent results from Alaska Survey Research. But he still has support in Wasilla.
That was evident even before dawn, said Crystal Howard, a healthcare provider who works night shifts. Howard said she saw several campers and cars parked at Church of the Rock at 3:45 a.m., several hours before the first shuttle buses were available to take attendees to the Menard Center.
Howard was not among the Trump fans. Instead, she swapped a work shift so that she could attend the anti-trump rally at Newcomb Park.
“I don’t know what prompted Trump to come up here, if he was asked or if he volunteered. That would be interesting to note,” she said.
Protestors line the Parks Highway in Wasilla on Oct. 13, 2026, in the afternoon of a campaign rally by President Donald Trump in the city. Trump was in Wasilla to stump for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: In swift reversal, Minneapolis Public Schools superintendant cancels plan to close schools
text:
Lyndale Elementary Schools students board the bus after school on Thursday, Jan. 9, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minn. (Photo by Ellen Schmidt/Minnesota Reformer)Minneapolis Public Schools Superintendent Lisa Sayles-Adams said she would no longer recommend closing any schools next school year, less than a month after first proposing closures. Board chair Collin Beachy said that he would not allow any resolutions to close schools for the 2027-28 school year to be placed on the board agenda this year. 
The state’s third largest school district runs 59 school buildings for approximately 29,000 students. The district recently analyzed buildings and determined more than half are considered “under-utilized,” or 70% of capacity or less. The district operates its buildings with significantly fewer students per building than other large Minnesota districts.
The announcement surprised some board members, including Director Sharon El-Amin, who said she was “blindsided” by the superintendent’s announcement at the beginning of the meeting. 
After seven community meetings over the prior two weeks, Sayles-Adams said the community made clear the district should not close schools. Sayles-Adams said this will mean the district will continue to spread its limited resources across schools in ways that do not provide equitable access to opportunities for all students. 
The district has not named specific inequities, but in recent years, parents have reported elementary students without access to music or art specialists, and middle and high school students who do not have access to world languages, music or art electives. The district’s high schools also have varying access to advanced coursework. 
By closing schools and concentrating resources in fewer buildings, the district’s plans would have guaranteed all students access to music, art and physical education in elementary schools, and diverse electives in middle and high schools, according to Sayles-Adams. The plan would have also provided all schools with academic interventionists to support students who are not meeting grade-level standards. Currently, academic interventionists are only available at schools with the federal low-income designation of Title I. 
The district is dealing with long-term fiscal issues related to declining enrollment — state aid is dependent on enrollment — and rising labor costs.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: TVA gets $250 million from U.S. Department of Energy for grid upgrades
text:
James Danly, center, assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy, announces TVA will get grant funds for grid upgrades. Mike Skaggs, president of the Tennessee Valley Authority, is on the left and U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann of Tennessee's 3rd Congressional District is on the right. (Photo: Angela Dennis for Tennessee Lookout)The U.S. Department of Energy plans to send $250 million to the Tennessee Valley Authority for grid upgrades that federal and TVA officials said Tuesday will lower power costs and ease congestion, though they did not say by how much.
The money will help fund 84 transmission and distribution projects across eight states, DOE said. With about $331 million in cost-share funding, the total investment is about $581 million. The department said the projects are expected to add about 2.5 gigawatts of grid capacity and support about 800 jobs.
“This is over half a billion dollars that is going into one of the fundamental requisites for America to function,” Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said during his announcement at TVA headquarters in Knoxville.
The award comes from DOE’s Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships, or GRIP, program, created under the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to help the grid withstand extreme weather and other disruptions. Final funding, project scope and schedules still depend on signed agreements and environmental, permitting and regulatory reviews, the department said.
The award builds on DOE’s earlier selection of TVA for its Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Transmission Technology Upgrades, SPARK, program. Under that $159.7 million project, TVA plans to upgrade about 125 miles of existing transmission lines in Tennessee, Alabama and North Carolina.
Tuesday’s award appears to stem from a grant first announced in October 2024, under President Joe Biden, when DOE selected TVA and 10 local power companies for $250 million in GRIP funding for 84 projects. At the time, TVA said the projects would help connect more solar power and link TVA to the Southwest Power Pool to tap up to 800 megawatts of wind energy. DOE’s release Tuesday did not say whether those plans remain part of the project. 
“The rates are going to go down because the cost of transmission will be dropped,” Danly said. He did not say when bills might drop.
Officials filled a conference room in TVA's downtown Knoxville headquarters for the Tuesday announcement the agency will get funds through a program initiated in 2024. (Photo: Angela Dennis for Tennessee Lookout)"The rates are going to go down because the cost of transmission will be dropped,” said Department of Energy Assistant Secretary James Danly in Knoxville, of updates to the power grid. (Photo: Angela Dennis for Tennessee Lookout)
Danly, who lives in Murfreesboro and called himself a TVA ratepayer, tied the grant to President Donald Trump’s declaration of a national energy emergency after taking office in 2025. He blamed “years of very, very bad policy,” including what he described as too much reliance on wind and solar power, for strained grids and rising power bills elsewhere. In a written statement, Danly attributed those policies to “the previous administration.”
“Tennessee is a boom state that’s open for business,” Danly said, adding that the state’s electricity rates are lower than those in 80% of states.
“While the rest of the country has been led astray, here in the Tennessee Valley, things are looking good, and they’re going to get better,” he said.
TVA President and CEO Mike Skaggs said the grants will help TVA deploy advanced technologies and make its system more efficient and reliable. The grants “provide meaningful investment into our system, which will benefit our ratepayers by supporting affordable, competitive rates as we prepare for the future,” he said.
Data centers have driven much of TVA’s growing demand for power. The utility has said data centers made up 18% of its industrial load in 2025, a share it expects to double in the region by 2030.
When asked how the grant relates to data centers, Skaggs said the money is tied to work on five transmission lines, none directly connected to a data center. He said the lines may still carry some data center load, but the upgrades are not being made to serve one. He did not say which lines.
U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann, who chairs the House appropriations subcommittee that funds DOE, praised Skaggs. “You stepped up at a time when we really needed a hero to lead TVA,” Fleischmann told him. TVA, he said, “is in a much better place today than it was four, six months ago, definitely a year ago.”
Fleischmann said TVA came up Saturday on Air Force One with Trump and U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty. “Only President Trump would say, ‘I like that guy,’” Fleischmann said of Skaggs, adding that the president asked, “What more can I do for TVA?”
“Other parts of the country are having brownouts,” Fleischmann said. “It is so important who governs.”
The grant comes as TVA works to meet rising demand, much of it from data centers, while trying to keep those costs off other customers’ bills. In August, TVA’s board approved a separate, higher rate class for data centers. Local governments across the state have paused data center projects due to resident concerns, and Gov. Bill Lee has signed onto a Trump administration pledge meant to protect ratepayers from data center costs.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s federal-only voter list grows to nearly 6,000, surprising some who are on it
text:
A voter fills out a ballot at a Brandon polling place during the runoff election for the South Dakota Republican nomination for governor on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Julian Winchester didn’t know he was one of South Dakota’s nearly 6,000 federal-only voters, let alone what that means, until South Dakota Searchlight found his name on the list and called him this month.
The Lake Area Technical College student registered through a voter registration drive on the Watertown campus this fall. His driver’s license predates a change that added a citizenship indicator to new licenses, making it ineligible as proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote in South Dakota.
A new South Dakota law says people who fail to produce proof of their U.S. citizenship are registered as federal-only voters. That means they can only vote in the two federal races on the Nov. 3 ballot, for U.S. House and U.S. Senate. They can’t vote on the governor, four state constitutional amendments, state lawmakers or local races.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Winchester will need to provide a copy of his birth certificate or other accepted proof of citizenship to the Codington County auditor by Monday, the voter registration deadline, to be able to receive a full ballot.
What’s happening to him “seems like voter suppression,” said Winchester, who added he’d have been angry if he hadn’t learned of his federal-only designation until he went to vote.
“That’s the whole point of democracy: Every person gets a vote,” Winchester said.
The number of South Dakotans restricted to voting in federal races has nearly quadrupled to 5,735 since May, driven by two recent laws passed by the state Legislature and signed by Gov. Larry Rhoden.
A 2025 law designates newly registering voters and voters requesting absentee ballots as federal-only when they list only a mail-forwarding service or post office box as their address, unless they can provide a physical description of their South Dakota residence and attest to 30 days of state residency. Targets of that law include people who drive recreational vehicles across the country year-round while registering in South Dakota.
A new law this year requires newly registering voters to provide a birth certificate, passport, driver’s license, non-driver’s identification card or tribal identification card, or “any other type of acceptable documentary evidence of citizenship” permitted under federal law. Photocopies can be used in place of all of them except driver’s licenses and state or tribal identification cards. 
Registrants who fail to document their U.S. citizenship are registered as federal-only. Courts have determined states can require citizenship documentation for state-level registration, but states must allow people to attest their citizenship without documentation when registering for federal elections.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



South Dakota Searchlight purchased a list of the state’s federal-only voters from the Secretary of State’s Office as of Oct. 6 and emailed county auditors about voters whose registration information — including their original registration date or mailing address — raised questions about whether they belonged on the list. In three instances, auditors said the voters had been mistakenly designated as federal-only and corrected their status.
Samantha Chapman, advocacy manager with the American Civil Liberties Union of South Dakota, said the errors flagged by Searchlight underscore the “stakes” of the recent law changes.
“When a law is so badly written and, in my opinion, carelessly implemented, the results of people being unfairly disenfranchised are inevitable and extremely upsetting,” Chapman said. “This is someone’s fundamental right to vote. They didn’t do anything to lose it — there was an error that nearly cost them a voice in key races in November.”
Voters might not realize they’ve been registered as federal-only. Some may not notice the designation on the postcard they receive from their county auditor confirming their registration. The state’s online Voter Information Portal does not tell voters if they are registered as federal-only. Voters can surmise their status if their sample ballot in the portal includes only federal races, or they can check their status by calling their county auditor.
More than 4,800 of the 5,735 federal-only voters on the list are registered using a commercial mail-forwarding address or post office box, indicating they may have failed to provide a physical address or prove 30 days of residency, although they also could have failed to prove their U.S. citizenship. Another roughly 800 listed residential addresses and are restricted solely because they didn’t provide proof of U.S. citizenship.
About 40% of federal-only voters are either independent or non-politically affiliated (meaning they left the affiliation portion of the form blank), 38% are Republicans, and 21% are Democrats. Libertarian and “other” registered voters make up 1% of federal-only voters.
When contacted by Searchlight, Gov. Rhoden’s office said he won’t comment on pending litigation. The South Dakota League of Women Voters and Sioux Falls resident Jaysen Hill sued the state earlier this year over the citizenship law’s implementation. Hill says he was unable to vote in local races in the June 2 primary election because of a registration error and was never given an accurate explanation or a chance to fix it before casting a ballot.
In response to some of the lawsuit’s claims, the Secretary of State’s Office instructed county auditors in September to send federal-only voters more accurate letters explaining their status. The move addresses part of the lawsuit, which remains pending in federal court.
Some federal-only voters Searchlight called knew about their status and had plans to fix it; others were unaware. Chapman led a group of volunteers to call voters on the federal-only voter list and remind them of their voter status ahead of Monday’s registration deadline.
“It’s heartbreaking,” Chapman said, “to see these numbers climb month after month.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis says Florida Isaias death toll reaches six; thousands still without power
text:
A tree crushed Cher Stanturf's home, completely ripping a wall off the front of it. The tree landed on her car, too. Hurricane Isaias wreaked havoc on the Pensacola, Florida community on Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida’s death toll following Hurricane Isaias has risen to six, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Tuesday afternoon during a press conference in the Panhandle.
That’s up from two previously reported Florida deaths due to the storm that made landfall in Destin on Oct. 8.
Meanwhile, about 41,000 customers in the northwest Panhandle remained without power Tuesday at 7 p.m., according to poweroutage.com. 
The governor explained that one of the fatalities resulted from a car accident at an intersection where the traffic light was out. But he provided no additional details.
2 deaths reported in Florida after Hurricane Isaias moves through

The governor attributed two additional deaths to what he described as “health care interruptions” due to the storm.
In an Oct. 10 report, the Division of Emergency Management reported that seven healthcare facilities had to evacuate during the storm: four assisted living facilities, one hospital,  one nursing home, and one center for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. According to the state report, 69 healthcare providers reported to the state they were having power shortages and  27 providers indicated they’d suffered damage.
No details were available about the other death.
The Florida Phoenix contacted the Florida Department of Emergency Management for additional information. DEM referred the question to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, which has not responded to the Phoenix’s request for additional information.
The first two deaths were confirmed by the Escambia County Sheriff’s Department. A spokesperson told the Phoenix Tuesday afternoon that it has only reported two deaths to the state.
The Phoenix made a public records request with the Santa Rosa Sheriff’s Department, which had not responded to the Phoenix’s request by deadline.

DeSantis described the deaths as “post-storm,” but said that’s how Florida typically collects the data.
“It’s not just if the storm knocks over your house and somebody gets killed for that counts. They kind of link anything that’s even a fallout from the storm,” DeSantis said. ” So, I would say those four are a little bit more post-storm, attenuated from the storm.”
The governor said he was “sad to hear” the rising death toll but added, “At the same time, I mean, we’ve had some [storms] where there’ve been a lot more [deaths]. So, I think people did take precautions, and I think the local officials did a really good job of helping spread the word.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Three takeaways from the latest Senate debate between Collins and Jackson
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins (left) and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson appeared on the debate stage for the third time on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photos by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)During their second to last debate Tuesday night, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson continued to make the case that their approach to a Donald Trump presidency would be best for Maine. 
The candidates had hammered this point in the first debate, when they blamed each other for Mainers’ struggles, and in the second, when they disagreed over how to address high energy costs. Discussion of tariffs, among several issues, again brought this fundamental disagreement into focus Tuesday night. 
Tuesday’s debate, hosted by WABI and WAGM, was the third of four scheduled debates, the last of which will occur Thursday in Bangor in front of a live audience. Here are three takeaways: 
Campaign finance 
After Jackson took aim at Collins for her campaign being financially supported by nearly 100 billionaires and their spouses, Collins criticized him for not yet having shared who is funding his campaign.  
“He promised to be completely transparent, yet he has not filed a single report,” Collins said, referring to Federal Election Commission filings. Due to his late entry into the race in July after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner dropped out, Jackson’s first FEC report is due on Thursday. 
Jackson responded, “I’ll give you the report tomorrow, and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday,” the next debate. 
“She didn’t deny that 90 billionaires are funding her,” Jackson added. 
Meanwhile, the first look at Jackson’s personal finances came last week. Senate candidates are typically supposed to file personal financial disclosure reports within 30 days of becoming a candidate, but Jackson requested a 55-day extension. The disclosure confirmed that Collins has far more personal assets than Jackson. 
Power
Tuesday’s debate put an even finer point on the candidates’ different approaches to legislating under Trump. 
Jackson described Mainers’ choice as one between “a senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine, then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price,” referring to the fatal U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shooting of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford three months ago. 
Meanwhile, Collins touted her ability to spare Maine from some of the Trump administration’s policy decisions. 
“Our Constitution guarantees that, regardless of population, each state has two senators, but it does not guarantee that all 100 senators will have the same knowledge, experience, and clout,” Collins said. “So when you live in a small state like Maine, who you send to Washington really matters.” 
How Collins has used her power also came up during debate about the president’s tariffs, when she mentioned that she got concrete, pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list. 
Trump had openly promised to impose sweeping tariffs before he took office, and Jackson said, “When they did it, she acts like she’s surprised: ‘I’ll send a letter.’ That is not how you’re supposed to be using your power as the most powerful U.S. senator chair of appropriations.”
Collins countered that Troy would not have been able to negotiate for the exceptions. 
“My point is that Troy would not have been able to convince the administration officials to remove these items from the tariff list,” Collins said. “I did.”
But Jackson called that work “a Band-Aid for a real big problem with a narcissist in the White House that is going to do whatever he wants.”
Immigration 
Both candidates turned statements their opponents made about ICE against them. 
After highlighting funding she helped secure for body cameras and de-escalation training, Collins said that ICE agents have not been properly trained. 
“I think what happened is far too many ICE officers were hired and deployed without adequate vetting and training,” Collins said.
Jackson then said the ICE agent who killed Guerrero was part of the agency that by her own admission has not had proper training. 
“He’s not coming back now because, in her words, no vetting,” Jackson said. “That is why I believe that this agency is just a rogue agency that’s doing Donald Trump’s bidding.”
Returning to his position that the agency should be abolished, he suggested Customs and Border Protection or the FBI could take on ICE’s work addressing things like sex trafficking, which Collins had pointed to in defending her stance that the agency should instead be reformed. 
Collins later seized on that, pointing out that a CBP agent fatally shot Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January. 
“So clearly, that is not the answer,” Collins said.
In turn, Jackson said, “so customs border patrol isn’t the answer either” — although still defended CBP in Maine — before criticizing the senator for continuing to back funding for ICE, an agency he said has created a “pack mentality.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Security volunteer ordered to stand trial in accidental shooting of Utah No Kings protester
text:
Matthew Scott Alder makes an appearance in 3rd District Court in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Jan. 6, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune) The armed volunteer accused of killing an innocent bystander at a Salt Lake City No Kings protest in 2025 has been ordered to stand trial for manslaughter, a second-degree felony. 
Third District Judge Derek Williams made the ruling at the conclusion of a preliminary hearing Tuesday, said Keith Chalmers, spokesperson for the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Prosecutors say Matthew Scott Alder, 43, of Murray, was aiming at a man carrying a rifle when he mistakenly shot Arthur “Afa” Ah Loo at the demonstration last year. They allege Alder committed a crime with one “reckless” gun shot that struck Ah Loo, of three total that he fired. 
The judge’s decision comes ahead of a new round of No Kings protests scheduled for Saturday across the country, including multiple events in Utah, to be held in opposition to President Donald Trump’s policies and rally voters ahead of the midterm elections. 
It also followed testimony in court Tuesday from other protest volunteers and argument from Alder’s defense lawyer that he did not act recklessly, KSL.com reported. His attorney Neal Hamilton entered a plea of not guilty on his client’s behalf and did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday evening. 
First responders tend to a man injured in a shooting at the “No Kings” protest in Salt Lake City on Saturday, June 14, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Ah Loo, a 39-year-old father of two, a fashion designer and the first Samoan contestant on TV’s “Project Runway,” had been marching with fellow demonstrators on State Street and taking video when he was shot. 
Alder told investigators he believed he saw a man “ducked down as he was loading his rifle” and who he thought was about to commit a mass shooting, charging documents say. He’s accused of firing at the man, toward a crowd. 
Salt Lake City police initially arrested the man with the rifle for investigation of murder, saying the volunteer saw him manipulating his gun. He was also shot and wounded, but was later released and has not been charged with any crime. Openly carrying a firearm, including at crowded events like protests, is allowed under Utah law.
Flowers and pictures are left at a memorial to Arthur “Afa” Ah Loo, Wednesday, June 18, 2025, at the site where he was shot and killed at the “No Kings” protest on State Street in Salt Lake City. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
In response to a pending lawsuit filed by widow Laura Ah Loo and other family members, attorneys for Alder have argued in a court filing that the demonstrator seen carrying a rifle is to blame for what happened that day.  
1 year on, widow of bystander killed at No Kings protest calls for ‘responsible gun laws’

As Afa Ah Loo’s community and family mourned his death, the events shined a spotlight on Utah’s permissive gun laws and raised questions about who’s responsible when a bystander is killed at a public event. Measures brought by Democrats to clarify that responsibility and restrict guns at protests failed in the overwhelmingly Republican state Legislature this year. 
Organizers of the 2025 march have also come under scrutiny for its use of armed volunteers at the event, leading the national 50501 organization to cut ties, and for the information it provided in its event permit application to Salt Lake City.
Alder returns to court for a pretrial conference on Dec. 11.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia voters kick off early voting with over 185,000 ballots cast
text:
Voters cast their ballots at a DeKalb County polling place on the first day of early voting in the midterm elections. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderThe polls are officially open for the midterm elections, and Georgia voters are ready.
About 185,000 people cast their ballots during the first day of early voting, surpassing the first day voter turnout during the 2022 midterms by over 50,000 votes.
The day also featured appearances from some of the biggest names in Georgia politics. U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for re-election against Republican Congressman Mike Collins, cast his ballot Tuesday morning at an Atlanta polling place. He also urged residents to proactively make a plan to vote and cautioned them not to wait until Election Day to cast their ballots.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks with reporters after casting his ballot at the Bessie Branham Recreation Center on the first day of early voting. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
“You don’t want to risk a bad alternator or a thunderstorm,” Ossoff said. “Go ahead and take care of things now.”
He also emphasized the importance of driving up the margin of victory for Democrats amid fears about potential intervention from federal officials.
“It’s up to citizens to use our constitutional rights to vote in unprecedented numbers, to vote early in person, make a plan to vote right now and ensure that we win decisively, so no meddling from this White House can foil the will of the people,” Ossoff said.
U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, a fellow Democrat, also cast his vote Tuesday as he appeared alongside Democratic nominee for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms in Decatur.
Prominent Republicans, including Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, also spent this week encouraging conservative voters to take advantage of the state’s early voting policies.
Bottoms faces empty podium on debate stage while Jackson campaigns with Kemp

“Y’all, we need to try to win the early voting battle,” Kemp told attendees during a Monday campaign appearance with Republican nominee for governor Rick Jackson near Augusta. “We got to get out and get there early.”
Across all of Georgia’s 159 counties, voters are doing just that. Jeff Hamm, a 64-year-old DeKalb County resident, said he was motivated to come vote early to avoid encountering any issues or long wait times at the polls.
“Historically, I didn’t like to vote on Election Day as much,” he said. “In my community, we didn’t have as much support in terms of the infrastructure and the voting and the polling places. There were less machines, and so the wait times were increased compared to some of the other counties around Atlanta.”
Maanasa Javangula, a medical student who lives in Augusta, said she drove two hours back to Atlanta and stayed an extra day in the city in order to cast her vote in person. Not having a printer made it more difficult to print out and submit an application for an absentee ballot, she said, and has been wary of voting by mail since a previous attempt to do so was unsuccessful.
Georgia “I voted” stickers line a table at a Fulton County polling place on the first day of early voting. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
“I previously used to only vote on an absentee ballot because I didn’t go to college here, but I’m glad I was able to (vote in person) now,” she said. “Now that I had that issue a couple years ago, I prefer to just come in in person.”
She came to vote at the Milton library alongside her parents and brother and said she was particularly excited to cast her vote for Ossoff. 
“We’re big Jon Ossoff people,” she said of her family. “We’ve always supported him. We care about immigration rights. We’re anti-ICE, we want better access to healthcare. My brother requires more healthcare than most people, so we want money put into that.”
But when it came to the governor’s race, voters from both parties seemed more motivated by disapproval of the opposing candidate than by enthusiasm for their own candidate of choice.
Sarah Roelle, a 47-year-old stay-at-home mom, said she was most concerned about voter integrity and lowering taxes. She cast her vote for Jackson, citing concerns about how Bottoms would govern the state.
“I don’t feel like Keisha did a very good job as a mayor,” she said. “That definitely swayed me big time.”
Mail-in voting is still an option for this year’s midterms. Here’s what voters should know.

Jane Uwhubetine, a 37-year-old management consultant and DeKalb County resident, said she was excited to cast her vote for Ossoff, citing his strong presence in the community and his responsiveness to the needs of his constituents. She cast her vote for Bottoms in the governor’s race but expressed less enthusiasm about her candidacy.
“I was here when she was mayor. I think that she did some things well,” she said. “I think there were issues, call it kind of a tough hand. But also in this case, I really don’t like Rick Jackson, so that was part of it as well.”
Sheila Livingston, an 83-year-old Roswell resident, said most of what she knew about Jackson was from the ads the billionaire healthcare executive has been running on TV. But she said she was optimistic that he would do a better job than Bottoms on issues that matter to her, such as keeping taxes low and keeping the city safe.
“I didn’t like her when she was in office, and I still don’t like her,” Livingston said. “So I didn’t have much of a choice.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: U.S. presidents in Mat-Su: A history of unlikely encounters of the Valley kind
text:
(Left) An advertisement for the 1960 Alaska State Fair includes a promotion of then-Sen. John F. Kennedy's upcoming visit and a visit by actor Mike Connors, later known as the star of the TV show "Mannix." (Frontiersman archive) (Right) President Warren Harding takes over the locomotive controls on a stretch of track between Wasilla and Willow. (Library of Congress)The history is clear, especially in more modern times. If a sitting U.S. president visits Alaska, it tends to mean a quick few hours in Anchorage, with as much refueling as anything else. Donald Trump in 2019 and 2025. Joe Biden three times from 2022 to 2023. George W. Bush in 2002 and 2005. Bill Clinton in 1994. George H.W. Bush in 1989. Ronald Reagan in 1983. Jimmy Carter in 1979. Gerald Ford in 1974. Richard Nixon in 1971. Lyndon B. Johnson in 1966. Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1960. Anchorage is the easy choice: a population center, a military base and runways long enough for Air Force One.
If a president is feeling spicy, they might mix in a trip to Fairbanks. Gerald Ford in 1975. Ronald Reagan in 1984. George W. Bush in 2008.
There are the wilder exceptions. Obama visited Anchorage in 2015 but also made it to Dillingham, Kotzebue and Seward. The sun will likely extinguish before a president visits Dillingham again.
Ford visited Pump Station 8 on the Alaska Pipeline during his 1975 visit, beyond the bright lights of metropolitan Salcha. Franklin D. Roosevelt fished on Buskin Lake at Kodiak in 1944. And Warren Harding touched soil at Metlakatla.
Then there is the Valley. If the history of presidential visits to a region is centered on an anecdote from 1923 — roughly 30 years before there even was an Air Force One — then it is safe to say that region is not presidentially favored.
The summer of 1923 meant it was Voyage of Understanding season, President Warren Harding’s doomed effort to combine a reelection campaign, public relations gesture, fact-finding mission and an escape from political scandals into a vacation. Upon departure, he never saw home again, killed by a heart attack in San Francisco on the long return. The long-tongued, facetious wags gossiped that Alaska had killed him, or of more literal murder, or of any number of crazy conspiracies.
Harding’s traveling company included Commerce Secretary and future President Herbert Hoover. Alaska, naturally, marked the distant end of the Voyage, beginning in Metlakatla and continuing through Ketchikan, Wrangell, Juneau, Skagway and Seward.
From Seward, his party took the train to Anchorage and arrived late on July 13, 1923. Like many tourists in the years since, Harding picked up a landscape painting, this one by Sydney Laurence.
From there, he continued north by rail. This marked the first presidential visit to the Valley, however in passing that it was, landscape seen through the windows of the train. The highlight was Harding’s brief turn at the locomotive controls, in the stretch from Wasilla to Willow.
On July 14, and after some brief instruction, he grasped the throttle under the watchful gaze of the first lady at the other side of the cab. It did not go well. Per the Anchorage Daily Times, “The president was described by the engineman as a good engineer, but the dining car steward as poor on stopping, as he slowed the train down with a jerk which broke eleven cups in the diner.” That was their Valley highlight.
At the Tanana River Bridge on July 15, he drove a golden spike to ceremonially mark the completion of the Alaska Railroad.
Unfortunately, the president was about as handy with a spike maul as he was with the train throttle. From The New York Times coverage, “The President lightly tapped the gold spike twice with a silver sledge hammer. Then Governor Bone quickly withdrew the spike and replaced it with one of ordinary steel…President Harding lifted the silver sledge higher for a more substantial blow on the steel spike. He missed it. A second attempt also went wild, the hammer striking the rail of the track. Then with determination in his eye the President took good aim. This time he drove the spike nearly to its head. Another blow finished the job.”
That was Harding’s — and Hoover’s — adventure in Alaska. The office of the president and the Valley then renewed their longstanding distance from one another.
John F. Kennedy was not quite yet elected when he made the journey to Palmer on Sept. 3, 1960. That election was the first where Alaskans could express their presidential preference with an actual ballot.
Both Kennedy and rival Richard Nixon campaigned in Alaska, but Kennedy deserves credit for going as far as the Alaska State Fair, where he did all the things a candidate does in hopes of an extra vote or two. He flew into the Palmer airport, traversed the few miles to the fairgrounds in a 17-car procession, posed with cabbages and donkeys and speechified in the looming shadow of a Ferris wheel.
For the youthful senator, it was an authentic Alaskan experience. Amid the carnival atmosphere, he battled the mud like all the regular attendees. Fairgoers helped push his car out of the muck. Others passed out anti-Catholic fliers to the crowd at the speech. Kennedy was the first Catholic president, only the second serious Catholic presidential candidate.
He spoke to a crowd of “between three and four thousand” who crowded into the grandstand and stood on the fairgrounds’ racetrack, according to an article in the Frontiersman recapping the visit.
Kennedy noted that he was from a small, old state, now standing in a new, large one, metaphorically and literally crossing the entirety of the country and its history. And he found insight in that transition.
He declared, “I do not say that the future will be easy—I do not say that the 60’s will be a golden age. But I do say that the opportunities are as unprecedented as the problems—that we need courage more than despair—and that all the challenges of the New Frontier can be met, and met successfully—if we only apply to that New Frontier the same dedication and spirit which you in Alaska applies to the ‘Last Frontier.’
Finally, as in before 2026 finally, there was President Jimmy Carter’s 1980 visit. In 1978, he invoked the 1906 Antiquities Act to create 15 national monuments in Alaska and enlarge two others, withdrawing 56 million acres from possible resource development, a step toward the 1980 Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act. And boy did that anger many Alaskans.
Carter effigies were burned in Fairbanks and drowned in Ketchikan. Protesters carried signs with him in a noose. Advertisements compared him to Hitler. Alaskans shot at Park Service planes and invaded what is now Denali National Park, intent on violating as many laws as possible.
Two years later, Carter was intent on seeing some of the land he fought to preserve. On July 10, 1980, a Marine helicopter flew him, Secretary of State Edmund Muskie and Alaska Gov. Jay Hammond north out of Elmendorf Air Force Base. They circled the mountains, gazed at majesties and briefly landed on a glacier. Then they took off for Clarence Lake in the Talkeetna Mountains.
Carter was an avid fisher, tied his own flies and everything. The Secret Service, attended by state Sport Fishing Director Rupe Andrews, scouted five potential lakes for the getaway and perhaps had their own fun along the way. A Hammond press aide told the Anchorage Daily News, “The Secret Service agents were even fishing each site as they went.” To them fell the burden of picking a site that matched weather, vistas and plentiful fish. And so, they settled on the picturesque Clarence Lake, perched in an alpine meadow, deep in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough.
It was a beautiful day as they worked one of the creeks feeding into the lake, what Carter called “one of the best days of fly-fishing” he ever had. At first, he tried some Alaskan-made ties without much success. From his hunting and fishing memoir, “An Outdoor Journal,” he switched to his own design, an imitation caterpillar he called Irresistible. Then he “began to catch fish regularly.” Over five hours, he caught 24 large grayling. Four of them were pan-fried on the spot as their breakfast. The rest were released.
“He’s one whale of a good fisherman,” said Gov. Hammond. “Frankly, he caught more than the rest of us put together. And he did it on his own flies.” He added, “Those fish knew who was president.”
The group included the president, assorted dignitaries, armed Secret Service agents, varied wildlife and a random family from Oakland, California. The Brauners — father Howard, mother Kathy and daughter Lori — had been there a few days, the centerpiece of a fishing trip they had spent months saving for, the escape people dream about their entire lives. Only, they hadn’t expected as many helicopters at an isolated mountain lake.
For some reason, Marines kept visiting, only they were vague about the reasons. Then, it just happened, the descent of a fleet of helicopters, one of them rather obviously featuring the presidential seal. The Secret Service escorted the Brauners out of the water, but Carter made a point to include them in the day, fishing and talking with them.
Howard stated, “Mostly I was tongue-tied and kind of nervous. We talked about fish, and the President showed me how to fly cast.” He continued, “He’s a good fisherman. I hadn’t caught anything until he showed me how to fish.”
And that is the history, pre-2026, of presidential visits to the Valley. History suggests it might be a while longer after this week.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee clashes with industry advocates again over critical speakers
text:
South Dakota's Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee listens to public testimony during its Oct. 13, 2026, meeting at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)PIERRE — Supporters of South Dakota’s medical marijuana industry clashed with a state oversight committee Tuesday about speakers invited to address the group.
The Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee is led by state lawmakers and also includes representatives of healthcare professions, a medical marijuana patient and law enforcement.
Ned Horsted, who operates 605 Cannabis in southeastern South Dakota, told the committee he was frustrated by the choice of speakers invited to make presentations Tuesday. They included a Harvard professor and Colorado doctor who opposed the federal government’s recent downgrading of medicinal marijuana to a less dangerous class of drugs, and a founder of a nonprofit that says it’s “taking on Big Marijuana.”
Medical marijuana home cultivation licenses surge in South Dakota

Similar clashes have occurred at past committee meetings. During this year’s legislative session, the state House approved a bill that would have eliminated the committee, but the bill failed in the state Senate.
Horsted referenced some of that history in his comments Tuesday.
“You’ve done quite the job once again in stacking the committee with anti-cannabis individuals from out of state,” said Horsted. “The agendas produced by this committee show evidence of a two-year war on patients, industry and, at times, the Department of Health.”
Rep. Josephine Garcia, R-Watertown, chairs the committee alongside co-chair Sen. John Carley, R-Piedmont. Both lawmakers lost their primary races in June.
Garcia, who has co-sponsored unsuccessful legislation to repeal medical marijuana, said Tuesday she believes the committee has “done a very good job” in aligning with what state law requires of it, including recommending legislation regarding patient access to medical cannabis.
Meeting attendees, “whether they’re from here or not,” have helped the committee meet its goals regarding medical marijuana, Garcia said.
“The bottom line is the people of South Dakota want it, and we need to make it right, to where it’s safe,” she said. “We learn from our other states. We learn how to not make the same mistake.”
South Dakota’s medical marijuana program began in 2021 after voters authorized it in 2020. There are 20,040 patient cards issued in the state to people with qualifying medical conditions.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaskans should consider candidates’ records on childcare and affordability at the polls
text:
Children's coats hang in a hallway at Hillcrest Childcare Center in Anchorage on April 18, 2024. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)For Alaskan voters this election, we may not have a candidate we love in every race, but we do have candidates who are much better poised to improve our lives in concrete ways. For families in Alaska, our biggest expense after our mortgage or rent is childcare. This recent article in the Beacon covers past votes and some candidate positions at the state level, but there are national policies that are important to highlight as well. 
Let’s take a look at the frontrunner candidates for U.S. Senate. Of them, Democrat Mary Peltola goes the furthest on the issue of affordability for families of young children. Her campaign proposes to reinstate a significant increase — from $2,200 to up to $3,600 — to the child tax credit. She noted that when the credit was higher as  part of the 2021 American Rescue Plan Act, it reduced child poverty by 40%. In addition to this, the policy stance she has on eliminating taxes for Alaskan families making less than $92,000 a year will help a critical industry: childcare workers. The high turnover because workers can’t afford to stay in their line of work contributes to a lack of affordable childcare and reduces the quality of available childcare. Peltola also endorses a tax credit for people who spend more than 30% of their income on housing; this tax credit would also benefit childcare workers and make it easier for them to stay in this vital industry. This is a hallmark of Peltola’s policies – practical, common sense approaches to help working families. 
Sullivan has a mixed record.  He supported some policies to help families, such as setting up a center to help families understand the tax breaks that are available to them. He reintroduced a bipartisan bill for $100 million dollars — over multiple years — for childcare worker training and improvement of facilities. This bill is welcome, but a drop in the bucket of what’s needed, and it doesn’t address the core issues of affordability. He’s never voted or voiced support for the American Rescue Plan, which put $39 billion towards childcare, and he voted against a budget resolution for the bipartisan infrastructure act that would have included childcare funding.  His overall voting record on affordability has set us back, and his tax cuts don’t go far enough to help families. He’s voted for work requirements for Medicaid and SNAP, adding an administrative burden to people who are working already and under significant stress — including childcare workers. He has also repeatedly – in votes and in rhetoric – supported the actions of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, which has conducted raids in childcare facilities in front of horrified children, and which has arrested thousands of people who are in the country legally. Given what a significant part of the childcare workforce is made up of immigrants and refugees, these actions – supported by Senator Sullivan – are having a real chilling effect on the childcare workforce in an already strained industry. 
Getting this issue right is important because it boosts our economy and invests in future generations of Alaskans by making it more possible for families with children that are born here to stay here. Hopefully, we can ask more from federal candidates about what they’re doing for Alaskan families and childcare affordability. Let’s continue to make this a front and center election issue; our children, our families and our economy needs it to be.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis says Florida Isias death toll reaches six; 41K still without power
text:
A tree took out a fence and landed on top of a power line in the backyard of a home near downtown Pensacola. Hurricane Isaias knocked down trees throughout the city and North Florida. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida’s death toll following Hurricane Isaias has risen to six, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Tuesday afternoon during a press conference in the Panhandle.
That’s up from two previously reported Florida deaths due to the storm that made landfall in Destin on Oct. 8.
Meanwhile,about 41,000 customers in the northwest Panhandle remained without power Tuesday at 7 p.m., according to poweroutage.com. 
The governor explained that one of the fatalities resulted from a car accident at an intersection where the traffic light was out. But he provided no additional details.
The governor attributed two additional deaths to what he described as” health care interruptions” due to the storm.
In an Oct. 10 report, the Division of Emergency Management reported that seven healthcare facilities had to evacuate during the storm: four assisted living facilities, one hospital,  one nursing home, and one center for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. According to the state report, 69 healthcare providers reported to the state they were having power shortages and  27 providers indicated they’d suffered damage.
No details were available about the other death.
The Florida Phoenix contacted the Florida Department of Emergency Management for additional information. DEM referred the question to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, which has not responded to the Phoenix’s request for additional information.
The first two deaths were confirmed by the Escambia County Sheriff’s Department. A spokesperson told the Phoenix Tuesday afternoon that it has only reported two deaths to the state.
The Phoenix made a public records request with the Santa Rosa Sheriff’s Department, which had not responded to the Phoenix’s request by deadline.
DeSantis described the deaths as “post-storm,” but said that’s how Florida typically collects the data.
“It’s not just if the storm knocks over your house and somebody gets killed for that counts. They kind of link anything that’s even a fallout from the storm,” DeSantis said. ” So, I would say those four are a little bit more post-storm, attenuated from the storm.”
The governor said he was “sad to hear” the rising death toll but added, “At the same time, I mean, we’ve had some [storms] where there’ve been a lot more [deaths]. So, I think people did take precautions, and I think the local officials did a really good job of helping spread the word.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: DNR issues notice of violation to Enbridge
text:
A billboard promoting Enbridge Inc. (Susan Demas | Michigan Advance)The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a notice of violation to the Enbridge Energy Company for incidents in Iron and Ashland counties, where the company is working on a controversial reroute of its Line 5 oil and gas pipeline. 
The notice includes violations of permit conditions of the reroute construction project, and violations of state environmental laws for the unpermitted construction of a bypass around the Saxon Line 5 spill site. It covers laws involving state water quality, wetlands, navigable waterways, air quality, storm water and endangered resources protection.
The violations are alleged to have occurred from March 30 through Sept. 21 of this year. In August, a section of the pipeline leaked natural gas liquid near the town of Saxon, with drone video of the leak showing plumes of smokey vapor pouring out of an area where trucks and equipment were parked. Enbridge said that the leak occurred when an unoccupied truck rolled over an open excavation site near a valve project. Environmental groups fear that the leak could have been the largest of its kind in Wisconsin history.
 
2026.10.13-Enbridge-NOV
 
The violation notice sets an enforcement conference, which is a standard step where the DNR and Enbridge will discuss the alleged violations. After the conference, the DNR can take further enforcement action such as issuing citations, referring the case to the Wisconsin Department of Justice for prosecution to seek forfeitures, or other court-related actions. 
A DNR press release notes that the notice of violation is separate from Enbridge’s responsibility under the spills law to respond to hazardous substances which may have been released during the August leak.
