Shelby called the LEARNS Act, Sanders’ signature 2023 education law that created the voucher program,  “the biggest failure of this administration.” He said teachers are unhappy while the educational gains cited by Sanders were based off a test “that the state made, that’s not nationally-recognized.”
“We need to scale it back, get it where we can afford it, and make the schools accountable for what’s going on,” Shelby said.
Sanders, however, said that LEARNS was working and improving outcomes for students. She pointed to literacy coaches that have been provided to struggling schools and increasing teacher pay as examples.
“What’s not fair is trapping kids in failing schools,” she said. “LEARNS is not just about educational freedom. While that is a key part of the legislation, it’s only a small part.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump administration seeks to rescind approval for Revolution Wind
text:
The Trump administration is once again seeking to interrupt the development of Connecticut’s first offshore wind project, Revolution Wind.
In a federal court filing on Friday, attorneys representing the U.S. Department of the Interior sought permission to rescind the agency’s three-year-old approval for the construction of the Revolution Wind project, which is now nearing completion.
The filing was made in a lawsuit filed in 2024 by Green Oceans, an anti-wind energy group, challenging the federal government’s approval of permits for Revolution Wind and its sister project, South Fork Wind.
“The Department of the Interior agrees that remand of its prior approval of the construction and operations plan (“COP”) for the Revolution Wind Project is warranted so that the agency can reevaluate its compliance with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act,” the filing states. “Given that remand, the Court need not reach Plaintiffs’ other claims challenging Interior’s COP approval.”
A spokesperson for the project’s developer, Ørsted, declined to comment on the filing Monday. The Department of Interior did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Revolution Wind’s 65th and final turbine was installed in September, and developers say the project is on track to begin producing its full, 704-megawatt output by the end of this year.
The project is located off the coast of Rhode Island, with onshore assembly taking place at the State Pier in New London. The project began supplying power to the New England electric grid in March, and is supported by contracts with utilities in Connecticut and Rhode Island. (South Fork Wind, which was not mentioned in the filing, was completed in 2024). 
The move also comes as Congress is mulling bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects, including offshore wind farms. A vote on that bill is not expected until after the midterm elections. 
National Ocean Industries Association President Erik Milito released a statement on Monday calling for Congress to vote on that legislation in response to the Trump administration’s latest efforts to interfere with Revolution Wind. The NOIA represents companies involved in offshore energy development for the wind, oil and gas industries.
“Predictable regulatory processes and timely decisions are important for offshore energy development of all kinds,” Milito said. “We recognize the federal government’s responsibility to review projects and ensure compliance with applicable requirements, and we hope the remaining process can move forward efficiently while Revolution Wind continues progressing toward full operations. The second-guessing of federal approvals that have already gone through a lengthy review process is precisely why Congress must pass comprehensive permitting reform legislation, specifically the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.”
Friday’s filing did not cite any specific concerns that prompted officials to reverse their stance on the Revolution Wind project. However, the filing criticized the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management’s original 2023 record of decision for failing to “adequately explain” how potential impacts fit within the agency’s mission to provide for other uses within U.S. waters, including fishing and recreation.
Previously, the Department of Interior has cited concerns about the impact turbine blades can have on military radar in its efforts to halt offshore wind development.
Those arguments, however, have failed to gain much traction within the courts. The judge overseeing the Green Oceans case, Royce C. Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, has twice sided with the developers of Revolution Wind in blocking the Trump administration’s efforts to halt work on the project.
Lamberth has yet to rule on Interior’s latest request to reconsider the project’s construction permit.
The Trump administration has had greater success stopping wind projects that have yet to begin construction. On the first day of his second term, Trump issued an executive order withdrawing all areas of the outer continental shelf from further leasing to wind developers, while also pausing permiting on any new projects.
Since then, several wind developers have reached agreements to relinquish their leases for areas of the U.S. coast, in exchange for billions in refunds and promises to develop oil and gas projects instead. Those agreements have prompted lawsuits from several state attorneys general, including Connecticut’s William Tong.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lawmakers concerned corrections agency may skip hearing on prison healthcare
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Lawmakers will hold a hearing on Thursday to look into dire problems with healthcare in Mississippi prisons and allegations of systemic failure to stop preventable deaths and illness.
Prison healthcare problems have been exposed through news investigations, legislative watchdog reports and first-person accounts from those working inside.
But apparently the Mississippi Department of Corrections will be a no-show at the hearing, a letter obtained by Mississippi Today shows.
In a letter on Tuesday to Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain, Public Health Chairs Rep. Sam Creekmore and Sen. Hob Bryan, along with Corrections Chairs Rep. Becky Currie and Sen. Lydia Chassaniol said they were “disappointed to learn that the Department of Corrections will not take part in Thursday’s joint hearing.”
“We want to be clear about the purpose of this hearing. It is not meant to assign blame. It is meant to help members of both chambers understand how health care is delivered behind the walls today, where the gaps are, and what the Legislature can do to help,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Department’s perspective is essential to that conversation. No one knows the day-to-day challenges better than the people responsible for meeting them.”
The letter does not say whether MDOC officials provided lawmakers with a reason for their avoidance. A department spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions about the matter.
The hearing comes after Mississippi Today’s Behind Bars, Beyond Care investigation documented potentially thousands of people living with hepatitis C going without treatment, amputations from delayed care and inmates having trouble getting cancer screenings. Such findings, as well as handwritten letters sent to lawmakers by prisoners seeking care and panicked messages from their family members, have drawn bipartisan condemnation in the statehouse and numerous hearings this year at the Capitol.  
In an interview, Currie, who has led the charge to improve healthcare in Mississippi’s prisons, said many prisoners are not getting cancer treatment in time to recover and are forced to languish for lengthy periods without care for ailments such as diabetes and hepatitis C, even as spending on prison healthcare has risen for taxpayers.
“Treatment could be less expensive and have better outcomes when treated early. Diabetic care is almost nonexistent. Many inmates complain to me that they have sugar drops when their blood sugar gets low, but they don’t have anything but the canteen to get a candy bar to get their sugar up, and then (prison medical staffers) put in the chart that the inmates are noncompliant.”
MDOC has the fourth-highest funding of any Mississippi state agency, set to receive over $430 million in the next fiscal year. The high costs for taxpayers can be attributed in part to its medical care contract and increased payments to private prisons, according to Rep. Currie, a top budget writer for corrections in the state Legislature.
The largest single chunk of the corrections budget goes to a prison medical contract currently held by Kansas-based VitalCore Health Strategies. The Kansas-based company was initially awarded four no-bid emergency contracts, for hundreds of millions of dollars, before securing a three-year contract worth over $357 million.
Mississippi Today’s investigation revealed that the same year the state agreed to keep paying VitalCore, a top official at the MDOC, remarking on a prisoner’s rotting leg, said the company “sucks.”
After she took over as House Corrections Chairwoman, Currie, a Republican from Brookhaven, began to notice what she described as disturbing instances of inadequate care under VitalCore’s contract. She embarked on a tour of Mississippi’s prisons and said she couldn’t believe what she found.
Currie encountered a wheelchair-bound man so jaundiced he appeared to glow in the dark. She met a 23-year-old woman with a lump growing out of her breast from untreated cancer. Other women were denied pap smears and mammograms. She met men with untreated HIV. Many more inmates were charged for care they never received.
“Since I began trying to hold VitalCore accountable to the contract they signed, they are doing somewhat better,” Currie told Mississippi Today. “They are now treating HIV, which they weren’t doing. They are treating 50 hepatitis C inmates a year, which is far below the necessary numbers if they want to eradicate (the illness), but better than they were doing. We still have a long way to go on many things.”
Currie said she wants to make it possible for other entities to compete for Mississippi’s prison health contract after Gov. Tate Reeves leaves office in 2027. 
As the healthcare problems roiling Mississippi’s prisons began to surface, Reeves dispatched Kenny Ellis, his former policy director, to keep an eye on the corrections committees in the Legislature. Cain then appointed Ellis as MDOC’s chief of staff in early 2026.
After numerous bills to reform prison healthcare passed the House unanimously, most of the measures were killed in the Senate by former Corrections Chairman Juan Barnett, a Democrat from Heidelberg and Vice Chair Chassaniol, a Republican from Winona. 
Rep. Justis Gibbs, a Democrat from Jackson, advanced the only prison health care reform to survive legislative negotiations last session. His measure requires that prisoners be provided with protective equipment while handling cleaning chemicals. The measure was inspired by the story of Susie Balfour, a Mississippi woman, who died of breast cancer last year at the age of 64.
In a lawsuit that her family eventually settled, she said her exposure to cleaning chemicals in prison might have led to her cancer, and that prison health providers delayed or failed to schedule follow-up cancer screenings for Balfour even though they had been recommended by prison physicians. 
In a statement ahead of Thursday’s hearing, Gibbs urged the Legislature to pass more legislation on prison healthcare in 2027.
“Meaningful, large-scale reform will require the commitment, collaboration, and support of an overwhelming majority of our Legislature,” Gibbs said. “We are talking about human rights here. It shouldn’t be such a hard lift.”
Creekmore, a Republican from New Albany, said he urged MDOC officials to participate with the hearing given the steady stream of stories emanating from Mississippi’s prisons about inadequate healthcare.
“There are very sad, unsuccessful stories about healthcare in prisons,” Creekmore said. “So I just hope that we can put everybody in the same room and figure something out.”
In the letter lawmakers sent to Cain, they said the issues of prison healthcare impact the state as a whole. 
“The health of the people in our correctional facilities is a public health issue for every Mississippian,” the lawmakers wrote. “Nearly everyone who enters our prisons will one day come home. Whether they return healthier, treated for addiction and mental illness, and ready to work, or return sicker and more likely to reoffend, affects our communities, our hospitals, our Medicaid program, and our public safety. A strong, rehabilitative corrections system is in everyone’sinterest, and we cannot build one without the Department at the table.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Secret deal with feds moves Iowa church closer to use of controlled substances
text:
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy has agreed to award the Iowaska Church of Healing the state certification that is needed to clear the way for the issuance of federal certificates to not only import a controlled substance, but also to manufacture from it a tea that is to be used in religious ceremonies. (Photo via Getty Images)After years of litigation over its nonprofit status and use of a hallucinogenic controlled substance, an Iowa-based church is one step closer to being able to import the drug.
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy has agreed to award the Iowaska Church of Healing the state certification that is needed to clear the way for the issuance of federal certificates to not only import a controlled substance, but also to manufacture from it a tea that is to be used in religious ceremonies.
State records indicate the church was formed in Iowa in September 2018 and is run by Admir Dado Kantarevic and by Shaman BaBa DaDo, the latter of whom the church describes as “an internationally renowned healer and clairvoyant.” For a time, the church’s official headquarters was Kantarevic’s former home in Des Moines.
Iowaska’s teachings are built around the use of ayahuasca, a tea that is brewed from the leaves of shrubs and vines found in the Amazon. The church has acknowledged that under the federal Controlled Substances Act, an ingredient of ayahuasca called dimethyltryptamine or DMT, is a Schedule I drug and a hallucinogenic alkaloid, and that there is no statutory exemption allowing for its use in religious ceremonies.
Church fights IRS and DEA in court
In January 2019, Iowaska filed an application with the IRS seeking tax-exempt status and was denied because, in the IRS’ view, the church’s use of the Sacrament of Ayahuasca in its religious practices was illegal.
In 2021, the church sued the IRS in U.S. District Court, challenging the federal agency’s decision. In court papers, the church argued the IRS was violating the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 and noted that the church’s mission was “to help individuals attain healing of the mind, body and spirit through the sacred Sacrament of Ayahuasca under the guidelines of North and South American indigenous traditions and cultural values. Ayahuasca is consumed in the form of a tea during religious ceremonies.”
At the same time, the church was asking the federal Drug Enforcement Administration for a religious exemption from the federal Controlled Substances Act. In court, the church argued the DEA never responded to its request, which then resulted in the IRS refusing to grant nonprofit status.
In March 2023, a federal judge at the district court level ruled in favor of the IRS and dismissed the church’s lawsuit. The church, the court noted, “has had as many as 20 members living in different states and foreign countries, and generally holds its ceremonies on weekends, with members staying in frequent contact with ‘healers’ to help guide them through their daily struggles.”
Organizations may be denied tax-exempt status if their activities violate public policy, the court ruled, adding the church’s activities violated public policy in that the use of ayahuasca remained illegal under the federal law for which the DEA had yet to grant an exemption.
In the meantime, the church continued to seek that exemption from the DEA. Earlier this year, the church went to federal court and argued the DEA and federal government had failed to discharge their duties for more than five years, thereby imposing a “clearly unjustified prior restraint on religion.”
Lawyers for the DEA argued the government “continues to act diligently in reviewing Iowaska’s request for an exemption,” but acknowledged its lack of a decision in the matter.
Confidential agreement reached with DEA
In June 2026, lawyers from the U.S. Department of Justice informed the court that the DEA and the Iowaska Church of Healing had settled their differences and signed a “memorandum of agreement” on the church’s request for a religious exemption to the Controlled Substances Act.
The DEA and the church then filed a joint motion to provide the court with a copy of their agreement only under seal, making the contents of the agreement inaccessible to the public.
“The parties agree that maintaining the memorandum of agreement under seal is necessary to protect important public and privacy interests,” lawyers for the DEA and the church told the court.
The agreement, they said, contained confidential information such as “personal identifying information” of church members, the names of individuals responsible for handling the controlled substances, security measures for storing the controlled substances and the manner in which the controlled substances were to be imported to the United States for the church’s use.
The agreement, they said, recognized the church’s “right under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act to practice its Sacrament of Ayahuasca, subject to agreed conditions.”
That agreement, they said, resolved only the first stage of the DEA’s two-step process for obtaining a religious exemption to the Controlled Substances Act. Step two, they said, involved the Iowa Board of Pharmacy awarding the church an Iowa Certificate of Registration, after which the DEA would “expeditiously” process the necessary exemption, registrations and permits.
On Oct. 5, 2026, the Board of Pharmacy agreed to provide the church the certificate of registration. In its order, the board stated the confidential agreement between the DEA and the church “effectively grants” the church a federal certificate to not only import “concentrated paste of ayahuasca,” but also a federal certificate to manufacture, in bulk, the ayahuasca tea used in ceremonies.
According to Board of Pharmacy records, the board-issued state certification will be placed on probationary status for one year. In addition, the church will be required to report to the board any “adverse events that occur with any participant in (the church’s) religious ceremonies using ayahuasca” if those events require some sort of off-site medical intervention.

title: Louisiana ends amberjack season for recreational fishermen
text:
A Greater amberjack swims in front of a reef. Louisiana is set to close its recreational amberjack season on Oct. 14. (Photo courtesy of NOAA Fisheries)Greater amberjack season will close in Louisiana waters overnight for recreational fishermen after anglers caught over 335,000 pounds in 43 days. 
The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries issued an emergency declaration to close the amberjack season for recreational fishers at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration determined that the annual amount of fish allowed to be harvested, just over 167 tons of fish, had been met in federal waters. 
State Wildlife and Fisheries Secretary Tyler Bosworth issued the declaration to close recreational fishing of amberjack in state waters to stay compatible with federal seasons, which helps state and federal officials maintain consistent rules and efficient enforcement to protect against overfishing.
Recreational fishers were limited to taking home one fish per person per day during amberjack season. Limits are put in place on the number of fish allowed to be taken by fishers to prevent long-term overfishing and decline of species like amberjack, which are currently considered an overfished population in the Gulf of Mexico. 
The 2026 recreational amberjack season started Sept. 1 and ran the full length of its projected 43 days. 
Commercial amberjack season typically spans from Jan. 1 through May 31 or until the total weight limit is met, which this year didn’t occur until Aug. 8.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT poverty rate above pre-pandemic levels, report says
text:
In recent years, the nation has seen two opposing shifts: a vast expansion of anti-poverty measures and public benefits during the height of the pandemic, followed by a drastic cutting of public benefits in the wake of sweeping federal legislation passed last year.
Now, a new report looks at how those shifts impacted poverty in Connecticut, finding that a drastic pandemic-era reduction in poverty within the state has already been reversed, with future increases likely as the newer cuts to public benefits continue to take effect. 
The report, released Tuesday morning by CT Voices for Children, a New Haven-based public policy group, aims to offer a closer look at how poverty has shifted in Connecticut in the past several years. The report focuses on three distinct periods: pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic.
The organization found that poverty in the state dropped from 9.3% in 2019 to 7% in 2021 as pandemic-era assistance and stimulus funds were released. But then the poverty rate increased to 10.6%, or about 385,500 state residents, including 91,400 children, by 2025. 
“The major changes in poverty in recent years largely reflect a historic but temporary shift in public benefits, and that another historic shift — this time in the opposite direction — is now underway,” said report author and CT Voices research and policy director Patrick O’Brien. “And if not offset, the new federal cuts will likely lead to more residents living in poverty.” 
To understand how the benefit cuts could impact state residents, the report examines a variety of federal data. It also looks at state data highlighting who is most likely to fall into poverty in Connecticut, including women, Black residents, Hispanic residents, noncitizens, and children.  
In doing so, the report adds new data to a growing pile of information about poverty and economic hardship in the state, showing that even before some of the upcoming federal benefit cuts take effect, a growing number of households are struggling. And with the benefit changes likely to increase poverty further, CT Voices argues that now is the time for the state to take action.  
Poverty on the rise
The report looks at three different types of poverty metrics: the Official Poverty Measure, which looks at pre-tax cash income; the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which adds in additional benefits like food and housing assistance;  and the Health Inclusive Poverty Measure, a third measure that includes health-related benefits like Medicaid. 
In addition to examining how poverty rates have increased as temporary pandemic-era assistance programs like stimulus programs and expansions to the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit ended, the report also examines who those changes have impacted the most. 
It dedicates much of its focus in this area to child poverty, noting that using SPM data,  the child poverty rate in Connecticut was more than halved during the pandemic, falling from 9.8%  in 2019 to 3.8% in 2021. By 2025, that decline was erased, with the rate hovering at 12.5%.
But other groups also stand to be affected by the recent ticks upward in poverty. The report shows that groups like women, noncitizens, and Black and Hispanic populations are more likely to face poverty or near poverty than the state population as a whole.  
The cuts to public benefits arrive at a time where populations in the state are less likely to be able to absorb the impact. That tracks with other CT Voices for Children reports, including its annual State of Working Connecticut report, which found that lower-income households are most likely to be hit by economic instability in the state, with higher than national unemployment, increased consumer costs, and public benefit cuts all colliding at an already complicated time for struggling households. 
Because of this, CT Voices for Children predicts that the looming benefits cuts, many of which are targeted at benefits programs that it says have had a tangible impact on reducing poverty in the state and nationally, will instead cause further increases in Connecticut. 
Gov. Ned Lamont’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Some of those effects are already beginning to be seen. In a different report published in August, CT Voices for Children found that in the past year, roughly 63,000 state residents lost benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, with people losing benefits faster than the state initially expected. 
The latest report notes that the public benefits most in jeopardy are also the ones with some of the largest effects in reducing poverty in Connecticut. SNAP, for example, was the fourth-largest poverty-reducing measure in CT in the state, pulling 48,100 residents out of poverty, including 15,900 children. 
Medicaid, meanwhile, will be subject to new work requirements and other rules in 2027 that could see roughly 110,000 adults removed from eligibility. It was the largest healthcare related poverty-reducing measure, reducing the poverty rate by 5.2 percentage points, lifting 189,400 residents out of poverty, including 72,800 children.
The largest poverty-reducing measure, Social Security, could also face changes in the coming years. If the program’s  funding shortfall is not addressed in the immediate future, benefits could be cut significantly starting in 2032.  
That could have a big impact in the state. “In Connecticut, the program reduced the poverty rate by 8.5 percentage points, lifting nearly 311,000 residents out of poverty, primarily seniors, but also children and working aged adults,” O’Brien said.
CT Voices for Children argues that the potential impact of the federal cuts reinforce the importance of benefit programs more broadly. While the latest report does not make policy prescriptions, the organization has already called for several changes that it says could help people in the state, including a state nutrition assistance program modeled after and capable of replacing parts of SNAP, and a state-funded public option for healthcare.
In recent months, state leaders have also advanced their own efforts to address the issue. The Lamont administration has used money to support Connecticut Foodshare and also pledged to issue grocery store gift cards to residents who have lost SNAP, but advocates say that a more permanent solution is drastically needed. 
With this new report, CT Voices hopes that it can provide data that shows the urgency of the issue facing the state. “As federal funding and benefits are cut, Connecticut faces important choices about how to respond,” Emily Byrne, executive director of CT Voices for Children, told reporters on Tuesday.  “We can allow federal budget cuts to deepen hardship, or we can make deliberate investments to protect Connecticut residents and strengthen economic security for everyone in our state.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: John Deere announces $13M to Iowa food banks, farm to plate support
text:
Deanna Kovar, left, with John Deere, speaks with Iowa farmer Emily Wynn about selling farm products to food banks. The two spoke at the Food Bank of Iowa in Des Moines Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/ Iowa Capital Dispatch) The John Deere Foundation announced Tuesday it was committing $18.5 million to support food banks across the country and their connections with farmers, with $13 million of the commitment to support food banks and farmers in Iowa.
Katie Sorrell, the executive director of the Iowa Food Bank Association, said the partnership was a “win-win-win investment” that would benefit food banks, families in need of food assistance and farmers who gain local market opportunities. 
Sorrell said food insecurity increased in every Iowa county over the past year. National data show 1 in 8 Iowans, about 12.4%, are food insecure. 
“Behind those numbers and statistics are our neighbors, seniors, coworkers, veterans, students, and working families doing their best to make ends meet. And the need continues to grow,” Sorrell said. “ … This investment will help bring fresh, nutritious, farm-grown food to the places where Iowans already turn for support.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The John Deere Foundation funding will support food bank operations and build up Iowa’s farm to food bank initiatives. The company made the announcement at the Food Bank of Iowa headquarters in Des Moines. 
While Food Bank of Iowa, Riverbend Food Bank and Northeast Iowa Food Bank currently purchase from about 20 producers, the food banks estimate the additional funding will allow them to expand to work directly with around 120 farmers. 
“That’s nearly 100 additional farmers participating across these three food bank networks, helping supply nutritious food to their communities through a model that is already proven successful,” said Deanna Kovar, president of worldwide ag & turf division at John Deere. 
Emily Wynn, a farmer with Brewer Family Farms, said her family has been selling pork products, like chorizo, to Food Bank of Iowa since 2024, when the food bank received funding for local purchases through the state-led Choose Iowa program. 
Brewer Family Farms sells beef and pork direct to consumers in addition to farming row crops. 
Wynn said being a farmer is a hard job but new opportunities like selling directly to a food bank help operations like hers, which has been in her family for more than 150 years, grow in new directions. 
“These are the types of opportunities that allow us, as those that are coming into owning the farm one day, the ability to hopefully keep it and own it until we’re in our late 70s and 80s, and then be able to give it on to the next generation,” Wynn said. 
In 2025, Choose Iowa allocated $200,000 in matching funds to Iowa food banks to purchase proteins, dairy, small grains, flour and honey from Choose Iowa member farms. Farmers have called for more local food funding since a federal procurement program was cut in 2025.
Wynn said even small farms that can only sell 50 or so pounds at a time to a food bank can take advantage of the partnership. 
“We grow the best protein, produce, crops in the nation here in Iowa, and it’s our duty to be able to spread that,” Wynn said. “So we love being able to partner and give back.” 
Emily Shearer, Food Bank of Iowa’s vice president of food acquisition, said the John Deere Foundation funding will more than double the local food procurement the food bank does currently. Shearer said Food Bank of Iowa intends to add 10-12 producers to its roster of vendors for each of the three years of the John Deere Foundation funding. 
Shearer said the food bank tries to prioritize things like protein and dairy with local food procurement because those are the items that are typically most expensive in a grocery cart, but she said this funding also allows the food bank the flexibility to purchase other things, like locally milled flour. 
According to Food Bank of Iowa’s 2026 fiscal year impact report, the nonprofit distributed more than 28 million pounds of food to the more than 700 food pantries and meal centers it serves. The report said 30% of the food was purchased by the food bank last year, 19% came from U.S. Department of Agriculture, 36% was rescued food and the final 15% was donated. 
Food banks across the state also saw increased need in late 2025 when the government shutdown temporarily suspended federal nutrition benefits. As the cost of food has increased over the past several years, Shearer said it has meant the food bank has to spend more on the food it purchases.
Shearer said she typically works directly with farmers for local food purchases and that often farmers are willing to cut a deal or donate some food in addition to the food bank purchase. 
Annette Hacker, Food Bank of Iowa’s chief communications and strategy officer, said the Des Moines-based food bank is set to receive $1 million from the John Deere Foundation each year for the next three years. Hacker said this funding will then be divided between three “buckets” at the food bank: one for farm to plate, another for operating expenses and the third for  volunteer programing with John Deere staff to pack items like snack packs and hygiene products. 
The John Deere Foundation announcement pledged $17 million, which includes the $13 million to be spent in Iowa, to Feeding America and an additional $1.5 million to The Farmlink Project, a nonprofit food recovery and delivery organization. 
“These investments will help recover surplus food, expand access to nutrition, nutritious meals and create stronger connections between farmers and food banks,” John Deere Foundation President Taryn Edgin said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Braun urges Hoosiers to apply for FEMA aid before Oct. 25 as storm recovery advances
text:
Indiana Department of Homeland Security Executive Director Jonathan Whitham, left, Gov. Mike Braun, center, and FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Darryl Dragoo discuss housing assistance for storm survivors Oct. 13, 2026, during a news conference in Indianapolis. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)About 200 Hoosiers remain in Indiana’s emergency shelter program two months after August’s storms, and officials are urging anyone impacted to apply for federal aid before an Oct. 25 deadline.

Gov. Mike Braun announced Tuesday that the Indiana Department of Homeland Security will lead a transition from state-funded hotel stays to rental housing and other longer-term arrangements for residents displaced by the severe weather and flooding.
The housing push follows a federal major disaster declaration approved in August, which opened individual assistance to residents in 21 counties.
Jonathan Whitham, the department’s executive director, said the roughly 200 people still in the shelter program are the first priority. Officials don’t know how many other displaced residents have yet to seek assistance.
At peak, some 360 households relied on vouchers for temporary shelter.


Hoosiers can apply for FEMA assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 800-621-3362. That deadline is Oct. 25. The state disaster relief fund’s application deadline is Nov. 24. Indiana 211 can help residents apply.


The state’s disaster services contractor, Tidal Basin, has begun contacting survivors to assess their housing needs and identify available state and federal help.
“Each survivor in this event, is going to have a different set of circumstances that needs to be addressed,” Whitham said. “They’re going to have opportunities for different types of assistance at both the state and federal level.”
Whitham warned, however, that some survivors may still be staying in tents or cars on their damaged properties. He encouraged residents to apply even if they don’t need assistance immediately so they can seek help if colder weather makes their current living arrangements untenable.
FEMA rental assistance can help eligible residents whose homes are uninhabitable pay rent for up to 18 months while repairs are made.
Darryl Dragoo, FEMA’s federal coordinating officer, said continued assistance involves working with the agency on a monthly basis.
The state is also seeking additional FEMA support that could include home repairs or direct housing assistance for families whose needs cannot be met through available rentals, according to Braun’s office.
Dragoo urged residents without insurance, or with losses their policies don’t cover, to apply.
“Please, register with FEMA,” Dragoo said. “That is the most direct way we can help you.”
More than 60,000 Hoosiers have applied for FEMA assistance, and about 34,000 have received help, Dragoo said. Federal assistance has topped $142 million, while the state has disbursed more than $32 million through its disaster relief fund.
Braun also said a statewide debris removal effort has cleared 80,000 cubic yards across more than 30 communities.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawsuit against vape retailers awaits hearing as lawmakers mull industry regulations
text:
The New Mexico Department of Justice in March of 2026 sued retailers and distributors of vape and nicotine products, alleging that colorful packaging and flavors including strawberry kiwi, raspberry lemon and pomegranate berry mint were meant to indirectly market to children. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)In a public hearing on Tuesday, New Mexico state Sen. Martin Hickey (D-Albuquerque) likened the state’s ongoing litigation against vape retailers and distributors to the decades-old struggle to convict Al Capone and his gang of “untouchables.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While prosecutors couldn’t successfully try the notorious bootlegger for selling alcohol during the prohibition era, they were able to convict him of tax evasion and send him to prison. Hickey, who chairs the Legislature’s interim Tobacco Settlement Revenue Oversight Committee, said that’s not very different from the New Mexico Department of Justice’s litigation strategy of suing Circle K, Alon and several other companies under the state’s consumer protection law for allegedly contributing to outsized rates of nicotine addiction among New Mexico’s youth.
NMDOJ has already proved it’s a workable strategy by using the same law to win a string of high-profile victories in court against the social media giant Meta, Hickey said.
Moreover, “in both that suit and in this one, these are selling products that are clearly hurtful to youth,” he said.
Defendants in the March NMDOJ lawsuit against the vaping retailers and distributors recently asked a judge to dismiss the case. New Mexico Department of Justice attorneys rebutted their request and are awaiting a hearing before Judge Bryan Biedscheid, who previously presided over two of the state’s cases against Meta.
The NMDOJ’s case alleges that retailers such as gas stations sell vapes and e-cigarettes in colorful packaging and bold flavors that appeal to children in “blatant disregard for public health and safety.”
New Mexico Democrats propose revamped consumer protection, digital safety laws

It seeks damages under the state’s Unfair Practices Act, a late-1960s consumer protection law that caps penalties at $5,000 per violation. Torrez, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and state Rep. Linda Serrato (D-Santa Fe) recently announced plans to attempt to overhaul the law in the 2027 legislative session. One proposed change would increase penalties to $50,000 per violation, which could increase further when companies target children, people with disabilities or people under a guardianship.
Studies have found that use of vapes and e-cigarettes during childhood and adolescence can lead to adverse health effects, such as increased suicide attempts. Studies have also found that young people who use e-cigarettes believe they’re a healthier alternative to traditional cigarettes, despite the common presence of chemicals like formaldehyde.
Hickey updated his fellow committee members on the litigation during a daylong hearing at the University of New Mexico Comprehensive Cancer Center in Albuquerque. Throughout the day, state lawmakers discussed how they could pursue legislation in the upcoming legislative session to further hold the industry to account.
They discussed whether to seek an increase to the state’s taxes on tobacco products. On cigarettes, the tax is currently $2 per pack, slightly below the national average of $2.05, but it varies significantly for other products. Taxes on e-cigarettes, for example, vary on how much liquid the cartridge contains.
Other potential ideas included limiting how these companies can market to young people by restricting what flavors stores can sell, and implementing greater taxes on alternative nicotine products, such as pouches. Currently, public health law consultant Megan Boelter told the committee, nicotine pouches are taxed at 25% of the manufacturer’s price, but that only applies to tobacco-derived nicotine. If the nicotine is synthetic, she said, it isn’t taxed.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan No Kings rallies aim to translate protest energy into early voting push
text:
Thousand of protesters demonstrated against the administration of President Donald Trump on Saturday at the "No Kings" rallies in Detroit on Oct. 18, 2025. (Photo By Erick Diaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)Organizers of the No Kings movement in Michigan are shifting their focus from street demonstrations to the ballot box, planning dozens of local rallies, marches and community gatherings Saturday, to encourage residents to vote early in the November election.
The latest mobilization, dubbed “No Kings 4: Vote Early,” will include events across Michigan, with organizers emphasizing voter registration, early voting and helping residents understand their voting options. The gatherings are part of a nationwide effort that organizers said includes thousands of events. They encouraged residents to find local events at NoKings.org
“This is not necessarily a numbers game when it comes to this particular protest,” said Eliza Sokoli, a senior at Oakland Early College in Farmington Hills and founder of the Teen Action Network, a youth-led chapter of the Indivisible progressive political movement. “This gathering is about getting neighbors to see neighbors, and to go and get them out and vote and use their voices.”
Sokoli noted that while she is not yet 18 and cannot actually cast a ballot in this election, she said it was important to still make her voice heard for those who will be voting.
“The American Dream is broken for this next generation,” Sokoli said. “We’re crushed with student debt, if we can even afford to go to college at this point … The price of everything has skyrocketed. It affects everybody, regardless if you’re like me going to the shawarma place after school or you’re an adult paying their rent.”
Eliza Sokoli, a senior at Oakland Early College in Farmington Hills and founder of the Teen Action Network, speaking on Oct. 13, 2026, during an online press conference promoting No Kings rallies in Michigan, set for Oct. 17, 2026. (Screenshot)
The Michigan Freedom Coalition initially announced 75 events in a news release, while speakers at Tuesday’s news conference said the number had grown to 78, including in Grand Rapids, Lansing, Traverse City, Bay City, Saginaw, Muskegon, Battle Creek, Canton and Ferndale.
While previous demonstrations have drawn large crowds protesting President Donald Trump’s administration and its policies, organizers said this time their emphasis is on turning that energy into civic participation ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
“It’s moving from protest to power,” Ryan Bates, executive director of End Gun Violence Michigan, said. 
Bates, who was serving as the press conference moderator, described the goal of the mobilization as one of motivation for voters to turn dissatisfaction into action. 
“We’ve convinced the country that there is an urgent danger to our democracy, and it’s time to move beyond standing with a sign and using our power as voters to try and protect our freedom,” Bates said.
Despite the explicitly anti-Trump framing, organizers insist the events themselves will be nonpartisan and will not feature political candidates, although they said elected officials may appear in their official capacities with a focus on voters rather than individual campaigns.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Emily Busch of the Michigan Freedom Coalition said the movement was responding to what she described as threats to democratic institutions, civil liberties and economic security under the Trump administration. She cited immigration enforcement, restrictions affecting universities and the news media, government data collection, health care costs and the administration’s trade policies.
“I’m calling on every Michigander to join us at No Kings: Vote Early events,” Busch said. “We’re still marching, but this time, we’re marching to the polls.”
Busch said she became involved in political organizing after her son was inside Oxford High School during the Nov. 30, 2021, mass shooting that left four of his classmates dead. She said the experience taught her that institutions intended to protect people only work when people actively defend them.
“I got into it because I watched what happens when people in power stop answering to the people they serve,” Busch said. “And that’s exactly what’s happening in this country right now. That’s why No Kings matters, and that’s why we’re all here.”
Angela Davenport, executive director of Voting Access for All Coalition, emphasized that Michigan residents have several ways to register and cast ballots. She said eligible residents can register in person at their city or township clerk’s office through Election Day, Nov. 3, with proof of residency.
The deadline to register online or by mail is Oct. 19, she said. Statewide early in-person voting is scheduled for Oct. 24 through Nov. 1, although some communities may begin earlier. Voters also can request and complete absentee ballots through their local clerks.
Davenport also urged residents not to assume that a criminal record disqualifies someone from voting.
“In Michigan, if you are not currently serving a sentence in jail or prison, you can vote,” she said, adding that people on probation or parole retain their voting rights. People held in county jails while awaiting arraignment, trial or sentencing also remain eligible, she said.
Angela Davenport, executive director of Voting Access for All Coalition, speaking on Oct. 13, 2026, during an online press conference promoting No Kings rallies in Michigan, set for Oct. 17, 2026. (Screenshot)
Davenport said misinformation and a lack of access to accurate information can prevent eligible residents from exercising their rights.
“Having a record does not mean that you lose your say in the decisions that affect your life,” she said.
During a question-and-answer session, organizers were asked what they hoped to accomplish that differed from previous No Kings demonstrations and whether they expected voters to change their minds about candidates ahead of the midterm election.
Organizers said they were not endorsing candidates or targeting voters based on their choices in past elections. Instead, they want to reach people who have not participated before, including young people newly eligible to vote.
“The battle is between the voting booth and the couch,” Bates said. “We need to beat the couch, if we’re gonna save this democracy.”

name: Delaware
title: Brad Jones Named General Manager of Delaware Blue Coats
text:
The Philadelphia 76ers have named Brad Jones general manager of the Delaware Blue Coats, placing an experienced NBA G League executive in charge of the organization’s Wilmington-based developmental affiliate. Image created with AI on 10/13
Former NBA G League basketball affairs executive takes over Delaware’s basketball operations as the Blue Coats prepare to open the 2026-27 season Nov. 6 in Wilmington.
WILMINGTON, Del. — The Philadelphia 76ers have named Brad Jones general manager of the Delaware Blue Coats, placing an experienced NBA G League executive in charge of the organization’s Wilmington-based developmental affiliate.
Jones will also serve as a 76ers pro scout. He becomes the seventh executive to lead the Blue Coats’ basketball operations department during the program’s 14-year history.
Jones spent the past eight years working in the NBA G League office, most recently as basketball affairs and player personnel lead. His responsibilities included player personnel, contracts, transactions and other basketball operations matters.
“Brad possesses a tremendous knowledge of the game and has natural leadership capabilities and a wealth of experience that will position him well as the next Blue Coats general manager,” 76ers President of Basketball Operations Mike Gansey said in the team’s announcement. “He’s a great addition to our organization and well respected throughout the league. We’re happy to have him on our side.”
Jones helped assemble the NBA G League United team that won the 2026 FIBA Intercontinental Cup championship in Beijing this summer.
Experience From the NBA and G League
Before joining the G League office, Jones worked as a consultant for USA Basketball after spending eight seasons in scouting and video positions with the Orlando Magic.
His time in Orlando also overlapped with current 76ers executive Jameer Nelson, who played for the Magic and previously served as general manager of the Blue Coats.
Jones earned a law degree from Florida Coastal School of Law and a master’s degree from the University of Florida.
He succeeds Ariana Andonian, who left the Blue Coats last month to become general manager of the WNBA’s Los Angeles Sparks.
Blue Coats Promote Marchesani
The organization also promoted CJ Marchesani to assistant general manager of the Blue Coats.
Marchesani spent the previous four seasons working in the 76ers scouting department. Before joining the Sixers organization, he served as director of recruiting for AMR Talent Agency.
The personnel moves come as the Blue Coats continue their role as a development program for the 76ers while competing independently for an NBA G League championship.
Season Begins Nov. 6
Delaware will open its 2026-27 season with back-to-back home games against the Capital City Go-Go on Friday, Nov. 6, and Saturday, Nov. 7, at Chase Fieldhouse in Wilmington. Sixteen of the Blue Coats’ 24 home games are scheduled for weekends this season.
The Blue Coats won the 2022-23 NBA G League championship and previously captured the 2021 Winter Showcase championship.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Michele Tafoya shrugs off Trump endorsement in close Senate race in Minnesota
text:
Republican Minnesota Senate candidate Michele Tafoya unveils a five-point public safety plan with law enforcement leaders at a news conference on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Michele Tafoya just got what most Republican candidates crave more than anything: President Donald Trump’s endorsement.
She demurred.
“I heard about that,” Tafoya said when asked about it Tuesday. “Look, this campaign is about bringing all Minnesotans together, whether they voted for President Trump or whether they voted for Kamala Harris.”
Was it a surprise to her?
“Most of the things that the president says are a surprise to somebody,” said Tafoya, who had called a press conference to talk about a public safety plan following a string of suburban shootings.
Tafoya’s tepid response to the endorsement reflects Trump’s toxicity in a state still reeling from his deadly immigration crackdown. Tafoya, a former NFL TV sideline reporter and conservative podcaster, has tried to balance her party’s allegiance to the president with his deep unpopularity in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican senator since 2002.
Tafoya did not acknowledge the endorsement on social media or in news releases, while her opponent seized on it. Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan posted a clip on social media of Trump telling supporters at a rally in Ohio on Monday that “you have to vote for Michele Tafoya” and then followed it up with a press release.
“She supported his war in Iran, she’s with him on his tariffs, his ICE and mass deportation agenda, and his attacks on abortion rights. She’s even defended January 6 rioters who tried to overturn a free and fair election for him,” Flanagan campaign spokesperson Lexi Byler said in a statement.
Tafoya pushed back on the ICE and mass deportation charge Tuesday, saying she’s the granddaughter of immigrants and the mother of an adopted Colombian-born daughter, and that she supports both law and order and the nation’s legacy of immigration.
Still, her Trump tightrope walk has included some flips and flops.
In 2022, she publicly asked Trump not to run again. Then she supported his candidacy and said she would be “honored” to have his support in her bid for Senate. Tafoya’s campaign ads describe her as a pro-abortion rights Republican and independent voice, but in fundraising messages she’s asked donors for their support to protect the “President’s Senate majority.”
Republicans are bullish on Tafoya because of her sharp television presence, high name recognition and moderate views on abortion as well as Flanagan’s weakness on fraud in state-run safety-net programs. (Though national Republicans are apparently not confident enough to put real money behind her.)
Tafoya worked in a couple of barbs at Trump and his administration in her prepared remarks on Tuesday at the Capitol, where she unveiled a five-point public safety plan alongside leaders from the Minnesota Police and Peace Officers Association, the state’s largest advocacy group for police officers.
The plan was a response to a string of shootings by young Somali Americans, and the arrest of a Somali American teenager for trying to conspire with a terrorist organization to carry out an attack at the Mall of America.
Point one: Say the phrase “Somali gang violence,” because, she said, “a politician who cannot even say the phrase Somali gang violence will never fix this problem.”
But don’t say it like Trump. Tafoya said Trump’s recent call for Minnesota to “fight back” against Somali immigrants was “not appropriate.”
Two of her public safety plan points address issues exacerbated by the Trump administration: working to improve cooperation between local, state and federal law enforcement as well as speed up federal prosecutions.
On improving coordination she said, “Our local officers should not be big-footed by the feds like we saw with ICE during Kristi Noem’s Metro Surge disaster, but we can get them more support.”
The comment was a reference to federal law enforcement blocking state investigators from the scene of the killing of Alex Pretti by Border Patrol agents and withholding evidence in the killing of Renee Good by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent during the incursion of some 3,000 federal agents to the state last winter.
Meanwhile, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minneapolis has seen a wave of career prosecutors resigning in protest over the Trump administration’s directives during Operation Metro Surge, including to open an investigation into Good’s widow.
She didn’t answer how she’d help rebuild the office.
“It’s a fair question, and I just met someone who just took a job there, so I think they’re working on filling those spaces,” Tafoya said.
Tafoya received the enthusiastic endorsement of law enforcement over Flanagan.
Dave Titus, executive director of the Minnesota Police and Peace Officers Association, said they’ve had more conversations with Tafoya than with Flanagan, even though Flanagan’s two terms in office included numerous public safety crises, such as the protests and riots following the murder of George Floyd.
“Regardless of one’s political party affiliation, we endorse candidates that are public safety-minded, support our mission, and are driven to assist us in making Minnesota a safer place,” he said.
Titus declined to say whether the organization would make an endorsement in the gubernatorial race. The association previously backed Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s campaigns for Senate.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Civil rights group loses effort to block Ocean County voter residency probe
text:
A state Superior Court judge rejected the ACLU’s argument that an investigation into the residency of some Bay Head voters is illegal. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A state judge refused Tuesday to block the Ocean County Board of Elections’ investigation into the voting eligibility of 37 voters registered in Bay Head.
Superior Court Judge Robert Lougy rejected the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey’s claim that the probe was a partisan effort to disenfranchise Democrats and unaffiliated voters there. The ACLU had sought an injunction on behalf of three of the voters targeted as well as the League of Women Voters, saying the board “bombarded” the voters last month with intimidating letters demanding proof of residency and threatening criminal sanctions if they failed to cooperate.
“This was bullying through bureaucracy,” ACLU-NJ attorney Liza Weisberg said.
But Deputy Attorney General Mark Gulbranson, who represents the board and its Republican chairman George Gilmore, insisted the board has the duty and authority to investigate all voter challenges regardless of any partisan motives the challenger might have.
“The board is keenly aware of how important the right to vote is,” Gulbranson said.
But the board also “has a very clear, unambiguous statutory duty to verify voter eligibility,” he added.
The legal fight stemmed from a list that Dennis Shaning, the chair of Bay Head’s all-Republican borough council, sent the board in August of Democratic and unaffiliated voters registered to vote in Bay Head whose tax bills get mailed to addresses outside the borough. Shaning, who excluded similarly situated Republicans from his list, urged the board to consider removing the listed Democrats and unaffiliated voters from the borough’s voter rolls.
Gilmore, who’s also the longtime chairman of the county’s Republican organization, then sent letters to those voters directing them to complete a “domicile questionnaire,” advising them to provide additional proof of residency and attend a board meeting, and warning they might be deemed ineligible to vote in the Nov. 3 election.
The ACLU asked Gilmore to stop the board’s probe, and when he refused, the group sued Gilmore and the board last Thursday.
Gulbranson noted that Shaning wasn’t listed as a defendant, so his motivations were irrelevant.
“Regardless of whether the Shaning letter was partisan, the board treats all complaints regarding registered voters’ eligibility the same,” he said.
He noted the effort already has resulted in three of the targeted voters voluntarily removing themselves from voter rolls because they no longer live in Bay Head. He denied the board bombarded voters with letters, saying they instead sent them to all addresses on file to ensure they were received.
“The board sends letters via certified and regular mail to every address it has for the challenged voter, precisely because it recognizes how important the right to vote is,” Gulbranson said.
In a 37-page opinion issued Tuesday, Lougy wrote that the ACLU failed to show irreparable harm, a requirement for an injunction.
He noted that state law doesn’t empower the board to outright purge voters it suspects are ineligible, instead allowing it only to put them on a challenge list maintained by a county’s election superintendent. Challenge-list voters denied a ballot can fight for their right to vote in state court, he added.
He conceded Gilmore’s letter “is susceptible to harsh or less harsh readings” but also found it “truthful” and largely a “request for information.”
“The Legislature has charged the Board with maintaining current voter rolls, investigating complaints, and applying the challenge list procedures. These critical functions outweigh any incidental burden on plaintiffs for having to fill out a questionnaire,” Lougy wrote.
Weisberg said the ACLU is disappointed in the decision but said the lawsuit has produced “important results.”
“At today’s hearing, the Board clarified its position and, contrary to the implication of its letter to the voters and certain public statements, it will not be making any decisions about voters’ eligibility at today’s meeting, nor at any point requiring the challenged voters to use provisional ballots. The Board also confirmed that having a tax bill mailed outside of Bay Head does not by itself make a voter ineligible to vote in Bay Head,” she said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Reykdal opposes federal tax credit program, urges gov to reject
text:
Washington State Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal discussed financial challenges facing public schools on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)The leader of Washington state public schools says the state should not join a federal tax credit program that would fund K-12 education. 
Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal views the tax credit as a way to expand school choice options without closing funding gaps for public schools. 
“Washington cannot in good faith participate,” Reykdal, who leads the nonpartisan state Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction, wrote in an Oct. 9 letter to Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson.
“This entire tax scheme will add significant federal debt, and that means more cuts to public education and programs in future years,” he added. 
Ferguson has yet to decide whether Washington will participate in the tax credit program. His office is reviewing new program rules released by the U.S. Department of Treasury last week, according to Brionna Aho, his communications director. 
Meanwhile, a growing movement of bipartisan supporters are urging Ferguson to join. 
Arne Duncan, who served as the U.S. secretary of education under President Barack Obama called the program a “moral obligation,” last month during a panel hosted by the Washington Policy Center. 
Thirty-one states have opted into the Education Freedom Tax Credit program, which is open to any state whose governor approves participation. While the program is widely adopted by Republican-held states, some Democratic-strongholds, including Colorado, Virginia, and more recently New York, are trickling in. 
Under the program, beginning in January, individuals can claim a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit of up to $1,700 for donations to certain nonprofits called scholarship-granting organizations. For married couples, credits can be up to $3,400. 
The contributions are meant to fund K-12 scholarships, primarily at private schools, though the scholarships also cover tutoring, books, supplies and disability services for public school students. 
The scholarships could reach a wide range of students with varying socioeconomic backgrounds. Eligible students are those whose household income is not greater than 300% of an area’s median income. 
The deadline for governors to approve participation is Jan. 1, 2027.
The Washington Student Success Coalition, an advocacy group whose members include Microsoft, the Seattle Metro Chamber, the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce and several educational associations, say the program would strongly benefit public schools. 
The program has been estimated to bring in $1.5 billion to Washington state if 30% of taxpayers contributed the full amount, according to the Democrats for Education Reform, a national advocacy group leading the push for states to adopt the tax credit.
“Superintendent Reykdal has repeatedly argued that Washington schools lack the resources to provide tutoring, afterschool programs, and other essential educational services,” Jill Jackson, managing partner of public affairs for Monument Advocacy, a public relations firm hired by the coalition, wrote in an email to the Standard. 
“Yet when Congress creates a new opportunity to help fund those very services – to the tune of $1 billion per year – he recommends that Washington turn it down,” she added. 
One of the core reasons Reykdal opposes the program is because states would have limited authority on the rules they could impose on scholarship-granting organizations, or SGOs. States could not limit scholarships to students from poor households, Reykdal said. 
Jackson says Reykdal is overlooking a key distinction: SGOs could impose their own restrictive criteria, for example limiting private school access.
“Washington organizations can focus on public-school students, struggling readers, mathematics tutoring, lower-income communities,” she wrote in an email.
Another reason for Reykdal’s opposition: it would cost the state money. State employees would be required to confirm that every SGO meets federal requirements. The U.S. Treasury Department estimated that at least 10 hours of state work per SGO would be required each year. 
“The costs borne by states to operate this program do not accompany any authority to actually regulate the program and ensure taxpayer money is used responsibly,” he said. 
Jackson argued that state resources needed to implement the program would be minimal compared to the amount in scholarships for students. 
On Tuesday, Reykdal called on the governor and the Legislature to fulfill their “paramount duty” of investing in public schools in a Seattle Times opinion editorial. 
The situation for public schools, he said, “continues to grow more dire.”
The review of the federal rules at the governor’s office “will take some time,” Aho said. “When the governor makes a decision, he will announce it.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: ‘Gus the Bus’ to provide free food at Lamprey Health in Newmarket
text:
Gather, a Portsmouth-based food pantry, is bringing its fresh food bus, nicknamed “Gus the Bus,” to Lamprey Health Care’s community health center in Newmarket.
The bus will be at the facility’s parking lot — 207 South Main Street in Newmarket — every other Thursday from 11:30 a.m. until 12:30 p.m. starting Oct. 15. The bus will provide free food to Lamprey patients and community members who show proof of New Hampshire or Maine residence or employment, Gather said. No financial information is required. The bus, which already operates in Portsmouth, Somersworth, Rochester and other towns and cities, provides fresh produce, dairy, meats and dry goods in an effort to address hunger and food insecurity in the region.
This comes amid growing food insecurity in New Hampshire. Feeding America, a national nonprofit, reports that 11.7% of New Hampshire residents were food insecure in 2024, the most recent data available. In 2023 that number was 10.7%. The problem is more severe among children. Child food insecurity rose in the state from 14.4% in 2023 to 15.5% in 2024. Food pantry and bank officials say they’re confident the problem has only worsened since that data was collected.
Meanwhile, the federal government has rolled back its investments in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP or food stamps. In 2025, Congress’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act implemented a number of cost-saving measures to the country’s marquee food assistance program. It decreased the share of program funding the federal government will cover, capped future rate increases at the rate of inflation and made work requirements stricter, among other things. Food pantry and bank officials worry these changes will worsen the problem.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV gives $2 million in Rural Health Transformation funds to community health centers
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey speaks to an audience in Bluefield, West Virginia, about the Rural Health Transformation Program in November 2025.  (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)The state of West Virginia is distributing more than $2 million in federal Rural Health Transformation program funds to community health centers in the state, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Tuesday.
The state will give $1,656,432 to the West Virginia Primary Care Association and $500,000 to the Monongahela Valley Association of Health Centers. 
“Community health centers are a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of West Virginians, especially in rural areas where access to healthcare can be a challenge,” Morrisey said in a news release. “These investments will give our healthcare providers better tools to spend less time on paperwork and more time caring for patients. That’s how we improve health outcomes, strengthen our communities, and help more West Virginians get healthy and return to the workforce.”
The money will “improve coordination among providers, strengthen data sharing and modernize clinic operations to deliver more efficient and accessible healthcare,” Morrisey’s office said in the news release. 
The West Virginia Primary Care Association will support the phased development of a statewide clinically integrated network that will deploy shared tools for care coordination, population health management, data analytics and quality reporting, creating a foundation for future statewide expansion, the news release says. The network will begin with 16 community health center organizations serving 40 West Virginia counties. 
The Monongahela Valley Association of Health Centers will “execute an operational transformation designed to significantly improve healthcare access, operational efficiency, care coordination and long-term health outcomes across its clinic locations in Fairmont, Shinnston and Mannington,” the release says. 
West Virginia received $199 million in federal dollars from the Rural Health Transformation Program for 2026. The five-year program from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending. 
The program aims to “empower states to transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable healthcare systems that expand access, enhance quality of care and improve outcomes for patients,” according to CMS.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware school board leaders unite to tackle literacy, accountability and school funding
text:
First State Educate’s new advisory structure is intended to help the organization develop resources that support those responsibilities. Image created on 10/13 using AI.
First State Educate launches 12-member advisory board to strengthen local school governance, improve student achievement and help districts navigate major changes in Delaware public education.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News.
WILMINGTON, Del. — As Delaware schools face growing expectations to improve student literacy, demonstrate academic progress and adapt to a new school funding system, First State Educate has assembled 12 current and former school board leaders to help strengthen the effectiveness of local school governance.
The nonprofit organization, whose mission is to empower school boards to improve public education, announced the formation of its new Advisory Board, bringing together representatives from all three Delaware counties with experience in education, business and community leadership.
The initiative comes at a significant time for Delaware public education, as state leaders advance changes to school funding and accountability while placing renewed emphasis on improving student outcomes.
First State Educate Executive Director Julia Keleher said the advisory group will help ensure the organization’s programs and resources reflect the practical challenges confronting local school boards.
“First State Educate has launched the Advisory Board to inform and ground our work; this esteemed group of Delaware leaders will ensure we are serving our state and schools in the most relevant, impactful ways possible,” Keleher said.
School boards play a critical role in student success
Although school boards often receive public attention for budgets, policies and controversial decisions, their responsibilities extend to establishing district priorities, evaluating superintendents and monitoring whether schools are delivering measurable academic results.
Delaware Secretary of Education Cindy Marten welcomed the initiative, emphasizing that those who serve on school boards should have a voice in developing the resources intended to help them succeed.
“School boards have an enormous responsibility. They set the direction for their districts, hire and hold superintendents accountable, and make decisions that directly affect students and classrooms,” Marten said.
“If we want board members to be effective, we need to understand what they need to succeed. I’ve always believed that if you want to know what works, ask the people doing the work.”
Marten said involving board members in shaping training and resources could improve the quality and relevance of those programs.
“The strongest solutions are built with people, not simply for them,” she said.
Literacy, accountability and funding top the agenda
The new Advisory Board will focus initially on five areas that could influence how Delaware school districts allocate resources, measure success and respond to community expectations.
Improving literacy outcomes: Members will help identify ways local school boards can support district literacy goals and align their priorities with the Delaware Department of Education’s strategic plan. This includes examining how board decisions about curriculum, instructional resources and student performance can contribute to improved reading achievement.
Strengthening academic accountability: The group will help school boards prepare for Delaware’s evolving performance and accountability framework, including the use of student achievement data to establish expectations, monitor progress and support continuous improvement.
The Delaware Department of Education is developing a School Performance and Support Framework intended to identify struggling schools earlier and provide increasingly intensive assistance when needed. The framework remains in draft form, with public feedback open through Nov. 1.


Delaware Department of Education


Preparing for school funding reform: Delaware’s proposed hybrid funding model represents a substantial change in how public education resources would be distributed and managed. Advisory Board members will help identify the guidance school boards need to understand funding decisions and oversee the use of public money.
The state’s Public Education Funding Commission has recommended a model combining core staffing support with additional resources based on student needs and operational expenses. The proposal also emphasizes transparency and accountability for how education dollars are spent.
Connecting employers and schools: Through initiatives such as the Delaware Education Performance Partnership, First State Educate intends to encourage greater engagement between school leaders and the business community. The goal is to strengthen connections between education, workforce needs and student opportunities.
Expanding access to school board resources: Members will provide feedback on First State Educate’s Knowledge Hub, an online resource designed to connect board members, parents and community leaders with information, tools and professional learning opportunities.
Together, these priorities reflect a broader challenge facing Delaware education: ensuring that increased resources, changing policies and new expectations translate into measurable improvements for students.
Bringing local experience to statewide discussions
First State Educate said the Advisory Board was intentionally designed to represent geographic, professional and community diversity, including newly elected and longtime school board members.
The organization also sought perspectives from individuals who have served in leadership positions and those with professional backgrounds outside education.
Patricia “Patty” Maull, a Cape Henlopen school board member, said the advisory group provides an opportunity to ensure statewide initiatives reflect the realities of local governance.
“The voice of local school board members is essential to shaping strong, community-focused educational leadership,” Maull said.
“I’m honored to join the FSE Advisory Board to continue to help ensure the voice and perspective of local governance remain front and center.”
The board will provide ongoing feedback on First State Educate’s research, training and initiatives, identify emerging challenges and recommend improvements to the organization’s work.
The advisory group will guide First State Educate’s efforts rather than replace the authority or responsibilities of locally elected school boards.

A greater emphasis on results
The launch of the Advisory Board also comes as Delaware policymakers reconsider how schools are evaluated and how education funding can be connected more closely to student needs and outcomes.
The state’s existing school accountability system measures academic achievement, student growth and other indicators of school success. Those measures provide information school boards can use to identify areas needing improvement and evaluate whether district strategies are working.
For local school board members, the challenge is translating that information into effective governance — asking the right questions, establishing clear expectations and evaluating whether educational investments are producing results.
First State Educate’s new advisory structure is intended to help the organization develop resources that support those responsibilities.
Its success will ultimately depend on whether the guidance and training provided help school board members make better-informed decisions, strengthen oversight and support improved academic outcomes.
For parents and taxpayers, those results may prove more important than the creation of another statewide advisory group.
