name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Ethics complaint over NJ school board member’s Facebook posts dismissed
text:
A state ethics board dismissed a complaint against a school board member accused of violating rules by soliciting feedback from residents on Facebook. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey School Ethics Commission has dismissed a complaint against an Alloway School Board member, rejecting allegations that she violated ethics rules when soliciting resident feedback on hypothetical school tax increases on social media.
The commission ruled there is insufficient evidence to lead a reasonable person to believe Gail Nazarene made improper promises, impermissibly directed school personnel, or disclosed confidential information when she asked about hypothetical tax increases in three Facebook posts.
Greg Greubel is a senior attorney at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which represented Nazarene in a legal dispute in federal court about the commission’s investigation of her.
“New Jersey did the right thing this time, and we are grateful Gail’s case brought more attention to the First Amendment rights of school board members. But this attack on Gail’s free speech rights never should’ve happened in the first place,” he said.
The complaint’s dismissal comes nearly a year after Nazarene sued state education officials, arguing the commission’s interpretation of the School Ethics Act impermissibly chills speech by exposing school board officials to legal sanctions for public statements.
Sara Cobb, a since-departed member of the Salem County township’s school board, filed an ethics complaint against Nazarene last year, alleging Nazarene violated ethics rules that bar personal promises that could compromise a school board and require members to keep confidential information that could injure the school or individuals, among others.
The complaint was spurred by social media posts where Nazarene asked residents for feedback on school tax increases ranging between 9% and 30%. After criticism from another board member and Alloway’s chief school administrator, Nazarene appended disclaimers to some posts that said she was asking in her capacity as a private citizen or not on the board’s behalf.
A federal judge dismissed Nazarene’s suit last month, finding she lacks standing because the School Ethics Commission had not ruled on her complaint, which it could not weigh while her lawsuit was ongoing.
Anyone can file a complaint with the school ethics commission, the judge reasoned, and the low bar meant any chilling of speech was self-imposed unless the commission moved to sustain a charge.
Still, the saga over Nazarene’s speech has spurred legislation that would bar officials from reading the School Ethics Act in a way that limits a board member’s speech on matters of public concern, including those related to schools they oversee.
The bill’s sponsor, Sen. Declan O’Scanlon (R-Monmouth), said the commission had issued a tortured interpretation of the law that resulted in the muzzling of elected officials.
“The resources that are wasted on this crap — it is outrageous,” he said. “Nothing like this exists for municipal officials, and it shouldn’t exist for school board officials. My bill needs to pass, and this is another great example of why the bill is needed.”

name: VTDigger
title: Newport mayor strives to revitalize city after years of struggle
text:
Newport Mayor Rick Ufford-Chase on Monday, October 5, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
NEWPORT — Rick Ufford-Chase hears what people say about Newport.
He sees what’s come to be known as “the pit,” an empty, fenced-in block of space that was once supposed to be a hotel before developers were caught in the EB-5 scandal, the biggest instance of fraud in Vermont’s history. He has witnessed a constant cycle of hopeful businesses shutter their doors on Main Street. So he knows how the city looks from the outside. 
But Newport’s mayor recalls a different downtown atmosphere when he visited in the 1960s and ‘70s, one with two vibrant dance halls, diverse shopping and restaurants. He also admires the beauty of the lakeside community and its vast opportunities for outdoor adventures.
The years have not been kind to Newport, Ufford-Chase admits. Even before the EB-5 scandal left an abandoned lot in the middle of downtown, Newport’s streets had started to empty.
Now, the city of about 4,400 people is trying to rebuild. In addition to filling the pit, the city needs to heal relationships with its Canadian neighbors and dramatically increase affordable housing, while fighting labor shortages in the dairy and construction industries. And one of its major employers, Galvion Inc., recently attracted controversy for supplying helmets to ICE operations. 
All of this work needs to happen without increasing the strain on Newport’s taxpayers, Ufford-Chase said.
As “the pit” nears new possibilities with an upcoming land sale, Ufford-Chase faces the same question every day.
 “How do you bring a city back to life?” he said.
A slow decline
When Ufford-Chase, 62, and his wife moved to the Northeast Kingdom from Rockland County, New York in 2020, they found a vastly different Newport than the one he remembered.
Growing up, Newport was the closest city to Ufford-Chase’s family home in Lowell. He lived full-time in Pennsylvania, but his mother was a fifth-generation Kingdom resident.
The family stopped in Newport during every visit.
“This was really quite a thriving place when I was a kid,” Ufford-Chase said. “This was the spot where everybody in the surrounding area came to do their shopping.”

Newport Mayor Rick Ufford-Chase on Monday, October 5, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Ufford-Chase spent his early adulthood in the West, attending Colorado College before becoming an immigration advocate in Tucson, Ariz., working with officials and families on the forefront of the border crisis.
“I thought I would go for a year as a volunteer, doing human rights work on the border, and instead I stayed 20 years,” he said.
During his time there, Ufford-Chase said he helped to start an organization called BorderLinks, which worked to help educate people about the border economy and the complicated situation of refugees.
Ufford-Chase and his wife eventually moved to New York state, and began to manage a conference center for the National Presbyterian Church. He continued his advocacy for peace, and was arrested while protesting the Iraq war in 2007.
Conference centers and COVID-19 don’t mix, he said, so they lost their jobs when the pandemic hit.
“We looked at each other and said, ‘Let’s go home to the place we’ve always gone to be with family and vacation,’” Ufford-Chase said. “So it felt very natural for us to come here.”
As Ufford-Chase made his way in the world, Newport’s once-vibrant streets began to struggle, according to Sharon Pare, a city council member who has always lived in Newport.
“I don’t think you can blame anybody because downtowns across the country suffered the same way,” Pare said, referring to the growth of online retail.  “And I think if we blame anybody, we can blame the dot-com era.” 
In the 2010’s, a team of developers came with big promises to build a grand hotel in the heart of Newport, Ufford-Chase said. But the team was caught in the EB-5 scandal — an instance of fraud that took advantage of the federal EB-5 immigrant investor program — and the project was demolished.
“It gave us such hope, that things were going to, you know, take off and bring businesses in,” Pare said. “And then it just kind of all came crashing down.”
Newport was left with a pit stretching for almost a block, where fully grown aspens interlace with dilapidated staircases and building facades.
The Pit in Newport on Monday, October 5, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The land deal, involving the sale of the property to the Northwestern Vermont Development Association which plans to transfer it to the city of Newport or another development partner, which Ufford-Chase hopes will finally fill “the pit” is expected to close this week, he said. But trust between the community and developers still needs to be rebuilt, too, Ufford-Chase said.
“I think almost without exception, people are thrilled that Newport has taken control of this critical piece of our destiny,” Ufford-Chase said in regards to the sale. “So I don’t hear anybody saying, ‘You shouldn’t have done that.’
“I hear a lot of people say, ‘I’ll believe something will happen there when I see it happen.’”
Headwinds from the borders 
Newport faces an unusual set of challenges as a small, remote city, Ufford-Chase said. Newport, located in northern Vermont, is the only city in Orleans County. Its proximity to the Canadian border comes with the presence of ICE in their community, which he said has an impact on both the dairy and construction industries.
Both industries in his area are struggling with labor shortages since many of their employees are afraid to go to work, he said. Orleans County is neck-and-neck with Addison County for second place in total dairy production in Vermont, surpassed only by Franklin County, according to 2024 data from the University of Vermont.
The economic realities of immigration are often overlooked, Ufford-Chase said, although he said he understands the necessity of a secure border.
“On this side of the border, you know, you talk to anybody right now in our area who’s a dairy farmer, Ufford-Chase said, “and they are really, really challenged by the current enforcement strategy here in Vermont, targeting workers from Mexico and other places in Latin America who are keeping our dairy industry alive right now.”
And in order to revitalize the city, Ufford-Chase said the city needs to build. And fast. 

A Canadian Pacific engine pulls cars along the waterfront of Lake Memphramegog in Newport on Monday, October 5, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Housing comes first, he said. 
The Newport City Master Plan Update, written in 2024, by the city and Newport Downtown Development, calls for 410 additional housing units to be built to meet the needs of the city and allow for expansion. Ufford-Chase said this is the goal, but the city must also contend with reality.
“If we build 410 units of housing, it will be nothing short of a miracle,” Ufford-Chase said. “If we built half that, I would think we had done an incredible thing.”
Most of the land has already been developed, he said, so the way to increase housing is to create a denser downtown with more varied types of housing options, such as affordable housing units and housing for seniors. 
To do that, Newport needs construction companies to invest in the community, a task complicated by the ICE presence on the Northern border, Ufford-Chase said. Many developers are hesitant to start projects in Newport for fear of being targeted, he added.
“I don’t understand why we would target people,” Ufford-Chase said of construction and dairy workers, many of whom are authorized to work in the U.S. “Because we do not have enough labor here to build what we need to build.” 
Newport is also home to Galvion Inc., a company which supplies helmets to ICE agents and U.S. military operations. The company provides essential jobs to the local community, he said. As someone who has spent a long time working as an immigration advocate, Ufford-Chase said it’s a “challenging juxtaposition” for him to face. But he said his duty is to help businesses thrive in the community.
“I feel about that not unlike I feel about a prison, which we also have in our city,” Ufford-Chase said. “Which is, I wish that there were ways that all of us could build an economy that is not dependent on aggressive military and policing behavior.”
The tariffs and trade hostilities between the U.S. and Canada have also had a noticeable effect on Newport, Ufford-Chase said.
“Where we see the impact the most is in our Canadian visitors,” Ufford-Chase said, “because our retail economy here in Newport has depended for years on the visitors who come, and there are very few people willing to come to the United States right now from Canada.”
Local limitations
The other challenge to development is much closer to home, Ufford-Chase said.
Newport has a small taxpayer base, he said. It’s also located in the county with the second highest rate of families below the poverty line in Vermont, according to the National Institute of Health, with neighboring Essex County ranking first. It’s difficult to sustain local services such as police, schools and infrastructure, let alone additional development. 
It’s an issue that came into full focus during a city council meeting last Wednesday, when discussions for the 2028 budget began.

Main Street in Newport on Monday, October 5, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

There’s many unknowns in the community, Pare said in the meeting. The education system is getting more expensive to fund, and the water and sewer plants need repairs.
“I’m a little frightened for everything that’s coming down the pike,” Pare added.
It can be difficult to balance downtown development with taxpayers’ concerns, Pare said, although Newport’s business leaders help by searching for grants and outside funding.
“And I’m often saying, great ideas, wonderful ideas, but you can’t ask the taxpayers to pay for that,” Pare said. “And they all say there’s money out there, you know. We’ve just got to find it and meet the guidelines.”
Ufford-Chase also attracted some controversy during his 2025 unopposed campaign for mayor, when former Mayor Linda Sullivan expressed concerns about a conflict of interest due to his position as executive director of Newport Downtown Development, according to past reporting from VTDigger. 
“We’re going to have to see if Rick can manage the inherent conflicts of holding both positions in a sufficiently transparent way as to assure our residents that his actions as Mayor are consistent with the interests of all of our constituents,” Sullivan wrote.
Ufford-Chase said he fully believed that he could juggle the two positions in an ethical way, although he understood where the concerns were coming from. He added that he reached out to the state’s ethics commission prior to joining the race, who confirmed that it would not be an ethics violation.
Efforts to reach Sullivan for an updated comment before publication were not successful.
There is also a new charter up for vote in Newport this November — the second attempt by the city council to pass a revised charter, Ufford-Chase said. Jay Walsh, a community member, took his complaints about the original amended charter to the Vermont Superior Court, but since the city voted down that version of the charter, Ufford-Chase said the case became a moot point.

Newport Mayor Rick Ufford-Chase on Monday, October 5, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Walsh also has raised complaints about the voting process for the charter, alleging that the changes to the charter should be voted on individually rather than grouped together.
Ufford-Chase and the council have repeatedly dismissed the concerns, and Ufford-Chase added that they have discussed the matter with the city attorneys. 
The revised document clarifies mayoral powers, Ufford-Chase said, but it does not change day-to-day operations. It also increases annual stipends to $5,000 for the mayor, $3,500 for the president of the council, and $3,000 for each member, and sets their compensation to increase as inflation increases.
The path forward
One of Newport’s young entrepreneurs, Dani Grant, who opened a yarn store downtown just a week earlier, attended last Wednesday’s meeting. She said she has recently witnessed energy being poured into Newport’s downtown and she’s learned more about Newport’s evolution through her work at the historical society.
A recent example of this energy is an effort by community members to launch a food co-op.
Grant knew that downtown was the place for her business to be.
“As I go through our archives, I see a lot of pictures of how downtown used to be,” Grant said. “There were so many different shops and so much culture.”
Ufford-Chase knows that reviving the community will not be easy, he said. But on summer evenings, he goes to downtown waterfront concerts on Lake Memphremagog, gazing out over 27 miles of water connecting his city to Canada.
“I sit on the lawn over there and listen to a band and watch the sun go down over the lake. And I think to myself, ‘If I had spent money to buy a plane ticket to Switzerland, I would be no less happy than I am right now.’ 
“And no more happy either.”

name: National
title: ‘Labor guides’ can help dispel myths pregnant women find online
text:
A sign outside a hospital’s maternal-fetal medicine department sets aside parking for patients. A new study suggests that giving “labor guides” to pregnant women helps combat misinformation that an increasing number of patients are getting from social media or artificial intelligence. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline)Providing “labor guides” to pregnant women helps combat misinformation that an increasing number of patients are getting from social media or artificial intelligence, according to a recent study.
Dr. Samuel Melville, a resident-physician in obstetrics and gynecology at Oregon Health & Science University and the lead author of the study, said he frequently hears patients quoting social media or AI when resisting medical interventions, such as inducing the pregnancy with medication to encourage stalled labor.
The study, published in the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine’s journal Pregnancy, found that in a group of about 200 patients, those who received the labor guide reported more satisfaction and a sense of control than those who did not receive it. Initial evidence also showed a potential to improve medical outcomes. Melville’s hospital recently made labor guides available to all patients admitted to its labor and delivery unit.
“What we found with this study was when patients have that autonomy and have that empowerment, they end up doing better,” Melville said. “They’re more satisfied in their labor process.”
Melville noted that trust in the medical community is down since the COVID-19 pandemic, something other researchers have also observed around vaccine hesitancy.
He said many patients falsely believe any kind of intervention will make it more likely they will have to have a cesarean section, major surgery that comes with more risks. But he and his colleagues try to reduce the need for C-sections, he said.
“There’s been a lot of people on social media with limited experience in obstetrics who are counseling folks to not get evidence-based things in their labor to avoid being induced, even when it’s for medically indicated reasons,” said Melville, noting conditions like hypertension and gestational diabetes can precipitate the need for certain interventions. “And those things can oftentimes make patients very hesitant to accept treatment or evidence-based practices.”
False birth control claims are proliferating, survey says

Melville believes the guides have the potential to be revolutionary, for his practice and nationwide if other hospitals adopt similar practices. In the group that got the labor guides, women had a higher rate of vaginal delivery, which corresponded with lower blood loss and better neonatal outcomes.
“Less babies in that group needed resuscitation, which was really exciting,” Melville said, noting the study did not measure the statistical significance of this trend but they will continue to study it as more patients use the labor guides.
He also acknowledged that pregnant patients have valid reasons to be concerned about not being able to consent for medical procedures, some that are based in history. The credited inventor of modern gynecology is J. Marion Sims, who performed gynecological surgeries on enslaved Black women without their permission or pain medication in the 1840s. Much more recently, ProPublica reported, patients have been forced by judges, particularly in Florida, to have C-sections against their will.
Black women especially report racial discrimination and not feeling heard by medical professionals around their labor and birth decisions and have higher rates of complications and deaths nationally.
“As long as human history has been around, we’ve always really oftentimes struggled with consent around the obstetric practice,” Melville said. “I often tell patients when they come in for labor, ‘Our team makes the recommendations, but you make the decisions for your body, and I will never go against the decisions that you make for your body.’ Sometimes my recommendations will be stronger than others.”

title: Upstate hospital building new training center to help address SC’s nursing shortage
text:
AnMed hospital system is building a 30,000-square-foot Education and Innovation Center beside AnMed Medical Center in Anderson, that will provide clinical classroom space for Tri-County Technical College’s expanding nursing program. (Photo courtesy of AnMed)An Anderson hospital is building a center to train more nurses in South Carolina’s Upstate.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Construction is under way on the AnMed Education and Innovation Center, a 30,000-square-foot space beside AnMed Medical Center that will provide clinical classroom space for Tri-County Technical College’s expanding nursing program.
As of last December, South Carolina had about 12,000 fewer nurses than it needed, according to the federal Health Resources and Services Administration. While the state is projected to narrow that gap to 7,250 by 2038, it will still have one of the largest shortages in the country.
Healthcare providers have advertised more than 2,000 nursing job openings in South Carolina in recent months, according to AnMed.
“No one organization can solve this challenge alone,” Tri-County Tech’s President Galen DeHay said in a statement. “It takes strong partnerships between healthcare providers and educational institutions who are willing to invest in the future of our region’s workforce.”
USC Beaufort nursing students to receive financial aid, job placements under $3.8M federal grant

Meanwhile, Tri-County Tech has a waiting list for its nursing program. The school can accept 60 nursing students a semester.
The partnership with AnMed is expected to bump that capacity to 160 students per semester within five years.
The new center, built by AnMed, will have classrooms, a computer lab and two patient simulation labs where students can train on medical-surgical care, critical care, labor and delivery, emergency care, and behavioral health procedures, under the guidance of two AnMed nurses.
Students also will perform their clinical rotations at the hospital and are eligible for paid part-time employment.
“This partnership is about building the future of nursing from within our own community,” Shaunda Trotter, AnMed’s chief nursing officer, said in a statement. “By connecting students directly with our caregivers and clearing their path into practice, we are creating a stronger, more sustainable workforce.”
The hospital system did not say how much it’s investing to build the center, nor did it give a timeline for opening.
SC spending $30M to tackle nursing shortage predicted to be nation’s 7th worst

AnMed already works with multiple colleges in the state to offer training for doctors, bachelor’s degree-level nurses, physical therapists, radiologic technicians and more.
Those students then graduate with an inside track to employment at AnMed, an independent, not-for-profit regional health system covering South Carolina’s Upstate and northeast Georgia.
The hospital system has 648 beds across four hospitals, employing more than 4,000 people, including 742 doctors. And it’s expanding.
In addition to the Anderson hospital, AnMed’s Piedmont campus and freestanding emergency department opened in 2025.
A new campus serving Clemson and Central is under construction.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Feds approve Nebraska’s request to block TANF funds for drugs, psychics, music, porn and more
text:
CEO Steve Corsi of the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services at an inaugural public roundtable of Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen's cabinet. April 20, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The federal government has approved Nebraska’s request to bar temporary financial assistance for tobacco, tattoos, psychic readings, video games and other “inappropriate and nonessential purchases.”
U.S. Assistant HHS Secretary Alex Adams, head of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Administration for Children and Families, approved the request Tuesday, just four days after Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen filed to change Nebraska’s participation in the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families’ Aid to Dependent Children benefits.
“ACF looks forward to partnering with governors and state agencies across the country to develop and implement common-sense EBT (electronic benefit transfer) purchase prohibitions that strengthen program integrity; protect taxpayer dollars from waste, fraud and abuse; and help ensure that TANF assistance is used for lawful, appropriate and effective purposes,” Adams wrote in a Tuesday letter to Pillen.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, seated at center, holds up a newly signed executive order barring state health officials from diverting federal survivor benefits for youths in foster care to cover the costs of their care. Behind the governor are, from left, State Sen. Brian Hardin of Gering, chair of the Legislature’s Health and Human Services Committee; U.S. Deputy Assistant HHS Secretary Martha Verno in the Administration for Children and Families; U.S. Assistant HHS Secretary Alex Adams, head of the federal department’s Administration for Children and Families; Dr. Alyssa Bish, director of the DHHS Division of Children and Family Services; and Nebraska DHHS CEO Steve Corsi, at right. Jan. 27, 2026. (Courtesy of Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services)
TANF helps low-income families with children pay for necessities, such as rent, childcare and utilities, as the families participate in workforce engagement programs. The benefits are provided through a prepaid debit card or direct deposit into a bank account.
Adams, speaking with the Nebraska Examiner on Tuesday, said “hats off” to Pillen for the changes. Other states are in “active conversations” to pursue similar action, Adams added.
“Really is a testament to Governor Pillen’s leadership to be the second state to do this,” Adams said. “I know it will for sure inspire others.”
A Nebraska DHHS spokesperson said that, as of January 2026, 2,856 Nebraska households were on TANF. The average benefit is $470 a month. The average household size is 2.7 people.
Pillen said in a Friday statement: “While Nebraskans are more than willing to help families in need, allowing hard‑earned taxpayer dollars to be spent on tobacco, gambling and video games is completely unacceptable. The inappropriate use of public funds will end at my direction.”
The state DHHS spokesperson said the agency will work toward implementation immediately, including engaging with the state’s ReliaCard vendor to implement the merchant category list. The agency will have a firmer timeline in the coming weeks for completion.
New purchase restrictions
Under federal law and prior Nebraska regulations, the temporary funds could not be used for liquor stores, casino gambling or retail stores providing adult-oriented entertainment.
With the accepted Nebraska TANF plan amendment, the list of prohibited purchases will soon expand to what Pillen’s office described as “inappropriate and nonessential purchases”:

Tobacco, nicotine, vaping and other associated products.
Drugs, intoxicants and related products.
Pornography, sexually explicit materials and adult-oriented goods or services.
Entertainment goods, subscriptions and services including entertainment tickets, theme parks and similar subscriptions or memberships.
Body art, body piercings, cosmetic services and luxury items such as tattoos, spa services and tanning.
Psychic, fortune-telling and divination goods or services.
Political contributions.
Lottery tickets and entries, sports wagers and bets.
Music, video and gaming streaming subscriptions.
Video games, in-game currency, downloadable content and virtual goods.
Jewelry and luxury watches.

Cash withdrawals of such funds will also only be permitted through cash-back transactions at financial institutions or SNAP-authorized retailers.
TANF now 30 years old
This summer, TANF celebrated its 30th anniversary, and HHS brought back some of the original architects, including former House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia and former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson. Adams said part of that conversation was that TANF was successful federally but that the feds wanted to “reinvigorate” state leadership in the program.
“It’s been a tremendous success in reducing caseloads and things like that, but it also, over time, has become a little bit stagnant,” Adams said.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen leads a news conference announcing he will seek changes to how Nebraska oversees the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program for low-income families on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, in the Nebraska State Capitol. (Photo courtesy of Gov. Jim Pillen’s office)
The push was in part to get TANF “back to its basics,” which Adams said is a “temporary bridge” for families to get back into the workforce, not a “catch-all” for the items soon to be banned. Adams said he’s aware of other states in “active conversations” to pursue similar action.
Florida became the first state to request such restrictions in late August.
Asked whether Adams’ agency would pursue congressional changes, Adams said TANF, by design, has always been intended to give states the creative control and flexibility they desire, an approach HHS has continued.
A ‘stigma’ of federal help?
Nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed said Friday that the state’s roughly 2,700 families use the assistance for basic necessities and that Pillen’s action is “an invention that stigmatizes low-wage parents and families in Nebraska who are working hard to get by. And it further shows the depth of disconnection leaders have with real Nebraskans.”
Said the nonprofit: “Today’s efforts from leaders in Nebraska are detached from reality and the opposite of what we need in Nebraska right now.”
Adams said the changes are the opposite and emphasize TANF is a hand up, not a handout.
“I think that takes some of the stigma away,” Adams said. “I think when things are seen as short-term bridges, I think when they’re seen as covering basic, legitimate needs, not superfluous purchases, I think that helps legitimize a program.”

name: VTDigger
title: Behind tinted windows, ICE is watching
text:
This commentary is by Devon Thomas, an ordained minister of the United Church of Christ.
On Monday, Oct. 5, I joined Vermont’s clergy in attending a funeral service at the doors of the Williston Immigration and Customs Enforcement office. This service of remembrance was to recognize 98 people who were killed by ICE or died in its custody, according to a bulletin given out at the service, and to highlight a system of cruelty our governing administration is using against our migrant neighbors and fellow citizens to win political power.
​In our time, we are seeing fellow human beings martyred in America’s culture war. The funeral service at the Williston surveillance center showed me how human atrocity can be permitted in a society such as our United States. It did not halt ICE activities, as it was made clear ICE was aware of and had prepared for our protest. Nor did it grant any meaningful sense of closure and comfort to the families and loved ones of victims.
This service demonstrated the eerie, callous strategy of fear ICE uses to disrupt the lives of millions of Americans and American migrant communities. Because as I stood looking over the shoulders of my esteemed clergy colleagues, hidden behind tinted windows, ICE was there.
As mourners laid down bricks etched with the victims’ names, ICE was there. As mourners wept on the streets, silently, ICE was there. As clergy nailed shut the coffin, ICE was there, apparently unremorseful. The system was ready to do its job. To burst from behind closed doors with crowbars and hammers to smash the painful memorial we put at their feet. They tore apart the coffin and threw the bricks bearing the names of the victims into the back of a pickup truck to be carted off as trash. That trash held the names of 98 people who died, directly or indirectly, because of ICE. The oldest was 85; the youngest was three.

READ MORE

​This funeral was a symbol, and as a person of faith, I believe symbols have meaning. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is part of us, as a people. It was created after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks because we, as a nation, were hurt and scared, and we wanted to protect ourselves. For a time, it seemed this fear brought us together, but it also, subtly, tore us apart. We turned a blind eye to how we treated those we saw as different and a threat. We treated people with different religions, skin tones and cultural backgrounds as dangerous to us, and we turned away when other Americans began to target and violate the sacred commandment to love those whom God loves, as described in Matthew 22:37-39. At first, the violence was open. ICE invaded cities such as Los Angeles and Minneapolis, but now the violence is behind tinted windows, and we become complacent.
​As I write, ICE is organizing surges into migrant communities across the United States. This surge is happening silently, avoiding headlines and the attention of American citizens. It is implementing new and cruel methods of deportation and detention, sending migrants to countries where they have no connections or resources to survive, or confining people far from home in underresourced detention facilities. 
Many Vermonters have never had to fear what lies beyond tinted windows. We have trusted law enforcement to protect us. That sense of security was a privilege many of our neighbors were never afforded. Now it is being stealthily stolen from the rest of us. 
Our migrant neighbors are being targeted first, and it is our moral responsibility to ensure this violence does not go unseen, so that we might avoid the fate of the German theologian Martin Niemöller, who said, “Then they came for me — and there was no one left to speak for me.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia lawmakers ask Flock representative to testify at November meeting
text:
A Flock Safety license plate-reading camera is seen at Colfax Avenue and Franklin Street in Denver, Colorado, on Aug. 5, 2025. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Still unsatisfied with written answers to their questions of Flock Safety, West Virginia lawmakers have requested to hear from the company in person again during an upcoming meeting.  
In a letter dated Monday, members of the House of Delegates Committee on Government Organization asked that a representative of the company — which manufactures artificial intelligence-driven surveillance technology — appear before the committee at 2 p.m. Monday, Nov. 9 during legislative interim meetings. 
Delegates are considering legislation that would put guardrails on Flock Safety, as more and more municipalities in the state consider or contract with the company to purchase and use its surveillance systems, including automatic license plate readers and audio detection equipment. The American Civil Liberties Union says the technology is “tracking, logging and sharing your movements without a warrant.” 
Flock Safety has been the subject of privacy and constitutional concerns nationally. The Institute for Justice has reportedly identified more than 100 incidents of Flock abuse, including law enforcement stalking romantic partners, wrongfully pulling people over and other misconduct. 
Kevin Kane, the director of Government Affairs for Flock, gave a presentation to the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization during August legislative interim meetings. Overall, some lawmakers on the committee were unimpressed with the few answers they received from Kane.
Delegates had given the company until last Friday to sufficiently answer a series of 19 questions on topics ranging from security incidents and unauthorized access to data governance and infrastructure. 
State lawmakers and the company had gone back and forth in letters over the questions after Kane’s presentation. 
In a 10-page response from Flock Safety on Sept. 1, Dan Haley, chief legal officer for Flock, wrote a broad response to each of the five categories of questions, but did not include specific answers to many of the questions lawmakers posed. Lawmakers said many of the company’s answers were not sufficient. 
State lawmakers also took issue with what they said was the company requesting to meet off the record away from public view.
In a letter to lawmakers Friday, Haley wrote that the company did not intend to request a meeting “behind closed doors.” 
“To be explicitly clear: we are proud of our record in West Virginia,” Haley wrote in the letter. “We are proud of our products, our safeguards and our ongoing efforts to continuously improve on each of those fronts. We extended offers to meet, in any setting, with members of the legislature to answer questions, provide a demonstration, and discuss in depth how Flock protects customer data in an effort to further dialogue and understanding. That offer stands. We are committed to continuing to voluntarily answer these questions and are available to meet at your convenience.”
Lawmakers have given the company until Monday, Oct. 19 to confirm they will attend the Nov. 9 meeting and provide the name of the witness expected to testify.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Detroit Democrats challenge Mike Rogers’ touted gains with Black voters in US Senate race
text:
Detroit City Councilmember Denzel McCampbell speaks during a news conference calling out former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers' record on education during his time in the state Legislature — where Rogers was the state Senate majority floor leader between 1999-2000 — on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Screenshot) A handful of Black civic leaders, Detroit elected officials and union heads said Tuesday that Republican U.S. Senate nominee and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers has a record of suppressing Black voting power in the city and across Michigan — an attempt to push back against Rogers’ claims that his Black voter outreach program is producing real results for his campaign against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
State Rep. Tonya Myers Phillips (D-Detroit) and Detroit City Councilmember Denzel McCampbell, along with the leaders of AFT Michigan, Detroit Action and the Detroit Federation of Teachers led the news conference held in Detroit Tuesday morning.
Each said that Rogers has a record dating back to the 1990s of demeaning Black voters and depriving them of real representation. They pointed to his time in the Michigan Senate, where he helped pass a law that the group said took away Detroiters’ right to elect their own school board, which they said resulted in Detroit parents having no vote over their children’s schools. The group, which advocated for Black voters to elect El-Sayed over Rogers, also said that those actions put Detroit schools in financial distress.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I know what students, families, and educators need,” said Terrence Martin, president of AFT Michigan. “They need safe schools. They need trusted teachers, and they need real voice and decisions that shape their futures. Detroit families have too often been denied that voice.”
Martin pointed to Public Act 10 of 1999, a bill co-sponsored by Rogers that originated in the Michigan Senate. He said that the law paved the way for state control of Detroit schools. Martin said that act led to decisions about Detroit schools from people who were not elected by Detroiters and were instead appointed by the state, leaving them unaccountable to the constituents they served. 
Rogers was the state Senate majority floor leader from 1999 to 2000.
“We simply can’t go back. Students felt the effects; their families lost a meaningful say in their schools,” Martin added. “Educators saw communities’ concerns pushed aside, and Detroit’s public school system went from a $100 million operating surplus to a $200 million deficit. PA 10 helped to set in motion years of financial crisis, instability that harmed students and made it harder for schools to provide the resources and reliable learning environments they deserve.”
Lakia Wilson-Lumpkins, president of the Detroit Federation of Teachers, said, “Our history matters.”
Lakia Wilson-Lumpkins, president of the Detroit Federation of Teachers, speaks during a news conference calling out former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers’ record on education during his time in the state Legislature — where Rogers was the state Senate majority floor leader between 1999-2000 — on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Screenshot)
“When our school boards have authority, our voters have authority,” Wilson-Lumpkins said. “Our school boards elect superintendents, and we do not want any reoccurrence of an emergency manager. We are the people, and we rebuke any attempt to remove power from the people.”
Scott Holiday, executive director of Detroit Action, said the group supported El-Sayed and his vision for policies that promote public education “and meaningful community control.”
McCampbell also noted Rogers’ record of supporting Trump’s tariff policies before seeking to distance himself from the president on the issue. 
“When we look at someone’s track record, you know they can go around on the campaign trail now and speak and act like they support Detroiters or act like they support Black Michiganders,” McCampbell said. “But Mike Rogers’ record speaks for itself.”
In response, Rogers spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet told the Advance that the press conference represented “fourth quarter theatrics” by the El-Sayed campaign and “don’t change the fact that he has a base problem.”
“Detroiters are tired of Democrats taking them for granted. And while Abdul gives them slogans, Mike Rogers is showing up in Detroit with real solutions,” Brouillet said. “He will put phonics and shop class back in schools to set students up for success — after Democrat failures dropped us to 45th in the nation for education.”
Rogers has said that he supports the president’s actions, and even championed them at one point, while more recently saying tariffs needed to be levied in a way that benefits Michigan. Rogers has called for an end to Trump’s tariff war with Canada — a comment featured most prominently in an ad in which Rogers talks about drinking LaBatt beer and watching the Red Wings.
Mike Rogers touts Democratic defectors as he seeks to exploit divisions over Abdul El-Sayed

Rogers’ campaign, in conversations with Michigan Advance and in comments during the first debate between Rogers and El-Sayed on Oct. 8, has said that its Black voter outreach operation is building a powerful coalition against El-Sayed in the general election. 
El-Sayed struggled to win over Black voters in the Democratic primary race, as a large portion of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) instead. El-Sayed has made it a point to court Black voters and has seen some gains — netting the support of Myers Phillips, McCampbell, Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield, a host of Black pastors and preachers, and groups like The Black Slate, Inc., Black Mayors of Michigan, the Kent County Black Caucus and Washtenaw County Democratic Party Black Caucus.
Still, the Republican nominee and his allies in Democrats for Mike Rogers, led by estranged Democratic State Rep. Karen Whitsett of Detroit — who has all but left the Democratic Party after much friction with her caucus — have been adamant that the Black voting bloc is a blind spot for his campaign.
Rogers has been working hard to chip away those blind spots by making campaign stops in Detroit and Pontiac, meeting with tutors, students and alumni at Beyond Basics, a reading remediation program, and discussed his education priorities. He also released a housing initiative to unlock home ownership, a platform unveiled in Detroit. Brouillet touted Rogers’ four-point plan for housing affordability “so that you don’t have to wait until age 40 to buy your first house.”
On Tuesday, Myers Phillips said Rogers and Trump were one and the same.
“Black people, we are not supporting Donald Trump. We are not. We might be able to find a few, but for the most part, voters in the cities of the city of Detroit, right here, our community has been devastated by Trump’s policies,” Myers Phillips said. “Not only the city of Detroit, no, the state of Michigan. We are experiencing so much harm. We just finished our budget process, and we have to do our best to continue to do what we can to provide for the least of these, but a lot of the trouble that we are experiencing right now, particularly at the state level, is because of the passage of the ‘Big Beautiful Bill.’”
Michigan state Rep. Tonya Myers Phillips (D-Detroit) speaks during a news conference calling out former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers’ record on education during his time in the state Legislature — where Rogers was the state Senate majority floor leader between 1999-2000 — on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Screenshot)
Rogers supported Trump’s signature 2025 tax and spending law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but was not in Congress when it passed and did not vote on it.
Still, Myers Phillips said Rogers “didn’t do one thing to stand up for our children, for the state of Michigan, for anybody but himself and his rich friends to let something so harmful pass.”
“When you think of Mike Rogers, that’s Donald Trump,” she said. “That’s the big, beautiful bill, and we are going to vote for someone, Dr. Abdul El Sayed, that’s looking out for us; that’s not just going to go along with the MAGA lines and follow Donald Trump to our community’s destruction. We are not going to do that.”

name: WyoFile
title: FBI’s touted Wind River enforcement surge includes three reindicted cases after prosecutorial misconduct
text:
When U.S. Attorney for Wyoming Darin Smith touted an enforcement surge on the Wind River Reservation, he included three defendants who were among cases he had to reindict after judges found the first-time federal prosecutor’s misconduct may have prejudiced jurors. 
The surge was part of an FBI and U.S. Department of Justice initiative called Operation Steadfast Promise, which aimed to address violent crime specifically in tribal communities across the country. 
As part of the national campaign, which occurred from April through September, the FBI assigned an additional 15 agents to Lander, who rotated through on one-month stints. The first temporary agents arrived in Lander in May, and the last left in September, FBI Denver Public Affairs Officer Vikki Migoya said via email. The 15 agents assisted the FBI’s resident agency in Lander, which is typically staffed with five people, Migoya said at a September press conference. 
Smith said at the press conference that an increase in meth dealings across the state precipitated the surge. “We’ve declared war at the Justice Department on drugs, and we’re committed to stamping that to the best that we can, and that’s like whack-a-mole, right? You whack them all down, and he pops up over here.” 
Following the surge of FBI agents to Lander starting in May, Smith’s office filed federal charges against 18 people for various violent crimes, including murder, assault, sexual abuse and drug distribution. 

FBI special agent Amanda Koldjeski briefs reporters about a surge in federal law enforcement presence on the Wind River Indian Reservation at a Sept. 29, 2026 press conference in Lander. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

“Because we had extra hands, we were able to investigate more quickly and get the cases to the prosecutors more quickly,” Migoya said at the press conference. “So while these may have been spread out over a longer period if we didn’t have the extra resources, we were able to get them done in a really timely fashion with that extra help.” 
It’s not clear how many federal charges prosecutors typically file in such a time frame. The Wyoming U.S. Attorney’s Office didn’t return WyoFile’s request for these numbers from previous years by publishing time. 
Of the 18 people Smith and the FBI cited at the press conference, 17 have been indicted, or formally accused of committing a crime by a grand jury, court records show. Another admitted guilt. 
“From doing the crime to doing the time, no district does a swifter job and more efficient job in the country of administering justice,” Smith touted at the September press conference. 
But according to a list of the 18 people provided by the FBI, three of the individuals counted — Dennison Antelope, Brian Johnson and Jose Ocon — were among a group of defendants that had to be reindicted after judges tossed their charges, citing misconduct by Smith that could have prejudiced the jurors. Antelope, Johnson and Ocon were initially indicted in March before the FBI surge, court records show. They were reindicted in May. 
Defense attorneys accused Smith, who at the time was the interim U.S. attorney, of improperly telling the grand jury the defendants were “bad guys,” stating they were “murderers” and that deliberations “won’t take long.”
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for Wyoming undertook a review of Smith, resulting in further disclosures about Smith’s interactions with grand jurors, including that he asked for the list of grand jury members and passed out business cards to them. Prosecutors are not permitted to have private communications with grand jurors.
The court empaneled a new grand jury after dismissing the initial indictments. The new jurors reindicted the group of defendants, including Antelope, Johnson and Ocon. 
The misconduct findings didn’t stall Smith’s U.S. Senate confirmation for Wyoming U.S. attorney in May. 
The episode sharpened tribal concerns over trust and federal prosecution on the reservation, and the Northern Arapaho and the Eastern Shoshone tribes were vocal in opposing Smith’s confirmation. The Wyoming U.S. Attorney’s Office holds particular weight on the Wind River Reservation, because federal prosecutors handle felony cases for crimes committed on the reservation by tribal members, and sometimes by non-tribal members.
A statement from the Eastern Shoshone Business Council addressing the imbroglio said that Smith’s “arrogant and unprofessional conduct speaks directly to the concerns the Eastern Shoshone Business Council has with the adequacy of the prosecution of crimes arising in Indian country.” 
Smith’s conduct, the statement continued, “created avoidable legal challenges that could result in indictments being dismissed or defendants avoiding accountability altogether because of prosecutorial misconduct or unfair grand jury proceedings.” 
An opinion piece by the Northern Arapaho Business Council published in the Riverton Ranger and the Lander Journal also condemned Smith’s alleged conduct and comments, noting that the U.S. Attorney’s Office “already faces longstanding criticism regarding the failure to adequately prosecute crimes arising on Indian reservations,” with many cases stalling before they get to a grand jury. 
“For Native victims and families, this means violent crimes often go unanswered, justice is delayed or denied, and faith in the federal system continues to erode,” the piece stated.
It’s not clear what steps, if any, Smith and his office have taken to build trust with the tribes since this incident. Smith’s office didn’t respond to WyoFile’s inquiry by publishing time. 
WyoFile reporter Mike Koshmrl contributed to this report.
The post FBI’s touted Wind River enforcement surge includes three reindicted cases after prosecutorial misconduct appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Cost of living looms over Nebraska Senate race
text:
Gas and diesel prices in Forest Glen, Maryland, on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)LINCOLN — Nebraska U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and his top opponent, registered independent Dan Osborn, agree the cost of living is top of mind for voters. 
As in nearly all midterm races across the country, Osborn and Ricketts have been trying to convince voters that they also feel the economy’s pain. Republicans capitalized on voters’ economic anxiety during the 2024 presidential election, but now the GOP could be punished for the same thing. 
Polling shows the cost of living is one of voters’ top concerns. Trump’s Iran war is about to enter its eighth month and has driven up gas prices and skyrocketed farmers’ fertilizer costs. 
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., greets thousands of Nebraskans gathered for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Osborn hopes to capitalize on it to pull off a prairie upset. Ricketts has highlighted relief provided by the tax cuts and increased child tax credit in President Donald Trump’s tax and spending law. Ricketts has also touted his vote for a landmark housing law, saying it “will help reduce housing costs.” 
Osborn has criticized the tax and spending law, saying it overwhelmingly benefits the wealthy “off the backs of people” losing benefits. Osborn rolled out his Nebraska “growth and fairness” plan that includes goals such as ensuring the “right to repair” to stopping “shrinkflation.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The tax and spending law made most tax cuts from the first Trump administration permanent, cementing most of its benefits for higher earners. Its new work requirements for Medicaid and other social safety net programs are meant to offset the costs of the tax cuts and other funding for Trump’s domestic agenda.
During the Senate Sept. 1 debate, Ricketts mentioned noticing the higher price of ground beef when he bought some for his mother and blamed the Biden administration. 
Ricketts has also acknowledged that Trump’s current actions have increased prices. 
“One of the biggest issues for everybody is cost of living,” Ricketts said after his August campaign event in Lincoln. “People were unhappy when grocery prices went up under Biden and gas prices came down. … now they’re back up again because of conflict in Iran.” 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Other Republican candidates across the country have shifted their tone on Trump’s actions that directly or indirectly affected the cost of living, such as tariffs and the Iran war. 
Mike Rogers, the Republican running in the Michigan Senate race, recently ran a campaign ad saying the trade war with Canada needs to end. In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson has called for an end to the war, citing high prices, though she voted last month against a Democrat-backed resolution that would have limited President Donald Trump’s powers in Iran. 
Those Republicans are in close races. Ricketts has consistently acknowledged the economic squeeze the voters are feeling but remained firm in defending the war, pointing to the importance of ensuring that Iran can’t get a nuclear weapon. During the Senate debate, Ricketts said Osborn would side with Democrats on ideas he argued would undermine Trump’s authority.
Osborn, a Navy veteran, has criticized the war and called for an end to the conflict, saying it has contributed to high gas, diesel and grocery prices. 
“We’ve been told time and time again that we are winning this war. … The people I talked to, their lives are exponentially harder because of this war,” Osborn said while receiving an endorsement in Papillion. 
Dan Osborn speaks at Red Cloud Community Center on Oct. 1, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Ricketts said in a statement about Trump’s recent executive order about red-dyed diesel that he “appreciate(s) the Administration’s willingness to find new ways to bring down costs for our farmers and ranchers during harvest.” 
Osborn also supported the order. But some Nebraska farmers and trucking organizations were cautious about how much impact the order would have. 
Tariffs have been a key tool for the Trump administration, which has used them as a bargaining chip with other countries. Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court dealt a major blow to Trump’s trade agenda, ruling that the tariffs he had issued under the International Economic Emergency Powers Act are illegal. But Trump still has some tariffs in place. 
Ricketts has generally supported most of Trump’s tariffs, saying the president is leveling the playing field for the U.S. In the Senate debate, he said he wants to keep using tariffs to protect Nebraska agriculture. In the same debate, Osborn said tariffs can help but argued that Trump’s “blanket” tariffs raise prices for Americans and that Congress should have tariff authority. 
The former governor — like most of the federal delegation — has spoken out against Trump’s plan to allow foreign beef to enter the U.S. without high tariffs. Ricketts recently released a “rebuilding the American cattle herd” plan.
Osborn has made a campaign ad trying to capitalize on Trump’s unpopular beef import plan, with ranchers and farmers saying that it is “selling out American farmers and ranchers.”
Three other candidates are on the ballot for the Senate race: Chuck Conboy, America First Party; Robin Richards, Working People Party; and Mike Marvin, Legal Marijuana NOW, who has suspended his campaign. Their answers are in the Examiner’s voter guide.
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already begun.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Memphis, Shelby County officials do little to mobilize voter engagement
text:
With the midterm election only three weeks away, Memphis and Shelby County elected officials are doing little to engage voters and promote turnout, writes Rev. Earle Fisher. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)I have spent much of this election cycle talking about political maturity. I have argued that this moment requires elected officials, faith leaders, organizers, advocates, and ordinary citizens to put aside personal grievances, bruised egos, and political ambitions long enough to recognize the magnitude of what is happening around us.
Now, with early voting approaching and the November midterm election less than a month away, I feel compelled to document something else.
I am deeply disappointed by how many of our local elected officials, especially Black elected officials, have failed to respond to this political moment with the fullest force of our collective potential.
Some have been virtually silent. Others have offered modest public statements without meaningful organizing behind them. Some have refused to publicly support nominees within their own political party. Others have mailing lists, social media platforms, donor networks, staffs, campaign organizations, and years of political relationships at their disposal, yet there is little visible evidence that those resources are being deployed toward voter registration, voter education, and turnout.
That should trouble all of us because this is bigger than any specific candidate. The most important question before Memphis and Shelby County is whether this community will exercise enough political power to demonstrate that efforts to divide and dilute Memphis’ electoral influence will not be met with political apathy.
That requires massive turnout.
I have been publicly calling for Shelby County to reach 75% turnout in November. In 2024, Shelby County turnout was barely above 54% and it was not even 30%in our August elections.  This left hundreds of thousands of registered voters on the sidelines. A 75 percent goal is intentionally ambitious. If the strategy is to weaken our political power by dividing our communities geographically, then our response must be to maximize our power through participation.
In the 2024 midterm election, Shelby County voters turned out at just over 54%. Photo taken at a Shelby County poll on Aug. 6, 2026, on primary Election Day. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)
Anybody who claims to care about the political future of Memphis should be working like hell to produce it. That includes me. 
Through UPTheVote901, the nonpartisan civic engagement initiative I founded in 2016 to spur voter education, engagement, and turnout in Memphis and Shelby County, we have spent months hosting voter education events, neighborhood canvassing, faith-based conversations, campus registration drives at LeMoyne-Owen College, and discussions like The Locker Room: The Bible, The Ballot & Black Men, a series of conversations engaging Black men around faith, politics, and civic responsibility.
We also convened Civics Conversation with the Nation (of Islam) and are helping coordinate a statewide Souls to the Polls effort on Oct. 17.
I am not listing those things to suggest that we have done enough. We have not. That is precisely the point. If a relatively small grassroots organization can host forums, canvass neighborhoods, organize volunteers, educate students and mobilize faith communities, then elected officials with greater political infrastructure should be capable of doing the same and more.
Many already possess the tools. They have campaign databases with thousands of names, phone numbers and email addresses. They have large social media followings, fundraising networks, volunteers, donor lists, constituent networks and the visibility that comes with public office.
You cannot enthusiastically ask people to vote when your name is on the ballot and then become passive when your own political future is not immediately at stake. You cannot build an operation capable of knocking doors, raising money, making calls and sending texts to get yourself elected, then behave as though voter mobilization is somebody else’s responsibility once you are in office.
This is not simply about endorsements. Elected officials may have ideological disagreements or political rivalries that influence whether they publicly endorse another candidate. But political maturity requires us to distinguish between our personal feelings and our public responsibilities.
If you cannot endorse somebody, endorse democracy. If you cannot campaign for a candidate, campaign for participation. If you cannot stand beside another politician, stand beside the people.
Host a voter forum. Sponsor a registration drive. Organize a neighborhood canvass. Encourage supporters to check their registration and develop voting plans. Help seniors get to early voting. Engage students and first-time voters. Partner with organizations already doing the work.
Because the absence of visible engagement communicates something too. If the reason for that absence is personal animus, bruised pride, political ambition or resentment toward another public figure, then personal political interests have become more important than the political interests of the people those leaders claim to represent.
Leadership does not require us to like everybody, and political maturity does not require artificial unity. But mature leaders know when history requires them to subordinate personal grievances to a larger collective responsibility.
November will reveal more than who wins these elections. It is already revealing who understands political power as something that belongs to the people and who seems primarily interested in political power when it belongs to them.
The 75 percent challenge is not merely about hitting a number. It is about refusing to allow low turnout to complete politically what redistricting began structurally.
This moment is asking all of us a question: What are we willing to do with the power we already have?
For those who hold public office, the answer should be visible by now.
