name: California
title: ¿Cómo gestionarían Xavier Becerra y Steve Hilton el recurso más preciado de California: el agua?
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El próximo gobernador de California deberá lidiar con un estado de extremos, donde el clima oscila entre la sequía y el diluvio, y el agua divide el territorio de las piscinas en los patios traseros de los lugares donde las abuelas temen bañar a sus nietos con agua del grifo.
 El cambio climático está elevando los riesgos, amplificando los ciclos de sequía y de lluvias, y alimentando los conflictos entre quienes tienen y quienes no tienen acceso al agua, conflictos que han caracterizado a California durante generaciones.
 El próximo gobernador, ya sea el republicano Steve Hilton o el demócrata Xavier Becerra, heredará estos desafíos y muchos más.
El uso excesivo de las aguas subterráneas y el hundimiento del terreno en la principal zona agrícola del estado siguen poniendo en peligro  tanto el suministro  de agua como sus sistemas de distribución . La industria pesquera está en crisis y los agricultores se sienten tan presionados que algunos están plantando paneles solares en lugar de cultivos.
 Además, cientos de miles de californianos siguen sin tener acceso a agua potable segura y asequible.
 Partiendo de esta realidad compartida, las estrategias de los dos candidatos divergen: Hilton se muestra muy crítico con sus planes de eliminar por completo las regulaciones ambientales para construir más formas de almacenar y transportar agua a las granjas y las ciudades.
 Becerra se apoya en su experiencia como fiscal general, el brazo legal de California en sus luchas contra el presidente Donald Trump durante su primer mandato. Sin embargo, Becerra no presenta propuestas específicas sobre el agua.
 “(Becerra) sabe que no le reportará muchos beneficios presentar planes detallados antes de las elecciones”, dijo Max Gomberg, consultor independiente en materia de agua y exgerente de clima y conservación de la Junta Estatal de Control de Recursos Hídricos, quien renunció en protesta por las políticas hídricas de la administración Newsom.
 “Porque diga lo que diga, siempre habrá alguien que lo critique.” 
 Más es más
 La estrategia hídrica del republicano Hilton es: más.
 Más agua para las granjas. Más almacenamiento. Más desalinización. Más reciclaje de agua. Más dinero del estado, destinado a reducir las costosas facturas de agua y construir más infraestructura. Menos regulaciones para proteger a las especies en peligro de extinción de los sistemas de suministro de agua de California, que, según él, obstaculizan la implementación de más medidas.
 “En California podemos y debemos tener agua en abundancia, y no hay ninguna razón para que no la tengamos, salvo malas políticas y una gestión deficiente”, declaró Hilton a CalMatters. “Se logra un suministro abundante con un plan mucho más ambicioso para la construcción y el funcionamiento de sistemas de captación, almacenamiento y distribución de agua en todas sus formas”. 
 El candidato republicano a gobernador, Steve Hilton, interviene durante un foro en la Universidad Estatal de Fresno, en Fresno, el 1 de abril de 2026. Foto de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters.
 Hilton, estratega político y antiguo presentador de The Next Revolution en Fox News, cambió el Reino Unido por California de forma permanente en 2012 y se instaló en el próspero enclave de Atherton, en el Área de la Bahía. En 2024, elaboró una estrategia de política hídrica junto con Edward Ring, del centro de estudios libertario California Policy Center.
 El plan, titulado “Lograr la abundancia de agua”, estima que hacer realidad la abundancia de agua podría costar hasta 150 mil millones de dólares, suponiendo que se implementen reformas regulatorias.
 Hilton y Ring propusieron una combinación de fuentes de financiación, incluida una asignación del 2% del fondo general del estado, obtenida mediante el recorte de programas ineficaces y derrochadores.
 Los expertos en agua se muestran escépticos.
 “Regla número 1. Hay agua de sobra, pero ya no hay agua barata”, dijo Greg Gartrell , exgerente de agua de un distrito de agua del norte de California y ahora investigador adjunto del Instituto de Políticas Públicas de California. “La única agua barata es la que alguien más paga y te ofrece por debajo del costo”.
 Hilton se muestra optimista respecto a la construcción. Esto incluye el embalse de Sites , un embalse en el norte de California cuyo costo se estima entre 6200 y 6800 millones de dólares y que está destinado a almacenar agua del río Sacramento para enviarla al sur. El proyecto está más cerca de superar un importante obstáculo en materia de permisos tras la presión ejercida por Newsom y otros partidarios para flexibilizar las restricciones destinadas a proteger a los peces y a otros seres vivos que dependen del agua del río, según informó el San Francisco Chronicle.
 Hilton también respalda la controvertida propuesta del gobierno de Trump de elevar la altura de la presa Shasta.
 El poderoso Distrito de Agua de Westlands, el mayor proveedor de agua para la agricultura del país y un actor importante en la industria agrícola de California, valorada en 60 mil millones de dólares, ha apoyado a ambos durante mucho tiempo.
 “Es positivo saber que el Sr. Hilton está considerando la infraestructura hídrica y que, de hecho, ya está evaluando proyectos relacionados con el agua”, declaró Allison Febbo, gerente general de Westlands. Según Febbo, ninguno de los candidatos se ha reunido con el personal de Westlands y el distrito no tiene permitido respaldar ni contribuir a las campañas electorales.
 Los opositores al proyecto del embalse y a la elevación de la presa, incluidos grupos de pescadores y ecologistas, así como la tribu Winnemem Wintu, temen que una mayor pérdida del caudal del río perjudique al salmón emblemático y a otras especies que ya se encuentran en peligro debido a la gestión del agua por parte de los gobiernos federal y estatal.
 Aunque Hilton afirmó que considera que la industria del salmón es “sumamente importante, tan importante como la industria agrícola”, su objetivo, según explicó, es “reequilibrar el sistema a favor de la agricultura y el consumo doméstico, alejándonos del enfoque tan limitado en lo que llaman uso ambiental, pero que en realidad es mucho más limitado que eso: se trata de un par de especies de peces”.
 La drástica disminución de la población obligó a cancelar la pesca del salmón durante tres años consecutivos durante el mandato de Newsom como gobernador.
 Lo único que Hilton se niega rotundamente a construir es el túnel del Delta, la versión de Newsom de un plan de hace décadas para desviar el agua alrededor del frágil Delta, en lugar de a través de él, con el fin de enviar más agua hacia el sur. Para Hilton, ese proyecto de construcción es demasiado ambicioso.
 “Estoy totalmente en contra”, dijo Hilton. “Es ridículo e innecesario”. 
 Abundancia: una palabra de moda bipartidista
 El favorito , Becerra , exmiembro de la Asamblea Estatal, congresista, fiscal general de California y secretario de Salud y Servicios Humanos de Estados Unidos, es mucho más cauto a la hora de hacer promesas. 
 El candidato demócrata a gobernador, Xavier Becerra, interviene en el escenario durante el Foro de Candidatos a Gobernador de California de Western Growers en Fresno State, el 1 de abril de 2026. Foto de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters.
 A diferencia de Hilton, Becerra no tiene planes detallados sobre el agua ni políticas específicas al respecto en el sitio web de su campaña. Rechazó varias solicitudes de entrevista de CalMatters sobre temas relacionados con el agua. Finalmente, CalMatters envió por correo electrónico a su campaña la misma lista de preguntas que Hilton había respondido por teléfono.
 Tras varios intentos de seguimiento, el portavoz Jonathan Underland respondió:
 “Como gobernador, Becerra reunirá a todos para modernizar nuestra infraestructura hídrica, garantizar agua potable segura y asequible para todos los californianos, brindar a las granjas y empresas el suministro confiable que necesitan para crecer y prepararse para los años de sequía y lluvia que se avecinan.”
 El silencio de Becerra es ensordecedor en un estado donde el 83% de los demócratas, el 77% de los independientes y el 67% de los republicanos afirman que es más probable que apoyen a un candidato que “priorice la mejora de la fiabilidad y la asequibilidad del agua en California”, según una encuesta realizada a principios de este verano por la Asociación de Agencias de Agua de California y FM3 Research.
 En cambio, Becerra ha dicho que escuchará.
 “Les aseguro, como gobernador, que cuando estén sentados a la mesa conmigo, escucharé lo que piensen que debemos hacer”, dijo ante el público en un foro celebrado en abril en Fresno, organizado por influyentes grupos agrícolas . “Porque el agua es más valiosa que el oro. ¡Hagámoslo posible!”.
 Algunos expertos en agua afirman que el enfoque reflexivo de Becerra resulta refrescante en un tema tan complejo como el agua en California.
 “La idea de un gobernador que quiera reflexionar sobre las cosas y hablar con todos me parece excelente”, dijo Felicia Marcus , quien dirigió la Junta Estatal de Control de Recursos Hídricos bajo el mandato del gobernador Jerry Brown. “Es algo que uno espera de un gobernador incluso después de ser elegido, en lugar de que ya esté completamente consolidado”.
 Otros son más cínicos.
 “Becerra tiene razón. Sería estupendo que todos participaran en la toma de decisiones”, dijo Peter Gleick , científico climático y cofundador del Pacific Institute, un centro de estudios sobre el agua a nivel mundial. “¿Pero qué se está ofreciendo?”
 Si bien Becerra no profundiza en los detalles, tiene un profundo conocimiento de la historia. Como fiscal general, demandó a la administración Trump en más de 120 ocasiones . Sus demandas frustraron un proyecto, con el apoyo de Westlands, para elevar la presa de Shasta , y se opusieron a una propuesta de Trump que afectaba los sistemas de suministro de agua y que, según temían los funcionarios estatales, perjudicaría al salmón y otras especies. 
 Presa Shasta en el condado de Shasta, 22 de julio de 2026. Fotografía de Salvador Ochoa para CalMatters.
 En su único debate cara a cara, Hilton describió este historial como una muestra de que Becerra está “demandando para impedir que nuestros agricultores reciban el agua que necesitan”.
 Becerra replicó: “Donald Trump estaba tratando de imponer sus estándares a California en lo que respecta a la infraestructura hídrica. Tenemos derecho a asegurarnos de que el agua en California esté regulada por California”.
 A pesar de todas las pullas de Becerra y Hilton, en cierto modo se hacen eco la una de la otra.
 En el foro de Fresno celebrado durante las elecciones primarias, ambos coincidieron en que proteger las aguas subterráneas es importante, y ambos coincidieron en que la histórica política estatal para controlar la sobreexplotación agrícola puede verse sobrecargada por la burocracia.
 Pero mientras Hilton afirmó que la solución reside en aumentar el agua superficial y que “todo esto es una locura. Hay que reducirlo todo y cerrarlo donde sea posible”, Becerra sostuvo que son necesarias las normas.
 No entiendo cómo algunas personas que quieren eliminar las normas que nos ayudan a gestionar las aguas subterráneas creen que podemos hacer lo correcto sin alguna guía. Estoy de acuerdo en que quizás hay demasiada regulación… y tenemos que reducirla. Pero seamos honestos: necesitamos las aguas subterráneas.
 Al igual que Hilton, Becerra también ha centrado sus escasas declaraciones públicas en la promesa de abundancia: suministros predecibles para las granjas, la conservación, la recarga de acuíferos y el reciclaje de aguas residuales.
 “Tenemos que mejorar mucho el almacenamiento, el transporte, la conservación y la distribución”, declaró Becerra en el foro de Fresno. “En California tenemos suficiente agua. Se está haciendo el mejor uso posible, y el estado tiene la obligación de ser el principal inversor para que beneficie a todos”.
 Sin embargo, a diferencia de Hilton, la versión de “más” de Becerra podría incluir el controvertido túnel del Delta, denominado Proyecto de Transporte del Delta.
 Al ser preguntado al respecto en un foro celebrado en enero y organizado por California Environmental Voters y otras organizaciones , Becerra reconoció las preocupaciones ecológicas que plantean los opositores al túnel, pero añadió: “Nunca deberíamos decir que no a nada hasta que lo hayamos examinado por completo… todo debería estar sobre la mesa, y todos deberían estar en la mesa”. 
 La historia de más
 La estrategia de “más” es algo que los gobernadores de California han intentado una y otra vez, con resultados dispares. Pero ninguno ha movido agua a la escala —ni con la arrogancia— del gobernador Edmund G. “Pat” Brown.
 En la década de 1960, en una proeza de ingeniería que desafió a la naturaleza, Brown lideró la construcción del Proyecto Estatal del Agua para transportar agua de los ríos del norte de California al centro y sur de California.
 “Quería que esto fuera un monumento a mi persona ”, dijo Brown sobre el proyecto, que ahora canaliza agua a través de 705 millas de acueductos y canales para abastecer a dos tercios de la población de California y las tierras de cultivo del Valle Central.
 El énfasis, señaló Norris Hundley, uno de los grandes cronistas del agua en California, era de Brown.
 Pero las medidas extremas que han tomado los líderes de California para desviar agua de ríos y acuíferos hacia ciudades y granjas tienen consecuencias. Un delta moribundo. Agua no potable. Especies en extinción. Hundimiento del suelo. 



 Primero: Niveles bajos de agua en el lago Shasta el 25 de abril de 2022. Último: Remolques y muelles vacíos en el delta de los ríos Sacramento y San Joaquín, cerca de Bay Point, el 19 de mayo de 2024. Fotografías de Miguel Gutierrez Jr. y Loren Elliott para CalMatters.
 En su novela de 1952, Al este del Edén , John Steinbeck describió cómo el giro de la gran rueda hidráulica de California borraba los recuerdos del pasado: «Y siempre ocurría que durante los años de sequía la gente olvidaba los años de abundancia, y durante los años de lluvia perdía todo recuerdo de los años de sequía. Siempre era así».
 Pero en esta nueva California, donde la rueda gira a toda velocidad, los californianos recuerdan ambas cosas. El estado se está recuperando del trienio más seco registrado hasta la fecha, seguido de inundaciones catastróficas . Los enormes embalses del río Colorado alcanzaron mínimos históricos el verano pasado. Ahora, California se encuentra al borde de un invierno de El Niño, con las lluvias e inundaciones que este podría traer consigo.
 La cuestión es si el próximo gobernador estará preparado para gestionar lo que se avecina. Gleick no está seguro.
 “Aquí está el problema: el problema es que lo que siempre hemos hecho con el agua en California ya no funciona”, dijo Gleick. “Y ningún gobernador ha podido ir más allá de enfoques graduales, cambios graduales a las políticas anteriores”.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana’s commerce secretary making overseas trip this week
text:
Commerce Secretary Chuck Goodrich speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The leader of Indiana’s business recruitment efforts is traveling to Japan for talks with executives of major automakers and other companies operating in the state.
Secretary of Commerce Chuck Goodrich is making the trip this week to the cities of Tokyo and Nagoya, state officials announced Tuesday.
Goodrich’s schedule includes meetings with leaders of Subaru, Toyota and Honda — all three of which have large assembly plants in Indiana.
“Japan is our most prominent international partner and the ideal destination for a strategic economic development trip,” Goodrich said in the trip announcement. “Our friendship with Japan has created thousands of career opportunities and investment in our communities over the last few decades, and we’re not slowing down.”
The trip by Goodrich will be the first for Gov. Mike Braun’s administration after he greatly scaled back the pace of foreign travel set by his predecessor, Gov. Eric Holcomb.
Holcomb made 27 foreign trade missions during his eight years as governor, including trips to Japan in 2017, 2019 and 2023.
Braun said he was proud that Indiana had built “a nearly 40-year partnership with Japan that has provided countless talent development and career opportunities for Hoosiers.”
“The state’s trip to Japan this week is a commitment to continuing our work together and advancing our shared strengths, particularly across the automotive and advanced manufacturing sectors,” he said.
Braun appointed Goodrich in July as commerce secretary, overseeing the Indiana Economic Development Corp., the Indiana Destination Corp. and other agencies, while Goodrich continues as CEO of Indianapolis-based Gaylor Electric.
Goodrich will be accompanied on the Japan trip by his wife, two officials from IEDC’s Indianapolis office and a representative of its Tokyo office, according to the announcement. Goodrich and his wife are paying for their travel expenses, with the Indiana Economic Development Foundation paying most of the expected $25,000 cost for others on the trip.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Hasbro gives 587 Pawtucket employees till Dec. 24 to agree to Boston move or face job loss
text:
A Mr. Potato Head sits outside Hasbro Inc's headquarters on Newport Avenue in Pawtucket. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Nearly 600 Hasbro workers currently based in Pawtucket will have to report to the company’s new Boston headquarters in January or else lose their jobs, according to an Oct. 8 notice filed with the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training.
The toy and gaming empire’s relocation across state lines has been in the works for more than a year. But Hasbro executives had provided few details after outlining a broad schedule for completing the move by the end of the calendar year, and listing the Newport Avenue headquarters for sale sometime after that.
The email notice from Holly Barbacovi, Hasbro’s chief people officer, offers two concrete dates: Dec. 24, 2026, will be the last day that 587 workers will work at their jobs in Pawtucket, and then they will start in Boston on Jan. 4, 2027.
Workers who choose not to move will lose their jobs as of Dec. 24. As of the email, Hasbro had not confirmed how many of its workers planned to accept the relocation offer, Barbacovi said.
Affected employees represent a wide range of positions, from a single intern, a clerk and a carpenter to dozens of senior and management roles in marketing, finance, product development and engineering.
Abby Hodes, a Hasbro spokesperson, said the notice filed with state officials is not a layoff notice, describing it as a “formality” under already public relocation plans. 
Under federal law, employers with more than 100 full-time workers have to give at least 60 days of notice before mass layoffs or facility closings.
“We communicated the move to employees on September 1, 2025 and have been providing support throughout the transition,” Hodes said in an email Tuesday.
The loss of one of the state’s top employers led many candidates for state and local office to bemoan Rhode Island’s lack of incentives and resources to attract business and grow jobs. 
Originally begun more than 100 years ago as a family-owned pencil box maker in Providence, Hasbro has grown to a 4,500-person, international public company with an $11 million operating profit for 2025. At the time it announced the move in September 2025, Hasbro employed 1,000 people in Rhode Island.
Pawtucket Mayor Don Grebien, who lost his reelection bid to Democratic primary challenger Adam Greenman, criticized the company for failing to communicate with its host city.
“Hasbro has an obligation to engage with the community that has supported it for generations,” Grebien said in a statement on Tuesday. “I strongly urge the company to meet with both my administration and the incoming administration to discuss the transition, the impact on its employees, and the future of its Pawtucket property. Pawtucket deserves that conversation, and we expect Hasbro to come to the table.”
Jennifer Almeida, a spokesperson for Grebien’s office, said in a follow-up email that the city wants a “meaningful conversation” about the transition, including more details on what happens with the circa 1900 industrial building when Hasbro moves out.
“While we recognize that Hasbro has decided to relocate, that does not eliminate its responsibility to engage with the community it has called home for decades,” Almeida said. “We expect a productive, transparent conversation about the transition and the future of this property.”
She did not say when the city was last in communication with or contacted Hasbro.
Hodes did not provide a response to Grebien’s statement.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Up to $6 million in tax rebates approved for South Dakota’s largest wind project
text:
The sun sets behind a South Dakota wind farm in 2023. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s Board of Economic Development voted Tuesday to authorize up to $6.1 million in tax rebates for the state’s largest wind energy project. 
The $750 million, 333-megawatt wind farm will span about 110 square miles of private land, located north of Philip and 85 miles east of Rapid City. State regulators described the project as the state’s largest wind facility when they approved a permit Feb. 12 for Philip Wind Partners, a subsidiary of Chicago-based Invenergy. Plans call for up to 87 turbines and 5.5 miles of electrical transmission line with a target completion date next year.
South Dakota regulators approve wind farm that will be the largest in the state

The company applied for the state’s Reinvestment Payment Program, which provides a rebate on sales taxes paid to upgrade equipment or build a new facility or expansion in South Dakota. The program is limited to building projects over $20 million or equipment upgrades over $2 million. 
According to the wind project’s regulatory application, it will create about 200 construction jobs and 12 long-term jobs. Over the next 30 years, the company anticipates paying about $85 million to landowners, $50 million in property taxes, and $10 million in other state and local taxes.
The board also approved a sales tax rebate of up to $8,845.87 for OmegaQuant Analytics from the state’s New Frontiers program, which supports qualifying research and clinical trials. OmegaQuant is a Sioux Falls lab that offers nutritional status testing to researchers, clinicians and the public. 
The board’s agenda said the rebate is for “a new or adapted research method, process, product or technology under approval by a federal authority.” OmegaQuant and the Governor’s Office of Economic Development did not immediately respond to South Dakota Searchlight questions seeking more information about the project.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Checking ‘I do’ regarding stock trades is an issue in Florida’s 7th Congressional District
text:
(Photo by CD Davidson-Hiers/Florida Phoenix)Banning congressional stock trading has become a big issue in this year’s midterm election in Florida, with both Republican and Democratic candidates including it in their agendas to clean up corruption on Capitol Hill.
In a campaign ad released Tuesday, Democrat Bale Dalton attempts to weaponize that his Republican opponent in Florida’s 7th Congressional District — former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah — indicated on a disclosure form that he intends to trade stocks if elected to Congress next month.
“Elijah admitted that he’ll trade stocks in Congress with inside information,” a narrator says in the ad.
But Elijah insists that although he did check the “I do” box on the disclosure form — introduced for the first time this year for federal candidates in Florida — he actually has no intention to trade stocks if elected.
“I checked ‘yes’ as I wasn’t sure how my retirement account would be managed,” Elijah told the Phoenix in an email message. “I do not intend to trade stocks. I actually have campaigned on not allowing members of Congress to trade stocks while they serve on committees that could lead to privileged information.”
Screenshot of new form that all candidates running for federal office in Florida must complete regarding whether they intend to trade stocks if elected to Congress.
Dalton’s ad also takes on Elijah’s stances on the economy, tariffs, and the Iran war. Elijah says the attack regarding stock trades isn’t fair.
“I have spoke out many times against members of Congress trading stocks,” Elijah says. “My opponent has deceived people about me from the very beginning — it’s all he has. Unfortunately for him, the people in this district know better.
Elijah defeated incumbent Cory Mills (who had been dogged by ethics issues) in the August Republican primary.
On Monday, Mills asked Elijah on X whether he and his spouse had committed to not trading stocks while in office, adding it’s “hard to say you support banning stock trading in Congress but signed on the official form ‘yes’ to planning to trade stocks.”
Elijah replied that it was not hard.
“I checked the box out of ‘full transparency ‘ because I wasn’t positive how my retirement account would be handled (others did also). I do not intend to trade stocks,” he wrote back to Mills.
“Intent is not the same as a pledge to Florida’s 7th not to trade or play the Pelosi game by putting in your wife’s name,” Mills responded, referring to Nancy Pelosi.
 Upon reading of Elijah’s comments, the Dalton campaign responded in a text message to the Phoenix.
“Ryan Elijah’s candidate form speaks for itself. Even disgraced Congressman Cory Mills saw the grift potential. Game recognizes game.”
Anti-corruption
Elijah’s primary campaign chances were boosted in the primary over Mills when he won endorsements by two members of Florida’s GOP congressional delegation — Mike Haridopolos and Anna Paulina Luna.
Luna is sponsoring federal legislation that would ban members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from trading or owning individual stocks, bonds, commodities, or complex investment vehicles. A similar bill, the Stop Insider Trading Act, passed in the U.S. House in July but failed in the Senate in late September.
This is the first time federal candidates in Florida are required to declare whether they’d trade stocks if elected to go to Washington. The provision was tucked into the Florida SAVE Act (HB 991), signed into law earlier this year by Gov. Ron DeSantis. It also will require Florida voters beginning next year to prove their citizenship when they next register or re-register to vote.
DeSantis indicated his support for a state law requiring all candidates running for federal office to check a form disclosing their intentions in January, during a press conference with Luna.
“It’s really odd,” DeSantis said in Clearwater. “You’ll have people get elected to Congress having never shown any investment acumen ever in their life, and then all of a sudden they become Warren Buffett on steroids. They’re putting some of the biggest hedge funds in America to shame with these stock trades that have these suspicious timings. Because, look, if you buy a stock and it goes up 400% in like a month? That’s like a once-in-a lifetime investment, and yet these guys seem to be doing this quite frequently. And they have access to certain information, I believe, that is helping to fuel that.”
The form asks congressional candidates whether they do or do not “intend to trade stocks, if elected, in a manner other than a trust or similar mechanism which strictly limits my ability to influence or exercise control over decisions regarding the management of assets.” It also asks whether they have previously traded stocks while serving in federal office.
Confusion
The Washington Sun reported Monday that the wording in that question has led to confusion not only for Elijah, but Florida District 27 Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez, as well. The Sun reported that Rodriguez also checked the “I do” box” when he did not intend to. (The Rodriguez campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment).
The form asks congressional candidates if they do or do not “intend to trade stocks, if elected, in a manner other than a trust or similar mechanism which strictly limits my ability to influence or exercise control over decisions regarding the management of assets.” It also asks if they have previously traded stocks while serving in federal office.
Other Florida congressional candidates from both major parties checked that they do intend to trade stocks if elected (or re-elected). They include Republicans Randy Fine and Scott Franklin and Democrats Lois Frankel and LaShonda J. Holloway, a candidate for Congress in Florida’s 4th Congressional District. The Phoenix reached out to them in the past 24 hours, but did not receive responses.
The idea of banning stock trading by lawmakers is extremely popular. An Economist/YouGov poll taken in May of 1,520 U.S. citizens found that 71% said yes about whether they supported it. Eight percent said no, while 21% were not sure.
The issue has been a hot one in several congressional races in Florida, most notably in CD 13, CD14, and CD 25.
Dalton, 45, was a U.S. Navy helicopter pilot who served in Iraq and Afghanistan and ultimately served in the Navy for 24 years. He served most recently as NASA chief of staff.
Elijah, 54, is a Fort Wayne, Indiana, native who stepped down from his news reporting and anchoring duties at WOFL, the Fox television affiliate in the Orlando market, after 14 years.
CD 7 encompasses all of Seminole County and a part of Volusia. It’s a red-leaning district that voted for Donald Trump by more than 12 points in 2024.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Trump official to host fundraiser for Shad White as he mulls run for governor
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Alex Meyer, a former White House official for President Donald Trump, will host a fundraiser in Oxford next month for state Auditor Shad White, who has been telegraphing a run for governor next year. 
White, a Republican, has not declared a gubernatorial run, but has long made it no secret that he’s considering it. The Nov. 11 fundraiser offers tickets ranging from $500 to $10,000, with proceeds directed to White’s campaign committee, an invitation obtained by Mississippi Today shows.  
White has long praised Trump, and Republican candidates in the GOP primary next year are likely to jockey for his endorsement. 
White has faced criticism from some in the Trump orbit and conservative media because of his legal battles with former NFL star Brett Favre, a close friend of Donald Trump Jr. Favre is suing White, alleging defamation over comments White made in a book he wrote about Mississippi’s welfare scandal and in media interviews.
Meyer, a University of Mississippi alumnus, led Trump’s 2024 campaign operation in the Iowa caucuses before working in the White House as director of intergovernmental affairs and deputy assistant to the president. He left the White House in June to work on the GOP’s political operation for the midterms, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles said. 
Meyer told Mississippi Today he hasn’t officially endorsed White, but agreed to host a fundraiser because White’s style of politics aligns with Trump’s. 
“Shad has a lot of the energy that I see in the Republican primary electorate in Mississippi, and across the country. They’re looking for someone who will go to war and will fight for them,” Meyer said. “And I think Shad is doing a great job of meeting the primary electorate where they’re at and giving them a fight on things that they haven’t felt like anyone’s fought for a while.”
READ MORE: Shad White running for governor as pro-Trump candidate. But does MAGA have a problem with him?
Meyer, without speaking for the president, said he predicted Trump would wait until well after the midterms to endorse in Mississippi’s Republican primary for governor, if he gets involved at all. But he said an endorsement is likely still up for grabs.
Arthur Schwartz, a Washington political operative who’s close to the Trump family and has been an adviser to Donald Trump Jr. for years, has traded barbs with White on social media, telling the auditor he was not “getting anywhere near a Trump admin” and that the “transition team has already been warned about you.” 
The late Charlie Kirk, a prominent conservative media personality who was assassinated in 2025, once dedicated a segment of his show to defending Favre and criticizing White.
Neither the president himself nor his White House administration has said anything publicly about the state auditor.
Republican candidates running for governor in Mississippi appear to be working hard to win over Trump and his supporters, often in strikingly similar terms. 
Republican Attorney General Lynn Fitch launched her gubernatorial campaign calling herself a “Trump conservative who doesn’t back down from a fight.” In his rollout, Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson said he’s  “always been in the fight with President Donald J. Trump.” White, touting his record as auditor, has said voters are “ready for a pro-Trump governor” focused on ending government fraud.
While many polls indicate Trump’s approval rating has cratered nationally, his endorsement is still considered a powerful factor in Mississippi Republican primaries. Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 points in 2024. 
If White enters the race for governor, he will square off against a Republican primary field to replace term-limited incumbent Gov. Tate Reeves that includes Fitch, Gipson and former House Speaker Philip Gunn. Former U.S. Rep. Gregg Harper and billionaire businessman Tommy Duff are also considering entering the race on the Republican side. 
Priscilla Williams Till, a cousin of Emmett Till who ran unsuccessfully for U.S. Senate in 2026, is the only Democratic candidate to have entered the race thus far
White has over $3.8 million in cash on hand, leading a fundraising battle that is sure to accelerate before the Aug. 3 primary.

name: Mississippi Today
title: In Major League Baseball this season, Brewers show that money isn’t even close to everything
text:
Call me Old School. I don’t mind. Actually, you can just call me old. That’s OK. I am. 
Rick Cleveland
And it seems the older I get, the more I hate how much the almighty dollar defines sports, especially at the college and professional levels. The teams that spend the most usually win the most. Its true on the college level, just as it has nearly always been true in the pros.
Seven teams in the Top 10 in the Associated Press college football poll this week are also among the top 10 spenders on their rosters, according to a report in The Athletic. That includes the Ole Miss Rebels, who ranked eighth in roster spending and rank ninth in the AP poll. Only three teams that are not in the top 10 in spending are actually in the AP Top 10. So let’s raise a glass to Indiana (No. 5), BYU (No. 8) and Texas Tech (No. 10), which crack the top 10 without spending top 10 money. Don’t raise it too high for Texas Tech, however. The Red Raiders do have all that backing from Permian Basin oil money and they do rank No. 11 on The Athletic’s list of big spenders.
Major League Baseball? The Los Angeles Dodgers have by far the highest payroll in the big leagues. So it shouldn’t surprise anyone that the Dodgers are the two-time defending World Series champions. They spend big bucks. They win big, too. 
Case in point: The Dodgers faced a (for them) severe pitching shortage back in August. So they just went out and traded three top prospects to the Detroit Tigers for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, despite the fact Skubal will become a free agent after this season and thus will command a salary that would pretty much buy Tupelo or Meridian or maybe both.
Don’t bet against Dodger Blue as a permanent home for Skubal, who, seriously, is expected to command a contract of somewhere between $400 million or $500 million over nine or 10 years. Of course, the Yankees, Mets, Red Sox and Phillies, all large market teams, will be bidding, too.
Brewers spend less but still win
One franchise that most likely will not be bidding for Skubal’s services is the Milwaukee Brewers, the primary reason I write what I write today. These are the Brewers, a small market team that has never, ever won a World Series. These are the Brewers who currently defy all baseball odds. These are the Brewers who spend about $146 million on player salaries, far less than half of the roughly $340 million the Dodgers spend.
And, yes, these are the Milwaukee Brewers who now lead the Dodgers two victories to none in the best of seven series to determine the National League pennant winner. These are the Brewers who are fighting the almighty dollar by playing Old School baseball. 
The modern game of baseball has morphed into something far different from the sport I dearly loved as a child and am still trying to love today. Today’s game is defined by two factors: home run power and power pitching. That’s where the Dodgers have spent so many of those millions: on guys who can hit the ball out of the yard and guys such as Skubal, who can throw a sinking fastball at 97 miles per hour. 
In fact, the Dodgers spent a king’s ransom on one player who, when healthy, can do both. Shohei Ohtani, the Japanese version of Babe Ruth, throws 100 mph fastballs and has also averaged 51 home runs per season over the previous three. The Dodgers are paying Ohtani $700 million over 10 years. That’s $70 million per year, which is roughly what the entire Washington Nationals team makes this year.
So how can the Brewers compete against all that money? Well, they play Old School baseball. They bunt. They steal bases. They take the extra base. They hit behind the runner. They play clean defense. They always hit the cut-off man. Their manager, Pat Murphy, came up through the college ranks, stresses fundamentals and looks like he just walked out of central casting for a 1950s black and white baseball movie, square jaw and all. He has made all the right calls.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, a solid and likable baseball guy, may have said it best about Murphy’s team.
“They play baseball the way it was intended,” Roberts told reporters. “They value 90 feet. They take extra bases. They defend well. They’re athletic. They prevent runs with really good pitching and then with the defense layered in. They don’t give pitches away.” 
The Brewers do sometimes hit home runs. But they are more likely to score with an opposite field single, a stolen base, a grounder to the right side to move the runner to third and then a sacrifice fly. They manufacture runs. This old school baseball guy loves it. 
A rookie from Mississippi
I also love it that they have a 22-year-old rookie shortstop named Cooper Pratt from Magnolia Heights School in Senatobia. Pratt had two hits in the Brewers’ 7-4 victory Monday night. He hit .280 as a rookie. His on-base percentage for the National League Championship series is .500.
True story. I grew up a New York Yankees fan, mostly because my folks were Yankee fans. I ditched the Yankees during the George Steinbrenner years when pulling for the Pinstripes seemed too much like pulling for Chase Manhattan. 
I switched my Major League allegiances years ago to the Atlanta Braves, who were once the Milwaukee Braves. And now that the Dodgers have eliminated the Braves, I turn to the small-market Brewers and their Old School approach.
Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians lead the Tampa Bay Rays 1-0 in the American League playoff series, despite the fact that you could combine the salaries of both those ballclubs and not get to even half of what the vaunted New York Yankees pay their players.
In Major League Baseball, at least this year, money isn’t everything. For me, at least, that’s refreshing.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Supreme Court to hear cases in eastern Idaho’s Idaho Falls and Pocatello
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)The Idaho Supreme Court will travel to the eastern Idaho cities of Pocatello and Idaho Falls this week to conduct hearings, the state judicial system announced.
The court is set to consider three cases starting at 8:45 a.m. Wednesday in Idaho Falls at the Bonneville County Courthouse, according to the court’s schedule. The following day, the court is set to consider two cases starting at 8:45 a.m. Thursday in Pocatello at the Bannock County Courthouse. 
The state’s highest court is based in the capital city of Boise, but the Idaho Constitution and state law requires the court to travel across the state to hear cases. 
Hearings of the Idaho Supreme Court — which handles appeals and some cases that go directly to the court —  are open to the public. Food, beverages and backpacks are not allowed in the courtroom, and cell phones and electronic devices should be silenced. Cameras and recording devices are not allowed without permission from the court ahead of time.

name: Source New Mexico
title: US House Speaker Johnson returns to New Mexico for GOP congressional hopeful’s fundraiser
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, pictured above at a rally for Republican congressional candidate Greg Cunningham on Aug. 26, 2026, returned to New Mexico for a closed-door fundraiser Oct. 12 on the candidate’s behalf. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) made his second New Mexico visit Monday evening in support of Republican Greg Cunningham, where he led a fundraiser in Las Cruces in the final stretch of the closely watched 2nd Congressional District race.
Johnson last visited New Mexico in late August to stump for Cunningham, a retired Marine and Albuquerque detective who is challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) for the state’s southernmost congressional district. Johnson stood alongside Cunningham at a rally in Albuquerque and said he and President Donald Trump agree that Cunningham is “straight out of central casting.”
The speaker’s Monday visit, this time in a closed-door fundraiser, comes on the heels of an Albuquerque Journal poll released Monday that found Vasquez, who is seeking re-election to his third term, with a narrow lead but one within the margin of error. 
The poll found 48% of likely New Mexico voters said they would vote for Vasquez, while 44% said they would for Cunningham, with a 5-percentage-point margin of error. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Josiah Ward, a spokesperson for Cunningham, told Source NM in a text message Monday that the slim margin shows that Vasquez has “stalled and Greg is closing the gap.”
“This is a margin of error race and Greg has the momentum because New Mexico voters know Gabe Vasquez has sold out our district,” he said. “That’s why Speaker of the House Mike Johnson is in Las Cruces today campaigning with us.” 
Vasquez held a news conference earlier Monday in anticipation of the fundraiser. He said Johnson came to Las Cruces to fundraise because “MAGA wealthy elites” think they can buy the seat for Cunningham. 
“It’s clear that Mike Johnson wants to help buy Greg’s ticket to Mar-a-Lago,” Vasquez said. “I’ve been in Congress for four years now, and I can tell you, once Trump picks you and buys your seat, you owe him his complete and total loyalty.”
Trump also earlier this month released a nearly two-minute video endorsing Cunningham and railing against “radical left Democrat” Vasquez. 
New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District race is regularly one of the closest in the country and is one of 13 congressional districts in the nation that voted for Trump in 2024 while also electing a Democrat. 
National political observers at the Cook Political Report have rated the race as “leaning” toward Democrats this year. 
The race has drawn interest from campaign donors and interest groups across the country. According to Federal Elections Commission Records, Vasquez has raised approximately $3.8 million this election cycle. Cunningham has raised a little over $1.5 million.

name: WyoFile
title: Following primary squabble, DOJ says it will ‘have presence in Wyoming’ in November
text:
The Department of Justice plans on “having a presence in Wyoming in the general election,” a department spokesperson confirmed to WyoFile on Monday. That decision comes after the Justice Department’s conduct in Wyoming during the primary raised concerns from Gov. Mark Gordon and others.
The plans are part of a larger effort by the Trump administration to send 1,000 monitors to various polling places across the country in November, when voters will decide who controls Congress. 
In August, local and state officials in Wyoming butted heads with the feds after two DOJ election monitors appeared at a Cheyenne polling place on primary election day, catching the governor and local election officials off guard. Email records indicate Secretary of State Chuck Gray was the only state official to be notified in advance that federal agents would monitor voting in Cheyenne, the Wyoming Tribune Eagle reported in September. 
At the state canvassing board meeting following the election, Gordon described the federal monitors’ conduct as “aggressive” and “irregular.” Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee said it “was a poorly managed exercise and one that showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections.” 

Gov. Mark Gordon during his 2026 State of the State address at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

In the weeks afterwards, Gordon met with the DOJ officials to discuss the matter. 
The meeting, which occurred sometime in September, was “cordial and helpful,” according to a statement from the governor’s office. “There was a discussion of the facts on election day as we understood, and both parties agreed to disagree.”
Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon “had a cordial meeting with Governor Gordon, the Wyoming Attorney General, and the county clerk for Laramie County,” Kiersten Pels, spokesperson for the DOJ, said in a statement. 
“We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were ‘aggressive’ or did anything improper,” she said. “The discussion with the governor and his team was helpful, and we look forward to having a presence in Wyoming in the general election.” 
How we got here
At the canvassing board meeting, Gordon raised concerns about the federal government overstepping its authority.  
“I feel very strongly about [the] federal government coming in and taking our guns,” Gordon said at the state canvassing board meeting a week after the primary election. “I don’t like that. And I don’t like [the] federal government coming in and taking our votes either.”  
Gordon wasn’t “objecting to the observers,” he said, but “their behavior seemed to exceed what the authority that Congress had given them was.” 
The governor also asked the attorney general to “examine” the matter. Those findings, however, are a matter of attorney-client privilege, according to the governor’s office, which pointed WyoFile to Clerk Lee’s account as an accurate representation of what happened the day of the primary election.  
Lee wrote in an Aug. 26 statement that “two individuals, identifying themselves as DOJ election monitors, informed our poll worker that they were here to monitor Wyoming’s Primary Elections.”
The two officials “did not offer their credentials until I requested they do so,” Lee wrote. 
“Shortly after learning of their presence, I spoke with a DOJ official in Washington who informed me that the decision to deploy monitors to Wyoming was made on short notice, and an email had been sent to me, but it may have gone to the wrong address,” Lee wrote.  
The monitors arrived at a busy time and asked questions, according to Lee, that appeared “outside the scope of federal voting rights laws. They included questions about the nature, length, and timing of poll worker training. Monitors requested training guides, asked how our new election equipment was acquired, and wanted to examine our tabulators.” 
When she learned that the monitors also planned to interview voters “to assess compliance with federal civil rights and voting rights law,” she denied that request. “We do not allow interviews to be conducted in polling places,” Lee said. 
Poll workers signal to voters as they enter the polling station during the 2026 Wyoming primary elections at North Christian Church on Tuesday, Aug. 18, in Cheyenne. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
Federal election observers aren’t new to Wyoming or other states across the country. However, the Trump administration says it’s ramping up those efforts and planning to dispatch about 1,000 staff members across the country in November, when voters will decide who controls Congress. 
At publishing time, state officials had not yet been notified by the federal government of their plans. 
“We have not yet received formal notice from the Voting Rights Section,” Secretary of State Chuck Gray wrote in a statement. “But there has been public reporting about all 50 states, including the following article,” he wrote, pointing to an Oct. 5 story by The Hill, in which Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the federal government’s plans. 
The governor’s office also said it had not been notified about whether federal agents would return to Wyoming in November. The governor’s meeting with the Justice Department in September, however, “was very helpful leading to agreement that there needed to be better communication between the Department of Justice and the county clerks, particularly if the federal monitors are seeking voting related documents and what activities are allowed at voting precincts under Wyoming law,” according to a statement from the governor’s office. 
“The Governor also found it was important to clarify the role our county clerks play in the prosecution of our elections here in Wyoming,” according to the statement. 
In her statements in August, Lee offered advice to “fellow county clerks in Wyoming and to election administrators in other ‘red’ states.” 
“Don’t think this won’t happen to you,” she wrote. “Know what the law allows monitors to do and what it does not, and what the monitors’ intentions are.
“Make plans now in case unannounced federal election monitors show up at your polling places on Election Day.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Advocates: Even in Mississippi, data center opposition spans political spectrum. But are politicians listening?
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

Opposition to data centers is at an all-time-high across the country. We are no outlier here in Mississippi. The opposition to data centers spans across the political spectrum. “Data centers are a unique issue where ‘MAGA Republicans and liberal Democrats’ land in the same place,” NPR recently reported, quoting the co-director of a group that tracks political advertising.
Yet in Mississippi, the battle around data centers looks like a game of two-on-two. On one side is team “people and communities,” versus team “data centers” made up of corporations and politicians across the political spectrum. 
Even though communities across the state are resoundingly rejecting data centers, very few officials are responsive to the concerns of these communities. Who even asked for these data centers, anyway? What regular citizen wants these data centers in their backyards? Rather, it’s the politicians and corporations telling us from on high that we should want these data centers and they will be good economic opportunities. The divergence between the people and the state is stark. 
State and local officials in Madison County, along with the corporations behind them, claimed in late August that data centers will help fund public schools. You know what could have funded public schools? It’s this thing that most civilized societies use to fund public education, along with infrastructure projects and hospitals, called taxes. But, we cut the income tax last year with even some Democrats voting for the cut. 
At this moment, we need state lawmakers who will actually listen to the community, not the corporate interests that lobby them. Early on, lawmakers had very limited information about the harms of data centers and were swayed by big corporations to sign legislation in support of data centers.
Sen. Hillman Frazier was one of those lawmakers. Sen. Frazier penned an August op-ed calling for data center regulations, maybe trying to right the wrong of having sponsored the “Data Center Giveaway” bill, Senate Bill 2001 from 2024. 
In his op-ed Sen. Frazier says that Mississippi should create laws that protect our communities, and he advocates for statewide policies and regulations around data centers. He says it’s not an all-or-nothing proposition between “economic growth and protecting our communities,” but says there needs to be more rules and regulations “before Mississippi sees another wave of data center development.” 
Well, the future is here. We are presently experiencing a wave of data center development that needs to be halted before further irreparable harm occurs to our environment, people and communities. People are already feeling the effects of data centers in their communities, including health issues.
We need regulation, public transparency and corporate accountability; and we need more legislators speaking up and revoking their sponsorship. To do anything else feels a bit tone-deaf. We know too much now of the economic and physical harms data centers cause. These harms far outweigh any imaginary benefit. 
Gov. Tate Reeves signs an Amazon beam during an announcement about an Amazon data center planned for Ridgeland on Thursday, April 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
S.B. 2001 (2024), codified at Miss. Code Ann. § 77-3-271, made it easier for Amazon and Entergy Mississippi to build their Madison County data centers. The bill provides heavy tax incentives to the companies and helps Entergy to create the infrastructure – power plants and grid – to power Amazon’s data centers. The bill made the projects exempt from the Public Service Commission’s review, and shielded the deals from the Mississippi Public Records Act designating the deals “trade secrets.” Thus, members of the public have no way to know the terms or rates Entergy charges.
We should be concerned because S.B. 2001 also “makes it easier for Entergy to build new power infrastructure serving Amazon’s data centers and recover expenses from customers,” the Mississippi Free Press reported. Money used to construct the data center infrastructure is deemed “used and useful,” which means Entergy can pass the costs onto residents.
Entergy can, and very likely does, pass costs along to its customers by increasing residential rates. There are serious “fears that Entergy could be undercharging Amazon while raising rates for other customers,” the Mississippi Free Press reported.          
A report commissioned by Environmental Advocates MS and EarthJustice estimates that: “Entergy’s residential ratepayers in Mississippi have already paid approximately $38 million as of March 2026 for investments related to serving data centers, and that they will contribute $74 million by the end of 2026. As a result, the average residential customer’s bill is now about $10.60 per month higher,” according to the report.
Now, these are just estimates because S.B. 2001 shields all the deal’s terms and rates from the public. But under S.B. 2001, Entergy can raise rates higher than the annual 4% rate increase cap under existing state law. This “allows the company to raise rates in excess of that to fund the construction of energy plants that power data centers.” Mississippi residents rightfully are skeptical of the corporations’ claims because the people clearly see their bills increasing. Corporate gaslighting is nothing new. These corporations will tell us the sky is green when we can clearly see it is blue.
While Sen. Frazier likely meant well with his op-ed, we still must ask who is responsible for S.B. 2001? Republican Sen. Josh Harkins was the lead author of S.B. 2001 and the senators who signed on as “authors” or “sponsors” represent a multigenerational, multiracial and cross-party coalition of politicians. All but one state senator, and all but two House members voted for the bill. Republican Rep. Dan Eubanks, Democratic Rep. Solomon Osborne and Republican Sen. Kathy Chism were the only legislators who voted no.
This, unfortunately, is an example of the Mississippi Legislature coming together seamlessly to enact public policy that the public never asked for and now communities across the state must fight retroactively against.
S.B. 2001 has been discussed and criticized by community members across the state. Groups such as Environmental Advocates Mississippi, Mississippi for a Just World and Mississippi Rapid Response Coalition are actively organizing communities to fight against data centers. Legislation like this further entrenches us in a world where corporations lack oversight and accountability, while members of the public, particularly our most marginalized and economically vulnerable communities, will continue to be left holding the bag while corporations profit. 
It’s a cruel reality that Mississippi politicians willingly allow corporations to pollute communities, then turn around and tell us that is the best way to fund public schools. Yet we know the corporations are trying to get out of paying their fair share. Our budget reflects our values. We could simply choose to fund public education without polluting and poisoning the kids first.
The politicians don’t speak for us, and we see this every day. This summer, we attended multiple People Over Politics sessions about data centers and community members discussed planned data centers across Mississippi, particularly in the Jackson metro area. Overwhelmingly, community members are against data centers and worry about the impact on their health and wellbeing.
This summer, we saw true people power with residents showing up to Jackson City Council meetings and demanding limits on data centers emerging in Jackson. Then we saw the Jackson City Council pass the first data center moratorium in the state, and now the people are pushing for a permanent ordinance to prevent data centers in our backyard. 
Nationally, data center opposition is at its highest politically. So why do Mississippi politicians continue to choose corporations at the expense of our health and wellbeing? The consequences to the public are here and felt, from the financial harms with higher bills to the very real and known environmental harms that data centers cause, such as the deprivation of natural resources like water needed to cool the data centers.
In fact, the Sierra Club just gave Entergy Mississippi a failing grade on “clean energy,” because it is adding 3500 megawatts of gas-powered energy to meet the needs of Amazon’s data centers in central Mississippi. There is an ever-present risk of pollution, including noise pollution, from data centers that can and will cause long-term health issues. For instance, the Madison County data centers use hundreds of diesel generators that “emit toxic pollutants linked to a range of chronic illnesses, from nitrogen oxides and particulate matter to cancer-causing chemicals like benzene,” the Mississippi Free Press reported. And yet politicians will say we “just have to take the good with the bad,” of data centers. Well, “the bad” may very well be cancer. 
The corporations behind the data centers will continue to claim that the benefits outweigh the negatives, that jobs and economic growth outweigh the human and environmental harms. Yet, the number of jobs being promised are minimal (Amazon claims its data centers will create 2,000 jobs, statewide).
The recently announced Jefferson County data center is only expected to create 200 permanent jobs. Construction jobs will be created as data centers are built. However, those jobs by definition are temporary and often given to out-of-state contractors. Plus, with the tax incentives given to these corporations, we will never receive a true fair share back. 
At the end of the day, AI is meant to replace humans. People use ChatGPT so they don’t have to write that email or do their own research. Why would we trust corporations behind AI data centers claiming to create long term jobs? Are we naïve enough to believe in 30 years people will be retiring from and living comfortably off pensions from data center jobs? We don’t even have a state minimum wage in Mississippi, and the conditions for workers across this state is abysmal. Corporations come to this state because our lawmakers don’t make them pay their fair share. They take advantage of workers and maximize their profits. 
In recent months, in community meetings across Mississippi, residents have asked their legislators about S.B. 2001, and we’ve heard multiple reports of legislators admitting they didn’t even know what was in the bill but voted yes. It’s a grim political reality when state lawmakers don’t carefully review legislation before signing onto or voting for it.
Mississippians deserve so much more. The Legislature can do so much more. They can shield consumers from rate hikes, make data center operators and utility corporations like Entergy pay their fair share, require environmental and community impact studies of the data centers before they are built, require proper permitting and Public Service Commission review, and increase – not decrease – public transparency while creating processes for public review of these deals being struck.
Members of the Mississippi Legislature, especially those authors of S.B. 2001 (2024), must right their wrong. Legislation prioritizing corporations over the people is always wrong. An August tweet can sum up the impact of S.B. 2001:


Brooke Floyd is a daughter of Mississippi. She has a master’s in education from Jackson State University, a master’s from Belhaven University and an undergraduate degree in English from Tougaloo College. She is the director of programs and community-led governance at People’s Advocacy Institute. Brooke continues to call Jackson home, with her husband and two children. 
Korbin Felder is a civil rights attorney who lives and works in Jackson.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia AG launches voter protection unit ahead of midterm elections
text:
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced a new Voter Protection Section Tuesday to investigate barriers to voting and enforce the state’s election laws. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones on Tuesday announced a new Voter Protection Section, creating a team of dedicated lawyers to investigate voting rights violations and enforce state election laws three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. 
The section will investigate improper voter registration cancellations, absentee ballot denials, voter intimidation and interference with election administration. 
Jones, a Democrat, said the moves comes as federal voting rights protections face challenges and President Donald Trump’s administration seeks greater control of how states conduct elections. 
Early voting is underway in Virginia, where a recent court battle has kept new federal restrictions pushed by Trump on mail ballots from taking effect this fall. 
“This work now has a permanent home, and a team focused every day on defending voting rights and enforcing Virginia law,” Jones said in a statement. “Virginia votes every year, and protecting the franchise must be a year-round responsibility. In Virginia, the right to vote will be defended.”
Ajay Saini, who will lead the section, said its attorneys will review proposed election changes and investigate complaints involving discriminatory redistricting, polling place changes and language access. The section will also address barriers facing voters with disabilities, students and military personnel. 
Saini said his team would coordinate with the Virginia Department of Elections and the attorney general’s Federal Accountability Unit. 
“At a time when the Trump administration has sought to push the federal government further into the administration of state elections, we will work … to protect Virginia’s authority, the integrity of our elections, and every eligible voter’s right to be heard,” he said. 
The announcement did not specify the section’s staffing, budget or how voters could submit complaints. 
The unit’s central responsibility will be to enforce the Virginia Voting Rights Act, which lawmakers passed in 2021 to prohibit election practices that discriminate based on race, color or membership in a language minority group. 
Then-state Sen. Jennifer McClellan, now a Democratic congresswoman representing Richmond, helped lead passage of the law, making Virginia the first Southern state to establish its own voting rights act. 
The legislation followed years of reduced federal oversight after the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2013 ruling in Shelby County v. Holder, which struck down the formula determining which states and localities needed federal approval before changing election rules. Virginia had been subject to that requirement. 
Another Supreme Court decision this May raised concerns among Virginia Democrats and civil rights advocates. In Louisiana v. Callais, the justices rejected Louisiana’s second Black-majority congressional district, prompting warnings about the erosion of minority representation in other states. 
Virginia’s law requires local governments to provide public notice and an opportunity for comment before making certain election changes. Voters can challenge those changes in court, or localities can seek certification from the attorney general that the changes do not violate the law. 
The requirements cover redistricting, polling places relocations and consolidations, restrictions on language assistance and changes to how governing bodies and local school boards are elected. 
The new section’s focus on registration cancellations follows a dispute during Virginia’s 2024 presidential election, when then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration removed about 1,600 people from voter rolls under a program intended to identify non-citizens. 
Voting rights organizations challenged those removals after eligible citizens reported their Department of Motor Vehicles records contained errors that raised questions about their citizenship.
A federal court ordered the registrations restored, but the Supreme Court blocked that order after then-Attorney General Jason Miyares appealed that decision. Some affected voters corrected their registrations through local elections offices, and same-day registration offered another day to cast ballots. 
More recently, Virginia joined other states in challenging federal restrictions on mail voting. 
A March 31 executive order from Trump directed the U.S. Postal Service to stop transmitting mail ballots to voters who were not on a federally controlled list. 
A subsequent postal rule would have required states to register eligible mail voters with the agency and submit ballot envelope designs for approval.
In September, the Supreme Court allowed an injunction blocking the rule to remain in effect, leaving Virginia’s existing mail-voting procedures in place for November. 
Jones subsequently encouraged Virginians to use mail ballots, drop boxes and early voting.
The attorney general, who is Black, also spoke about the personal significance of voting rights enforcement. 
“I was raised by people who understood that the right to vote was never simply given. Generations of Americans had to sacrifice, organize, and show extraordinary courage to claim that right,” Jones said. “That history is personal to me, and it reminds us that the work of civil rights and voting rights is never finished.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Trump asks Guilfoyle to resign after texts with former KY candidate
text:
From left to right, Republican gubernatorial candidates Eric Deters, Daniel Cameron, Kelly Craft, Ryan Quarles and Alan Keck take their seats before the KET debate. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)President Donald Trump has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign after texts between her and former Kentucky governor candidate and suspended attorney Eric Deters became public, according to published reports. 
The Wall Street Journal reported last week on text messages between Guilfoyle, Donald Trump Jr.’s former fiancée, and Deters, where she requested Deters pay $100,000 to American Express in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail ahead of her confirmation hearing.
“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she texted Deters in July 2025, the Journal reported, along with a prayer hands emoji and a PDF with bill payment instructions from American Express. He didn’t make the payment, saying it would cost him his marriage. 
Guilfoyle resigned Tuesday morning and shared a statement on X saying the allegations “are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
From left, Bernie Moreno, Vivek Ramaswamy, Kimberly Guilfoyle, and Donald Trump, Jr. speaking before a campaign rally in Butler County, Ohio in 2024. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Deters, a Republican, ran for governor in 2023 and for Congress in 2024. He hosts a political commentary show online and has led a conservative Patriots Day Freedom Fest in Northern Kentucky, though this year’s event was canceled after only six $1,000 VIP tickets were sold. 
After saying “rich people, as a whole, suck,” and that he planned for 100 VIP ticket sales to cover the cost of the free event, Deters said he was never ever, ever, ever, ever doing this event again,” USA Today reported. Trump Jr. spoke at the 2024 event. 
In media rounds after the Wall Street Journal story, Deters told CNN he was planning legal action against Guilfoyle and accused her legal team of making false claims about him. 
“It’s going to be fun,” he said. 
Deters is no stranger to courts. The Kentucky Bar Association filed a contempt motion against Deters after a 2021 Louisville Courier Journal story said Deters was behind two federal lawsuits aimed at stopping a vaccine requirement for federal employees, but he was suspended from practicing law. 
A couple years later, amid his gubernatorial run, Deters pled guilty to misdemeanor charges after police said he chased his nephew on a family farm and sent harassing messages to his sister-in-law.

name: VTDigger
title: Evelyn Beliveau
text:
Born: 04/08/1931
Maine
Died: 09/30/2026
Jericho, Vermont
Details of service:
Memorial Service

Sunday, November 22, 2026 at 2:30 p.m.


First Congregational Church
39 Main St
Essex Junction, VT 05452

A memorial service will be held on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 2:30 p.m. at the First Congregational Church of Essex Junction, 39 Main St, Essex Junction, VT 05452.





Evelyn Vinton Beliveau, 95, of Jericho, Vermont, died September 30, 2026, in her home.
Lyn was born in 1931. The second of four children of Bill and Catherine Vinton, she grew up on Kezar Lake in Maine, which continued to be her favorite spot in the world no matter how many places she traveled.
Lyn graduated from Gould Academy in Bethel, Maine, and Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, New York (1952), earning a degree in mathematics. She decided she would either be a doctor or get married. She worked briefly at GE, then met Maurice Beliveau, a mechanical engineer, on a blind date. They wed in 1953 and were married for 56 years, until Maurice’s death in 2009.
The couple lived in New York State and welcomed four children before moving to Essex Junction, Vermont, in 1965; a fifth child then completed the family. They named their kids in alphabetical order.
She lived a busy life as a wife and mother, and was a member of Home Dem and the League of Women Voters. Several of her close lifelong friendships began in Essex Junction.
In middle age and with some offspring still at home, Lyn went back to school and earned a nursing degree at UVM. She worked in gynecology at the hospital in Burlington. Although she was a professional nurse for less than a decade, it was highly meaningful to her and became an important part of her identity.
Her childhood home in Maine had been a family-run summer camp for visitors from the early 1930s to the early 1950s. When she was young, Lyn worked there as a chambermaid, and her sister Fran worked as a cook. After the camp became a vacation place for family only, Fran and Lyn spent many summers there, where they more or less assumed their teenage roles and “ran camp.” These were some of Lyn’s happiest times.
Maurice retired in the early 1980s, and the couple became avid world travelers and Elderhostel attendees. Lyn was especially fond of overnight train travel, and believed each Elderhostel to be “the best one yet.”
In 1983, Lyn and Maurice moved into a house in Jericho, Vermont, that he had built himself. She embarked on a 10-year project of transcribing the diaries of her grandfather, General Francis Henry French, whom she had never met. She enjoyed this project so much she had business cards printed with “Evelyn Beliveau, Curator” on them.
Lyn was a deacon of her church and a volunteer with the church thrift shops in both Essex Junction, Vermont, and Lovell, Maine.
Lyn was not a braggart, except when the stakes were low. She often boasted to family about her naturally curly hair, which did not begin to go gray till she was in her 70s; her collection of (three!) cashmere sweaters; and her color-coding system for bedsheets—“green for queen, blue for two”—of which she was so ridiculously proud she insisted it be put in her obituary. (Here you go, Mom.)
Her character was outstanding. Lyn was an unflappable, reassuring, kind, loving presence, a bottomless well of patience and generosity. She seldom complained, and she was empathetic toward people who were struggling. Being inclusive was important to her. She could talk to anyone about anything, and was always interested in what they had to say. She was exceptionally easy to please, and a great travel companion. She was more fun than a barrel of monkeys. Her home was the family gathering place, and she was the magnetic center.
Things Lyn loved: roller-coasters, puzzles, blue cheese, new places, storytelling, gadgets, Disney World, hauling out an aphorism for every occasion, reading (history and biography for herself; nursery rhymes and chapter books for the children in her life), playing games, baking with kids, hearing others play the piano.
Things Lyn was good at: knitting; she made countless sweaters, scarves, mittens, and baby blankets, and taught herself entrelac in her 80s. Playing along with Jeopardy; she once passed a Jeopardy test administered in Burlington, but unfortunately was never called to be on the show. Reciting “The Cremation of Sam McGee” by Robert Service. Cake decorating, including making elaborate themed cakes for grandchildren on request.
Lyn had a frightfully large collection of the Three Wise Monkeys. At some point a visitor referred to “hear no evil, see no evil, speak no evil” as her motto. She seemed astonished at that idea, but considered the possibility it was true.
In her later years as a widow, Lyn still traveled, but closer to home. She once tied a rope around a ball-shaped LL Bean ice cream maker and made ice cream by letting it bob around in the Atlantic Ocean. She became a “pub crawl” enthusiast, meeting up with family and friends for one drink at one establishment, where she would invariably order an Old Fashioned cocktail. She played a daily game of cribbage with one son in a tournament that went on for years. She wanted to remain in her own home, and she did.
Lyn was predeceased by her husband Maurice, her brother John, her sister Frances, and her three cousins. She is survived by her five children and their spouses: Catherine (Robert), Joe (Julie), Paul (Constance), Teresa (Steve), and Victoria (Stephen). Also 15 grandchildren: Christine (Jeff); Averil, Aliza, Jordan, and Marley; Annie, Evelyn, Arthur, and Jessica; Katherine (Gus), Alexander (Ellis), Ethan, and Jordan; and Andrew (Jessica) and Derrick (Emily). Also six great-grandchildren: John, Ben, and Connor; Grace; Eowyn; and Nicholas. She is also survived by her sister Elizabeth Powel of South Dartmouth, Massachusetts, as well as many extended family members on both the Vinton and Beliveau sides. Also mourning Lyn are an unusual number of people who considered her a surrogate mother, and the members of her vast fan club.
The family thanks UVM Home Health and Hospice for its excellent care and counsel in the last week of Lyn’s life.
A memorial service will be held on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 2:30 p.m. at the First Congregational Church of Essex Junction, 39 Main St, Essex Junction, VT 05452.
Memorial gifts may be sent to the Fistula Foundation: https://fistulafoundation.org/how-to-help/.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Trump to rally in Northern Kentucky on Saturday

President Donald Trump dances on stage during a March 11 event in Kentucky. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)President Donald Trump will be in Northern Kentucky on Saturday, Oct. 17.
