name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Yes, end gun crime and fraud — and stop scapegoating the community for actions of a few
description: Somali Minnesotans have unfairly been forced to answer for the actions of a very few, following a recent string of shootings involving Somali youth and continued revelations involving large-scale fraud schemes in our social service programs. Election season has only exacerbated this dynamic, with cynical politicians deploying Somali Minnesotans as a politica[...]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office on August 6, 2026. Trump recently slandered tens of thousands of Somali Minnesotans on his social media network: “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back."  (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Somali Minnesotans have unfairly been forced to answer for the actions of a very few, following a recent string of shootings involving Somali youth and continued revelations involving large-scale fraud schemes in our social service programs. Election season has only exacerbated this dynamic, with cynical politicians deploying Somali Minnesotans as a political cudgel. 
Public safety and fraud should be central campaign issues in this election, and candidates for public office should be able to talk about these issues without scapegoating.
Unfortunately, what we are seeing in Minnesota is yet another attempt by the right-wing propaganda machine to whip up hatred against Somali Americans. 
The president’s recent social media post instructing Minnesotans to “fight back” against their Somali neighbors deserves condemnation. This is just his latest inciteful smear job: About a year ago the president called Somali Americans “garbage” while amplifying debunked vulture journalism. 
Even though nearly 90% of Somali Minnesotans are U.S. citizens, Operation Metro Surge came shortly thereafter, resulting in the death of two Minnesotans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, at the hands of masked ICE agents, sent under the pretext of rooting out fraud. 
The Trump administration has hampered efforts to investigate the deaths of Good and Pretti, reportedly resulting in key federal prosecutors working the Feeding Our Future fraud and related Medicaid fraud cases to resign.
Short staffed and inundated with immigration cases, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota has had to dismiss drug cases to focus on charging protesters, with some of those cases later dismissed. 
Moreover, federal judges across the country, including here in Minnesota, have sounded the alarm on the Trump administration’s relentless assault on our courts and the rule of law. 
Minnesota Republicans have been silent throughout this entire ordeal, when not cheering on Trump’s relentless focus on Minnesota and Somali Minnesotans. 
Two things can be true: Our community is being unfairly targeted based on the actions of a few, and those actions — gun violence and social service fraud — should be rooted out. The exploitation of these issues by bad-faith actors for political gain only highlights why our elected officials should address these matters substantively. Doing otherwise breeds resentment, erodes credibility and feeds harmful narratives.
The failure to address fraud in public programs — beginning with the first revelations of the Feeding Our Future scandal in early 2022 — has done exactly that. The fraud problem has eroded confidence in our government and its ability to manage safety net programs. 
The same could happen when it comes to the recent string of senseless shootings. Beginning about a decade ago —  and here in Minnesota after the murder of George Floyd — progressive prosecutors were elected throughout the country, including in Hennepin County. They have made rehabilitation — rather than incarceration — a priority. They have a point: Most young people age out of crime, and far more should be done to invest in marginalized communities. But second and third chances for offenders cannot come at the expense of public safety, and spiraling rounds of Somali youth gun violence — exploited by racist demagogues — risk undermining the project to make the criminal justice system more humane. 
The overwhelming majority of Somali Minnesotans are law abiding citizens and are just as horrified to see young men in our community engaging in senseless acts of violence. After all, the victims in these shootings, just as in the fraud cases that have made headlines, are also from our community. 
My community asks for what every citizen is owed: fair governance. That means without scapegoating, but also without special protection from accountability. Investigate and prosecute without fear or favor, but don’t blame an entire community.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Gov. Ferguson calls for salary survey after WA ferry sickout
description: After a sickout crippled Washington’s ferry system last week, Gov. Bob Ferguson ordered a new evaluation of its engineers’ salaries ahead of wage negotiations with union workers next summer. Negotiators for Ferguson refused to offer a wage increase to members of the Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association in months of talks on a new two-year collective […]
text:
Washington State Ferries' Wenatchee approaches the Bainbridge Island terminal in fall 2025. (Photo by Tom Banse)After a sickout crippled Washington’s ferry system last week, Gov. Bob Ferguson ordered a new evaluation of its engineers’ salaries ahead of wage negotiations with union workers next summer.
Negotiators for Ferguson refused to offer a wage increase to members of the Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association in months of talks on a new two-year collective bargaining agreement. The union did not ratify an agreement, and the contract dispute went to a third-party arbitrator, who sided with the state and awarded no wage hike amid the state’s budget woes. 
“Given the significant financial challenges we face in our near-term budget, this is not a problem that can be solved immediately,” Ferguson wrote to the union following the mass sickout last week. “However, I am committed to the goal of correcting pay disparities between deck and engine.”
The union said it didn’t organize last week’s sickout. Strikes and work stoppages among ferry workers are illegal under state law. Ferguson has made consistent ferry service a top priority in his administration.
“Going forward, in order to maintain a constructive partnership, it is imperative that there are no further service disruptions,” Ferguson told the union in his letter.
Members have long complained of uncompetitive wages and a reliance on overtime that drives burnout. Many engineers work between 500 and 1,500 hours of overtime per year, according to the union. A survey of 80-plus members in June found more than 60% were either somewhat or very likely to retire or leave the ferry system for another job. Over half reported poor morale among their colleagues.
They say their wages are now 20% below above-deck ferry workers.
“I work a second job in my off weeks just to make ends meet,” Nick Twietmeyer, an oiler, said in a statement. “I’m hopeful the state is serious about fixing this system. That would be a win for WSF crew and more importantly the thousands of people and businesses in our communities who depend on ferries to get around.”
Many state worker unions are also not getting a wage increase in their contracts. But most call for negotiations next summer on potential pay hikes for the second year of the contract, which spans July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2029. This is the case for the Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association.
Union representative Eric Winge said in a statement it was “encouraging to see Governor Ferguson acknowledge the essential role marine engineers play in keeping our ferry system going and commit to taking the steps necessary to address our workforce crisis.”
On Oct. 5, 23 engine room workers called out sick, and their replacements declined to fill in for them, leaving most state ferries docked and stranding travelers. Thirteen of the system’s 18 vessels were out of commission at various points of the day as the U.S. Coast Guard requires a minimum number of engine room employees to sail. Ferguson urged the workers to return the next day, and they did, allowing the system to return to a mostly normal schedule.
The ferry system has long faced crew shortages, especially in the years immediately after the COVID-19 pandemic. 
This led the state to prioritize increasing captains’ pay to attract more and help keep pace with retirements, according to Steve Nevey, head of Washington State Ferries. This widened the gap between licensed deck and engineering staff. 
Since Ferguson took office in January 2025, ferry system leaders have discussed this disparity with the Democratic governor. The two-year collective bargaining agreement that began in 2025 gives engine room staff an 8% wage hike, 4% each year.
“We are aligned that the gap between licensed deck and engineering pay needs to be brought back within the range you would normally expect in the maritime industry,” Nevey wrote in a blog post last week. “I have said many times over the past two years that my three biggest priorities are 1. Engineers’ pay, 2. Engineers’ pay, and 3. getting new boats. That has not changed.”
Nevey acknowledged the state’s fiscal situation “means we cannot resolve it as quickly as any of us would like.”
Other ferry workers are set to get raises to varying degrees in their next union contracts between 2027 and 2029.

name: Mississippi Today
title: All’s Fair in love and biscuits: A first timer’s perspective on the Mississippi State Fair
description: A dog waits at a "Fetch N Fish" show at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Dogs draped in American flags jump through hoops, little kids wrestle to catch free biscuits flying through the sky, and a giant pink and purple teddy bear sits down at a table like it’s about to eat lunch.
Welcome to the 167th Mississippi State Fair, where I learned that everything can be fried, put on a stick or both at the same time.
A giant Teddy Bear sits for lunch at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
It’s nothing like the Santos Populares, the traditional street festival in Lisbon, Portugal, where I grew up. We eat sardines, dance to pimba folk music and toast to Saint Anthony with Sagres beer.
This fair is bigger, more extravagant, more kitsch. In other words, it’s American. Bruce Springsteen’s “Born in the USA” blared through the loudspeakers as I strolled the fairgrounds, feeling like Dorothy in the Land of Oz.
Kelly Shannon, public relations specialist at the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce, met me at the entrance to the fair, handing me a biscuit oozing with cane syrup. As a reporter, you don’t usually get to participate in the events you cover. But this time it would be different.
Children enjoy warm biscuits from the “Biscuit Booth” at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Shannon took me to the back of “Biscuit Booth,” where Aguster Lewis whisked flour off her apron. Lewis has been baking biscuits at the state fair for over 30 years. She’s now the manager of the Biscuit Booth, where Mississippians can get free biscuits in between Sky Screamer rides and Fetch N Fish dog shows. Last year, they gave out over 110,000 biscuits in the course of 12 days.
The tradition was started by late Agriculture Commissioner Jim Buck Ross in the 1970s after taking inspiration from a biscuit booth at the Missouri state fair. Despite its long-standing history, there is still room for innovation: This year for the first time, veterans and active-duty military can get a “Brisket Biscuit” for free.
Aguster Lewis makes biscuits at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Lewis mixes, kneads and folds. One bag of flour makes 75 biscuits — each of which should be half an inch thick. If the biscuits in a batch are too small, they go in the trash. Pro-tip: If you come back to the Biscuit Booth enough times during the fair, Lewis will give you a goody bag of biscuits to take home.
With a full stomach, I make my way to the show ring with Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, where children wrangle their sheep around and around. I am incredibly amused at how regal and luxurious the sheep look with the tufts of fur around their legs.
Children wrangle sheep in the ring at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
The Mississippi State Fair began in 1859, two years before the Civil War, when a group of farmers decided to have a fair to see who had the best cows, hogs, goats and sheep. Today, at over 100 food vendors and over 10 daily shows, it’s a far-cry from the small, informal cattle show it once was. But its agricultural heart remains the same.
“Farmers are the first ones here, and they’re the last ones to leave, because this event is theirs,” said Gipson as he walked me through the livestock barns, gliding much more skillfully through the straw and animal muck than me.
People explore the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
We strike up a conversation with a farmer from Wiggins, who is amused at how little I know about cows, livestock and anything farming. He introduces me to Mr Wxc Long Haul Jim, one of White’s Crossing Cattle’s most prized bulls, who is nurtured all year around to win all the blue ribbons at the fair.
His dedication reminds me of Jack Jones from Blackburn Syrup, who told me that “biscuits are eaten with cane syrup and not maple syrup, and to please get it right in my article because maple syrup is produced in the northeast and therefore not local at all.” To me, these men embody the best of the fair: the beautiful craftsmanship that keeps Mississippian traditions alive.
Tray of biscuits, milk and Blackburn syrup at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Having moved to Mississippi after a year living in New York City, a place where life happens on street corners and in subway cars and firescapes, it was hard to adjust to the silos of suburban life. It felt strange that living was often saved for the inside of homes and cars, and I missed third spaces. I missed the unexpectedness that can happen when strangers come together. But at the fair, Mississippians have no option but to be on foot. And the best part about third spaces in Mississippi is that no one really feels like a stranger.
The way I see it, stereotypically American symbols fall into two categories: ones that have become partisan and corrupted to some (the flag) and ones that are still generally harmless and neutral (Stanley cups, air conditioning and ice – that’s “ice” in lower case). An all-American state fair falls into the latter category. It’s nothing but family, giggles and funnel cakes.
As the day drew closer to an end, I put my camera away, sat down next to a “fried Oreos” sign, and felt wistful. After all that unabashedly Americana fun, returning to real life seemed unappealing. I wasn’t the only one who thought so: A little girl with butterflies painted on her face cried while her mother dragged her toward the exit. 
A man and a dog perform in the “Fetch N Fish” dog show at the Mississippi State Fair in Jackson on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri pushes nuclear power to reduce reliance on out-of-state electricity
description: Missouri energy leaders are all in on nuclear power. A new state energy plan from Missouri’s Department of Natural Resources prioritizes new nuclear plants, as well as energy independence and grid reliability. Missouri uses eight times more energy than it produces, a statistic state energy leaders want to change by building more nuclear power plants, […]
text:
Ameren Missouri operates the state’s only commercial nuclear power plant in Callaway County. The utility aims to add additional nuclear power facilities in 2040 (Jana Rose Schleis/KBIA).Missouri energy leaders are all in on nuclear power. A new state energy plan from Missouri’s Department of Natural Resources prioritizes new nuclear plants, as well as energy independence and grid reliability.
Missouri uses eight times more energy than it produces, a statistic state energy leaders want to change by building more nuclear power plants, increasing transmission capacity and reusing closed power plants.
“In recent years, Missouri has become more dependent on electricity from outside our state borders. The State Energy Plan provides a roadmap for reversing that trend,” Gov. Mike Kehoe said in the report.
With electricity demand expected to rise from the development of artificial intelligence data centers, Missouri Department of Natural Resources Director Jake Buxton said nuclear power is best suited to provide the state around the clock electricity.
“Really, the only one that’s on the table that doesn’t have the emissions that has the ability to flip the switch on and provide that dispatchable power is nuclear,” Buxton said.
Missouri lawmakers debated how to pay for new multibillion dollar nuclear power plants in the last legislative session. The discussion was partly fueled by the public’s concerns about rising energy bills and the increasing cost of living.
“Anticipated increases in demand due to AI and other data center load could drive energy bills even higher. Continued reliance on importing electricity generated in other states exposes Missourians to these strings and risks further escalation of energy bills,” the report said. “Although building new generation in Missouri carries costs, it can help limit the pace of future bill increases for Missouri customers.”
Missouri’s new state energy plan says replacing the electricity produced by power plants set to retire, in addition to meeting projected future energy demand, means the state would need to produce 2.6 times more energy than it does now.
Buxton and Department of Natural Resources energy leaders want lawmakers to designate “priority energy zones” across the state — areas such as brownfields, former power plants and industrial-ready sites to redevelop.
Buxton leads a nuclear power task force assembled by Kehoe that is expected to bring the new report’s policy recommendations to lawmakers. Buxton said the plan reflects Kehoe’s energy priorities.
“When you have a nuclear plant, it is producing energy 97% of the time that it’s in operation, that’s true dispatchable power,” he said.
Ameren Missouri operates the state’s only commercial nuclear power plant in Callaway County.
Ajay Arora, Ameren’s chief generation development officer, said gas is the company’s “anchor” generation resource for the future, but the utility aims to add additional nuclear power facilities in 2040.
“Over the last year, we have really focused on assessing the various technologies — whether it’s large nuclear or small modular nuclear reactors — and also understanding policy aspects at the state in order to enable us to make that investment,” Arora said.
Electricity demand is projected to spike in Missouri, due to current and future development of AI data centers. The state energy plan notes Missouri has moved from a “minor data center market to a rapidly expanding hub” — with construction concentrated in the Kansas City corridor and more planned along Interstate 70 and Interstate 44.
Two large data center projects are in development in Montgomery County, which have brought varying levels of community pushback and concerns.
This story originally appeared at KBIA. It can be republished in print or online.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska attorney general candidates take differing approaches to campaign trail
description: LINCOLN — While Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said he views his public service one term at a time, it was a quick decision to seek reelection. With an upcoming U.S. Supreme Court case concerning Colorado’s water rights with the South Platte River, his ongoing legal battle with TikTok and other pending lawsuits, Hilgers said […]
text:
The 2026 candidates for Nebraska attorney general: Republican Attorney General Mike Hilgers, seen speaking at a midterms rally headlining President Donald Trump in Grand Island on Oct. 5, 2026, and Democrat Jocelyn Brasher of Omaha, seen speaking at a small campaign town hall with a small group of Lincoln voters on June 22, 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — While Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said he views his public service one term at a time, it was a quick decision to seek reelection.
With an upcoming U.S. Supreme Court case concerning Colorado’s water rights with the South Platte River, his ongoing legal battle with TikTok and other pending lawsuits, Hilgers said he has unfinished business.
“(I) want to see those fights through,” Hilgers said.
The GOP incumbent faces a challenge from Democrat Jocelyn Brasher, who said she decided to run after watching Hilgers take the Attorney General’s Office in what she believes is the “completely wrong direction.” She said Hilgers seemed to have brought his work as a former lawmaker into the office with him and is legislating based on his personal political views.
The 2026 candidates for Nebraska attorney general: Republican Attorney General Mike Hilgers, left, and Democrat Jocelyn Brasher of Omaha. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Mike Hilgers has forgotten that he’s no longer the speaker of the Legislature,” Brasher said.
Hilgers served six years as a state senator before becoming attorney general, including two years as speaker. He described his approach to AG as trying to “really conserve our democratic republic” and seeking to uphold the framework of the U.S. Constitution and the Nebraska Constitution.
Brasher is a deputy Dodge County attorney and previously worked five years in the Nebraska AG’s Office in its Consumer Protection Division under former Attorney General Doug Peterson.
The two have taken vastly different approaches to the campaign trail. Being a new name on the ballot, Brasher said she has visited “all four corners of the state,”putting herself in front of voters directly. She said many of her conversations have involved telling voters specifically what Hilgers has been doing as AG, as she argued that Hilgers has not been transparent to his constituents.
Hilgers, meanwhile, has focused on running positive advertisements that focus on his accomplishments. He has continued his work as AG through the race, and he said as an incumbent with a history in elected office, his campaign strategy is less traditional.
“You have a resume, a track record, and so in many ways, it is easier to campaign,” Hilgers said.
Brasher has been endorsed by several known Democrats, including former U.S. senator and governor Ben Nelson, Omaha Mayor John Ewing and Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird. Hilgers has gathered endorsements from several organizations, including the Nebraska Farm Bureau, the Nebraska Professional Fire Fighters Association, the Lincoln Police Union and the Omaha Police Officers Association.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Under Hilger’s leadership, the AG’s office has pursued legal battles against Google, Facebook/Meta, TikTok, the Biden administration, China-based Temu and Lorex, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, California, Colorado, a Swiss billionaire, General Motors, Change Healthcare and more. He said he believes he has built the “best pound-for-pound law firm” in the U.S.
Brasher argued that engaging in national lawsuits and “culture wars” is not what the AG is meant to do, particularly,she said, when the subjects of the lawsuits have nothing to do with Nebraska or its residents. From her conversations with voters, she said, Nebraskans care about strengthening public safety and cracking down on data centers, human trafficking and violent crime, among other issues.
Hilgers has incurred criticism due to his role in the fight against cannabis legalization in Nebraska. His office has accused petitioners of fraud in a successful 2024 ballot initiative that legalized medical cannabis in Nebraska, with certain restrictions, and is part of a multistate lawsuit seeking to stop the Trump Justice Department’s order reclassifying marijuana as a less harmful drug.
From his perspective, Hilgers said, cannabis doesn’t appear to be a big issue for voters this election. His conversations with voters have mostly centered on issues his office has already been involved in, such as consumer fraud protections and Nebraska’s water rights concerning Colorado.
“(Cannabis) has hardly come up at all,” Hilgers said. “And when it has, (it’s) people thanking me for ensuring that people aren’t cheating when they’re trying to get things on the ballot.”
Brasher said she wasn’t surprised that Hilgers doesn’t think cannabis is a big issue to voters because he hasn’t been on the campaign trail the same way she has. However, from her view, cannabis legalization might be the biggest topic on voters’ minds.
Concerning the 2024 medical cannabis initiative, Brasher argued that Hilgers was trying to overturn election results that he doesn’t agree with. She said she believes he would continue to fight against legal marijuana access if reelected.
If elected, Brasher said, she would pursue regulations for medical cannabis, but would align the regulations with what voters requested. She said this would likely involve setting guidance for law enforcement.
Brasher argued that Hilgers has allowed irresponsible spending at a time when the state is facing a continued budget deficit, saying that he has “blown” the AG’s budget for multiple years.
Hilgers countered that his office has actually been a net positive for Nebraska’s budget due to the influx of settlement revenues. He noted that Nebraska is slated to receive more than $200 million in a settlement with Facebook’s parent company, Meta, which will be paid out over 10 years into the state’s consumer protection cash fund.
“Nebraskans can actually add up and tally the inflows and outflows of the consumer cash fund and see that we will have added more to it than we have taken out,” Hilgers said.
If reelected, Hilgers said, he plans to double down on his past promises, which include building his solicitor general team, working on mental health and technology issues, and supporting law enforcement, particularly in rural Nebraska.
“You never know what the fight’s gonna be in, say, 2029,” Hilgers said. “But you have to think enough ahead to know what you want to accomplish, and we’ve got a good sense of that.”
If elected, Brasher said, she wants to bring the AG’s office “back to basics,” which to her involves enforcing Nebraska’s laws as they are written. She said she hopes voters understand how important the AG’s office is, saying it is supposed to be “the people’s lawyer.”
“I know how much good this office can do when it is actually focused on the people here at home,” Brasher said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Why St. Louis parents demanded accountability for their public schools
description: As a local, Black-led, community-based nonprofit, Coalition with STL Kids spent months talking to hundreds of parents about the troubling state of St. Louis Public Schools (SLPS). We wrote and spoke to the Missouri state auditor’s office and pleaded for an audit of SLPS. We raised concerns about the district’s academic performance, financial management and [[...]
text:
(kali9/Getty Images)As a local, Black-led, community-based nonprofit, Coalition with STL Kids spent months talking to hundreds of parents about the troubling state of St. Louis Public Schools (SLPS).
We wrote and spoke to the Missouri state auditor’s office and pleaded for an audit of SLPS. We raised concerns about the district’s academic performance, financial management and treatment of parents who tried to make their voices heard, including during the tenure of former school board President Toni Cousins and Vice President Matt Davis.
Those concerns were not unfounded.
The auditor’s 2025 report documented serious financial problems, including $266,780 in purchases that improperly bypassed competitive bidding requirements, salary increases that exceeded approved pay schedules and approximately $3.5 million in employee attendance incentives that auditors concluded violated the Missouri Constitution.
A second audit, released this August, found additional failures of oversight. Board members spent approximately $75,000 on conference travel over 13 months that auditors considered unnecessary, sometimes without obtaining required approval.
Our organization also participated in a federal lawsuit alleging that school officials violated community members’ First Amendment rights by restricting public comment and removing critics from board meetings. The district settled the lawsuit earlier this year.
We asked for an audit because parents deserved answers about how their children’s schools were being managed and how taxpayer money was being spent. The findings confirmed that our concerns warranted attention.
We recognize that the auditor’s office cannot investigate every school district at once. Other districts and charter schools deserve the same scrutiny when serious problems arise. But our responsibility as a community organization is to advocate for the children and families of St. Louis.
Black communities have historically faced inequities in education, and we understand why additional state scrutiny can raise concerns. But accountability is also welcomed by many Black parents, particularly when they are the ones demanding it.
We also hope that accountability will come with increased support and resources to improve our schools.
The audits raise serious questions about district priorities, particularly when classrooms need more resources, students need academic intervention and teachers need additional support.
We believe the teachers union should be using these findings to press district leaders for more resources for teachers and students. Auditors documented hundreds of thousands of dollars in purchases that improperly bypassed competitive bidding requirements, along with other questionable expenditures. Those findings should be part of a larger conversation about district spending priorities and whether enough money is reaching classrooms.
And the stakes are especially high in a district that the Missouri State Board of Education placed on provisional accreditation status earlier this year.
We understand that state intervention has sometimes been used to diminish the power of Black communities. That history deserves consideration whenever questions arise about local control of our schools.
But concerns about possible state intervention should not prevent an independent examination of how public money is spent and whether district leaders are fulfilling their responsibilities.
The audits largely examined practices from 2023 and 2024, and current district leaders have said they are working to address many of the problems identified. We welcome those efforts. What matters now is whether they produce lasting improvements.
We asked for accountability because we believe St. Louis Public Schools can and must do better.
The audits have provided information that parents, teachers and district leaders can use to demand improvements. The next step is making sure those findings lead to meaningful changes in how the district operates and how it serves students.
Missouri is developing an A–F grading system for public schools and charter schools statewide. We welcome accountability that applies fairly and consistently to every school, regardless of the community it serves.
Our goal has never been to punish our public schools. It is to make them better for the children who depend on them.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Housing a key issue for NJ congressional candidates campaigning on affordability
description: Democratic and Republican congressional candidates agree that housing is a key affordability issue. They differ on how they want to bring down costs.
text:
Democratic and Republican congressional candidates agree that housing is a key affordability issue. They differ on how they want to bring down costs. (Photo by Anne Marie-Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]As prices on gas, groceries, healthcare, utilities, and more soar, candidates running to represent New Jersey in Congress say housing has become the biggest affordability issue of all.
The concern is bipartisan, though they diverge on how to rein in runaway housing costs.
“Obviously, we want to bring down the cost of groceries and gas and things like that. But housing is the basis of generational wealth for so many Americans, and right now, the average first-time home buyer is 40 years old. That is a terrible statistic for our country,” said Zack Mullock, a Democrat looking to unseat Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) in South Jersey’s 2nd District.
Skyrocketing housing costs impact people of all ages, as well as renters and owners alike, agreed Michael McGuire, a Republican challenging Rep. Herb Conaway (D) in Central Jersey’s 3rd District.
“If I had to buy my home today, my wife and I couldn’t afford this home that we’re in right now,” he said. “It’s absolutely absurd. The younger generation can’t afford to get into homes, and the older generation is dealing with the ridiculous real estate taxes here in New Jersey, which sometimes unfortunately force people out.”
Experts attribute rising housing costs to colliding trends that have driven young adults to live with their parents longer and delayed home ownership for those who regard renting as cheaper than buying.
High mortgage rates and a housing shortage have inflated prices for homebuyers nationally, while New Jersey’s highest-in-the-nation property taxes compound the problem here. Yet apartment rents simultaneously have crept up, making it challenging for renters to save for house down payments, said Jung Hyun Choi of the Housing Finance Policy Center at the Washington, D.C.-based Urban Institute.
Rising labor, fuel, materials, and other building costs have deepened the housing shortage and worsened affordability, with both new construction and renovations of existing homes more expensive, Choi added.
But delaying home ownership, or rejecting it altogether, can cause harm for a lifetime — and beyond, she added.
“Access to homeownership and building wealth have really long-term implications, not only on your own wealth, but then the wealth of the future generation,” Choi said.
Most of those campaigning for Congress have focused on financial assistance as a key strategy for easing housing unaffordability.
“I think we need to look at the thresholds for these first-time homebuyer programs and make sure that the cap aligns with the actual fiscal reality that we’re facing currently,” said Rachel Peace, a Democrat hoping to flip the 4th District in Central Jersey that Rep. Chris Smith (R) has held since 1981. “We absolutely want to focus on people whose parents never were able to purchase homes, so that they can start to build their own generational wealth.”
Rachel Peace (D) is challenging Rep. Chris Smith (R) in the state’s 4th Congressional District. (Photos by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor and Kris Connor/Getty Images)
Mullock, who’s mayor of Cape May, supports such aid too, saying he personally benefited from it when he bought his first home in his early 20s.
“I bought a junky house — and it was junky! It was under $100,000, and it needed a ton of work. But that started my life. It was 3% interest on the mortgage, and 3% down. Otherwise, I wouldn’t have been able to do it,” Mullock said. “That kickstarted how we raised our family, and we sold that house eventually and did make a profit and used that to build our next house. That aim for so many people right now seems completely unattainable.”
Republican Joe Hathaway, who’s challenging Rep. Analilia Mejia (D) in North Jersey’s 11th District, proposes a temporary freeze on federal taxes for first-time homebuyers.
“So in that first year of initial home purchase, rather than sending more money down to Washington, those are dollars they can keep in their own pockets,” Hathaway said.
Hathaway, a Randolph councilman, also supports eliminating the cap on what’s known as the SALT deduction. That itemized deduction allows taxpayers to reduce their federal taxable income by deducting certain state and local taxes they paid, so it especially benefits high earners in high-tax states like New Jersey. It had been unlimited until President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress capped it at $10,000 in a tax bill they passed in 2017. Trump raised the cap to $40,000 in the spending bill he signed in July 2025.
“Quadrupling that cap from 10,000 to 40,000 was huge for New Jersey homeowners, but I’d like to see it get completely removed because it’s always going to be a challenge for New Jersey families,” Hathaway said.
Joe Hathaway (R) is challenging Rep. Analilia Mejia (D) in New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District. (Photos by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Sagging salaries that haven’t kept pace with inflation also have kept homeownership out of some hands, added Sean Kirrane, a Republican challenging Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D) in North Jersey’s 5th District.
“It used to be you could work a blue-collar job, make a normal salary, support a family of four with a mom at home, and you lived a good middle-class lifestyle,” Kirrane said. “Now you’ve got two working adults in every house, and they’re struggling just to keep their head above water, even making professional salaries.”
He and McGuire support mortgage portability, which would enable people to move without getting a new mortgage at a potentially higher rate.
Rep. Tom Kean Jr., a Republican in the 7th District hoping to be reelected, proposed such a change in a bill dubbed the Making Ownership Viable for Everyone (MOVE) Act that he introduced in August. Homeownership is an important way to build equity, stability, and long-term financial security, Kean said in a statement then.
“I have heard directly from residents across our state who feel stuck in homes that no longer meet their needs because moving would mean giving up their mortgage rate,” Kean said. “I wrote this bill, the MOVE Act, to give homeowners more freedom, help put more homes on the market, and make the American Dream of owning a home more attainable for families across New Jersey.”
Kean’s challenger, Democrat Rebecca Bennett, agreed “creativity” is needed to ensure high mortgage rates and other financial stressors don’t discourage homeowners from selling, essentially trapping people in homes they’ve outgrown and limiting inventory for homebuyers.
Bennett also proposes stopping algorithmic price-fixing in the rental market and ending tariffs Trump enacted that she blames for driving up building costs.
“Different generations have different challenges when it comes to housing,” Bennett said. “When I talk to somebody in their 20s, they’re like, ‘I’m never going to be able to buy a house.’ People that are my age are in starter homes, and they’re looking at, ‘I can’t afford to buy another home.’ And then you have people that are empty nesters that are trying to downsize, but they’re not able to because of the housing inventory.”
Bennett, Mullock, Kirrane, and Hathaway support banning institutional investors from buying up homes, a trend that has sent housing prices soaring in many communities. Congress passed a bill largely barring this practice in June, and it became law in July.
“I don’t believe that large financial institutions should be getting in the business of buying up those single-family homes and then flipping them and artificially driving up the market. That was a really good move on the part of Congress,” Hathaway said.
Peace also proposes reevaluating federal poverty standards, both to put home ownership within reach for more people and to improve affordability more broadly.
“Money is not stretching as far as it once did, and we need to look at the models that we’re using to determine this,” she said.

name: WyoFile
title: Amid Wyoming’s mental health struggles, governor hopes successor prioritizes the issue
description:
Gordon has made mental health a policy focus with initiatives to increase access and destigmatize. 
The post Amid Wyoming’s mental health struggles, governor hopes successor prioritizes the issue appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
JACKSON—Wyoming is among five states with the highest suicide rates in the nation. In recent years, it has fallen from No. 1 to the second and third spots.
“It’s got a long way to go,” Gov. Mark Gordon told WyoFile on Friday. That the state is no longer in the top spot, however, is proof to him that the mental health initiatives he has championed in office are moving the needle. Campaigns to destigmatize mental illness are shifting the culture, access is improving and more people are seeking the care they need, he said. 
With just three months left in his second term, Gordon, who did not run for reelection, said he hopes the candidate who succeeds him on Nov. 3 continues to tend the effort. 
Republican primary winner Eric Barlow faces Democrat Ken Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel in the general election. 
“I would hope the next administration would understand that we’ve now got little flowers growing all over the state,” Gordon said. 
Those “flowers” were featured last week during a mental health conference Gordon hosted in Jackson. The Western Governors’ Association’s Health Beyond Healthcare summit brought together government administrators, researchers and industry professionals to discuss mental health policy lessons and successes. The summit came on the heels of a similar Jackson gathering, the Intermountain West Youth Mental Health Symposium, organized by the Ortus Foundation.
Gov. Mark Gordon, center, joined Western Governors’ Association President Jack Waldorf and Ortus Foundation founder Sabrina Gracias in Jackson for a conversation on rising behavioral health needs in the West on Oct. 8, 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
Along with celebrating small gains, participants agreed that Wyoming and Western states have much work to do to meet steep challenges around mental health access in rural states. Workforce shortages, youth suicide prevention and an uptick in demand were among the issues addressed.
Cowboy up, cupcake
Wyoming consistently ranks among the worst states in terms of higher prevalence of mental health and substance use disorders and lower rates of access to care. 
Growing up in Wyoming, Gordon said, cowboy culture dictated things like good manners, respect and the willingness to help neighbors in need. He posited that too much emphasis in the broader culture on the rugged individualism element of cowboys tipped led to a growing belief that asking for help is a sign of weakness. 
By the time he was elected in 2018, Wyoming led the nation in suicide rates, and it was apparent to Gordon that nearly everyone experiences or knows someone who has experienced trauma, loss or mental illness. The state could do better, he recalled thinking at the time.
Back then, he said, “This was a topic nobody wanted to talk about.” 
In July 2022, Wyoming and the rest of the country transitioned to a uniform 988 number for suicide lifeline services. Gordon championed an effort to offer full-time Wyoming-based coverage so that callers would end up on the line with individuals who understood the nuances of life in this rural state.  
He was also instrumental in launching a mental health policy roadmap, a public awareness campaign to destigmatize mental illness and suicide, annual meetings and efforts to better fund behavioral health resources. 
The Wyoming Legislature in 2021 redesigned Wyoming’s behavioral health system with a goal of focusing resources on those in highest need, such as acute psychiatric patients and children. Gordon supported that. 
“In my time, we’ve really tried to take this on,” he said. 
So are the efforts resulting in change? More people are accessing behavioral health resources, officials report, including via telehealth expansion. And the state’s suicide rate has fallen.
Annette Bollinger hikes through lupines on Rattlesnake Mountain in July 2021. Research shows that spending time outdoors can improve mental health. (Kinley Bollinger) 
But pain points still exist, with statistics painting a picture of huge swaths of unserved patients and critical provider shortages. 
The issues are shared by many Western states, and the Health Beyond Healthcare event in Jackson was designed to offer participants opportunities to learn how to tap into federal resources, develop new funding streams and implement effective policy. 
Experts from across the country sat on panels to discuss issues like the effects of the outdoors on mental health, suicide prevention, gun safety measures and philanthropic opportunities. The Western Governors’ Association will form recommendations based on the discussions for the members to consider adopting.
Alarm bells
Though much of the summit focused on Western or national policy, several Wyoming-specific tidbits stood out. 
Central Wyoming Counseling, based in Casper, is experiencing major spikes in demand, CEO Jim Cowser said. 
“This year, we saw two and a half times more clients than three years ago,” Cowser said. The clinic is experiencing upwards of 200 walk-ins a month, he said, and its call volume is ballooning. 
“Some of the calls are duplicative, but the sheer demand in the area is overwhelming for our workforce,” he said.
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming has also observed growing use of mental health and substance use disorder services in the state, said Amy Scharaswak, director of population health for the organization. One alarming area experiencing the opposite trend has been in postpartum depression screening and counseling, she said, which may be attributed to the state’s overall erosion of maternity care services. 
Daniel Cossaboon, school psychologist at Cody High School, discusses suicide prevention with students. (Mike Vanata for the Hechinger Report)
Along with the provider side, speakers addressed ways to ensure access to mental health resources for a workforce of teachers, lawyers, miners, construction workers, emergency responders and others. 
Mike Wandler, CEO and president of the heavy machinery design and manufacturing company L&H Industrial in Gillette, has invested a great deal of money to hire a mental health coach to counsel employees and their family members, he said. The result, he reported, is an extremely low turnover rate and healthier, happier workers. 
“There is a massive return on investment,” Wandler said, “but you have to do it for the right reasons.”
His sentiment underscores a theme many circled back to: Mental health improvements can contribute to a healthier overall economy. 
Such solutions often require money, and one opportunity for Wyoming to tap into funding is the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion, five-year program meant to bolster rural health systems. Wyoming was awarded $205 million in year-one program funds this summer.
The state plans to invest about $38 million in Rural Health Transformation funds annually into workforce development, including programs focused on behavioral health, Wyoming Innovation Partnership Executive Director Lauren Schoenfeld said. But in the country’s least-populated state, where more than 70% of youth leave by age 25, turning the trends around won’t be easy, she added.
“We have some unique challenges that are amplified by the ruralness of the work that we’re doing, and so I think we have our challenge cut out for us,” Schoenfeld said.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming health insurance task force deserves another year on the job
description:
"BearCare” catastrophic coverage plan wasn’t found to be as helpful as expected to reduce costs, but there are many ideas to explore, columnist Kerry Drake writes.
The post Wyoming health insurance task force deserves another year on the job appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When I first heard about the Legislature kicking the tires last year on a state vehicle to offer catastrophic health insurance to Wyomingites who have been priced out of the market, I had some hope for the proposal.

Opinion

I admit that hopeful part didn’t sound like me when the topic is what the state is willing to do to lower healthcare costs. After rejecting Medicaid expansion for 14 years, to the point where no one will even mention it at the Capitol, it inspires zero confidence in legislative leadership.
Still, I know that it’s imperative for Wyoming to search for solutions to the healthcare affordability and access problems of people who, through no fault of their own, lost coverage.
I’m talking about the more than 9,000 state residents who saw their premiums on the federal Health Insurance Marketplace jump at the highest rate in the nation this year after Congress in late 2025 refused to extend enhanced premium tax credits that had kept Affordable Care Act premiums low. 
Some Wyoming families were hit with premiums that increased more than 400%, and they decided to take the risky but fiscally understandable move to go without any health insurance coverage at all.



The Wyoming Department of Health recommended creating a catastrophic  insurance program called BearCare. It would at least provide coverage for extremely expensive healthcare problems that can bankrupt people, like being injured in a car accident or attacked by a bear.
BearCare was originally part of Wyoming’s application for Rural Health Transformation funding passed by Congress as part of President Donald Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill” that also provided huge tax breaks for the wealthy.
But the far-right Freedom Caucus, which controlled the state House, balked at BearCare because it contended state government should not be running any healthcare program, and it objected to its reliance on federal funds.
Before the 2026 session ended, the Legislative Management Council appointed the Wyoming Health Insurance Affordability Task Force that was tasked during the interim to study proposals to reduce healthcare costs. Its mission was given funding for one year.
The task force included legislators, hospitals, medical associations, insurance companies and the health department. It decided to further investigate whether BearCare could help reduce Wyoming health insurance costs for residents and also keep hospitals from absorbing uncompensated care costs when patients didn’t have catastrophic coverage.
But last week the task force, at its final meeting, decided not to advance BearCare. After extensive study, Legislative Service Office Attorney Anna Johnson said the program’s premiums “would probably actually have to be fairly high to cover everybody in the pool,” so any cost savings wouldn’t have been as high as previously hoped.
The task force also nixed another leftover proposal from this year’s budget session to create a state-administered division to negotiate, purchase and distribute medical devices to participating healthcare facilities in an attempt to reduce costs through coordinated purchasing. 
After doing its due diligence on both proposals over several months and reaching the same conclusion, the task force explored some other creative ideas.
One of the most intriguing is another proposed by the health department. It’s not a finished product, and I have reservations about some pieces of this complex puzzle, but it would seem to have the potential to provide some significant health cost savings.
Lawmakers begin to trickle into the House chamber on the first morning of the 2026 budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
Wyoming would create a list of expensive, yet-to-be-determined “core” health services and reduce what individuals are charged for them. The state would use a block grant to help cover hospitals’ costs.
By regulating those core services under a public utility-like commission, health department officials believe the cost of premiums will decrease while procedures that people can shop for would be more affected by the free market.
Franz Fuchs, deputy director of the health department, said because the state would be severing its ties to core services, insurers may not be required to have those core services offered in-network.
“You let those insurers have more free reign in terms of negotiating prices and steering patients and sending patients to the most-cost effective places for care,” Fuchs said. “So you’re essentially unchaining the free market to do what it does best, which is drive, you know, hopefully innovation and drive costs down.”
Phrases like “essentially unchaining the free market” don’t give me any comfort at all, because it doesn’t automatically ensure a positive result no matter how hard the speaker hopes it will.
The amount of money the state may have to spend on the block grant also gives me heartburn. Depending on rates paid by insurers and other payers, the plan could require Wyoming to pay between $100 million to $350 million annually.
That’s a wide gap and some very serious money. And given the Legislature’s disdain for any kind of taxes, I don’t think Fuchs’ remark that the money could be generated by a premium tax or a payroll tax on large corporations, plus using state investment income, is likely to result in its favorable consideration.
But there are aspects of this proposal that deserve to be studied. Payers — whether self-pay, private insurance, Medicaid, Medicare or employer plans — would all be charged the same amount for the core services. 
Billing would be consolidated to one state-administered clearinghouse. The rate for the core services would be between 100% and 200% of the Medicare rate, which Fuchs pointed out is significantly less than what private insurers are usually billed for.
Before it ended its work for the year, the task force approved a motion to ask the Legislative Management Council for a second year of funding for another round of work to consider the core services package and other ideas.
In general, I’m not a big fan of multi-year interim studies, but when it comes to making healthcare more available and affordable, Wyoming needs to be all in.
Wyoming can make strides to improve rural healthcare through the millions of dollars in federal funds the state will receive over the next decade under the Rural Healthcare Transformation plan. But we have so many health-related problems to fix that there’s no need to limit whoever is involved.
Whether it’s a single lawmaker, a committee, a caucus or a coffee klatch, good ideas can come from anybody. We need to have people available to listen and make good informed judgments about whether any of these concepts will work. The legislative task force didn’t approve the pair it was handed, but studying them and concluding neither was up to snuff was valuable work.
There will be other ideas for the task force to explore after the 2027 session. BearCare may not have made the grade, but a different catastrophic health insurance plan might work. And how about a serious look at Medicaid expansion? 
One thing is clear: It would be a mistake to tell task force members to fold their cards and go home.

title: Idaho’s top officials keep getting these common election questions. Here’s the answers to your FAQs.
description: As the 2026 Nov. 3 general election approaches, Idahoans have been asking questions about filling out ballots, write-in candidates, online voter registration searches, and more as they gear up to vote.  The Idaho Capital Sun spoke to Secretary of State Phil McGrane and his staff about some of the top concerns that have arisen this […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the primary election on May 21, 2024, at Linden Park Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
As the 2026 Nov. 3 general election approaches, Idahoans have been asking questions about filling out ballots, write-in candidates, online voter registration searches, and more as they gear up to vote. 
The Idaho Capital Sun spoke to Secretary of State Phil McGrane and his staff about some of the top concerns that have arisen this election season. 
Here are some of the most frequently asked questions: 
 If I don’t fill in a response to every question, does my ballot still count? 

Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane attends the State of the State Address at the State Capitol building in Boise on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
Voters can skip any question or race on their ballot if they choose to. 
McGrane had heard concerns from voters worried that if they didn’t fill out a response to one of the ballot questions, that the rest of their ballot would be thrown out. This won’t happen, he said. 
“Voters are not required to vote in every race on their ballot for it to count,” the secretary of state’s office spokesperson Joe Parris said in an email. “If they skip a question or contest, the remaining selections on their ballot will still be counted.”
 Can I write in a candidate or write in an answer to the state gun advisory question? 

Prospective write-in candidates in Idaho must file a “Declaration of Intent” to run with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, and the deadline to do so was Sept. 4. Voters may still write in a name, but that vote won’t count if it doesn’t go toward a registered write-in candidate. 
This year, the only write-in candidate who filed this declaration is independent gubernatorial candidate Jacob Burnett, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. 
For House Joint Resolution 4, House Joint Resolution 6, and Proposition 1, there are only “yes” or “no” options to fill out on the ballot. The advisory question about selecting an official state gun has six choices of gun and no option to write in a response. 
 Are signatures on absentee ballots verified, and how? 

Signatures on all absentee ballots are verified, Idaho Secretary of State’s Office officials said. 
Election staff members compare signatures on the ballots with voter registration, signature history on previous ballots, and driver’s license records to confirm a match before ballots are counted, Parris said. 
“Make sure you sign your own absentee ballot,” Parris said. “A common mistake is a spouse putting their return ballot in the wrong return ballot envelope.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 I can’t find my voter registration. Have I been purged from the voter rolls? 

Voters who have moved, changed their name or haven’t voted in the past four years will need to update their voter registration. 
Eligible voters who are still having a hard time finding their voter information in the Secretary of State’s online voter look-up tool at VoteIdaho.Gov may be running into the tool’s more stringent search requirement.
“No one’s being removed,” McGrane said. “It’s our search function on VoteIdaho(.gov) got tighter, and so we’ve been working to try and resolve it.” 
The tool was previously updated after several people were unable to find their voter registration and expressed concern that they’d been removed from the voter rolls, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. The issue was previously linked to people searching on their cellphones, but other voters have run into challenges finding their information. 
“Voters need to use their name exactly as they registered it,” Parris said. “If a user, for example, registered as ‘Elizabeth,’ the short name ‘Beth’ won’t yield results. Make sure no extra characters, like a space, are at the front or back end of the submission. If there are questions, don’t hesitate to call the Idaho Secretary of State’s office to confirm voter registration.”
Some voters who tried to use the polling location look-up tools to find their polling location or sample ballots ran into hurdles if they put a period in the directional abbreviations for cardinal directions — such as “W. Jefferson St.” 
To avoid this, don’t add periods after the directional abbreviations and try to allow the search bar to auto-populate once there’s enough information in it. If you lived at the Idaho State Capitol, the correct search would be “700” in the “House No” search bar, and “W Jefferson St, Boise 83702” under “Street Name.” 
 I’ve seen lists online of people who signed the petition to get Proposition 1 on the ballot — are those real? Is that allowed? 

Conservative North Idaho blogger Summer Bushnell has posted several lists of people who signed petitions to get the proposed abortion rights initiative, now called Proposition 1, on the ballot in the November election. The lists are broken out by county. 
Signatures on initiative petitions are a public record. McGrane confirmed that the information came from his office from public records requests. 
However, the names appear to be from the unverified lists, he said. This means that all of the names are real, but some of them might have been thrown out in the official signature count because there were duplicates, the person wasn’t a registered voter, or other reasons for ineligibility. 
“While initiative signature lists are published using valid public record information, there are nuances in the lists being published that need to be detailed,” Parris wrote. “For example, voters may appear on the list more than once, but that only means they signed a petition more than once. A signature is counted only once. All signatures are validated as a part of the process on the county level during the petition-gathering cycle.”
McGrane said his office has been getting questions about the eligibility of the initiative because people have noticed some names appearing on multiple lists. 
In Idaho, a ballot initiative allows residents to directly propose and decide whether to enact a new law. To qualify for the ballot, initiative supporters must collect the signatures from a total of at least 6% of registered voters statewide, as well as 6% of registered voters in at least 18 of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. 
The supporters of the initiative, Idahoans United for Women and Families, turned in over 110,000 signatures, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. The group needed 70,725 valid signatures to qualify. 
County clerks first checked the signatures turned in from their county and then the Secretary of State’s office performed a final verification. McGrane said he’s confident the signatures were valid and sufficient to qualify the initiative for the Nov. 3 ballot.

text:
Members of the Alabama State Board of Education pose for a picture after its meeting on Oct. 8, 2026. Board members Thursday voted to approve a $6.8 billion budget request for fiscal year 2028.(Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama State Board of Education Thursday approved a $6.8 billion budget request for fiscal year 2028, a 4% increase over the current year.
The request, which must be approved by the Alabama Legislature, includes increases for Struggling Readers Beyond Grade 3, school breakfast and transportation.
The Alabama State Department of Education last year requested $6.59 billion and received $6.58 billion in the FY27 Education Trust Fund Budget, the current budget. The FY28 budget will go into effect on Oct. 1 of next year.

“We want to make sure that every student, every adolescent is also a good reader, and that when they’re leaving third grade on grade level, they’re staying on or above grade level in fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth too,” said Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey during the meeting. “So when they get in high school, they’re above grade level going into those high school courses.”
The request is the largest component of the ETF, which funds public K-12 and postsecondary education in the state. The ETF this year is budgeted at $10.4 billion.
The department wasn’t given any money for Struggling Readers Beyond Grade 3, a program to increase literacy for students after third grade, in the FY27 ETF. Officials are seeking $45 million for the program from the budget.
The board also requested a $56.1 million increase (9%) for the transportation program for local education agencies and a $2.4 million increase (20%) was requested for parental leave. Mackey said during last month’s board meeting the increase was to help with the rising costs bus drivers face such as rising diesel prices.
The department wants to maintain funding in other programs. 
The department is asking for $58 million for the RAISE Act, which aims to create a needs-based funding model for K-12 schools. The appropriation would be the same as FY27. The RAISE Act aims to get additional money to populations such as rural students, students in poverty and English Language Learners. 
The request will come in a year where funding is expected to be tight due in part to health insurance pressures and uncertainty and tax revenues. Mackey said he doesn’t anticipate getting the full amount funded.
“We’ll obviously work with the new governor, incoming governor’s office, and legislature about what that number looks like in the end,” Mackey said. “The request is close to $50 million. I doubt we’ll get all of it, but I do think we’re making a good case for why that needs to continue to grow.”

title: Tennessee Senate leaders predict no move to expel member before speaker vote
description: Tennessee’s Senate Republican Caucus won’t try to remove a member for a rogue endorsement before the election of a new Senate speaker, two key lawmakers said Monday, a move that could affect the outcome of a tight race. Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson of Franklin, who is running against Sen. Paul Bailey for the speaker’s […]
text:
Tullahoma Republican Sen. Janice Bowling, with former state Rep. Jerry Sexton. photographed at the June unveiling of the "Monument to Unborn Children," earned the ire of fellow Republicans for endorsing an independent in the governor's race instead of party nominee, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s Senate Republican Caucus won’t try to remove a member for a rogue endorsement before the election of a new Senate speaker, two key lawmakers said Monday, a move that could affect the outcome of a tight race.
Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson of Franklin, who is running against Sen. Paul Bailey for the speaker’s post, said in a Monday statement, “The Senate Republican Caucus stands firmly behind the Republican nominee for governor. There are no plans to change the makeup of the caucus’s membership prior to the November 10 caucus elections.”
Sen. Ferrell Haile of Gallatin, who serves as Senate speaker pro tempore, acknowledged Monday “gossip” exists about a vote to expel Sen. Janice Bowling of Tullahoma from the caucus after she endorsed independent gubernatorial candidate David Hatley over Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn.
But Haile said the “proper time” for any discussion about removing Bowling from the caucus should be after the race for the speaker’s seat, which also determines Tennessee’s lieutenant governor.
“I don’t think the caucus will consider it until after the lieutenant governor’s race, and I don’t know that they’ll consider it then,” Haile said. “There’s a few folks around that are calling for that, but I haven’t heard much of that. In other words, I don’t think that’s gonna take place.”
Republican TN state senator spurns party, backs independent candidate Hatley

Bowling is said to be a supporter of Bailey of Sparta, who is running against Johnson of Franklin in the speaker’s race to replace outgoing Lt. Gov. Randy McNally of Oak Ridge. Bowling could not be reached for comment during the last week and a half.
Bailey said Monday he doesn’t know “officially” whether Bowling is backing him in the race but called her an “independent thinker” and a friend for 30-plus years and “assumed she may be supporting” him.
The competition is close as a Nov. 10 officer vote approaches for the 27-member caucus that holds a supermajority in the 33-member Senate and, because of that advantage, selects the Senate speaker no matter how Democrats vote in the ultimate election. Whoever is selected as Senate speaker also serves as lieutenant governor in Tennessee and is first in the line of succession to serve as governor in case that person is incapacitated or has to leave office. 
Removing a vote for Bailey would bolster Johnson’s chances of election with at least two of the Republican senators believed to be uncommitted.
Senate Republican Caucus Chairman Ken Yager, who is seeking the caucus leader’s post again, downplayed the matter Monday, saying he is “not aware of any organized effort to remove” Bowling from the caucus.
Nor is any meeting to be held in advance of the caucus vote scheduled for Nov. 10 to expel any member from the caucus, Yager said.
“There have certainly been some members (who) have offered opinions, but there’s been no organized effort to have any such meeting,” Yager said. 
Bailey, who chairs the Senate Commerce and Labor Committee but isn’t a member of Senate leadership, said Monday “there was quite a bit of chatter going on” about the potential removal of Bowling for backing Hatley. But he said he believes such talk has “died down now.”
“No members of leadership have discussed that with me,” Bailey said, only rank-and-file members who’ve called him to ask what’s happening.
